There is no difficulty in this reading. The manner of pronouncing those opening letters that are not single letters, like (ص), nor in a form matching a single word, like (حم), is, as mentioned in al-Kitab (Sibawayh's *al-Kitab*), merely quotation, with the final letter at rest as in pause (waqf, stopping at the end of a word). This holds whether they are treated as names or recited in the manner of enumeration. Even if this entails the meeting of two sukun letters, that is certainly tolerated in the domain of pause. For this reason the reading of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd with a kasra on the mim is deemed weak. The majority pronounce the mim with a fatha and drop the hamza from the noble name. It has been said:

[Page 74]

The mim was given a fatha only so that the vowel of the hamza is transferred onto it, to indicate that it is in the status of what is retained, since the hamza was dropped for lightness and not for connected speech. The mim is in the status of pause, like his saying (واحد اثنان, "wahid ithnan," counting "one, two"), not because of the meeting of two sukun letters as Sibawayh said, since that is not objectionable in pause. For this reason it was not vowelled at the lam. To this view al-Farra' went. In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is said that this is weak, because there is consensus that the connecting alif of the definite article drops in connected speech, and what drops does not have its vowel transferred, as Abu 'Ali said. Their claim that the mim is in the status of pause and its vowel is a vowel of transfer contradicts the consensus of the Arabs and the grammarians that one never pauses on a vowelled letter at all. This applies whether the vowel is a case-marking vowel, a fixed vowel, a transferred vowel, a vowel due to the meeting of two sukun letters, a vowel of quotation, or a vowel of imitation. Thus, in (قد أفلح, "qad aflaha"), when the hamza is dropped and its vowel transferred to the dal, one may not pause on the dal of (قد) with a fatha. Rather, one must make it sukun, by unanimous agreement. As for their comparison with (واحد اثنان), where the vowel of the hamza is placed on the dal: Sibawayh mentioned that they pronounce the final letter of (واحد) with a light vowel (ishmam) because it is firmly established, and the kasra is not reported as a dialect form. If the kasra is sound, then (واحد) is not pausal, as they claimed, and its vowel is not a transferred vowel from the hamza of connection. Rather, it is joined to their saying (اثنان). Two sukun letters meet, the dal of (واحد) and the tha' of (اثنين), so the dal takes a kasra because of their meeting, and the hamza is dropped because it does not occur in connected speech. As for their claim that it is not objectionable in pause, and therefore it was not vowelled at the lam: the answer is that the one who said the vowel is due to the meeting of two sukun letters did not mean by them the meeting of the ya' and the mim of (ألم) in pause. Rather, he meant the final mim of (ألم) and the lam of the definite article. This is like the meeting of the nun of (من) and the lam of (الرجل) when you say (مَنِ الرَّجُلُ؟, "who is the man?"). Moreover, their claim is self-contradictory: the sukun of the final mim is on the intention of pausing on it, while placing the vowel of the hamza on it is on the intention of connection. The intention of connection requires dropping the hamza, and the intention of pausing on what precedes it requires its retention and its being cut off. This is contradictory. For this reason al-Jarbardi said: "The correct view is what Sibawayh said." Most grammarians hold that the mim is vowelled because of the meeting of two sukun letters, and the fatha is chosen for its lightness and to preserve the emphatic pronunciation of the glorious name. Ibn al-Hajib chose this view and claimed that al-Farra's position involves reliance on a weak basis, because treating connection as pause is not strong in the language.

Others have said: it is necessary to say that connection is treated as pause. The claim that this is weak is not accepted, and even if it were accepted, it would not be decisive, because it is strong in the matters where lightness is the aim, as in (ثلاثة أربعة, "thalatha arba'a"). Here the need for lightness is more pressing, and for this reason they made it one of the things that require the fatha. It has been said: it is an attribute of the subject, or a substitute (badal) for it, or for the first predicate. Or it is the predicate, and what precedes it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject and the predicate, confirming what the noble name conveys. Or it is a circumstantial state (hal) of it, according to the view of one who holds that this is valid. Whichever it is, it serves as evidence that the entitlement to worship is exclusively His, glory be to Him.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have transmitted, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Greatest Name of Allah is in three surahs: the Surah of al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, and Ta-Ha." Abu Umamah said: "So I searched for it and found it in al-Baqarah [255]: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾; and in Al 'Imran: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾; and in Ta-Ha [111]: ﴿And faces shall be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾."

'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, and 'Alqamah read (الحي القيام, "al-Hayy al-Qayyam"). This is a refutation of the Christians who claim that 'Isa (peace be upon him) was a lord. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir have transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "A delegation from Najran came to the Prophet (ﷺ). They were sixty riders, among them fourteen men of their nobles. Among them, Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, al-'Aqib, 'Abd al-Masih, and al-Ayham al-Sayyid spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He was from Christianity, on the religion of the king, while their opinions differed. They said: 'He is Allah, the Most High.' They said: 'He is the son of Allah, the Most High.' They said: 'He is the third of three.' This is the saying of Christianity. They argued for their statement, 'He is Allah, the Most High,' saying: 'He used to give life to the dead, heal the sick, inform of the unseen, and create from clay the likeness of a bird, then breathe into it and it became a bird.' They argued for their statement that he is the son of Allah, the Most High, by saying: 'He had no father known to him, he spoke in the cradle, and he did what no one from the children of Adam had done before him.' They argued for their statement that he is the third of three: 'Allah, the Most High, says: "We did, We commanded, We created, We decreed." If He were one, He would have said only "I did, I commanded, I created, I decreed." Rather, He is He, and 'Isa, and Maryam.' All of that from their saying was revealed in the Qur'an, and Allah, the Most High, mentioned to His Prophet (ﷺ) their saying in it. When the two rabbis, al-'Aqib and al-Sayyid, spoke to him," as in the narration of al-Kalbi and al-Rabi' from Anas, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'Submit (aslima).' They said: 'We submitted before you.' He said: 'You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim that Allah has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of pork.' They said: 'Then who is his father, O Muhammad?' He remained silent and did not answer anything." So Allah, the Most High, revealed concerning that, and concerning their saying and the whole variance of their affairs, the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran up to some eighty-odd verses of it. He opened the surah by declaring Himself exempt from what they said and by affirming His unity in creation and command, with no partner in it, and He refuted the disbelief they had innovated and the rivals they had set up alongside Him. He argued against them with their own saying about their companion, to make them recognize their error through it, and said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah: there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ That is: there is no partner with You in His command, the Living who does not die, whereas in their saying 'Isa (peace be upon him) has died. (القيوم, "al-Qayyum") means the one who stands over His dominion and does not cease, whereas 'Isa has ceased.

In the narration of Ibn Jarir from al-Rabi' it is said: "The Christians came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disputed with him concerning 'Isa son of Maryam. They said to him: 'Who is his father?' They attributed to Allah, the Most High, falsehood and slander. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'Do you not know that there is no child except that it resembles its father?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you not know that our Lord is living and does not die, whereas 'Isa will undergo annihilation?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you not know that our Lord is the Self-Subsisting over everything, who sustains it, guards it, and provides for it?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Does 'Isa possess any of that?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Do you not know that nothing is hidden from Allah, the Most High, in the earth or in the heaven?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Does 'Isa know any of that except what he was taught?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Do you not know that our Lord shaped 'Isa in the womb however He willed, that our Lord does not eat food, does not drink drink, and does not void waste?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you not know that 'Isa was carried by his mother as a woman carries, then she gave birth to him as a woman gives birth to her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, then he ate food, drank drink, and voided waste?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then how can this be as you claim?' They recognized it, but then refused except in denial. So He revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah: there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾: that is, the Qur'an, which comprises the foundations and the branches of the law, and what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection. The expression of it by the generic noun (ism al-jins) signals its superiority over the rest of the individual books in comprising the perfections of the genus, as though it alone deserves to be called "the Book" to the exclusion of all others, as is hinted at by the explicit naming of the Torah and the Gospel. In the use of the prepositional phrase (al-zarf), its placement before the direct object, the choice of the second-person pronoun, and the use of ʿalā (upon), there is an evident glorification of him (ﷺ) and an indication of the elevation of his station, peace be upon him. The sentence is either a new, independent sentence, or a further predicate of the noble Name (Allah), or it is the predicate itself, and everything preceding it is either a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ is either an attributive adjective (ṣifah) or an appositive (badal). Al-Aʿmash read nazala (with the light form) and raised al-Kitāb, in which case the sentence is then detached from what precedes it. It has also been said that it is connected to what precedes it, with the implied phrase "from Him" (min ʿindihi). ﴿With the truth﴾: that is, with truthfulness in its reports, or with justice, as al-Rāghib explicitly stated, or with what establishes that it is from Allah the Exalted, through decisive proofs. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "accompanied by the truth" or "as one who is true." In al-Baḥr it is said that the bāʾ may be causal, meaning "because of the establishing of the truth." ﴿Confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the Book following another circumstantial clause, or an appositive to the position of the first circumstantial clause, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive. In every case it is an emphatic circumstantial clause. ﴿That which is before it﴾: that is, the earlier books. The prepositional phrase is the object of "confirming," and the lām is for strengthening the government of the verb. How it confirms what came before has already been explained.

﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [3]: He mentioned them specifically as a clarification of "that which is before it," and as a demonstration of the elevation of its station through this. It is an emphasis on what precedes and a preparation for what follows. The one upon whom they were sent down is not mentioned in these two, because the discourse concerns the two books, not those upon whom they were sent down. The use of the verb (anzala) for both is to indicate that they had only a single descent. This is unlike the Qur'an, which had two descents: a descent from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ) to the House of Honor (bayt al-ʿizzah) in the lowest heaven, all at once, and a descent from that to him (ﷺ) in installments over twenty-three years according to the well-known view. For this reason it is said of it: nazzala and anzala. This view is better than what has been said, namely that nazzala implies gradualness and anzala implies a sudden descent. The latter is problematic in view of the verse: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾, where nazzala is joined with "all at once," and the verse: ﴿He has already sent down to you in the Book﴾. Some of the scholars of verification (al-muḥaqqiqūn) mentioned for this context that gradualness is not multiplicity, but rather the act occurring little by little, as in a sequence. Words necessarily include this, so the form nazzala indicates it. Anzala is absolute, but when there is an indicator, gradualness is meant by it as installments (tanjīm), and by anzala, the sudden descent that is contrasted with it, or it is absolute according to what the context requires.

The derivation of "al-Tawrah" and "al-Injīl" has been disputed. It was said that the derivation of the first is from warā al-zind, when the flint struck and fire appeared from it, because it is light and illumination in relation to all other than the Qur'an, dispelling the darkness of error. It was also said that it derives from warrā in speech, when one alludes, because it contains many symbols and noble allusions. Its pattern according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is fawʿalah, like ṣawmaʿah, and its original form is (wawriyah) with two waws. The first was changed to a tāʾ, the yāʾ became vowelled, and the letter before it took a fatḥah, so it was changed into an alif, and it became tawrāh. It was written with a yāʾ to point to the original, and for this reason it is pronounced with imālah. Al-Farrāʾ said its pattern is tafʿilah with a kasrah on the ʿayn; the kasrah was changed to a fatḥah, the yāʾ was changed to an alif, and this was done for lightness, as they said in tawṣiyah, tawṣāh. The Basrians objected to this, saying that this pattern is rare, and that it entails the addition of a tāʾ at the beginning, which is not added in that way except in certain positions, and this is not one of them. Some of the Kufians held that its pattern is tafʿalah with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, so the yāʾ was changed to an alif. It was said that the derivation of the second is from al-najl, with a fatḥah and then a sukūn, which is the water that oozes from the earth, and from it comes al-najīl, for what grows in it. It is also applied to the father and the son, and this is better known, so it is a homonym (ḍidd), as al-Zajjāj said. It is from najala meaning "to appear," and it was named so because it is extracted from the Preserved Tablet and manifest from it, or from the Torah. It was also said: it is from al-najal, which is expansion, and from it comes ʿayn najlāʾ, a wide eye, because in it there is an expansion not found in the Torah, since it made lawful some of what the Torah made unlawful. It was also said that it is derived from al-tanājul, which is mutual contention; one says tanājala the people when they contended. It was named so for the abundance of contention concerning it. This is what has been said. But it is not hidden that the matter of derivation and pattern, on the assumption that the two words are Arabic, is clear. As for the assumption that they are foreign words, the first of which is Hebrew and the second Syriac, which is the more evident view, then there is no meaning to it in actual fact, because derivation from other foreign words is not something whose establishment is possible, and derivation from Arabic words, as the case of ḍabb (lizard) derived from ḥūt (fish) is heard, is not established. What remains is that after arabization they treated them according to the patterns of their own forms regarding augmentation and originality, and they assumed an original root for them so that this could be known, as we indicated before. The argument for their Arabic origin from the entry of the definite article (lām) is a matter for consideration, because its entry into foreign proper names is disputed. For they made the alif and lām obligatory as a sign of definiteness for some foreign proper names, as in al-Iskandariyyah. Abū Zakariyyā al-Tibrīzī said that it is not used without it, with agreement on its foreignness. Among the things that support the foreignness of "al-Injīl" is what is narrated from al-Ḥasan, that he read it with a fatḥah on the hamzah, and ifʿīl is not one of the patterns of the Arabs.

﴿Min qablu﴾ ("before") is connected to ﴿wa-anzala﴾ ("and He sent down"). That is, He sent down both (the Tawrah and the Injil) before the revelation of the Book. It was also said: "before you" (i.e., before you, O Muhammad). The explicit mention of it, despite the matter being clear, is for the sake of emphasis in clarification. This is what they all say in full. I say: the explicit mention of it is a hint that their being sent down contains an *irhas* (a preparatory sign, a foreshadowing announcing a prophet's coming) for his mission ﷺ, since the descent, qualified by ﴿min qablu﴾, is further qualified by His words, glorified is He: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾. That is, He sent them down in this way for the sake of guiding the people to whom they were sent down, to the truth, of which belief in him ﷺ and following him is a part, since they contain the good news of him and the exhortation to obey him, upon him be blessings and peace. Guidance through them, after their rulings were abrogated (*naskh*) by the Qur'an, is only from this aspect and no other. The claim that one may also be guided by them in matters other than the abrogated laws, in matters which the Qur'an confirms, is nothing, because guidance at that time comes through the confirming Qur'an and not through them, as is not hidden from the fair-minded. It is permissible for ﴿hudan﴾ to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of both of them, and the singular form is because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), making the guidance itself (a form of) emphasis, or the genitive phrase has been elided, meaning "possessors of guidance." Making it a circumstantial state of "the Book" is not what should be adopted.

﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾. ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported on the authority of Qatadah that it is the Qur'an, by which He distinguished between truth and falsehood, so He made lawful in it its lawful things, made unlawful its unlawful things, legislated its laws, set its limits and obligations, clarified its clarifications, commanded obedience to Him and forbade disobedience to Him. The mention of it under this title after the mention of it by its generic name is to magnify its status and elevate its station. Ibn Jarir reported on the authority of Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr that it is that which separates truth from falsehood in what the factions differed about concerning the matter of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and other matters. This is supported by the fact that the beginning of the surah, as we have mentioned, was revealed in the dispute of the Christians with the Prophet ﷺ concerning the matter of his brother ʿIsa, peace be upon him. In that case, by *al-Furqan* is meant part of the Qur'an, and it was not satisfied with its inclusion within the whole, out of special concern for it. Similar to this view is what is related from Abu ʿAbd Allah, may God be pleased with him, that what is meant by it is every clear (*muhkam*) verse. It was also said: what is meant by it is the genus of divine books. He expressed them by a description encompassing what was mentioned of them and what was not mentioned, by way of completion through generalization after particularizing some of their famous ones by mention. It was also said: it is the very books mentioned, mentioned again with a special description not mentioned previously, by way of conjunction, repeating the verb "sending down," treating the descriptive difference as if it were an essential difference. It was also said: what is meant by it is the Zabur (Psalms). The placing of the Injil before it, despite its being later in revelation, is because of the strength of its relation to the Tawrah in containing rulings and the commonness of their being mentioned together. It is objected that the Zabur is admonitions, so there is in it nothing that distinguishes truth from falsehood in terms of rulings. It is answered that admonitions, because of their warning and encouragement, are also distinguishing, and because the distinction in them is hidden, they were specifically described by it. It is objected to this that mentioning the description without the thing described implies its fame by that attribute, to the point that it dispenses with mentioning what it describes, whereas hiddenness only implies the affirmation of the attribute, not expressing it by that term. It was also said: what is meant by it is the miracles accompanying the sending down of the mentioned books, which distinguish the one who is right from the one who is wrong. In any case, it is in origin a verbal noun like *al-ghufran* (forgiveness), used for the agent by way of emphasis.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God﴾. The annexation may be to a known referent (*ʿahd*), pointing to the verses of the previously mentioned revealed books, and it may be generic, so that "the signs" applies to what is realized within what was previously mentioned and to other things, such as miracles. He attributed them to the divine Name, to specify the aspect of their disbelief, to magnify their matter, and to emphasize their deserving of punishment. By the relative pronoun is meant either those mentioned earlier in the occasion of revelation, or the People of the Two Books, or the genus of disbelievers. On both assumptions, those (earlier) enter it by primary inclusion. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾: a subject and predicate, in the position of the predicate of *inna*. It is permissible for "the punishment" to be nominative by the prepositional phrase (as its subject), and the indefiniteness is for magnification. In this there is an indication that its measure cannot be determined. This is the point of the restriction derived from fronting the prepositional phrase. The attaching of the judgment to the relative clause, which has the force of a derived noun (*mushtaqq*), indicates causation, and this is the meaning which the conditional form contains, and the particle *fa* is omitted because it is evident, so it is more eloquent when the context calls for it.

﴿And God is Mighty﴾, that is, dominant over His affair, doing what He wills and judging what He desires. ﴿Owner of retribution﴾ [4]: an *ifti'al* form from *al-niqmah*, which is power and dominance. It is said: *intaqama minhu* ("he took vengeance on him") when he punished him for his offense. Its base form is *naqima* (with *fath* and *kasr*), and some have taken it to mean only "disliked." The tanwin is for magnification. He chose this structure over *muntaqim* despite its brevity, because it is more eloquent: one is not called "possessor of a sword" except one who kills much, not one who merely has a sword with him. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiradh tadhyili*), confirming the threat and emphasizing it.

[Page 78]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him.﴾ [5] This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) to show the breadth of His knowledge, glorified is He, and His encompassing of everything in the world, of which the faith of those who believe and the disbelief of those who disbelieve are part. It comes right after the demonstration of His perfect power and great might. Showing this serves as a warning (*tarbiyah lil-wa'id*, a preparatory reinforcement of the threat), and it points to the proof that He is living. It also alerts the reader that knowing some of the unseen, as happened with Jesus, peace be upon him, is far from reaching the rank of the divine attributes. By "the earth and the heaven" is meant the whole world. Many scholars took this as a figurative usage (*majaz*) in which the part is mentioned and the whole is intended. Whoever said that the word "kull" (all) cannot properly apply to a whole and a part, based on the condition of real composition and on the whole ceasing to exist when the part ceases, made the mention a metonymy (*kinayah*) rather than a figure of speech. The earth is placed before the heaven to show concern for the affairs of its inhabitants and attention to what points to the threat against those among them who are astray, and so that the mention of the heaven afterward comes as an ascent (from the lower to the higher). It is said that for this reason the negative particle was placed between the two. The negated clause is the predicate of *inna* (indeed). Repeating the predication strengthens the judgement. The phrase "fi" (in) is attached to an omitted element and functions as an attribute of "shay'" (thing), emphasizing its generality, which is derived from its occurrence in the context of negation. That is: nothing whatsoever that exists in the entire world is hidden from Him, however its being "in" (location) is conceived. The expression "non-concealment" is more eloquent than the expression "knowledge." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the adverbial phrase be attached to "yakhfa" (is hidden).

He (Allah) says, ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾. This is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) according to the sound view, expressing some of the rulings of His self-subsisting sustainment (qayyumiyyah), and pointing to the affirmation of His knowledge along with a further clarification of His relation to things before they exist. Al-taswir (forming) is making a thing into a form it did not have, and al-surah (form) is the configuration a thing takes through composition. Al-arham is the plural of rahim (womb), which is well known. It may be that it is derived from al-rahmah (mercy), because it is that by which one shows mercy and compassion. The word fi (in) is connected to yusawwiru (He forms). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: He forms you while you are in the wombs as a lump of flesh (mudgha). Kayfa (how) is in the accusative position with yasha'u (He wills), and it is a circumstantial expression (hal), and the object is omitted, its estimated meaning being "He wills your forming." It has also been said that kayfa is an adverbial of time or manner (zarf) for yasha'u, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial expression, meaning: He forms you according to His will, i.e., willing, if the circumstantial expression is from the subject; or He forms you, changing you according to His will, following it in accepting the differing states: being drops of semen (nutfan), then clots of blood (alaqan), then lumps of flesh (mudgha), then (further stages), and in the attribution of differing qualities, of maleness and femaleness, of beauty and ugliness, and other things. In this there is, among the indications of the falsity of the claim of those who claim the lordship of Jesus, peace be upon him, despite his changing through the stages and his revolving in the orbit of these phases as the King, the Subduer, willed, and the feebleness of their intellects, which is not hidden.

Tawus recited (taṣawwarakum) in the past form of the taf'"ul pattern, meaning: he took your forms for himself and for his worship. It is then of the same type as (tawassada al-turab), meaning he took it as a pillow. What has been said, that it is as if it is from tasawwartu al-shay' in the sense of tawahhamtu suratahu (I imagined its form), is then [to be affirmed as] a pure fancy.

﴿There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the Wise﴾ [6]. He repeated the sentence that indicates the negation of divinity from anything other than Him, exalted is He, and the restriction of divinity to Him, as an emphasis on what came before it and as an intensification in refuting the one who claimed the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him. Its coming after the two preceding attributes of knowledge and power is fitting, since the one to whom these two attributes belong is the one who is characterized by divinity and no other. Then He brought the attribute of might (al-'izzah), which indicates the absence of a peer, or the limitlessness of power and wisdom, because their creation in the wondrous pattern mentioned is one of the effects of that.

[Page 79]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 1 of 4):

﴿He it is Who has sent down to you the Book﴾. This is a resumption (istinaf) to refute the doubts of the delegation (al-Wafd) and their like, which arose concerning what the Qur'an stated about the Messiah, peace be upon him, right after the explanation of the exclusivity of lordship (rububiyyah) and its basis being with Him, glory be to Him. It is said: the delegation said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Do you not claim that Jesus is the Word of Allah, exalted is He, and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us." (So He, glory be to Him, censured their deviation (zaygh) and their trial (fitnah)), and He made clear that the Book is founded on firm principles (usul) and branches built upon them, speaking the truth and decisively refuting what they held. This is what has been said, and from it the connection of the verse with what precedes it is known. It has been objected that this report has no trace in the "Sahihs" (al-Sihah), nor any chain of narration that can be relied upon outside of them; the most that has been found from al-Rabi' is that the intended meaning of the relative pronoun that follows is the delegation. In reply: the same report was recorded by Abu Hatim and Ibn Jarir from al-Rabi' in "al-Durr al-Manthur" (by al-Suyuti), and from some of them: "that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by (a man of the Jews came to the Messenger) of Allah ﷺ while he was reciting the opening of Surah al-Baqarah [1-2]: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾. So he came to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab among a group of Jews and said: 'Do you know, by Allah, I heard Muhammad reciting in what was revealed to him: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾.' He said: 'Did you hear it yourself?' He said: 'Yes.' So he went until he came with those men to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'Did he not mention that you recite in what was revealed to you ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Allah, exalted is He, sent prophets before you, and we do not know that He explained to any of them what the duration of his reign or the term of his community would be, except you. Alif is one, Lam is thirty, and Mim is forty: this is seventy-one years. Is there anything else with this?' He said: 'Yes.' (Al-Mas) He said: 'This is heavier and longer.' Alif is one, Lam is thirty, Mim is forty, and Sad is ninety: this is one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything else with this?' He said: 'Yes.' (Ar) He said: 'This is heavier and longer. Is there anything else with this?' He said: 'Yes.' (Al-Mar) He said: 'This is heavier and longer.' Then he said: 'Your matter has confused us, so that we do not know whether you were given little or much.' Then he said: 'Stand up.' Then Abu Yasir said to his brother and those with him: 'What do you know? Perhaps he has gathered all of this for Muhammad?' They said: 'His matter has become confused for us.'"

This was recorded by al-Bukhari in "al-Tarikh" and Ibn Jarir and others from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, except that in it is the phrase "they claim that these verses were revealed concerning them," which indicates that there is no certainty about this. Yet the report previously cited, "that Allah, exalted is He, revealed concerning those delegates, from the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran, about eighty-some verses," further weakens it. Setting this aside, the connection of the verse with what precedes it may be that in the ambiguous (mutashabih) there is obscurity, just as the shaping of what is in the wombs is so; or that in this verse is the shaping of the spirit by knowledge and its perfection by it, while in what precedes is the shaping of the body and its formation. Since each of them contains shaping and perfection in general, it is appropriate to mention it alongside it. And since there is such difference and contrast between the physical, corporeal shaping and what is not so, of the spiritual kind, the conjunction was omitted.

As for His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Among it are verses﴾. The prepositional phrase (al-zarf) here is the predicate (khabar) placed first, and "verses" (ayat) is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), or the reverse. The first was preferred on the ground that it better accords with the rules of grammatical craft (sina'ah); the second on the ground that it is more fitting to the eloquence of meaning, since the primary intent is the division of the Book into the two well-known categories, not that they are from the Book. The sentence is either a new resumption, or in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book," meaning: He it is who sent down to you the Book in this state, that is, divided into the decisive (muhkam) and other than it. Or the prepositional phrase alone is the circumstantial clause, and "verses" is raised by it as its agent (fa'iliyyah). ﴿Decisive (muhkamat)﴾ is an adjective of "verses," meaning: clear in meaning, manifest in indication, precise in expression, protected from possibility (ihtimal) and confusion (ishtibah). ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾: that is, its origin, and its foundation, to which the others are referred back. The Arabs call every comprehensive thing that serves as a point of return a "umm" (mother). The sentence is either an adjective of what precedes it or a new resumption. The noun "umm" is given in the singular although the verses are many, because the intent is to show the originality of each one of them, or to show that all of them are like a single verse. ﴿And others (akhar)﴾ is a qualifier of an omitted noun conjoined to "verses," meaning: and other verses, ﴿akhar﴾ being the plural of ﴿ukhra﴾, the feminine of ﴿akhar﴾, whose meaning originally is "more extremely late." So the meaning of "a man came to me and another man (rajul akhar) came to me" is: a man came to me and a man more extremely late than him in some respect. Then it was transferred to the meaning of "other," so that "rajul akhar" means a man other than Zayd. It is not used except of what is of the same kind as what was mentioned first; so one does not say "Zayd came to me and a donkey (himar) other" nor "a woman (imra'ah) ukhra." And since it departed from the meaning of comparative (tafdil), it is used without the features of the elative (af'al al-tafdil), namely min, the genitive construction, and the definite article, and it agrees with what it qualifies in the unmarked form without the article or genitive construction: e.g., "rajulan akharan," "rijal akharun," "imra'ah ukhra," "imra'atan ukhrayan," and "niswah ukhar."

Most of the grammarians hold that it is not declinable (ghayr munsarif), because it is a qualifier deviated (ma'dul) from "akhar." They said: because the original rule of the elative is that it should not be pluralized except when combined with the definite article, as in "al-kibar" and "al-sigar"; so it was deviated from its original form and given, in the unmarked state, the plurality that other [forms] receive only when accompanied by the article. It was also said: the proof of the deviation of "ukhar" is that if it were with the implied min as in "Allahu akbar," it would necessarily be said "bi-nisswatin akhar" on the pattern af'al, because the elative, as long as it is with min, explicit or implied, may not agree with what it qualifies, but must be kept singular. Nor can it be by the implied genitive construction, because the genitive complement is not omitted except with the construct being indeclinable, or with something standing in the place of the complement, or with the indication of the complement by what follows the construct, as derived from the inductive study of their speech. So there remains only that its original form was with the definite article. Abu 'Ali objected to this, saying: if it were so, it would have to be definite, like "suhar" (the adverb meaning "at dawn").

It was answered: it does not follow of what is deviated from something that it must be in every respect the same as that thing; what follows is only that it has been taken out of what it deserves and what is its analogical form into another pattern. Indeed, it may be intended to make it definite after the transfer, either by the definite article whose meaning is incorporated, so that it is built (fa-yubna), or by proper-name status, as in "suhar," so that it is prevented from declension. Since in "ukhar" the intention of the definite article was not meant, it is declined. It is not valid to intend proper-name status, because that contradicts the descriptive character that is intended from it. Ibn Jinni said: it is deviated from "akhar min," and Ibn Malik claimed this is the correct view, and Abu Hayyan's apparent statement favours it; they argued for it with evidence that is not free from scrutiny.

﴿Ukhar﴾ is described by His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾. In reality it is a qualifier of an omitted noun, meaning: admitting of meanings that are ambiguous, none of which is distinguished from another in deserving to be intended, and the matter is not made clear except by close examination. Lack of clarity may be due to homonymy (ishtirak) or to generality (ijmal), or because its apparent sense is resemblance (tashbih). So "mutashabih" in reality is a qualifier of those meanings, and it was applied to the verses in the manner of describing the signifier with what is a description of the signified. Thus the objection falls away: that the singular of "mutashabihat" is "mutashabihah," and the singular of "ukhar" is "ukhra," and the singular here cannot be described by this singular, so one does not say "ukhra mutashabihah," unless some part of one [verse] resembles some other part, which is not the meaning here. Rather the meaning is that each verse resembles another verse. So how is it valid to describe the plural by this plural, while it is not valid to describe its singular by its singular? No need arises for the strained answer that it is not a condition of the validity of describing a dual or plural that every individual adjective applies to every individual of what is described, just as predication to two or more does not necessarily imply predication to each one, as in ﴿and he found in it two men fighting﴾, since the man does not fight. It was also said: since it is the nature of ambiguous matters that reason is unable to distinguish them, everything that reason does not reach is called ambiguous, even if that is not because of resemblance, just as "mushkil" (problematic) originally denotes what has entered among its like and similars and whose exact identity is not known; then it was applied to every obscure thing even if its obscurity is not from that aspect. In that case "mutashabih" is a metaphor or a metonymy for what its meaning does not make clear, and so the objection is a sophistry that does not arise at all. This explanation of the decisive and the ambiguous is the doctrine of many people, and the Shafi'is adhere to it.

The division of the Book into these two is a division of the whole into its parts, on the basis that by "the Book" is meant what lies between the two covers (al-daftayn), and its article is for definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd). In that case, either by the second "Book," the one in the genitive construction, is meant the "umm" of the first, which occurs as the divided whole, as the saying "the repetition of a thing is definite" indicates; and placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is to give attention to the apparent noun and to magnify it; and the genitive relation is in the sense of "in," as in "one of ten," so it does not follow that a thing is the origin of itself. For the meaning is that the decisive verses, which are part of what lies between the two covers, are the origin, within what lies between the two covers, to which the ambiguous within it is referred. Considering the containment of the whole in the part averts the assumption that the thing must be contained in itself. This is preferable to the view that a noun is to be supposed between the two genitive terms, so that the sense would be "the mother of part of the Book," for although the word "Book" remains in its state, that involves some strain.

Or by it is meant the genus (jins). It is like the Qur'an, which is applied to the common notion between the whole collection and each part of it, having with it a kind of particular connection, as explained in the principles of jurisprudence. By this genus is meant what is within the ambiguous verses. In that case the article is for the genus, and the genitive relation has the sense of the article. The hadith of repetition does not oppose this, since it is a principle from which one often departs, and it is not understood from it that a thing is the mother of itself as its origin, nor that the context is one of pronominalization needing an answer to that. Some of the excellent scholars of this age, the essence of knowledge by the generosity of their noble minds, the best of ages, permitted that the genitive relation be of the sort denoting the "lam" (of possession/belonging), and that the "Book" in the genitive is the very same first Book, with no omitted noun in the construction. What follows from this, that a thing is a mother and origin for itself, does no harm, since the notions differ: its being a mother to other ambiguous verses is by the consideration of referring them back to it and returning them to it, and its being a mother to itself is by the consideration that it does not need anything other than itself for its meaning to become manifest. It should not escape you that if "mother" is in both considerations literally true, it involves using a homonym in both its meanings; and if it is metaphorical in both, it involves combining two metaphorical meanings; and if it is literal in origin in respect of what other things return to, as some of their expressions imply, and metaphorical in origin in the sense of what is self-sufficient needing nothing else, it involves combining literal and metaphorical. There is no escape from this except by accepting the generality of the metaphor.

That said, it has also been permitted that the division into the two categories, decisive and ambiguous, is a division of the universal into its particulars. Thus the article in "the Book" is for the genus both times, except that by "the Book" in the first occurrence is meant the quiddity as such (al-mahiyyah min haythu hiya), as is the well-known practice in such divisions; and in the second occurrence, the quiddity considered as realized within some of its instances, namely the ambiguous. It is also permitted that by the second be meant the whole of what lies between the two covers, and the discussion there proceeds in the manner already described. It has been said: the most that follows from this division, after accepting the view, though it is contrary to the apparent sense, is the applicability of the term "Book" to its parts, and this

The chain of authorities and the grammatical discussion are rendered as they stand. Qur'anic verses are given in their meaning within ﴿ ﴾.

...something that cannot be avoided. Indeed, this is the aim of those who interpret the Book as having only the common meaning. You know that the verse has other meanings as well, but this can be resolved by careful attention, so reflect on it.

Our masters of the Hanafi school hold that the *muhkam* (the clear, definitive verses, whose meaning is evident and which do not admit abrogation) and the *mutashabih* (the ambiguous, hidden verses whose meaning cannot be grasped by reason or by transmission, namely what Allah Most High has reserved knowledge of for Himself, such as the Hour of the Last Day and the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs). It is also said that the *muhkam* are the obligations, the promises and the threats, and the *mutashabih* are the narratives and the parables. Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The *muhkamat* are its abrogating (*nasikh*) and abrogated verses, its permitted and forbidden matters, its limits and its obligations. The *mutashabihat* are what is believed in but not acted upon." Al-Firyabi reported from Mujahid, who said: "The *muhkamat* are those containing the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever is other than that is *mutashabih*." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "The *muhkamat* are what has not been abrogated, and the *mutashabihat* are what has been abrogated." Al-Mawardi said: "The *muhkam* is what has an intelligible meaning, and the *mutashabih* is its opposite, such as the number of the prayers and the specification of fasting for Ramadan rather than Sha'ban." It is also said: "The *muhkam* is that whose words are not repeated, and the *mutashabih* is what stands opposite to it." And it is said: "Other than that." This disagreement concerning the *muhkam* and the *mutashabih* applies here; otherwise the term *muhkam* is sometimes used to mean that whose composition is perfectly firm, and the term *mutashabih* to mean that whose parts resemble one another in eloquence. In this sense both terms are applied to the whole Qur'an, and on this basis Allah Most High said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿a Book resembling itself, in pairs (*mathani*)﴾.

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation (*zaygh*)﴾, that is, a turning away from the truth and an inclination toward desires. Al-Raghib said: "*Zaygh* is inclining away from uprightness toward one of the two sides." *Zaagha*, *zalla* and *mala* are close in meaning, but *zaagha* is used only for what moves from truth to falsehood. Its verbal nouns are *zaygh*, *zayghughah*, *zayaghan* and *zuyugh*. The intended referents of the relative clause are the Christians of Najran or the Jews, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said that they are the deniers of resurrection, and it is said that they are the hypocrites. Imam Ahmad and others reported from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that they are the Kharijites. The apparent wording is general, covering everyone who deviates from the truth, so what has been mentioned should be understood as an explanation of some of what the general term applies to, not as a restriction. In making their hearts the place of deviation there is an intensification of their turning away from the paths of right guidance and their persistence in evil and corruption. *Zaygh* is either the subject or the predicate of the nominal sentence. ﴿So they follow that of it which is *mutashabih*﴾, that is, they cling to it alone, without looking at what agrees with it from the *muhkam* and referring it back to that. This is either by taking its apparent sense, which is not what Allah Most High intended, or by taking one of its false inner meanings. In that case they set the Qur'an against itself and display contradiction among its meanings, out of heresy and disbelief, and they bend its wording to one of its possible senses that suits their corrupt purposes. This is what is meant by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿seeking discord and seeking its interpretation (*ta'wil*)﴾, that is, seeking to lead the believing men and women astray from their religion through doubt and confusion, and through setting the *muhkam* against the *mutashabih*, as was reported from al-Waqidi; and seeking to interpret it as they desire. Therefore the genitive in ﴿its interpretation﴾ is of a specific reference, namely a specific interpretation, which is one that does not agree with the *muhkam* but rather one that accords with mere whim.

*Ta'wil* means *tafsir* (exegesis), as many have said. Al-Raghib said: "It derives from *awwal*, which means returning to the origin; from it comes *mawil*, the place to which one returns. It is the bringing of a thing back to the purpose intended by it, whether in knowledge or in action. From the first sense is what is mentioned here; from the second is his (the poet's) saying:

*wa li-l-nawa qabla yawm al-bayni ta'wil*
(And for the separation there is an interpretation before the day of parting.)

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on the day its ta'wil comes﴾, that is, its explanation, which is its intended goal. And His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿that is better and more excellent in *ta'wil*﴾ — it has been said: more excellent in translation and meaning; it has been said: more excellent in reward in the Hereafter." End of quotation.

It is permitted to read these two aims as distributive: ﴿seeking discord﴾ being the aim of some, and seeking interpretation according to their desire being the aim of others. It is also permitted that the following applies to both aims together, and this befits the obstinate person, since by the strength of his obstinacy and his great corruption he clings to both at once. It is also permitted that it applies to each of them in succession, and this suits the state of the ignorant, for he is bewildered: at times he follows its apparent sense, and at times he interprets it according to what he desires, since he is in the grip of his desire and follows it whenever it calls him. Some people have taken *fitnah* (discord) to mean wealth, since Allah, glory be to Him, has called it *fitnah* in several places in His speech. But it is clear that this is an assertion that does not stand as proof. In giving as the cause of following the phrase "seeking its interpretation" rather than "seeking its *ta'wil*" in plain form, and in stripping *ta'wil* of any description of soundness or correctness, there is an indication that they have no share in *ta'wil* at all, neither in a small nor in a large matter, and that what they follow is not *ta'wil* in any way. It does not mean that it is an unsound interpretation of which its holder might be excused.

﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in (*yattabi'una*, they follow), in terms of the final cause; that is, they follow the *mutashabih* in order to seek its interpretation, while the case is that the interpretation which corresponds to reality, as the expression by "knowledge" and its attribution to Allah Most High indicates, is specific to Him, glory be to Him, and to whomever of His servants He has granted success, the firmly rooted in knowledge, that is, those who were steadfast and established in it and did not waver at the slippery places of feet and the refuted places of understanding, unlike others who are far from that rank. This is what the apparent sense requires in the explanation of "those firmly rooted". Ibn 'Asakir reported through 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Azdi, who said: "I heard Anas ibn Malik say: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: Those whose speech is truthful, who are dutiful in their oaths, and whose stomach and private parts are chaste; these are those firmly rooted in knowledge.'" Perhaps this is an explanation of their sign and of what they ought to be like. The knowledge meant is the sacred knowledge drawn from the niche of prophethood, for its people are the praiseworthy ones.

﴿They say: We believe in it﴾. This is a resumptive clause clarifying the state of those firmly rooted, and for this reason it is separated. The grammarians always supply for it a subject, that is, "they say". It has been said that there is no need for this, and the reason for their insistence on this has not been known, so let it be considered. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from "those firmly rooted", and the pronoun in the genitive refers to the *mutashabih*. Its not being contrasted with their belief in the *muhkam* is because the latter is evident. If the pronoun refers to the Book, this also has a valid sense, because its ultimate reference is that each part of the Book, or each of its particulars, is so. That does not escape either of the two matters. Then, although this statement does not restrict itself to the firmly rooted, it contains an implicit reproach: the requirement of belief in it is that no improper path of interpretation be followed, as has passed, so it is as if the others are not believers.

﴿Each is from our Lord﴾. This is part of their speech, confirming what precedes and establishing it, that is, each one of it and of the *muhkam* — or each one of its *mutashabih* and *muhkam* — is sent down from Him, Exalted is He, with no contradiction between them. In the expression "Lord" there is an indication of the secret of sending down the *mutashabih*, and its wisdom: it contains the meaning of nurturing, of considering the benefit, and of bringing one step by step to the heights of perfection. They have said: the *mutashabih* was sent down for this reason, so that the excellence of the scholars might appear, and their zeal for diligent reflection on it and for acquiring the sciences upon which the derivation of the real legal rulings intended by it depends might increase. Thus they attain, by exhausting their faculties and by extracting the refined aims and fitting meanings, lofty stages, and by reconciling it with the *muhkam* they ascend to the canopy of certainty and the throne of tranquillity, and they win the exalted visions. Then the veil is lifted from them and their station becomes pleasant in the gardens of correctness. This is of the nurture and guidance at the furthest extent, a utmost purpose in the observance of benefit beyond which there is no further end.

﴿And none takes heed except those of understanding﴾ [7]. It is coordinated with the clause ﴿they say﴾. It is introduced from His side, Exalted is He, as praise for those firmly rooted, for their keenness of mind and fine reflection, since their intellects are free of what covers them of inclination toward the deviant desires which cloud them, and they have prepared themselves to be guided to the landmarks of truth and to ascend the stairs of sincerity. To indicate this, the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun (*wa dha'a al-zahir mawdi' al-damir*). This holds on the supposition that the pause is at "those firmly rooted", which is the view of the Shafi'is and of all who explain the *mutashabih* as what has no clear meaning. As for the supposition that the pause is at ﴿except Allah﴾, which is the view of the Hanafis who hold that the *mutashabih* is what Allah Most High has reserved knowledge of for Himself, then "those firmly rooted" is the subject, and the clause ﴿they say﴾ is its predicate. The first view has been preferred for several reasons. First: if the purpose were to state the share of those firmly rooted in contrast to the statement of the share of the deviants, then the proper phrasing would have been "as for those firmly rooted, they say". Second: because in that case the qualifier of firm rootedness would serve no purpose, since this would be the ruling for all people. Third: because in that case the Book would not be limited to *muhkam* and *mutashabih* as the apparent wording requires, since he did not say "and among it are *mutashabihat*". For what has no clear meaning, which the scholars arrive at the interpretation of and refer back to the *muhkam*, is neither *muhkam* nor *mutashabih* in the sense mentioned, and this is very numerous. Fourth: because the *muhkam* in that case would not be the "Mother of the Book" in the sense of the *mutashabih* returning to it, since there is no return to it concerning what Allah Most High has reserved knowledge of, such as the number of the guardians of hell, for example. Fifth: because it is established in the authentic collection that "he (ﷺ) prayed for Ibn 'Abbas, saying: 'O Allah, grant him understanding of the religion and teach him the *ta'wil*.'" If *ta'wil* were something that none knows except Allah, the prayer would have no meaning. Sixth: because Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "I am among those who know its interpretation." Seventh: because Allah, glory be to Him and Exalted, praised those firmly rooted for taking heed in this context, and this indicates that they have the greatest share of knowledge of it. Eighth: because it is unlikely that Allah Most High would address His servants with something for which no path exists for any of creation to know.

As for the claim that *amma* (as for) is for distinction, so that the ruling on the deviants must be matched by a ruling on those firmly rooted for the distinction to be complete, with the result that *amma* and the *fa*' have been omitted, and that the verse belongs to the category of combination, division and differentiation: the combination is in His saying ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, the division is in His saying ﴿of it are verses that are *muhkam*, they are the Mother of the Book, and others that are *mutashabih*﴾, and the differentiation is in His saying ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ etc. Therefore the counterpart to this must include a ruling connected with the *muhkam*, namely that those firmly rooted follow it and refer the *mutashabih* back to it, according to the content of His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ etc. The answer to this is that the distinction in *amma* is mostly, not entirely; and even if it were granted, mentioning the counterpart explicitly is not necessary. Furthermore, even if it were granted that the verse belongs to the category of combination, division and differentiation, the mention of the counterpart by way of resumption or circumstance, namely "they say" etc., is sufficient for that. The second view has been preferred because it is the position of most of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), of the Successors and their followers, especially the People of the Sunnah; and it is the most authentic of the reports from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. No one has adopted the first view except a small group compared to the majority, as Ibn al-Sam'ani and others have stated explicitly. The hand of Allah is with the community.

Many reports indicate the soundness of their position:

**First**: what 'Abd al-Razzaq reported in his *Tafsir*, and al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak*, from Ibn 'Abbas: that he used to recite, "And none knows its interpretation except Allah," and would say, "And those firm in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'" This indicates that the *waw* (and) is for resumption (*li-l-istinaf*), because even though this narration does not establish a recitation, its lowest level is that it is a report with a sound chain of transmission to the interpreter of the Qur'an (*turjuman al-Qur'an*), so his words are given precedence over those of anyone else. Al-Farra' also related that in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b as well it reads, "And those firm in knowledge say." Ibn Abi Dawud, in *al-Masahif*, related through al-A'mash that in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it reads, "And its interpretation is only with Allah, and those firm in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'"

**Second**: What al-Tabarani reported in *al-Kabir* from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "I do not fear for my community except three things: that wealth increases among them, so they envy one another and fight; and that the Book is opened to them, so the believer takes it, seeking its interpretation, while none seeks its interpretation except Allah, the Exalted."

**Third**: What Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed the Qur'an was not sent down so that some of it would contradict other parts. So what you know of it, act upon it, and what is *mutashabih* (ambiguous), believe in it."

**Fourth**: What al-Hakim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The first Book was sent down from one gate, upon one letter (*harf*). The Qur'an was sent down from seven gates, upon seven (modes): a warner, a commander, the permitted, the forbidden, the *muhkam* (clear, decisive), the *mutashabih* (ambiguous), and parables. So make lawful what it makes lawful, forbid what it forbids, do what you are commanded, refrain from what you are forbidden, take lessons from its parables, act upon its *muhkam*, believe in its *mutashabih*, and say: 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Shu'ab*, related something similar from Abu Hurayrah.

**Fifth**: What Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Qur'an was sent down upon four modes: the lawful and the unlawful, which no one is excused for not knowing; an explanation which the scholars explain; the *mutashabih*, which none knows except Allah, the Exalted; and whoever claims to know it apart from Allah, the Exalted, is a liar."

And there are other reports besides these indicating that the *mutashabih* is among what none knows the interpretation of except Allah, the Exalted.

Some verifying scholars (*muhaqqiqun*) held that both pausing (*waqf*) and continuing (*wasl*) are permissible, and each has a sound basis. Al-Raghib explained this by saying that when the Qur'an is considered in relation to its parts, it has three kinds: *muhkam* absolutely, *mutashabih* absolutely, and *muhkam* in one respect and *mutashabih* in another. The *mutashabih* in general has three kinds: *mutashabih* from the standpoint of the wording alone, from the standpoint of the meaning, and from both together. The first has two types: one returns to the individual words, either because of their strangeness, such as *al-abb* (fodder) and *yazuffuna* (they hasten), or because of their homonymy, like *al-yad* (hand) and *al-'ayn* (eye). The second returns to the whole structure of the composite sentence, and this has three types: one for the brevity of the speech, such as ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾; one for its elaboration, such as ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, because if it were said, "Nothing is like unto Him," it would be clearer to the listener; and one for the arrangement of the speech, such as ﴿He sent down to His servant the Book and did not place in it any crookedness, [but made it] straight﴾, since its implied sense is "He sent down to His servant the Book, straight, and did not place in it any crookedness." The *mutashabih* from the standpoint of the meaning is the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, and the attributes of the Day of Resurrection, for those attributes cannot be conceived by us, since no image forms in our souls of what we have not perceived or of what is not of its kind. The *mutashabih* from both standpoints has five types:

The first: from the standpoint of quantity, like the general and the specific, such as ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾.
The second: from the standpoint of modality, like obligation and recommendation, as in ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾.
The third: from the standpoint of time, like the abrogating (*nasikh*) and the abrogated (*mansukh*), such as ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾.
The fourth: from the standpoint of place and the circumstances in which the verse was revealed, such as ﴿And it is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the postponing (*nasi'*) is an increase in disbelief﴾; for whoever does not know their customs in the time of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*) will find it impossible to interpret these.
The fifth: from the standpoint of the conditions by which an act is validated or invalidated, such as the conditions of prayer and marriage.

Then he said: When this whole division is considered, it becomes known that everything the exegetes mentioned in interpreting the *mutashabih* does not go beyond these divisions. Then all of the *mutashabih* falls into three kinds: a kind for which there is no way to know, such as the time of the Hour, the emergence of the beast, and other such things; a kind for which there is a way for a human being to know, such as strange words and difficult rulings; and a kind that lies between these two, which only some of the firm in knowledge know and which is hidden from those below them. This is what is referred to in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Allah, grant him understanding in the religion and teach him the interpretation." When you know this, it becomes clear to you that both are permissible: pausing at ﴿except Allah﴾ and pausing at ﴿the firm in knowledge﴾.

Some leading verifiers said: The truth is that if by the *mutashabih* is meant what there is no way for created beings to know, then the truth is to pause at ﴿except Allah﴾. And if what is meant is what is not clear, such that it encompasses the general (*mujmal*) and the like, then the truth is to continue (the sentence), though pausing is also permissible, because no one knows all of it, or no one knows its reality (*kunh*) except Allah, the Exalted. But when it is interpreted by what a decisive proof (*qati'*), that is, a textual transmitted proof (*nass naqli*) or a decisive rational proof (*dalil jazim 'aqli*), shows that its apparent meaning is not intended, and no proof has been established for what is intended, then there are two positions. Some permit delving into it and interpreting it in a way that accords with the correct path in its like, so for them both pausing and not pausing are permissible. Others prohibit delving into it, so interpreting it is forbidden and pausing is obligatory for them.

Those who hold the position of pausing among the Hanafi masters (*al-sada al-Hanafiyyah*) answered what others mentioned in support of their own positions as follows:

Regarding the first: the purpose was to state the portion of the firm in knowledge in contrast to the statement of the portion of those who deviate, except that He did not say "As for the firm in knowledge..." out of emphasis on the importance of the firm in knowledge, for He did not put them in a verbal parallel with those deviators, and they were protected from being mentioned together as opposites are usually mentioned in such contexts. Similar to this is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (*taghut*)﴾, where He did not say "And the *taghut* are the protectors of those who disbelieve," nor "And the protector of those who believe is Allah," glorifying His own station and taking care of the importance of the believers.

Regarding the second: the benefit of the qualifier of firmness (*rusukh*) is to strongly restrict knowledge of the interpretation of the *mutashabih* to Allah, the Exalted, because if they (the firm) do not know it, as the judgment about them that they say "We believe in it" implies, then others are even more deserving of not knowing it. Thus no one knows it except Allah, the Exalted.

Regarding the third: it is necessary to say that the statement follows after the restriction. In *al-Itqan* it is mentioned that some said: The verse does not indicate restriction to the two things, since it does not contain any of its (the restriction's) means. Otherwise, His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ would be problematic, because the *muhkam* does not depend on explanation for its understanding, and the *mutashabih* is not expected to be explained. So what is it that the Prophet (ﷺ) explains?

Regarding the fourth: by committing to the view that the idiom "mother of the Book" (*umm al-Kitab*) is in the sense of "in," and the *muhkam* is a "mother" within the Book, but not for the *mutashabih* which Allah, the Exalted, has kept exclusively for His knowledge. Rather, it is a mother and a root in understanding the legal acts of worship, such as the obligation to know Him, to affirm His messengers, to comply with His commands, and to avoid His prohibitions. And if one holds that the idiom is a possessive (*lamiyyah*), one commits to the Book's being a mother in relation to a part of it, namely the intermediary between the two kinds, because what is clear in its indication is often referred to in order to clarify what is obscure in it, among what has not reached the limit of being kept exclusively (for Allah).

Regarding the fifth: the interpretation for which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed for Ibn 'Abbas is not necessarily to be understood as the interpretation of what is exclusively known to Allah, the Exalted, but it is permissible to understand it as the explanation of what is hidden in its explanation from the kind that lies between the two matters which al-Raghib mentioned, as he (al-Raghib) mentioned.

Regarding the sixth: the report from Ibn 'Abbas that he said, "I am among those who know its interpretation," is contradicted by what is more authentic than it by several degrees, so it drops from the level of consideration. And even if its authority is granted, it is possible to say that his intention, may Allah be pleased with him, was: "I am among those who know its interpretation," that is, the *mutashabih* in general, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed for me. And although this is said to be *mutashabih*, in reality it is an intermediary between the *muhkam* and the *mutashabih* in the intended sense.

Regarding the seventh: the praise of the firm in knowledge with "remembering" (*tadhakkur*) is not because they have a share in knowing it, but because they took admonition, opposed their desires, stopped at what their Master set as a limit for them, did not take the path of those who deviate, and did not plunge in with the plungers. It is possible, though remotely, to intend by "remembering" the meaning of "benefiting" metaphorically, that is, the firm in knowledge are those who benefit from it, since they believe in it because their minds are purified of the veil of desire, just as they believe in the unseen. This is in contrast to those who deviate, for the *mutashabih* has become a harm to them and a calamity, since they go astray in it greatly and lead others astray from the right path. And He, glorified, has already said earlier, concerning the parable He struck: ﴿He misleads many by it and guides many by it, and He misleads by it none but the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Regarding the eighth: there is no impossibility in Allah, the Exalted, addressing His servants with what no created being has a way to know, and that this would be part of a trial, just as He, glorified, tested His servants with many obligations and abundant acts of worship whose true secret no one has understood. The secret in this trial is clipping the wing of reason, breaking the wings of thought, and removing the vanity of the peacock of the self, so that the heart turns with all its being toward the Ka'bah of servanthood, submits beneath the canopies of lordship, acknowledges deficiency, and confesses inability to reach what is within those palaces. In that is the ultimate of upbringing and the final benefit. This is when what is meant by "what no created being has a way to know" is what none of them has a way to know through reflection. But if what is meant is what there is no way to know absolutely, whether in summary or in detail, through revelation or inspiration to a prophet or a saint, then the existence of such a thing being addressed in the Qur'an is ruled out. Perhaps the one who holds that the *mutashabih* is among what Allah, the Exalted, has kept exclusively for His knowledge does not prevent its being taught to the Prophet (ﷺ) through revelation, for example, nor its being cast into the heart of a perfect saint in detail. But it does not reach the level of comprehensiveness of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted; and even if it is not in detail, then at least it is in summary. Denying this and that is something that one who knows the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the rank of the perfect saints of his community would hardly say. Rather, the prohibition is only from comprehensiveness and from knowing it through reflection and reasoning, which is the customary way and the path taken in knowing difficult matters and deriving theoretical conclusions. And because this meaning is what comes to mind for anyone who knows, when it is ascribed to the firm in knowledge, one refuses to ascribe it to them. But if what is meant by knowledge is knowledge not through the path of reflection, then the ascription is valid and the conjunction (*'atf*) is permissible. However, to think of this intention from the apparent wording of the speech is like pulling out thistles (*kharṭ al-qatad*, i.e., an extremely difficult task). Therefore the view of not conjoining became widespread, and holding it is safer.

[Page 88]

This is supported by what Imam al-Sha'rani related: "Our shaykh, 'Ali al-Khawwas (may Allah sanctify his secret), informed me that Allah Most High granted him insight into the meanings of Surat al-Fatiha, and from it he extracted two hundred thousand, forty thousand, and nine hundred and ninety 'ilms (branches of knowledge)." He used to say: "None is called a scholar, among the people of Allah Most High, except one who knows every word the Sharia has brought." In *al-Kashshaf*, concerning such letters as Qaf, Sad, Ha Mim, and Ta Sin, he said: "Perhaps the understanding of what lies beneath them, for their people, is like our understanding of the self-evident truths (awwaliyyat). This is not far-fetched. The overflowing bounty of the Creator is unlimited in its reach, and the readiness of the perfect human being to receive it is not exhausted. Whoever does not affirm in general that behind the objects of thought and their starting points there is a stage or stages, where the intellect's share of them is like the senses' share of intelligibles, has not freed himself from the narrow path of either negation (ta'til) or anthropomorphism (tashbih). Even if he does not rectify his state, he will remain, after the veil is lifted, in this bewilderment. To confirm this: the levels differ, and comprehensive knowledge of the Divine Realities, as it is, is impossible except for the Creator, may His remembrance be exalted. The knower, even if he reaches the highest levels, must retain something that must be believed in as unseen. This is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters of which those firmly grounded in knowledge say: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾. This is what must be believed, so that one does not fall into heresy (ilhad)."

Then know that many people have classed the transmitted attributes, such as istiwa' (being established), the hand, the foot, descent to the lowest heaven, laughter, wonder, and their like, as ambiguous matters. The position of the salaf (the early predecessors) and of al-Ash'ari, may Allah have mercy on him, who is among their notables, as his *al-Ibanah* makes clear, is that these are established attributes beyond the reach of the intellect. We are only obligated to believe in their affirmation, together with the belief that they involve no embodiment (tajsim) or likening to creation, so that transmission does not contradict reason. The khalaf (later scholars) went to ta'wil (interpretation) and to specifying what Allah Most High intends by them. They say, for example, that istiwa' means istila' (dominion) and domination. That is an effect of some of the eight attributes, beyond which, according to them, Allah has no attribute. Al-Sukuti claimed (and I wish he had kept silent) that whatever lies beyond these is impossible, since its negation entails no absurdity, and whatever's negation entails no absurdity is not necessary, while Allah Most High is described only by what is necessary.

Al-Sha'rani mentions in *al-Durar al-Manthurah* that the position of the salaf is safer and more judicious, because the interpreter has moved from explaining the bodily istiwa' upon a spatial throne, by declaring God exempt from it, to a created, sovereign likening, namely dominion over a place. This is a shift from likening to one created thing to likening to another created thing. Whoever's intellect does not reach in declaring God's transcendence the level that the Sharia reaches in His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾... Do you not see that he cited, in rational declaration of transcendence regarding istiwa', the verse of a poet:

*"Bishr has become established over Iraq,*
*without war or spilled blood."*

And where is Bishr's istiwa' over Iraq from the istiwa' of the Most Merciful upon the Throne? The final outcome requires saying that what is meant is a dominion befitting the majesty of the Most Merciful, may His glory be exalted. So whoever interprets should, before bearing the burden of this interpretation, say: an istiwa' befitting the One whose glory is great and whose sovereignty is exalted beyond the grasp of intellects. This is more fitting to good manners and more consistent with perfect servanthood. The leading early generations and their masters followed this, and the imams of the jurists and their leaders chose it, and the imams of hadith, past and present, called to it. So much so that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said, as al-Lalika'i transmitted from him: "All the jurists, from East to West, agree on affirming the attributes without explanation or likening."

It is reported from Sulayman ibn Yasar that a man called Subaygh came to Madinah and began asking about the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) sent for him, having prepared palm fronds for him, and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am 'Abd Allah Subaygh." 'Umar took one of those palm stalks and struck him until his head bled. In another narration, he struck him with the palm branch until his back and rear were torn open.
