Then he left him until he healed, and then he came back to him, then left him again until he healed. He then called for him to return, and he said: "If you intend to kill me, then kill me with a beautiful killing." So 'Umar permitted him to return to his land, and wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that no Muslim should sit with him.

It cannot be said: if such ambiguous matters are left in their apparent meanings, they indicate embodiment; and if their apparent meanings are not intended, they have been interpreted, because ta'wil, as they say, is turning the speech away from its apparent meaning. We reply: we choose the second alternative and do not grant that ta'wil is turning speech away from its apparent meaning absolutely. Rather, it is turning it toward a specific, known meaning, as one says istiwa' means istila' (dominion). Moreover, ta'wil has two well-known meanings, neither of which applies to negating the apparent meaning without specifying the intended meaning. The first: the translation of a thing and its explanation that clarifies it. The second: stating its reality and bringing it out, either through knowledge or through reason. Whoever says, after declaring God's transcendence, "I know nothing of these ambiguous matters except that Allah Most High described Himself by them and intended by them a meaning befitting His majesty, but I do not know that meaning," has not been said to have translated, clarified, stated the reality, or brought out the intended meaning, so as to be called one who interpreted. Whoever carefully examines the basis of ta'wil will not doubt the soundness of what we have said.

Yes, a small group of the salaf went to leaving such matters in their apparent meanings, except that they negate their evident implications that come to the mind, which would attribute deficiency to Him, may His glory be exalted. They say: these are implications that cannot be separated from what they imply in our created attributes. But regarding the attributes of the One to whom nothing is like, they are not implications in reality, so that asserting their separation would be sophistry. And how far is dust from the Lord of lords! It seems they only said this because they supposed that the saying of the other salaf was ta'wil, which those firmly grounded in knowledge do not follow, or because they found some reports suggesting this, such as what Muqatil and al-Kalbi related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *istawa*, that it means *istaqarra* (settled). And what Abu al-Qasim transmitted through Qurrah ibn Khalid, from al-Hasan, from his mother, from Umm Salama, regarding the verse ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾, that she said: "The how is unknown, the istiwa' is not unknown, belief in it is faith, and denial of it is disbelief."

Close to this view is what many of our Sufi masters explicitly state. They said: these ambiguous matters are taken in their apparent meaning, together with affirming transcendence, as indicated by His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. The Truth's existence, may His glory be exalted, is not confined by created beings, even though He manifests in whatever He wills of them, since He possesses perfect absoluteness, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. It is not hidden that taking the ambiguous matters in their apparent meaning, together with the transcendence befitting the majesty of His essence, is a stage beyond the stage of reason, and a sea in which no one swims except the one who attains nearness through supererogatory acts.

Some of the masters of precise investigation mentioned that the path of reason to knowing the eight well-known attributes is like its knowledge of those attributes to which the khalaf claim these others return, when it sharpens its inquiry. Proof and witnessed evidence establish the absence of resemblance in essence and in attributes too. But His exalted attributes and His Beautiful Names are of two kinds. One kind bears some relation, however distant, to what we have of attributes. Yet one cannot say: in our understanding, we who are deficient must name Him with these familiar names, so He is called "knowing," for example, and not "inkwell" or "pen." The other kind is not like that, and this is what is referred to in His (ﷺ) saying: "...or You have kept it to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You." Thus He may be described by names that evoke longing, because among them is what the perfect human being has a share of through being shaped by it and realizing it. So he mentions at times the hand, descent, the foot, and similar imaginings, together with demonstrative knowledge and experiential witnessing of God's transcendence above every perfection that a human can conceive and encompass, let alone any deficiency. He knows that he is pointing to that kind which he knows in general, and at that moment he turns with his whole being toward the Kaaba of majesty and beauty, and there is poured upon him from the spring of perfection what he finds comforting, and the reality of the matter is revealed to him. Since it has no relation to what we have, no expression can be found to translate it except by way of imagery. To this refers his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever knows Allah, his tongue becomes incapable (of describing Him)." And another matter: he explains the aim of all, and whoever loves Him, glory be to Him, is protected from the suspicion of grasping what is for others, through such opening letters. Perhaps their understanding, for their people, is like understanding self-evident truths, except that there is no comprehensiveness; rather, some remainder must persist, as has been indicated. On this basis too, the most fitting is that one stops (at the words "except Allah"), because this is the motto of those whom we have as a good example, though its face is evident. But the verse should not be made a proof against one who interprets such a verse as ﴿And the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection﴾, for example, since it is not granted that it falls under that ambiguous category. Reading it as the common metaphor of Arabic speech, and a kinaya (metonymy) so famous as to be as established as the literal, is clearer than reading it as an unknown meaning. Yes, if it were said that depicting greatness in this way indicates that reason is not independent in grasping it, and that it is too majestic for intellects to encompass, then the reality (kunh) is among the ambiguous matters that the verse indicates and that must be believed, and this would be good. It would be a combination of what the salaf held and what the khalaf followed, and this is what must be believed, so that no one is disparaged among either group, as Ibn al-Qayyim did, until he said: "The lam of the Ash'aris is like the nun of the Jews. May Allah protect us from that." Based on this, the ambiguous element in the verse must be explained as covering both categories. The muhkam ("the clear," "the mother" of the Book) is the reference for distinguishing the two categories: one is its faith-based branch, and the other its certainty-based branch.

Ibn Daqiq al-'Id took a middle course in the question of ta'wil. It is possible that this precise scholar, in his final statement, did not leave the ambiguous. He said: "If the interpretation is close to the language of the Arabs, it is not rejected. If it is distant, we refrain from it and believe in its meaning in the way it was intended, together with transcendence. Whatever its meaning is among these words, apparent and familiar in Arab discourse, we affirm it without hesitation, as in His saying: ﴿Oh, my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah﴾. We interpret it as relating to the right of Allah Most High and what is due to Him." Let this position be understood, for many peoples have slipped in it, one after another.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 8:

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ It is possible that this is part of the statement of those firmly grounded in knowledge, and it is possible that it is meant as an instruction, i.e., "Say: Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate from the path of truth to following the ambiguous (mutashabih) with an interpretation You do not approve of, after You have guided us to the landmarks of truth, whether through delegation (tafwid) regarding the ambiguous, or through faith in both categories, or through correct interpretation (ta'wil)." The meaning reverts to: "Do not lead us astray after guidance," because the deviation of hearts is in opposition to guidance, and the opposite of guidance is misguidance (al-idlal). The attribution of this to God Most High is valid according to the Sunni position on the actions of servants, while the Mu'tazilah interpret this with something like: "Do not afflict us with trials through which our hearts would deviate, and do not withhold Your kindnesses from us after You have shown us kindness." They made this supplication, or were commanded to make it, because hearts are subject to turning.

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often supplicate, 'O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how often you make this supplication!' He said: 'There is no heart except that it is between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful. If He wills to keep it upright, He keeps it upright, and if He wills to make it deviate, He makes it deviate.'"
Page 90

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated through the route of 'Utbah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Faith is only like a shirt: at one time you wear it, and at another time you take it off." There are many reports with this meaning, and they indicate the permissibility of disbelief occurring after faith, through the arising of doubt, for example, and we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted. Also in the words of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, there is something that indicates this. Ibn Sa'd narrated from Abu 'Attaf that Abu Hurayrah used to say: "O Lord, let me not commit adultery! O Lord, let me not steal! O Lord, let me not disbelieve!" It was said to him: "Do you fear?" He said: "I have believed in the Turner of hearts," three times.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi also narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, whenever he met me, would say: 'Sit down, O 'Uwaymir, so that we may believe for a while.' So we would sit and remember Allah the Exalted as He willed. Then he said: 'O 'Uwaymir, these are the gatherings of faith. The likeness of faith and of you is like the likeness of your shirt: while you have taken it off, you have worn it, and while you have worn it, you have taken it off. O 'Uwaymir, the heart is swifter in its turning than a cooking pot when it has gathered up its boiling.'"

And from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari: "There will come upon a man times when there is not in his skin a place the size of a needle's point of hypocrisy, and there will come upon him times when there is not in his skin a place the size of a needle's point of faith."

Some have claimed that this applies to incomplete faith, and that only those who turn back did so from the path. As for after the attainment of complete faith, firm assent and established knowledge that corresponds to reality, a return and disbelief are not conceivable at all, lest knowledge be turned into ignorance, which is impossible; and they obligated the interpretation of everything that indicates this. It is not hidden that this view almost leads to feeling safe from the plotting of Allah Most High, and to the obligation of interpreting the texts because of a doubt that arose in the breast, which, in verification, is weaker than a spider's web, and which no one with even a little sense would embrace, as is not hidden. So reflect.

"Ba'da" (after) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its governing element is "tuzigh" (do not let deviate). "Idh" (when) is a noun in the genitive by its being governed by "ba'da" as its complement, and it is inflectionally variable (mutasarrifah), as the eminent grammarians have mentioned. As for the view that it means "an" (that) the masdariyyah with a hamzah that is opened, so that the meaning is "after our guidance," this is something mentioned by al-Hawfi in "I'rab al-Qur'an," and it is not seen from anyone else. What is mentioned in grammar is that it is a particle of causation, so it is construed with what follows as a verbal noun, as in ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged [idh zalamtum]﴾, i.e., because of your wronging. If it was taken from this, then it is as you see. And it has been read "lā tuzigh" with the yā' and the tā' and with the raising of "al-qulūb" (the hearts).

﴿And grant us from Yourself﴾ Both prepositional phrases are connected to "hab" (grant). The first is placed first out of concern for it and to create anticipation for the second. It is permissible for the second to be connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning "being from You." "Min" is for the figurative beginning of the end-point. "Ladun" is an adverb, and it is for the first end-point of time, place, or other entities, as in "min ladun Zayd." It is not synonymous with "'inda" (with/at), but it may sometimes have its meaning. Some restrict it to the adverb of place. It is always attached to a noun in the genitive, so it is never separated from it in any case: sometimes it is attached to a singular noun, and sometimes to a nominal or verbal clause, and it is rarely free of "min." It has two dialects: the inflected form, which is the dialect of Qays, and the indeclinable form, which is the well-known dialect. The reason for indeclinability is its resemblance to a particle in always being used in one form and in not being predicated, unlike "'inda" and "ladayya," which are not always used in one form, since they can be an adjunct, a principal element, an end-point, or not an end-point. It is said that because of the strength of this resemblance, it is not inflected when attached, in the well-known usage. The two dialects mentioned, of inflection and indeclinability, are specific to "ladun" with an open lam, a closed/raised dal, and a final nun. As for its remaining dialects, they are indeclinable in the usage of all the Arabs. Its well-known dialects include the aforementioned, and "ladun" with an open dal and a kasra, "ladun" with an open lam and a damma with a sukun on the dal, and "ladut" with an open lam and a damma on the dal, with the dal changed to a sukun tā'. Whenever the nun-less form is attached to a pronoun, it is obligatory to restore the nun.

﴿Mercy﴾ is the object of "hab," and its tanwin is for magnification. By "mercy" is meant kindness and bounty in general. It is said: it means a specific bounty, namely, divine success (tawfiq) in steadfastness upon the truth. In asking for this with the term "gift" there is an indication that this is from Him, Exalted, a pure bounty without any trace of obligation upon Him, glorious is His majesty. The postponement of the explicit object is for creating anticipation.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [8] This is a causal clause explaining the request or the granting of what is asked. "Anta" is either a subject, or a separator (fasl), or an emphasis for the noun of "inna." The object is omitted to convey generality, as in their saying: "So-and-so gives." The choice of the intensive form over "fa''al" is said to be for harmony with the rhyme endings of the verses.

﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind﴾, meaning those who are obligated and those who are not, ﴿for a Day﴾, that is, for the reckoning of a Day, or for the recompense of a Day. The genitive noun has been elided and the noun in the genitive has been put in its place, to convey the dread of what happens on that Day. It has also been said that the lam means "to," so the meaning is: "You gather them in the graves until a Day," ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾, that is, it is not fitting for anyone to doubt its occurrence or the occurrence of what it contains of resurrection, reckoning, and recompense. It has been said that the pronoun in the genitive refers to the ruling, so the meaning is: there is no doubt about this ruling. On the first view, the clause is a qualifier of "a Day"; on the second, it is an emphasis of the ruling. Their purpose in this, as more than one commentator has said, is to display their deep need for mercy, which they regard as the highest aim, and the emphasis serves to show their complete assurance and strong certainty regarding the conditions of the Hereafter, in order to increase their desire to draw down the bird of response. It has also been recited as ﴿Gatherer of mankind﴾ with tanwin.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [9]. This is a reason for the content of the emphasized clause, or for the negation of doubt. It has been said that it is an emphasis after an emphasis of the preceding ruling, and the mention of the Glorious Name together with the shift in address points to the magnification of what is promised and the reverence arising from mention of the awe-inspiring, terrifying Day, and it also indicates the cause of the ruling, since divinity is incompatible with failing [to fulfil a promise]. This differs from what is at the end of the surah, where the address is in the second person, because its context is one of seeking bounty. Al-Karkhi said: the difference between them is that what is here is connected to what precedes it only verbally, whereas what is at the end is connected both in meaning and in wording, since the word "promise" precedes it. It is also permissible that this clause be part of the speech of Allah Most High, to confirm the statement of those firmly grounded in knowledge, not part of the speech of those firmly grounded in knowledge; in that case there is no shift of address. Al-Saffaqsi said: this is the apparent meaning.

The word ﴿al-mi'ad﴾ (promise) is a mimi noun meaning the event itself, not a time or place, and this is the most appropriate reading given that it is the object of ﴿yukhlifu﴾; its yā' is converted from a wāw because of the kasra before it. The Wa'idiyya (those who hold that punishing the disobedient is obligatory upon Allah) have used this verse as evidence for the obligation of punishment for the disobedient upon Allah, for otherwise failing would be entailed. It has been answered that the threat against the sinners is conditional upon the absence of pardon, by separate proofs, just as it is conditional upon the absence of repentance, by consensus. It has also been said that it is an act of creating speech (insha'), so no prohibited consequence follows from its not being fulfilled. It has also been said that what is in the verse is not a point of dispute, because the promise in it is a verbal noun meaning the promise, and from the non-failure of a promise it does not follow that threats are not failed, since the former is a requirement of generosity, as he said:

"When I threaten someone, or promise him, I am one who breaks my threat, and one who fulfils my promise."

It was objected that the threat which is the point of dispute falls under the promise, as proven by His saying: ﴿We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾. It was answered that we do not concede that it falls under it, and the verse is in the manner of mockery, like "so give them the good news of a painful punishment." It was also objected that the failing of a threat being a requirement of generosity does not permit failing on the part of Allah Most High, because it would then follow that it is valid to name Allah Most High "one who contradicts His own self," and no Muslim would venture this. It was answered that leaving this aside is more correct than mentioning it; so the truth is to return to the first answer.

* * *

Furthermore, from the allusive interpretations of the verses: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾. The discussion of it has already passed. Some of our masters have mentioned concerning it that it indicates all existence as such, as a whole, because (alif) is an indication of the Essence, which is the first of existence and the station of absoluteness; (lam) indicates the intellect called Gabriel, which is the middle of existence, which overflows from the origin and pours out to the end; and (mim) indicates Muhammad (ﷺ), who is the last of existence, and by him its circle is completed, and for this reason he is the Seal. Some of them said: (lam) is composed of two alifs, that is, it is placed in correspondence with the Essence together with the attribute of knowledge, which are two of the three Divine worlds that we have indicated [page 92] to, so it is one of His Names, Exalted is He. As for (mim), it is an indication of the Essence together with all the attributes and acts by which it has veiled itself in the form of the Muhammadan reality, which is the Greatest Name of Allah Most High, such that none knows it except those who know it. Do you not see that (alif), which is for the form of the Essence, how it is veiled within it, for the mim in it is a yā', and in the yā' there is an alif? And because (alif-lam-mim) includes an indication of the stations of existence and the Muhammadan reality, it was fitting that these verses, which include a refutation of the Christians who erred in tawhid and did not know it as it truly is, be opened with it. For this reason He, glorified is He, followed it with His saying: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him﴾, since there is no existent in all the worlds in truth except Him, since none is more jealous than Allah Most High, may His majesty be exalted. ﴿The Living﴾, that is, the one characterized by complete life in a manner befitting His Essence. ﴿The Self-Subsisting﴾, the one who sustains the management of the fixed entities by His manifestation in them according to their eternal readiness, which is not made by another.

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, which is the knowledge that yields the station of unification, which is tawhid in which multiplicity passes away and plurality is not witnessed, clothed ﴿in truth﴾, which is the established, which does not undergo change in its Essence, ﴿confirming what came before it﴾ of the first, eternal tawhid, previously known in the first covenant, stored in the unseen of readiness. ﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ ﴿before, as guidance for mankind﴾, to the landmarks of tawhid. ﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾, which is detailed tawhid, the truth in terms of differentiation, and it is the source of uprightness and the origin of the call. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, that is, who veiled themselves from these two tawhids by the appearances and the cosmos and by seeing other than Allah, and did not believe ﴿in the signs of Allah﴾, Most High, which indicate that He, glorified is He, has the station of absoluteness, and that He has manifestation and self-disclosure as He wills. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾ in distance and deprivation from the enclosures of gnosis. ﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, the Subduer, ﴿Lord of retribution﴾, severe according to the requirements of His majestic attributes.

﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ in the wombs of existence ﴿as He wills﴾, because you are the manifestations of His Names and the mirror of His Essence. ﴿There is no god﴾ in existence ﴿except Him, the Mighty﴾, who subdues the fixed entities, so the scent of existence is never smelled from them by themselves, ﴿the Wise﴾, who manifests them by His true existence and discloses Himself through them as wisdom requires.

﴿He is the One who sent down to you the Book﴾, varied in manifestation. ﴿Of it are clear verses﴾ which are made firm so that probability and confusion cannot reach them, so they admit only one meaning, ﴿they are the mother of the Book﴾, the origin, ﴿and others are allegorical﴾, admitting two or more meanings, in which confusion occurs. This is because the Most High has one aspect, which is the absolute that remains after the passing away of His creation, and it does not admit of multiplicity from that aspect; but He has many aspects according to the mirrors and manifestations, and by these confusion occurs, so the revelation came in this way. ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, that is, inclination away from the truth, ﴿they follow what is allegorical of it﴾, because they are veiled by multiplicity from unity. ﴿And none knows its interpretation﴾, which is the final point to which it returns, ﴿except Allah﴾. And those firmly grounded in knowledge know it, those who were not veiled by one of the two matters from the other, by their knowledge which they were granted through the nearness of supererogatory works, not by discursive knowledge obtained through logical syllogisms. By this the joining of the pause at ﴿except Allah﴾ and the pause at ﴿those firmly grounded﴾ is achieved.

﴿And none takes heed﴾ through that one knowledge, detailed in the many allegorical details that are multiplied, ﴿except the people of understanding﴾, whose intellects are purified by the light of guidance and who are stripped of the husk of desire and habit. ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾ by looking at the cosmos and being veiled by it from its Originator, ﴿after You have guided us﴾ by Your light to Your straight path, and by witnessing You in the stations of existence and the multiple mirrors. ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾, a special one, which erases our attributes with Your attributes and our darkness with Your lights. ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾, who gives to the receptacles according to their receptivities. ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer of mankind﴾ across their different stations, ﴿for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾, which is the Day of Gathering, which is the arrival at the station of unity when the veil is lifted and the sun of direct vision rises. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾, so that His beautiful and majestic attributes may appear; and for this He created creation and manifested Himself to the fixed entities, so He displayed them as He willed.

Here, then, when Glorified is He had explained the true religion and tawhid, and mentioned the conditions of the Books that speak of it, [page 93] and described the state of the Noble Qur'an and the manner of the faith of those firmly grounded in it, He followed that with an explanation of the condition of the one who disbelieves in it, with His saying, majestic is His glory:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ The apparent meaning is that by them is intended the category of disbelievers, comprising all of its types. It has also been said: the delegation of Najran, or the Jews of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, or the idolaters of the Arabs. ﴿Will not avail them at all﴾, i.e., will not benefit them. It is also read with the masculine form (lan yughniya) and with the yā' silent, and this is from al-jidd (the verb with a weak-letter root), in the dislike of the vowel on the letters of softness. ﴿Their wealth﴾ which they prepared to repel harms and to attract benefits, ﴿nor their children﴾ who support them in important matters and whom they rely upon in dark and grave calamities. Their being mentioned after wealth with the particle of negation placed between them, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is either because of their nobility in removing distresses, or because wealth is the first resource to which one turns when calamities descend. ﴿From Allah﴾, i.e., from His punishment, the particle min here denotes the starting point of the action, as al-Mubarrad said. The words of the Exalted, ﴿anything﴾, are in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., "anything of benefit." It is also permitted that it be an object for what the verb (aghnā) contains of the meaning of repelling, and the min is partitive, and it is related to an omitted element which occurred as an adjective to it, except that it was placed before it and so became a circumstantial (ḥāl). And it is permitted that it be a second object, based on the notion that aghnā ʿanhu means kafāhu (sufficed him), and the flaw in this is not hidden. Abu ʿUbayda said: min here means ʿinda (with/at), and this is weak. Many others said: it is substitutive (badaliyyah), like it in the verse of the poet:

"Would that for us, of the water of Zamzam, [there were] a cool draught that had spent the night on Ṭahyān."

And of this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The possessor of wealth will not benefit from You, the wealth [of this world]" (wa lā yanfaʿu dhā al-jidd minka al-jidd), and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made of you angels upon the earth succeeding⦆. The meaning is: "will not avail them, in place of Allah's mercy or in place of His obedience, the Exalted, their wealth nor their children." He, the Exalted, negated that, although the possibility that their wealth and children might take the place of Allah's mercy and obedience, the Exalted and Mighty, is far-fetched, indeed scarcely occurs to the mind so as to be taken up in its negation. This is an indication that these disbelievers have been diverted by their wealth and children from Allah, the Exalted, and from considering what is fitting for Him, to the point that it appears to the observer that they are among those who believe that these would take the place of Allah's mercy and obedience. Similar to this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And neither your wealth nor your children are that which brings you near to Us in position﴾. It was objected that most grammarians, as in "al-Baḥr," deny that min can be substitutive, and that the first (the partitive/other reading) is more fitting apparently for the magnification of the disbelievers' affair, and more suitable to the Exalted's saying: ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire﴾ [10], and so on with what follows.

Al-waqūd, with a fatḥa on the wāw, is the reading of the majority, and means firewood, i.e., those characterized by disbelief, removed from the honor of presence, are the firewood of the Fire by which it is kindled because of their disbelief. It has been said: al-waqūd with a fatḥa is a dialectal form of al-wuqūd with a ḍammah, and Ḥasan read it so; it is a verbal noun in the sense of kindling, and then a noun is to be understood, i.e., the people of its fuel. The first is the correct view. The choice of the nominal sentence is either to indicate the affirmation and establishment of the matter, or to make known that the reality of their state is that, and that while they are in this world they are, in their very persons, the fuel of the Fire. It is either resumptive, confirming the non-avail, or conjoined to the first sentence which is the predicate of inna, and hum may be a subject or a separating pronoun (faṣl).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 11:

﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ Al-da'b (habit, custom, way of doing things) and al-sha'n (affair, state). Its root is from "da'aba fi al-shay'" (da'ban wa du'ūban), meaning to strive at a thing and exert oneself in it, i.e., the condition of these people in disbelief and in deserving punishment is like the condition of the family of Pharaoh. The prepositional phrase (al-jār wa al-majrūr) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is detached from what precedes it and begun as a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'nāf bayānī), by estimating the question "what is the cause of this," according to what some of the verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqūn) have said. Among the people there are those who permitted that the prepositional phrase be attached to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of the verbal noun of ﴿tughnī﴾, i.e., "an enriching that is like the non-enriching,"
Page 94
or to "waqūd" (fuel), i.e., they are set alight by them just as those were set alight. The defect of both possibilities is not hidden. As for the first: Abū Ḥayyān said regarding it that it is weak, because of the separation between the governing element and the governed by the sentence which is (ulā'ika) etc., if it is estimated as conjoined. If it is estimated as resumptive, which is distant, it is permissible.

As for the second: al-Ḥalabī objected to it that "al-waqūd," according to the well-known and more apparent view, is a noun for that which is set alight by it, and when it is a noun it has no governing effect. If it is said that it is a verbal noun, as in the reading of al-Ḥasan, it would be valid, but it is not valid. Both of them together were also raised as an objection: that they are contrary to the apparent meaning, because what is mentioned in the explanation of al-da'b is only denial and seizing, without reference to the absence of enriching, especially according to the estimate that (man) is in apposition (badal), nor to kindling the fire. So let this be understood.

﴿والَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ And those before them, who are the disbelievers of the past nations. The pronoun then refers to the family of Pharaoh; it is said that it refers to "those who disbelieved," and what is meant by the relative clause is the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا﴾ is an explanation of their habit which they did, by way of resumptive explanatory sequence (isti'nāf bayānī). What is meant by the signs is either those recited in the books of Allah the Exalted, or the indications that point to the oneness of Allah the Exalted and the truthfulness of His prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿فَأخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ is an explanation of their habit which was done to them, i.e., Allah the Exalted punished them, and they did not find from the might of Allah the Exalted any refuge. It is said that the sentence ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ etc. is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿āli Fir'awn wa-alladhīna min qablihim﴾ with "qad" implied; and it is permissible, though distant, that it be in the place of the nominative, as a predicate about "alladhīna." The shift (iltifāt) to the first person first, in "āyātinā," follows the customs of majesty, and then to the third person, and then by making the Divine Name explicit, to train awe and to introduce dread. ﴿بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ means because of them, or while being entangled in them without repenting. What is meant by sins according to the first is the denial of the many signs; the causal form was used to emphasize what the fa' indicates. According to the second, it is all other sins; and in this is an indication that they had other sins. The root of sin (dhanb) is the following and the follower; then it was applied to the crime, because its punishment follows (yatlū, i.e., yatba'u) its doer. ﴿واللَّهُ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ [11] and for whoever disbelieves in His signs. The sentence is a concluding summation (tadhyīl) confirming the content of what precedes it of the seizing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 12:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome"﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Jews of Madinah said when Allah defeated the polytheists at the Battle of Badr: "By Allah, this is surely the Unlettered Prophet whom Musa (upon him be peace) gave us good news of, and we find him in our Book by his description and attributes, and that his banner will never be turned back." They wanted to affirm him and follow him. Then some of them said to others: "Do not hasten until you see another encounter of his." So when the Day of Uhud came and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were afflicted, they complained and said: "No, by Allah, he is not the one." Wretchedness overcame them, and they did not submit. There was a treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a set period, but they broke that treaty. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with sixty riders to the people of Makkah, Abu Sufyan and his companions, and they agreed with them and unified their decision, saying: "Our word shall be one." Then they returned to Madinah, and Allah revealed this verse concerning them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq and al-Bayhaqi also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, likewise: "When the Messenger of Allah returned to Madinah after what befell [the polytheists] at Badr, he gathered the Jews in the market of Banu Qaynuqa' and said: 'O assembly of Jews, embrace Islam before Allah afflicts you with what He afflicted Quraysh.' They said: 'O Muhammad, do not let yourself be deceived by the fact that you killed some men of Quraysh who were inexperienced and did not know fighting. By Allah, if you were to fight us, you would know that we are the people, and that you are not like us.'" So Allah revealed: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿for people of insight﴾.

The relative pronoun refers to the Jews. The sin (in sa-tughlabun) indicates the nearness of the occurrence, i.e., "you will be overcome soon," and it refers to this world. Allah, exalted is He, has indeed fulfilled His promise to His Messenger (ﷺ). As it is said, He killed six hundred of the Banu Qurayzah in a single day. He gathered them in the market of Banu Qaynuqa', commanded the executioner to strike their necks, ordered a trench dug and them thrown into it. He expelled the Banu al-Nadir, conquered Khaybar, and imposed the jizyah (poll tax) upon them. This is among the clearest proofs of prophethood.

﴿And you will be gathered﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you will be overcome﴾, and what is meant is in the Hereafter, ﴿to Hell﴾, which is the end and limit of their gathering, so "ila" retains its evident meaning. It is said that it means "in" (fi), and the meaning is that they will be assembled within it. The verse serves as an emphasis of what precedes it, for overcoming is achieved by their failure to benefit from wealth and children, and the gathering to Hell is the beginning of their being fuel for it. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read (sa-yughlabuna wa-yuhsharuna) with the ya', while the rest read with the ta'. The two readings are distinguished in that, according to the ta' of address, the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to inform them from himself of the content of the statement, so that if they denied it, the denial would return to him; and according to the ya' of the third person, he was commanded to convey what Allah, exalted is He, had informed him of, the ruling that they would be overcome, such that if they denied it, the denial would return to Allah, exalted is He.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿And evil is the resting place﴾ may either be part of what is said to them, or a new statement to magnify the terror of Hell and the horror of the state of its people. Mihad, like firash, is both in form and meaning (a bed/resting place). The object of the dispraise is implied, and it is Hell, or what they have prepared for themselves.

[Page 96 begins]

﴿There has already been for you﴾ is part of the statement that was commanded. It is included to confirm and establish the content of what precedes it. The address is also to the Jews. Shaykh al-Islam (a title for a senior scholar of Islamic law) chose this reading, and al-Balkhi adopted it. That is, "There has already been for you, O Jews, who are deceived by their number and their equipment, (a sign), meaning a great sign indicating the truth of what I say to you: that you will be overcome. ﴿In two groups﴾, meaning two companies or two parties of people, of which the defeated one was conceited about its numbers and proud of its might, so what befell it befell it. ﴿Met﴾ on the Day of Badr, ﴿one fighting in the way of Allah﴾. So it is at the highest levels of faith. He did not say "believing" (mu'minah), praising them in a manner fitting to the occasion and signalling the importance of their fighting. It has also been read as yuqatilu ("fighting," masculine), taking fi'ah (group) to mean qawm (people) or fariq (party). ﴿And another disbelieving﴾ in Allah the Exalted, so it is further from fighting in His way. The reason it was not described with the opposite of the first group's description is that their fighting is removed from the level of consideration, and as a notification that they did not confront the believers because awe and fear had overtaken them."

Kana (was) here is a defective (incomplete) verb, which is the view of most grammarians of i'rab (grammatical analysis). Ayah (sign) is its subject. The verb is not feminine because the noun in the nominative is not truly feminine, because it is separated from the verb, and because ayah and dalil (proof) have the same meaning. Regarding the predicate, there are two possibilities. The first is (lakum) (for you), and ﴿in two groups﴾ is an adjective (na't) of ayah. The second is that the predicate is this adjective, and (lakum) is connected to kana according to the view of those who hold that. It is also permitted that (lakum) be in the accusative position as a circumstantial (hal) phrase. It has been mentioned many times that when the adjective of an indefinite noun is placed before it, it becomes a circumstantial phrase. The word (iltaqata) (met) is in the genitive position as an adjective of fi'atayn (two groups). (Fi'ah) (group) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "one of them is a group," and (ukhra) (another) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "and another group." The sentence is a new (resumptive) clause to confirm the sign contained in the two groups. It has also been said that fi'ah and what is joined to it are a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in iltaqata, and what follows them are adjectives. Then there must be an omitted pronoun referring back to the noun being replaced, which justifies describing the substitute with a clause that lacks a pronoun. That is, "a group from among them fights," and so on. It is also permitted that each of the two conjoined nouns be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate follows, meaning "a group from among them fights," and so on, "and another group is disbelieving." It has also been said that each of them is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "from among them is a group," and so on. It has been read as (wa ukhra kafirah) (and another disbelieving) in the accusative in both cases. This is accusative of praise in the first and of blame in the second. It has also been said that it is accusative of specification (ikhtisas), but Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the noun in such an accusative cannot be indefinite. It was answered that the one who said this did not mean the specification that is classified in grammar, as in the hadith "We, the company of prophets, leave no inheritance." He meant the accusative with an implied suitable verb. The rhetoricians call this type of construction specification, as al-Halabi stated.

It is also permitted that the two terms be circumstantial phrases, as if it had been said: "They met as a believing group and a disbelieving group." On this reading, fi'ah and ukhra are a preparatory introduction to the circumstantial phrase. It has been read in the genitive for both, as a substitution of a part for a whole (badal ba'd min kull) from (fi'atayn) (two groups). The pronoun referring back to the noun being replaced is implied in the manner mentioned above. This is called a detailed substitution (badal tafsili), as in the verse:

*"I was like one with two legs: one leg sound,*
*and a leg struck by the arrow of the vicissitudes."*

His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿they see them as twice their number﴾, is in the nominative position as an adjective of the last group, or it is a new clause explaining how the sign appeared. The meaning, as al-Suddi said, is that the last group, the disbelieving one, sees the first group, the believing one, as twice the number of those who see, and they were nine hundred and fifty fighters, all armed. It is reported from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were a thousand. A roof of a house covered them, and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah ibn Abd Shams bound them. Among them were some of the leaders of Quraysh and chiefs of misguidance, Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan, and others. They had seven hundred camels and one hundred horses. Muhammad ibn al-Furat narrated from Sa'id ibn Aws that he said: The polytheists captured a man from the Muslims and asked him, "How many were you?" He said, "Three hundred and some ten." They said, "We did not see you except as those who would overwhelm us," and they meant a thousand and nine hundred, and this is what is meant by ﴿they see them as twice their number﴾. Al-Farra' claimed that it may mean three times their number, because when you say, "I have a thousand and I need twice that," you mean two thousand added to it, not as a substitute for it. So they were seeing them as three times their number. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view as contrary to the apparent meaning of the words. Or it means twice the number of those who were seen, that is, about six hundred and some twenty, since the number of the Muslim fighters was seventy-seven men from the Emigrants and two hundred and thirty-six from the Helpers. The standard-bearer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and of the Emigrants was Ali al-Karrar, may Allah ennoble his face, and the standard-bearer of the Helpers was Sa'd ibn Ubadah. With them were seventy camels and two horses: one horse belonged to al-Miqdad ibn Amr and one to Marthad ibn Abi Marthad. Their weapons were six coats of mail and eight swords. Most of them were on foot. Fourteen of them were martyred that day: six from the Emigrants and eight from the Helpers. This has already been alluded to. Allah the Exalted showed them in this way, although they were not in that state, so that the polytheists would fear them and shrink from fighting them. This is a kind of support and spiritual reinforcement. This happened when the two groups drew near to each other, after Allah had made the Muslims seem few in the eyes of the polytheists at the moment of seeing each other, so that they would be bold against them and not be frightened and flee, where fleeing would be of benefit.

A group of scholars held that what is meant is that the believing group sees the disbelieving group as twice the number of themselves, even though the disbelievers were three times their number, so that the believers would stand firm and be reassured by the promised victory in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾.

Shaykh al-Islam, our master, the Mufti of the Rumi lands, said: The first view is preferable, because seeing twice their number is not specific to the believers. Indeed, seeing an equal number, or even less, has occurred. It is related that Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We looked at the polytheists and saw them as a number slightly more than ours. Then we looked at them again, and when we saw them exceeding us by only one man, Allah the Exalted made them seem few in our eyes, until we saw them as a small number, fewer than ourselves." Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They were made to seem few in our eyes on the Day of Badr, until I said to a man beside me: 'Do you see them as seventy?' He said: 'I see them as a hundred.' Then we captured a man from among them and asked, 'How many were you?' He said: 'A thousand.'" So if the intended meaning were the believers seeing the polytheists as fewer than their actual number, as in al-Anfal, their seeing them as fewer than themselves would be more deserving of mention as a sign than their seeing them as twice their number. Moreover, displaying the traces of Allah's power and wisdom to the disbelievers, by showing them the few as many and the weak as strong, and casting terror into their hearts because of this, is more fitting as a sign for them and as a proof against them. It is also closer to the acknowledgement of the addressees, because of their close association with the disbelievers who witnessed the situation. Likewise, the connection of the verb to the subject is stronger than its connection to the object. Thus the nearer of the two previously mentioned items was made the subject and the more distant one the object. Whether the clause is made an adjective or a new clause, this is preferable to the reverse. End of quotation.

[Page 97 begins]

It may be said, on behalf of the majority who hold that what is meant is the believers seeing the polytheists as twice their number, that this is the interpretation transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. We do not accept that their seeing them as fewer than themselves is more deserving of mention as a sign than their seeing them as twice their number. This is because the sign and the indication for the Jews would be that they will be defeated by these polytheists in fighting the believers, and that the believers will defeat them, even though there was a natural cause for cowardice, namely the believers seeing the polytheists as more than themselves and greater in number than they actually were. So it is as if it had been said: "O company of Jews, be certain that the Muslims will fight you and overcome you. Do not be deceived by their knowledge of their own small number and your large number. They will advance to fight those whom they see as more numerous than themselves. They will not be cowardly, nor fearful, and they will be victorious. This is only because Allah the Exalted has filled their hearts with faith and firmness against those who oppose them, and has surrounded them with His support and victory, and has promised them the good promise."

It may not be said: "The more suitable thing for this purpose is that the believers see the polytheists as they are, with the polytheists being three times their number, or that they see them as more than that, because their advancing to fight them at that point is a stronger indication of the cause of the victory over the Jews." We reply: Yes, the matter is as stated. However, this vision, because it fulfils the purpose and includes the praise of the believers for their steadfastness, which arises from the strength of faith in the promised victory mentioned at the end in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾, was chosen over a vision that contains only one matter and does not include that specific praise. On this basis, it is not necessary to commit to the view that the dual form is a metaphor for multiplicity, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then return the vision twice﴾ (67:4). Nor is it necessary to hold that the pronoun in ﴿twice their number﴾ refers back to the last group, meaning that the believing group sees the disbelieving group as twice the number of the disbelieving group, namely about two thousand, even though some have taken that view.

This also is refuted in his statement: "Because the clarification of the signs of Allah's power and wisdom..." After granting that the seeing itself was the sign, it is objected that the seeing of the few as many did not happen to the Jewish addressees in the opening of the verse, so that the clarification of the signs of His power through it would be more fitting as a sign and proof for them. Also, the claim that this is closer to their acknowledgement, because of their close association with the disbelieving witnesses, depends on the witnesses having informed them of it and on them having believed it and not having taken it as an illusion caused by fear, since they lacked knowledge of war. The frightened person imagines that the trees of the desert are brave warriors and that lions are attacking. Proving each of these matters is difficult. Moreover, among what Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ after that event: "Do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were ignorant and had no knowledge of war, so you gained an opportunity against them. If you fight us, you will know that we are the real men." This indicates in general that if they had informed them of it and they had believed it, they would have taken it in the way we have mentioned. As for what was said about the connection of the verb to the subject being stronger, etc., this is granted. However, we do not accept that it requires that making the first of the two previously mentioned items the subject and the more distant one the object is always preferable to the reverse. Rather, that applies only when the reverse does not contain a subtle meaning that it is good to observe in view of the context. Here that is the case, especially since the praise of the first group for fighting in the way of Allah the Exalted has already been mentioned, and the praise of them by faith, which is the foundation, was set aside. There is no doubt that their fighting the polytheists while seeing them as more than themselves, and as twice their number, is more praiseworthy and far more praiseworthy, as is not hidden.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read (*tarawnahum*) with the *ta'* (ت), addressing the audience directly. This reading raises a difficulty if the address is taken to be to the Jews: they did not see the believers as twice themselves, nor as twice the disbelievers, and they did not see the disbelievers as twice themselves, nor as twice the believers. It is answered that it is valid to say that they saw the believers as twice themselves or as twice the disbelievers in a figurative sense (*majaz*), since the seeing of the polytheists was treated as their seeing because of the unity between them in disbelief and their agreement in word, especially after the covenant and pact had been made between them through Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. So the seeing is attributed to them for emphasis in explanation and to confirm that such a condition had befallen them. Likewise it is valid to say that they actually saw the disbelievers as twice the believers. The seeing may be understood as knowledge and conviction arising from fame and widespread report. It is also necessary that the verse mean that for them there was fighting between the believers and the disbelievers, and the victory of the first over the second, although the latter were more numerous than them; but only the least of the necessary implications was stated. From this it is known that the fighting of the believers and their victory over the disbelieving group, which in reality was three times their number, is also known to them as a sign, *a fortiori* (*min bab awla*).

Because of what is in these two answers, whichever way they go, some scholars held that the address from the outset was to the polytheists, so that the matter of this reading would be clear. This requires that His words ﴿There has already been for you﴾ be an address to them after that, and not be included under the command, on the basis that the threat was with the battle of Badr, and there is no sense in citing it before it occurred. Making that part of the object of the command is also acceptable, except that He expressed the future with a past-tense form because its occurrence is certain, which is not free of some difficulty.

Some scholars made the address in Nafi's reading to the believers, and held that the preceding address to them is also the case, as the beginning of an address in the context of bestowing favour upon them with what the promise had been given for. It was said that it is addressed to all the disbelievers. One of the leading scholars of verification (*tahqiq*) said: the view that the address is general to the believers, the Jews and the polytheists of Makkah is what the context requires, so that the speech is not cut off, and so that the concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) with His words ﴿And God supports﴾ etc. falls in the place of musk at the end. Then, whoever counts the expression about a group by one of the three modes, followed by an expression about a part of it by another mode that differs from it, as a shift (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical person or address), has said it exists in the verse according to some of its possibilities; and whoever does not count that as such, as is apparent, denies that there is an *iltifat* in it. By this the differing views of those who examine the verse on this point, and their disagreement over whether an *iltifat* exists in it or not, can be reconciled. So consider carefully, for this whole discussion is reserved for such a topic.

Ibn Musarrif read (*yurawnahum*) in the passive voice with the *ya'* and *ta'*, meaning God shows them that by His power.

﴿with their own eyes﴾ (*ra'y al-'ayn*) is an emphatic infinitive (*masdar mu'akkid*) for (*yarawnahum*) if the verb is taken as a verb of sight. Then (*mithlayhim*) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). It may also be a figurative infinitive of comparison (*masdar tashbihi*) if the verb is taken as a verb of knowledge and belief, meaning an opinion like the opinion of the eye. Then (*mithlayhim*) is the second object. It was said that (*ra'y*) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "in the view of the eye." ﴿And God﴾, who is characterized by the attributes of beauty and majesty, ﴿supports﴾, that is, strengthens, ﴿with His help﴾, that is, with His aid. It was said: with His proof, but this is not strong. ﴿whomever He wills﴾ to support, without the intermediary of ordinary causes, as He supported the fighting group in His way. This is part of the statement that was commanded.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in the mentioned help, and it was said: in that seeing, ﴿is surely a lesson﴾, that is, an admonition and an indication. It is a form (*fi'lah*) from *al-'ubur* (crossing over), like *rikbah* and *jilsah*, which means passing across; from it comes "I crossed the river" (*'abartu al-nahr*). Admonition is called *'ibrah* because the one who takes admonition crosses over from ignorance to knowledge and from destruction to salvation. The nunation is for magnification, meaning a great lesson ﴿for those of insight﴾ [13]. *Absar* is the plural of *basar* in the sense of *basirah* (insight) figuratively, or in its well-known meaning: that is, for those possessing minds and perceptions, or for those who saw them with the eyes of their heads. This sentence is either part of the speech falling under the statement, confirming what precedes it by way of concluding summary (*tadhyil*), or it comes from Him, the Exalted, confirming the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

[Page 99]

﴿Adorned for people is﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that picks up the thread) brought to make people averse to the carnal pleasures, which are often the cause of fighting. It follows the description of the state of the disbelievers and the explicit statement that their wealth and children will not benefit them, though they used to take pride in these. By "people" is meant the category of humankind. ﴿The love of desires﴾: "desires" here means the desired things. Making them the very desires themselves points to the love of them and the eagerness for them that are fixed in human nature, to the extent that it is as if people desire to desire them. This is like what was said to a sick man: "What do you desire?" He said: "I desire to desire." Or it is a warning about their baseness, because desires are base in the view of the wise and the intelligent. In this there is an aversion from them and an encouragement toward what is with Allah, exalted is He. The one who adorns is Allah, exalted is He, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. It is related from al-Hasan that the adorner is Satan, and that Allah adorned them for people, because we do not know anyone who condemns them more than their Creator. In *al-Intisaf* it is said: "The adorning of desires is used in two senses. It may mean creating the love of them in hearts, and in this sense it is truly attributed to Allah, since there is no creator but Him. It may also mean urging people to indulge in forbidden desires, and in this second sense the adorning is attributed to Satan, treating his whispering and his making them appealing as if it were a command to them and an urging to indulge in them. The saying of al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, is to be understood in the second sense and not the first, for he would be too reverent to attribute the creation of Allah to anyone else." The attribution in each case is literal, as we have indicated earlier. As for the one who said: "It appears that this is of the type of 'bring me to your city, I have a right over you,' since there is no bringing here but only mere coming, so He established a bringer for the sake of emphasis," and that the meaning is that the desires were adorned in their eyes because of their deficiency, and there is no adornment for them in reality without there being an adorner, but He established an adorner for the sake of emphasis in the adornment, and treated the cause of the adornment as the doer, then he has gone to extremes and affected pretension. And the one who said: "The adorner in reality is Satan, because adorning is an attribute that subsists in him," and the one who said it is Allah, exalted is He, "because He is the Creator of actions and motives," is mistaken in the claim and incorrect in the proof. So the mistaken one is the nephew of his maternal aunt's son (a proverbial description of someone who is wrong). Mujahid read ﴿zayyana﴾ in the active voice with ﴿ḥubba﴾ in the accusative.

﴿From women and children﴾ is in the place of an accusative of circumstance (*ḥāl*) with respect to ﴿the desires﴾, and it explains them in meaning. It was also said that ﴿min﴾ is for specifying the kind. Women are mentioned first because of their prominence in the meaning of desire, and they are the snares of Satan. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have left after me no trial more harmful to men than women." It is also said that there are two trials in them: severing family ties and gathering wealth from lawful and unlawful sources. Children are mentioned after them because they are fruits of women in trials. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A child is a cause of miserliness and cowardice." It is also said that there is one trial in them, which is gathering wealth. Daughters are not specifically mentioned because love for them is not consistent. It was also said that the word "children" includes them by way of predominance (*taghlīb*, where the masculine form covers both sexes).

﴿And the heaped-up hoards of gold and silver﴾: ﴿qanāṭīr﴾ is the plural of ﴿qinṭār﴾, which is a large amount of wealth, as Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak. Ahmad related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A qinṭar is twelve thousand ounces." al-Hakim related from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, and he said: "A qinṭar is a thousand ounces." In the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim from him: a qinṭar is a thousand dinars. Ibn Jarir related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A qinṭar is a thousand ounces and two hundred dinars." And from Muʿadh: a thousand and two hundred ounces. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: twelve thousand dirhams and a thousand dinars; in another narration from him: a thousand two hundred dinars, and of silver a thousand two hundred mithqals. From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri: the filling of an ox's hide with gold. From Mujahid: seventy thousand dinars. From Ibn al-Musayyib: eighty thousand. From Abu Salih: a hundred ratls. From Qatadah who said: We used to narrate that a qinṭar is a hundred ratls of gold or eighty thousand of silver. From Abu Jaʿfar: fifteen thousand mithqals, and the mithqal is twenty-four qirats. It was said: the qinṭar among the Arabs is a weight without limit. It was said: it is whatever is between heaven and earth of wealth and other things. Perhaps the best view, as has been said, is what was related from al-Dahhak. The specification of a definite quantity in these statements is to be understood as an example and not as a restriction, and abundance varies according to considerations and relations.

It has been disputed about its pattern: it was said it is ﴿fiʿlāl﴾, and it was said it is ﴿fiʿnāl﴾. So the nun is original according to the first, and extra according to the second. The word ﴿muqanṭarah﴾ (heaped-up) is derived from it. It is a common habit of the Arabs to describe a thing by what is derived from it for emphasis, like "a shade that is shady" (*ẓillun ẓalīl*). This is frequent in the pattern of the active participle (*fāʿil*), and it also occurs in the passive participle (*mafʿūl*), like ﴿ḥijran maḥjūran﴾ (a barrier that is barred) and ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾ (forgotten and forgotten). It was said: ﴿muqanṭarah﴾ means doubled. Some restricted it to nine qanatir. It was said: ﴿muqanṭarah﴾ means firmly tied and secured, from "I qanṭartu the thing" when you tie it and make it firm. It was said: it means minted dinars or dirhams. It was said: it means arranged, some piled upon others. It was said: it means buried and hoarded.

﴿Of gold and silver﴾ is an explanation of ﴿qanāṭīr﴾, and it is in the place of a circumstantial accusative with respect to them. ﴿Dhahab﴾ (gold) is feminine; one says "she is the red gold," and for this reason its diminutive is ﴿dhuhayba﴾. Al-Farra said: it may be treated as masculine. Its plurals are ﴿adhhāb﴾, ﴿dhuhūb﴾, and ﴿dhuhbān﴾. It was said: it is a collective in meaning to ﴿dhahaba﴾ (a piece of gold), and its derivation is from ﴿dhahāb﴾ (going away). Silver (﴿fiḍḍa﴾) is pluralized as ﴿fiḍaḍ﴾, and its derivation is from "the thing dispersed" (*infaḍḍa*) when it scatters.

﴿And horses﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to ﴿women﴾ or to ﴿qanāṭīr﴾, not to ﴿gold and silver﴾, because they are not called qinṭar. Its singular is ﴿khāʾil﴾, which is derived from ﴿khuyalāʾ﴾ (pride), like ﴿ṭāʾir﴾ and ﴿ṭayr﴾ (bird and birds). Some people said: it has no singular from its own form, but is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*) whose singular is ﴿faras﴾ (horse), and its form is that of a verbal noun. It is permitted that it is a lightened form of ﴿khayl﴾. ﴿Al-musawwamah﴾ means grazing, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in one of his narrations. So it is from ﴿sawwama māshiyatahu﴾ when he sent his livestock to pasture. Or it means the handsome and beautiful, said by Mujahid; then it is from ﴿al-sīmā﴾ in the sense of beauty. Or it means marked with a white blaze and white markings on the legs, said by ʿIkrimah; then it is from ﴿al-simah﴾ or ﴿al-sūmah﴾ in the sense of a mark.

﴿And livestock﴾, that is, camels, cattle, and sheep, and they are so named because of the softness and gentleness of their walking. The term ﴿naʿam﴾ is specifically for camels. ﴿And tilth﴾ is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, that is, what is planted, whether grains, herbs, or fruit.

﴿That﴾, that is, what has been adorned for them of what was mentioned. For this reason the demonstrative is masculine and singular. It is also possible that ﴿that﴾ is for making the predicate masculine and singular, and the predicate is ﴿the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, that is, what is enjoyed for a few days, then it passes away from its owner. ﴿And with Allah is the best return﴾ [14], that is, the good place of return. ﴿Maʾāb﴾ is a noun of place from ﴿āba yaʾūbu﴾, meaning returned; its original form was ﴿maʾwab﴾, then the vowel of the waw was moved to the preceding unvowelled hamza, then it was changed to an alif. It is a noun of the verbal noun form (*ism al-maṣdar*), and it may be used as a noun of place or time, and the verbal noun is ﴿awb﴾ and ﴿iyāb﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi that he said: "the best return" is the best place to return to, and it is Paradise. In repeating the attribution to the Glorious Name there is an increase in emphasis and magnification, and greater concern in encouraging what is with Allah, exalted is He, of everlasting bliss, and in making one disinclined toward the pleasures of this world that quickly vanish. Among the strange deductions drawn from the verse, as Abu Hayyan said, is the obligation of zakat on grazing horses, because they are mentioned together with what zakat or alms are due on. The second deduction: women and children are mentioned, and what is in this is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 3, verse 15:**

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ This is an affirmation and confirmation of what was understood from what precedes it, namely that the reward of God, exalted is He, is better than the pleasures of this world. By "informing" (al-inba') is meant "telling" (al-ikhbar). ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier concerning women and what accompanies them.

Regarding the reciters (al-qurra') when two hamzas come together, the first vowelled with a fatha and the second with a damma, as here and as in Surah Sad (38:8) ﴿Was the Reminder sent down (أأُنزِلَ) to him?﴾ and Surah al-Qamar (54:25) ﴿Was the Reminder cast down (أأُلقِيَ) upon him?﴾, there are five modes:

First: the mode of Qalun, which is softening (tas-hil) the second hamza to a sound between hamza and vowel (bayn bayn) and inserting an alif between the two hamzas.

Second: the mode of Warsh and Ibn Kathir, which is also softening the second hamza bayn bayn, but without inserting an alif between them.

Third: the mode of the Kufans and of Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, which is full articulation (tahqiq) of the second hamza without inserting an alif.

Fourth: the mode of Hisham, for it is related from him that there are three ways. The first is full articulation without inserting an alif between the two hamzas. The second is full articulation with an alif inserted between them in the three surahs. The third is differentiation between the surahs, so that he fully articulates and shortens here, and lengthens (mad) in the last two.

Fifth: the mode of Abu 'Amr, which is softening the second hamza, with and without inserting the alif.

As for the first adverbial phrase (al-zarf al-awwal), it is linked to the verb before it. The second is linked to the comparative adjective (af'al al-tafdil). It is not permissible for it to be a qualifier (sifah), as Abu al-Baqa' said, because that would entail that Paradise and what is in it are a part of what they desired, while they had renounced some of the wealth and the like.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿For those who are mindful of God, with their Lord are gardens﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that clarifies that undefined good, on the basis that ﴿for those who﴾ is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿gardens﴾ is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿With their Lord﴾ may have two possibilities: that it is an adverbial complement of location (zarf li-l-istiqrar), or that it is a qualifier of the gardens which in origin was placed later, then was moved forward and so became a circumstantial accusative (hal) for them. In mentioning this there is an indication of the high rank of the gardens and the elevation of their status. In referring to the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with the attachment to the pronoun of the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) there is an announcement of greater kindness toward them. By them are meant those who devote themselves wholly to Him, exalted is He, and turn away from anyone other than Him, as the attributes that follow indicate. The attainment of the gardens and what comes after is linked to this title in order to encourage its pursuit and steadfastness in it.

It is also permitted that the particle (al-lam) be linked to "good" (khayr), or to a deleted qualifier of it. In that case "gardens" (jannat) is a predicate of a deleted subject, meaning "they are gardens," and the sentence clarifies "good." "With their Lord" in that case may be linked to the verb, meaning that their God-fearing has been established with Him, as a testimony to their sincerity. It may also be made a fronted predicate, so that the subject need not be deleted. It has been objected that one says "with God is the reward," but one does not say "with God is the Garden." The words of al-Sa'd and others make this clear, and there is something in the soul about it.

"Gardens" (jannatin) has also been read with a kasra on the ta'. In this there are two possibilities: first, that it is genitive by substitution (badal) from the word "good" (khayr). Second, that it is accusative by the implied "I mean, for example" (a'ni mathalan), or by substitution from the position of "bi-khayr."

﴿Flowing﴾ (tajri) is in a position that may be nominative, accusative, or genitive, as a qualifier of "gardens" according to both readings. ﴿Beneath them rivers﴾: what is involved in this has already been discussed. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a delayed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun concealed in "for those who" (li-alladhina), and the governing element is the sense of settledness contained in it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the ha' in "beneath them" or from the pronoun in "were mindful" (ittaqaw), but what is in it is not hidden.

﴿And purified spouses﴾, that is, free from what is repulsive in women, in form and in character. The conjunction is with "gardens" according to the nominative reading. As for the accusative reading, it is necessary to supply "for them" in the sentence. ﴿And approval﴾, that is, a great approval, according to what the tanwin (nunation) implies. 'Asim recited it with a damma on the ra', and both are two dialects and two canonical readings throughout the Qur'an, except in God's words ﴿those who follow His approval in the paths of peace﴾ (5:16), where it is with a kasra by agreement. It has been said that the kasra form is a noun and the damma form is a verbal noun (masdar), but this is an opinion without proof. ﴿From God﴾ is a qualifier of "approval," emphasizing what the tanwin conveys of majesty.

﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾ [3:15]. That is, He is Knowing of them and of their conditions and actions, so He rewards the good-doer by grace and punishes the wrongdoer by justice. Or it means He is Knowing of the conditions of those who were mindful, and for that reason He has prepared for them what He has prepared. On the first reading "servants" is general; on the second it is specific.

In this verse, He, glorified is He, began first by mentioning the abode, which is the gardens. Then He doubled back to mention what brings complete intimacy, which is the purified spouses. Then He made a third mention of what is the greatest elixir and the spirit of the heart of the one who is passionately enamoured, which is the good pleasure of God, mighty and majestic is He.

In a hadith: "He, glorified is He, asks the people of Paradise, 'Are you pleased?' They say, 'Why would we not be pleased, O Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' Then He, majestic is His state, says, 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say, 'O Lord, and what is better than that?' He says, 'I shall cause My good pleasure to descend upon you, so I shall never be displeased with you ever again.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 16:

﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed"﴾ may be in a nominative position (*raf'*), as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject, as if it had been said, "Who are they?" and the answer was, "They are those who..." etc. It may also be in an accusative position (*nasb*) by way of praise (*madh*). It may also be in a genitive position (*jarr*) as a follower (*tabi'*) of ﴿those who are God-fearing﴾, either as a qualifier (*na't*) or as an apposition (*badal*). Or it may be a qualifier of "the servants" in the same way. The view that it is a qualifier of "the servants" has been objected to on the grounds that it would restrict the seeing (*ibsar*) to some of the servants. The reply is that this restriction does not imply exclusivity, since the matter is evident, but rather expresses concern for their affair and the elevation of their station. It has also been objected that it is a follower of "the God-fearing," on the grounds that this is very remote, especially if the *lam* (of *lilladhina*) is taken as connected with *khayr* (good), because of the many intervening elements between the follower and the one followed. The reply is that there is no harm in this intervening element, just as there is no harm in the separation between the one praised and the praise, since the detached descriptive qualifier (*al-sifah al-madihah al-maqta'ah*) is a follower in meaning. For this reason the omission of the governing verb (*nasib*) or the subject (*mubtada'*) is obligatory, so that the speech does not depart from the form of following. The difference between this and other followers, regarding the ugliness or absence of ugliness of the intervening element, is obscure and requires a noble proof. It has also been objected that analogizing following in both form and meaning to following in meaning alone is not appropriate for an ignorant person, let alone a learned, excellent scholar. As for the obligatory omission of the governing verb or the subject in the case of detachment for praise or for blame, it may be said that this is to avert the supposition of informative statement, whereas the intended meaning is performative (*insha'*), not in order to prevent the speech from departing from the form of following. The emphasis of the clause (*ta'kid al-jumlah*) serves to show that their faith arises from abundant desire and perfect eagerness. In the ordering of the request for forgiveness in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ [16] after mere faith, there is evidence that faith alone is sufficient to merit forgiveness and protection from the Fire, without dependence on acts of obedience. By "sins" is meant both major (*kaba'ir*) and minor (*saghair*) sins.

[p. 102]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 17:

﴿the patient﴾ may be in the genitive or the accusative, as an attribute (ṣifah) of ﴿those﴾ if you take it to be in a position of genitive or accusative. If you take it to be in a position of nominative, then it is in the accusative of praise (al-madḥ). The meaning of ﴿patience﴾ is patience in obedience to God, the Exalted, and patience in refraining from His prohibitions. This was said by Qatadah. The omission of the object (muta'allaq) suggests generality, so it includes patience in hardship, in adversity, and at the time of battle. ﴿the truthful﴾ in their intentions and their words, in private and in public. This is also related from Qatadah. ﴿the obedient﴾, that is, those who obey. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. Or ﴿those who persist in obedience and worship﴾. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Or ﴿those who stand in the performance of obligations﴾. This was said by al-Qadi. ﴿the spenders﴾ from their wealth for the right of God, the Exalted. This was also said by Ibn Jubayr. ﴿those who seek forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours﴾ [17]. Mujahid, al-Kalbi and others said: that is, those who pray at the pre-dawn hours.
