Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: They are those who attend the dawn prayer. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Umar that he used to spend the night in prayer, and then he would say: "O Nafi', has the dawn (saḥar) come for us?" He would say: "No." So he would resume prayer. When he said: "Yes," he would sit, seeking forgiveness from God, the Exalted, and supplicating until morning. Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded us to seek forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours seventy times." Al-Ridha related from his father, from Abu 'Abd Allah: "Whoever seeks forgiveness from God, the Exalted, at the time of saḥar seventy times, is among the people of this verse." The ba' in ﴿bi-al-asḥār﴾ (بِالأسحار) means fi (فِي, "in"). It is the plural of saḥar (سَحَر), with an unpointed ḥ, pronounced with a fatḥah or sukūn. The last hours of the night were so called because of the obscurity in them, like the saḥar (concealment) of a hidden thing. Some said: saḥar is from the last third of the night until the rising of dawn.

The specification of the pre-dawn hours for seeking forgiveness is because supplication at that time is closer to being answered, since worship at that time is more difficult, the soul is purer, and the spirit is more gathered. In the Ṣaḥīḥ: "He, the Exalted, and Holy, who is free from the marks of createdness, descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night and says: 'Whoever calls upon Me, I will answer him. Whoever asks Me, I will give him. Whoever seeks My forgiveness, I will forgive him.' He continues thus until dawn rises." Ibn Jarir and Ahmad related from Sa'id al-Jarīrī, who said: "It reached us that Dawud, upon whom be peace, asked Jibril, upon him be peace: 'O Jibril, which part of the night is best?' He said: 'O Dawud, I do not know, except that the Throne shakes at the pre-dawn hours.'"

The insertion of the conjunction waw (وَ) between these mentioned attributes is either because those described by them are many, or to indicate the independence of each one of them and their perfection in them. As for Abu Hayyan's statement, "We do not know that coordination with waw in an attribute indicates perfection," al-Halabi refuted it, saying that the scholars of rhetoric (al-bayan) knew it, and they are the authorities.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses: ﴿There has indeed been for you﴾, O assembly of wayfarers toward the goal of all, ﴿a sign﴾ indicating your perfection and your arrival at the summit of monotheism. ﴿In two hosts that met﴾ for battle, ﴿one of them﴾ is the host of the spiritual powers, which are the armies of God, the Exalted, ﴿fighting in the way of God﴾ and the path of arrival to Him. ﴿And another﴾ of them is the armies of the soul and the helpers of Satan, ﴿disbelieving﴾, concealing the truth and veiled from the enclosures of truthfulness. The latter host sees the former host, due to the squint of its insight, ﴿twice their number﴾ at the moment of encounter in the battlefield of the body, with a plain and manifest vision with no concealment in it, like the vision of the eye. This is for the support of the believing host with the divine lights and the sublime illuminations, and the abandonment of the disbelieving host by what has overcome it of the accumulation of the darknesses of nature and the humiliation of distance from the Presence. ﴿And God﴾, the Exalted, ﴿supports with His help whom He wills﴾, supporting him for accepting his readiness for that. ﴿Indeed in that﴾ support ﴿is a lesson﴾, that is, a consideration or a matter by which one takes lesson to arrive at the desired goal, for those who see clearly, who open the eyes of their insight to witness the eternal lights in the horizons of divine manifestations.

﴿Made attractive to people is the love of desires﴾ because of what is in them of the lower world, the natural veil, and the bodily coverings: ﴿of women﴾, which are the souls; ﴿and sons﴾, which are the imaginings born of them and arising from them; ﴿and heaped-up sums of gold and silver﴾, which are the widely circulated sciences and those not widely circulated, or the roots and the branches; ﴿and branded horses﴾, which are the vehicles of desire and the steeds of amusement; ﴿and cattle﴾, which are the mounts for gathering worldly goods and the means of bringing worldly benefits; ﴿and tilth﴾, which is the seed of greed and long hope. ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, which passes away after a little, by returning to the original origin and the ancient homeland.

You may also leave these mentioned things on their apparent meanings, for souls immersed in the states of nature have a total inclination toward that as well. ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ that is mentioned, ﴿for those who are mindful﴾ of looking at others. ﴿Gardens﴾: a garden of certainty, a garden of unveiling, a garden of witnessing, a garden of contentment, and a garden that I do not name, which is the one in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. There is nothing in that garden, according to the knowers, except God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, the rivers of theophanies (tajalliyyat, divine self-disclosures), filled with the water of the unseen. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ through their subsistence after their annihilation. ﴿And spouses purified﴾, which are the holy spirits, sanctified from the filths of nature, confined in the tents of the divine attributes. ﴿And God's good pleasure﴾, whose measure cannot be estimated. ﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾ in the fluctuation of their spirits in the world of dominion, burning from the assaults of the lights of majesty, out of love for His proximity and longing for His meeting. He recompenses them according to the measure of their concerns in seeking His eternal Face and His everlasting beauty. ﴿Those who say: Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾ by the lights of Your actions and attributes, ﴿so forgive us﴾ the sins of our existences by Your essence, ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, the fire of deprivation and the existence of remnants.

﴿the patient﴾ under the pain of striving and discipline; ﴿the truthful﴾ in love and in will; ﴿the obedient﴾ in the journey toward Him; ﴿the spenders﴾ of whatever other than Him they have in Him; ﴿those who seek forgiveness﴾ for the sins of their variations and their particularizations at the pre-dawn hours of theophanies. It is said: (﴿the patient﴾) are those who were patient in the pursuit and were not ashamed of the weariness; they abandoned every comfort and delight, and they were patient under trial and rejected complaint until they reached the Master, and nothing of this world or the next cut them off. (﴿the truthful﴾) are those who were truthful in the pursuit: they reached the watering place, then they were truthful and witnessed, then they were truthful and found, then they were truthful and were effaced. Their state is intention, then arrival, then witnessing, then existence, then extinction. (﴿the obedient﴾) are those who clung to the door and persisted in drinking the cup of sorrow and abandoning the beloved things until they realized nearness. (﴿the spenders﴾) are those who gave of their souls in terms of actions, then gave of what was within their means of wealth, then gave of their hearts for the sincerity of states, then gave of every share they had in the immediate and the deferred, consuming it in the lights of union. (﴿those who seek forgiveness﴾) are those who seek forgiveness for all of that when they return to sobriety at the time of the Lord's descent to the lowest heaven and the shining of the lights of His beauty over the horizons of the soul, and His call: "Is there any who asks? Is there any who seeks forgiveness? Is there anyone who ...? Is there anyone who ...?" Then, when He, glorified be He, praised His beloved ones, the lords of religion, and censured His enemies, the disbelievers, He followed that with an explanation of the true religion and the firmest handhold in the most complete and emphatic manner, so He, glorified be He, said:

﴿God bears witness that there is no god but Him﴾. Al-Kalbi said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became manifest in Medina, two rabbis (aḥbār, plural of ḥabr, meaning scholars of the Jews) from among the rabbis of the people of al-Sham came to him. When they saw Medina, one of them said to his companion: 'How much this city resembles the description of the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) who will emerge at the end of time.' When they entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), they recognised him by the attribute and description, and they said to him: 'Are you Muhammad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Are you Ahmad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'We will ask you about a testimony. If you inform us of it, we will believe in you and affirm you.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Ask me.' They said to him: 'Inform us about the greatest testimony in the Book of God, the Exalted.' So God, the Exalted, revealed the verse, and they both embraced Islam."

It is also said that it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they disputed about the matter of Jesus (peace be upon him). This is what is indicated by the reports we mentioned earlier, and the words of Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr incline toward it. It is also said that it was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians when they abandoned the name of Islam and called themselves Jewish and Christian. It is also said that they said: "Our religion is superior to yours," and so it was revealed.

The majority reads (شَهِدَ) with the past tense and the opening hamza of (أنَّهُ) pronounced with a fatḥa, meaning "that He" or "because He." It was also read (إنَّهُ) with a kasra on the hamza, either by treating (شَهِدَ) as (قالَ) (that is, as introducing direct speech), or by making the clause a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) and placing the verb upon ﴿Indeed, the religion...﴾ etc., according to the reading of the one who opens the hamza, as you will see. The pronoun refers to Him, the Exalted, and it is possible that it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn).

It was also read (شُهَداءَ لِلَّهِ) with the accusative and the nominative, as the plural of (شَهِيدٌ), like (ظُرَفاءُ) as the plural of (ظَرِيفٌ), or as the plural of (شاهِدٌ), like (شُعَراءُ) as the plural of (شاعِرٌ). The accusative may be a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the two mentioned, or an accusative of praise (manṣūb ʿalā al-madḥ). The nominative is the predicate of an omitted subject, and its implication is praise, meaning: "They are witnesses." In both cases the sacred Name is in the genitive by the preposition (لام), attached to what precedes it. It was also read (شُهَداءُ اللَّهِ) with nominative and as a construct phrase.

With (شَهِدَ) attributed to God, the Exalted, there is a explicit subsequent metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya tabaʿiyya), because what is meant is that He, glory be to Him, indicated His oneness, and indeed all His perfections, through His particular acts which no other can achieve, and through the signs of creation He established in the horizons and in the souls, and through what He revealed of His verses that express this, such as Surat al-Ikhlāṣ and Āyat al-Kursī and others. So He likened that clear indication to the testimony of a witness in making things evident and disclosed. Then the term of the thing likened to was borrowed for the thing being likened, and then the metaphor spread from the verbal noun to the verb. It is also permitted that there be a subsequent loose metonymy (majāz mursal tabaʿī), since clarification is a necessary consequence of testimony, and the word signifying the necessary consequence has been mentioned while the consequence itself is intended. This interpretation is necessary according to the reading of the majority, but not according to the anomalous reading.

﴿and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ is conjoined to the sacred Name. In that case it is necessary to take the testimony in a figurative sense that includes what is ascribed to these two groups through a general metaphor. That is: the angels acknowledged this, and the learned believed in it and argued for it. Some have supposed, for each of the two conjoined items, the verb (شَهِدَ) intended in the sense that is valid to ascribe to what it is attributed to. Perhaps the view of a general metaphor is preferable to this. It is said that by "those of knowledge" the prophets (peace be upon them) are meant. It is said: the Emigrants and the Helpers. It is said: the scholars among the believing People of the Book. It is said: all the scholarly believers who knew His oneness, exalted be He, through decisive proofs and dazzling arguments. He mentioned the angels first because among them are those who are intermediaries for conveying knowledge to their recipients. It is also said: because all their knowledge is necessary (ḍarūrī), unlike humans, whose knowledge is both necessary and acquired (iktisābī).

Then, the nominative of these two nominatives, according to the anomalous reading, is the inceptive (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate is omitted, indicated by the sense of the speech. That is: "And the angels and those of knowledge are witnesses to this." It is also said: by conjunction upon the pronoun in (شُهَداءُ), and this is valid because of the intervening separation. It has been objected that this, according to the accusative reading as a circumstantial state, leads to restricting the state of those mentioned to the testimony of the angels and those of knowledge, and there is not much benefit in it, as is not hidden.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿standing in justice﴾ is an explanation of His perfection in His acts, following the explanation of His perfection in His essence. (القِسْطُ) means justice, and the (باء) is for transitivity, meaning: "establishing with justice." As for the accusative of ﴿standing﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that it is a necessary circumstantial state (ḥāl lāzima) from the subject of (شَهِدَ). It is permissible to make the conjoined item share the circumstantial state with the first item alone when a contextual or verbal indicator is present, such as in ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾. The state has been delayed after the two conjoined items to indicate the high rank and nearness of their station, and the hastening to establish the witnessing of divine oneness out of concern for its matter. Perhaps this is the secret of placing it before the two conjoined items, together with the indication of His being the origin of the witnessing to it.

The second: that it is in the accusative of praise. Though it is well known in definites, it is also established in indefinites.

The third: that it is an adjective of the name (لا), not the one built on it (the mabnī). This has been considered unlikely, because they only allow separation between the modified and the adjective by a separator that is not entirely foreign in every respect, and the conjoined item upon the subject of (شَهِدَ) is entirely foreign to what is in the complement of (أنَّ) both verbally and in meaning. It is also objected that it is linked to the circumstantial state, so on this view it should be put in the nominative by analogy to the position of the name of (لا), not as an actual nominative, to avoid ambiguity.

The fourth: that it is the object of knowledge, meaning: "and those of knowledge [who know] standing in justice." Its remoteness is not hidden.

The fifth, and perhaps the most correct: that it is a circumstantial state from the pronoun, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the clause, meaning: "He alone [is to be recognised as] established," or "He is entitled to it," because it is a confirming circumstantial state (ḥāl muʾakkida). The intervening of the two conjoined items here does no harm, unlike in the case of the adjective, because the confirming circumstantial state in this category functions as an explanatory clause of a certain kind. So it is fitting that the two conjoined items be placed first, because the one witnessed to is one, and so this is a kind of its confirmation, completed by the explanatory circumstantial state. On the supposition of it being a circumstantial state from the subject and the object of knowledge, it does not fall within what is witnessed to. On the supposition of the accusative of praise, it may or may not fall within it. On the last two suppositions, it necessarily falls within it.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd) read (اَلْقائِمُ بِالقِسْطِ) as the predicate of an omitted subject. That it be a substitute (badal) for (هُوَ) involves some difficulty. Abu Hanifa read (قَيِّمًا بِالقِسْطِ).

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a repetition of the thing witnessed to, for emphasis. In it there is an indication of heightened concern for knowing its proofs, because establishing the claim is only through proof, and concern for it requires concern for its proofs. So that upon it there may be built His saying, exalted be He: ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [3:18], so that it is known that He is the one described by both of them. It has been said: there is no repetition, because the first is God's testimony alone, and the second is the testimony of the angels and those of knowledge. This is clear according to those who read the angels as nominative by a hidden verb. The reason for the order is that knowledge of His power, which is conveyed by (اَلْعَزِيزُ, the Mighty), is mentioned before knowledge of His wisdom, which is signalled by (اَلْحَكِيمُ, the Wise). Some have made (اَلْعَزِيزُ) refer back to His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, and (اَلْحَكِيمُ) refer back to His saying, exalted be He, ﴿standing in justice﴾. Their nominative is as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a substitute for (هُوَ), or as an adjective of it, based on what al-Sakkaki held concerning the permissibility of describing the pronoun of the absent. To make them adjectives of the subject of (شَهِدَ) is remote.

Reports have been narrated about the excellence of the verse. Al-Daylami narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, and Āyat al-Kursī, and ﴿God bears witness﴾, and ﴿Say: O God, Owner of Sovereignty...﴾ up to ﴿without reckoning﴾ were revealed, they clung to the Throne and said: 'Will You send us down upon a people who disobey You?' He said: 'By My might, My majesty, and the loftiness of My station, no servant will recite you at the end of every obligatory prayer except that I will forgive him what was in it, and I will settle him in the garden of Firdaws, and I will look upon him every day seventy times, and I will fulfil for him seventy needs, the least of which is forgiveness.'"

Ibn ʿAdi, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi (who declared it weak), al-Khatib, and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ghalib al-Qattan, who said: "I came to Kufa and lodged near al-Aʿmash. One night I wanted to descend, and he stood and performed the night prayer. He passed by this verse, ﴿God bears witness﴾ etc., and said: 'And I too bear witness to what God, the Exalted, bore witness to, and I entrust to God, the Exalted, this testimony, and it is for me a deposit with God, the Exalted,' repeating it several times. I said: 'He must have heard something about it, so I asked him.' He said: 'Abu Wa'il ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to me, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection its reciter will be brought, and God, the Exalted, will say: My servant made a covenant with Me, and I am the most worthy of those who fulfil covenants. Admit My servant to Paradise."'"

It is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Around Medina there were three hundred and sixty idols. When this noble verse was revealed, they fell down prostrate toward the Kaʿba."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 19:**

﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam.﴾ This is a independent nominal sentence, placed as an emphasis of the first. The definiteness of both parts (the predicate and subject) indicates restriction (al-hasr), meaning: there is no religion acceptable to God Most High other than Islam. According to what Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah, Islam is "the testimony that there is no god but God Most High, and the acknowledgement of what has come from God Most High. It is the religion of God Most High, which He legislated for Himself, sent His messengers with, and which His friends (awliya') pointed to. Nothing else is accepted, and no reward is given except by it."

ʿAli ibn Ibrahim related from the Commander of the Faithful, may God honour his face, that he said in one of his sermons: "I will certainly attribute Islam to a lineage to which no one before me has attributed it. Islam is submission (al-taslim), submission is certainty (al-yaqin), certainty is affirmation (al-tasdiq), affirmation is acknowledgement (al-iqrar), acknowledgement is fulfilment (al-ada'), and fulfilment is action (al-amal)." Then he said: "Indeed, the believer took his religion from his Lord and did not take it from his own opinion. Indeed, the believer is one whose faith is recognised in his action, and indeed the disbeliever is recognised by his disbelief in denial. O people, your religion, your religion! For a misdeed within it is better than a good deed outside of it. Indeed, a misdeed within it is forgiven, and indeed a good deed outside of it is not accepted."

Ubayy recited (Indeed, the religion with God is surely Islam) (inna al-din ʿinda Allah la-l-Islam), and al-Kisa'i recited (that the religion) (anna al-din) with a fatha on the hamza, as a substitution of one thing for another (badal al-shay' min al-shay'), if Islam is interpreted as faith (al-iman) and what is meant is the acknowledgement of God's oneness and affirmation of it, which is the greatest part. Likewise, if it is interpreted as affirmation of what the Prophet ﷺ brought, of what is known of the religion by necessity, because that is essentially the testimony to what was mentioned, considering what it necessitates; so it is its very essence in outcome. But if it is interpreted as the sharia (sharia'), then the substitution is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because the sharia encompasses faith and the acknowledgement of God's oneness. Some of them interpreted it as the knowledge of the rulings (ʿilm al-ahkam), and claimed the priority of this option in view of the context of the speech, arguing that the knowledge of the fundamentals (ʿilm al-usul) was not restricted by "with God," because these are matters according to the reality itself, not revolving around consideration; for this reason, the true religions all coincide in them. The description of the religion as Islam was restricted by "with God," because the sharia revolves around the consideration of the Lawgiver, and for this reason it changes and is altered according to interests and times. What this implies is not hidden.

Or (that he bore witness) is governed by it, on the assumption of reading (innahu) with a kasra, as has been indicated. And (with) (ʿinda) in every case is an adverbial phrase (zarf) whose governing element is the stability (al-thubut) indicated by the sentence. It was said: it is connected to a specific verb (kawn khass) that the mind inclines towards, which is understood as definite and is a description of the religion, meaning: indeed, the religion that is approved with God is Islam. It was said: it is connected to something omitted that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of the religion. It was said: it is connected to it. It was said: it is connected to something omitted that functions as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is parenthetical, meaning: this ruling is established with God. I consider all of these to be nothing. As for the first, it is because it contradicts the known rule regarding adverbial phrases when they occur after indefinite nouns. As for the second, it is because it is well known that (inna) does not govern a circumstantial state. As for the third, it is because there is no basis for connecting it to the word (al-din) except by accepting that it originally carries the meaning of recompense. As for the fourth, the artificiality in it that could be dispensed with is clearer than to be hidden.

Furthermore, there has been disagreement about applying the term Islam to what other than what our Prophet ﷺ brought. Most scholars permit this application. I think that after clarifying the dispute, there should be no room for disagreement.

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after the knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves.﴾

It was said: what is meant by them is the Jews, who differed concerning what Moses, peace be upon him, had entrusted to them. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Rabi' who said: "When death approached Moses, peace be upon him, he called seventy rabbis from the rabbis of the Children of Israel, entrusted them with the Torah, appointed them as its custodians, and designated Joshua son of Nun as successor. When the first generation, the second, and the third had passed, division occurred among them. They were the people of knowledge from among the sons of the seventy, until they shed blood among themselves, and strife broke out seeking worldly authority, its dominion, its treasures, and its adornments. So God Most High empowered their tyrants over them." It was said: the Christians, who differed concerning the Oneness (al-tawhid). It was said: the relative pronoun refers to both Jews and Christians, and "the Scripture" refers to the category, and they differed concerning the Oneness. It was said: concerning his prophethood ﷺ. It was said: concerning faith in the prophets. The apparent meaning is that the relative pronoun refers to what encompasses both groups, and that what they differed about is Islam, as the context indicates. Referring to them by this title is an additional censure of them, since difference after the coming of the Scripture is more reprehensible.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except after the knowledge had come to them﴾ is another increase (in censure), since difference after the coming of knowledge is more reprehensible in ugliness. The exception is an exceptive construction without a stated positive element (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states or the most general of times. What is meant by the coming of knowledge is either the capacity to attain it because its proofs are clear, or it means the actual attainment of the knowledge of the reality of the matter for them, in fact. He did not say "they knew," although that is more concise, to indicate that it is knowledge by way of revelation. And His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿out of rivalry among themselves﴾ is an increase in condemnation. The noun in the accusative is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for what is indicated by (ma) and (illa) of the establishment of difference after the coming of knowledge, just as you say: "I did not strike except my son, as discipline." So the sentence has no indication that the motive is restricted. Some of them claimed that the motive for their differing is rivalry and envy, not doubt and the obscurity of the matter. Perhaps this is understood from the situation or from the speech, based on permitting the multiplicity of exceptive constructions without a stated positive element, meaning: they did not differ at any time for a purpose except after knowledge, for the purpose of rivalry, just as you say: "No one struck except Zayd, Amr," meaning: no one struck anyone except Zayd struck Amr.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of God﴾. It was said: what is meant by them is His proofs. It was said: the Torah. It was said: it is the Torah and the Gospel. It was said: the Qur'an. It was said: His signs that declare that the religion with God is Islam. The apparent meaning is generality, meaning: whatever sign it may be. What is meant by "whoever" is also more general than the aforementioned differing parties and others, and you may restrict it to them.

﴿Indeed, God is swift in reckoning﴾ [19]: this stands in place of the answer of the conditional, as a cause for it, meaning: whoever disbelieves, God will punish him and requite him soon, for He is swift in reckoning, meaning His reckoning comes soon, or that is accomplished quickly. It was said: the swiftness of reckoning requires the encompassing of knowledge and power, so the sentence conveys a threat, and by this consideration the conditional and the response are coherent without need for an elided element. Perhaps this is more appropriate and more precise in consideration. In the manifestation of the glorious Name there is an instilling of awe and an infusion of dread. In arranging the punishment upon disbelief in general, immediately after explaining the condition of those mentioned, there is an indication of the severity of their punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 20:

﴿And if they argue with you﴾, i.e., dispute with you concerning the religion after you have presented the proofs. The pronoun refers to those who were given the Book, the Jews and the Christians. This is the view of al-Hasan. Abu Muslim said it refers to all people. It was also said that it refers to the delegation of the Christians of Najran. This is what the statement of Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr points to. ﴿Then say: I have submitted my face to God﴾, i.e., I have sincerely devoted myself,
Page 108
and I have humbled my heart and my body to God, associating no partner with Him. This contains an indication that disputing with them is not appropriate, because argument occurs only regarding a hidden matter, whereas what they dispute is an evident matter, and the judgment of its state is known, namely the upright religion. Therefore, argument and dispute would be nothing but arrogant obstinacy. In that case, this statement is a turning away from disputing with them. It was also said that it is an argument, and its explanation is that the people acknowledged the existence of the Creator and that He deserves to be worshipped. So it is as if he said: this statement is agreed upon by all, so I hold fast to this agreed-upon measure, and the call of creation is directed to it. The disagreement lies only in matters beyond that. The Jews claim anthropomorphism and corporeality, the Christians claim the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the polytheists claim the obligation of worshipping idols. These are the ones making claims, so the burden of proof is upon them. A parallel to this is ﴿Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but God, and that we associate nothing with Him﴾. It is narrated from Abu Muslim that the verse in this place is like the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾. So it is as if it was said: if they contend with you, O Muhammad, over these details, then say: I hold to the way of Abraham, peace be upon him, and you acknowledge that he was right in his statement and truthful in his religion. This falls under the category of holding to what is binding on the opponent (ilzamat), and it enters under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾. Perhaps the statement of turning away is preferable, because of what it contains of indicating their wretched condition and the lowering of their status. He expressed the whole by "the face" because it is the most noble of the outward members, the place where the faculties and senses manifest, and the gathering of most of what worship is performed with, and through it one turns toward everything. Nafi', Ibn Amir and Hafs read the yā' (of "wajhiya") with a fatha, and the rest read it with a sukun.

﴿And whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the attached pronoun in ﴿aslamtu﴾, and it is permissible because of the separation. Or it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu). It is objected to both of these that they require that they share with him, peace be upon him, in submitting their faces, and the meaning is not: "I have submitted my face, and they have submitted their faces," since "I ate a loaf and Zayd" cannot be said to mean that each of them ate a loaf. Therefore, it is necessary that "man" (whoever) be a subject (mubtada') and its predicate be omitted, i.e., "and whoever follows me likewise," or that it be conjoined to the Name of God, and [the meaning is] his submission, peace be upon him, to whoever follows him, by protecting and advising them. It was answered that understanding the meaning and the absence of ambiguity permits both matters, and by that one dispenses with the burden of omission and the great strain of departing from the apparent meaning. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' kept the yā' in "ittaba'anī" according to the original form, while the rest omitted it. Omitting it is better for conforming with the orthography of the codex. Omission has come in such cases frequently, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

"Will my wandering through the lands prevent me from the fear of death, that it (will) come to me?"

﴿And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered﴾ is conjoined to the conditional clause. The meaning is: if the People of the Book argue with you, then address them with that; and if it proves fruitless, then generalize the call and say it to the black and the red alike. ﴿Have you submitted?﴾, following me as the believers did, for there has come to you of the signs what necessitates it and requires it? Or are you upon your disbelief in the signs of God, exalted is He, and your persistence in obstinacy? This is like what you say when you have summarized a matter for a questioner and have left no path of explanation unexplored: "Have you understood it?" It is in the pattern of ﴿So will you desist?﴾ after the detailing of the obstacles to engaging in what is forbidden. In this there is a rebuke to them for obstinacy and lack of fairness, and a reproach for dullness and the sterility of their disposition. Most scholars hold that the interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir), and that it implies a command. Placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun is to observe the correspondence between the two conjoined terms. By "the unlettered" are meant those who do not write among the polytheists of the Arabs. This was said by Ibn Abbas and others.

﴿Then if they submit﴾, i.e., they become characterized by Islam and the true religion, ﴿then they have been guided﴾, according to the inclusion of the meaning of "going out" (of error), i.e., they were guided, departing from misguidance. This is what was said. Some interpret guidance as its necessary consequence, which is benefit, meaning: then they have benefited themselves. They said: the reason for
Page 109
removing it from its apparent meaning is that submission is the very essence of guidance, and if it is interpreted in its original sense the condition and the consequence become identical, and this has an evident objection.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., they turn away from Islam and do not accept it, ﴿then upon you is only the conveyance﴾ stands in the place of the response, meaning: it will not harm you at all, for upon you is only the conveyance, and you have delivered it in the most complete and eloquent manner. This was before the command to fight, so it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword. ﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾ [20] is a concluding statement containing a promise of reward for submission and a threat for turning away from it.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ (whatever sign it may be). This includes, as a primary category, those who disbelieve in the clear signs that establish the truth of Islam. ﴿And kill the prophets without right﴾: they are the People of the Book who lived in his time (ﷺ), since warning those who came before them would have no meaning. Al-Qutb (Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi) said: The attribution of killing to them, though none of them actually killed, is for two reasons. First, this course of action was the course of their predecessors, so it is correct to attribute it to them, since the deed of a father may be attributed to a son, especially if he is pleased with it. Second, the meaning is that killing is characteristic of them if no obstacle is found. The restriction "without right" is for what has already been stated. The definite article *alif-lam* (ال) is omitted here, unlike in the preceding clause, because the two clauses differ in their point of origin (*makhraj*). What benefits you regarding this verse has already been explained, so reflect on it. Al-Hasan recited (يَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ).

﴿And kill those who enjoin justice among people﴾, i.e., enjoin justice. Perhaps the repetition of the verb is to indicate the difference between the two killings, or because the two killings differ in time. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, 'Who among people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection?' He said: 'A man who killed a prophet, or a man who enjoined what is good and forbade what is evil.' Then he recited the verse. Then he (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Ubayda, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day, in a single hour. Then a hundred and seventy men from the servants of the Children of Israel stood up, and they enjoined upon those who were killing them what is good and forbade them from what is evil, so they were all killed at the end of that same day. They are the ones whom Allah the Exalted mentioned.'" Hamza recited (ويُقاتِلُونَ الَّذِينَ). Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) recited (وقاتَلُوا). Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) recited (ويَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ والَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ).

﴿So give them the tidings of a painful punishment﴾. This is the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna* [21]. The *fa'* (فاء) entered the predicate because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional. The abrogating particle (*nasikh*, i.e., *inna* and its sisters) that does not change the meaning of the inceptive (*ibtida'*) does not prevent this entry. When it changes the meaning, as *layta* (ليت, "would that") and *la'alla* (لعل, "perhaps") do, this is prohibited by consensus (*ijma'*). Sibawayh and al-Akhfash prohibit it absolutely with the abrogating particles. Therefore, according to them, the predicate is the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void﴾.

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The clause ﴿So give them good tidings﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) introduced by the فاء (fa'), as in your saying: زيد فافهم رجل صالح (Zayd, fa-fham, is a righteous man). The grammarians (nuhat) have made this explicit in the verse:

"So know, for a person's knowledge benefits him, that whatever is decreed will surely come to pass."

Whoever does not grasp this says that the فاء is a conditional particle (jaza'iyya) whose response is fronted from a delayed position, the estimate being: "Zayd is a righteous man." And when we have said that to you, then understand. According to the first view, the clause is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), and ﴿Those﴾ (أولئك) is the subject (mubtada'), with the distal demonstrative used, according to the well-known view, to signal the great remoteness of their rank in the gravity of their condition. The relative clause is its predicate, meaning: those who possess these dreadful attributes, whose deeds have been nullified and have fallen out of the sphere of consideration, and are empty of any fruit in this world, since their blood and property were not protected by them and they did not thereby deserve praise and commendation; and in the Hereafter, since they did not avert punishment from them and did not attain reward through them. This applies both to deeds that depend on intention (niyyah) and to those that do not.

Some people hold that deeds that do not depend on intention, such as charity and kinship ties, benefit the disbeliever in the Hereafter and are not nullified by disbelief. On this view, the deeds meant here are those of the first category. If the verse is taken to include both categories, then this ruling must be restricted to a particular group of disbelievers, namely those described by the attributes mentioned above. But this requires reflection.

﴿And they have no helpers.﴾ [22] That is, no one will help them against the might and punishment of God the Exalted, in either of the two abodes. The word ﻧﺎﺻﺮﻳﻦ (nasirin, "helpers") is in the plural to correspond with what stands in opposition to it (namely, the plural in the earlier clause), not to negate that each of them has multiple helpers. It may be claimed that the plural is better here than the singular because it is the verse's closing rhyme (ra's ayah). What is meant by the negation of helpers is the negation of the benefits and advantages that result from help. If these are negated for a plurality, their negation for a single helper is all the more so.

Furthermore, although this ruling is general for all disbelievers, as the words of God the Exalted indicate, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, it has a particular relevance here, since these disbelievers are described as killing those who command justice, while they themselves are the upholders of truth. This is as the hadith indicates. No helper exists among them who would prevent them from killing those noble people, so they are repaid with a punishment for which they have no helper and no one to assist them.

Some people have claimed that the verse contains a correspondence of three things with three things: disbelief with punishment, the killing of the prophets with the nullification of deeds, and the killing of those who command justice [with justice] with the absence of helpers. But, as you see, this is far-fetched.

[p. 111 is marked in the source at this point.]

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ This is an expression of wonder directed at the Prophet ﷺ, or at everyone who is capable of seeing, regarding the condition of the People of the Book: that when proof overwhelms them, they flee to clamor and turn away from the right path. It also confirms what preceded, that the disagreement occurred only after knowledge had come. It has also been said that it is a means of negating any helper for them, since they become defeated when their Book is made the judge. By "those who were given" is meant the Jews, and by "portion" is meant share. The "min" (from/of) may be partitive (tab'id) or explanatory (bayan). If it means that "a portion" is the Book itself, or a portion of it, because reaching the essence of the speech of God, exalted is He, is impossible, then if it is explanatory the meaning is the sending down of the Book upon them, and if it is partitive the meaning is their guidance to understanding what is in it. On both readings, the "al" in "al-Kitab" (the Book) is for prior reference, and the Book meant is the Torah, which is what many of the early scholars narrated. The tanwin (indefiniteness) is for magnification.

It is also permitted that the "al" in "al-Kitab" be for prior reference with the meaning being the Preserved Tablet, and that it be for the genus; in the latter case, "the portion" is the Torah. "Min" is for beginning in the first reading, which also admits it, and for partitive in the second. The tanwin is for exaltation. You may also make it so in the earlier way as well. It is also permitted, on the assumption that "portion" means what they obtained of knowledge, that the tanwin is for belittling. It was objected that this does not fit the context of emphasizing the ugliness of their condition. It was answered that it is possible the intended purpose is to rebuke them for their rebelliousness and arrogance, through a meager portion, against following One who has knowledge that the knowledge of all the messengers cannot equal. Expressing what they were given as a "portion" indicates its complete specificity to them and that it is a right among their rights which must be observed and acted upon according to its requirements.

God the Exalted's saying: ﴿They are called to the Book of God﴾ is either a resumed sentence clarifying the place of the wonder, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun. The "Book of God" is the Torah. The explicit noun in place of a pronoun is for compelling response, and the idafa (construct) is for honor and for stressing the obligation of referral. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, and others went to this view.

Ibn Ishaq and a group narrated from him, saying: "The Messenger of God ﷺ entered the house of study (bayt al-midras) upon a group of Jews, and he called them to God, exalted is He. Al-Nu'man ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said: 'Upon what religion are you, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Upon the creed and religion of Abraham.' They said: 'Abraham was a Jew.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said to them: 'Then come to the Torah, it is between us and you.' They refused him, so God the Exalted sent down the verse." In al-Bahr: "A Jewish man committed adultery with a woman, and in our religion there was not yet stoning at that time. They brought their dispute to the Messenger of God ﷺ, seeking leniency for the two adulterers because of their nobility. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'I judge by your Book.' They denied stoning, so the Torah was brought, and their rabbi Ibn Suriya placed his hand on the verse of stoning. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: 'Pass beyond it, O Messenger of God,' so he uncovered it, and they were stoned. The Jews became angry, and so it was revealed."

This is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him. Al-Hasan and Qatadah went to the view that by "the Book of God" is meant the Qur'an, to which they were called, because what is in it agrees with what is in the Torah regarding the fundamentals of the religion and the pillars of the law, and the attribute whose good news preceded, or because they do not doubt that it is the Book of God, exalted is He, sent down upon the Seal of His messengers.

﴿That He may judge between them﴾: It was said, meaning: that He may distinguish the truth from falsehood between those who were given (who are the Jews) and the one who calls them, who is the Prophet ﷺ, regarding the matter of Abraham, peace be upon him, or regarding the ruling of stoning, or regarding the affair of Islam; or between those among them who embraced Islam and those who did not, since disagreement about the true religion occurred among them. According to this view, which is preferred by some even though it does not agree with the occasion of revelation, it may sometimes require the use of a metaphor (majaz, figurative usage) in the referent of the pronoun, and it is not determined that the one calling must be the Messenger of God ﷺ. It was also read as "liyuhkama" (in the passive), and this is attributed to Abu Hanifa.

﴿Then a party of them turns away﴾: it is coordinated with "they are called," and "then" (thumma) is for remoteness in rank. It implies the improbability of their turning away after knowing the obligation to return to it. The "from them" is a qualifier of "a party." Perhaps the intended party here is the most knowledgeable of them, so that the turning away of the rest may be known by a fortiori reasoning. It has been said: this is the reason for the shift from "then they turn away" (thumma yatawallawna). It has also been said: those who did not embrace Islam. The reason for the shift on this view is clear, so reflect.

﴿And they are averse﴾ [23]: It is permitted that it be a qualifying attribute coordinated with the attribute before it, so the waw is for coordination. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the hidden pronoun in "minhum" or from "fariq," since the party is specified by the attribute; in that case the waw is for the circumstantial clause, and it is either emphatic, because turning away and aversion have the same meaning, or explanatory, because their objects differ, on the basis of what has been said: that turning away is from the caller and aversion is from what he calls to, or that turning away is physical and aversion is of the heart, or that the first was from the scholars and the second from their followers. It is also permitted that it have no place in the grammatical structure, by being a concluding remark (tadhyil) or a parenthetical insertion (mu'tariḍah), and the meaning is: they are a people whose habit is aversion. Some explained the sentence this way while still considering it circumstantial, and perhaps he saw that this is not prohibited from that status.

ذَلِكَ (That) — i.e., the aforementioned turning away and aversion (al-tawalli wa al-i'rad). It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿بِأنَّهم قالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلا أيّامًا مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ (This is because they said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days"). That is, it befalls them because of this statement, whose belief had taken firm root in them, by which they made calamities seem light, and with which they did not mind committing sins and wrongdoings. What is meant by "the numbered days" is the days of their worship of the calf. Here ﴿مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ comes in the plural form, whereas in al-Baqarah [80] it is ﴿مَعْدُودَةً﴾ in the singular form, as a variation in expression (tafannun fi al-ta'bir). This is because the broken plural (jam' al-taksir) for non-rational beings may be treated as a singular feminine noun at times and as a plural of feminines at other times. So one says: "hadhihi jibalun rasiyah," and if you wish you may say "rasiyat"; and "jimalun mashiyah," and if you wish "mashiyat." The plural is specified here because of what it indicates of fewness, as with its qualified noun (mawsufuhu), and that is more fitting to the context of wonderment and censure.

﴿وغَرَّهم في دِينِهِمْ﴾ (And their religion deceived them) — that is, it made them hope for what was not to be hoped for, and deceived them. ﴿ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ (what they used to invent) [24] — that is, their fabrication and their lying; or that which they used to fabricate, namely their saying "The Fire will not touch us," etc., as Mujahid said; or their saying "We are the sons of God and His beloved," as Qatadah said; or what includes that and similar things, such as their saying: "Indeed our forefathers, the Prophets, will intercede for us, and God the Exalted promised Ya'qub that He would not punish his sons except for the fulfilment of an oath (tahillat al-qasam)." The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is related either to what is before it (mā 'indahu) or to (yaftarun). al-Khatib objected to this, saying that what follows the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) does not govern what precedes it; and it was answered that this is permitted by extension (bi al-tawassu').

"So how [will it be]?" — an expression of awe and dread, and a demolition of what they relied upon. The interrogative word (kayfa) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (ḥāl), and its governing element is omitted; that is, "how will their condition be?" or "how will they act?" or "how will they be?" It is also permitted that it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, meaning "how is their condition?"

His saying, exalted is He, "when We gather them" (idhā jama'nāhum) is a pure temporal adverb (ẓarf maḥḍ), without any implied conditional sense. The element governing it is the same element governing (kayfa), if kayfa is considered to be in the accusative governed by an implied verb. If we say that it is the predicate of an implied subject, then the governing element of (idhā) is that implied verb, meaning: "how will their condition be at the time of their gathering" — "for a Day" (li-yawmin), meaning on a day, or for the recompense of a day, "about which there is no doubt" (lā rayb fīhi), meaning about its occurrence and the occurrence of what is in it. It is narrated that the first banner raised for the people of the standing place (ahl al-mawqif) among the banners of the disbelievers will be the banner of the Jews, whereupon Allah will expose them before the eyes of the witnesses, then He will command that they be taken to the Fire.

"And every soul will be paid in full what it earned" (wa-wuffiyat kullu nafsin mā kasabat) — meaning what it did of good or evil. What is intended is the recompense for that, but the earned deed has been put in the place of its recompense, signifying the complete connection and inseparability between them, to the extent that they are as one thing. "And they will not be wronged" (wa-hum lā yuẓlamūna) [25] in anything, so they will not have any of their reward reduced, nor will their punishment be increased; rather, each of them is given the measure of what he earned. The pronoun refers to "every person" (kull insān), which is implied by "every soul" (kull nafs). And since "kull" may have its meaning taken into account, the pronoun is made plural; the reason for the masculine gender is evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "O Allah, Master of the Kingdom"﴾. This is an affirmation of what the preceding verse implies of the greatness of His exaltation and the immensity of His power. It also contains a silencing of whoever denied the Prophet ﷺ and objected to him, especially the hypocrites, who are in a worse state than the Jews and Christians. It is also good news to him ﷺ of physical victory over those who opposed him, just as he was victorious by argument over those who disputed with him. Through this, this noble verse is connected with what precedes it.

Al-Wahidi related from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas ibn Malik that "when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Mecca, he promised his community the kingdom of Persia and Byzantium. The hypocrites and the Jews said: 'Far-fetched, far-fetched! How could Muhammad obtain the kingdom of Persia and Byzantium? They are mightier and better protected than that. Was it not enough for Muhammad to have Mecca and Medina, that he should covet the kingdom of Persia and Byzantium?!' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse."

Abu al-Hasan al-Tha'alibi related from Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who said: My father told me from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ dug the trench in the year of the Confederates, then he assigned forty cubits to every ten [men]. 'Amr ibn 'Awf said: I, Salman al-Farisi, Hudhayfah, al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin al-Muzani, and six men from the Ansar were assigned forty cubits, and we dug. Then Allah the Exalted brought out from the belly of the trench a round rock that broke our iron and was hard upon us. We said: 'O Salman, go up to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and inform him of the matter of this rock, so that either we may turn away from it or he may command us concerning it with his order, for we do not wish to go beyond his line.' He said: So Salman went up to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was pitching a Turkish tent over himself, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a white round rock has come out from the belly of the trench, and it has broken our iron and been hard upon us, until not a little or much of it can be cut. So command us concerning it, for we do not wish to go beyond your line.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ descended into the trench with Salman, while the nine were on the edge of the trench. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the pickaxe from Salman and struck it a blow that split it, and a flash of lightning came from it that lit up what lay between its two lava plains, until it was as if a lamp were in the inside of a dark house. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cried out 'Allahu akbar' with the cry of conquest, and the Muslims cried out too. Then he ﷺ struck it a second time, and a flash came from it that lit up what lay between its two lava plains, until it was as if a lamp were in the inside of a dark house. He ﷺ cried out the cry of conquest, and the Muslims cried out. Then, peace be upon him, he struck it a third time and broke it, and a flash came from it likewise; he ﷺ cried out the cry of conquest, and the Muslims cried out. He took Salman by the hand and went up. Salman said: 'My father and mother be ransomed for you, O Messenger of Allah, I have seen a thing the like of which I have never seen before.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned to the people and said: 'Did you see what Salman says?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'I struck my first blow, and there flashed for me what you saw; there were illuminated for me from it the palaces of al-Hira and the cities of Kisra, as if they were dog's fangs. Jibril informed me that my community will prevail over them. Then I struck the second, and there flashed for me what you saw; there were illuminated for me from it the red palaces of the land of Rome, as if they were dog's fangs, and Jibril informed me that my community will prevail over them. Then I struck my third blow, and there flashed for me what you saw; there were illuminated for me from it the palaces of San'a, as if they were dog's fangs, and Jibril informed me that my community will prevail over them. So rejoice.' The Muslims rejoiced and said: 'Praise be to Allah, a true promise, He has promised us victory after digging.' The hypocrites said: 'Do you not wonder? He promises you falsehood and tells you that he sees from Yathrib the palaces of al-Hira and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be opened to you, while you are digging the trench out of fear, unable to come out to fight!'" So Allah the Exalted revealed the Qur'an: ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion"﴾ [33:12], and revealed this verse, ﴿Say, "O Allah"﴾ and so on.

The original form of (اَللَّهُمَّ) is (يا اللَّهُ) ("O Allah"). The (يا) was dropped, and the (مِيم) was substituted for it. It was preferred because of its closeness to the (واو), which is a weak letter (حرف علة) (a letter of prolongation/weakness). It was doubled because it is a substitute for two letters. Its combination with (يا), as in the words of the poet:

"Whenever a calamity befalls me, I say: O Allah-mma, O Allah-mma"

is anomalous (شاذ). This is among the peculiarities of the Name of Majesty (الاسم الجليل): the vocative particle is not dropped from it without (مِيم); it may be preceded by the definite article and its hamza is cut; the oath particle (تاء القسم) enters upon it, as does the lam of the wondering oath, as in (لَلَّهُ لا يُؤَخِّرُ الأجَلَ); (اَيْمُنُ) and (يَمِينٍ) also enter upon it in oaths; the mim is in (م اللَّهِ); and the interrogative hamza occurs in place of the oath particle, as in (أللَّهِ); and the particle of admonition occurs in phrases such as (لاها اللَّهِ ذا), and other things. Glory be to Him, a God whose every affair is strange.

The Kufans claimed that its original form is (يا اللَّهَ آمَنّا بِخَيْرٍ), meaning "we intended by it," which was lightened by dropping the vocative particle, the related elements of the verb, and its hamza. According to them, combining (يا) with (مِيم) is permissible without harm, and the wonder of what this entails is not hidden: it implies that no other supplicatory imperative may follow this word except through the artifice of substitution from that verb, or of coordination with it by dropping the conjunction. (الـ) in (الْمُلْكِ) is for the genus or for comprehensiveness.

(اَلْمُلْكِ) with a damma, according to what some of the leading verifiers (أئمة التحقيق) mentioned, is a relation between the one who holds it and the one to whom it is attached. If you wish, you may say: it is an attribute subsisting in His essence, related to others by a relation of complete disposal, which entails the independence of the one who disposes and the dependence of the one disposed of. For this reason it is not validly applied absolutely except to Allah the Exalted alone. It is more specific than (المِلْك) with a kasra, because the latter is a relation of possession with control and capacity to dispose of the linguistic object, and it additionally carries the legal status of a right, without regard to independence or dependence. So, "Master of the Kingdom" is the true King who disposes as He wills, however He wills, in creating and annihilating, giving life and causing death, punishing and rewarding, without partner and without hindrance. For this reason one does not say "King of the Kingdom" except in a figurative sense. Taking (اَلْمُلْكِ) in this meaning is more suitable to the context of praise. It was also said: what is meant is prophethood, and this is the view of Mujahid. It was said: wealth and slaves. It was said: this world and the Hereafter.

The accusative of ﴿مالِكَ﴾ as an attribute, according to al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and Sibawayh, requires that it be a second vocative. It cannot be an attribute of (اَللَّهُمَّ), because its joining with the mim makes it resemble sound-names (أسماء الأصوات), and these are not described. Sibawayh's argument has been challenged by Sibawayh himself, for he, despite it being a sound-name, describes it. It was answered that the sound-name has become compounded with it and has become like part of the letters of a word, unlike what we are concerned with here. From this, Abu 'Ali said: "Sibawayh's view is more correct in my opinion, for there is nothing among described names of the type of (اللهم), and for this reason it differs from all other names and enters the category of what is not described, such as (حَيَّهَلَ), for both have become like a sound joined to a name, and so are not described." Al-Taftazani

(Continued on the next page.)

The existing (occurring) kinds of these categories in the world are the first and second, and the evil found in it is not intended in itself; rather, God Most High has decreed it only for a profound wisdom, and it is a means to a greater good that is more widely beneficial. A small evil, whenever it is a means to abundant good, its commission is a benefit that wisdom requires, and the absolute generosity (al-karam al-mutlaq) does not reject it. Do you not see that bloodletting, cupping, drinking a bitter medicine, cutting off a growth (al-sil'ah), and similar painful things, because they are a means to attaining health, it is good to commit them in accordance with wisdom, and they are counted as good and not evil, and as health and not sickness? And every decree of God Most High of what we see as evil of this kind is so. For this reason it is reported in the hadith: "Do not accuse God Most High on your own account," and it has been reported: "Do not dislike trials, for in them is the harvest of the hypocrites," and it has come: "Were you not to sin, I would fear for you something greater than that: self-admiration, self-admiration." And from here it has been said: "O you whose corruption is a reform, whatever corruption He has decreed for the sake of its containing great benefits, overlook that small measure in comparison to them, because it is a means to them, and what leads to good is itself good." So every evil God Most High has decreed, because it was not intended in itself, since the rulings of qada' and qadar, as they have said, run according to the patterns on which all the sharia agree, from the viewpoint of bringing benefits and warding off harms; rather, it is intended incidentally (bi'l-'arad) because of the greater good and the most complete benefit it necessitates. In this sense it is truly said of it that it is good, and it enters into His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾. Therefore He restricted it to "the good," in a manner that it encompasses what is intended originally and what occurs as a necessary consequence. This is from the category of "it is not possible for there to be anything more wondrous than what is," and the philosophers of Islam have followed this path, and one should not heed those who aim the arrows of criticism at it. In Sharh al-Hayakil it is stated that evil is decreed incidentally and proceeds by way of consequence, because some of what contains abundant goods may necessitate a small evil, so abandoning the abundant goods for the sake of that small evil would be a great evil. Thus that good proceeds from You, and so the occurrence of that evil necessarily follows; and it, from the standpoint of its proceeding from You, is good, since its non-proceeding would be evil, as it entails the loss of that good. So You are exalted above indecency, although nothing operates in Your dominion except what You will. This is not from the saying that the optimal (al-aslah) is obligatory, and it is not contradicted by ﴿He is not asked about what He does﴾, since He does not do what one would ask about, out of generosity, wisdom, bounty and favour. "And if you were to perceive the unseen, you would choose what has occurred."

[p. 116]

**"You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night."** *Wulūj* (ولوج) originally means entering, and *iwlāj* (إيلاج) means causing to enter. The expression is used figuratively for the increase of the length of day at the expense of night and its reverse, according to the risings and settings in most lands. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. The equality of night and day that occurs always at the equator (*khatt al-istiwa'*) does not contradict this, because the increase and decrease in both are sufficient in the general case. Al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of causing one of them to enter the other is bringing each of them into existence immediately after the other. The first interpretation is closer to the wording. Under both interpretations, the apparent meaning of night and day is the night and day of revolution (*layl al-takwīr* and *nahāruhu*), which are the well-known ones among the common people who understand the apparent sense of speech. Beyond this are the days of stripping (*ayyām al-salkh*), which those who know recognize, and the days of potential entering (*ayyām al-iwlāj al-sha'niyya*), which the wise scholars comprehend.

[p. 117 (as marked in source)]

An explanation of this in summary: the day, according to what the divine (*ilāhiyyūn*) philosophers have mentioned, is an expression for one single revolution of the cycles of the celestial sphere. It runs from *al-naṭḥ* to *al-naṭḥ*, from *al-shartayn* to *al-shartayn*, from *al-buṭayn* to *al-buṭayn*, and so on to the end of the lunar mansions, and from the degree of a mansion and its minute to the degree of a mansion and its minute, and more hidden than that to the furthest point at which one can stop. Every day among the days known to the common people, which runs from sunrise to sunrise, or from sunset to sunset, or from noon to noon, or whatever lies between these to the same between these, contains the completion of three hundred and sixty days. Thus the length of the day is three hundred and sixty degrees, because in it the whole sphere appears and movement encompasses it. This is the physical day (*al-yawm al-jusmānī*). In it there is the spiritual day (*al-yawm al-rūḥānī*), in which the intellects take their knowledge, the insights take their witnessings, and the spirits take their secrets, just as bodies in this physical day take their nourishment, growth, development, health, sickness, life and death. The days, in respect of their apparent judgments in the world, issuing from the active power of the universal soul, are seven, from Sunday to its end. These days have spiritual days, which have judgments on spirits and intellects, emanating from the knowing power of the Truth by which the heavens and the earth subsist, which is the divine Word (*al-kalima al-ilāhiyya*). Upon these seven revolving days the sphere of inquiry turns. So we say: God the Exalted said, regarding the observed days of the sensible world: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ (39:5). He then clarified two realities by way of judgment, after this, when He said in another verse: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ (36:37). This verse informs that the night is the origin and the day was hidden within it, then it was stripped off. The meaning of stripping is not the meaning of wrapping, so it is necessary that the night of each day be known apart from it, so that every garment is attributed to its wearer, every branch is returned to its root, and every son is joined to his father. And He said in the noble verse, revealing another reality: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾. He thus made between night and day a spiritual marriage, since things are generated from both together. He confirmed this meaning by His saying, Mighty is He: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ (7:54). For this reason each of them is both causing-to-enter and caused-to-enter-into. Each of them is for its companion both origin and spouse. Whatever is generated in the day, its mother is the day and its father is the night; and whatever is generated in the night, its mother is the night and its father is the day. Therefore the judgment of entering is not the judgment of stripping, for stripping occurs only at the time when the day returns from being causing-to-enter and caused-to-enter-into, and likewise the night. However, He mentioned one stripping and did not mention the other stripping, for the sake of the apparent and the hidden, the unseen and the witnessed, the spirit and the body, the letter and the meaning, and the like. So entering is entirely spirit, and wrapping is the body of this entering-spirit. For this reason He repeated night and day in entering, as He repeated them in wrapping: this in the world of bodies and that in the world of spirits. Thus the wrapping of the day is for the entering of the night, and the wrapping of the night is for the entering of the day. And stripping came singular for the sake of its apparent people.

The Persians (*al-'ajam*) and the Arabs differ regarding the priority of which of the two wrapped things is over the other. The Persians put the day before the night, and their reckoning is solar. Thus the night of Saturday, for example, in their reckoning is the night whose dawn is Sunday, and so on. The Arabs put the night before the day, and their reckoning is lunar. ﴿Those—He has written faith in their hearts﴾ (58:22). Thus the night of Friday, for them, for example, is the night whose dawn is Friday. They are closer to knowledge than the Persians, for the stripping supports them in this view, but they did not know the judgment. So they attributed the night to other than its day, as the people of the sun did. That is because their common people know only the days of wrapping, while the knowers of this community and the heirs of the prophets know what lies beyond that: the days of stripping and the days of potential entering.

Since days are a thing, and everything for them has an outer and inner, a hidden and witnessed, a spirit and a body, a dominion (*mulk*) and a kingdom (*malakūt*), a subtle and a dense, they said: the day is a day and night in correspondence to inner and outer. The days are seven, and each day has a day and night of its own kind. The day is a shadow of that night and in its form, because it is its origin: it is included in it, and it is stripped from it by the divine breath. The Glorified has left unspecified in the verse of stripping which day was stripped from which night, and He did not say: "the night of such-and-such, from which He stripped the day of such-and-such," so that whoever God the Exalted has inspired with His right guidance may understand it and attain the decisive word (*faṣl al-khiṭāb*). According to what is understood from the Arabic language by the lunar reckoning, that is: the night of Sunday, God the Exalted stripped from it the day of Wednesday; and from the night of Monday He stripped the day of Thursday; and from the night of Tuesday the day of Friday; from the night of Wednesday the day of Saturday; from the night of Thursday the day of Sunday; from the night of Friday the day of Monday; from the night of Saturday the day of Tuesday. Thus the Glorified placed between each night and its stripped day three nights and three days, so they were six. This is your creation with its directions (*nash'atuka dhāt al-jihāt*). The nights among them are for the below, the left, and the behind; the days among them are for the above, the right, and the front. Thus a human being does not become a day and light, whose sun rises and whose earth shines by it, until he is stripped from the night of his desire. And he does not turn toward one who does not accept directions, until he distances himself from the directions of his temple (*haykal*). They attributed this relation to the commonality of the apparent matter, in order to conceal the divine wisdom at the hands of those entrusted with the hours. In the entering-day of potential character they consider night and day as well, and it is for them twenty-four hours, in which the matter has become one, so that nothing issues in it except one meaning, which diversifies among existents according to their readiness. For this reason the Glorified said: ﴿Every day He is in a task﴾ (55:29), and He did not say "in tasks." Its tanwīn is for glorification, the apparent glorification through the difference of receptacles and the multiplicity of persons. So when the hours of that day are under one judgment and one governing gaze, the one appointed by Him who is not in His dominion except as He wills, and He has assigned it and singled it out with that movement and made it commander in that, and the true disposer is God the Exalted, not it in itself. Thus the potential day is that whose hours are all equal. Whenever they differ, it is not one day. This is not found in the days of wrapping, nor in the days of stripping except rarely. So we sought that in the entering days and found it fully realized in them. The Glorified has sent down the verse of entering and did not say: "He causes to enter the night whose dawn is Sunday into Sunday," nor "the day whose evening is the night of Monday into Monday." Therefore it is not required that the night of Sunday be the night of the wrappings or the night of stripping. Rather, the oneness of the day is sought for the sake of the oneness of the matter, so one looks only at the unity of the hours. The governing one is a master appointed by a master. So the night of entering-Sunday is composed of: the first hour of the night of Thursday, the second of it, the third of Thursday day, the tenth of it, the fifth of the night of Friday, the twelfth of it, the seventh of Friday day, the eighth of the night of Saturday, the ninth of it, the fourth of Saturday day, the eleventh of it, and the sixth of the night of Sunday. These are the hours of its night.

As for the hours of its day from the days of wrapping: the first of Sunday day, the eighth and third of Monday day, the tenth of it, the fifth of Monday day, the twelfth of it, the seventh of the night of Tuesday, the second of Tuesday day, the ninth of it, the fourth of the night of Wednesday, the eleventh of it, and the sixth of Wednesday day. These are twenty-four apparent hours like the sun, for the entering-Sunday potential day, all of them like one soul, because they are from one substance. And so you say of the rest of the days until seven days are complete, distinguished from one another, entering into one another, its day in its night and its night in its day, for the wisdom of procreation and generation, and that is like the flowing of one judgment through the days. This appears from the days of wrapping.

Our master, the Greatest Shaykh (*al-Shaykh al-Akbar*, Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, mentioned the matter (*sha'n*) of each day in his treatise called *al-Sha'n al-Ilāhī* (*The Divine Matter*). Perhaps, God the Exalted willing, I will mention that at His saying: ﴿Every day He is in a task﴾. These days are also other than the Day of the Parable, which is the lifespan of the world (*'umr al-dunyā*), the Day of the Lord, the Day of the Ascensions (*al-ma'ārij*), the Day of the Moon, the Day of the Sun, the Day of Saturn, the Day of Aries. Each star among the planets and the zodiacal signs has a day. All of that has been mentioned in *al-Futūḥāt* (*al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya*). We have touched upon this measure, though exhaustive explanation of the way of this people is not novel in this book. It is an instruction for some students of knowledge about what the night and day are, since they have, through their ignorance, assumed what they assumed due to an inquiry that has led us to conjectures. In this is sufficiency for whoever gives ear while he is a witness. So praise be to You, O God, for what You have taught, and to You be thanks for what You have bestowed.

[p. 118]

**﴿And You bring forth the living from the dead﴾**, that is, the animals come from their materials, or from the sperm drop. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and a great many. **﴿And You bring forth the dead from the living﴾**, that is, the sperm drop from living animals, as the majority of the early generation (*al-salaf*) said. Ibn Mardawayh reported, through the route of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, from Salman al-Farisi, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God the Exalted created Adam, peace be upon him, He brought forth his offspring, and He grasped a handful with His right hand and said: These are the people of Paradise, and I do not care. He grasped another handful with the other hand and in it was every wicked one, and He said: These are the people of the Fire, and I do not care. Then He mixed some of them with others, so He brings forth the disbeliever from the believer and the believer from the disbeliever." That is His saying: ﴿And You bring forth the living from the dead﴾, the verse. To this view al-Hasan went, and it is reported from the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt. So "living" and "dead" are figurative. The conjunction of this sentence after the first is not hidden. Those who hold that the figurative sense is general said: the meaning is that You bring forth animals from drops, and drops from animals; the palm tree from the date-stone, and the date-stone from the palm tree; the good from the bad, and the bad from the good; the knowing from the ignorant, and the ignorant from the knowing; the intelligent from the dull, and the dull from the intelligent; and so on.

It does not follow from the verse that every living thing comes from a dead thing and every dead thing from a living thing, such that an infinite regress would result on the side of the originator. What the verse implies at most is that God the Exalted has this attribute. As for whether He creates nothing except from something, that does not follow, as is not hidden. It is read *al-mayt* with lightening (*takhfīf*) in both places.

The place-expression (*al-zarf*) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) relating to the object: "You provide for whom You will without reckoning," i.e., without holding him to account.
