Or it relates to the subject: "You provide for him without reckoning with him," or "without restricting him." It is also permitted that it be a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*) or an omitted object, meaning "provision that is not little." In the mention of these great acts, which bewilder the intellects, and their attribution to Him, exalted is He, there is an indication that whoever is able to do that is not incapable of stripping sovereignty from the non-Arabs (*ajam*) and humbling them, and of granting it to the Arabs and honoring them. Rather, that is easier for Him than any easy thing.

Indeed, what points to the virtue of this verse has already been mentioned. Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "I complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about a debt I had, and he said: 'O Mu'adh, would you like your debt to be settled?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You strip sovereignty from whom You will, and You honor whom You will, and You humble whom You will; in Your hand is all good; indeed You are over all things powerful.' Lord of this world and the Hereafter and their Merciful, You give from both to whom You will and withhold from both whom You will. Settle my debt for me, for even if you had upon you the weight of the earth in gold, it would be paid on your behalf.'" In a narration of al-Tabarani, the verse is cited in its entirety.

* * *

From the approach of allusion (*al-ishara*) in the verses: "Allah bears witness that there is no god but He" (3:18), i.e., He manifested, through the signs of the horizons and of the souls, that there is no deity in existence besides Him. Or: He bore witness by His Essence, in the station of unification (*maqam al-jam'*), to His oneness, where there is no witness and no witnessed other than Him. The angels and those of knowledge also bore witness to this, and that is the witnessing of His manifestations (*mazahir*), may He be glorified, in the station of differentiation (*maqam al-tafsil*). Among the people there are those who distinguished between the two testimonies: the testimony of the angels is from the standpoint of certainty (*yaqin*), and the testimony of those of knowledge is from the standpoint of direct witnessing (*mushahada*). They also said: the testimony of the angels is from seeing the actions, and the testimony of those of knowledge is from seeing the attributes. It was said: the testimony of the angels is from seeing the majesty (*azama*), which is why fear predominates over them; and the testimony of the scholars is from seeing the beauty (*jamal*), which is why hope predominates over them. The testimony of the scholars varies: the testimony of some is from states (*ahwal*), the testimony of others is from stations (*maqamat*), the testimony of a group is from unveilings (*mukashafat*), and the testimony of a party is from witnessings (*mushahadat*). The elite of the people of knowledge bear witness to Him with the attribute of perceiving eternity (*qidam*) and the emergence of the light of oneness (*tawhid*) from the beauty of unity (*wahdaniyya*). Thus their testimony is absorbed into the testimony of the Truth, because they are in the place of effacement (*mahw*).

"Standing in justice" (3:18): i.e., establishing justice by giving each manifestation what is its due according to its readiness (*istid'ad*), so He is unveiled to it according to the measure of its supplication (*du'a'*).

"There is no god but He, the Mighty" (3:18): so no one reaches the knowledge of His essence (*kunh*) or the knowledge of the knowledge of His essence. "The Wise" (3:18): who governs everything, so He gives it from the degrees of oneness what it can bear.

"Indeed, the religion" (3:19) that is pleasing "with Allah is Islam" (3:19), which is the Abrahamic station (*al-maqam al-Ibrahimi*) alluded to by His saying: "I have submitted my face" (6:79), i.e., my self and my whole being, and I have stripped myself of my vessels for Allah, may He be exalted, so I passed away (*fana'*) in Him.

"Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah" (3:21): these are the veiled from the religion and the concealers of the Truth through inclination toward the desires. "And they kill the prophets" (3:21): those who call to oneness; these are the servants and the perfect realized ones (*wasilun*). "And they kill those who enjoin justice" (3:21): which is the negation of the others (*aghyar*) and the restriction of true existence to Allah, may He be exalted. "From among the people" (3:21). It may be that by "those who disbelieve" is indicated the powers of the commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammara*), by "the prophets" are indicated the prophets of the hearts, which are honored with the inspiration of hidden knowledge (*ilham al-ghuyub*), and by "those who enjoin justice" are indicated the spiritual powers which are among the armies of those prophets and their followers. So give good tidings to those disbelievers (3:21) "of a painful punishment" (3:21), which is the punishment of the veil and of distance from the presence of the Lord of lords. "Those are the ones whose deeds have become void" (2:217; 3:22), i.e., they have been nullified and fallen out of the sphere of consideration. "In this world" (2:217; 3:22), which is the world of witnessing, "and in the Hereafter" (2:217; 3:22), which is the world of the unseen. "And they have no helpers" (2:270; 3:22), due to their ill fortune and the weakness of their readiness.

"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture" (3:23), like the scholars of evil and the rabbis of misguidance, "who are called to the Book of Allah" (3:23), which speaks of the station of unification and differentiation, "that it may judge between them" (3:23) and between the monotheists.

"Then a party of them turn away while they are refusing" (3:23): from accepting the Truth, because of the excess of their veiling and their deception by what they have been given. "That is because they said: the Fire will not touch us" (3:24), the fire of distance, "except for numbered days" (3:24), i.e., few and brief. "And their religion has deceived them" (3:24), the religion they adhere to, "regarding what they used to invent" (3:24): of premises and syllogisms which their intellects brought, mixed with the darkness of illusion and imagination.

"Then how will it be" (3:25) with their condition "when We gather them" (3:25) after their dispersal in the desert of doubts and the tearing by the beasts of illusions, "for a Day about which there is no doubt" (3:25), which is the Great Day of Resurrection, on which the Truth becomes manifest to its denier. "And every soul will be paid in full for what it earned" (3:25), whether righteous or wicked, through the medium of its readiness, "and they will not be wronged" (3:25) in the recompense for that.

"Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty" (3:26): i.e., sovereignty that disposes of Your manifestations without opposition or resistance, as wisdom requires. "You give sovereignty to whom You will" (3:26): and he is the one You have chosen for inner leadership, and You have made him one who disposes by Your will and power. "And You strip sovereignty from whom You will" (3:26): by transferring it to another, after completing the term of his stay in the world of bodies and the perfecting of his creation; or You deprive whom You will of being granted that sovereignty, because of his injustice, which prevents him from attaining Your covenant or being given Your bounty. "And You honor whom You will" (3:26) by casting upon him a light from the lights of Your might, for might belongs to Allah entirely. "And You humble whom You will" (3:26) by stripping from him the garment of Your might, so he remains humbled. "In Your hand is all good" (3:26), and You are the absolutely capable: You give according to Your will, You manifest according to Your intention, and You grant according to the capacity of Your manifestations.

"You cause the night to enter the day" (3:27): You cause the darkness of the self to enter the light of the heart, so it becomes dark. "And You cause the day to enter the night" (3:27): and You cause the light of the heart to enter the darkness of the self, so it becomes illuminated; and You mix the two together despite the distance of their affinity. "And You bring out" (3:27): the living heart from the dead self, and the dead self from the living heart; or You bring out the living knowledge from the dead ignorance, and the dead ignorance from the living knowledge. "And You provide for whom You will" (3:27) with the blessings, apparent and hidden, or with one of the two only, "without reckoning" (3:27), since there is no restriction upon You.

Now, since He, may He be glorified, has made clear that the giving of sovereignty and honor is from Allah, exalted is He, and that He is over all things powerful, He admonished the believers that they should not befriend the enemies of Allah, exalted is He, out of kinship, or jahili friendship, or the like, nor seek support from them, because He, exalted is He, is the Honorer, the absolutely Capable, by His saying, mighty is He, saying:

[p. 120]

**Qur'an 3:28: "Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies"**

Ibn 'Abbas said: "It concerned al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, Kahmas ibn Abi al-Haqiq and Qays ibn Zayd, all of them Jews, who were secretly befriending a group of the Ansar in order to turn them away from their religion. Rifa'ah ibn al-Mundhir, 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr and Sa'id ibn Khaythamah said to those men: 'Avoid these Jews and beware of staying close to them and befriending them, lest they turn you away from your religion.' But those men refused except to continue befriending and associating with them, so God revealed this verse."

al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. They would take the Jews and the polytheists as allies, bring them news, and hope that victory over the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would be theirs. So God revealed the verse and forbade the believers from their conduct."

al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit al-Ansari, who was a veteran of Badr and a chief (naqib), and who had Jewish allies. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out on the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), 'Ubadah said: "O Prophet of God, I have five hundred Jews with me, and I think they should go out with me so that I may seek their support against the enemy." So God revealed: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies...﴾, etc.

The verb is in the jussive mood because of the prohibitive particle *la* (the negative particle used for prohibition). al-Kisa'i (a famous grammarian of Kufa) permitted the verb to be in the nominative, as a statement, while the meaning remains a prohibition. The verb is transitive to two objects, but it may also be read as transitive to one object, in which case *awliya'* is the second object or a circumstantial state (hal). *Awliya'* is the plural of *wali* (ally, friend), meaning one who is close (*al-wali* means nearness). The meaning is: they should not observe the ties that existed between them in the pre-Islamic period, but should observe what they now hold through Islam, namely the legally valid forms of hatred and love that make the obligation (taklif) valid. We specified this because some have said that love for kinship, old or new friendship, is outside the scope of choice, is pardoned, and does not fall under consideration.

Understanding *muwalah* (alliance, allegiance) to include seeking help from them in military expeditions is the view of some scholars. Our school, and the majority, hold that it is permitted, and that they may be given a share (yurdah lahum), but only that they may be sought as help against polytheists, not against rebels (bughat), as they have explicitly stated. As for what is reported from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out for Badr, and a polytheist man who was bold and brave followed him. The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were pleased when they saw him, but the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Go back, for I will never seek help from a polytheist,'" this is abrogated (mansukh, superseded by a later ruling) by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) sought help from the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa' and gave them a share, and he sought help from Safwan ibn Umayyah in the battle of Hawazin.

Some scholars mentioned that seeking help is permitted on condition of need and trustworthiness; without these two conditions it is not permitted. On this the report of 'A'ishah is interpreted, and likewise what al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas about the occasion of revelation. Through this the evidence for prohibition and the evidence for permission are reconciled. Some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) mentioned that the forbidden seeking of help is only when a weak person seeks help from a mighty one; but when it is from the category of a mighty person seeking help from a weak one, it has been permitted for us. From this is the taking of disbelievers as servants and attendants, and marrying women from the People of the Book. This is a good statement, as is not hidden.

Some people used the verse as evidence that it is not permitted to appoint them as officials or employ them in government affairs and other matters. Likewise, they included among the forbidden forms of alliance greeting them with peace, honouring them, addressing them by kunyah (a respectful name), and showing them deference in gatherings. In the *Fatawa* of the scholar Ibn Hajar it is stated that standing in a gathering for the People of the Dhimmah (protected non-Muslims) is permitted, and he counted this as part of goodness and kindness, which is permitted by His saying: ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not drive you out of your homes, that you be kind to them and deal justly with them. Indeed God loves the just.﴾ Perhaps the correct view is that everything that custom counts as honour, and that Muslims regard as alliance, is forbidden, even with the People of the Dhimmah, especially if it puts something into the hearts of weak believers. I do not see standing for the People of the Dhimmah in a gathering as anything other than a prohibited matter, because its indication of honour is strong, and I do not see making it a form of kindness as kindness, as is not hidden.

﴿rather than the believers﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject (the believers), meaning: going beyond the believers to the disbelievers, either independently or jointly. This adverbial phrase carries no implied restriction (mafhum), either because it was revealed concerning specific people who took the disbelievers as allies and not the believers, so it describes the actual situation; or because its mention is to indicate that those truly worthy of alliance are the believers, and that allying with them is a substitute for allying with the disbelievers. That this nuance would require saying, when the believers are present, without ﴿rather than the believers﴾, is within the scope of prohibition. That it indicates that their alliance does not combine with the alliance of the believers is very obscure.

It has been said that the adverbial phrase modifies *awliya'* (as a qualifier). It has also been said that it is connected to the act of taking (ittikhadh), and *min* (from) indicates the starting point: meaning, do not make the starting point of alliance from a place other than the place of the believers.

﴿And whoever does that﴾: that is, the taking (of allies). The act is expressed by the verb, as Shaykh al-Islam said, for brevity, or to suggest disapproval by mentioning it. *Man* (whoever) is conditional, ﴿does﴾ is the conditional verb, and its response is ﴿then he has nothing to do with God in anything﴾. The statement is elliptical, with an omitted noun: "from His alliance" or "from His religion." The first adverbial phrase is a circumstantial state of (thing), and the second is the predicate of *laysa* (is not). The tanwin on (thing) is for belittlement: meaning, he is not in any thing that could be called alliance or religion, because allying with opposites hardly ever enters the realm of actuality. For this reason it was said:

"You wish harm to my enemy, then claim that I am your friend; the folly is not far from you."

It was also said:

"When your friend allies with one you oppose, he has become your enemy, and talk is over."

The clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah). His saying, ﴿except when you fear a danger from them﴾, in the form of address by way of third-person narration (ghaybah), is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh), taken from the most general category of circumstances. Its governing element is the prohibitive verb, understood as addressed to you: meaning, do not take them as allies in any circumstance except the circumstance of guarding yourselves.

It has also been said that it is an exceptive clause from the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih): meaning, a believer should not take a disbeliever as an ally for any reason except out of taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation to protect oneself from harm). Here *min* (from) indicates the starting point, connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial state of His saying ﴿taqiyyah﴾, because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun, and it has been placed before it. The meaning of *taqiyyah* is what is guarded against. It may mean the act of guarding (ittiqa'), which is the common usage. In the first reading it is the direct object of ﴿tattaquu﴾; in the second it is an absolute object of purpose, with *minhum* connected to it. It takes *min* because it means "to fear," and "to fear" is followed by it, as in: ﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband﴾ and ﴿whoever fears bias or wrongdoing from a testator﴾. The prepositional phrase stands in the position of one of the two objects, and the other object is omitted because it is known: that is, harm or the like.

The original form of *taqah* was *wuqayah*, with a dammed waw and a moving ya' after the fathah-marked qaf. The dammed waw was changed to ta', as in *tujah*, and the moving ya' was changed to alif because it was moving and the letter before it had fathah. Its pattern is *fu'alah*, as in *tukhamah* and *tu'adah*. In verbal nouns it is not regular; the regular form is *ittiqa'*, like *iqtida'*. Abu al-Rajā' and Qatadah read *taqiyyatan* with a doubled ya', with pattern *fa'iilah*, and the ta' is again a replacement of the waw.

The verse is evidence for the legitimacy of taqiyyah. Scholars defined it as protecting the self, honour or property from the harm of enemies. The enemy is of two kinds. The first: one whose enmity is based on difference of religion, like the disbeliever and the Muslim. The second: one whose enmity is based on worldly aims, like wealth, goods, kingship and command. From here taqiyyah became two kinds.

As for the first kind: the legal ruling is that every believer who finds himself in a place where he cannot display his religion because of the hostility of opponents is obliged to emigrate (hijrah) to a place where he can display his religion. It is not at all permitted for him to remain there, conceal his religion, and cling to the excuse of weakness, for the earth of God is wide. Yes, if he is among those who have a legitimate excuse for not emigrating, such as children, women, the blind, and prisoners, and those whom the opponents frighten with killing or with the killing of their children, parents or mothers, by a threat that makes it likely that what they threatened will be carried out, whether this killing is by beheading or by withholding food or the like, then it is permitted for him to stay with the opponent and to outwardly conform as far as necessity requires. He must strive to find a way to leave and flee with his religion. Even if the threat is the loss of a benefit or the infliction of a hardship he could bear, such as imprisonment with food provided or light non-lethal beating, it is not permitted for him to conform to them.

In the case where it is permitted, conformity is a concession (rukhsah), and openly displaying his creed is the strict requirement (azimah). If he loses his life for that, he is certainly a martyr. Among what shows that it is a concession is what is reported from al-Hasan:

"Musaylimah the liar seized two men from among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said to one of them: 'Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he called the other and said to him: 'Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?' He said: 'I am deaf.' He said it three times, and each time he answered him, 'I am deaf.' So he struck his neck. The news reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: 'As for this one who was killed, he has passed away in his truthfulness and certainty, and has been honoured with His favour; so congratulations to him. As for the other, God has granted him a concession, so there is no blame upon him.'"

As for the second kind: the scholars differed on whether emigration is obligatory in it or not. Some said: it is obligatory, because of His saying ﴿and do not cast yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾, and by the evidence of the prohibition on wasting property. Others said: it is not obligatory, since emigration from that place is a worldly benefit, and no loss in religion results from abandoning it, because the religion is one, and an enemy who is strong and a believer is not harmed by him merely for being a believer. Some said: the truth is that emigration here may also be obligatory if one fears the destruction of his own self or of his relatives, or the violation of his sanctity through excess; but it is not an act of worship or a means of drawing near to God, so that reward would follow from it. Its obligation is for the sake of a purely worldly benefit for that emigrant, not for the correction of religion, so that reward would follow from it. Not every obligation earns reward, for the verified view is that not every obligation is an act of worship. Many obligations carry no reward, such as eating at the height of starvation, avoiding known or presumed harms during illness, and avoiding taking poisons while healthy, and other such things. This emigration is also of this kind, and it is not like emigration to God and His Messenger (ﷺ), which entails reward in the Hereafter by God's grace.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 3, verse 28 (part 2 of 3):

Some scholars counted, under the heading of *taqiyya* (precautionary dissimulation, concealing one's true position to avoid harm), courtesy toward disbelievers, sinners and oppressors: being gentle in speech toward them, smiling in their faces, being open and friendly with them, giving them something to stop their harm, silencing their tongues, and protecting one's honour from them. Such conduct is not counted among the forbidden *muwalat* (taking them as close allies). Rather, it is a sunna and a prescribed matter. Al-Daylami narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted has commanded me to be courteous (*mudara*) to people, just as He commanded me to establish the obligatory duties." In another narration: "I was sent with courtesy (*mudara*)." In *al-Jami'*: "There will come to you a riding party who harbour hatred, so when they come to you, welcome them." Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated: "The head of intellect, after belief in Allah the Exalted, is courtesy toward people." In the narration of al-Bayhaqi: "The head of intellect is courtesy." Al-Tabarani recorded: "Courtesy toward people is charity." In another of his narrations: "Whatever a believer uses to protect his honour is charity." Ibn 'Adi and Ibn 'Asakir recorded: "Whoever lives courteously dies a martyr. Protect your honour with your wealth, and let each of you guard his religion with his tongue." From Burda, from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "A man asked permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while I was with him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What an evil son of the tribe, or brother of the tribe.' Then he admitted him and spoke gently to him. When he had left, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you said what you said, then you spoke gently to him?' He said: 'O 'A'isha, among the worst of people is the one whom people abandon or leave alone to avoid his obscenity.'"

In *al-Bukhari*, from Abu al-Darda': "Indeed, we smile in the faces of some people, while our hearts curse them." In the narration of al-Kushmayhani: "while our hearts despise them." In the narration of Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibrahim al-Harami, with an addition: "and we laugh with them." Beyond these, there are many other hadiths. However, courtesy must not be carried to the point where religion is undermined, wrongdoing is committed, and suspicions arise.

Behind this investigation lie two opinions of two opposing groups of people, namely the Kharijites and the Shi'a. As for the Kharijites, they held that taqiyya is not permissible under any circumstances, and that wealth, the preservation of life and the preservation of honour are not to be weighed against religion at all. They have strange rigidities in this matter. Among them: if someone is praying and a thief or usurper comes to steal or seize his valuable property, he must not break off the prayer; rather, it is forbidden for him to break it. They also criticised Buraydah al-Aslami, a Companion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the ground that he used to keep his horse in view during his prayer so that it would not run off. It is not hidden that this doctrine is an extreme of negligence.

As for the Shi'a, their statements on this point are inconsistent. Some of them said: taqiyya is permissible in all kinds of speech when there is necessity, and it may even become obligatory in them for a kind of kindness and expediency; but it is not permissible in actions, such as killing a believer, nor in anything that is known, or strongly presumed, to cause corruption in the religion. Al-Mufid said: it may sometimes be obligatory, its performance may at some times be better than its abandonment, and its abandonment may sometimes be better than its performance. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi said: the apparent meaning of the narrations indicates that it is obligatory when one fears for one's life. Others said: it is obligatory when one fears for one's wealth as well, and recommended for the protection of one's honour; so much so that it is prescribed for one who is with the People of the Sunna to agree with them in their prayers, their fasting and all the other matters they follow. They also narrated from some of the Imams of the Household: "Whoever prays behind a Sunni out of taqiyya, it is as though he prayed behind a prophet." Among them there is disagreement over whether that prayer must be made up. Similarly, there are two opinions on whether one who breaks the fast out of taqiyya, when breaking it is not lawful, must make up the fast. There is also disagreement over whether it is better to practise taqiyya before a single Sunni in order to protect the Shi'i school from criticism; and many of them issued rulings that it is better. Some of them held that it is permissible, indeed obligatory, to display disbelief for the slightest fear or greed. It is not hidden that this is an excess. They also interpreted most of the actions of the Imams that agree with the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, and for which there is evidence, as cases of taqiyya, in order to refute the doctrine of the Sunnis. They made this a fundamental principle among themselves and built their religion upon it. This is what is widespread among them today, to the extent that they attributed it to the Prophets (peace be upon them). The main aim of all this is to nullify the caliphate of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs (may Allah be pleased with them all), and Allah refuses that.

In their books there is what refutes the claim that Commander of the Faithful 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and his sons (may Allah be pleased with them all) were people of taqiyya; indeed, it also nullifies the excellence of taqiyya that they claimed. In *Nahj al-Balagha*, which in their view is the most authentic book after the Book of Allah the Exalted, the Commander (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The sign of faith is that you prefer truthfulness where it harms you over lying where it benefits you." Where is this from their interpretation of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you with Allah is the most righteous of you﴾, as "the one with the most taqiyya"?! Also in it: "By Allah, if I were to meet them alone while they filled the whole earth, I would not care, nor would I feel lonely. Indeed, concerning their misguidance in which they are, and the guidance upon which I am, I am upon insight from myself and certainty from my Lord, and I await the meeting with Allah and His good reward, hoping for it." In this there is evidence that the Commander did not fear, even when alone against the enemies' armies, which were numerous; and it is inconceivable that such a man would resort to something whose effect would be the destruction of the religion.

Al-'Ayyashi narrated from Zurara ibn A'yan, from Abu Bakr ibn Hazm, that he said: A man performed ablution and wiped over his leather socks, then entered the mosque. 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) came, struck him on the neck, and said: "Woe to you, you pray while you are not in a state of ablution!" He said: "'Umar ordered me to do so." 'Ali took him by the hand and led him to him ('Umar), then said: "Look at what this man says about you," and he raised his voice against 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). 'Umar said: "I ordered him to do that." Observe how he raised his voice and denounced him, and did not hold back.

Al-Rawandi, the commentator on *Nahj al-Balagha* and a reference of the Shi'a, narrated from Salman al-Farisi that 'Ali learned that 'Umar had mentioned his Shi'a. So he met him on one of the roads of the gardens of Medina, with a bow in 'Ali's hand, and said: "O 'Umar, I have heard that you have mentioned my Shi'a." 'Umar said: "Four cubits on your bald head!" 'Ali said: "You are here," then threw the bow on the ground, and behold, it was a serpent like a camel, its mouth open, coming toward 'Umar to swallow him. 'Umar said: "By Allah, by Allah, O Abu al-Hasan, I will never return to anything after this!" and he began to implore. 'Ali struck the serpent with his hand, and the bow returned to what it had been, and 'Umar went off to his house. Salman said: When night came, 'Ali called me and said: "Go to 'Umar, for money has been brought to him from the eastern region, and he has resolved to hide it. Say to him: 'Ali says to you: bring out what has been brought to you from the East, and distribute it to those it belongs to; do not hide it, lest I expose you.'" Salman said: "I went to him and delivered the message. He said: 'Tell me, from where did your companion learn of this?'" I said: "Is such a thing hidden from him?" He said: "O Salman, accept from me what I say to you: 'Ali is nothing but a sorcerer. I am certain of you, and the right course is that you part from him and become one of us." I said: "It is not as you say, but he has inherited from the secrets of prophethood what you have seen from him, and he has even more than this." He said: "Return to him and say: 'I hear and obey your command.'" So I returned to 'Ali, and he said: "I will tell you what passed between you two." I said: "You know better than I do," so he spoke of what had passed between us. Then he said: "The terror of the serpent will remain in his heart until he dies." In this narration there is also a refutation of taqiyya, since the owner of this bow is sufficed by his bow and not compelled to give his daughter Umm Kulthum in marriage to 'Umar out of fear of him or taqiyya.

Al-Kulayni narrated from Mu'adh ibn Kathir, from Abu 'Abd Allah, that he said: "Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent down a book to His Prophet (ﷺ), and Jibril said: 'O Muhammad, this is your testament to the noble ones.' He said: 'And who are the noble ones, O Jibril?' He said: ''Ali ibn Abi Talib and his son.' There were golden seals on the book. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave it to 'Ali and ordered him to break one seal and act upon what was in it. Then he gave it to al-Hasan, and he broke one seal and acted upon what was in it. Then he gave it to al-Husayn, and he broke a seal and found in it: 'Go out with your people to martyrdom, for they will have no martyrdom except with you, and sell yourself to Allah the Exalted.' He did so. Then he gave it to 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and he broke a seal and found in it: 'Be silent, keep to your dwelling, worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.' He did so. Then he gave it to his son Muhammad ibn 'Ali, and he broke a seal and found in it: 'Narrate to the people and give them rulings, spread the knowledge of your Household, confirm your righteous forefathers, and fear no one but Allah the Exalted, for no one has any power over you.' Then he gave it to Ja'far al-Sadiq, and he broke a seal and found in it: 'Narrate to the people and give them rulings, fear none but Allah the Exalted, spread the knowledge of your Household, confirm your righteous forefathers, for you are in safety and security.' He did so. Then he gave it to Musa, and so on to the Mahdi."

He narrated it by another route, also from Mu'adh, from Abu 'Abd Allah. In the fifth seal: "Speak the truth in security and in fear, and fear none but Allah the Exalted." This narration too is explicit that those noble ones did not have taqiyya as their religion, as the Shi'a claim.

Salim ibn Qays al-Hilali, a Shi'i, narrated in a long report that the Commander of the Faithful said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away and people turned to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and pledged allegiance to him, Fatima carried her sons al-Hasan and al-Husayn by the hand and left out none of the people of Badr and the people of precedence among the Emigrants and the Helpers without imploring them by Allah concerning my right and calling them to support me. Yet of all the people, none responded to me except four: al-Zubayr, Salman, Abu Dharr and al-Miqdad." This indicates that taqiyya was not obligatory upon the Imam, for this act, in the view of those who pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), has within it what it has.

In the *Book of Aban ibn 'Ayyash* it is related that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), when the people had pledged allegiance to him and 'Ali had not pledged allegiance, sent Qunfudh to 'Ali and said: "Go to 'Ali and say to him: respond to the Caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So he went and conveyed it. 'Ali said to him: "How quickly you have lied against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and turned back! By Allah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed no one as successor but me." It is also in it that he did not respond, and 'Umar in his anger set fire to the door of 'Ali, burned it, and entered. Fatima met him and cried out: "O my father! O Messenger of Allah!" 'Umar raised the sword, still in its sheath, and struck her blessed side with it, and raised the whip and struck her udder, and she cried out: "O my father!" Then 'Ali seized 'Umar by the collar, shook him, and struck his nose and neck. It is also in it that 'Umar said to 'Ali: "Pledge allegiance to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him)." He said: "And if I do not?" He said: "Then, by Allah, I will strike off your neck." He said: "You lie, by Allah, O son of Suhak; you cannot do that, you are meaner and weaker than that." These reports clearly show that taqiyya was far removed from that Imam, for there is no sense in this dispute and abuse if taqiyya were obligatory.

Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated that the Commander of the Faithful said to 'Umar: "O deceived one, I see you in this world slain by a wound from the hand of Umm Ma'mar, who judges unjustly against him, and he will kill you, and by that enter Paradise in spite of you."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 28 (part 3 of 3):

It is also narrated that he said to ʿUmar once: "Indeed, for you and your companion, the one you took his place, there is disgrace and crucifixion. You will leave the neighborhood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you will be crucified upon a dry tree, which will then sprout leaves, and by this those who follow you will be put to trial. Then the fire that was kindled for Ibrahim will be brought, and Jurjis and Daniyal and every prophet and truthful one will come, and you will be crucified in it, and you will be burned and become ashes. Then a wind will come and scatter you into the sea, scattering." So consider, by Allah the Exalted upon you, who narrates these lies about the Imam, may Allah ennoble his face. Is it fitting for him to say, attributing taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation) to him? Glory be to Allah the Exalted! This is a strange and wondrous matter, and an incurable disease.

Among the things that also refute their claim is that taqiyyah exists only out of fear, and fear is of two kinds. The first is fear for one's life, and this is absent with regard to the honored Imams for two reasons. One of them is that their natural death came about by their own choice, as al-Kulayni proved this matter in *al-Kafi*, devoted a chapter to it, and all the Imamiyyah agreed upon it. The second is that the Imams have knowledge of what has been and what will be, so they know their appointed times, the manner of their deaths, and their times in detail and in particular. Thus, before their time, they do not fear for their own selves, and they do not exercise taqiyyah in their religion, nor do they deceive the common believers. The second kind is fear of hardship, bodily harm, abuse, insult, and violation of honor. There is no doubt that bearing these things and being patient over them is the duty of the righteous. They always endured affliction in carrying out the commands of Allah the Exalted, and at times they confronted tyrannical rulers. The People of the Prophet's House are more worthy of bearing hardships in support of the religion of their grandfather (ﷺ).

Also, if taqiyyah were obligatory, the Imam of the Imams would not have delayed the allegiance to the Caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for six months, and what would have prevented him from fulfilling an obligation at the very first moment?

Among the things that also refute their claim of attributing taqiyyah to the prophets, peace be upon them, in the sense that they intended, is the saying of Allah the Exalted about them: ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him, and fear no one except Allah. And Allah is sufficient as Reckoner.﴾ And His saying, glory be to Him, to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people.﴾ And other verses besides these. Yes, if they meant by taqiyyah the courteous dealing (mudarah) that we have pointed to, then there would be a basis for attributing it to the prophets and the Imams. This is one of the two interpretations of what ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan, that he said: "Taqiyyah is permissible until the Day of Resurrection." The second interpretation is that taqiyyah is to be understood in its apparent sense, and its permissibility is only in the detailed manner that we have mentioned.

Among the people there is one who made obligatory a particular kind of taqiyyah specific to the elite among the believers, namely guarding the divine secrets from disclosure to outsiders, since disclosure would entail total corruption. So you find them, whenever they are asked about a secret, leaving it ambiguous and speaking in words which, if presented to the common people, or even to their scholars, they would not understand. They pour it into molds, and only one who has drunk from their cup, or whose inner regions have been perfumed by the fragrance of their breaths, understands the meaning from them. Although many people go astray because of this, and it has led to slander against those noble and wise masters, to the extent that many of them were accused of heresy, and whoever heard their words and did not investigate them issued a ruling for their execution, nevertheless they saw this harm as less than the corruptions that would result from disclosure, which would spread throughout the earth:

"Have mercy, some evil is easier than other evil."

Concealing secrets from their people entails the loss of great good and brings painful punishment. It may be said: this is not at all a matter of taqiyyah, but the people spoke of what overflowed upon their tongues and appeared openly, and the meanings they intended were such that expression falls short of them, and none approaches their sanctuary except allusion. Whoever follows their example and walks in their footsteps with detachment understands what they said and realizes what they inclined toward. This is supported by what al-Shaʿrani, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in *al-Durar al-Manthurah fi Bayan Zubdat al-ʿUlum al-Mashhurah*, the text of which is: "As for the essence of the science of Sufism (tasawwuf), in which these people wrote their treatises, it is the fruit of acting upon the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever acts upon what he knows speaks as they spoke, and all that they said becomes only a part of what he possesses, because whenever the servant advances in the station of courtesy with Allah the Exalted, his speech becomes more subtle for minds to grasp. Thus one of them said to his shaykh: 'The speech of my brother so-and-so is too subtle for my understanding.' He said: 'Because you have two shirts and he has only one shirt, so he is higher in rank than you.'" And this is what led the jurists and their like, from the people of the veil, to call the science of the Sufis "the science of the inner" (ʿilm al-batin). But it is not inner, since the inner is only the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. As for all that the creatures know, across their different levels, it is of the outer knowledge, because it has appeared to the creatures. Know this. End of quotation.

Based on this, the denunciation of these people is not in its proper place.

﴿And Allah warns you about Himself﴾, i.e., the punishment of His self, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said. In it is a great threat, indicating the extreme ugliness of what is forbidden, since the warning was attached to Himself.

The application of the term "self" (nafs) to Allah the Exalted in the sense intended is permissible without mushakalah (a figure of speech by association) according to the sound view. It was said: "self" here means essence (dhat), and the permissibility of applying it in that sense without mushakalah is something not disputed among the earlier scholars, although some later scholars explicitly stated its impermissibility even if it is meant as essence, except by mushakalah.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ [28], i.e., the place of return. The explicit mention of the Name in place of a pronoun is to cultivate awe and to instill reverence. It was said that there is an omitted modifier in the sentence, i.e., "to His judgment" or "to His recompense," but this is not necessary. The sentence is a concluding statement that confirms what precedes it and establishes that it will certainly occur.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 29:

﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts﴾ i.e., keep secret what is in your hearts of inner dispositions, among which is allegiance to the disbelievers. He mentioned the breast (ṣadr) because it is the place of the heart. ﴿Or reveal it﴾ i.e., make it manifest among yourselves.

﴿Allah will know it﴾, and so He will call you to account for it when you return to Him, and concealing it will not benefit you. As for placing concealment before revealing, its secret has already been pointed out. ﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾ — this is the introduction of the general after the specific, for emphasis and confirmation. The clause is a fresh sentence (mustaʼnafah), not conjoined to the answer of the conditional. ﴿And Allah is powerful over everything﴾ [29] — an affirmation of the attribute of power after the affirmation of the attribute of knowledge, and with this the aspect of warning is completed. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, because He is characterized by an essential knowledge encompassing all known things and an essential power comprehensive of all things that can be done, so do not dare to disobey Him or to take His enemies as allies, for there is no act of disobedience, whether hidden or manifest, except that He is aware of it and able to punish for it. The use of the apparent noun (Allah) in place of the pronoun is for the reason you already know.

[p. 127]

**"On the Day every soul will find (*tajidu*) whatever good it has done"** — from among the souls that are responsible — **"in the world,"** **"even if it be the weight of an atom,"** **"present"** (*muhdaran*) before it, observed in the records. It is also said: "manifest in forms." It is also said: "it will find the recompense of its deeds present, by the command of God, the Exalted." In this there is an intensification of terror that is absent in *hadiran* (present). *Muhdaran* is the second object of *tajidu*. **"And whatever evil it has done"** is conjoined to **"whatever it has done"**. *Muhdaran* carries the same meaning here, but it was singled out for mention with regard to good, to indicate that good is intended in itself, and that the presentation of evil is one of the requirements of the legislative wisdom, as Shaykh al-Islam said. The supplying of *muhdaran* in the text and its omission for brevity, by the indication of its mention in the first clause, is what most of the scholars have said. In this case it is a conjunction to the two objects. This is permissible, as in *al-Durr al-Masun*. They did not treat it as in the construction *"I knew Zayd excellent and ʿAmr"*. That is not a case of limiting to the first object, but rather like *Zayd qa'imun wa-ʿAmrun* (Zayd is standing, and ʿAmr [is standing]), in which the predicate has been omitted, as they have stated explicitly. Therefore limitation necessarily follows. The distinction between the subject and the object in this matter is an error. You may also make *tajidu* mean *tuṣību* (to reach/find), so that it takes one object, and *muhdaran* is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*).

**"Wadda"** — i.e., *tatamannā* (wishes). It governs the adverbial of time (*ẓarf*), i.e., "it wishes on that day." **"Were there between it and that"** — i.e., between that day — **"a long term"** (*amadan baʿidan*). It is also said: the pronoun refers to *mā ʿamilat* because of its proximity, and because the day in which good and evil are presented, while the wish is after evil, not after whatever is in it absolutely. Therefore it is not good to return the pronoun to the day. This is the view taken in *al-Bahr*. It was refuted on the ground that this is more eloquent, because it wishes for distance between itself and the day, together with the good that is in it, lest the evil in it be seen.

*Al-amad* is the end and limit of a thing. The difference between it and *al-abad* (eternity) is that *al-abad* is a period of time without limit, while *al-amad* is a period having an unknown limit. What is meant here is a long extent. It is also said: the measure of a lifetime. It is also said: the amount of distance covered from east to west. Some have held that what is meant by "a long term" is a long distance, and this is perhaps the more apparent. So the wish here is of the same kind as the wish in His saying, *"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts"* (43:38). What has been mentioned concerning the structure of the verse is what many of the imams of tafsir have adopted. Abu Hayyan said: it is the apparent meaning at first glance, and is based on a matter about whose permissibility the grammarians have differed: that the subject be a pronoun referring back to something connected to an element governed by the preceding verb, as in *ghulamu Hindin ḍaraba-hā hiya* ("the slave of Hind, she struck him herself"). The verse is of this kind according to that analysis, because the subject of *tawaddu* refers back to something connected with a complement of *tawaddu*, namely "a day," since it is annexed to *tajidu kullu nafsin*. The sense is: "Every soul wishes, on the day of its finding whatever good and evil it has done present, that between it and that [evil] there were a long term, etc." Most of the Basrans hold that this is permissible, and this is the correct view. From it is the verse:

*Ajalu al-mar'i yastaḥithth wa-lā yadrī, idhā yabtaghī ḥuṣūla al-amānī.*
(The lifespan of a man hastens on, and he does not know, when he seeks the attainment of his wishes.)

That is: at the time he seeks the attainment of his wishes, his lifespan hastens on and he does not know. Al-Farra', al-Akhfash, and others of the Basrans hold that it is not permissible, because this complement is a superfluous element (*faḍla*), so one may dispense with it. Returning the pronoun to what is connected with it removes it from this, because it requires mention of the complement so that the subject pronoun may refer back to what is connected with it. Its weakness is not hidden.

**Other views on the verse:**

Among them: the governor of the adverbial of time is *qadīr* (powerful). It is not objected that His power, glory be to Him, is restricted to that day, because if He has power in its like, His power in other than it is known a fortiori.

Among them: it is governed by *al-maṣīr* (the returning), or by *al-dhikr* (the mention), or by *yuḥadhdhirukum* (He warns you) supplied, so that it is an object; or by the suppressed punishment (*al-ʿiqāb al-muḍāf*) which the speech of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, implies. They stated explicitly that on the supposition that it is connected to something like *udhkurū* (remember), it is permissible for *mā ʿamilat* to be a subject whose predicate is the clause *tawaddu*, or to be conjoined to the first *mā*. The clause *tawaddu* is either a fresh resumptive sentence answering an implied question, as if a questioner said, when they were commanded to remember that day: "What will happen then?" and it was answered: "She wishes, if only between her and it, etc." Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *tajidu*, i.e., "remember the day on which every soul finds whatever good and evil it has done present, and wishes distance between itself and it."

It was permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *ʿamilat*, because of its proximity. It was objected that the wishing is at the time of finding the deed present in the Hereafter, not at the time of doing the deed in this world, and that the circumstantial state from the pronoun in *ʿamilat* requires that it be [at the time of doing], so there is no basis for it. It was answered that it is a *ḥāl muqaddarah* (a predicated future circumstance), in the sense: "On the day every soul finds such and such, its wishing being determined," i.e., being in a state in which its wishing is fixed in Our decree. So the wishing, although not concurrent with the deed, yet its being fixed in God's decree and judgment is concurrent with it. This is like what has been said concerning His saying, *"And We gave him the good tidings of Isaac, a prophet among the righteous"* (37:112). It was also objected that on the supposition of the circumstantial state from the pronoun in *ʿamilat*, it would entail specifying the deed, and the context does not suit this. It was answered that the aim is not specification, but to show the evil of their state and their regret, and there is no harm in it.

Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that *mā* in *"mā ʿamilat min sūʾin"* [30] be conditional (*sharṭiyyah*), and al-Saffaqsi inclined to this. The raising of *tawaddu* is not an obstacle, because when the condition is in the past tense and the consequent in the present tense, the consequent may be in the raised or jussive form, without distinguishing between *in* as conditional and the conditional nouns. It was objected that raising the present tense in the consequent is anomalous, like raising it in the condition, as the Mubarrad stated explicitly, and usage bears this out, since it is not found except in the verse of Zuhayr:

*Wa-in atāhu khalīlun yawma maspabatin ... yaqūlu lā gha'ibun mālī wa-lā ḥarami.*
(And if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger, saying: "My property is not absent, nor is it forbidden [to you]...")

[p. 128]

So the agreed-upon reading is not to be easily explained on this basis. Yes, there is no harm in explaining the anomalous readings, like the reading *"Wherever you are, death will overtake you"* (4:78) with *yudrikukum* raised. It was answered: we do not concede anomaly. Abu Hayyan mentioned that the raised form is heard much in the language of the Arabs, to the point that some of the Maghribis claimed that it is better than the jussive. Zuhayr's verse is similar to the saying of Abu Sakhr:

*Wa-lā bi-lladhī in bāna minhu ḥabībuhu ... yaqūlu wa-yukhfī al-ṣabra innī la-jāziʿu.*
(Nor is he one who, when his beloved departs from him, says and hides his patience: "Indeed I am distressed.")

And the saying of another:

*In yas'alū al-khayra yuʿṭūhu wa-in khubirū ... fī al-jahdi udrik minhum ṭība akhbāri.*
(If they ask for good, they give it; and if they are tested in hardship, I find among them the goodness of news.)

With the raising of *udriku*, which is present tense and occurs as the consequent of the condition. And his saying:

*Wa-in baʿudū lā yaʾmanūna iqtirābahu ... tashawwufa ahli al-ghā'ibi al-muntaẓiri.*
(And if they are far away, they do not feel safe from its approach — the longing of the people of the absent one who awaits.)

And other examples. In *al-Bahr*: the weakness of the raised form on this basis is not so, as you know. However, it is impossible that what is in the verse be a consequent of what Sibawayh mentioned, that the intention in the raised form is the anteposition (*taqdīm*), and then it would be an indication of the consequent rather than the consequent itself. In that case it would lead to anteposing the pronoun before its noun in other than the excepted cases, because it is a pronoun whose referent is the conditional noun *mā*; so the sense would become: "every soul wishes, if between it and that there were a long term, whatever evil it has done," and that is not permissible. Al-Saffaqsi replied that even if we adopt Sibawayh's view, no problem follows, because the clause, by containing a pronoun referring to the conditional, must be delayed, even if it is anterior in intention. Do you not see that when the subject contains a pronoun referring to the object, it is forbidden according to most to anteposed it before the object, even though it is anterior to it in intention?

And ʿAbdullah [Ibn Masʿud] read *waddat* (feminine), and with this reading the objection regarding the prevention of raising is removed by consensus, and the conditional reading is sound. But the second *ʿAllamah* said: there is a difficulty in its soundness, because the clause on the supposition of a relative (*mawṣūlah*) is a circumstantial state or a conjunction to *tajidu*, and the conditional clause does not occur as a circumstantial state nor as a clause annexed to the adverbial of time. So there remains only its conjunction to *udhkurū*, and this, given its soundness, disturbs the meaning, which is that this state and wishing occur on that day. There is no escape except making it a circumstantial state with an implied subject, i.e., "and it is: *mā ʿamilat min sūʾin waddat*" ("and it, [which] whatever evil it has done, wished"). The difficulty in this is not hidden, for they have said that the relative clause with its sentence is a circumstantial state, and the grammarians did not explicitly forbid its annexation. Many of the imams said that the relative reading agrees better with the reading of the majority and is more in accordance with the right course, because it is a statement like a narration of the state existing on that day, so it must be taken to indicate occurrence. The conditional does not indicate this, since it indicates futurity, and there is no evil deed in the future of that day. This does not negate soundness, for although it does not indicate occurrence, it does not contradict it. The objection of futurity is answered by the supposition *wa-mā kānat ʿamilat* ("and what she had done"), as in its parallels. So reflect and understand, perhaps nothing will divert you from choosing the relative reading.

**"And God warns you of Himself"** (3:28/30). It has been said: His mention first was to prevent the taking of unbelievers as allies, and here [it is] an incitement to doing good and a prevention from doing evil in general. It is permitted that it be conjoined to *tawaddu*, i.e., "she dreads that day and the evil deed, and God warns you of Himself by manifesting His dominance (*qahhāriyyah*)." This is something that the Glorious Book should hardly be made to convey. Easier than this is to conjoin it to *tajidu*, with the adverbial of time governed by *udhkurū* — i.e., "remember that day, and remember the day on which God warns you of Himself by manifesting His majesty and dominance." It may be said: this is a repetition of what preceded and a restatement of it, but not for emphasis alone; rather, to convey what it conveys.

As for His saying, **"And God is Compassionate toward the servants"** (*raʾūfun bi-l-ʿibād*): [this may mean] that His warning of Himself arises from His vast mercy toward the servants, for when they know Him and fear Him, that leads them to seek His pleasure and avoid His wrath, and that is the great triumph. Or [it may mean] that His warning, glory be to Him, is not founded on forgetting the attribute of mercy, but is established together with its establishment as well.

So the clause, on the first view, is a concluding remark (*tadhyīl*), and on the second view a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). To the first view the speech of al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, points. The *al* in *al-ʿibād* is for comprehensiveness (*istighrāq*). The repetition of the Glorious Name is to instill awe and to remove heedlessness by directing the mind to this ruling with the fullest attention.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 31:

﴿Say: If you truly love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Most of the theologians (mutakallimun) held that love (mahabbah) is a kind of will (iradah), and that it truly relates only to meanings (ma'ani) and benefits (manafi'). Thus it is impossible for it to relate to the Essence of Allah and His Attributes. Accordingly, here it means the servant's will to single Allah out for worship. This is either by way of mentioning the necessary consequence and intending its implied meaning (ithlaq al-malzum wa iradat al-lazim), or by way of metaphor in a verb-based sense (al-isti'arah al-tab'iyyah), by likening the servant's will and desire for this to the inclination of the heart of a lover toward the beloved, an inclination in which nothing else is attended to except him; or by way of the metonymy of deficiency (majaz al-naqs), meaning: if you love the obedience of Allah or His reward, then follow me in what I command you and forbid you. This is what has been said; but it contradicts the position of the gnostics (al-'arifin) among the People of the Sunnah and the Community, for they said: love truly relates to the Essence of Allah, and it is fitting for the perfected person to love Allah, glorified is He, for His own sake; as for loving His reward, it is a lower rank. Al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*: "Love (hubb) is an expression for the inclination of the nature toward a thing that gives pleasure. If that inclination is strengthened and intensified, it is called 'ishq (passionate love). Hatred (bughd) is an expression for the aversion of the nature from what is painful and wearying; when it intensifies, it is called maqt (loathing). One should not assume that love is confined to the objects of the five senses, so as to say: He, glorified is He, is not perceived by the senses and is not imagined by the faculty of imagination, so He is not loved. For the Prophet ﷺ called prayer the coolness of the eye and made it the most beloved of things, and it is known that the five senses have no share in it. Rather there is a sixth sense whose seat is the heart, and the inner insight is stronger than outward sight, and the heart is more intense in perception than the eye, and the beauty of the meanings perceived by the intellect is greater than the beauty of the forms visible to the eyes. Therefore, without doubt, the heart's pleasure in what it perceives of the noble divine matters, which are too exalted for the senses to perceive, is more complete and more eloquent; so the inclination of the sound nature and the correct intellect toward it is stronger. And love has no meaning except the inclination toward what contains pleasure in its perception. Thus none denies the love of Allah, exalted is He, except one whom deficiency has confined to the rank of beasts, so that he does not allow the senses to perceive Him at all." Yes, this love necessitates obedience, as al-Warraq said:

You disobey God while you show His love; by my life, this is a wondrous analogy.
If your love were sincere, you would have obeyed Him; for the lover is obedient to the one he loves.

As for the claim that love requires kinship (jinsiyyah) between the lover and the beloved, so that it cannot relate to Allah, it is baseless, for love indeed relates to accidents (a'rad) without doubt, and there is no kinship between an accident and a substance.

﴿Allah will love you﴾ is the answer to the imperative, and this is the view of al-Khalil; but most later scholars hold that such a construction is the answer to an implied condition, i.e., "if you follow me, He will love you," meaning He will bring you near (yuqarribkum). This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah. It was also said: "He will be pleased with you." This was expressed by love by way of metonymy (majaz mursal), or metaphor, or the figure of similarity (mushakalah). Some have also held that attributing love to Allah is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose interpretation none knows except Allah.

﴿And He will forgive you your sins﴾, i.e., He will overlook them for you, ﴿and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [31], i.e., to those who make themselves beloved to Him through His obedience and draw near to Him by following His Prophet ﷺ. The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyil) confirming what preceded, with the added promise of mercy. The placing of the noble Name together with the pronoun is for what has passed and to indicate that the attribute of divinity entails forgiveness and mercy. It was also read as (tuhibbunni), (yuhibbakum), and (yuhbibkum), from habbahu yuhibbuhu, and from it is his saying:

I love Abu Tharwan for the sake of his dates, and I know that gentleness toward the neighbor is gentler.
By Allah, were it not for his dates, I would not have loved him, nor would he have been nearer to me than a slave or a Mashriqi.

Page 130
The connection of the verse to what precedes is, as al-Tibi said: when He, glorified is He, magnified His Essence and showed the greatness of His sovereignty by saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O Allah, Master of the Kingdom...﴾ etc., the heart of the believing servant became attached to a Lord of great station, possessor of dominion, sovereignty, majesty and might. Then, when He followed this with the prohibition on believers taking the disbelievers as allies, and warned against this in the utmost degree by saying, He, the Mighty, said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies...﴾ etc.; and He drew attention to the eradication of that alliance by saying, exalted is His affair: ﴿Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it...﴾, and confirmed this with a severe threat, that attachment increased to its utmost extent. So He resumed with His saying, majestic is His majesty: ﴿Say: If you love Allah...﴾, to point to the path of reaching this Master, exalted is He. It is as if a questioner asks: by what is the perfection of love and the allegiance of the Lord attained? It was said: after cutting off the alliance with our enemies, that rank is attained by turning to following our beloved, for every path other than his is blocked, and every deed other than what he has permitted is rejected.

It was disputed concerning the occasion of its revelation. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: "Groups at the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ claimed that they loved Allah, the Exalted, so they said: O Muhammad, we love our Lord, and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ stood before the Quraysh in the Sacred Mosque, and they had set up their idols, hung ostrich eggs upon them, placed earrings in their ears, and were prostrating to them. He said: O assembly of Quraysh, you have opposed the religion of your father Ibrahim and Isma'il, and indeed they were upon Islam. The Quraysh said: O Muhammad, we only worship these out of love for Allah, the Exalted, so that they bring us near to Allah, glorified is He, in closeness. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: If you love...﴾ etc." In the narration of Abu Salih: "When the Jews said: 'We are the sons of Allah and His beloved,' He revealed this verse. When it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented it to the Jews, but they refused to accept it." Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr who said: "It was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, for they said: 'We only exalt the Messiah and worship him out of love for Allah and to glorify Him.' So Allah revealed this verse as a refutation of them." It is related that when it was revealed, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: "Muhammad makes his obedience like the obedience of Allah, and commands us to love him as the Christians loved Jesus." So the saying of Allah, exalted is He, descended:

Say: Obey God and the Messenger﴾ — i.e., in all commands and prohibitions. The preceding command is included in this by primary inclusion. The use of the explicit noun instead of a pronoun, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in discourse), serves to specify the aspect in which obedience is owed and to indicate its reason. In this there is also an allusion to refuting the doubt of the *munafiq* (hypocrite), as if he were saying: "God, exalted, has made my following obligatory upon you not because of what the Christians say about Jesus, but because I am the Messenger of God." ﴿But if they turn away﴾ — i.e., they turned away, or they put themselves in that position, on the understanding that one of the two *ta'*s is elided, so that the clause then falls within the scope of what is spoken. In omitting mention of the possibility of obedience there is a hint that it is not to be expected from them. ﴿Then God does not love the disbelievers﴾ [32] — i.e., He does not draw them near, or is not pleased with them; rather, He distances them from the proximity of His holiness and the enclosures of His might, and is displeased with them on the day He is pleased with the believers. The intended "disbelievers" are those who turned away. He did not express this with a pronoun, to indicate that turning away from obedience is disbelief, and that His love, exalted and majestic, is specific to the believers. Because negating it from these disbelievers entails negating it from all others, since the cause is shared, this requires restriction (*hasr*) to their opposites.

[p. 131]

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran over the worlds.﴾ [33] It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Jews said: "We are the sons of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, peace be upon them, and we are upon their religion," so this was revealed. It was also said that when the Christians of Najran exaggerated regarding Jesus, peace be upon him, and made him the son of Allah, glorified is He, and took him as a god, this was revealed as a refutation of them and to inform them that he was from the offspring of human beings, who pass through the stages (al-atwar) that are impossible for God. This is the aspect of the connection (munasabah, the link between one verse and what precedes it) of the verse to what came before it.

[p. 131 continues in the source]

Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding the aspect of the connection: When Allah, glorified is He, explained that the religion with Allah is Islam, and that the disagreement of the People of the Two Books concerning it is only out of rebellion and envy, and that success in His good pleasure, His forgiveness and His mercy depends upon following the Messenger (ﷺ) and obeying him, He began to establish his mission, and that he is from the household of the ancient Prophethood. So He began by explaining the high rank of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and followed this with mention of the origin of Jesus and his mother, and the manner of his calling people to faith, establishing the truth and nullifying what the People of the Two Books held of excess and deficiency regarding both of them. Then He explained the falsehood of their argument about Abraham and their claim of belonging to his creed, and He cleared his exalted station of what they were upon of Judaism and Christianity. Then He stated explicitly that all the Messengers were callers to the worship and monotheism of Allah, the Exalted, and that all their nations are commanded to believe in whoever comes to them from a Messenger confirming what is with them, establishing the obligation of faith in the Messenger (ﷺ) and the necessity of obeying him, as its detail will come. End of quote. This is a sound aspect.

He began with Adam, peace be upon him, because he is the first of the human species, and mentioned Noah, peace be upon him, second, because he is the second Adam and the second father; no one on the face of the earth is except from his offspring, due to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We made his offspring the survivors﴾. He mentioned the family of Abraham to encourage those who acknowledge their being chosen to believe in the prophethood of the one who is the centre of their pride, and to incline them toward acknowledging his being chosen through his being of their company. He mentioned the family of Imran, although they are included in the first "family," to show further concern for the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, because the disagreement about his affair is deeply rooted. This is what calls for adding "family" (al) in the last two and not in the first two. It was also said that the meaning of "family" in both places is "self" (nafs), i.e., He chose Adam, Noah, Abraham and Imran, and He mentioned "family" in them out of concern for their matter; but this is not worth anything. The intended meaning of the family of Abraham, as Muqatil said, is Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes (al-Asbat). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them, that they are whoever was upon his religion, like "the family of Muhammad" (ﷺ) in one of its usages. The intended meaning of the family of Imran is Jesus, peace be upon him, and his mother Mary, daughter of Imran son of Mathan, from the descendants of Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both; this was said by al-Hasan and Wahb. It was also said that the intended meaning is Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and so Imran is then Imran son of Yashhar, father of Moses, as Muqatil said; and between the two Imrans there are one thousand and eight hundred years. The first opinion is apparent, because the surah is called "Al ʿImran," and the story of Jesus and Mary is not explained in any surah more extensively than in this surah, whereas nothing of the story of Moses and Aaron is mentioned in it at any length. This indicates that the Imran mentioned is the father of Mary. Also, what favours the meaning being the father of Mary is that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned her chosen status afterward and stated it explicitly, and He said, glorified is He: ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ etc. It is apparent that this explains the manner of the choosing referred to by His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and the family of Imran﴾; so this is of the type of repeating a name in two sentences, where the mind immediately takes the second to be the first, like "Honour Zayd; indeed Zayd is a virtuous man." If the intended meaning of the second were other than the first, there would be confusion for the listener. The preference for the last opinion on the ground that Moses is mentioned alongside Abraham in remembrance is not as strong as the preference for the first, as is not hidden.

Istifa' (choosing) means selection, and its origin is taking the choicest part of a thing, like istisfa'. Because it implies the meaning of preference, it takes ʿala ("over"). The intended meaning of "the worlds" is the people of the time of each one of them, i.e., each of them was chosen over the worlds of his time. Kingship enters into this, and interpretation contrary to the basic meaning is not preferred. From here, some have used the verse as evidence for the superiority of the Prophets over the angels. The aspect of choosing all the Messengers is that He, glorified is He, specially endowed them with holy souls and what befits them of spiritual qualities and bodily perfections, until they were distinguished, as it has been said, over all creation in form and character. They were made treasuries of the secrets of Allah, the Exalted, places where His names and attributes appear, the locus of His special manifestation among His servants, the place of descent of His revelation, and the conveyors of His command and prohibition. This is evident regarding the chosen ones mentioned in the verse among the Messengers. As for Mary, she has the greatest share of some of this.

It was also said: He chose Adam by creating him with His two Hands, teaching him the names, commanding the angels to prostrate to him, and settling him in His proximity. He chose Noah by making him the first Messenger sent with the prohibition of daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, and all other close relatives; and that he was the father of mankind after Adam; and by the answering of his supplication regarding both the disbelievers and the believers. He chose the family of Abraham by placing prophethood and the Book among them, and it suffices them as honour that the master of the chosen ones is from them. He chose Jesus and his mother by making them both a sign for the worlds.

If the family of Imran is meant as Moses and Aaron, then the aspect of Moses' being chosen, peace be upon him, is that Allah, the Exalted, spoke to him and that He wrote the Torah for him with His own hand. The aspect of Aaron's being chosen is that He made him a minister to his brother. As for the choosing of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is understood by way of priority, and not stating it explicitly is to indicate that there is no need for it, because the matter of his intimate friendship (khullah) is thoroughly famous, and because he is the elder of the Prophets and the exemplar of the Messengers. As for the choosing of our Prophet (ﷺ), it is understood from his inclusion in the family of Abraham, as we have indicated; and it is reinforced by the fact that the context of this discussion is for his sake, as the explanation of the connection in the words of Shaykh al-Islam indicates. It is also narrated from the leaders of the People of the House that they recite (and the family of Muhammad over the worlds), and according to that there is no difficulty.

Some people said: the intended meaning of the family of Abraham is Muhammad (ﷺ), who is treated as if he were the whole family, as hyperbole in praising him. In this there is the objection that our Prophet, although in reality he is on a level with all the Prophets, let alone the family of Abraham only, nevertheless this intention here is remote. Similar to this in remoteness, and even more so, is what some have mentioned concerning the verse: that when He commanded them to follow him (ﷺ) and obey him, and made obeying and following him a cause of Allah's love for them, and not obeying him a cause of Allah's wrath upon them and the removal of His love from them, He confirmed that by following it with what is the habit of Allah, the Exalted, regarding the choosing of His Prophets over their opponents and the subduing, humiliating and destroying of those opponents, as a warning to these rebels against following him (ﷺ). So He mentioned the choosing of Adam over the higher world, for He preferred him over all the angels, made them prostrate to him, and put Satan under a curse for his rebellion; and the choosing of Noah over the world, along with the extreme multitude of them, so He destroyed them by the flood and preserved Noah and his followers; and the choosing of the family of Abraham over the world, although the whole world was disbelieving, so He made their religion spread and humbled their opponents; and the choosing of Moses and Aaron over the world, so He made the magicians, despite their multitude, defeated before them, and Pharaoh, despite his greatness and the overpowering of his armies, defeated, and destroyed them. For this reason He specifically mentioned Adam, Noah and the two families, and did not mention Abraham and our Prophet, may Allah, the Exalted, bless them both and grant them peace, since Abraham was not overcome. This statement is to show that our Prophet (ﷺ) will prevail, and the intended meaning is not choosing through prophethood, so that the reason for the specification would be obscure. With this, the weakness of using it as evidence for the superiority of the Prophets over the angels became clear. End of quote.

It is objected that what is understood from choosing (istifa') is selection and preference, not victory over enemies. Moreover, the context is far from this interpretation. Ibn ʿAsakir and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he explained the choosing here as choosing for the mission (risalah), and similar is what Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan. Also, taking the family of Imran as Moses and Aaron is something the mind does not naturally move toward, as you have known. It seems that the one who said this, since he could not make choosing carry the meaning he intended regarding Jesus and his mother, was compelled to interpret it against the apparent meaning.
