You know that the verse is independent of entering into such narrow difficulties.

[Page 133 appears in the original here.]

﴿offspring, one of another﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute (badal, a substitution in apposition) for "the two families" (al-ālīn), or as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, circumstantial accusative) of them both. It was also said that it is a substitute for "Noah" and what follows him. It was permitted that it be a substitute for "Adam," with "and" (ma) as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to him. Abu al-Baqa' rejected this, saying that Adam is not among the offspring. The objection was answered: this rests on what al-Raghib and others have stated explicitly, that offspring (dhurriyya) may be applied to both fathers and sons, because it derives from dhara'a, "to create," and the father has offspring produced from him, while the offspring is produced from the father. However, the word dhurriyya most readily signifies progeny, and the discussion of it has already passed. The meaning is that they are one offspring, branching out, some from others in lineage, as the specification of them being "offspring" indicates. This was related from Abu ʿAbd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), and al-Jubba'i chose it. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Qatada, who said: ﴿some of them from others﴾ in intention, deeds, sincerity and monotheism.

The particle "min" (from) according to the first view is for the beginning of origin (ibtida'iyya), and the implication is one of approximation (taqribiyya). According to the second view it is for connection (ittisaliyya), and the implication is one of proof (burhaniyya). It was also said that it is for connection in both cases.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of the words of His servants, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ [34] of their deeds and of what their breasts conceal, so He chooses from among them whom He wills. The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) that confirms the meaning of what came before it.

[Page 134 marker appears in the source here.]

﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ is an explanation of the (divine) choosing and a description of how it occurred. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative position as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "Mention to them the time when she said (it)." It has also been said that it is accusative as an adverb modifying what precedes it, and that the phrase ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is (placed) in a manner of condescension (tanazzul), or that the phrase is "the All-Hearing." The separation between them by a foreign element is not harmful, because the grammarians allow wide latitude with adverbial phrases. It has also been said that it is an adverbial phrase modifying the meaning of choosing (al-istifa') implied by the verb "chose" (isṭafā) mentioned earlier, as if it were said: "And He chose the family of 'Imran when the wife said..." etc. In that case it is a coordination of sentences with sentences, not of single words with single words, so that it would not entail that the choosing of all of them occurred at that time.

The wife of 'Imran was Hanna daughter of Faqudha, as narrated by Ishaq ibn Bishr from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and by al-Hakim from Abu Hurayrah. She was the grandmother of 'Isa, peace be upon him. She had a sister named Ishaa', who was married to Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and she was the mother of Yahya. Thus 'Isa was the son of the daughter of the maternal aunt of Yahya, as many of the historians (akhbariyyun, transmitters of reports) mentioned. This is problematic in light of what al-Bukhari and Muslim reported in the hadith of the Mi'raj, in his (ﷺ) saying: "Then behold, I was with the two cousins: 'Isa son of Maryam and Yahya son of Zakariyya." The author of "al-Taqrib" replied that the hadith is to be understood figuratively, for a man often calls the daughter of his maternal aunt by the title "maternal aunt" out of honour towards her. The point is that between the two of them, peace be upon them both, there is this kind of kinship, namely the maternal relationship. It has also been said that Ishaa' was the sister of Hanna through the mother, and the sister of Maryam through the father, on the basis that 'Imran first married the mother of Hanna, who bore him Ishaa', then he married Hanna, based on the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters (rabā'ib) in their law, and she bore Maryam. Thus Ishaa' was the sister of Maryam through the father and her maternal aunt through the mother, since she was the sister of Hanna through the mother. However, this is contrary to what Muhyi al-Sunna (the Reviver of the Sunna, al-Baghawi) mentioned, that Ishaa' and Hanna were the two daughters of Faqudha. This (latter view) is distant, because there is no narration in either matter.

Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that Hanna, the wife of 'Imran, had been prevented from bearing a child and from menstruation. Then one day, while she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and her soul was stirred towards having a child. So she supplicated Allah, the Exalted, to grant her a male child. She then menstruated at that very moment. When she became pure, her husband came to her. When she became certain of the pregnancy, she said: "If Allah, the Exalted, saves me and I deliver what is in my womb, I will dedicate it (to Your service) as a liberated one (muharrar)." At that time only boys were dedicated in this way. Her husband said to her: "Do you think, if what is in your womb is a female, and a female is 'awrah (a matter of shame or weakness), what will you do?" She was distressed by this, and at that point she said: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as a dedicated one, so accept it from me.﴾ In reality this is a request for a male child, since a female is not accepted (for this service). The meaning is: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, so make it male," in the manner of "Free your slave on my behalf."

Some of the scholars (al-a'imma) took it as an emphasis of her vow, and as removing it from the form of a conditional (ta'liq) to the form of an unconditional statement (tanjiz). The lam in ﴿for You﴾ is the lam of causation (ta'lil), and the meaning is "for the service of Your House." A muharrar is one who does not work for worldly affairs, does not marry, devotes himself to the work of the Hereafter, worships Allah, the Exalted, and serves in the church. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Mujahid said: "The muharrar is the servant of the church (bay'a)." In another narration from him: "The pure one, who is not mixed with anything of worldly affairs." Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: "She meant a freed one, pure for Your obedience, whom I will not put to use for my own needs." In any case it derives from freedom (hurriyya), which has two aspects: that the rules of captivity (sibbi) do not apply to him, and that bad character traits and worldly vices do not dominate him.

Its accusative case is as a circumstantial (ḥāl) modifying "what" (mā), and its governing element is ﴿I have vowed﴾. It has also been said that it modifies the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, in which case the governing element is "being established" (al-istiqrar). The preference for the first view is not hidden. The circumstantial clause is either anticipated (muqaddara) or simultaneous (musahiba). Abu Hayyan permitted that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning "dedication," because it has the sense of the vow. The emphasis of the sentence indicates the intensity of desire for its content. The fronting of the prepositional phrase indicates the complete concern with it. The expression of the child with "mā" indicates the vagueness of his condition and his shortfall from the rank of the rational. Taqabbul (acceptance) means taking a thing with pleasure, and its origin is the exchange of a thing for a reward. Here taqabbal means iqbal (accept).

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing﴾ of all things heard, so You hear my supplication; ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ [35] of what has been and what will be, so You know my intention. This is a reason for the request for acceptance, in that His knowledge of the soundness of her intention and her sincerity necessitates that (acceptance), by His bounty and kindness. The emphasis of the sentence is for the purpose of the strength of her certainty in its content. The restriction of the attributes of hearing and knowledge to Him, the Exalted, is for the purpose of specifying her supplication and severing the rope of her hope from anything other than Him, glory be to Him, completely, in exaggeration of humility and entreaty. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam. The attribute of hearing is placed first because, although its objects are endless, they are not as numerous as the objects of the attribute of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when she gave birth to her﴾ The pronoun in "lamma" (when)... Since the speaker knew that what it refers to is feminine, it was permissible for him to feminize the pronoun that refers back to it, even though the word is masculine. As for the feminine in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said, "My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female"﴾, it is not on the basis of knowledge, but on the basis that every pronoun that falls between a masculine and a feminine, both of which are expressions of one referent, may be masculine or feminine, like: "al-kalam yusamma jumlah" (speech is called a sentence). And ﴿unthā﴾ (a female) is a state (ḥāl) in the position of the predicate, so the pronoun referring to (mā) was feminized, looking to the state, without considering in it the meaning of femininity, lest it be meaningless; or on the basis of interpreting it as a feminine word that is applicable to both masculine and feminine, like al-nafs (the soul), al-ḥablah (the pregnancy) and al-nasamah (the breath). So the feminine is not problematic, and ﴿unthā﴾ is not superfluous, but is a clarifying state. This is what has been said, and it is not free from scrutiny. The truth is that the pronoun refers to (what is in my womb), and the feminine in the first case is because the context calls for the manifestation of her femininity and its consideration within the scope of the condition, since the answer of (lamma) is built upon it, not upon the mere giving birth to some child. The feminine in the second is for the haste to present what overtook her of the disappointment of hope and the severing of the rope of expectation. ﴿Unthā﴾ is a confirmatory state of the pronoun, or a substitute for it. The purpose of this statement is not to inform, because information is either for benefit or for what follows from benefit, and the knowledge of God, exalted is He, encompasses both. Rather, it is merely for lamenting and grieving. Imam al-Marzuqi has said: the predicate may come in form for purposes other than informing, as in his saying:
"My people are those who killed Umaym, my brother; so when I shoot, (my arrow strikes me)"
For this statement is grief and lamentation, not information. The gist of the meaning here, as established, is: when she gave birth to a girl, she lamented to her Lord and grieved, since her hope had failed. On this basis there is no difficulty at all regarding the feminine, nor regarding the answer itself, nor regarding its following upon the condition. As for what has been said: it may be that the benefit of this statement is the belittling of the one dedicated, in order to attract acceptance, because whoever humbles himself before God Exalted, God raises him. So it is belittled in speech in comparison to what we have mentioned. As for the emphasis here, it has been said it is to refute her false belief; and perhaps it returns to care and emphasis on the lamentation she intended, and an allusion that it came from a broken heart and a soul captive to the bonds of deprivation.
Page 135
﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to﴾ The intent is not to refute her in her report of what He, exalted is He, knows better, as appears from the context. Rather, the clause is parenthetical, brought to exalt the newborn she gave birth to, to magnify its status, and to make her ignorant of its worth. That is: God knows best the thing she gave birth to, and what is attached to it of great matters, subtle secrets and clear signs, while she is unaware of all of that. "Mā" in this sense refers to "the thing placed (al-mawdu'ah)." It has been said that using "mā" rather than "man" suits the ignorance, for it is often used for what is unknown. Some took it as referring to the one who gave birth, meaning: God Exalted knows best the matter of Mary's mother when she lamented and grieved over the illusion of the failure of her hope, and that she has no connection to God Exalted whatsoever, since she has a great rank, and her dedication is a dedication that is not found in it, something without basis, and the eloquence of the composition rejects it.
Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, read ﴿what you gave birth to﴾ as God's address to her, and its purpose is also the magnification of the status of what was born: that is, you do not know the extent of what you have given birth to, and what God Exalted has placed in it.
Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ya'qub read (what I have given birth to) as being from her speech, which she said as an apology to God Exalted, for having given birth to a child unsuited to the purpose, or as consolation for herself: that is, God Exalted perhaps has a secret and wisdom in that, and perhaps this female is better than the male. The clause then serves to negate knowledge, not to make ignorant, because the servant looks to the outward condition and does not stand upon what lies within it of secrets. Taking Ibn 'Abbas's reading to this meaning, by making the address from her to herself, is very far-fetched; and the placement of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun of the addressee shows extreme exaltation.
﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ Another parenthetical clause, explaining what the first contains of magnification. It is not an explanation of its explicit statement, so as to be like an appositive, which is disallowed to be conjoined. The "al" in "al-dhakar" (the male) and "al-unthā" (the female) is for prior reference: as for the one in "al-unthā," it is because her mention preceded explicitly in His saying, exalted is He, in quotation: ﴿I have given birth to her as a female﴾; and as for the one in "al-dhakar," it is because of her saying: ﴿I vowed﴾ etc., since it is what she asked for, and dedication is only for a male. This is called the presumed reference (al-'ahd al-taqdiri), which is other than the mental reference, because her saying ﴿what is in my womb﴾ is suitable for both kinds, and her saying ﴿dedicated﴾ is a wish that it be male, so reference is made to what is in the womb according to her hope. It is also permissible that the clause be from her speech, so her intent would be the negation of the male's similarity to the female, and then the "al" is for the genus, as is apparent, because she did not intend a specific male and female, but rather that this genus is not like that genus. It is objected that the presumption that this is from her speech requires that it be "and the female is not like the male," because her intent is to belittle the female in comparison to the male, and the custom in such a case is that the likeness of the deficient is negated from the complete, not the reverse. It is answered that it proceeds according to the custom in such a case too, because the intent of Mary's mother is not to prefer the male over the female, but the reverse, magnifying God's gift over what she asked for. That is: the male whom I sought is not like the female whom God has given me, knowing that what the Lord does is better than what the servant wills. There is scrutiny in this: first, because the "al" in "al-dhakar" and "al-unthā" would then be for prior reference, which is contrary to the apparent meaning that most exegetes adopted; and second, because it contradicts the lamentation and grief derived from her saying: ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female﴾, for her grief is only because she preferred the male over the female, while what is understood from this answer is her preference of the female over the male. Unless her saying is taken as consolation for herself after she grieved over the gift of a female in place of the male she had asked for; yet the contradiction of the apparent meaning remains as it is. So it is better in the answer not to depart from the apparent meaning, and to examine what custom requires. Al-Zamakhshari in "al-Intisaf," after relating the objection and mentioning the rule, said: I have found the matter in this to be varied, and it has not been established for me that what they said is fixed. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾, where He negated the likeness of the deficient from the complete, since the perfection of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ is established in relation to women in general; and on that the expression of the wife of 'Imran came, and also His saying: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ End.
Page 136
The complete discussion on this point is what some researchers mentioned: that when a negation enters with "la" or other particles, or what has its meaning, upon an explicit comparison with its elements or some of them, it may bear two meanings: the preference of the compared, by meaning that it is not compared to such-and-such because its aspect of resemblance in it is superior and stronger, as in your saying: "Zayd is not like Hatim in generosity." And the opposite may be meant, by meaning that it is not compared to it because of the great distance between them, like the saying of the Arabs: "water, but not like Sada'; pasture, but not like al-sa'dan; a youth, but not like Malik," and his saying:
"The phantom's glance, but not like the night of the traveler by night."
It occurred in the "Commentaries on the Maqamat" and elsewhere that the Arabs did not use the negation with "la" in this way except for the second meaning, and that its use for preferring the compared is from the speech of the later writers, to the point that they objected to al-Hariri's saying:
"You arrived, but not like the going of the crow."
And the saying of the author of "al-Talwih" in his preface was criticized: "He attained a share of fame, but not like the fame of the sun at midday." The basis of the objection is on this, though perhaps it is not necessary, as indicated by the author of "al-Intisaf" with the verses he cited; and what al-Tha'alibi cited contrary to it in his book "al-Muntakhab": "So-and-so is good, but not like the moon; generous, but not like the rain." Even if what they mentioned is granted, meanings are not restricted by it, and what came in the negation with "la" intervening between the two sides is not in every negation. End. And it is as he said: among the precious meanings that should be preserved.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I have named her Mary﴾ is conjoined to ﴿I have given birth to her as a female﴾, which is in the accusative position as the object of "said"; and what lies between them, as you know, is a parenthesis of two clauses that are not reported speech, the second being a continuation of the first in meaning, as explained. For this reason some treated it as a parenthesis within a parenthesis, making it like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾. It was objected: how is it permissible for a parenthesis to come between the speech of Mary's mother and the speech of a speaker who is not permitted to be a parenthesis between the speech of another speaker? It was answered: the speech of Mary's mother is the speech of God Exalted, related from Mary's mother, and there is no distance in His speech, exalted is He, being a parenthesis between her two statements, which are the speech of God Exalted related from her. This is on the assumption that those two clauses are not from Mary's mother's speech. As for if they are from her speech, based on what preceded of the reading and the possibility, then there is no parenthesis.
It has been said: the purpose of presenting the naming before the One who knows the unseen is to draw near to Him, exalted is He, and to seek protection for her. For Mary in their language means "worshipper." Its remoteness is not hidden, for mere mention of naming her Mary hardly draws her near to Him, exalted is He, since drawing near to Him, exalted is He, occurs only through worship, and mere presentation of a name is not worship, so how could it draw near? Unless it is said: drawing near to God Exalted is through her love for worship, which her naming her daughter "worshipper" indicates, or the belief that God Exalted is one sought for refuge, who grants protection to whoever seeks refuge in Him from what he fears.
It is objected that this does not remove the doubt; rather it remains too, because what draws near in that case is what is in the heart of love and belief, not presenting that to One from whom no hidden thing is concealed. The better view is that the purpose of this is to show that she has not retracted her intention, even though what she gave birth to is a female, and that although she was not suited to the custodianship of the Bayt al-Maqdis, let her be among its female worshippers; and that she independently named her because her father had died while her mother was pregnant with her. Thus the fronting of the subject for restriction means: the naming is from me, and her father does not share it with me.
It has been said: in that there is an allusion to her orphanhood, seeking His compassion and making her orphanhood an intercessor for her. The view that the purpose of presenting her naming was lamentation and grief, that is, "I named her, not her father, because he did not care for her and did not turn to her, since men in general dislike daughters," is, along with being contrary to what most reports indicate and what most accounts state about her father's death while she was pregnant, something that leads to ascribing to the sacred ground of the righteous man 'Imran what ought to be exalted above, as is not hidden.
The discussion of Maryam in terms of form and meaning has already been presented. Some later scholars chose that it is an arabized form of "Mariyah," meaning "servant girl" (jariyah), and this is close to being the relied-upon view. The verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of naming infants on the day of birth rather than on the seventh day, because the apparent meaning is that she said this immediately upon the delivery. It has also been used as evidence, by the difference between the two objects, for the difference between the name and the named; and the discussion of this has already passed.

﴿And indeed I seek refuge for her in You﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction) with "indeed I have named her." He used the predicate of inna as a present-tense verb, ﴿uʿīdhuhā﴾, to indicate that the request is for continuous seeking of refuge without interruption. This differs from ﴿waḍaʿtuhā﴾ and ﴿sammaytuhā﴾ ("I gave birth to her" and "I named her"), where he used the two predicates in the past tense to indicate that those actions were completed. He placed the object of seeking refuge before the coordinated verb to give it emphasis.

The meaning of ﴿uʿīdhuhā bika﴾ is: I protect her and grant her protection by Your safeguarding. The root meaning of ʿawdh, as al-Rāghib said, is seeking refuge in another and clinging to him, as in the saying "fulān ʿādha bi-fulān" when he sought protection from him. From this comes ʿawdhah, which means an amulet or a charm. Abū Jaʿfar and Nāfiʿ read ﴿innī﴾ with a fatḥah on the first-person ya', and likewise in all places where the ya' is followed by a dammed alif, except in two places: ﴿biʿahdī﴾ and ﴿ātūnī ufrigh﴾.

﴿Dhurriyyatahā﴾ is coordinated with the object pronoun (the pronoun in the accusative). In specifying both her protection and the protection of her offspring there is an allusion to requesting that the child remain alive until she grows up, and a request for her to have descendants. This is the case when ʿiʿādhah (protection) is taken in its sense of protection from harm.

﴿Min al-shayṭān al-rajīm﴾ [36]: that is, the one who is driven away. The root of rajm is throwing stones. It means safeguarding her from his seduction, which leads to sins, since that begins only after puberty, for there is no legal obligation before it. If the protection is understood to be a safeguard from him in general, then both requests are understood from the final expression.

This is supported by what al-Shaykhān (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No child is born except that Satan touches him when he is born, and so he cries out from his touch, except Mary and her son." In some of its chains: a screen was set up between him and her, and Satan intended to stab with his finger, but the stab fell upon the screen. In the narration of Isḥāq ibn Bishr from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child of Adam is touched by Satan, who stabs him with his finger when he falls to the earth, and for this reason he cries out, except for Mary and her son, for Iblīs did not reach them."

The judge ʿAbd al-Jabbār struck at these reports with the finger of his thought, saying that they are khabar al-wāḥid (solitary reports) contrary to evidence, because Satan only calls to evil those who have discernment. Also, if he were able to do this act, he could destroy the righteous. Furthermore, why did it single out ʿĪsā and his mother over all the other prophets? And if the touch or prodding were present, its effect would remain, but it does not. Al-Zamakhsharī claimed that, if the report is accepted as sound, the meaning is that every newborn is one whom Satan hopes to seduce, except Mary and her son, for they were protected (maʿṣūmān), and likewise everyone who shares their attribute, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾. His crying out from the touch is an imaginative representation (takhyīl) and depiction of Satan's desire for him, as if he touches him and strikes him with his hand. Similar to this imaginative expression is the saying of Ibn al-Rūmī:

"When the world announces through its vicissitudes what is to come, the crying of the infant at the hour of birth is its announcement."

As for the true nature of prodding and touching, as the ignorant literalists (ahl al-ḥashw) imagine, no, for even if Iblīs were given power over people to prod them, the world would be filled with screaming and wailing because of the prodding by which he tests us. End of quote.

It is not hidden that reports on this subject are numerous, and most of them are recorded in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the Sahih collections). The matter is not impossible, and the truthful one (peace and blessings be upon him) has informed of it, so it should be received with acceptance. The imagery upon which al-Zamakhsharī relied is worth nothing, for touching with the hand may indeed be suitable for that, but crying out is not. Moreover, most of the narrations do not allow such an interpretation. As for his saying "the world would be filled with wailing," we say: it is already full, for no child is born except that he cries out. Being able to inflict that prod does not mean he can do it at all times. How could it be otherwise, when in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Were it not that the angels guard you, the devils would surround you as flies surround honey." In another narration: "The jinn would snatch you away." The words of God Most High ﴿For him are successive guardians before and behind him﴾ have been explained in one of the views as referring to this. By this, the objection of the judge is also refuted, that if he were able to do this act he could destroy the righteous. The lasting of the mark, indeed even its occurrence, is not necessary for touching or prodding. The restriction (ḥaṣr) is made with regard to what is usual, and the singling out of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and his mother is an announcement that the supplication of the wife of ʿImrān was answered in the most complete way, so that those who seek the Lord turn to God Most High with all their hearts. Or one may assume a specification that restricts it. On both assumptions, the Prophet (ﷺ) is excluded from the generality, so there is no implication that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, is superior in this respect. This is supported by the speaker being excluded from the generality of his own speech, and a group of scholars held this view. It is confirmed by what al-Jalāl narrated in al-Bahjah al-Saniyyah from ʿIkrimah, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, the earth was lit with light. Iblīs said: "Tonight a child has been born who will corrupt our affairs." His troops said to him: "Go to him." So he came, and Jibrīl, peace be upon him, pushed him, and he fell at ʿAdan. This is better than leaving the general term on its generality.

The statement that it is not improbable that ʿĪsā and his mother alone have this virtue, to the exclusion of the other prophets, peace be upon them, and that this does not imply that he is superior to them, since something may be found in the one who is less excellent that is not found in the more excellent, is acceptable. Under either case, whether the one is excellent or less excellent, there is no difficulty with the reports from that perspective. Yes, it may appear problematic for their apparent meaning that the protection of Mary's mother was after the birth, so it cannot be taken as protection from the touch that occurs at the time of birth. It is answered that the touch is nothing but at the separation, which is the birth, and the protection comes with it. The only difference is that he expressed it with the present tense, as we have indicated, for the purpose of continuity. So let this be considered.

And it is strange that some of the people of the Sunnah follow the Muʿtazilah in interpreting such sound hadiths, merely out of inclination toward the nonsense of the philosophers, when leaving them on their apparent meaning does not muddy anyone's drink nor narrow their path. We ask Allah, Exalted, to grant us success in what pleases Him, and to make our future state better than our past.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 37 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾, meaning He was pleased with Maryam in the vow in place of a male. In this there is a comparison of the vow to a gift, and of God's good pleasure to acceptance. ﴿Her Lord﴾, meaning the Lord of Maryam, who brings her to the perfection fitting for her. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the wife of 'Imran, as evidenced by the fact that she is the one who addressed and called out with her words: ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to her﴾, etc. But the first view is preferable. ﴿With a good acceptance﴾. The *ba'* (with) here is like its use in "I wrote with the pen." *Qabul* (acceptance) is that by which a thing is received, like *su'ut* (a nasal medicine) and *ladud* (a medicine poured into the side of the mouth), which is what is poured into the nose or the mouth. That is, He accepted her in a good manner by which vows are accepted, which is His singling her out to take the place of a male in the vow, and He did not accept any female before her. Or, He received her from her mother immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for service and ministry. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: When she gave birth to her, Hannah feared that a female would not be accepted as a dedicated offering, so she wrapped her in a cloth and placed her in the Temple of Jerusalem among the readers (of the Torah). The readers cast lots over her, because she was the daughter of their leader. Each asked who would take her. Zakariyya, who was the chief of the rabbis, said: "I will take her, and I am the most entitled among you to her, because her aunt is with me." The readers said: "But we will cast lots over her, and whoever's lot comes out is the most entitled to her." So they called for their pens with which they wrote the revelation, gathered them in one place, and covered them. Zakariyya said to one of the boys who had not reached puberty among those in the Temple of Jerusalem: "Put your hand in and bring out one." He put his hand in and brought out Zakariyya's pen. They said: "We are not satisfied. Rather, let us throw the pens into the water. Whoever's pen goes against the current of the water and then rises, he is the one who will take care of her." So they threw their pens into the River Jordan, and Zakariyya's pen rose against the current. They said: "Let us draw lots a third time. Whoever's pen flows with the water, he is the one who will take care of her." So they threw their pens, and Zakariyya's pen flowed with the water, while their pens rose against the current. At that point Zakariyya took her. It is also permissible that the *ba'* is for accompaniment (*mula-basah*).

*Qabul* is a verbal noun, and it is one of the irregular verbal nouns. There is an omitted modifier, and the meaning is: He was pleased with her, while she was characterised by something acceptable and by a face of good pleasure, namely that which places her in the place of males because of the honour she was singled out for. It is also permissible that *tafa''ala* here means *istaf'ala*, like *ta'ajjala* meaning *ista'jala* (to hasten). The meaning would then be: her Lord received her and welcomed her from the very first moment of her birth with a good acceptance, and He showed honour to her at that time. There is a proverb: "Take the matter by its counterparts." It is also permissible that the *ba'* is extra (*za'ida*), and *qabul* is a verbal noun emphasising the preceding verb with the augmentations removed, meaning: He accepted her with a good acceptance. The apparent sense was deviated from to indicate that the acceptance was accompanied by complete good pleasure and was in harmony with the divine care, for the form *tafa''ala*, in its basic usage, indicates effort and that the act is contrary to the nature of the doer. Although what is meant with regard to God, exalted is He, is what results from it of perfect strength and abundance of the act. It is also conceivable, though at a very remote distance, that the *ba'* is for accompaniment, in the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: He accepted her vow together with a good acceptance of her mother's supplication for her and for her offspring, since He protected both of them from the accursed Satan from the first moment of birth to the end of life.

﴿And He made her grow with a good growth﴾, meaning the Lord raised her with a good upbringing in worship and obedience to her Lord. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. In another narration from him, he said that He perfected her creation, so she would grow in one day what others grow in a year. It has also been said: He took care of her with what would benefit her in all her conditions. So in the speech there is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*) or a metonymy (*majaz mursal*) through the relation of concomitance (*'alaqat al-luzum*), since the farmer tends his crop by watering it when needed, protecting it from calamities, and uprooting whatever plants choke it. ﴿Growth﴾ here is a verbal noun not from the verb's own form, and it stands in for *inbat* (causing to grow). It has been said that the implied construction is: "so she grew a growth." *Nabat* and *nabt* have the same meaning, and both may be used to refer to what grows.

﴿And Zakariyya took charge of her﴾, and he was of the descendants of Sulayman son of Dawud, peace be upon them both, meaning God joined her to him and made him her guardian and the guarantor of her welfare, as mentioned in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. All of this is among the effects of His power, exalted is He, and there was no revelation to him about that. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read the *fa'* with a doubled consonant (*kaffala*), and they read ﴿Zakariyya﴾ as a short form (with the final vowel without the *alif* of length), except that 'Asim in the narration of Ibn 'Ayyash read it with the *alif*. It is then the object of *kaffala*. The rest read the *fa'* without doubling (*kafala*), and they lengthened ﴿Zakariyya﴾ and put it in the nominative as the subject. There are two other dialectal forms for it: first, *Zakariyy* with a doubled *ya'* and without *alif*; second, *Zakar* without *ya'*, and it is not declined because of being a proper noun and a foreign word. It has been said that it is because of the feminine *alif* (of the ending). Ubayy read *wa-akfalaha* (and he made him take charge of her). Mujahid read *fa-taqabbalha rabbaha wa-anbitha wa-kaffilha* (so accept her, O her Lord, and make her grow, and make Zakariyya her guardian) in the form of supplication for the three verbs, and the word *rabbaha* in the accusative as an address, meaning: accept her, O her Lord and her Lord, and make Zakariyya her guardian. God has responded to her supplication in all of this. What the majority hold, and what the reports attest, is that Zakariyya's guardianship of her was from the very beginning of her affair. Some have claimed that he took charge of her after she was weaned and had grown good growth, but this is not a strong view.

﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary﴾. This is an explanation of her acceptance, and for this reason it is not joined with a conjunction. According to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, the *mihrab* was a chamber built for her in the Temple of Jerusalem, whose door was in the middle of the wall, and one could not ascend to it except by a ladder, like the door of the Ka'ba. It has been said that what is meant is the mosque, for their mosques were called *mahareeb*. It has also been said that it is the most honoured place and its foremost part, which in one opinion is the place of the imam in the mosque. Its origin is the form *mif'al*, an intensive form like *mit'an*, and so the place was named with it because the warriors (*muharibin*) in it are many. It has also been said that it is a noun of place, and it was named that because it is the place where the battle with Satan takes place, or because people compete for it. One of the Maghribis said in praise:

*He combined bravery and humility before his Lord; how beautiful is the sanctuary in the sanctuary!*

The placing of the adverbial phrase before the subject is to show the full care for her affair. The accusative of ﴿the sanctuary﴾ is by extension (*tawassu'*), since the verb properly takes *fi* (in) or *ila* (to). The mention of the subject is said to be for the separation of the clause. ﴿Whenever﴾ (*kullama*) is an adverb of time, on the basis that *ma* is verbal (*masdariyya*), and the time is omitted, or it is an indefinite noun described by a relative clause whose meaning is "time," and the returning pronoun is omitted. Its governing element is its answer clause, by agreement, since what is in the place of the object of a preposition does not govern what precedes it, and the difference mentioned concerning conditional particles does not apply to it. Some people have erred, saying that it is governed by the verb of the condition, and they claimed that this is more fitting in meaning, and so they added a camel to the chess (i.e., they went beyond what is right). The meaning is: every time he entered upon her, or every moment in which he entered upon her.

﴿He found with her provision﴾, meaning he found and came upon it in her presence, or that it was present in her presence. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Rabi' who said: No one entered upon her except him, and when he went out he locked seven doors upon her. He would find with her summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. The *tanwin* (indefiniteness) is for glorification. From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, it is reported that this was from the fruits of Paradise. But what most people hold is that this was provided to her in place of breastfeeding, for it has been reported that she never suckled from a breast at all. It has also been said that this occurred after she had grown up. In the narration of Ibn Bishr from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: "Zakariyya, peace be upon him, hired a wet-nurse for her. When two years had passed for her, she was weaned and left alone in the sanctuary, and he locked the door upon her, and no one else took care of her affairs."

﴿He said: O Maryam﴾. This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*). ﴿From where is this to you?﴾, meaning: from where to you is this provision, which does not resemble the provisions of this world, while the doors are locked behind you? The coming of *anna* with the meaning of "from where" or "how" has been discussed before. He cited for the first meaning the verse:

*He desired, in the valley of the tamarisk, Zaynab as a stray; so how, and from where, will she come to the tamarisk-place?*

And for the second meaning, the verse:

*From where and how did the longing pull you back, from a place with no youthful inclination and no doubt?*

The preposition is omitted from *anna*, as *fi* is omitted from certain adverbs that are obligatorily adverbial, such as *ma'a* and *saharin*, because when a thing is known in one place it may be omitted. The verified view is that adverbs are the place of extension, because of the frequency of their use, and every adverb is used with the preposition connected to it, with which its use is common, because its connection to what it modifies is by these prepositions, and so it may be omitted, just as *fi* may be omitted. However, since the basic meaning is what is used for the sense of place, its omission is regular in the inflecting and non-inflecting adverbs. Other prepositional connectors of adverbs are not omitted except with what is frequent among non-inflecting adverbs, to lower their rank below that of *fi*, as in *al-Kashf*.

The verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of *karama* (miraculous favour) to the saints (*awliya'*), because Maryam, according to the prevailing view, had no prophethood. This is the view held by the People of the Sunna and the Shi'a, while the Mu'tazila disagreed. Al-Balkhi among them answered concerning the verse that it was a *irhas* (preliminary sign) and a foundation for the prophethood of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Al-Jubba'i answered that it was a miracle for Zakariyya, peace be upon him. The latter view was refuted by saying that the confusion of the matter for him precludes that. Perhaps this is based on the outward sense; otherwise, whether this expression necessarily implies actual confusion is open to question, for it may be intended to show the wonder in what is there, through her speech and the like. The claim that Zakariyya's confusion about whether it was a miracle does not conflict with its being a miracle, because of his confusion about whether it came from Paradise or from the gardens of this world, is not a valid point, as is not hidden.

﴿She said﴾. This is a resumption like the one before it. ﴿It is from God's presence﴾. It has been said: she meant from Paradise. It has been said: from what God has provided me, not through the agency of any human, so do not be astonished or find it strange. It has been said that she spoke these words when a child, as 'Isa did. Those who spoke in this manner have been gathered, and they number eleven persons, and al-Jalal al-Suyuti has put them into verse, saying:

*The Prophet Muhammad spoke in the cradle, (and Yahya, 'Isa, al-Khalil and Maryam);
and Jurayj in his cradle, the witness of Yusuf, and a child of the People of the Trench, as Muslim narrates;
and a child to whom the slave-woman passed, who is called "She commits fornication" yet does not speak;
and the child of the hairdresser in the time of Pharaoh; and in the time of al-Hadi, the blessed one concludes.*

[Page 141]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 37 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah provides for whomever He wills﴾ of His servants, without reckoning ﴿without reckoning﴾ [37]. Its meaning has already been explained. The clause gives the reason for its being "from the presence of Allah." Apparently it is part of Mary's speech, in which case it occupies a place in the accusative case, falling under the verb of saying. Al-Tabari said that it is not part of her speech but is a new statement from Allah, the Exalted, informing His Prophet (ﷺ). The first view is preferable.

Abu Ya'la transmitted from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spent several days without eating any food, until it grieved him. He went around the houses of his wives, but found nothing with any of them. He came to Fatimah and said: "O my daughter, do you have anything I may eat, for I am hungry?" She said: "No, by Allah." When he left her, a neighbour of hers sent her two loaves and a piece of meat. She took it from her and placed it in a dish of hers, and said: "I will prefer the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with this over myself and those with me," and they were all in need of a satisfying meal. So she sent Hasan or Husayn to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he came back to her. She said to him: "May I be your ransom, my father, Allah, the Exalted, has brought something that I have kept hidden for you." He said: "Bring the dish, O my daughter." She uncovered the dish, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. When she looked at it she was astonished, and she knew that it was a blessing from Allah, the Exalted. So she praised Allah, the Exalted, and brought it to the Prophet (ﷺ). When he saw it, he praised Allah, the Exalted, and said: "From where is this for you, O my daughter?" She said: "O my father, it is from the presence of Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whomever He wills without reckoning." Then he praised Allah, the Glorified, and said: "Praise be to Allah, who has made you resemble the chief of the women of the Children of Israel." For she, whenever Allah, the Exalted, provided her with sustenance and she was asked about it, would say: "It is from the presence of Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whomever He wills without reckoning." Then he gathered Ali, Hasan and Husayn, and gathered the people of his household, until they were satisfied, and the food remained as it was. Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, then generously gave to her neighbours.

* * *

Furthermore, from the approach of allusive interpretation (ishara) in the verses: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾. He forbade the believers from befriending the disbelievers, because in reality there is no affinity between them, and because of the difference between darkness and light, and shade and scorching heat. Friendship requires affinity, and when it is not present, the friendship is merely out of show or hypocrisy, and Allah, the Exalted, does not love the showy nor the hypocrites. For this reason, the people of Allah, the Exalted, forbade the aspirants from befriending those who deny. For the darkness of denial, Allah forbid, resembles the darkness of unbelief, and it may accumulate and block the path of faith. ﴿And whoever does that has nothing of﴾ the allegiance of ﴿Allah﴾, the Exalted, ﴿in anything﴾ worthy of consideration, since there is in him no pure luminosity by which he could become suitable for the Divine Presence. ﴿Except when you fear from them a fear﴾, then friendship becomes permissible outwardly. This applies to the weak. As for one whose certainty is strong, he fears none but Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, that is, He calls you to the tawhid of vision (tawhid 'iyani), so that your fear is not of anyone else. ﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾, so fear none but Him. Most of them hold that this is an address to the elite of the knowers, for one does not fear the Self of One whom he does not know. He warned those beneath them with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾.

Ibrahim al-Khawwas said: The sign of fear in the heart is the constancy of watchfulness (muraqabah), and the sign of watchfulness is the attentiveness to the states that descend. ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts﴾ of friendship ﴿or reveal it, Allah will know it﴾, for He is with every breath and every passing thought. ﴿And He knows what is in﴾ the heavens of spirits and ﴿the earth﴾ of bodies. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾, so no affair preoccupies Him from another affair, and no manifestation restricts Him from another manifestation. ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil﴾, because everything a person does or says leaves an imprint upon his self and is inscribed upon the pages of the heavenly souls. However, because he is occupied with sensory preoccupations and imaginative and fanciful perceptions, he does not see those imprints nor perceive those lines. But when he is stripped of the world of density, he sees, witnesses and beholds what the pen of readiness has written. Then, if he finds evil, ﴿his self wishes﴾ and desires ﴿that between it and that there were a great distance﴾, so that it may punish it with it. ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾. He repeated it for emphasis, lest they do what deserves His punishment. ﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, that is, to all of them, and therefore He warned them. Or it means to those who have attained the station of servanthood and cut themselves off to Him entirely.

﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾, for I am the master of the lovers, ﴿and Allah will love you﴾. In the view of the knowers, the reality of love is the burning of the heart with the fires of longing, the spirit's refreshment with the pleasure of passion, the immersion of the senses in the sea of intimacy, the purification of the self with the waters of holiness, the seeing of the Beloved with the eye of totality, the closing of the eye of totality to the two worlds, and the flight of the secret into the unseen of the unseen, and the lover's taking on the character of the Beloved. This is the root of love.

As for its branch, it is conformity with the Beloved in all that He is pleased with, and accepting His trial with the attribute of contentment, and submission to His decree and destiny, on condition of fidelity, and following the Sunnah of the Chosen one (ﷺ).

As for its etiquette, it is detachment from desires and permissible pleasures, tranquillity in solitude and watchfulness, inhaling the fragrances of the attributes, and humility and lowliness in movements and stillnesses:
"The wretched people of passion, even their graves
are upon them the dust of humiliation among the tombs."

This cannot occur except after the spirit sees with the eye of the secret the witnessing of the Truth in the attribute of beauty and the goodness of eternity, not in the attribute of bounties and blessings. For when love arises from the perception of blessings, it is conditioned. The reality of love is that which has no cause in it between the lover and the Beloved except the essence of the Beloved. For this reason they said: Love is not valid from one who distinguishes between Fire and Paradise, between joy and affliction, between obligation and recommendation, or between compensation and objection. It is valid only from one who has forgotten everything and been immersed in witnessing the Beloved and annihilated in Him:
"O my two companions, if you had loved, you would know
the place of passion from the heart's lover, its pain.
Remember, and remembrance inspires longing, and the one in passion
yearns, and whoever clings to love is afflicted by it.
A passion upon the despair of passion and its hope,
and a longing upon the distance of the desired and its nearness."

It is said: Love is of three kinds. The first kind: the love of the common people, which is looking at the favour, from seeing the kindness of the benefactor. Hearts are created to love whoever is kind to them. This love changes, and it belongs to those who follow deeds, seeking reward for what they do. About this Abu al-Tayyib says:
"I am not one who seeks love in exchange for a bribe,
weak in passion, hoping for reward upon it."

The second kind: the love of the elect who follow the moral qualities, who love Him out of veneration and magnification, and because He is worthy of that. To this kind the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded when he said: "What an excellent servant Suhayb is! If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." And Rabi'a, may Allah have mercy on her, said:
"I love You with two loves: love of passion,
and love because You are worthy of it."
This love does not change, forever, because beauty and majesty endure into eternity.

The third kind: the love of the elect of the elect who follow the states. It arises from the divine attraction in the hiding-places of "I was a hidden treasure." The people of this love are those prepared for the perfection of knowledge. Its reality is that the lover is annihilated by its power, so that he remains without "he." Perhaps its possessor remains bewildered and intoxicated, neither alive so that he may be hoped for, nor dead so that he may be wept over. Concerning this it has been said:
"They say love is like fire in the inner parts.
Indeed they lied; fire flares and dies down.
It is nothing but a spark touched by its wood
moist, so it neither flares nor blazes."

The word of love is sufficient in explaining it, for it consists of ḥ and b. The ḥ is one of the throat letters, and the b is a labial. This contains an allusion that passion, so long as it has not taken hold of his heart, his tongue, his inner and outer, his secret and open, is not called love. A full explanation of that would be lengthy. This is the love of the servant for his Lord. As for the love of His Lord for him, it is also varied, even if it proceeds from one source. It attaches to the common people from the aspect of mercy, as though it were said to them: follow me with righteous deeds, and Allah, the Exalted, will single you out with His mercy. It attaches to the elect from the aspect of grace, as though it were said to them: follow me with noble morals, and He will single you out with the manifestation of the attributes of beauty. It attaches to the elect of the elect from the aspect of attraction, as though it were said to them: follow me by giving up existence, and He will single you out by drawing you to Himself. There the distance is removed from the separation, and the dawn appears to the one who has two eyes. A drop of this love suffices in place of a river:
"In an intoxication from it, even if he lived a single hour,
you would see the age a servant obedient, and the command His."

﴿And He will forgive you your sins﴾, that is, your disobediences which preceded from you, contrary to following, and He will not punish you for them. Or it means He forgives your sins by covering the darkness of your attributes with the lights of His attributes. Or it means He forgives the sins of your existence and gives you in their place an existence that does not perish, as He said: "When I love him, I become his hearing by which he hears, and his sight by which he sees," the hadith. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾, who expiates your errors and erases the sins of your attributes and your existence, ﴿Merciful﴾, who grants you in exchange for that good deeds, attributes, and a true existence better than that.

﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾, for the aspirant must follow what is desired. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, if they turn away, then they are disbelievers, denying, veiled. ﴿Then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾, because of the deficiency of their readiness to manifest His beauty in them. ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of Imran over the worlds﴾. Choosing (istifa') is more general than love and intimacy, so it includes all the prophets, and their ranks differ in it, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾. The most distinguished rank is love, and His saying, the Exalted, points to it: ﴿And He raised some of them in degrees﴾. Then intimacy (khullah), and in its wording there is an allusion to that through the articulation points of the letters. The most general is choosing. He chose Adam by teaching him the attributes, uniting his two hands, and causing the cosmos to prostrate to him. He chose Noah, who is the second father, by that fatherhood and by what he had with his people. He chose the family of Abraham, namely the prophets from his descendants, by the manifestation of the lights of His special self-disclosure upon the horizons of their existence. He chose the family of Imran by making them a sign to the worlds, descendants some of whom are from others in religion and reality, for birth is of two kinds: physical and spiritual. Every prophet who followed a prophet in tawhid and gnosis, and in what relates to the inner dimension of the foundations of religion, is his son, like the spiritual sons of the shaykhs. The son is the secret of his father. It is possible to say: Adam is the Spirit at the first of its stations of manifestation; Noah is it in its second station of descent; Abraham is the heart, which Nimrod of the self threw into the fires of trials and hurled into them with the catapult of desires; his family are the spiritual powers. Imran is the intellect, the leader, in the sanctuary house of the body, and his family are those who follow him in that house and take him as a model. All of that is descendants, some from others, by the unity of origin and the agreement of the path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 37 (part 3 of 3):

﴿When the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, freed (for Your service)﴾ — freed from the bondage of the self, sincerely devoted to Your worship, free from inclination toward what is other than You. ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance﴾. Al-Wasiti said: she was preserved from being perceived by creation. ﴿And He made her grow a goodly growth﴾, in that He watered her with the waters of power and made her a tree bearing the fruit of prophethood. ﴿And Zechariah became her guardian﴾, because of the purity of his inner secret, and a thing's likeness is drawn toward it. ﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the mihrab (the sanctuary, or prayer niche), he found provision with her﴾: this is what you have known. It is also permissible that what is meant is spiritual provision, namely the knowledge, realities, sciences and wisdoms that were poured upon her from Allah, the Exalted. The specification by "with her" (ʿindahā, "from the presence of") indicates that it is more noble than bodily provisions.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, through some chains, from Mujahid that he said: "provision" means knowledge. It may also be said, in a manner similar to the first, so that the correspondence of what is in the horizons with what is in the souls may be complete. ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾: she is the soul in the first of the stages of its obedience to 'Imran, the intellect. ﴿I have dedicated to You what is in my womb﴾: and it is the boy of the heart. ﴿Freed﴾: not in bondage to any of the created things. ﴿So when she gave birth to her, she said: My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾. She is also a soul, except that she is more perfect than it in rank, and a kind gives birth to its kind. ﴿And Allah knows best what she bore﴾, for He knew that from this female there would appear a wondrous marvel, whereas the secrets are hidden from anyone other than Him, glorified is He. ﴿And I have named her Mary﴾, and she is the worshipper.
Page 144
﴿And I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from Satan the accursed﴾: and he is the carnal appetites, which veil the holy soul from the gardens of the dominion. ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance﴾: and this is His singling her out by pouring His lights upon her. ﴿And He made her grow a goodly growth﴾: and He elevated her in that by which her development is completed, a good ascent, untainted by obstacles and attachments. ﴿And Zechariah became her guardian﴾: the readiness. ﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her﴾: and he turned toward her in the mihrab of her worship, which was built for her in the house of the holy place of the heart. ﴿He found provision with her﴾: by which the spirits are nourished in the world of the dominion. ﴿He said: O Mary, from where is this for you?﴾, this great provision. ﴿She said: It is﴾ bestowed ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾, exempt from being carried by the hand of thoughts. ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, who combines the attributes of beauty and majesty, ﴿provides for whom He wills﴾, and He pours upon them from His knowledge according to their capacities ﴿without reckoning﴾. Glorified is He, the God, the Generous, the Noble, the Bestower.

[Page 145 of the original]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 38:**

﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord﴾. This is an independent narrative, placed in the course of the story of Maryam for the sake of complete connection with it, and because mentioning it confirms the purpose for which the story was told. (*Hunā*) is a *ẓarf makān* (adverbial of place), the *lām* indicates distance, and the *kāf* indicates address. The meaning is: in that place, where he was sitting beside Maryam in the *miḥrāb* (prayer niche). *Hunālika* is a *ẓarf* that is always used adverbially, and it may be governed by *min* and *ilā*. It has also been allowed that it refers to time, metaphorically, since *hunā*, *thumma* and *ḥaythu* are often used in that sense. It is connected to *daʿā* (called upon). The placing of the adverb first indicates that he turned to supplication immediately, without delay. Al-Zajjaj said: *hunā* here is used metaphorically for direction and state, meaning: from that state Zakariyya called upon (his Lord), just as you say: "From here I said such-and-such," and "From *hunālika* I said such-and-such," meaning: from that direction and that place.

Ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: When Zakariyya found with Maryam winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter, which Gabriel brought to her, he said to her: "From where do you have this out of season?" She said: "It is provision from Allah. Allah brings it to me; indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning." Zakariyya then longed for a child and said: "Indeed He who brought Maryam this fruit out of its season is capable of making my wife fit for childbearing and granting me a child from her." At that point he called upon his Lord. This was three nights before the end of Muharram. Zakariyya rose, performed ghusl (ritual washing), and then earnestly supplicated Allah, the Exalted.

It is also said that (the angel) made him hopeful for a child, so he prayed, even though he was an old man in decline and his wife was barren. The circumstance alerted him to the possibility of a barren woman bearing a child in old age, in several ways. The first is what the report indicates: that a child is like fruit, and barrenness is like being out of season. The second: when he saw a female accepted in place of a male, he became aware that an old man may stand in place of a young man, and a barren woman in place of one who bears. The third: when he saw that a child was accepted in place of an adult for the purpose of service, he took note of this. The fourth: when he saw Maryam speaking out of season, he took note that his wife might give birth out of season. The fifth: when he heard from Maryam, ﴿Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾, he took note that she might bear without preparation. The defects in some of these aspects are not hidden. In any case, what he saw alone was not the sole cause that prompted him to turn to supplication. Rather, it was a part of the complete cause, among which was his advanced age, the weakness of his strength, and his fear of his successors (*mawālī*), as explained in the surah of Maryam.

(*Qāla*) is an explanation of the supplication and a statement of its manner: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself﴾. The two prepositional phrases (*al-jārrān*) are connected to what precedes them, and this is permitted because their meanings differ. *Min* here indicates the starting point metaphorically, meaning: give me from Your presence ﴿good offspring﴾, that is, blessed, as al-Suddi said. It was also said: righteous, pious, and pure in deed. It is permitted that the last prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted element that functions as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of *dhurriyya*. The request came in the form of *hibah* (gift), because a gift is pure benevolence that is not given in exchange for anything. This suits what the father had no part in, because of his old age, and what the mother had no part in, because she was barren and could not bear. It is as if he said: give me offspring without the usual means. *Dhurriyya* in the common usage means offspring. It applies to the singular and the plural, and to the male and the female.

Here the intended meaning is one child. Al-Farrāʾ said: he made *al-ṭayyiba* feminine because the word *dhurriyya* is feminine in form. Feminine and masculine forms sometimes follow the wording and sometimes follow the meaning. This applies to common nouns (*asmāʾ al-ajnās*), as in the verse:

"Your father is a caliph whom another bore, and you are the caliph of that perfection."

This differs from proper names, since one cannot say "*jāʾat Ṭalḥa*" (for the masculine name Ṭalḥa), because a proper name refers only to that particular person, so if it is masculine, only the masculine form is permitted.

﴿Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ [38]. He meant: the one who answers much those among His creatures who call upon Him. This is a reason for what precedes it and a stirring of the chain of answering. In this there is a following of his great forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah who granted me in old age Ismaʿil and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾.

It was said: Allah, the Exalted, mentioned three formulations of his supplication. The first is this one. The second is ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾, etc. The third is ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone﴾, etc. This indicates that the supplication was repeated by him three times, each time in a different formulation. It also indicates that there was a period of time between the supplication and the answer, and this is made explicit by what has been reported in some traditions, that between them was forty years. But this is clearly open to objection, since the three formulations may be the narration of one single supplication, sometimes in brief, sometimes in extended form, and sometimes in a middle form. And this narration in these formulations is by meaning, since their language was not Arabic. For this reason it is reported from al-Ḥasan that when he (peace be upon him) called upon (his Lord) he said: "O Provider of Maryam's summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer, grant me from Your presence offspring," and he did not mention "O my Lord" in the supplication.

It was said: What indicates that it was one supplication followed by the announcement of good news is the particle *fa* (then/so) in the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 39 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the angels called him﴾. And in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya﴾.

The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is His majesty, in Maryam: ﴿Indeed We give you good tidings﴾ is that the good tidings followed the supplication immediately and were not delayed after it. As for the report that there was a period of forty years between the supplication and the answer, we have not found any trace of it in the "Sahihs" (the authentic collections). Yet some transmitted reports (mawquf, those ending with a companion) may suggest that there was an interval between the birth and the good tidings, as we will shortly indicate, God willing.

By "the angels" is meant Jibril (peace be upon him) alone, since he was the one who called out, as Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad mentioned that he used to recite (fa-nadahu Jibril, "Jibril called to him"). So the plural here is a figurative use for the singular, for glorification, or this is the attribution of an act of some to all. It was also said that the plural here is like your saying: "So-and-so rides horses and wears brocade." This was objected to on the grounds that this is only valid when an unspecified one is meant, whereas here a specific one is meant; so what came before is more likely to be intended. It was also said that the plural remains as it is and the caller was a group of angels. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (fa-nadihi) with imala and the masculine form.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "They mentioned the angels," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females﴾, and he used to recite it as (fa-nadahu al-mala'ikatu), and he would make it masculine throughout the Qur'an. Al-Khatib narrated from him that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it likewise.

﴿while he was standing﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of the calling, confirming what the fa' indicated, as we have pointed out. His saying, exalted: ﴿praying﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿standing﴾, or another circumstantial clause from the object, on the view that multiple circumstantial clauses may occur without conjunction or apposition; or it is a second predicate of the subject, according to the opinion of one who holds such a view. It was also said that the clause is a qualifier of "standing," and by prayer is meant the prayer consisting of words and actions, as is apparent and as most exegetes hold. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Thabit who said: "Prayer is service to God Almighty on earth. Had God Almighty known of anything better than prayer, He would not have said: ﴿So the angels called him while he was standing, praying﴾." It was also said that by it is meant supplication; the first view indicates that prayer was prescribed in their law.

﴿in the mihrab﴾, that is, in the masjid, or in the place of the imam within it, or in Maryam's chamber. The adverbial phrase is connected to ﴿praying﴾ or to ﴿standing﴾, on the assumption that ﴿praying﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿standing﴾, because the governing element for both is one thing, so no separation by a foreign element is required, as is required under the other possibilities. Thus they said. But what appears is that the matter falls under the category of dependence (tanazu'), for each of ﴿standing﴾ and ﴿praying﴾ may govern ﴿in the mihrab﴾ according to any of the grammatical possibilities mentioned. So reflect.

Then know that prayer in the well-known mihrabs present today in the masajid of the Muslims has been disliked by a group of imams, and 'Ali, may God honour his face, and Ibrahim, may God have mercy on him, held this view, as Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from them both. They are among the innovations that did not exist in the first era. On the authority of Abu Musa al-Juhani, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My community will remain in good as long as they do not take in their masajid altars like the altars of the Christians." And on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Ja'd who said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) used to say: Among the signs of the Hour is that altars will be taken in the masajid." And on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of these altars," meaning the mihrabs. The narrations on this are numerous, and al-Imam al-Suyuti has a separate treatise on it.

﴿That God gives you good tidings of Yahya﴾: that is, that God [gives good tidings]. After the removal of the preposition, which is regular with "anna," though in the resulting phrase it is permissible to consider either the accusative or the genitive case. The first is the view of Sibawayh, the second the view of al-Khalil. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited the hamzah of (inna) with a kasrah, and this is explained as an implied "say," which is the view of the Basrans, or as treating the calling as a kind of saying, which is the view of the Kufans. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (yubshiruka) from al-ibshar, and recited (yabshuruka) from the triliteral. Ibn Jarir narrated from Mu'adh al-Kufi who said: Whoever recites (yubashshiru) with the doubled letter, it is from bishara (good tidings); whoever recites (yabshuru) with a light form and a fatha on the ya', it is from surur (joy).

Yahya is a non-Arabic name according to the correct view. It was also said to be an Arabic name derived from the verb. The reason for its being diptote is, according to the first view, being a proper name and being non-Arabic; according to the second, being a proper name and the form of a verb. The claim that there is no decisive reason for its diptoteness, since it may be indeclinable, making the proper name a sentence by having a pronoun in it, as in the line of verse: "I was informed that my maternal uncles are the Banu Yazid," is not valid, because of the unnecessary strain in that possibility, which hardly serves as conclusive proof. Those who hold that it is Arabic include some who explain its naming by saying that God revived through him the womb of his mother, a view narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Others explain it by saying that God revived his heart with faith, a view narrated from Qatadah. It was also said he was named Yahya because God taught him to seek martyrdom, and martyrs are alive with their Lord, being provided for. It was also said because he lives by the knowledge and wisdom given to him. It was also said because God gives life to people through him with guidance. Al-Qurtubi said: "His name in the earlier Scripture was Hayy (living)." I have seen in the "Gospel of Matthew" that he, peace be upon him, was called John the Baptist, because he baptized people in his time, as the books of the Christians report.

The plural of Yahya is Yahyuna in the nominative and Yahyin in the genitive and accusative. Its dual is similarly Yahyayan and Yahyayayn. In the relative form, it is said Yahyi, by deleting the alif; Yahyawi, by changing it into a waw; and Yahyawi, by adding an alif before the waw that replaced the original alif. Its diminutive is Yuhayyi, on the pattern of fu'ayil. Our master Shaykh al-Islam said: "It is fitting that this statement to its end be reported in words from God, glorified and exalted, in the manner of: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ and so on, as the reply addressed by him (peace be upon him) directly to God, not through the angel, hints at. The departure from attributing the good tidings with the plural of majesty, as occurred in Surat Maryam, is for the sake of following the customs of grandeur, as in the saying of the caliphs: 'The Commander of the Faithful orders you such-and-such.' It also signals that what is related there of the calling, the good tidings, and the dialogue that follows was all through the angel, by way of narration from Him, glorified is He, not directly, as is the apparent meaning. With this, the unity of meaning in the two noble surahs becomes clear, so reflect." End of quotation.

What prompted treating what is here as reported in words from God, exalted, is the evident invalidity of the claim that what is in Surat Maryam is the angel's words and not reported from God, exalted, and that the apparent reading is the unity of the two supplications. Otherwise, what is here does not necessarily have to be read as stated, were it not for that, and the hint is not binding, as is not hidden. In both places, a genitive-annexed element must be supplied, such as "birth," since good tidings do not attach to substances; its meaning returns to what is there, namely: that God gives you good tidings of the birth of a boy named Yahya.

﴿confirming a word from God﴾ is put in the accusative as a presumed circumstantial clause from (Yahya). The word here is Isa (peace be upon him), as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, and is the view of the leading exegetes. Isa (peace be upon him) was called this only because he came into being by the word "Be," without an ordinary intermediate cause, and so resembled the wondrous things that belong to the world of command. (min) is for the starting point, figuratively, and is attached to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier of "word," meaning: a word issuing from Him, exalted. By this confirmation is meant belief; he was the first to believe in Isa (peace be upon him) and to confirm that he was the word of God, exalted, and a spirit from Him, according to the well-known view.

Ahmad narrated on the authority of Mujahid who said: "The wife of Zakariyya said to Maryam: 'I find that what is in my belly moves toward what is in your belly.'" Ibn Jarir narrated through Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Yahya and Isa were cousins through the maternal side, and the mother of Yahya used to say to Maryam: 'I find that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly.'" That is his confirmation of him. He was six months older than Isa, as al-Dahhak and others said; it was also said three years. It was said: in every case there was a long period between Yahya's birth and the good tidings of him, because Maryam gave birth when she was thirteen or ten years old. This was objected to on the grounds that this holds only if Zakariyya's supplication took place during Maryam's childhood, before ten or thirteen; but the verse contains nothing except an indication that when Zakariyya repeatedly entered upon Maryam, witnessed the provision with her, asked her, and heard from her that answer, he longed for a child and so supplicated with what he supplicated. This supplication may have been at the beginning of the matter, and it may have been near the end, just before Maryam conceived. Its being near the end is not unlikely, since his desire was then stronger, for he had seen the matter's continuity and steadiness during her childhood and after it. Such a thing is rare among children, for many of them are given by God words upon their tongues in youth that may be far removed from what they later become. So we have no clear evidence that there was a long period between the birth and the good tidings, nor between the supplication and the good tidings either. Yet we do have evidence that Yahya was older than Isa, peace be upon them both, which is agreed upon by Muslims and others.
