The "Gospel of Matthew" explicitly states that he was born before him, and that Herod killed him before Isa's ascension, and that he baptized the Messiah. And God knows best the reality of the matter. It is reported from Abu 'Ubayda that the meaning of ﴿a word from God﴾ is a book from Him, namely the Gospel, and calling it a word is like calling a poem a word, as in their saying "the word of al-Huwaydara," referring to the famous 'Ayniyya, known for its eloquence.

﴿and a master﴾ is conjoined to (confirming). Ibn 'Abbas explained it as "noble," Qatadah as "forbearing," al-Dahhak as "of good character," Salim as "pious," Ibn Zayd as "honourable," Ibn al-Musayyib as "a learned jurist," Ahmad ibn 'Asim as "content with God's decree," al-Khalil as "obeyed, surpassing his peers," Abu Bakr al-Warraq as "reliant upon God," al-Tirmidhi as "of great aspiration," al-Thawri as "one who does not envy," Abu Ishaq as "one who surpasses his people in goodness," and some lexicographers as "the owner whose obedience is obligatory," and other sayings besides these. Every attribute among them is suitable for Yahya (peace be upon him), for they are attributes of perfection, and the people most worthy of attributes of perfection are the prophets. However, the verified view is that the original meaning of sayyid is one who leads his people and has followers, and then it was applied to everyone who excels in religion or in worldly affairs. It is also possible that it means here one who excels in religion, since he (peace be upon him) never intended any disobedience at all, as this is reported through many routes.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary on surah 3, verse 39 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every son of Adam will meet Allah with a sin he has committed; He will punish him for it if He wills, or have mercy on him, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." It is also permissible that what is intended is its original meaning: he (peace be upon him) was the chief (sayyid) of his people, and had followers among them. The only difference is that this leadership was a legislated one (riyasah shar'iyyah). The mention of him right after the words of Allah, ﴿confirming﴾, is to indicate that he was a prophet like 'Isa (peace be upon him), and not one of his followers, as the words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾ might suggest at first glance.

﴿And chaste﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it. Its meaning is one who does not approach women despite having the ability to do so. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in one of the reports from him. In some of his reports, it is said that it means the impotent man (al-'innin) who has no organ with which to consummate marriage and does not ejaculate. The memorizers of hadith have related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that what he (peace be upon him) had was like a fingertip (al-unmulah). In some reports it is like a speck (al-qadhah), in another like a date stone (al-nawah), and in some like the lint of a garment (hudbat al-thawb). It has been said: the most sound is the first, since impotence (al-'unnah) is a defect that cannot apply to prophets. And even if we accept that it is not a defect, at the very least it is not a quality of praise, whereas the statement is meant to praise. As for what al-Hafiz related, if it is authentic, it may be said that it is of the category of metaphor (al-tamthil), and the indication is to his (peace be upon him) not benefiting from what he had, because he had no inclination toward marriage, being occupied with a preoccupation that distracted him from it. Hence it has been said that devoting oneself (al-tabattul) to voluntary acts of worship is superior to occupation with marriage, citing the condition of Yahya (peace be upon him). Whoever holds the opposite argues with what al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four have been cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and the angels have said Amen: a man whom Allah made male but who feminized himself and imitated women; a woman whom Allah made female but who masculinized herself and imitated men; one who leads the blind astray; and a man who is hasur, and Allah has not made any hasur except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." In another report: "Allah and the angels have cursed a man who became hasur after Yahya ibn Zakariyya."

It is also permissible that by hasur is meant one who is extreme in restraining the self and holding it back from desires while having the ability, and his (peace be upon him) condition was indeed also like this. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Qatadah as a mawquf report, and Ibn 'Asakir from Mu'adh ibn Jabal as a marfu' report: "When he (peace be upon him) passed by children playing in his youth, they invited him to play, and he said: 'I was not created for play.'"

﴿And a prophet﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, consequent upon the praiseworthy qualities enumerated, ﴿among the righteous﴾ [39]. That is, arising from them, or counted among them. Thus "min" in the first case is for origin (li'l-ibtida'), and in the second for partition (li'l-tab'id). It has been said that its meaning in the first case is "of noble lineage," and in the second "protected from sin (ma'sum)." Under both interpretations, its mention after "prophet" is not superfluous. It may also be said that what is meant by righteousness is that which goes beyond the righteousness that is absolutely necessary for the station of prophethood, reaching its farthest ranks. Upon this is based the supplication of Sulayman (peace be upon him): ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾. And perhaps this is better than what came before.

[Page 149]

**"He said: My Lord, how can I have a son?"** This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), answering an implied question: "What did Zakariyya, peace be upon him, say at that time?" So it was said: **"He said: My Lord..."** etc. He, peace be upon him, addressed his Lord, glory be to Him, and did not address the angel who had called out to him, dispensing with intermediaries out of intense supplication and sincere devotion to Him. The word *anna* (أنّى) here means "how" or "from where." It could be a complete verb (*tammah*) with *ghulam* ("a boy") as its subject, and *anna* and the *lam* would then both be attached to it. It could also be a deficient verb (*naqisah*), with *li* ("for me") attached to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because if it were postponed it would be a qualifier (*sifah*). In that case, the predicate has two possible readings. The first is *anna*, since it means "how" or "from where." The second is that the predicate is the prepositional phrase, and *anna* is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*). Mentioning the boy explicitly indicates that he had already been informed of him at the time of the good news, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾ (19:7).

**"And my wife is barren"**, and the phrase **"old age has overtaken me"** is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the *ya'* of the speaker (me). That is, old age has reached me and affected me. The verb "overtake" (*balagha*) is attributed to old age figuratively, as if old age were seeking him and he were the one sought. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when he was given the good news of a son, Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was one hundred and twenty years old, and his wife was ninety-eight years old. It was also said that his age was ninety-nine, and it was said ninety-two, and it was said eighty-five, and it was said seventy-five, and it was said seventy, and it was said sixty.

**"And my wife is barren"** is also a circumstantial clause, either referring to the *ya'* in "for me" or to the *ya'* in "has overtaken me." *'Aqir* (عاقِر) means one who cannot bear children, from *'uqr*, which means "cutting," because she is cut off from offspring. The form *fa'il* here indicates attribution, and in meaning it is passive, i.e., *ma'qurah* ("one who has been cut off"). For this reason the feminine *ta'* is not added. This was said by Abu al-Baqa'. The first clause is verbal because old age comes upon a person gradually, and it was not a fixed attribute. The second clause is nominal because her being barren is a fixed attribute of hers and not something that happened to her afterwards. He, peace be upon him, said this even though he had previously made this supplication and had strong certainty in God's power over it, especially after witnessing earlier signs. He was seeking clarification about how the child would come about: would it be given to him in his present state of old age and with a barren wife, or would the situation change? This was said by al-Hasan. It was also said that the matter was confusing to him: would the child be given to him from his aged wife, or from another, younger woman? So he said what he said. It was also said that he said this as an expression of amazement at God's power, and the wonder that arises in a person when a great sign appears, like someone who says to another: "How could your soul allow you to part with that precious possession?!", expressing astonishment at his generosity. It was also said that when the angels gave him the good news of Yahya, he did not know whether he would be given the child through adoption or from his own loins, so he said those words to remove this possibility. It was also said that when a servant is intensely eager for something and asks his master for it, and the master promises to give it, the servant may often speak in a way that prompts the answer to be repeated, so that he may enjoy the repetition and find peace in hearing that answer once more. So it is possible that the speech of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was of this type. It was also said that he said this to express improbability according to customary practice, because when he made the supplication he was young, and when he was answered he was an old man, based on what was said: that between the supplication and the answer there were forty or sixty years, as related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, and that he had forgotten his supplication. The defects in most of these views are not hidden.

Even more remote than these is what is related from al-Suddi, that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, heard the good news, Satan came to him and said: "This voice is from Satan, and he has mocked you," so the matter became confused for him, and he said: "My Lord, how can I have a son?" His intention in this was that God would show him a sign indicating that those words were revelation and not from Satan. Similar to this is what Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrima, who said: "Satan came to him and wanted to spoil his Lord's blessing upon him, so he said: 'Do you know who called you?' He said: 'Yes, the angels of my Lord called me.' Satan said: 'No, it was that Satan. If this had come from your Lord, He would have concealed it from you, as you concealed your call.' So he said: 'My Lord, how can I have a son?...'"

Al-Qadi and others objected to this, saying: it is not permissible for the speech of the angels to be confused with the speech of Satan at the time of revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, for if we allowed that, trust in all the laws would be lost. It was answered that one may say: since miracles have established the truth of revelation in everything concerning religion, there is therefore certainty there that the revelation is from God through the mediation of the angel, and Satan cannot enter into it. As for matters concerning worldly welfare and a child, which most resemble such matters, these may not have been confirmed by a miracle. Therefore the possibility remained that those words were from Satan, and for this reason he turned to God, asking Him to remove this possibility from his mind. You know that the objection is masculine and the answer is feminine (i.e., the objection is strong while the answer is weak). Perhaps this discussion will come to you, God willing, in full detail when explaining His saying: ﴿We never sent before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke, Satan cast into his wish...﴾ (22:52), and so on.

In sum, saying that the matter was confused for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, is extremely remote, especially since Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada, [Page 150] that he said: "The angels spoke to him directly, face to face, with this, and gave him the good news of Yahya."

**(He) said**, i.e., the Lord. The sentence is resumptive, in the same manner as what has preceded. **"Thus God does what He wills"** (3:40), i.e., God does whatever He wills to do of extraordinary acts that break customary habits, an act like that act, the wondrous deed and marvelous creation which is the creating of a child in a state where creation seems improbable according to custom. Thus the *kaf* (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), and the demonstrative refers to that verbal noun. The prepositional phrase is placed first to indicate restriction in relation to what is lower than the thing pointed to. The *kaf* is considered superfluous (*muqhamah*) to emphasize the grandeur which the demonstrative noun implies, as was indicated earlier in a similar case. The sentence may bear other possible readings:

First: the *kaf* may be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the implied pronoun of the verbal noun, being definite, i.e., He does the deed being in a state like that. Second: it may be in the nominative position as the predicate of a fronted subject, with "God" as a postponed subject, i.e., the affair of God, Exalted is like this wondrous affair, and the clause "He does what He wills" is an explanation of that vague affair. Third: "thus" may be in the position of a predicate for an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is thus, and the clause "God does what He wills" is also an explanation. Fourth: that "thus" may refer to what was mentioned about the state of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, as if he said: "My Lord, in what condition will the boy be mine?" and it was said to him: "Just as you are, the boy will be yours." In this case the sentence serves as a justification for what precedes it, as they have said. The defects of some of these readings are not hidden. In any case, the expression with the Exalted Name is for the purpose of magnifying (the matter).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 41 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ That is, a sign by which I may know the conception has taken place. He asked for it out of eagerness for the joy of it, as al-Hasan said. It was also said that he asked so that he might receive that blessing with thanks at the moment it occurred, and not delay until it became apparent in the usual way. This is perhaps the more fitting view for the situation of such figures, peace be upon him. As for al-Suddi's view, that he asked for the sign so that he could be certain that the good news came from God and not from Satan, it is worthless, as we have indicated above. The word "ja'ala" (appoint) may be taken in the sense of "make" (taṣyīr), in which case it takes two objects: the first is "āyatan" (a sign) and the second is "lī" (for me). The fronting of "lī" is because it is what justifies "āyatan" being the subject (mubtada') when the sentence is analysed. Or it may be taken in the sense of "create and bring into being," in which case it takes one object, which is "āyatan," and "lī" is then in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "āyatan," because if it came after it, it would be a qualifier of it. A qualifier of an indefinite noun, when it comes before it, is parsed as a circumstantial qualifier of it, as the reference to this has been made more than once. It is also permissible that it be connected to what is in front of it, and its placement serves to draw attention to it and to create anticipation for what follows.

﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people"﴾ That is, that you will not be able to speak to them without an impediment. This is the most fitting reading for it being a sign, and the most consistent with what is in surah Maryam. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jubayr ibn Mu'tamir that he said: "His tongue swelled in his mouth until it filled it, and so it prevented him from speaking." The sign in this case is that it did not prevent him from remembrance (dhikr) and glorification (tasbih). Under both interpretations, the inability to speak is involuntary. Abu Muslim said that it was voluntary, and the meaning is: your sign is that you will become commanded not to speak except in remembrance and glorification. The remoteness of this view is not hidden here. In light of this, and in light of the two views before it, it is possible that what is meant by not speaking is its apparent meaning only, and this is the apparent meaning. It is also possible that it is a metaphor for fasting, because at that time they would not speak to anyone when they fasted. Atā' went to this view, but it goes against the apparent meaning. Moreover, its acceptance depends on a textual basis (tawqīf). He specified "speaking to the people" only to indicate that he was not prevented from speaking with the remembrance of God, exalted is He.

﴿three days﴾ That is, consecutive. Some of them said that what is meant is three days and their nights. It was also said that the expression contains an omitted modifier, meaning "the nights of three days," due to His saying, exalted is He, in surah Maryam: ﴿three nights﴾. The truth is that the sign was non-speech for six periods, but it was sometimes limited in mention to three days from among them, and at other times to three nights, and what was not mentioned in each case was treated as following what was mentioned. It has been said: the expression was framed in terms of days because the day of each night comes before it in the reckoning of people at that time, and its coming after it is only in the case of the Arabs specifically, as the reference to this has been made before.

It has been objected that the sign of the nights preceded in revelation, because the surah in which it appears is Meccan, and the surah in which the sign of the days appears is Medinan. In light of this, the first appearance of this sign would be at night, and the day would follow the night before it, according to the reckoning of the Arabs. So reflect upon this. The question still requires further examination. The binding of the tongue was made the sign of conception so that the period would be free for the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and for thanking Him, in fulfilment of the right of the blessing. It is as if it was said to him: the sign of the blessing's arrival is that you be prevented from speech except in thanking for it. The best answer to this, as has been said, is what is taken from the question itself, just as it was said to Abu Tammam: "Why do you say what we do not understand?" He replied: "Why do you not understand what is being said?" This is based on the premise that his request for the sign, peace be upon him, was only in order to receive the blessing with thanks. Perhaps the indication of his speech towards this is through the context, otherwise there is obscurity in this, as is not hidden.

Abd al-Razzaq and others related from Qatada that the restraint of his tongue, peace be upon him, was by way of punishment, since he asked for the sign after the angels had spoken to him directly with the good news. Perhaps the fault at that time was of the kind of "the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near." Yet good opinion inclines to the first view. The position of Qatada: "I am not safe from weak feet."

﴿except by gesture (ramzan)﴾ That is, by signalling. Its root meaning is movement; it is said: "irtamaza," meaning he moved. From this, the sea is called "al-ramūz." Al-Tibi related from Ibn Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about the gesture (ramz), and he said: "A signal with the hand and an indication with the head." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes, indeed. Have you not heard the words of the poet:

"Nothing in the heavens of the Merciful is signalled (murtamaz) except towards Him, and nothing in the earth is a refuge (wazar)."

It was related from Mujahid that the gesture here was the moving of the two lips. It was also said: writing on the ground. It was also said: a signal with the forefinger. It was also said: a faint voice. It was also said: anything that causes confusion in understanding is a gesture. The exception here is discontinuous (munqati'), on the basis that the gesture is a signal and conveying meaning without speech, and in that case it is not of the same kind as what is excepted from. It was permitted that it be continuous, on the basis that what is meant by speech is that by which the intended meaning is understood, and there is no doubt that the gesture belongs to that category. It is not hidden that this interpretation goes against the apparent meaning, and it entails that the exception would never be discontinuous at all in this world, for there is no exception except that it can be interpreted in a similar way so as to make it continuous, and no one holds this. Ibn al-Shajari criticized the accusative case of the exception here in all cases, and claimed that "ramzan" is an object in the accusative, governed by an elided preposition, and the original form is: "that you will not speak to the people except by a gesture." So the governing element before "illa" is "mufarragh" (left without a complete object) in this type of construction for what follows it. The evidence is that if you were to delete "illa" and the negative particle, the sentence would be sound. You say, in a construction like "I met no one except Zayd," "I met Zayd," and in "Nobody went out except Zayd," "Zayd went out." Similarly, if you said: "Your sign is that you speak to the people by gesture," it would be sound. But this is not the case with the exception proper. If you said: "The people are not in the house except Zayd, or except Zayd," then deleted the negation and "illa," saying: "The people are in the house, Zayd, or Zayd," it would not be sound. Likewise the discontinuous exception, as in: "The people did not go out except a donkey," if you said: "The people went out, a donkey," it would not be sound. This was said by al-Saffaqisi.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "illa rumuzan" with two dammas, the plural of "rumūz," like "rasūl" and "rusul." It was also read "ramazan" with two fathas, the plural of "rāmiz," like "khādim" and "khadam," and this is among the rare plurals. On both readings, it is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the subject and the object together, meaning "mutual gesturing." A similar usage is the words of Antarah:

"Whenever you meet me in pairs (fardayn), the fleshy parts of your buttocks tremble and are scattered."

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "illa rumuzan," on the reading with the damma, be a verbal noun (maṣdar). He took it to be originally with a sukun on the mim, and the damma is incidental, for the sake of harmony, like "al-yusr" and "al-yusur." On this view its i'rab (grammatical parsing) does not change. So understand.

﴿And remember your Lord﴾ That is, during the days of confinement, in thanks for that blessing,

[152]

as the reference to the title of Lordship (rubūbiyya) indicates. It was also said that it is possible that the command to remember is a thanks for the blessing in general and not specifically for those days, and that it may apply to all the days of the pregnancy, so that its blessings return to him. What comes to the mind directly is the first view. The sentence confirms what precedes it and explains the purpose behind it. The conjunction has been questioned on two grounds. The first: conjoining a command to a statement. The second: conjoining an emphatic to what is emphasized. It was answered that it is conjoined to something omitted, that is: "give thanks and remember." It was also said: it is not far-fetched to make the command have the meaning of a report, conjoined to "that you will not speak," so that it is in the sense of: "that you will not speak and will remember your Lord." What is wrong with this is not hidden. ﴿much﴾ is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, or of an omitted time expression of the same kind, meaning: a much remembrance and a much time.

﴿And glorify [Him] in the evening﴾ and it is from the decline of the sun to sunset, said Mujahid. It was also said: from the afternoon to the passing of the early part of the night. ﴿and in the morning (al-ibkar)﴾ [41] That is, its time, and it is from dawn to forenoon. The noun was supposed to have an omitted element because "al-ibkar," with a kasra on the hamza, is a verbal noun and not a time, so the contrast would not be appropriate. This is what has been said. It is based on the view that "al-ashiyy" is the plural of "ashiyya," a specific time. This is the view of Abu al-Baqa'. What the majority hold is that it is also a verbal noun, on the pattern "fa'il," and not a plural. Al-Jawhari's statement points to this, so understand. It was also read "wal-abkar" with a fatha on the hamza, which is then a plural of "bakar," like "sahar," in form and meaning, and this is rarely used. It was said: by glorification is meant prayer, on the evidence of its being restricted to a time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. It was also said: it means oral remembrance, just as remembrance means inward remembrance. On both interpretations, there is no repetition in mentioning glorification together with remembrance. The "al" in both times is for generality. It is more remote to take it as referring to a specific reference, meaning the evenings and mornings of those three days. The prepositional phrase is connected to what is before it, and it is not of the type of "tanāzu'" (competition between governors) according to the well-known view, though some permitted it, in which case the command to remember would also be restricted to these two times. Some claimed that restricting it with "much" indicates that it does not mean repetition. There is remoteness in this, since granting that it is restricted to this alone, "much" is more specific than repetition.

Moreover, among the inner meanings (buṭūn) found in these verses is that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was an elderly guide to the people. When he saw what he saw, that is, the zeal of prophethood was stirred, he asked his Lord for a true child who would take his place in the upbringing and guidance of the people. So he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾, that is, purified from the defilement of preoccupation with other than God, detached from its own desires, sanctified from its appetites. ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing﴾ in the posture of service ﴿praying in the sanctuary﴾, which is the place of watchfulness and combat with the soul ﴿that God gives you good news of Yahya﴾. He was named so because whoever witnesses the Truth in the beauty of its prophethood, his heart is revived from the death of spiritual lethargy. Or because he himself is alive through prophethood and witnessing. ﴿confirming a word from God﴾, which is what the angel brings down upon the sanctified hearts. ﴿and a master (sayyid)﴾, who is the one whose light of the awe of the might of the Truth prevails over him. Al-Sadiq said: he is the one who is distinct from creation in attribute, state and creation. Al-Junayd said: he is the one who gave both worlds in seeking his Lord. Ibn Ata' said: he is the one who is realized in the reality of the Truth. Ibn Mansur said: he is the one who is free of human attributes and adorned with the qualities of lordship. Muhammad ibn Ali said: he is the one whose states are equal in withholding and giving, in rejection and acceptance. ﴿and chaste (ḥaṣūr)﴾, who is the one who was confined and restrained from all desires, and was protected by eternal protection. Al-Iskandarani said: he is the one who is transcended above the cosmos and what is in it. ﴿and a prophet (nabiyyan)﴾, that is, raised in rank by the descent of revelation upon him, and counted ﴿among the righteous﴾, who are the people of the first row among the rows of the souls that are arrayed and that witness the Truth in the mirrors of creation.

﴿He said﴾, magnifying the blessing: ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son, when old age has already reached me﴾, and the situation is that "old age has indeed reached me," which is one of the customary obstacles, ﴿and my wife is barren﴾, which is another obstacle. ﴿He said: "Thus God does what He wills"﴾, according to what wisdom requires. ﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign"﴾ of the conception, ﴿so that I may thank You for this blessing, since thanking the benefactor is obligatory, and by it divine gifts endure.﴾

[153]

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people"﴾, by having your tongue confined from conversing with them, so that your inner secret may be devoted to your Lord and your outward and inward being may be occupied with Him ﴿except by gesture (ramzan)﴾, by which you relieve the constriction of the heart when there is need. The reality of the gesture according to the knowers is the presenting of the secret to the secret and the informing of the thought to the thought, by way of setting in motion the chain of connection between the one who addresses and the one addressed. ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾, by purifying the intention from passing thoughts and gathering the concerns, by way of clarifying the secret in intimate conversation and the bewilderment of the spirit in contemplations. ﴿And glorify﴾, that is, declare your Lord free from partnership in existence, ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾, with passing away and subsistence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 41 (part 2 of 2):

If you wish to apply what is in the horizons (al-afaq) to what is in the souls (al-anfus), you would say: ﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾ — the readiness (al-isti'dad) — ﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾ — and this is the pure soul, sanctified from defects — ﴿Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ — from one who is sincere in seeking — ﴿Then the angels called him﴾ — the angels of the spiritual powers — ﴿while he was standing﴾ — rising up to perfect the stage of creation — ﴿praying﴾ and supplicating in the niche of humility to God, the Exalted, who bestows upon the receptive recipients according to their capacities — ﴿that God gives you good tidings of Yahya﴾ — who is the living spirit, alive through the Spirit of Truth and the divine attributes — ﴿confirming a word from God﴾ — which is what the angels of inspiration cast, from the Absolute Overflowing One — ﴿and a lord (sayyid)﴾ — not overcome by the carnal appetites — ﴿and chaste (hasur)﴾ — that is, one who thoroughly abstains from worldly pleasures — ﴿and a prophet﴾ — by what he receives from the world of the dominion — and counted ﴿among the righteous﴾ — those in that presence who uphold the rights of the Truth and of creation, because of his being characterized by subsistence after annihilation.

﴿He said: My Lord, how (anna) can I have a boy, when old age has overtaken me﴾ — that is, how — ﴿and my wife is barren﴾ — the animal soul, barren from bearing such a boy, since a living thing gives birth only to a living thing — ﴿He said: Thus God﴾ — in the strangeness of the matter — ﴿does what He wills﴾ — of the wonders which he who is bound by the gaze upon familiar things deems improbable, and remains a captive in the prison of habits. ﴿He said: My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾ upon that, so that I may thank You, seeking the increase of Your blessings, which have no end. ﴿He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to people﴾ — and they are what one finds pleasant of permissible delights — ﴿for three days﴾ — which are the day of annihilation in actions, the day of annihilation in attributes, and the day of annihilation in essence — ﴿except by gesture (ramz)﴾ — that is, a small amount which necessity calls for. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ — who nurtured you until He brought you to this goal — ﴿much﴾, for He has bestowed upon you much good — ﴿and glorify﴾ — that is, declare your Lord free from the defects of being bound to appearances — ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾ — that is, the times of sobriety and of effacement.

Some of those committed to mentioning the inner meanings (al-butun) have, in applying what is in the horizons to what is in the souls, stated that the bodily powers, the wife of Imran, the Spirit, vowed what was in her strength of the tranquil soul; she gave birth to the female soul, and Zakariya, the reflective faculty, took charge of her. Zakariya entered upon her in the niche of the brain and found with her provision of intuitive meanings which were revealed to her through her purity. There Zakariya, the reflective faculty, called upon [God] by composing those meanings, and asked for a holy offspring, free from the impurity of nature. God, the Exalted, heard his supplication, and the angels of the spiritual powers called him while he was standing in his task of composing knowledge, communing with his Lord by drawing down lights in the niche of the brain: ﴿that God gives you good tidings of Yahya﴾ — the intellect — confirming Isa — the heart — who is a word from God, because of its sanctity from the world of bodies — ﴿and a lord﴾ over all kinds of powers — ﴿and chaste﴾ from contact with nature — ﴿and a prophet﴾ by informing of knowledges and realities and teaching morals — and included among the righteous, who are the immaterial beings and those brought near to the Presence. ﴿He said: My Lord, how can that be﴾ — ﴿when old age has reached me﴾ — the greatest old age of the stage — ﴿and my wife﴾ — who is the nature of the psychic spirit — ﴿is barren﴾ — with the pure light. So he asked for a sign for this, and it was said to him: the sign of that is refraining from speaking with the bodily powers in attaining their aims of pleasures — ﴿for three days﴾ — each day a complete cycle of the stages of life, which is ten years, except (illa) by hidden allusion. He was commanded to remember in these days, which together with the first ten years, the age of discernment, make forty years.

End. This is close to what I have mentioned, though what I have mentioned, despite my weakness, is perhaps more preferable than it. The door of interpretation is wide, and the inner meanings of the words of God, the Exalted, cannot be counted.

﴿And when the angels said﴾ is a continuation of the explanation of the rulings concerning the chosenness of the family of 'Imran. The story of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, came in between because it contains elements that confirm that chosenness. The "idh" (when) is, according to the well-known view, in the accusative case governed by a verb meaning "mention." The sentence is coordinated with the preceding sentence as the coordination of one story with another, and there is complete suitability between them, because the earlier one is directed first and foremost at explaining the condition of the mother, while this one explains the condition of the daughter. By "the angels" is meant their chief, Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. What is said here is like what was said regarding what came before. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the adverbial phrase be coordinated with the preceding adverbial phrase and that its governing verb be the same as its governing verb, but the first view is more preferable. The meaning is: "Mention also, among the signs of the chosenness of those noble ones, the time when the angels, peace be upon them, said: ﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you﴾," that is, He selected you from the beginning, showed kindness to you, distinguished you above every woman dedicated [to worship], and singled you out with exalted honors. The emphasis (through "indeed") is an expression of concern for the importance of the announcement. The angels' saying this to her was verbal, as the reports indicate and the apparent meaning of the text expresses. In some narrations there is something that implies that this statement was repeated by the angels to her. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Ishaq that he said: Maryam was confined in the sanctuary (kanisa), and with her there was a boy named Yusuf, whose mother and father had dedicated him as a devoted servant confined there. So they were both in the sanctuary together. Whenever Maryam's water ran out, and Yusuf's water as well, they would take their two pitchers and go to the cave where there was water, fill them, and then return. While they were doing this, the angels were approaching Maryam with glad tidings: ﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you﴾, and so on. When Zakariyya, peace be upon him, heard that, he said: "Indeed, the daughter of 'Imran has a matter [of great importance]." It has also been said that the angels, peace be upon them, inspired her with that. It is not hidden that interpreting the "saying" as inspiration (ilham) and attributing it to the angels goes against the apparent meaning, although there is no objection to its being through their mediation as well. Moreover, it is a statement that no report at all supports. According to the first view, the speaking is among the category of honors which Allah, glorified is He, bestows upon His chosen servants. Whoever denies it claims that it was a foreshadowing (irhas) and a preparation for the prophethood of 'Isa, peace be upon him, or a miracle for Zakariyya, peace be upon him.

It is objected to the first [view] that irhas, according to the well-known definition, is that before the claim of prophethood there occurs something resembling a miracle, such as the shading of a cloud over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the speaking of a stone with him. Its apparent meaning requires that an extraordinary event occurred at the hand of the prophet, but before he was given prophethood, and not at the hand of someone else, as in what we are discussing. It can be answered through the (special) care [of Allah]. It is objected to the second [view] that it is very far-fetched, since no conversation took place with Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and this was not accompanied by a challenge either, so how could it be a miracle for him?

Whoever holds that Maryam was a prophetess has used this verse as evidence, because the angels speaking to her requires it. Al-Laqani refuted this by saying that the angels have spoken, by consensus (ijma'), to someone who is not a prophet. It has been narrated that they spoke to a man who went out to visit a brother of his for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He, and they informed him that Allah, glorified is He, loves him as He loves his brother for His sake, and no one has claimed that he was a prophet. He claimed that whoever imagines that prophethood is merely revelation and the speaking of an angel has deviated from the truth.

Among people there are those who used the consensus on the non-prophethood of women as evidence, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾. But what is in this is not hidden. As for first: the reporting of a consensus is extremely strange, for the disagreement regarding the prophethood of women such as Hawwa' (Eve), Asiya, the mother of Musa, Sarah, Hajar, and Maryam exists, especially Maryam, for the view of her prophethood is well-known. Indeed, Shaykh Taqi al-Din al-Subki in "al-Halabiyyat" and Ibn al-Sayyid leaned toward preferring it, and [al-Subki] mentioned that her being mentioned together with the prophets in their chapter (surah) is a strong indication of that. As for second: the use of the verse as evidence is not valid, because what is mentioned in it is the sending (irsal), and this is more specific than prophethood (istinba') according to the correct and well-known view. Negating the more specific does not entail negating the more general. So understand.

﴿And purified you﴾, that is, from the impurities and filths that afflict women, such as menstruation and postnatal bleeding, until you became fit for serving the mosque. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was narrated from al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr that the meaning is: He purified you through faith from disbelief and through obedience from disobedience. It has also been said: He cleansed you from blameworthy character traits and base dispositions. The preferable reading is to take it in its generality, that is, He purified you from physical, moral, inward, and outward filths.

﴿And chose you above the women of the worlds﴾ [42]. It is possible that by this choosing is meant something other than the first choosing, namely the last [act of] His bestowing upon her a child, 'Isa, peace be upon him, without a father, a thing that was not granted to any other woman, and His making her and him a sign for the worlds. It is also possible that what is meant is the first [choosing], and it was repeated for emphasis and to clarify who it was that He chose above them. According to the first [view], the mention of this dialogue before the mention of the glad tidings of 'Isa, peace be upon him, is for alerting that each of them deserves to be mentioned independently. There are parallels to this, some of which have already passed. According to the second [view], there is no difficulty regarding the order, and the wisdom of placing this dialogue before the glad tidings is an indication that she, peace be upon her, before that was prepared to receive the overflow of the Spirit upon her through her devotion (tabattul) and submission in accordance with the command. And the first is likely more preferable, as al-Imam said, because establishing a new matter (ta'sis) is better than emphasizing (ta'kid).

As for the meaning of "the women of the worlds," it has been said: all women in all eras. It was used as evidence for her superiority over Fatima, Khadija, and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them. This is supported by what Ibn 'Asakir reported in one of its chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mistress of the women of the People of Paradise is Maryam bint 'Imran, then Fatima, then Khadija, then Asiya the wife of Pharaoh." And by what Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Makhul. Something close to it is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of women who rode camels are the women of Quraysh: they are the most compassionate toward a child in its infancy and the most protective of a husband in his property. And if I knew that Maryam bint 'Imran had ridden a camel, I would not have preferred anyone over her." And by what Ibn Jarir reported from Fatima, may Allah's blessings be upon her and her father and upon her, that she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "You are the mistress of the women of the People of Paradise, except Maryam the virgin."

It has been said: what is meant is the women of her own world (alamiha), so it does not follow from this that she is superior to Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her. This is supported by what Ibn 'Asakir reported through the route of Muqatil from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Four women are the masters of their worlds: Maryam bint 'Imran, Asiya bint Muzahim, Khadija bint Khuwaylid, and Fatima bint Muhammad (ﷺ), and the best of them in her world is Fatima." And what al-Harith ibn Usama reported in his "Musnad" with a sound chain, but it is mursal: "Maryam is the best of the women of her world." This is the view of Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is what is well-known from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt.

What I incline toward is that Fatima al-Batul is the best of women, both former and latter, because she is a part of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and even for other reasons as well. The earlier reports do not conflict with this, since it is possible that what is meant by them is the superiority of others over her in some respects and from some aspect of consideration. By this the reports are reconciled. This is also valid according to the view that Maryam was a prophetess, since being a part of him (bid'iyya) is from the spirit of existence and the lord of every existent; I do not see it being compared with anything.

And how far is the Pleiades from the hand of the one who reaches for it.

From here it is known that she is superior to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. Many have gone to the opposite view, citing His saying (ﷺ): "Take two-thirds of your religion from the Humayra'," and his saying, may the prayers and peace be upon him: "The superiority of 'A'isha over women is like the superiority of tharid over food," and that 'A'isha on the Day of Resurrection will be in Paradise with her husband, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while Fatima on that day will be there with her husband 'Ali, may Allah honor his face. And there is a great difference between the station of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the station of 'Ali, may Allah honor his face.

You know what is in this argument, and that it is not an explicit text (nass) for the superiority of the Humayra' over the Zahra'. As for first: the most that can be said about the first hadith, if it is established, is that it proves she was knowledgeable to the extent that two-thirds of the religion may be taken from her. This does not indicate negating knowledge similar to hers from his daughter, peace and blessings be upon him. And since he (ﷺ) knew that she would not remain after him for a considerable time in which the religion could be taken from her, he did not say that about her. Had he known, he might have said: "Take all your religion from al-Zahra'." The absence of this statement regarding one whose knowledge is established by reason and transmission does not indicate that she is lesser (mafdula). Otherwise 'A'isha would be superior to her father, may Allah be pleased with him, since little was narrated from him concerning the religion because of the brevity of his life after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the great burden of his responsibilities. Moreover, his saying, may the prayers and peace be upon him: "Indeed I have left among you the two weighty things, the Book of Allah and my 'Itrah, which will not separate until they come to me at the Pool," serves as a substitute for that report and more, as is not hidden. How could it not, when Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, is the mistress of that 'Itrah?!

As for second: the second hadith conflicts with what indicates the superiority of someone else over her, may Allah be pleased with her. Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ammar ibn Sa'd that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Khadija has been preferred over the women of my community as Maryam was preferred over the women of the worlds." Indeed this hadith is more evident in superiority and more complete in praise to the one whose inner vision is not blinded by the eye of partisanship and rigidity. For although that report is apparent in superiority, it has been said, even if from a distance, that the "al" in "al-nisa'" (the women) there is for specification (al-'ahd), and what is meant by it is the pure wives who were present at the time of the announcement. And nothing like that was said regarding this hadith.

As for third: the third proof requires that all the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) be superior to all the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, because their station is undoubtedly not like the station of the one who holds the Praised Station (ﷺ). So if sharing a dwelling required superiority, that would necessarily follow, and no one holds that.

After all this, what occurs to my mind is that the best of women is Fatima, then her mother, then 'A'isha. Indeed, if someone said that all the daughters of the Prophet (ﷺ) are superior to 'A'isha, I would see no harm in it. In my view there is a suspension of judgment between Maryam and Fatima with respect to absolute superiority. As for superiority with respect to a particular aspect, you have known what I incline toward. Imam al-Subki was asked about this question and said: "What we choose and what we hold Allah, Exalted is He, to be pleased with is that Fatima bint Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best, then her mother, then 'A'isha." Al-Bulqini agreed with him in this. Ibn al-'Imad has affirmed that Khadija is also superior to 'A'isha, because it is established that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said to 'A'isha when she said: "Allah has given you something better than her," so he said to her: "No, by Allah, Allah has not given me anything better than her. She believed in me when people denied me, and she gave me her wealth when people deprived me." This is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed the greeting to Khadija from Jibril, and that Jibril conveyed the greeting to Khadija from her Lord. Some of them, when they saw the conflict of the proofs in this question, suspended judgment on it. The judge Abu Ja'far al-Istarushani from among us inclined to suspension, while Ibn Jama'a went to the view that it is the safest position.

The most problematic matter in this topic is the hadith of the tharid (the dish of bread soaked in broth), but perhaps the abundance of reports that speak against it makes its interpretation easier. The interpretation of one (report) in light of many is easier than the interpretation of many in light of one. And God Most High is the One who guides to the right path.

[p. 157]

﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is also part of the speech of the angels. They commanded her to guard her prayer after informing her of the elevation of her rank and the completeness of her nearness to God, Exalted is He, so that she would not slacken or become heedless of worship. The repetition of the address (yā Maryam) serves to draw attention to what follows, as though it were the true object of the discourse, and what precedes it is a preparation for it.

Qunut (devout obedience) means prolonging the standing in prayer, as said by Mujahid; or persisting in obedience, as said by Qatadah, and al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) also held this view; or sincerity in worship, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr; or simply standing in prayer, as said by some. It also contains a reference to the title of Lordship (al-Rubbūbiyyah), to indicate the reason why obeying the commands is obligatory.

﴿And prostrate yourself and bow with those who bow.﴾ [43] It is possible that all of this is a command to pray, but God, Glorified is He, commanded it by mentioning its pillars (arkān), in order to emphasise the obligation of guarding it, since mentioning a thing in detail establishes it more firmly than a general statement. Perhaps the prostration is mentioned before the bowing because that was their order in their prayer. It has also been said: because prostration is the most excellent of the pillars of prayer and the highest degree of humility. In a report it is said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." Or it is to alert that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. Or so that "bow" (irka'ī) is paired with "with those who bow," to signify that whoever has no bowing in his prayer is not one who prays.

Each of these views is not free from difficulty. As for the first: it holds only on the view that standing is not more excellent than prostration, as is reported from Imam al-Shafi'i. As for the second: the Qur'an's address is to one who knows the Arabic language, not to one who is learning it from it. As for the third: its completeness depends on explaining why it did not say "with those who prostrate," to alert that whoever has no prostration in his prayer is not among those who pray. Perhaps the explanation for this is what is derived from the words of al-Zamakhshari, where he said: "It is possible that in her time there were those who would stand and prostrate in their prayer without bowing, and among them were those who bow. So she was commanded to bow with those who bow, and not to be with those who do not bow." So the point in the expression is what was made the point in the mention of "bow with those who bow." Some have also objected to this, saying: if the bowing were placed first, and it were said, "bow with those who bow and prostrate," that purpose would be achieved, and placing it first or last has no bearing on conveying it. It has also been said: by "prostration" alone is meant prayer, as in His saying: ﴿and after the prostrations﴾ (Q 50:40). Expressing prayer by this is a case of mentioning a part to mean the whole. And "bowing" is meant as humility and submissiveness. It seems that her being commanded to do this was a protection for her from falling into the pits of arrogance and self-exaltation on account of the elevation of her rank. The first possibility is the apparent one, and it is supported by what Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Awza'i, who said: "She would stand until pus flowed from her feet." And by what Ibn 'Asakir narrated concerning the verse from Abu Sa'id, who said: "Mary used to pray until her feet swelled."

Most scholars hold that the purpose of His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿with those who bow﴾ is to direct to congregational prayer (ṣalāt al-jamā'ah). This is the view of al-Jubba'i. Some researchers have mentioned that the point of expressing it this way in this context, rather than "prostrate with those who prostrate," is to indicate that whoever catches the bowing with the imam has caught a unit (rak'ah) of the prayer. This was objected to by saying: if it were said, "prostrate with those who prostrate," it might have contained an indication that whoever catches the prostration with the imam has caught the congregation. Perhaps this indication is better than the first in this context. However, the implication of that is that whoever catches only what comes after the prostration with him does not catch the congregation, which falls under prohibition. It is not hidden that the objector and the objected-to are of no account in the eyes of fair-minded people. Better than both is what the author of al-Kashshaf indicated. Some have also claimed that "ma'a" (with) is a metaphor for agreement in action only, without actual joining together. That is: "act as the bowers act," even if you do not perform the prayer together with them. He said: because she used to pray in her sanctuary (miḥrāb), and also because she was a young woman, and the prayer of young women in congregation is disliked. This was objected to by saying: it is an employment of metaphor, which is contrary to the original sense, without any need. That she used to pray in her sanctuary at times is granted, but this does not prove the claim; that she did so always is something for which there is no evidence. And even if granted, it still does not prove the claim, since it is permissible for her to follow an imam while she is in the sanctuary. As for the dislike of a young woman praying in congregation, its establishment in the law of earlier communities has not been confirmed for us. Moreover, al-Maturidi denied the dislike of Mary's praying in congregation even though she was young, and we say that the dislike of young women praying in congregation was also in their law. He explained this by the fact that the people with whom she prayed were her relatives and kin, which is why they disputed over her custody and keeping. Perhaps it is also explained by the absence of fear of temptation even if they were strangers. In support of this is her going with Joseph to fill the jar in the cave. Perhaps those with whom she bows are of this kind. And if we say that she follows an imam while in her sanctuary, either alone or with women, the difficulty is removed.

And ﴿with those who bow﴾ came rather than "with those who bow (feminine)"

[p. 158]

because this plural form is more general, as it includes men and women by way of predominance (taghlīb). It also suits the rhyme endings of the verses (ru'ūs al-āy). And because following men is more excellent, if we say that she is commanded to perform congregational prayer. Some have claimed that in this expression there is an implicit praise of Mary, peace be upon her. The last two commands are not restricted by what restricted the first command, relying on the restriction that comes at first glance. Shaykh al-Islam said: "The stripping of the last two pillars from what the first was restricted by is because the intent is to restrict the command to prayer by this, and this was done when the first pillar of it was restricted by it." Perhaps what we have mentioned is better, because it applies consistently to all the views on qunut.

Ibn Abi Dawud, in al-Masahif, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to recite: "irka'ī wa-asjudī fī al-sājidīn" (bow and prostrate among those who prostrate).

﴿That﴾ refers to the preceding accounts, those wondrous narratives whose strangeness reaches the highest degree. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His words, ﴿from the news of the unseen﴾, meaning from reports of what is hidden from you and from your people, which can only be known through revelation, as the context indicates. The clause is a new sentence (mustaʼnafah) with no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab). His words, ﴿We reveal it to you﴾, form an independent clause that explains the first. Revelation (al-iyha') means conveying a meaning to another in a hidden manner. It can mean sending an angel to the prophets, or it can mean inspiration (al-ilham). The pronoun in *nuhihi* ("We reveal it") refers, according to the well-known view, to ﴿that﴾. It has been deemed preferable to refer it to "the unseen," because then it includes both the stories already mentioned and those not yet mentioned. By contrast, if it refers to ﴿that﴾, it gives the false impression of being restricted to what has passed. It has also been allowed that this clause is the predicate of the subject before it, and that ﴿from the news of the unseen﴾ is either related to *nuhihi* or is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its object. That is, "We reveal it while it is part of the news of the unseen." Making it a circumstantial clause of the subject is the opinion of some. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the sense is: "The matter is that," so that *dhalika* ("that") is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause of it. This is a rejected view, and the speech of the Glorious King should not be interpreted in this way. According to some, the use of the future form (*nuhihi*) indicates that revelation has not yet ceased.

﴿You were not with them﴾, that is, with the disputants. The pronoun refers to something unmentioned but implied by the meaning. The purpose of this clause is to establish that the reports of these matters came through revelation, by way of mockery toward those who deny it. It is as if it were said: "Our Messenger has informed you of what cannot be known by reason, while you acknowledge that he neither heard it nor read it in a book, and yet you deny that it is revelation. Therefore, nothing remains that needs negation except witnessing, which is the most evident of things to negate, because its impossibility is known to all rational people." It also draws attention to the authenticity of the story of Maryam, even though what is known through revelation includes the story of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, too. This is because that story is the one primarily intended by the reports, and the other story came incidentally, and because part of Zakariyya's story is included in the mention of who undertook her guardianship. Thus the clause is not devoid of an allusion to his story in general. It is related from Qatada that the purpose of this clause is that God, glorified is He, marvels at His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, at the intense eagerness of the people to take responsibility for Maryam and to care for her affairs. This is brought as an emphasis on her chosen status, peace be upon her. However, this separation between the emphasizer and the emphasized is far-fetched. Nevertheless, this is preferable to the view that its purpose is to marvel at their pushing to take responsibility for her because of the severity of the situation and the great need that befell them, until the best of guardians, Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was granted success. Rather, this view is almost incorrect in both reason and transmission. In any case, negating witnessing presents no difficulty, since its non-occurrence is evident to everyone.

﴿When they cast their pens﴾, that is, they threw them and cast them for drawing lots. *Aqlam* is the plural of *qalam*, the instrument with which they used to write the Torah, and they chose them seeking blessing through them. It has been said that they were arrows of the crossbow, which are the arrow-shafts. Al-Kazaruni related that they were made of copper. The word is derived from *al-qalm* meaning cutting, from which comes *qulamat al-zufr* ("the paring of a fingernail"). The manner of casting has been explained earlier. There is disagreement about the number of pens. It is reported from al-Baqir that they were six. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is governed by the stabilizing verb (*al-istiqrar*) that operates in ﴿with them﴾. Making it an adverb of *kana* ("was"), as Abu al-Baqa' said, is not valid. ﴿Which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾ belongs to the first statement. Making it the beginning of an interrogative sentence corrupts the meaning. Since *yulquna* ("they cast") cannot be linked to the interrogative, it is necessary to supply something that connects the structure. Al-Jull mentions three possibilities. The first is to supply: *yanzurun* ("they look") *ayyuhum yakfulu* ("which of them would take charge"). Since looking leads to perception, it is permissible for it to govern the interrogative word, like the verbs of the heart, as Ibn al-Hajib and Ibn Malik stated in *al-Tashil*. The second is to supply: *li-ya'lamu* ("in order that they might know") *ayyuhum yakfulu*. According to the first, the sentence is a circumstantial clause of what precedes it, and according to the second, it is in the position of the object of purpose. It is not hidden that casting is a cause of knowledge itself, but it is a distant cause. The immediate cause is looking at what rose from the pens. The third is to supply: *yaqulun* ("they say") or *liyaqulu* ("in order that they say") *ayyuhum*. It was objected that supplying *yaqulun* yields no meaningful benefit, and the meaning does not flow toward it, but is merely a verbal adjustment for the position of *ayyuhum*. It was answered that it is beneficial, and the meaning flows toward it on the basis that the intended meaning of "saying" is saying for clarification and specification. It was also objected that supplying the verb of saying combined with the particle of causation is meaningless here. It was answered by interpreting it as was done with the previous one. It was also said that it is interpreted as "judging": that is, *liyaqulu* and *liyahkumu* ("in order that they say and judge") *ayyuhum*, etc. Al-Sakkaki supplies here *yanzurun li-ya'lamu* ("they look in order that they know"), and perhaps this is to observe both meaning and wording, since otherwise the supplying of looking or knowing would suffice in place of the other. Some researchers supplied nothing at all and made *ayyuhum* a substitute (badal) for the plural pronoun, meaning: each one who intends to take charge and is capable of it casts his pen. It is not hidden that this is highly forced.

﴿And you were not with them when they disputed﴾ concerning her, competing for her guardianship. According to one opinion this dispute occurred after the drawing of lots, and according to another it occurred before it. The repetition of "you were not with them" along with the attainment of the purpose through the conjunction of ﴿when they disputed﴾ to ﴿when they cast﴾ is to indicate that each of the two, the absence at the casting and the absence at the dispute, independently serves as evidence for his prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him. This holds especially according to the second opinion regarding the time of the dispute, because changing the order in the mention emphasizes this. So said Shaykh al-Islam.

There is disagreement about the time of this drawing of lots and contention, with two views. The first, which is the well-known one on which reliance is placed, is that it occurred at her birth, when her mother carried her to the church, as we indicated earlier. The second is that it occurred when she grew old and Zakariyya, peace be upon him, became unable to raise her. This view is less preferred, and weaker than it is the view of those who claimed that the drawing of lots happened twice, once in childhood and once in old age.

This verse indicates that lots have a role in distinguishing rights. It is related from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "No people cast lots and then entrusted their affair to Allah, mighty and majestic, except that the lot of the one who is right came out." He also said: "What judgment is more just than the judgment when the matter is entrusted to Allah, glorified is He? Does not Allah say: ﴿Then he cast lots and was among the losers﴾?" Al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The first person upon whom lots were cast was Maryam bint 'Imran," and then he recited: ﴿You were not with them when they cast their pens﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 45 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When the angels said﴾ marks the beginning of the account of ʿIsa, peace be upon him. By "the angels" is meant, according to the well-known view, Jibril, peace be upon him. The speech was verbal, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah. The (idh) that is prefixed to what follows is a substitute for its earlier counterpart, a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull). It has also been said that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). The intervening clause does no harm, since the parenthetical clause that comes between the substitute and what it substitutes is an interjection (i'tiraḍ), brought in as a confirmation of what preceded it and as an alert to its independence and to its being genuine enough to be counted on its own among the proofs of prophethood. They said: the conjunction is omitted on the basis that the addressee and the one addressing are one, and to signal that the two addresses are concurrent or close together in time. Abu al-Baqa' permitted the adverbial phrase to be in the accusative governed by an implied (udhkur, "mention"), and that it be an adverbial complement of (yakhtasimun, "they dispute"). It has also been said that it is a substitute for the (idh) that is prefixed to it. This was objected to on the grounds that the time of the disputing precedes the time of the glad tidings by a considerable period, so this substitution is not valid; and maintaining that it is a substitution is an error, since it does not occur in eloquent speech. The answer given is that a continuous extended period is considered, in part of which the disputing occurred and in part of which the glad tidings occurred; and on this basis it is correct to say that they were in one time, just as one says that fighting and reconciliation occurred in one year, although the fighting took place at its beginning, for example, and the reconciliation at its end. It was said: this is not needed on the second possibility mentioned by Abu al-Baqa', based on what is narrated from al-Hasan, that she, peace be upon her, was rational in childhood, so it is possible that the glad tidings came to her at that time. But this is far-fetched, and the reports speak clearly against it.

﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you glad tidings of a word from Him﴾. The word (min, "from") is used figuratively to indicate the starting point, and it is connected to an implied element which occurs as a qualifier of "word". The application of the term "word" to the one to whom it is applied is on account of his being created without the mediation of a father, but only through the mediation of "Be" alone, unlike the rest of the children of Adam. Thus the effect of the word in his case was more manifest and more complete. It is like your saying to someone who is overcome by generosity, for example: "pure generosity." Most of the exegetes hold this view, and they supported it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed the likeness of ʿIsa with Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. It has also been said: it was applied to him because Allah, exalted is He, gave glad tidings of him in the earlier scriptures. In the Torah, in the twentieth chapter of the fifth book: Allah, exalted is He, came from Sinai, appeared from Seir, and manifested Himself from the mountains of Paran. Sinai is the mountain of Allah's manifestation to Musa; Seir is the mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis, where ʿIsa used to worship; and Paran is the mountain of Makkah, where the master of the messengers, ﷺ, used to seclude himself. This is like the saying of one who announces a matter when it comes out in conformity with what he reported: "My word has come." It has also been said: because Allah guides through him just as He guides through His word.

Some people claimed that the word here means glad tidings, as if it were said: "with glad tidings from Him." The apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He, rules this out: ﴿The Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam, is only the messenger of Allah and His word which He conveyed to Maryam﴾. Perhaps the first of the views is preferred, as the lack of consistency in the other views also favors it, although this is not necessarily binding in such matters. As for the readings of ﴿gives you glad tidings﴾ here, they are like those mentioned earlier.

﴿His name﴾: the pronoun refers back to "word", and its being masculine is in observance of the meaning, since it is an expression for a masculine referent. (ism, "name") is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿al-Masih﴾. The phrase "ʿIsa" may be a substitute, or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayan), or an emphasis by synonym, as al-Dunushari indicated, or another predicate, or the predicate of an implied subject, or accusative governed by an implied verb: "I mean, as praise." The omission of the subject and of the verb: it was said that this is permissible, and what they mentioned concerning the cut-off qualifier (naʿt maqtuʿ) requires that it be obligatory. The phrase ﴿son of Maryam﴾ is a qualifier of ʿIsa, and on the assumption that it is accusative, it must be held to be cut off, being a predicate of an implied subject. Whoever made these three into predicates of the subject raised an objection: that the name in reality is ʿIsa, al-Masih is a title (laqab), and "son" is a qualifier; how then are all three made predicates of it? The answer: the intended meaning of "name" is its technical sense, namely a proper name (ʿalam) in general, not in the sense of being opposed to a title, but encompassing it and other things; and its being annexed gives generality, since the annexation of a common noun may be intended to cover all instances; and its application to the son of Maryam is by way of predominance (taghlib).

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "name" is its lexical meaning, namely a mark and a distinguishing sign, not a proper name. There is then no obstacle to making the three together a predicate, since distinction by all of them is stronger than distinction by each one alone, and the meaning returns to your saying: "The one by which he is known and distinguished from others is the three together." On this basis, as in al-Intisaf, there is a release from an objection they raise, saying: ﴿al-Masih﴾ in the verse, if it means the designation, which is the apparent sense, then what is the position of ﴿ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾, since a designation cannot be described as a prophet? And if it means the one bearing this designation, it does not agree with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿his name﴾. The way of release is clear. Because this way was not apparent to some of them, they took the release to be that al-Masih is a predicate of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿his name﴾, meaning the designation; while ﴿ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject whose estimate is "he," and the pronoun refers to the one named by the designation mentioned, detached from "al-Masih".

It is well known that al-Masih is his title, peace be upon him, and it is among his honorific titles, like al-Faruq. Its original form in Hebrew is mashiha, and its meaning is "the blessed." It is reported from Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi that it means "the truthful" (al-siddiq). It is reported from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' that it means "the king." ʿIsa is an arabicized form of Yeshua, and its meaning is "the lord." It is reported from many of the early scholars that al-Masih is derived from masḥ (wiping). They differed about the reason for applying it to ʿIsa, peace be upon him. It was said: because he was anointed with blessing and good fortune; this is reported from al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr. It was said: because he used to wipe the eye of the blind man and he would see; this is reported from al-Kalbi. It was said: because he did not wipe anyone afflicted with an ailment with his hand except that he was healed; this was related by ʿAta' and al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Jubba'i said: because he used to wipe with oil of olive that was blessed, and the prophets used to anoint themselves with it. It was said: because Jibril wiped him with his wings at the time of his birth, so that he would be a protection from the accursed Satan. It was said: because when Allah, exalted is He, wiped the back of Adam, peace be upon him, and brought forth from it the particles of his offspring, He did not return him to his place as He did with the other particles, but kept him with Himself until He cast him to Maryam; so the name al-Masih, that is, "the wiped one," remained upon him. And it was said, and it was said.

These views indicate that the word is Arabic, not Hebrew, and many of the verifiers hold the second view, and Abu ʿUbayda chose it; on this view there is no derivation, since derivation does not truly apply to foreign names. In al-Kashf: the apparent view regarding it is derivation, since it is Arabic, to which the particular features of their speech have been applied; it was made a title of honour for him, peace be upon him, like "the Friend" for Ibrahim. Making it arabicized, and then treating it as an adjective in the admission of the definite article, is contrary to the apparent sense, since in their speech it has the meaning of a descriptive epithet.

Some people claimed that the entry of the definite article does not contradict foreignness, for the Torah, the Gospel and Alexander were only heard with it, although they are foreign; and perhaps this does not contradict the stronger likelihood that the subject of dispute is Arabic. Yes, it was said about ʿIsa that he is derived from ʿIs, and that he was named by it, peace be upon him, because in his colour there was ʿis, that is, whiteness with a reddish tinge, as the report "as if he had come out of a bathhouse" indicates. But what is relied upon in this is that it has no derivation, and that the one who says so is like one who inscribes on water. This disagreement pertains only to this al-Masih. As for al-Masih al-Dajjal, it is Arabic by consensus, and he was so named either because one of his eyes is wiped out, or because he wipes the earth, that is, traverses it in a short period. Al-Nakhaʿi distinguished between the title of the Spirit of Allah and that of His enemy: the first, with a fatha on the mim and light pronunciation; the second, with a kasra on the mim and a shadda on the sin, like sherrir ("very wicked"). Others denied this, and it is the well-known view.

Then, those who hold that it is a title in the verse, and that ʿIsa is a substitute for example, mostly restricted the prohibition of placing the title before the name to cases where it is not more famous than the name in reality or in supposition. But if it is more famous, as here, then placement is permissible, as Ibn al-Anbari explicitly stated, and it is not limited to non-eloquent speech as in cases where it is not so. The well-known view, when both the name and the title are single words, is that the first is annexed to the second; in al-Mufassal it is said that this is definite, and Sibawayh's practice indicates this. Whoever permitted following (tabaʿiyya) relied on the saying: "This is Yahya, two eyes" (ʿaynan), for if it were annexed, one would say ʿaynayn. Its being read as ʿaynān with a damma on the nun is taken to be in the dialect of those who make the dual end in alif; this is rejected by the fact that the reading is with a damma. If the reading were with a kasra, that interpretation would be possible and the argument would not hold; likewise if it were with a fatha, since it would then be possible for the title to be genitive by annexation, except that the fatha in it stands in for the kasra, on the basis of the view that a named word may be inflected as well as left undeclined. But you know that the most that this argument establishes is that it occurs in this particular instance, and not that it is a general rule. Perhaps the one who prevents this claims that the rule is annexation, but only on condition that nothing blocks it; so it is not permissible when the definite article is attached to a title, because it prevents annexation; hence one does not say "al-harth Karaz" with annexation. Likewise when the title is originally a descriptive adjective, as in Ibrahim al-Khalil, according to what Ibn al-Hajib stated explicitly in his commentary on al-Mufassal, since in the familiar view a modified noun is not annexed to its qualifier.

Some people made what we are discussing of this kind, and that is based on the view of one who holds that al-Masih is an adjective in Arabic; yet in this matter there is a disagreement of Ibn Hisham, for he permits annexation in this category too. The full discussion is in our grammatical books, so let it be understood.

The phrase ﴿son of Maryam﴾ was said although the address is to her, to indicate that he would be born without a father; for had he had a father, he would have been ascribed to him. In this there is also an allusion to the excellence of the mother. It has been said that in this there is a refutation of the Christians. And the furthest in this is the one who claimed that this annexation is for the praise of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, because the sense would then be like "son of the Worshipper (ʿAbida)." Know, moreover, that the word (ibn, "son") in the verse is written without a hamza, on the basis that it occurs as a qualifier between two proper names. The rule is that whenever it occurs in this way, its hamza is not written but is omitted in the script, following its omission in pronunciation because it is so frequently used in this way.
