Whenever a proper name precedes it but it is annexed to a non-proper name, as in Zayd ibn al-Sultan, or whenever a non-proper name precedes it and it is annexed to a proper name, as in al-Sultan ibn Zayd, or whenever it occurs between two items neither of which is a proper name, as in Zayd al-ʿAqil ibn al-Amir ʿAmr, the alif is written and not omitted in the script in all those cases. Scribes often make mistakes in this and omit the hamza in writing wherever it occurs; Ibn Qutaybah and others have explicitly stated their error in this.

From here it has been said that the orthography favours the following of the qualifier (tabaʿiyya). Yes, there is a disagreement as to whether this is a consistent rule when the annexed-to word is the mother's proper name; and what I myself choose is also omission, when this is well known.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 45 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Honored (wajihan) in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ Al-wajih is one who possesses standing (jah), nobility (sharaf) and rank (qadr). It has also been said: one who is esteemed by the one he asks, so that, because of the nobility of his face before Him, He does not turn him away, unlike one who offers his face to a request and is turned away. His honor in this world lies in prophethood and his precedence over people; in the Hereafter, in the acceptance of his intercession and the elevation of his rank. It has also been said: his honor in this world lies in the acceptance of his supplication, by which the dead were brought back to life and the blind and leper were healed. It has also been said: it is due to his being free of the defects which the Jews falsely attributed to him. As for the Hereafter, it is as previously mentioned. Honor (wajahah) here does not mean outward appearance and splendor, such that one would ask: how was he honored in this world when the Jews, may God curse them, treated him as they did? Moreover, if the meaning were that, that treatment would not detract from him, just as it does not detract on the earlier interpretations, as will not be hidden from the careful reflector.

The accusative of ﴿wajihan﴾ is because it is a presumed (muqaddarah) circumstantial clause (hal) of "kalimah" (word). What permitted a circumstantial clause to come from it, although it is indefinite, is that it is described by what follows it. The masculine form is due to consideration of the meaning, as has been pointed out. The circumstantial clause was made presumed because honor came after the glad tidings. Some people made the circumstantial clause from (Isa). Abu al-Baqa said: this is not permissible; likewise it is not permissible to make it a circumstantial clause from ﴿al-Masih﴾ or from ﴿Ibn Maryam﴾, because these are predicates (akhbar), and the governing element in them is the inceptive (ibtida') or the subject (mubtada') or both, and none of these governs a circumstantial clause. Likewise it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in his name (ismihi), because of the intervening separation between them and because there is no governing element for the circumstantial clause. The adverbial phrase is connected to what precedes it, because it contains the sense of a verb.

﴿And among those brought near﴾ [45] — that is, in the presence of God on the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Qatadah. It has also been said: it refers to his being raised to heaven and his companionship with the angels. It has also been said: "among those brought near" means among people who are drawn near by acceptance and response, and it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿wajihan﴾, that is, "and one brought near from among those brought near."

﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ is coordinated with the earlier circumstance (ḥāl) as well. Coordinating a verb with a noun (ʿaṭf al-fiʿl ʿalā al-ism) is permissible and common, because the verb is taken to be equivalent to a noun in meaning (taʾwīl), and it is frequent in the Qur'an. The adverbial phrase "in the cradle" (al-ẓarf) is a circumstantial element (ḥāl) of the pronoun hidden within the verb. It was not made a loose adverbial (ẓarf laghw, an adverbial dependent on nothing in particular) attached to the verb, even though that is grammatically valid, because "and in maturity" is coordinated with it. The meaning is: he will speak to them while being a child and while being a grown man. The intent is to equate speech in childhood with speech in maturity. Otherwise, speech in the second state would not be anything peculiar to him, peace be upon him, nor would there be anything strange in it. On this reading, the whole phrase is one circumstance, not two independent ones. It has also been said that each of the two is a separate circumstance. On the second view, the words "and in maturity" give good news of his reaching the age of maturity and specify his age.

The cradle (al-mahd) is the place where the infant rests during nursing. Its root is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that became a name. His speech in the cradle lasted a single moment, as God has related to us. Then he did not speak again until he reached the age for speech. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also been said that he spoke continuously, and that his speech in the cradle was a foundation (taʾsīs) for his prophethood and a preliminary sign (irhāṣ) of it, according to the view of Ibn al-Ikhshid. On this view, God's words "and He made me a prophet" are a report of what he would become.

Al-Jubba'i said that God perfected his intellect, peace be upon him, at that time, and revealed to him what he said, joined with prophethood. It is also permitted that this was a miracle (karāma) for Mary, indicating her purity and the clearing of her name from what the people of slander attributed to her. The claim that it was a miracle (muʿjiza) for her is far-fetched, even if we hold that she was a prophetess.

The Christians claim that he, peace be upon him, did not speak in the cradle and did not speak in defense of his mother's innocence while he was an infant. Rather, he remained silent for thirty years. The Jews accuse his mother of having relations with Yusuf the carpenter. This is among the greatest of their manifest disgraces, refuting what they hold about his divinity, peace be upon him. Likewise, his passing through different and contradictory stages refutes divinity, because one whose condition is this is far removed from divinity. They raised the objection that his speech in the cradle is among the most astonishing of matters, so if it had occurred it would have been transmitted, and if it had been transmitted the Christians would be the people most entitled to know it. The answer is that those present at that time did not reach the level of mass transmission (tawātur). When they reported it, they were denied and fell silent, and the matter remained concealed until the Qur'an spoke of it. This is plausible on the view of Ibn ʿAbbas that he spoke only for an hour of the day. On the other view, that he continued to speak, it is said that people subsequently occupied themselves with transmitting things even more astonishing about his condition, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, reporting the unseen, and creating from clay something like the form of a bird. As a result, speech was mentioned by them only rarely, and the matter kept dwindling until no one remained who reported it, and it remained hidden until the Qur'an made it known.

After all this, you may say: we do not concede that the Christians agree that he did not speak in the cradle. The apparent sense of the reports, some of which have already been mentioned, indicates that some of them held this view. Even granting their consensus, the most that follows is improbability, and that improbability is of no benefit, nor does it satisfy hunger, for one whose faith is firm and whose certainty is strong. How often have the people of the two Books agreed on things that the true Qur'an contradicted, and the truth is more deserving of being followed. Perhaps their aim in this is to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, "but God refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it" [cf. 61:8].

The kahl (the one in maturity) is the one between youth and old age. From it comes the verb iktahala, said of a plant when it grows tall and strong. Many have mentioned that the son of Adam, as long as he is in the womb, is a janīn (fetus). When he is born, he is a walīd (newborn). As long as he is nursing, he is a raḍīʿ (suckling). When he stops drinking milk, he is a faṭīm (weaned). When he crawls and grows, he is dārij. When he reaches five spans, he is khumāsī. When his milk teeth fall out, he is mathghūr. When his permanent teeth come in, he is muthghir, with the letters tāʾ and thāʾ, as Abu ʿAmr said. When he approaches ten years or exceeds it, he is mutarraʿriʿ and nāshiʾ. When he is about to reach puberty or has reached it, he is yāfiʿ and murāhiq. When he has had a wet dream and his strength has gathered, he is ḥazawwar. His name in all these states is ghulām (boy). When his beard begins to show green and his sideburns hang down, it is said: his face has become green (baqala wajhuh). When he attains vigor and becomes a fatā (young man) and shārikh, and when his beard is full and he reaches the peak of his youth, he is mujtamiʿ. Then, as long as he is between thirty and forty, he is shābb (youth), and then kahl (middle-aged) until he completes sixty. It is said of one in whom the signs of old age have appeared and whitening has marked him: then it is said shāba, then shamiṭa, then shākha, then kabura, then haruma, then dalafa, then kharifa, then ihtarra. His shadow is effaced when he dies. This sequence applies to males. For females, while she is young, she is called ṭiflah. Then she is walīdah when she has begun to move. Then kāʿib when her breast has begun to swell. Then nāhid. Then muʿṣir when she has reached puberty. Then ʿānis when she has passed the limit of the age of puberty. Then khawd when she is in the middle of youth. Then musallif when she has passed forty. Then naṣaf when she is between youth and decrepitude. Then shahlah kahlah when she has reached old age while still having some remnant and vigor. Then shahrabah when she has become feeble while still holding herself together. Then ḥayzabūn when she has reached great age and diminished reason. Then qalʿam and liṭlaṭ when her body has bent and her teeth have fallen out.

According to what has been mentioned regarding the age of maturity, his speaking to them as a man (kahl) refers to his speaking to them in the same way after descending from heaven and reaching that age. This is based on the view of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Zayd ibn Aslam, and others, that: "He was raised to heaven when he was thirty-three years old, and he will descend to the earth and remain alive there for twenty-four years," as Ibn Jarir related with a sound chain of narration from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse. He said: "ʿIsa spoke to them in the cradle, and he will speak to them when the Dajjal is killed, and he will then be a man (kahl)."

﴿And among the righteous﴾ [46]: that is, and counted among them. It is coordinated with the preceding circumstances.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 47:

﴿She said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did she say when the angels told her that?" So it is said: ﴿She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child?"﴾ The interrogative may be figurative, meaning wonder at this and a customary sense of its being unlikely. It may also be literal, meaning: how will it happen, by marriage or otherwise? It has been said that it may be a question about whom the child would be from. The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of this sentence is like the analysis of the preceding sentence in the story of Zachariah, peace be upon him. ﴿No man has touched me﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) that confirms what came before and strengthens it. Here *massis* (touching) is a metaphor for sexual intercourse, and this is a general negation covering marriage and other means. *Bashar* (human, man) applies to the singular and the plural, and the indefinite form indicates generality. What is meant is the generality of the negation, not the negation of generality. He was called *bashar* either because of the visibility of his skin (*bashara*) or because God Most High touched his father and created him with His own hands.

(She was told) is a resumptive sentence like the previous one. The subject of the verb is the pronoun referring to the Lord, and the angel conveyed to her the words that were spoken, which are His, glorified is He: ﴿Thus does God create what He wills﴾. This is either without change, in which case there is a shift (*iltifat*) in it, or with change. It has been said that God Most High said this to her without an intermediary angel. The first view is based on the position that God Most High did not speak to anyone other than the prophets, or rather other than their elect, upon them be prayer and peace. It has been said that the speaker was Gabriel, peace be upon him, and that this is not in the mode of reported speech. The indication for this is the mention of the angels, peace be upon them, before it. Taking ﴿She said: "My Lord"﴾ in what preceded to refer to that is an extremely distant interpretation. The discussion of a sentence like this has already passed over you, except that the expression here is *yakhluqu* (creates), while there it is *yaf'alu* (does), because the two stories differ in strangeness, for the second is stranger. Creation, which indicates origination (*ikhtira'*), is more suitable for it, and for this reason He followed it with an explanation of its manner. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾, that is, wills something. *Al-amr* is the singular of *al-umur* (affairs), and *al-qada'* originally means judgments. It is applied to the definitive divine will related to bringing the non-existent into being and annihilating the existent, and it is so called because it makes necessary whatever it relates to, absolutely. It is also applied to command, as in ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾.

﴿Then He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [47]: that is, then it exists, that is, comes into being. According to most scholars, this is an analogy (*tamthil*) for the effect of His power on what He wills, by the command of one obeyed to one who obeys in bringing about the commanded thing without hesitation, pause, or need to undertake work or use an instrument. So the analogue is a thing that comes into being swiftly without work or instrument, and the analogue-source is the command of a commander obeyed by one commanded who obeys immediately. This expression is borrowed for that from it. You know that it is possible for it to be literal, in that what is meant is the relation of the inner speech (*kalam nafsi*) to the thing that comes into being, with the manner of creation being in this way. On both assessments, the purpose of this answer is to show that God Most High is not unable to create a child without a father, because it is a thing possible in itself, so it can be the object of will and power. How not, when we often observe the coming into being of many animals by spontaneous generation (*tawallud*), such as mice arising from mud, snakes from rotting hair, scorpions from *badhurij* (a kind of plant or herb), flies from broad beans, and so on. The only thing this implies is improbability, and that does not produce even a presumption, let alone knowledge. After the true reporter has informed us of the existence of that possibility, it is necessary to be certain of its soundness. As for the claim that the matter (material) exists in the cases enumerated and similar ones, and that after its existence there is no doubt about possibility, but not in our case, because the material of a human is two seeds, while there is only one seed here or none at all, so how can creation be possible?—this is nothing. As for our school, the origination does not depend on the prior existence of material, otherwise the matter would be an infinite regress. As for the school of the deniers, it is possible that the female's seed by itself, or with what joins it of which only God Most High has knowledge, is in a state suitable to be material. The most that follows from this is improbability, and that is of no benefit in matters of this kind. It is also possible that God Most High makes something other than seed take the place of seed. What absurdity follows from that? Do you not see how dust was made to take the place of seed in the origin of the species? The claim that substitution is conditional on that other thing being outside the womb, while substitution inside the womb is something for which there is neither clear possibility nor clear proof, is not correct. Rather, reason does not distinguish between the two matters in terms of possibility. It only distinguishes between them in terms of agreement with habit and its absence, and that is a matter beyond what we are discussing.

Some people have explained this question by saying that mental imaginings often become causes for the occurrence of events, such as imagining the presence of something repugnant causing anger, and imagining a fall causing a fall in one who walks on a log laid across an open space, unlike if he were on level ground. The philosophers have made this like a principle in explaining the possibility of miracles and marvels (*karamat*). So what prevents us from saying: when she imagined the form of Gabriel, that was enough for a child to form in her womb, because a man's seed is only for the purpose of conception, so when conception takes place for a woman's seed by another means, it is possible for a child to form. End of quote.

This is nothing, because it leads to deficiency in the status of the virgin, and she would purify her sanctuary from such imagining, as is not hidden. In the reply of this pure woman to Joseph the carpenter there is something that supports what we have said. Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Wahb that he said: When Mary's pregnancy was established and Gabriel gave her good news, she was reassured by God Most High's honour, and she was content and her soul was at ease. The first person to notice her pregnancy was a maternal cousin of hers named Joseph, and he was concerned about it and was grieved by it, and feared trouble from it, because he used to serve her. When he saw the change in her color and the enlargement of her belly, this weighed heavily on him, and he said, alluding to her: "Can there be a crop without seed?" She said: "Yes." He said: "How can that be?" She said: "God Most High created the first seed without a plant, and He made the first crop grow without seed. Perhaps you will say: why can He create the first crop only with seed? Perhaps you will say: if God Most High had not been assisted in it by seed, He would have overcome it so that He could not create or grow it?" Joseph said: "I seek refuge in God from saying that. You have spoken truly, and I have said it with light and wisdom. Just as He was able to create the first crop and make it grow without seed, He is able to make a crop without seed. So tell me: does a tree grow without water or rain?" She said: "Do you not know that seed, water, rain, and tree have one Creator? Perhaps you will say: if not for water and rain, He would not have been able to make the tree grow?" He said: "I seek refuge in God Most High from saying that. You have spoken truly. So tell me your story." She said: "God Most High gave me good news of a word from Him whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary," up to His words, Most High: ﴿and among the righteous﴾. Joseph knew that this was a command from God Most High for a good reason He intended concerning Mary, so he remained silent about her. She remained in that state until the pangs of labour seized her, and she was called: ﴿"Come out from the sanctuary"﴾, and she came out.

[p. 165–166]

﴿And He will teach him the Book﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with ﴿He gives you good news﴾, meaning: God gives you good news of a word, and He will teach that child, who is referred to by the word, the Book. The lengthy intervening clauses do not weaken this, because it is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtiraḍ*), and such an insertion does no harm. It may instead be coordinated with ﴿He creates﴾, meaning: thus God creates what He wills and teaches him. Or it may be coordinated with ﴿He speaks﴾, in which case it occupies the position of an accusative circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the sense is: He gives you good news of a word, speaking to people and teaching the Book. Or it may be coordinated with ﴿honourable﴾. It is also permitted that it be an independent sentence (*jumla mustaʾnafa*) that is not within the scope of the speech of the angels, peace be upon them. In that case the *wāw* is for resumption (*istiʾnaf*) and occurs at the beginning of a speech, as the grammarians have explicitly stated. Therefore, as al-Shihab said, there is no need to interpret it as coordinated with an earlier independent sentence, namely ﴿And when the angels said﴾ etc., nor to any implied element. There is no difficulty in the coordination, as al-Nihrir said. Likewise, it cannot be claimed that the *wāw* is superfluous, as Abu Hayyan said. These are several grammatical possibilities, differing in preferability. The strangest thing I have seen is what al-Tabarsi transmitted from some people: that the coordination is with the clause ﴿We reveal it to you﴾. Indeed, one whose taste is sound would hardly find it agreeable.

﴿The Book (*al-kitāb*)﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning writing, i.e., He teaches him writing with the hand. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Juraij adopted it. It is narrated from him that he said: God gave Jesus, peace be upon him, nine parts of writing, and gave all other people one part. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i held that what is meant is some of the books that God sent down to His prophets, peace be upon them, other than the Torah and the Gospel, such as the Psalms and others. Many scholars held that the definite article *al-* here is generic (*lām al-jins*), and what is meant is the genus of divine books. However, the transmitted position is the first. As for the view that by "the Book" is meant the genus, but within two particular instances, namely the Torah and the Gospel, and that the *wāw* in what follows is considered superfluous and inserted, with what follows it being a substitute or an appositive (*ʿaṭf bayān*), this is far from sound.

The people of Medina, ʿĀṣim, Yaʿqub and Sahl read ﴿He will teach him﴾ with *yāʾ*, and the rest read it with *nūn*. It has been said that on this reading some of those possibilities are not good unless the verb "say" is implied, meaning: God gives you good news of Jesus and says: "We will teach him," or: honourable and spoken of as: "We will teach him the Book."

﴿And wisdom (*al-ḥikma*)﴾ means understanding (*al-fiqh*) and knowledge of what is lawful and unlawful. This was said by Ibn Abbas. It has also been said that it is all that He taught him of the matters of religion; that it is the practices (*sunan*) of the prophets, peace be upon them; that it is correctness in speech and action; and that it is mastery of the rational sciences. The discussion of this has already passed.

﴿And the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [48] are mentioned separately on the assumption that "the Book" is meant to include them, because of their great merit and the elevation of their standing above others. As for His teaching him these, it has been said that it was by inspiration, that it was by revelation, and that it was by granting success and guidance to learn. It is authentically reported that when he grew up... and in the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas: when he reached seven years of age, his mother placed him with a teacher. However, the reports are consistent that he kept asking the teacher whenever the teacher mentioned something to him, about matters on which he could not utter a word. This supports that his knowledge was purely a divine gift and a lordly bestowal. The mention of the Gospel is because it was known to the prophets and scholars, and it was firmly established in their minds that it would be sent down.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose sense is drawn from the context and which is conjoined to "yu'allimuhu" (he teaches him). The meaning is: "and We make him a messenger." This is the view preferred by Abu Hayyan. It has also been said that it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb which is itself governed by an implied "saying" conjoined to "yu'allimuhu," meaning: "and Jesus says, 'I have been sent as a messenger.'" It is not hidden that conjoining this saying to "yu'allimuhu" is not seriously objectionable if it is taken as a new sentence. But if it is conjoined to ﴿yubashshiruki﴾ (He gives you good news) or ﴿yakhluqu﴾ (He creates), al-Allamah al-Taftazani has criticized it, on the grounds that the sense would be: "Indeed God gives you good news," or "Indeed God creates what He wills and Jesus says such-and-such." This involves conjoining to a predicate, and there is no link between the two except with great strain. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, "The Surrounding Sea," the commentary of Abu Hayyan), it is said that this view, in every case, is weak, since it involves implying two things, the saying and its object, and dispensing with them by a noun in the accusative as a emphasizing circumstantial (hal). Some have preferred to conjoin it to the preceding circumstantial phrases, with the verb implicitly carrying the sense of speaking. Its being in the sense of an absent party does not harm this, since the phrase is in the sense of speaking. The meaning then is: "while he is dignified and a messenger who speaks such-and-such." The word "messenger" in all the other interpretations is an adjective, like "grateful" (shakur) and "patient" (sabur). Here "fa'ul" (the pattern fa'ul) has the sense of "mif'il" (the pattern af'al, the active participle of causation). It is also possible that it is a verbal noun (masdar), as Abu al-Baqa stated, in the same way as in the line of the poet:

*Convey to Abu Salma a message (rasulan) that will startle him*

And it may be made conjoined to "al-kitab" (the Book), meaning: "and He teaches him the message (risalah)." This is distant both in wording and in meaning. As for the first point, the apparent sense is the adjectival and not the verbal-noun form. As for the second, the teaching of a message is hardly ever found in their speech.

The prepositional phrase "to the Children of Israel" either relates to "messenger," or to an implied word that functions as an adjective to it, meaning: "a messenger present to the Children of Israel," that is, all of them. It has been said: their being singled out for mention is to signal the specificity of his mission, or to refute those among the Jews who claimed that he was sent to others.

I have some hesitation about attributing this claim to some of the Jews. It is not in the well-known books. What we have found in them is that concerning Jesus, whose story God has related to us, there are two groups. One group slanders him, and God forbid, with the most abominable accusations a community has ever leveled against its prophet; they are the majority of the Jews. The other group is called the 'Ananiyyah, the followers of 'Anan ibn Dawud, the head of the Exilarchate (ra's al-jalut). They accept his admonitions and allusions, and they say that he did not oppose the Torah at all, but rather affirmed it and called people to it, and that he was among those who responded to Moses, peace be upon him, and among the Children of Israel who worshipped God, and that he was not a messenger or a prophet. They say that the rest of the Jews wronged him, in that they denied him at first without understanding his claim, and then killed him without understanding his purpose and aim. Yes, there is among the Jews a group called the 'Isawiyyah, the followers of Abu 'Isa Ishaq ibn Ya'qub al-Isfahani, whom some call "Bi'arqid al-Wahim." They claim that God, exalted is He, has a messenger after Moses, peace be upon him, named the Messiah, though he has not yet come. They claim that he has five messengers who will come before him, one after another, and that this man of theirs is one of His messengers. Each of these views is miles away from what the proponent of the claim asserts. Perhaps he found something that agrees with his claim. And the one who has memorized (the Qur'an) is a proof against the one who has not memorized it.

That said, there is disagreement about the time of his prophetic mission, peace be upon him. It has been said that it was in childhood, when he was three years old. In al-Bahr it is said that revelation came to him after puberty, when he was thirty years old, so his prophethood lasted three years. It is said also three months and three days, after which he was raised to heaven. This is the well-known view. But against it is that the first of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Joseph. It has been said also that it was Moses, and the last of them was Jesus, and he is the best of them all, with the most perfect blessings and the fullest peace.

Al-Yazidi read ﴿wa-rasulin﴾ (and a messenger) in the genitive, as conjoined to "kalimatin" (a word), meaning: "He gives you good news with a word and with a messenger."

﴿That I have come to you﴾ is governed by "rasulan" (messenger), because it contains the sense of speaking. Abu al-Baqa allowed that it is governed by an implied word which functions as an adjective to "rasulan," meaning: "a messenger speaking or informing that I..." It may also be an apposition to "rasulan" if you make it a verbal noun, meaning: "and We teach him that I have come to you"; or a predicate of an implied subject on the same assumption of its being a verbal noun, meaning: "it is that I..." Thus the clause that is formed is either in the genitive, the accusative, or the nominative position.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with a sign﴾ is in the place of a circumstantial phrase, meaning: "bringing evidence" or "endowed with a sign." Or it relates to "I have come to you," with the preposition "bi" (with) being for accompaniment or for transitivity. The nunation (tanwin) of "aya" (sign) is for magnification, not for unity, because what contradicts unity is evident. It was also read as ﴿bi-ayatin﴾ (with signs).

﴿from your Lord﴾ relates to an implied word which functions as an adjective to "aya" (sign). It was also permitted that it relates to "I have come." In both cases "min" (from) is for the starting point of the action, in a figurative sense. The mention of the title of Lordship with the pronoun of the addressees is to emphasize the obligation to obey the commands that will follow, or because the attribute of Lordship suits the situation of being sent to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that I shape for you from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ is an apposition to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿that I have come to you﴾, or to "aya" (sign), or it is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul) of an implied verb, meaning: "I mean," or in the nominative as a predicate of an implied subject, meaning: "it is that I..." etc. Nafi' read ﴿inni﴾ (I) with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence. What is meant by "creating" (khalq) is shaping and fashioning into a specific measure, not bringing into existence from nothing, as the mention of the material indicates. "Hay'ah" (the likeness, form) is a verbal noun in the sense of the thing that has been formed, just as "khalq" (creation) is in the sense of the thing created. It has been said that it is a noun for the state of a thing and not a verbal noun. The verbal noun is "hay'" and "tahayyu'" (the act of getting ready). On the first reading it is a substance (jawhar); on the second it is an accident ('arad). They have explained it as the configuration resulting from the enclosing of a single boundary or several boundaries around a body. The meaning is: "I determine, for the purpose of securing your faith and repelling your denial of me, from clay something like a bird that has been prepared, or a form that is like its form." The particle "ka" (like) is either a noun, as Abu al-Hasan held, in the accusative position as the object of "akhluqu" (I shape), or an adjective to an implied object of it. Or it is a particle, as the majority held, and then it relates to an implied word which is also an adjective, since the thing it modifies is an adjective, on the assumption that it is a noun.

Yazid and Hamzah read ﴿kahayyati﴾ with a doubled ya'. Ibn al-Muqsim used to say: "It has reached me that Khalaf says that Hamzah drops the hamza and moves the ya' with its vowel." The people of Madinah and Ya'qub read ﴿al-tair﴾ (the bird) with the definite article, and similarly in al-Ma'idah.

﴿Then I breathe into it﴾: the pronoun refers to the form that is implied in the structure of the speech, but in the sense of the thing that has been prepared, not in the sense of an accident that subsists in it, since that cannot be a place for breathing. The pronoun is mentioned here in consideration of the meaning, just as it is made feminine in al-Ma'idah in consideration of the wording. It has been said that this is valid because there is no ambiguity. It occurs in the speech of more than one commentator that the pronoun refers to the particle "ka" (like), on the basis of its being a noun. This amounts in reality to the pronoun returning to the thing described by it. Ibn Hisham objected to this: "If it were as they claim, it would be heard in speech as 'I passed by like a lion' (marartu bi ka-al-asad)." Some have answered that the return of the pronoun to it is not customary. It was also read as ﴿fiha﴾ (into it, feminine).

﴿And it becomes a bird﴾: a living bird that flies, like all other birds. Al-Mufaddal read ﴿fa-takunu﴾ (so she becomes) with the feminine ta'. Ya'qub, Abu Ja'far and Nafi' read ﴿ta'iran﴾ (a flying bird).

﴿By God's permission﴾ relates to "yakunu" (it becomes) or to "tiran" (bird). What is meant by it is the command of God. By this he indicates that its being brought to life is from God, exalted is He, but through the means of the breathing. This is not a peculiarity specific to Jesus, peace be upon him, namely his being formed from the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him, who is pure spirit, as has been said. Rather, if God, exalted is He, willed the bringing to life through the breathing of any person whatsoever, it would happen without failure or refusal. It has been said that in this miracle there is an appropriateness to his creation without a father.

It has been disputed whether this occurred at the request of the people as a demand or not. The majority took the first view. They said: the Children of Israel asked him, as a way of challenging him, in keeping with their habit with their prophets, that he create for them a bat. When he did so, they said, "He is a sorcerer." They asked for this particular kind and not another because it is the most perfect of birds in its creation and the most eloquent proof of power, since it has teeth and molars, menstruates and gives birth, and flies without feathers. It has ears, nipples and an udder, and milk comes out of it. It appears to laugh as a human laughs. It cannot see in the light of day or in the darkness of night, but it sees only in two hours: one hour after sunset, and one hour after dawn before it becomes very bright. The well-known view is that he created nothing but the bat. Abu al-Shaykh narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. Wahb said: it flew as long as people were looking at it, and when it disappeared from their eyes, it fell dead, so that it would be distinguished from God's creation without an intermediary. It has been said that he created various kinds of birds. Others took the second view. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Ishaq that Jesus, peace be upon him, sat one day with boys from the school, took some clay and said: "Shall I make for you a bird from this clay?" They said: "Can you do that?" He said: "Yes, by the permission of my Lord." Then he shaped it until, when he had made it in the form of a bird, he breathed into it and said: "Be a bird, by God's permission, exalted is He." It flew out from between his two palms, and the boys went out with this by his command, told their teacher about it, and spread it among the people.

﴿And I heal the one born blind﴾ is conjoined to ﴿I shape﴾, so it falls within the scope of ﴿that I﴾. The "akmah" (one born blind) is the one who was born blind. Ibn Jarir narrated it through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through 'Ata' from him that it is the one whose eye is smoothed over, whose sight has not been split open, and who was not created with a pupil. It has been said that there was no one in the early part of this community who was born blind in this sense except Qatadah ibn Di'amah al-Sadusi, the author of the Tafsir. From Mujahid: it is the one who sees by day but does not see by night. From Ikrimah: it is al-A'mash. That is: "I free the akmah from his blindness."

﴿And the leper﴾ is the one who has the well-known white patch. The specifying of these two matters is because they are two troublesome matters that baffled the physicians, who were extremely skilled, and were numerous in his time. For this reason God, exalted is He, showed them a miracle of the kind of medicine, just as He showed the people of Moses, peace be upon him, the miracle of the staff and the white hand, since sorcery predominated among them, and the Arabs the miracle of the Qur'an, since eloquence predominated among them in the time of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. Limiting the mention to these two matters does not indicate the negation of what is other than them, for it has been narrated that he, peace be upon him, also healed other things. It is narrated from Wahb that sometimes there gathered around Jesus, peace be upon him, fifty thousand sick people. Whoever was able to reach him did so, and whoever was not able to, Jesus, peace be upon him, went to him on foot. He would treat them by supplicating God, exalted is He, on condition of faith. His supplication, with which he would pray for the sick, the disabled, the blind, the insane, and others, was: "O God, You are the God of whoever is in the heavens and the God of whoever is on the earth; there is no god in them besides You. You are the Almighty of whoever is in the heavens and the Almighty of whoever is on the earth; there is no almighty in them besides You. You are the King of whoever is in the heavens and the King of whoever is on the earth; there is no king in them besides You. Your power on earth is like Your power in heaven, and Your authority on earth is like Your authority in heaven. I ask You by Your Noble Name, Your Radiant Face, and Your Eternal Kingdom, indeed You are over all things Powerful." Among the special properties of this supplication, as Wahb said, is that if it is recited over the frightened person or the insane person, and it is written out for him and he drinks from it, it benefits him, God willing, exalted is He.

And I will raise the dead by the leave of Allah. This is coordinated with the predicate of (Indeed, I...). The raising of the dead is qualified by "by the leave of Allah," as was done in the first case, because it is an extraordinary feat (khāriq, a miracle that breaks the normal order of nature) so great that one might imagine from it the divinity (ulūhiyyah) of its doer, since it is not of the kind of the works of humans. His giving life was by supplication, and his supplication was: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting."

The report: "When he wished to raise the dead, he would pray two rak'ahs. In the first he would recite: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion﴾, and in the second: The Prostration (As-Sajdah). When he finished, he would praise Allah the Exalted and extol Him, then supplicate with seven names: O Eternal (Qadīm), O Hidden (Khafī), O Everlasting (Dā'im), O Singular (Fard), O Odd (Witr), O One (Aḥad), O Eternal Refuge (Ṣamad)." Al-Bayhaqī said: "It is not strong (in its chain)." It was also said: when he wished to raise a dead person, he would strike the dead person, or the grave, or the skull, with his staff, and the person would live by the leave of Allah the Exalted, speak with him, and die quickly.

Muḥyī al-Sunnah (al-Baghawī) narrated from Ibn 'Abbās that he said: "He (peace be upon him) raised four souls: 'Āzar, the son of the old woman, the daughter of the tax collector ('āshir), and Sām son of Noah. As for 'Āzar, he was a friend of his. His sister sent to 'Īsā: 'Your brother 'Āzar has died.' Between him and 'Āzar was a three-day journey. He came with his companions and found that he had died three days earlier. He said to his sister: 'Come with us to his grave.' She went with them to his grave. 'Īsā prayed to Allah the Exalted, and 'Āzar rose, his shroud dripping, and came out of his grave. He lived for a time and had children. As for the son of the old woman, he passed by him dead, on a bier carried by men. 'Īsā prayed to Allah the Exalted, and he sat up on his bier, got down from the shoulders of the men, put on his clothes, carried the bier on his neck, and returned to his family. He lived for a time and had children. As for the daughter of the tax collector, her father was a man who collected tithes. His daughter had died the day before. He prayed to Allah the Exalted and she was brought back to life. She lived for a time and had children. As for Sām son of Noah, 'Īsā (peace be upon him) came to his grave and called upon Allah the Exalted by His Greatest Name, and he came out of his grave, his hair half-grey from fear of the Hour, for in that time people did not turn grey. He said: 'Has the Hour come?' He said: 'No, but I called you by the Greatest Name of Allah the Exalted.' Then he said to him: 'Die.' He said: 'On condition that Allah the Exalted protects me from the agonies of death.' He prayed to Allah the Exalted for him, and it was done."

In some reports, the raising of Sām was after they said to him (peace be upon him): "You revive only one who was recently near death, and perhaps they did not die, but a stroke struck them. So raise Sām son of Noah for us." He raised him, and between him and his death there were more than four thousand years. He said to the people: "Believe him, for he is a prophet." Some of them believed in him and others denied him. They said: "This is sorcery. Show us a sign." So he told them what they eat and what they store.

It has also been reported that he (peace be upon him) raised the son of a king so that he might succeed him, in a lengthy story, and he raised a young deer, a sheep, and a cow. The word "the dead" (al-mawtā) encompasses all of this.

﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses.﴾ "Mā" in both places is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) or an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawṣūfah), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "what you eat of it and what you store of it." The adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf) is connected to what is with him (i.e., what he informs of), and it is not from the category of tanāzu' (the grammatical competition of two governing words for one complement). Al-idkhār means storing away and concealing. The original form of "tadakhirūn" is "tadhtakhirūn," with a dhāl (with a dot) and then a tā', so the tā' was changed into a dhāl, then the dhāl was changed into a dāl and assimilated (idghām, merging of two identical consonants). Some Arabs change the tā' to a dāl and assimilate. This informing was after prophethood and after his raising of the dead (peace be upon him), according to some reports. It was also said: it was before. Ibn 'Asākir narrated from 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr ibn al-'Āṣ that he said: "'Īsā (peace be upon him), while still a boy, was playing with children. He would say to one of them: 'Do you want me to tell you what your mother has hidden for you?' He would say: 'Yes.' He would say: 'Your mother has hidden for you such and such.' The boy would go to his mother and say to her: 'Give me what you have hidden for me.' She would say: 'And what have I hidden for you?' He would say: 'Such and such.' She would say: 'Who told you?!' He would say: 'Jesus son of Mary.' They said: 'By Allah, if you leave these children with 'Īsā, he will corrupt them.' So they gathered them in a house and locked it on them. 'Īsā went out looking for them and did not find them until he heard their clamour in a house. He asked about them. He said: 'What are these? Are these the children?' They said: 'No, they are only monkeys and pigs.' He said: 'O Allah, make them monkeys and pigs.' And they became so."

Some hold that this happened after the revelation of the Table (al-Mā'idah), and this is supported by what 'Abd al-Razzāq and others narrated from 'Ammār ibn Yāsir (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning the verse: "﴿And I inform you of what you eat﴾ from the Table, ﴿and what you store﴾ from it." He had taken a covenant from them concerning the Table when it was sent down, that they would eat and not store, but they stored and betrayed, so they were turned into monkeys and pigs. It may be said that all of this has occurred, and under all interpretations the meaning is the informing of these two specific matters, as the apparent sense indicates. It was also said: the meaning is informing of the unseen (al-mughayyabāt), but he limited himself to mentioning two of them. Perhaps the reason for specifying the informing about their circumstances is that they were certain of them, so no doubt would remain for them. The secret of mentioning these two matters specifically is that most of a person's striving and attention is directed to obtaining food, by which he sustains himself, and to storing, by which most hearts are reassured and most souls are at rest. So let it be understood.

It is read "tadhkharūn" with the dhāl (with a dot) and without the shaddah (tashdīd, doubling).

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., what was mentioned of the four great extraordinary acts. This is from the speech of 'Īsā (peace be upon him), which Allah the Exalted related from him. It was also said: it is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, brought for rebuke. ﴿is a sign﴾, i.e., of its kind. It is read "lā'ayāt" (signs, plural). ﴿for you﴾ indicates the truth of the message with clear proof, since that did not occur through the intervention of instruments or the mediation of ordinary causes, as physicians and astrologers do.

From here it is known that the sciences of al-jafr (numerological divination) and astronomy and the like, since they are tied to principles and rules, are never called "knowledge of the unseen," because the condition of knowledge of the unseen is that it be free of material causes and natural intermediaries, and these sciences are not like that, because they are arranged according to rules known to their practitioners, without which those sciences would not be known. This is unlike knowledge through revelation, for it is not acquired; rather Allah the Exalted singles out whomever He wills with it. Likewise knowledge through inspiration, for it has no source except the divine gift and the eternal bounty. Moreover, some have held that those sciences do not produce the certainty that is the opposite of conjecture, but rather at most a dominant conjecture, and between it and knowledge of the unseen there is a vast gap. This matter will have a continuation, Allah willing.

﴿If you are believers﴾ [49]. In it is the metaphorical usage of approach (majāz al-musharafah), i.e., if you are those granted success in faith. It is possible that the meaning is: if you are affirmers. The response of the conditional, under both interpretations, is omitted, i.e., you have benefited from that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 50:**

﴿And confirming what was before me of the Torah﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) either upon the implicit element to which his words ﴿with a sign﴾ are attached, meaning: "I have come to you as one presenting proof or bearing a sign, etc., and confirming what [was before me]..." or upon "a messenger" (rasulan), which carries the sense of speech, like it. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative governed by a verb indicated by ﴿I have come to you﴾, meaning: "and I have come to you confirming, etc."

His, glory be to Him, words ﴿of the Torah﴾ are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), and the governing element is the state of being established (al-istiqrar). Or the adverbial phrase itself, since it takes the place of a verb. It may also be a circumstantial clause from "what" (ma), in which case the governing element is "confirming." The meaning of his confirmation of the Torah, peace be upon him, is the belief that everything in it is wisdom and correctness. It has also been said that his confirmation of it is his coming as a messenger in accordance with what the Torah had given good news of.

﴿And to make lawful for you﴾ is the object of an implied element after the conjunction "and," meaning: "and I have come to make lawful for you." It is thus a conjunction of one clause upon another. Or it is conjoined to ﴿with a sign﴾ from his, glory be to Him, words: ﴿I have come to you with a sign﴾, since it carries the sense of "to show you a sign and to make lawful." Thus there is no objection that the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) cannot be conjoined to the direct object (maf'ul bih). Or it is conjoined to "confirming" (musaddiqan), and the interpretation is adopted that makes both of the same type, even though the first is a circumstantial clause and the second an object of purpose. It is as if it were said: "I have come to you to confirm and to make lawful." It has also been said: it is necessary to supply "I have come to you" in all of them, since one type of object cannot be conjoined to another type.

﴿Some of that which was forbidden to you﴾, that is, in the law of Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' that he said: "What Isa brought was more lenient than what Musa brought, peace be upon them both. What had been forbidden to them in what Musa, peace be upon him, brought was the flesh of camels and the fat [thurub]. So he made these lawful to them through the tongue of Isa. Also forbidden to them was the fat of camels, and it was made lawful for them in what Isa brought, as well as some kinds of fish, some kinds of birds that have no spur, and other things which he [Musa] had forbidden to them and made strict upon them. So Isa brought leniency from him in the Injil." ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah something similar.

This indicates that the Injil (Gospel) contains rulings that differ from those in the Tawrah (Torah), and that the law of Isa abrogated part of the law of Musa. This does not undermine his being a confirmer of the Torah, for abrogation (naskh) is an explanation of the end of the time of the first ruling, not its removal and nullification, as has been established. This is like the Qur'an abrogating some of itself by other parts. Some scholars held that the Injil did not specify rulings, nor did it contain lawful and unlawful things, but rather it consisted of allegories, parables, admonitions and warnings, and whatever else concerns laws and rulings is referred back to the Tawrah. They also held that Isa, peace be upon him, did not abrogate anything of what is in the Tawrah; that he observed the Sabbath and prayed towards the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis), forbade the flesh of swine, and affirmed circumcision. However, the Christians changed this after his being raised up. They adopted Sunday instead of Saturday, because it is the first day of the week and the beginning of the outpouring [of grace]. They prayed towards the east, for the reason mentioned earlier. They interpreted circumcision as circumcision of the heart, meaning cutting it off from worldly attachments and from obstacles to the Divine Presence. They made the flesh of swine lawful. Yet Mark related in his Gospel that the Messiah destroyed the swine and drowned a large herd of them in the sea, and said to his disciples: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the swine," thus pairing them with dogs. The cause of this is their claim that Peter saw in a dream a sheet descending from heaven, containing images of animals and the image of a swine, and he was told: "O Peter, eat of whatever you wish from them." This statement is attributed to Wahb ibn Munabbih. Those who hold this view interpreted the verse as meaning what their scholars had forbidden through personal desire or error in judgment, and they cited as evidence that the Messiah, peace be upon him, said in the Injil: "I did not come to abolish the Torah, but to fulfil it."

It is not hidden that interpreting the verse in the way they have interpreted it is remote in itself. What makes it even more remote is that it has been read as (ḥarrama) with the active voice, its subject being the pronoun referring to "what was before me," or Allah, exalted is He. It has also been read as (ḥaruma) on the pattern of (karuma). Also, what they mentioned from the words of the Messiah, peace be upon him, does not contradict abrogation, since you know that it is not nullification but an explanation of the end of the first ruling. The meaning of "fulfilment" is the addition of the inner policy with which he came to the outer policy with which Musa, peace be upon him, came, as has been said. Or it is the abrogation of some rulings of the Torah by rulings that are more in accordance with wisdom, more fitting to the public good, and more suitable to the time. On this view, the words of the Messiah are evidence for the former [the majority view], not against them. Perhaps what they adopted is the position relied upon, as is not hidden from those of knowledge.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾. The discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding its counterpart. It has been read as (with signs) [bi-ayatin]. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ in not accepting what I have brought you, ﴿and obey me﴾ [50] in what I command you and forbid you [from] by the command of Allah, exalted is He.

[page 172]

[p. 172]

**"Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path"** (3:51). This explains the sign mentioned earlier, which is the saying: "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord." Since this statement is one that all the messengers agreed upon as true, and they called people to it, it was a sign indicating his prophethood. The "sign" here does not mean a miracle, so that it would not be objected that such a statement may come from some of the common people. Rather, the meaning is that once prophethood was established by a miracle, this statement, being the method of the prophets (peace be upon them), was a sign of his prophethood that brings peace to the souls. It is also permissible that the "sign" means a miracle of the kinds already mentioned. It is also said that the attainment of knowledge, monotheism, and guidance to the straight path in beliefs and acts of worship, by someone who grew up among a people who had altered their religion, distorted the books of Allah the Exalted that were sent down, and killed their prophets, and who had not learned it from remnants of their reports, is among the greatest miracles and extraordinary events. Or it may be said: it is possible that Allah the Exalted had mentioned in the Torah: "When a person comes to you with such and such a description, calling you to such and such, follow him, for he is a prophet sent to you." So when he says, "I am the one whom I mentioned with such and such descriptions," this is among the greatest extraordinary signs.

It was also read as *"Anna Allaha"* with the *hamza* of *anna* opened, so that the clause formed by *anna* is in apposition to *"ayah"* (sign), or the meaning is: "I have come to you with a sign indicating that Allah..." etc. Something similar is possible with the reading with the *kasra* as well, but with the implied "saying" (qawl). On both estimations, His saying the Exalted, *"So fear Allah and obey me"* (3:50), is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ).

Many have mentioned that the apparent meaning is that this sentence is conjoined to the first sentence, *"I have come to you,"* and was repeated so that a further meaning would be connected to it, namely His saying, glorified is He, *"Indeed, Allah is my Lord."* Or it is for comprehensiveness, like His saying the Exalted, *"Then return the gaze twice"* (67:4). That is: "I have come to you with a sign after another of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of birds, the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, my birth without a father, my speaking in the cradle, and the like." The first statement is to lay the groundwork for the argument against them, and the second is to bring it closer to the ruling, which is the obligation of the ruling of the fear of Allah the Exalted and obedience to Him. For this reason the *fa'* is used in *"So fear Allah,"* as if it were said: "Since I have come to you with dazzling miracles and manifest signs, so fear Allah," etc. On this view, His saying the Exalted, *"Indeed, Allah..."* etc., is the beginning of a speech and the start of the call referred to by a general statement. The nominal sentence emphasized with *inna* points to the perfection of the theoretical faculty through the true belief whose ultimate aim is monotheism. His saying the Exalted, *"So worship Him,"* points to the perfection of the practical faculty, for it entails obedience, which is carrying out the commands and abstaining from the prohibitions.

[p. 173]

Following these two matters with His saying, glorified is He, *"This is a straight path,"* confirms what preceded by showing that combining the two matters, true belief and righteous action, is the path witnessed to be straight. The meaning of the reading with *fath* according to what has been mentioned is "because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," so it is like His saying the Exalted, *"For the security of the Quraysh"* (106:1), etc. The demonstrative refers either to the two matters together, or to the second matter which is the effect of the first. The *tanwin* (nunation) in "path" is either for magnification or for partitiveness. The sentence *"This is..."* etc., is, as has been said, a resumptive sentence (istinaf) explaining what the call requires.

Moreover, the indications in these verses are as apparent as the expression, except that applying what is in the horizons to what is in the souls needs explanation. So we say: Allah, glorified is He, said: *"And when the angels said"* — that is, the angels of the spiritual faculties — *"to Mary,"* the pure and chaste soul, *"'Indeed, Allah has chosen you,"* for the perfection of your readiness and the abundance of your receptivity; *"and purified you"* from base vices and ugly characteristics; *"and chosen you above the women"* of the appetitive souls, clad in the cloak of blameworthy deeds. *"O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord"* — that is, persist in obedience to Him by complying with what He has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden; *"and prostrate, and bow with those who bow"* — in the places of humility, in the niches of submission, along with those who humble themselves, for in that is the establishment of the rites of servanthood and the discharge of the rights of lordship. Glory be to Allah the Exalted, how well one has said:

*It is good to show fortitude before enemies, but only helplessness is ugly before the beloved.*

*"That is among the news of the unseen"* — that is, among the reports of the unseen of your existence — *"which We reveal to you,"* O prophet of the spirit, *"and you were not with them"* — that is, with the spiritual and soul faculties; the meaning is that you were not paying attention to them but were preoccupied with a preoccupying matter that kept you from them, *"when they cast"* the pens of their readinesses with which they write the scrolls of their states and the Torah of their conditions, and throw them into the sea of management, *"which of them would take charge of Mary"* — the soul — and manage her according to his own opinion and the requirement of his nature. *"And you were not with them when they disputed"* in the station of the breast, which is the place of the dispute of the faculties over seeking leadership before discipline and during it, *"when the angels said"* — the angels of the spiritual faculties, when they prevailed — *"O Mary, Allah gives you good news"* according to the requirement of being turned toward Him, *"of a word from Him"* — comprehensive of the letters of existences, and this is the heart that encompasses the worlds — *"whose name is the Messiah"* because He wipes you with light, or because he was anointed with it, *"honored in this world"* for his management of the affairs of livelihood, so that the human faculties of the outer senses and the jinn of the inner faculties obey him; *"and honored in the Hereafter"* for his standing in the management of the return, so that the dominion of the heaven of spirits obeys him. Or "honored" means exalted and elevated in this world, which is an expression for the manifestation of the acts, and in the Hereafter, which is an expression for the manifestation of the Names. *"And one of those brought near"* — that is, counted among the company of those brought near to the Presence, who are capable of the manifestation of the Essence. In a report: "My earth and My heaven do not contain Me, but the heart of My believing servant contains Me."

*"And he will speak to the people"* — with what guides them in the cradle of the body at the time of its nourishment with the milk of conduct toward the King of kings; *"and in maturity"* — reaching the stage of the elder of the spirit and arriving at the middle of the path. *She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child"* like this *"when no man has touched me?"* This is an expression of wonder at her giving birth in that way without the upbringing of a human teacher, since custom has it that reaching the lofty stations is only through a guiding shaykh who knows the way and repels the calamities. It is well known that whenever a person travels by himself he goes astray or does not attain much. Among their sayings is: "The tree that grows by itself does not bear fruit."

*He said: "Thus Allah creates what He wills."* So He may choose whomever He wills without the upbringing of a trainer or the guidance of a guide, but by the mere divine attraction. This is the condition of those who are drawn and some of those who seek:

*Many a person is led by destinies toward lofty heights, though choice has no part in it;*
*he is heedless while happiness embraces him, yet he shies away from it, fleeing.*

*"And He will teach him"* by divine teaching, which is free from the intermediaries that are customary: the book of rational sciences, the rulings of the laws, and the knowledge of the divine books, from the Torah of the outward and the Gospel of the inward; and He will make him *"a messenger to"* the spiritual ones among *"the Children of Israel"* of the spirit, saying:

[p. 174]

*"Indeed, I have come to you"* from the world of the unseen *"with a sign,"* a great one, which is *"that I create for you"* through upbringing *"from clay"* of human souls *"the likeness of a bird"* flying toward the sanctuary of holiness on the two wings of hope and fear; *"then I breathe into it"* by breathing the divine knowledge and the soul of true life, *"and it becomes a bird"* — that is, a living soul flying in the space of beauty and majesty toward the gardens of the presence of the Truth, glorified is He; *"by Allah's permission."* *"And I heal the blind"* — that is, the one veiled from the light of the lights by seeing others, *"and the leper"* — afflicted with diseases of vices and corrupt beliefs that caused the color of his natural skin to change; *"and I raise the dead"* of ignorance to the true life of knowledge, *"by Allah's permission. And I inform you of what you eat"* — that is, what you consume of appetites and pleasures, *"and what you store"* in the houses of your intentions of hopes that are like a mirage in a desert plain. *"Indeed, in that"* just mentioned *"is a sign for you"* that is beneficial, *"if you are believers."* *"And confirming what was before me of"* the Torah of the outward, for it is one of the manifestations; *"and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you"* because of your obstinacy and your restricting the Truth to some of its manifestations. By this is indicated the knowledge of the inward. The "some" may refer to the whole, according to what has been said about His saying: *"Some of what He promises you will befall you"* (40:77). Or it may be its apparent meaning, and then it indicates that among the inward things there is what it is forbidden to disclose. For our master Zayn al-'Abidin said:

*Many a jewel of knowledge, if I were to disclose it,*
*they would say to me: "You are among those who worship idols."*

*And people who call themselves Muslims would have made my blood lawful,*
*seeing the worst of what they do as good.*

*Before this, Abu Hasan*
*went before Husayn, and before him he had bequeathed to Hasan.*

*"And I have come to you with a sign"* after another *"from your Lord; so fear Allah"* in opposing me, *"and obey me"* in what contains the perfection of your growth. *"Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord,"* so He is the One who brings you to what contains your perfection. *"So worship Him"* with humility and brokenness, standing at His door in helplessness and need, and comply with His command and His prohibition. *"This is a straight path"* that brings you to Him and makes you reach Him by it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 52 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when Jesus perceived disbelief from them﴾ This begins the explanation of the outcome of his situation, peace be upon him. It has been said: it is possible that all of this is from the speech of the angels, as an elaboration of a part of it that falls within the speech. It is also possible that the speech was complete at the words of His, the Exalted, ﴿and a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾, and that ﴿that I have come to you﴾ is not connected to what precedes it, and is not included within the speech; and the omitted element there would be: "So Jesus came, just as Allah the Exalted had announced, a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying]: 'I have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord,' etc." In this case the fa' here is explanatory, expressing something like what is implied there on the second interpretation. The root meaning of ihsas (perception) is awareness through one of the five outward senses, and it has here been used, by way of metaphor in a subordinate form (isti'arah tab'iyyah), for knowledge, without doubt. It has also been said that it is a metonymic figure (majaz mursal) for that, by way of mentioning the necessary concomitant and intending the consequent, the motive for that being that disbelief is not something that can be perceived by the senses. The claim that what is meant is perceiving the traces of disbelief is not worth anything. What is meant by disbelief is their persistence in it and their obstinacy in it, together with their determination to inflict harm upon him, peace be upon him. It is established that he, peace be upon him, encountered many hardships from the Jews, may Allah the Exalted fight them.

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir related through various chains from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Jews used to gather around Jesus, peace be upon him, mocking him and saying to him: 'O Jesus, what did so-and-so eat last night, and what did he store in his house for tomorrow?' He would inform them, and they would scoff at him, until that affected him and them. Jesus, peace be upon him, had no fixed abode and no known place; he was a wanderer on the earth. One day he passed by a woman sitting at a grave, weeping. He asked her, and she said: 'My daughter has died; I had no child other than her.' So Jesus prayed two rak'ahs, then called out: 'O so-and-so, arise by the permission of the Most Merciful!' She came out. The grave stirred; then he called a second time and the grave split open; then he called a third time and she came out shaking the dust from her head. She said: 'O mother, what made you make me taste the agony of death twice? O mother, be patient and seek reward; I have no desire for this world. O Spirit of Allah, ask my Lord to return me to the Hereafter and to ease for me the agony of death.'
Page 175
He prayed to his Lord, and she was taken back to Him, and the earth closed over her. The Jews heard of this and their anger against him increased." It is related from Mujahid that they intended to kill him, and that is why he sought help from his people. The particle min (from) is for the starting point of the action and is connected to ahassa (perceived): that is, the perception began from their direction. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to an omitted element, as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to disbelief, meaning: when he perceived disbelief as it proceeded from them.

﴿He said: "Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah?"﴾ Those addressed were the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun), as indicated by the verse of al-Saff [61:14]: ﴿as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the Disciples﴾, and the verse. That it was all of the Children of Israel, on the basis of His, the Exalted, words: ﴿so a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved﴾, is not valid, since the verse is not explicit in the claim, for the division only requires that the call reached everyone. The word ansar is the plural of nasir, like ashraf is the plural of sharif. Some people said it is the plural of nasr, but Abu al-Baqa' considered this weak unless a genitive noun is understood before it, meaning "from among those who are with my support," or you make it a verbal noun described by it. The prepositional phrase either is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause of the ya' (the first person pronoun), which is in meaning the object, and the meaning is: who will support me while I am seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted or going toward Allah; or it is connected to ansari with the sense of addition implied, meaning: from among those who attribute themselves to Allah in supporting me.

In al-Kashshaf, in its commentary on Surah al-Saff, there is a summary, differing from what is mentioned here, that the addition of ansar to the ya' is an addition of association, i.e., "from my party and those who share with me in my orientation to support Allah the Exalted," so that it corresponds to their answer that follows; and it is not valid that its meaning be "who will support me along with Allah," because of the lack of correspondence. In this there is the point that the lack of correspondence is not accepted, since the support of Allah the Exalted in the answer is not in its apparent sense, but there must be some figurative usage, or an implied element in their support for Allah the Exalted, and what achieves the correspondence is implied. Yes, the use of ila in the sense of ma'a (with) is not free of difficulty; al-Farra' mentioned that it is only so when one thing is joined to another, as in: "al-dawd ila al-dawd ibil" (a herd added to a herd is camels), meaning: when you join one to the other it becomes camels. Do you not see that you say "Zayd came, and with him is wealth," and do not say "wa-ilayhi"? The similar cases are likewise. So the interpretation that is free of this carrying, with its inclusion of less implied material, is preferable. For this reason some chose that ila means lam, and others that it means fi.

In al-Kashf, it is said: "Perhaps the most fitting meaning of the verse, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is to take it as: 'who will support me, making his support end in Allah the Exalted,' as the particle of ending requires, without an addition of meaning; as if he, peace be upon him, asked them to support him for the sake of Allah the Exalted and for no other purpose, implicitly connecting the support of Allah the Exalted with the support of His messenger. Their reply, reported by His, the Exalted, words: ﴿The Disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾, is very closely matched to it, as if they said: 'We are your supporters, because it is the support of Allah the Exalted for the purpose He alluded to.' Had they said instead 'We are your helpers,' it would not have fallen into this position." End of quote. You know that making ila mean lam, or fi in the causal sense, achieves the aim of the Messiah alluded to, in a way that is perhaps less forced than what was mentioned. The reason for choosing that seems to be what al-Zajjaj said: it is not permissible to say that one of the particles of meaning is in the sense of another, but two particles may come close in usefulness, so the one weak in knowledge of the language supposes their meaning is the same, and it is not so. So let this be understood.

﴿Al-Hawariyyun﴾ is the plural of hawari. It is said: "Fulan is the hawari of Fulan," meaning his particular companion and helper. The hawari is not a plural like karasi, as is mistakenly thought, but is a singular noun that is declinable, as the scholars have stated explicitly. Allamah al-Taftazani mentioned that it is singular and its alif is one of the alterations of the relative adjective. But in this there is the point that when an alif is added in the relative form and the word is changed by it, the ya' is lightened in the most eloquent usage for such words, whereas hawari is different, because lightening its ya' is anomalous, as they have stated explicitly, and it was read so in the verse. Its root is from tahwir, meaning whitening, and from it comes khubz hawari, bread sifted repeatedly. The hawariyyat are the urban women, the women of cities and villages, because whiteness predominates among them, owing to their not being exposed to the sun. Hawari is also applied to launderers, because they whiten clothes; in the Nabatean language it is huwari, with a damma on the ha', a shadda on the waw, and a fatha on the ra', as said by al-Dahhak. There is a difference over why those people were given this name. It has been said: they were named so for the whiteness of their garments, and this is what is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has been said: because they were launderers who whitened clothes for people, and this is what is related from Muqatil and a group. It has been said: for the purity of their hearts and the goodness of their character, and Qatadah's statement points to this. There is also a difference over which of the groups of people they belonged to. It has been said: they were a people who fished, among them Ya'qub, Shim'un and Yuhanna. Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by them and said to them: "You catch fish; if you follow me, will you become such that you catch people with eternal life?" They said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Jesus son of Mary, the servant of Allah and His messenger." They asked him for a miracle. Shim'un had cast his net that night and caught nothing, so Jesus, peace be upon him, ordered them to cast it into the water again, and they did, and caught enough to fill two boats. At that they believed in him, peace be upon him. It has also been said: they were twelve men, or twenty-nine men from among other people, who followed Jesus, peace be upon him. Whenever they were hungry they said: "O Spirit of Allah, we are hungry," and he struck the earth with his hand and two loaves came out for each one; and when they were thirsty they said: "We are thirsty," and he struck the earth with his hand and water came out, and they drank. They said: "Who is better than us? When we wish, you feed us, and when we wish, you give us drink, and we have believed in you." He said: "The better of you is one who works with his hand and eats from his earnings." So they began washing clothes for hire and eating from it.

It has also been said: a king prepared food and gathered people around it, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was at a dish, and the dish did not diminish. This was mentioned to the king, and he went to him with his relatives. They said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Jesus son of Mary." The king said: "I am leaving my kingdom and following you," and he followed him with his relatives; those are the Disciples. It has also been said: his mother gave him to a dyer, and whenever he wished to teach him something, he found him more knowledgeable in it than himself. The dyer was once away on an urgent matter and said to him: "Here are garments of various kinds, and I have marked each of them; dye them with those colours." Jesus, peace be upon him, boiled one grain and put all of them into it, and said: "Be by the permission of Allah as I wish." The dyer returned and was told what he had done. He said: "You have ruined my garments." He said: "Get up and look." So he kept bringing out a red garment, a green garment and a yellow garment, just as he had wished, and those present marvelled at him, believed in him, and they were the Disciples.

A group reported from al-Qaffal that it is possible that some of them were from kings, some from fishermen, some from launderers, some from dyers, and some from other people, and they were all called Disciples because they were the helpers of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the sincere ones in his love and obedience. Derivation, however it occurred, is derivation; its source may be taken literally or figuratively, and the figurative is more fitting to the circumstances of those helpers. It has also been said that it is derived from haar, meaning returned, and from it His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Surely he thought he would never return﴾ [84:14]; and as if they were named so for their returning to Allah the Exalted.

Some people explained hawari as "warrior" (mujahid). If by jihad is meant what is immediately understood from it, that is problematic, since it is not established that Jesus, peace be upon him, commanded it; some claimed it, citing His, the Exalted, words: ﴿so a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved, then We strengthened those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant﴾. But it is not hidden that the verse is not explicit in the intended point, since "strengthening" may mean strengthening by proof and the elevation of the word. If by jihad is meant the struggle against the self, by enduring its bitter obligations, then that is not problematic.

Yes, it has been raised as a difficulty: if Jesus, peace be upon him, was not commanded to fight, what is the meaning of his seeking helpers?
