It has been answered that when he, peace be upon him, knew the Jews intended to kill him, he sought support for protection from them, as al-Hasan and Mujahid said, and he did not seek support for fighting alongside them for faith in what he brought. This is what he was not commanded to do, not that; indeed it may be claimed that this was commanded, because of the obligation of preserving
Page 177
the soul's safety. It is related that when the Jews sought him in order to kill him, he said to the Disciples: "Which of you loves to be my companion in Paradise, on condition that his likeness be cast upon him and he be killed in my place?" One of them agreed to that. In some of the Gospels it is said that when the Jews seized Jesus, peace be upon him, Shim'un drew his sword and struck with it a servant among them belonging to a great rabbi, and cut off his ear. Jesus, peace be upon him, said to him: "Enough," then he touched the servant's ear and restored it to its place, and it became as it had been. It has also been said: it is possible that the seeking of support was for enabling the establishment of proof and for distinguishing the agreeing from the opposing, and that does not require an order to fight, just as our Prophet, the Spirit of the existence of creation, peace be upon him, was commanded to; and this is the apparent meaning for one who is fair. The meaning of "the helpers of Allah" is the helpers of His religion and His messenger, and those who assist them both, according to what is most well known.

﴿Āmannā bi-llāh﴾ (We believe in Allah) is the basis of that claim, serving as its reason. ﴿Wa-ashhad﴾ (and bear witness) is conjoined to ﴿Āmannā﴾. The difference between them, one being an act of inshā ʼ (performative speech) and the other a khabar (informative statement), does no harm, as has been established in its proper place. It has been said that ﴿Āmannā﴾ is also for the inshā ʼ of faith, so there is no difference. ﴿Bi-annā muslimūn﴾ [52] means: submitting to what You want from us, and this includes, as a primary matter, their support of him. Or it means: our religion is Islam, which is the religion of the prophets before you, so it is in meaning an affirmation of the prophethood of those before him, peace be upon him. This is a request from them for his testimony on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, when the messengers testify for their peoples and against them, as an announcement, as al-Karkhi said, that the aim of their intention is the happiness of the Hereafter. In al-Ma'idah [111] it came as ﴿Bi-annanā﴾ because what is there, as has been said, is the first speech of the disciples, so it came in its original form. What is here is a repetition of it in meaning, so the lightening (of the form) is appropriate here, because each of the lightening and the repetition is a derivative, and a derivative with a derivative is more fitting.

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾ is a presentation of their state to Him, Exalted, after presenting it to His Messenger, seeking to draw down the clouds of the answer to their supplication that follows. It was also said that it is an exaggeration in displaying their situation. ﴿And we have followed the Messenger﴾, meaning: we have obeyed what he brought to us from You. ﴿So write us down among the witnesses﴾ [53], meaning: among Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, because they bear witness to the Messengers that they conveyed (the message), and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness for them to their truthfulness. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Abu Salih narrated from him that they are those who believed among the nations before them. It was also said that what is meant by ﴿the witnesses﴾ is the Prophets, because every Prophet is a witness for his community and against it. Muqatil said: they are the truthful ones. Al-Zajjaj said: they are those who bear witness for the Prophets through confirmation. It was also said: they meant "with those who are absorbed in witnessing Your majesty, to the extent that we do not care about the hardships and pains that reach us, so that fulfilling what we have committed ourselves to in support of Your Messenger becomes easy for us." It was also said: they meant "record our remembrance among the company of those who attended Your presence from the nearest angels," like His saying, ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin﴾. The strain in this last view is not hidden. The meaning according to the other views is: "include us in the count of those (witnesses), or in the count of their followers." It was said: they expressed Allah's act of that by them with the word ﴿write us down﴾, since writing binds and fixes what needs to be verified and known at a later state. It was also said: what is meant is "make that and decree it in the leaves of the pre-eternity (al-azal, the eternal past)." Some people took the writing to be a metaphor for their being made firm in faith at the end (of their lives). The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of "write us down" (uktubnā).

[p. 178]

﴿And they plotted﴾: that is, those whom he sensed to be disbelievers, for they appointed someone to kill him by stealth. ﴿And Allah plotted﴾: by casting his likeness (peace be upon him) onto another, who was then crucified, while He raised him up to Himself. Ibn 'Abbas said: When the king of the Children of Israel wanted to kill 'Isa (peace be upon him), he entered a small door in which there was an aperture, and Jibril (peace be upon him) lifted him through the aperture to the heaven. The king then said to a wicked man among them: "Go in to him and kill him." He entered the small door, and Allah the Exalted cast onto him the likeness of 'Isa (peace be upon him). He came out to his companions and informed them that 'Isa was not in the house. So they killed him, crucified him, and thought that he was 'Isa.

[p. 179 — continued]

Wahb said: They captured him and set up a wooden cross to crucify him, and the earth became dark. Allah sent the angels, who came between him and them. They then seized a man called Yahuda, who was the one who had guided them to 'Isa. This happened because 'Isa had gathered the al-Hawariyyun (the disciples) that night and given them his instructions, then said: "One of you will disbelieve in me before the rooster crows, and will sell me for a small sum of dirhams." They left and scattered. The Jews were seeking him, and one of the al-Hawariyyun came to them and said: "What will you give me if I show you where he is?" They set for him thirty dirhams, so he took them and showed them where he was. Allah the Exalted then cast onto him the likeness of 'Isa (peace be upon him). He was taken into the house and then raised up, and he said: "I am the one who showed you where he is." But they paid no attention to his words, and crucified him while thinking that he was 'Isa. When the likeness of 'Isa was crucified and seven days had passed, Allah the Exalted said to 'Isa: "Descend to Maryam, then let the al-Hawariyyun be gathered for you, and disperse them in the earth as callers (to the faith)." He descended to her, and the mountain was illuminated with light. She gathered the al-Hawariyyun for him, and he dispersed them in the earth as callers. Then Allah, glorified is He, raised him up. That night was the night in which the Christians became divided, and when the al-Hawariyyun rose in the morning, each of them went toward the town of the one whom 'Isa had sent to them.

It is related from more than one narrator that when the Jews resolved to kill him (peace be upon him), the al-Hawariyyun gathered in an upper room, and the Messiah entered upon them through the niche of the room. Iblis informed the Jews' assembly of this, and four thousand men of them mounted and seized the door of the room. The Messiah said to the al-Hawariyyun: "Which of you will go out, be killed, and be with me in Paradise?" One of them said: "I, O Prophet of Allah." He cast upon him a woolen cloak, a woolen turban, and handed him his staff, and cast upon him the likeness of 'Isa (peace be upon him). He went out to the Jews, and they killed him and crucified him. As for 'Isa (peace be upon him), Allah clothed him in light, cut off from him the desire for food and drink, and raised him up to Himself. Then, when his companions saw that, they split into three groups. One group said: "Allah was among us, then He ascended to the heaven." Another group said: "The son of Allah, mighty and majestic, was among us, then Allah, glorified is He, raised him up to Himself." And another group among them said: "The servant of Allah and His messenger was among us for as long as Allah willed, then He raised him up to Himself." These are the Muslims. The two disbelieving groups then united against them and killed them. Thus Islam remained with its traces effaced until Allah the Exalted sent Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is related from Ibn Ishaq that the Jews tortured the al-Hawariyyun after the raising of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and inflicted great hardship upon them. This reached the king of the Romans, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects; his name was Dawud ibn Nudha. He was told: "A man from the Children of Israel, among those under your command, used to inform them that he is the messenger of Allah the Exalted, and showed them the reviving of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper, and did such and such." He said: "If I had known that, I would not have left them between them and him." He then sent for the al-Hawariyyun, snatched them from their hands, and asked them about 'Isa (peace be upon him). They informed him, so he pledged allegiance to them upon their religion. He took down the crucified one, buried him, and took the cross and honoured it. He then campaigned against the Children of Israel and killed a great multitude of them. From this, the origin of Christianity appeared among the Romans. Then there came after him another king called Titus, who attacked Bayt al-Maqdis about forty years after the raising of 'Isa (peace be upon him). He killed and took captives, and did not leave a stone upon a stone in Bayt al-Maqdis. At that time Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz.

This is all. As for the origin of makr (plotting), it is said to be evil; from it comes "makara al-layl" (the night plotted), meaning it grew dark. It is also said to be turning and twisting; from it comes "al-mukur," a type of tree with twisting branches, whose singular is "makr," and "al-mamkura" among women is the one whose frame is tightly folded. Some explained it as diverting another from what he intends by a stratagem, and others as deceiving a person in order to bring him into harm. They distinguished it from hila (cunning/stratagem), since hila may be used to bring about what is difficult in an action without intending harm. Makr is a stratagem against a person that brings him into something like a snare (wahq). They said: it is not applied to Allah the Exalted except by way of musha-kalah (consistency of wording), because He is exalted above its literal meaning and does not need a stratagem; therefore one does not say, initially, "the makr of Allah, glorified is He." Al-'Adud and a group held this view, but al-Abhari and others disagreed with them and permitted the application without musha-kalah, citing His saying: ﴿Then do they feel secure from the plot of Allah? For none feels secure from the plot of Allah﴾, since here makr is attributed to Him, glorified is He, initially.

It is related from the Imam that makr is causing harm to reach another in a manner that is concealed, and that it is permissible for it to proceed from Him, the Exalted, in its literal sense. Many others said that it is an expression for a firmly planned arrangement, and this is not impossible for Him, the Exalted. In a hadith: «O Allah, plot for me and do not plot against me.» Those who held that it may be applied only by way of musha-kalah answered the argument from this verse and similar verses by saying that this is musha-kalah in estimation (al-musha-kalah al-taqdiriyya), as in His saying: ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾. The weakness of this is not hidden. Therefore, the better view is that it is valid to apply it to Him, glorified is He, initially, with the meaning befitting His majesty, may His majesty be exalted. Among what supports this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah is the best of planners﴾ [54], meaning the most powerful of them in plotting and the most severe, or that His plotting is better and more fitting in its place, being far removed from injustice; for musha-kalah is far from it.

﴿When God said﴾ is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) modifying the plotting (makr) or an implied verb, such as "that happened." If one supposes the implied verb is "remember," as in similar constructions, it is not far-fetched. Its attachment to "the plotters" is distant, since no good reason appears for restricting the power of God's plotting to this time.

﴿O Jesus, indeed I will take you in death and raise you to Me﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada that he said: "This is from what is advanced and what is delayed. That is: I will raise you to Me and cause you to die." This is one of the interpretations required by the apparent meaning of the verse conflicting with what is well known and explicitly stated in another verse, and with the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed Jesus did not die, and he will return to you before the Day of Resurrection."

Second: the meaning is "I will complete your term and cause you to die a natural death; I will not give power over you to anyone who would kill you." The statement is then a metaphor for his protection from enemies and from what they intended for him, peace be upon him, because God's completing his term and his dying a natural death entails that.

Third: the meaning is "I will receive you and take your person from the earth," from the expression "tawaffā al-māl," meaning he took and received the property in full.

Fourth: the meaning of death (wafāh) here is sleep, since they are siblings and each is used for the other. It has been related from al-Rabi' that God raised Jesus, peace be upon him, to heaven while he was asleep, out of kindness toward him. This view and the preceding one are also reported from al-Hasan.

Fifth: the meaning is "I will make you like one who has died," because being raised resembles that.

Sixth: the meaning is "I will take you, having received you with your spirit and body," so that "and raise you to Me" serves as an explanation of what precedes.

Seventh: the meaning of death is the death of the appetitive faculties which prevent him from connecting with the realm of the unseen (malakūt).

Eighth: the meaning is "I will receive your deeds," meaning "your future action." Most of these views are not free from remoteness, especially the last.

It has been said: the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense. Ibn Jarir related from Wahb that he said: "God caused Jesus son of Mary to die for three hours of the day, until He raised him to Himself." al-Hakim related from him that God caused Jesus to die for seven hours, then revived him, and that Mary conceived him when she was thirteen years old, that he was raised when he was thirty-three, and that his mother remained for six years after his being raised. This is reported in a weak narration from Ibn Abbas. The correct view, as stated by al-Qurtubi, is that God raised him without death or sleep, and this is the choice of al-Tabari. The authentic narration from Ibn Abbas agrees with this. As for the report that God caused him to die for seven hours, Ibn Ishaq mentioned that it is from the claims of the Christians. They have in this context statements that make the skin shudder, and they claim that it is in the Gospel. God forbid! It is nothing but slander and a great calumny. There is no harm in quoting it and refuting it, for in that is a refutation of their claim concerning him, peace be upon him, of lordship in the fullest manner. So we say:

They said: While the Messiah was sitting with his disciples on the night of Friday, the thirteenth night after the month of Nisan had passed, Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, came with a group who had swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people. Judas had said to them: "The man who approaches is he; seize him." When Judas saw the Messiah, he said: "Peace be upon you, Teacher," and then they seized him. Yasu' said: "As one does to thieves, you have come out to me with swords and clubs. I was among you in the Temple every day teaching, and you did not lay hands on me, but this is the hour of the authority of darkness." They took him to the chief priest, where the elders gather. Butrus followed him from afar and entered the house with him at night, sitting in a corner of it disguised, to see what would become of him. The elders sought testimony against Yasu' by which they might kill him. Some false witnesses came, and two of them testified that Yasu' had said: "I am able to destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days." The chief priest said to him: "Will you not answer anything in your own defense?" Yasu' was silent. The chief priest then adjured him by the living God: "Are you the Messiah?" He said: "You have said it. And I tell you, from now on you will not see the Son of Man until you see him seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven, and that some of those standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." When the chief priest heard this, he tore his garments and said: "What need have we of the testimony of Judas? You have heard; what do you see concerning his matter?" They said: "He deserves death." Then they spat in the face of the one afar, struck him, mocked him, and began to slap him and say: "Tell us who struck you."

When it was morning, they delivered him to Pilate the governor. The whole people shouted, "Crucify, crucify!" Pilate was reluctant to kill him and said: "What evil has this man done?" The elders said: "His blood is upon us and upon our children." Then the governor's soldiers led him to the praetorium. The people gathered around him, stripped him of his garments, dressed him in a red robe, wove a crown of thorns and placed it on his head, and put a reed in his hand. Then they knelt before him mocking him, saying: "Peace be upon you, King of the Jews," and they began to spit on him and strike his head. Then they took him, carrying his cross, to a place known as Golgotha, and crucified him and nailed his hands to the wood. He asked them for a drink of water, and they gave him vinegar mixed with myrrh. He tasted it and did not swallow it. The guards sat, and they divided his garments among themselves by lot. They placed above his head a board on which was written: "This is the King of the Jews," in mockery of him. Then they brought two thieves and placed them on his right and left, as a humiliation of him. The Jews were saying to him: "O destroyer of the Temple and builder of it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God as you claim, come down from the cross!" The Jews also said: "He claims that he saved others; how is it that he could not save himself? If he trusts in God, let Him rescue him from what he is in." When it was six hours into Friday, Yasu' cried out on the cross with a loud voice, "ʾĀlawī ʾĀlawī ʾImā ṣāṣā" (that is: "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?"). The Jews took a sponge filled with vinegar, one of them raised it on a reed and gave him to drink, and another said: "Leave him, until we see who will save him." Yasu' cried out again, bowed his head, and yielded up the spirit. The veil of the Temple was torn, the rocks split, the graves opened, and many of the holy ones arose from their graves, entered the holy city, and appeared to the people. When evening came, a man from his disciples called Yusuf took him in clean linen and placed him in a tomb he had hewn in the rock, then rolled a great stone over the door of the tomb. On the day after Friday, the elders of the Jews came to Pilate the governor and said: "Sir, we recall that this deceiver said to his disciples, 'I will rise after three days.' So order that the tomb be guarded until the period passes, lest his disciples come, steal him, and then tell the people that he has risen, and the second error will be worse than the first." The governor said to them: "Go and seal it and guard it as you wish." They went and did what they wanted. On the evening of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and her companion Mary came to look at the tomb.

In the Gospel of Mark: Mary came only on Sunday at dawn, and behold, an angel descended from heaven with a great earthquake, rolled away the stone from the tomb, and sat upon it, wearing white garments like lightning. The guards nearly died from fear of him. Then he said to the women: "Do not fear. I know that you came seeking Yasu' who was crucified. He is not here; he has risen. Come and look at the place where the Lord was. Go and tell his disciples that he has gone ahead of you to Galilee." So they went and informed the disciples. The guards entered and informed the chief priests of the news.

[p. 181]

They said: "Do not speak of this," and they bribed them with silver to keep the matter secret. The guards accepted this from them, and spread the report that the disciples had come and stolen him. The elders prepared an excuse for them before the governor. The eleven disciples went to Galilee, though some of them doubted. Yasu' came to them, spoke to them, and said: "Go and baptize all nations and teach them what I have commanded you. Behold, I am with you until the end of the age." End of quotation.

Here are several matters. First: it is said to the Christians: the killing and crucifixion of the Messiah which you claim, do you transmit it by mass transmission (tawātur, a report so widely transmitted that its agreement on falsehood is impossible) or by solitary reports (āḥād, reports transmitted by individuals or small numbers)? If they claim it is by solitary reports, then no proof is complete by it and knowledge is not established, since solitary reports are not safe from inattention, heedlessness, and collusion in lying. If solitary reports are subject to these, how can their testimony be relied upon in certainties? If they attribute it to mass transmission, we say to them: one of the conditions of mass transmission is that the chain be uniform at its two ends and in its middle, such that the reporting at every level comes from people who could not have colluded on a lie. If you claim that the report of the killing of the Messiah is of this kind, then you have contradicted the texts of the Gospel which you hold, for its transmitters, who wrote it down for you and on which you rely, said: "The one seized for killing was among a small group of his disciples. When he was arrested, they all fled, and none followed him except Butrus from afar. When he entered the house where they had gathered, a maidservant among them looked at him and recognized him, and said: 'This man was with Yasu.' He swore that he did not know Yasu' and would not speak his words, and he deceived them until they left him, and he went away, and he had barely gone. A young man followed him wearing a loincloth, and they seized him, but he left his loincloth in their hands and fled naked." So these were his companions and followers, and none of them was present according to the testimony of the Gospel. As for his enemies, the Jews, whom you claim were present at the event, we do not grant that they reached the number required for mass transmission. Rather they were solitary individuals, and they are enemies who could collude in a lie against their adversary, to give the impression that they had gained the upper hand over him and achieved their aims. Thus the condition of mass transmission is broken. This is supported by the fact that the chief priests, according to your claim, bribed the guards. So it is not far-fetched that this band of Jews crucified a person from among the companions of Yasu' and led the people to believe that he was the Messiah, so that their aims would be accomplished. Moreover, the historians mentioned that Nebuchadnezzar killed the scholars of the Jews in the east and west of the earth, because they had altered the Torah, added to it, and removed from it, until only a small remnant of them remained. Thus the transmitters did not reach the level of mass transmission in the middle tier either.

Second: in this section there is that which sound reason judges to be false, that which the bereaved mother would laugh at, and that which the intellect rejects, such as his saying to the priests: "From now on you will not see the Son of Man." They mean by "the Son of Man" the Lord, glory be to Him, but no such designation for Him is found in any Book. And his saying: "Some of those standing here," and so on, for no one among those standing there was seen before the death of Jesus, peace be upon him, coming in his kingdom. And the angel's saying to the women: "Come and look at the place where the Lord was," for it is said about this: "A lord who is buried, and a god who is laid in the grave! Woe to the dust that covered the face of this god! Perish the shroud that concealed his beauty! Wonder at the heavens, how they were not dissolved though he holds them up; at the earth, how it was not spread out though he holds it; at the seas, how they did not subside though he runs them; at the mountains, how they were not moved though he set them firm; at the animals, how they were not struck dead though he feeds them; at the universe, how it was not annihilated though he originated it. Glory be to God! How did existence remain upright while the Lord was in the tombs, and how did the world remain in order while the god was in the dust? To God we belong and to Him we return, for the calamity of this Lord and the disaster of this god! Verily his mother was bereaved, and as for his people, may you have no father!"

Ruh al-Ma'ani by al-Alusi, commentary on surah 3, verse 55 (part 2 of 2)

As for his words, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me," this contradicts contentment with the bitter decree and conflicts with submission to the rulings of the All-Wise. Such a statement is not befitting for the righteous, let alone for the messengers. Moreover, it nullifies the claim of lordship that you assert and the divinity that you believe in.

As for their saying that many of the saints (al-qiddisin) rose from their graves, etc., this is a plain lie. Had it been true, people would have unanimously transmitted it, and doubt would have been removed from those crowds regarding the matter of Yasu' (Jesus).

As for their saying, "Eleven disciples went to the Lord's house, etc.," the lamp of the twelfth disciple was extinguished in him, as the words of the Messiah require: "Woe to the one by whom the Son of Man is betrayed." Yet, according to your claim, Yasu' said to his twelve disciples, among whom was Judas Iscariot, who handed him over to be killed: "Truly, you will sit on twelve thrones on the Day of Judgment, judging the twelve tribes of the children of Israel."

As for their saying that they asked him for a sip of water, this is extremely far-fetched, because the Gospel explicitly states that the Messiah would fast forty days and forty nights. Someone like him would not be distressed by being separated from water for an hour, especially since he used to say to his disciples: "I have food that you do not know," and so on.

Third: What they mention about the Messiah's rising from his grave on the night of Saturday, despite his crucifixion on Friday, contradicts what Matthew related in his Gospel. He said in it: The Jews asked the Messiah to show them a sign, so he said: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah," meaning Yunus (peace be upon him), "for just as Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights."

Fourth: In this story there is a clear indication that the one crucified was a likeness, and that Allah the Exalted protected the Messiah (peace be upon him) from crucifixion, as will become clear to you with further verification at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾.

Furthermore, the previous ruling was emphasized out of concern for it, or because the domination of the disbelievers over him made the situation one of belief that they would kill him. By His saying: ﴿and raising you to Me﴾, He, glorified is He, meant: raising you to My heaven. It has also been said: to My honour. In either case, the speech contains an ellipsis (of a modifier), since it is known that the Creator, glorified is He, is not confined to a direction. Scholars differ regarding to which heaven he was raised. The view chosen by many of the knowers of God is that he was raised to the fourth heaven. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, related that He raised him to the lowest heaven, where he glorifies with the angels, and then Allah the Exalted will bring him down at the emergence of al-Dajjal (the Antichrist) onto the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). In al-Khazin it is mentioned that when Allah the Exalted raised him (peace be upon him) to Himself, He clothed him with feathers, dressed him in light, and cut off from him the pleasure of eating and drinking. So he flew with the angels, and he is with them around the Throne, becoming a human, angelic, earthly and heavenly being.

Some people raised several difficulties here. Allah the Exalted had strengthened him with Gabriel (peace be upon him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾. Moreover, a single wing of Gabriel's wings would suffice for the whole world, so how did it not suffice to prevent those Jews from him? Also, since he (peace be upon him) was able to revive the dead, heal the blind and the leper, how was he not able to cause their death, or to undo their power, or to strike them with illness and paralysis and palsy, so that they would be incapable of confronting him? Also, since He delivered him from the enemies by raising him to heaven, what is the benefit of casting his likeness upon another?

All of these were answered by saying that the basis of moral responsibility is free choice. Had Allah the Exalted empowered Gabriel or Jesus (peace be upon them both) to repel the enemies or to lift him up without casting his likeness to heaven, his miracle would have reached the level of compulsion. As for the claim that opening the door to the casting of likenesses would remove certainty regarding sensory perceptions, would lead to the abolition of the laws, and would nullify mass transmission (tawatur), and that in that casting there is deception and confusion, which is not befitting the wisdom of Allah the Exalted, this is nothing. First: Casting the likeness of one person upon another, although possible in itself, the default position is that there is no such casting, and that each animal exists independently in the form that is its own. Yes, if the truthful one informs us of the casting of the form of one person upon another, we would affirm it and believe it. In that case, certainty regarding sensory perceptions is not removed; rather, they remain on their default status concerning matters where the truthful one has not reported otherwise. Moreover, the claim that opening this door nullifies mass transmission is rejected, because it is not required that a report be about a fact existing in reality; it suffices that it be about something perceived by the senses, as some verifiers have said. Second: If the deception and confusion were directed at the enemies, we do not accept that this is something unbefitting to wisdom, especially if salvation could not be achieved without the casting. If it was directed at his allies, we do not accept that the casting involved deception, because they were certainly aware that the one sought was the likeness, not Jesus (peace be upon him), as you will come to know, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Then there is the claim that the one sought was established by mass transmission as having remained alive for a long time; so, had it not been Jesus, he would have displayed distress and identified himself. Had he done that, it would have become widely known and transmitted by mass transmission. This too is nothing. First: The claim of mass transmission that the crucified one remained alive for a long time has not been proven by any evidence. What is established is that the crucified one was crucified at the second hour of Friday, died at the sixth hour of that day, and was taken down and buried. A period of four hours is not considered a long time, as is well known. Second: The crucified one's not identifying himself is either because a bewilderment overcame him that prevented him from explanation and clarification, or because Allah the Exalted restrained his tongue so that he could not inform about himself, in order to protect His prophet (peace be upon him) from the man disclosing his affair; or because, out of his truthfulness (siddiqiyyah), the Messiah preferred another over himself, and did so in fulfillment of a covenant made to him, out of desire for martyrdom. For this reason he gave an evasive answer, as recorded by the Christians in the story. The Messiah (peace be upon him) had promised the disciples, as they related earlier, saying: "If we were to be delivered to death with you, we would die," and the likeness was among them. So he fulfilled what he had promised of himself, in the manner of the truthful companions of the prophets (peace be upon them). He is among "men who were true to what they covenanted with Allah."

As for the one who holds that the likeness was from the enemies, not from the allies, it has been narrated that he began saying to the Jews at the crucifixion: "I am not the Messiah; I am only your companion." But he was not heard, and his words were not heeded, and they crucified him. As for the claim that had that been so, it would have been mass-transmitted, what is wrong with it is not hidden from one who has comprehensive knowledge of what we have mentioned. So reflect.

﴿and purifying you from those who disbelieved﴾. It may be that his purification (peace be upon him) is by distancing him from them through the raising, and it may be that it is by his deliverance from what they intended to do to him by killing. In the first case, He made them like a filth; in the second, He made their act like that. The first is the apparent meaning, and al-Jubba'i went to the second.

The relative pronoun here refers to the Jews. The use of the explicit noun rather than a pronoun, as has been said, indicates the cause of the filth, which is disbelief. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that the relative pronoun refers to the Jews, the Christians, the Magians, and the disbelievers of his people.

﴿and making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾. Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ibn Juraij, and a large group said: they are the people of Islam who followed him in his religion and natural disposition, from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿superior to those who disbelieved﴾, who are the Jews, or all who are included in this concept. Believers overcome them by proof or by the sword in most cases. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd that the first relative refers to the Christians and the second to the Jews. Allah the Exalted has made the Christians superior to the Jews, for there is no land in which there is any Christian without them being above the Jews in the east and west of the world. On this view, the meaning of "following" is merely claiming and loving, and their domination over the Jews is not harmed by the domination of the Muslims over them. If "following" is taken to include the following of Muslims, then the followers may be understood to include Muslims and Christians in general, those who believed in him before the coming of our Prophet (ﷺ) and the abrogation (naskh) of his law, and those who believed, according to their claim, after that. "Following" may also be understood in the first sense, so the followers may be understood as Muslims and the first group of Christians. It is not proper for the Noble Book to be interpreted in a way such as restricting the followers to this community and taking "following" to mean coming later, just as the address being to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that the pause at ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ and ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to the making, or to the implied stability within the adverbial phrase. The intention is not that at that point it ends and those who disbelieved are freed from humiliation. Rather, the meaning is that the followers will dominate them until that limit; after that, Allah the Exalted does what He wills.

Some people understood superiority as elevation in rank, with superiority according to nobility, and understood the restriction "until the Day of Resurrection" as an expression of perpetuity, as in the saying "as long as the sky remains, and as long as the sphere turns," on the basis of the assumption that the non-cessation of the elevation of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers until that day requires this making. But that is not the case.

﴿Then to Me is your return﴾, that is, your destination after the Day of Resurrection and your return. The pronoun refers to Jesus (peace be upon him) and the two groups. In it there is predominance of the more apparent (reference). "Then" (thumma) indicates delay. The fronting of the adverbial phrase serves restriction, which conveys emphasis on promise and threat. It may be that the pronoun refers only to those who followed and disbelieved. In it there is a shift (iltifat) to indicate the intensity of the desire to deliver reward and punishment, because direct address indicates concern.

﴿So I will judge between you﴾, that is, I will decide between you after your return to Me and your standing before Me, ﴿concerning that about which you used to differ﴾ [ 55 ] among matters of religion, or regarding the matter of Jesus (peace be upon him). The adverbial phrase is connected to what follows it and is placed first for the sake of the rhyming endings (fawasil).

﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾. This is an explanation of the judgment implied by His words, glorified is He, ﴿I will judge﴾, and a detailing of it by way of division after a general statement. Many of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) held this view. It has been objected that the judgment is connected to the return to God, Exalted is He, and that this occurs on the Day of Resurrection without doubt. So how can it be correct to explain it as punishment restricted by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾? It has been answered in several ways.

The first: the intended meaning is perpetuity and non-cessation, without regard to this world and the Hereafter.

The second: what is meant by "this world and the Hereafter" is their linguistic meaning, namely "the first" and "the last", and this would be an expression for permanence. This is far more remote than the first.

The third: what the author of al-Kashf mentioned, that the return is more general than the worldly and the otherworldly, and His words, glorified is He, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ are the endpoint of the superiority (al-fawqiyyah), not the endpoint of the placing (al-ja'l). The return is delayed relative to the placing, and it is not bounded, in the manner of your saying: "I will lend you the use of this house for a month, then I will bestow upon you a robe of such and such a kind." For this implies that the bestowal is delayed relative to the lending, not that the bestowal is the delay. On this basis, the full recompense is for the benefit of both abodes. It is not hidden that in the word ﴿you were﴾ in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿concerning that about which you were disputing﴾, there is some remoteness from this meaning, and that the meaning is: "He will judge between you in the Hereafter concerning that about which you were disputing in this world."

The fourth: the punishment in this world is the superiority over them, and the meaning is: I add to the punishment of the earlier superiority the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Kashf said: "In it there is a fine antithesis, and this superiority is a prelude to the punishment of the Hereafter and its emphasis, and it includes the idea that it is a superiority of justice, not of domination by existence." It is not hidden that this is very remote from the wording, since the meaning of "I punish him in this world and the Hereafter" is nothing other than "I inflict the punishment of both abodes." Unless it is said that taking the whole does not require taking each part, so it is permissible that He inflicts on him in the Hereafter the punishment of both abodes, by inflicting on him the punishment of the Hereafter, and He has already inflicted on him the punishment of this world, so the completion of both punishments is in the Hereafter.

The fifth: that ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is connected to ﴿severe﴾, intensifying the matter of severity. But this is nothing, as is not hidden.

The better of all of this is what some of the verifying scholars mentioned: that the meaning of ("then", thumma) be taken as delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi) and ascent from one statement to another, not delay in time. Then it does not follow that their return to God, Exalted is He, must be delayed in time relative to the placing, whether His words, may His majesty be exalted, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ are an endpoint for the placing or for the superiority; so there is no objection. Furthermore, what is meant by punishment in this world is their humiliation by killing, capture, enslavement, the taking of the jizyah (poll tax), and the like. Whoever is not subjected to any of the forms of humiliation is nevertheless in apprehension, since it is known that Islam demands him, and that alone is sufficient as punishment. And what is meant by punishment in the Hereafter is the punishment of perpetual retribution in the Fire.

﴿And they will have no helpers﴾ [56]: that is, no assistants who will ward off the punishment of God from them. The plural form, as our master Mufti al-Rum said, is to correspond with the plural pronoun, i.e., none of them has a single helper.

Page 185

**﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾** is an explanation of the state of the second category. He began with the category of **﴿those who disbelieved﴾** because the mention of what came before it, namely the judgment of Allah Most High among them, first suggests a threat at first glance, so it was fitting to begin with them. Also, they are closer in mention, given His saying: **﴿above those who disbelieved﴾**, and because the discourse is with the Jews, who disbelieved in ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and plotted to kill him. **﴿Then He will pay them their rewards in full﴾**, meaning He will make it abundant for them, complete the recompense for their deeds, both of the heart and of the body, and give them the reward for that in full without any deficiency. Some have claimed that the full payment of rewards is the allotment of ranks in Paradise, but the apparent meaning is that it is more general than that. He linked the full payment to faith and righteous deeds, and did not link punishment to anything other than disbelief, as an alert to the degree of perfection in faith, an invitation to it, and a declaration of the great ugliness of disbelief. Ḥafṣ and Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read **﴿فَيُوَفِّيهِمْ﴾** (fa-yuwaffīhim) with the third-person masculine ya' (yā' al-ghayba), and Ruways additionally read the ha' with a ḍamma. The rest read it with the nūn, in keeping with the manner of majesty and grandeur. Perhaps the reason for the iltifāt (shift of grammatical person) to the third person in the first reading is to indicate that the full payment of the reward does not require the exertion of self, since it is among the effects of wide mercy, whereas punishment is not like that. The relative pronoun in the two verses is a mubtadaʾ (subject), whose predicate is what follows the fāʾ. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted that is explained by what was mentioned, and the place of the omitted verb is after the ṣila (relative clause), as Abu al-Baqāʾ said. It is not permissible to supply it before the relative pronoun, because **أمّا** (ammā) is not followed by a verb.

**﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾** [57]: meaning He does not wish to honor them, does not show them mercy, and does not praise them. Or the intended meaning is that He hates them, as is common in expressions of this kind. The sentence is a tadhyīl (concluding appendix) to what precedes it, affirming its content.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the aforementioned account of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. The use of what indicates distance is to point to the great status of the one referred to and his lofty rank in nobility. ﴿We recite it to you﴾, i.e., we narrate it and mention it piece by piece. What is meant is "We recited it," but he expressed it in the present tense to bring the resulting scene to mind, out of concern for it. It has also been said that it is possible to take it in its apparent sense, because the story of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, had not yet been concluded. ﴿Of the signs﴾, i.e., the proofs indicating the truth of your prophethood, since it informed them of things that none would know except a reader of a scripture (*qāriʾ kitāb*) or a teacher, and you were neither of these two. Nothing remains except that you came to know it through revelation. ﴿And the Reminder﴾, i.e., the Qur'an. It has also been said that it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*), and interpreting it as such is because the Qur'an is contained in it. The *min* (﴿of﴾) is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*) according to the first interpretation, and initial/origin (*ibtidāʾiyya*) according to the second. Taking it as explanatory (*bayān*), and intending a specific portion of the Qur'an, is far-fetched. ﴿The Wise﴾, i.e., the one who makes its composition firm and precise, or the one protected from falsehood, or the possessor of wisdom. In that case, its description with what proceeds from wisdom and includes its wisdom is either by way of a subordinate metaphor (*istiʿāra tabaʿiyya*) in the word *ḥakīm*, or by way of metaphorical attribution (*isnād majāzī*), by attributing to the Reminder what belongs to its cause and its possessor. As for making it a suggestive implicit metaphor (*istiʿāra makniyya takhyīliyya*), by likening the Qur'an to a speaker of wisdom and attributing to it the quality of *ḥakīm* imaginatively, this requires a well-known strain to remove the objection concerning mentioning both parties in that case, so reflect.

Several grammatical analyses (*i'rāb*) of the verse have been allowed. The first: *dhālika* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), ﴿we recite it﴾ is its predicate (*khabar*), ﴿to you﴾ is related to the predicate, and ﴿of the signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in the accusative, or a predicate after a predicate, or it is the predicate and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause from the demonstrative, on the basis that its governing element is the meaning of pointing (*maʿnā al-ishāra*), not the prepositional phrase. It has been said: this is because a circumstantial clause does not precede its implicit governing element (*al-ʿāmil al-maʿnawī*). The second: *dhālika* is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is that," and ﴿we recite it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from *dhālika*, and ﴿of the signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the *hāʾ*. The third: *dhālika* is in the accusative position governed by a verb indicated by *natlū* (we recite), so ﴿of the signs﴾ is also a circumstantial clause from the *hāʾ*.

[Page 186]

It was mentioned by more than one scholar: "The delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'What is wrong with you that you revile our companion?' He said, 'What do I say?' They said, 'You say that he is the servant of Allah.' He said, 'Yes, he is the servant of Allah, His messenger, and His word which He cast to the virgin, the pure one.' They became angry and said, 'Have you ever seen a human being without a father? If you are truthful, then show us one like him.' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dala'il*, related through Salama ibn Abd Yasu', from his father, from his grandfather: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to the people of Najran, before the revelation of (Ta Sin) (Sulayman) (In the name of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob), from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to the bishop of Najran and the people of Najran: If you accept Islam, then I praise Allah before you, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. To proceed: I call you to the worship of Allah instead of the worship of servants, and I call you to the guardianship of Allah instead of the guardianship of servants. If you refuse, then the poll-tax (jizyah); and if you refuse, then I have declared war upon you. Peace." When the bishop read the letter, he was terrified and greatly alarmed, so he sent for a man of the people of Najran called Shurahbil ibn Wada'a. He handed him the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he read it. The bishop said to him, "What is your opinion?" Shurahbil said, "I know what Allah the Exalted promised Abraham concerning the prophethood among the descendants of Ishmael. There is no assurance that this man is not a prophet. I have no opinion regarding prophethood. If it were a matter of worldly affairs, I would advise you on it and exert myself for you." The bishop then sent for the people of Najran one after another, and every one of them said the same as Shurahbil's statement. Their opinion united on sending Shurahbil, Abd Allah ibn Shurahbil and Hayyar ibn Qanas, so that they might bring them the news of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The delegation set out until they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He questioned them and they questioned him, and the questioning continued between him and them until they said, "What do you say about Jesus, son of Mary?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I have nothing to say about him today. Remain until I inform you of what is said to me about Jesus at the morning dawn." Then Allah revealed this verse, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus﴾, up to His words, ﴿and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾. They refused to acknowledge this. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose the next day, after having informed them of the news, he came out wrapped in a cloak over al-Hasan and al-Husayn, with Fatimah walking behind him, for the mutual cursing (mubahalah). On that day he had a number of wives. Shurahbil said to his two companions, "I see a grave matter. If this man is a prophet sent by Allah, and we invoke a curse upon him, not a hair or a nail on the face of the earth belonging to us will remain but will perish." They said to him, "What is your opinion?" He said, "My opinion is that we make him the judge, for I see a man who never judges unjustly ever." They said to him, "It is up to you." Then Shurahbil met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "I have seen something better than cursing you." He said, "And what is that?" He said, "Your judgment today until night, and your night until morning. Whatever you judge concerning us is binding." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned without cursing them, and he made peace with them on the poll-tax.

It has been related otherwise, as will come shortly. The word "likeness" (mathal) here is not the word used in the sense of comparison, and the particle "ka" (kaf) is not superfluous, as has been said; rather it carries the sense of "state" and "wondrous attribute." That is, the attribute of Jesus ﴿with Allah﴾, meaning in His decree and judgment, or in what is hidden from you, whose reality you have not perceived. The adverbial phrase is connected to what the preposition in His words ﴿like that of Adam﴾ is connected to, meaning like his attribute and his wondrous state, about which no doubter doubts.

﴿He created him from dust﴾: this is a independent clause having no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection). It explains the aspect of resemblance, in that both involve departure from habit and the absence of the two parents being complete. It is possible that it was brought to show that the one compared to (Adam) is more strange and more contrary to habit, so that this is more decisive against the adversary and more effective in cutting off the root of his doubt. The "min" (from) indicates the starting point and is connected to what follows it; the pronoun in the accusative refers to Adam, and the meaning is that He began the creation of his form from this kind of substance.

﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [59]: that is, "Become a human being," and he became. On this reading the sequence (tarakhi) is temporal, since between the fashioning of him from what was mentioned and the bringing of the spirit into him, and his becoming flesh and blood, there was a long period. It is related that after He created his form, it remained lying at the gate of Paradise for forty years, with the spirit not yet breathed into it. The expression is in the present tense although the context calls for the past, in order to depict that complete matter as if it were a sight being witnessed now, as a notification that it is among the strange and wondrous affairs. It has also been permitted that the expression is in this form because "becoming" is future relative to what precedes it. Many of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) went to the view that "then" (thumma) indicates sequence in the reporting, not in what is reported, and they took the statement at its apparent meaning. There is no harm in the saying preceding the creation in this order and sequence, as is not hidden. The pronoun in the genitive refers to what the pronoun in the accusative referred to; and the view that it refers to Jesus is not valid, for it involves a disconnection for which there is no reason and no indication that supports it.

It has been said: in the verse there is evidence for the validity of reflection and reasoning (nazar wa istidlal), for He, glory be to Him, argued against the Christians and established the permissibility of creating Jesus, peace be upon him, without a father, by the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, without a father or a mother. Moreover, the apparent meaning is that Allah the Exalted created Jesus, peace be upon him, from the seed of Mary, peace be upon her, by making her receptive and prepared for that, as we have indicated earlier. The claim that he was created from air, as Adam was created from dust, has no basis in either reason or transmission. And ﴿so We breathed into him of Our Spirit﴾ does not indicate that in any way at all.

The truth is from your Lord﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is the truth." This refers to the clarifications and the narratives mentioned earlier. The prepositional phrase "from your Lord" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in the predicate. It is also permissible for ﴿the truth﴾ to be the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿from your Lord﴾ as its predicate. The first reading is preferred because the intended meaning is to establish that Jesus, like Adam, peace be upon them both, was a created being, and that this is "the truth," not what the Christians claim. Taking them as subject and predicate for this meaning can only be achieved with the strained assumption that every truth, or its category, is from God Most High, and that this matter is among them. Alternatively, the definite article may be read as referring back to a known "truth" already mentioned. It is not hidden how delicate it is that the address uses the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) with the pronoun referring to him (ﷺ).

﴿So do not be of those who doubt﴾ [60]: This is an address to him (ﷺ). The impossibility of doubt occurring from him, peace and blessings be upon him, does not harm this reading, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And do not be of those who associate partners with God﴾. Rather, they have mentioned two benefits of this style. The first is that when he (ﷺ) hears such an address, a sense of joy (arīḥiyyah) stirs within him, so that he increases in steadfastness upon certainty, light upon light. The second is that the listener is alerted by this address to a great matter, so he refrains and restrains himself from what would produce doubt. For he (ﷺ), with his exalted station that no wishes can reach, when addressed with such words, then what might one suppose about others? Thus there is added firmness for him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and gentleness for others. It is also permissible that this be an address to everyone who encounters it and is fit to be addressed.

[p. 188]

﴿Whoever argues with you﴾ — i.e., disputes with you and contends against you, from the delegation of the Christians of Najran, since they were the ones who undertook this. (**about it**) — i.e., concerning the matter of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), because he is the one spoken of and the subject of the story. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the truth mentioned previously, due to its proximity and because the meaning is not thereby distant. ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾ — i.e., the signs that necessitate knowledge. Calling them "knowledge" is either a literal usage, since they are, as has been said, a kind of it, or a metonymic usage (*majaz mursal*), and the indication of this is the mention of argument, which requires proofs. The final prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject of ﴿came to you﴾, which refers back to the relative pronoun *ma*, and *min* (in "min dhalika") is partitive, though it has also been said that it is explanatory of the genus.

(**Say**) — i.e., to whoever argues with you: ﴿Come⁠﴾ — i.e., come forward with resolve and determination. Its original sense is requesting someone to come up to an elevated place, then it was broadened and used for the mere request to come. ﴿Let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves⁠﴾ — i.e., each of us and of you calls upon his sons, his women, and himself for *mubahala* (mutual imprecation, a mutual invoking of God's curse upon the liar). In placing those who were placed before the self in the mubahala, although the self is among the things most exposed to ruin, and the man risks himself on their behalf, there is a notification of his complete security [p. 188 continues] (ﷺ) and his complete certainty in the all-encompassing protection of God Almighty for them. For this reason, while observing the original form of the expression (since the non-speaker follows the speaker in the attribution), he (ﷺ) placed his own side before the side of those addressed.

﴿Then let us invoke⁠﴾ — i.e., let us mutually invoke (*natabahal*). So the form *iftaʿala* here carries the meaning of *mufaʿala*, and *iftaʿala* and *tafaʿala* are, in many instances, siblings, as in *ishtawara* and *tashawara*, and *ijtawara* and *tajawara*. The root meaning of *buhla* (with *ḍamma* or *fatḥa*), as has been said, is the curse and the invocation of it; then it spread to general supplication, as one says: "So-and-so invokes God Almighty earnestly concerning his need." Al-Raghib said: *bahl* of a thing or of a camel is leaving it unattended and letting it go, and then it was used for pouring out supplication, whether it was a curse or not. However, here it is explained as a curse, because that is the intended and actual meaning, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿so that we may place the curse of God upon the liars⁠﴾ [3:61] — i.e., concerning the matter of ʿIsa (peace be upon him). For it is conjoined to "let us invoke" and explains what is meant by it: i.e., we say, "The curse of God upon the liars," or "O God, curse the liars."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated: "That al-ʿAqib and al-Sayyid came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he wished to invoke a curse upon them both. One of them said to his companion: 'Do not invoke a curse upon him, for by God, if he is a prophet and invokes a curse upon us, we shall never prosper, neither we nor our descendants after us.' They said to him: 'We will give you what you ask; send with us a trustworthy man.' He said: 'Stand up, O Abu ʿUbayda.' When he stood, he said: 'This is the trustworthy one of this community.'"

Abu Nuʿaym narrated in *al-Dalaʾil*, through the chain of ʿAta' and al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "That eight of the bishops of the people of Najran came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among them al-ʿAqib and al-Sayyid, and God Almighty revealed ﴿Say: Come⁠﴾ — the verse. They said: 'Give us respite for three days.' So they went to the Banu Qurayza, the Nadir, and the Banu Qaynuqaʿ, and consulted them. They advised them to make peace with him and not to invoke a curse upon him, saying: 'He is the Prophet whom we find in the Torah.' So they made peace with the Prophet (ﷺ) for a thousand garments in Safar and a thousand in Rajab, and dirhams." It is also narrated that they made peace with him on condition that they give him each year two thousand garments, thirty-three coats of mail, thirty-three camels, and thirty-four horses.

He also narrated in *al-Dalaʾil*, through the chain of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas: "That the delegation of Najran from among the Christians came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they were fourteen men of their nobles, among them al-Sayyid, who is the elder, and al-ʿAqib, who is the one after him and the man of their opinion. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Submit (become Muslims).' They said: 'We have submitted.' He said: 'You have not submitted.' They said: 'Yes, we have submitted before you.' He said: 'You lie. Three things prevent you from Islam: your worship of the cross, your eating of pork, and your claim that God has a son.' And God revealed ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿIsa⁠﴾ — the verse. When he recited it to them, they said: 'We do not understand what you are saying.' And God revealed ﴿Whoever argues with you⁠﴾ — the verse. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'God Almighty has commanded me, if you do not accept this, to invoke a mutual curse upon you.' They said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, rather we will return and consider our matter, then we will come to you.' Some of them withdrew with others and they agreed among themselves. The Sayyid said to the ʿAqib: 'By God, you know that this man is a sent prophet, and if you invoke a curse upon him, it will be your annihilation, and no people has ever invoked a curse upon a prophet, for their elder would remain and their young would not grow up. If you will not follow him and insist only upon the faith you have, then make peace with him and return to your lands.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had gone out with ʿAli, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, and Fatima. He said: 'If I supplicate, then you say āmīn.' They refused to invoke the curse with him, and they made peace with him for the poll-tax (*jizya*)."

From al-Shaʿbi: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The bearer of good tidings has come to me about the destruction of the people of Najran, even the birds on the trees, had they persisted in the mutual cursing." From Jabir: "By Him who sent me with the truth, had they done it, He would have rained fire upon the valley over them both." It is also narrated that the bishop of Najran, when he saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approaching, with ʿAli, Fatima, and the two sons (al-Hasan and al-Husayn), may God be pleased with them, said: "O assembly of Christians, I see faces which, if they asked God Almighty to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it. So do not invoke the curse and perish."

Now, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) joined the sons and women to himself, although the purpose of mubahala is to make clear the truthful from the liar, and this belongs to him and to the one with whom he invokes the curse, because that is more complete in indicating his trust in his own state and his certainty of his truthfulness, more complete in striking the enemy, and more abundant in harming him, should the mubahala take place.

In this story there is the clearest proof of his prophethood (ﷺ); otherwise they would not have refrained from invoking the curse with him. Its indication of the excellence of the family of God and His Messenger (ﷺ) is something about which no believer doubts, and the Nasibi (the one who harbours enmity to the Prophet's household) is firmly outside faith.

The Shiʿa have cited it as evidence for the priority of ʿAli (may God ennoble his face) for the caliphate after the Messenger of God (ﷺ), on the basis of the narration of ʿAli (may God ennoble his face) coming with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the argument that "our sons" then means al-Hasan and al-Husayn, "our women" means Fatima, and "ourselves" means the Commander (ʿAli), who came to be the self of the Messenger. It is evident that the literal meaning is impossible, so it is determined that the intended meaning is equality, and whoever is equal to the Prophet (ﷺ) is more excellent and more entitled to the disposal of affairs than others, and there is no meaning to the caliphate except that.

This is answered as follows. First: we do not accept that "ourselves" means the Commander; rather the intended meaning is his noble self (ﷺ), and the Commander is included among the sons. In custom, a son-in-law is counted as a son without doubt, and metonymy is necessarily general if we say that applying "son" to a daughter's son is literal; and if we say that it is metonymic, there is no need to say it is general, and its application to the Commander and his two sons (may God be pleased with them) is equal in being metonymic. The statement of al-Tabrisi and other scholars of theirs, that taking "ourselves" to mean his own noble self (ﷺ) is not permissible because of the presence of "let us call" and that a person does not call himself—this is raving talk, since it has spread and become widely known in old and new usage that "his self called him to such-and-such," "I called myself to such-and-such," "his self made it easy for him," "I commanded my self and consulted it," and other valid usages found in the speech of eloquent writers. Thus the result of "let us call our selves" is "let us bring our selves forward." And what harm is there in that? Moreover, even if we established the Commander as the referent of "ourselves" on behalf of the Prophet (ﷺ), who then would we establish as the referent from the side of the unbelievers, since they share in the form "let us call," for there is no meaning to the Prophet's calling them and their sons and women after his saying ﴿Come⁠﴾, as is not hidden.

Second: even if we grant that the intended meaning of "ourselves" is the Commander, we do not accept that the intended meaning of "self" is the person's essence, since the word "self" has come to mean a relative and a partner in religion and community. Among that is His saying: ﴿Do not expel yourselves from your homes⁠﴾ and ﴿Do not defame yourselves⁠﴾ and ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and women not think well of their own kind?⁠﴾ Perhaps when the Commander had a connection with the Prophet (ﷺ) through lineage and marriage and unity of religion, it was expressed by "self." And in that case, the equality on which their argument rests is not required, namely their argument that if the meaning were equality in all attributes it would entail sharing in prophethood, finality, being sent to all creation, and the like, which is false by consensus (*ijmaʿ*), since the follower is inferior to the one followed. And if the meaning were equality in some respects, the purpose would not be achieved, since equality in some attributes of the more excellent and more entitled to the disposal of affairs does not necessarily make the one to whom they belong more excellent and more entitled to disposal.

Third: even if that indicated the caliphate of the Commander, as they claim, it would entail that the Commander was imam during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is false by agreement. If it is restricted to a period and not another, then, apart from the fact that restriction is something for which there is no indication in the wording, it would not be conclusive for their claim, since it is not a point in dispute, because the People of the Sunna affirm his imamate for one period and not another. Thus this proof does not stand on the point of contention. Because of the weakness of the argument from it on this question, and indeed the invalidity of it—like arguing from it for the excellence of the Commander ʿAli (may God ennoble his face) over the prophets and messengers (peace be upon them), on the claim that his equality with the most excellent of them is established in it—the verifying scholars of the Shiʿa did not stand upon more than the assertion that the Commander, the Virgin (Fatima), and al-Husayn were dear to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as ʿAbd Allah al-Mashhadi did in his book *Izhar al-Haqq* (*The Manifestation of the Truth*).

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and others narrated from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿So say: Come, let us call⁠﴾ etc., the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called ʿAli, Fatima, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, and said: 'O God, these are my family.'" This which we have mentioned of his (ﷺ) calling these four, who are fitting (for the purpose), is the well-known narration on which the scholars of hadith rely. Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad from his father, may God be pleased with them: "That when this verse was revealed, he brought Abu Bakr and his sons, and ʿUmar and his sons, and ʿUthman and his sons, and ʿAli and his sons." This is contrary to what the majority have narrated.

Ibn Abi ʿIllan of the Mu'tazila also used this story as evidence that al-Hasan and al-Husayn were legally responsible (*mukallaf*) at that time, because mubahala is not permissible except with adults. The Imamiyya held that it requires perfection of intellect and discernment, and attaining that does not depend on puberty, for perfection may be attained before it, which may even exceed the perfection of adults. So there is nothing to prevent al-Hasan and al-Husayn at that time from being non-adults while being at an age in which they could have perfect intellect. Moreover, it is possible that God Almighty breaks ordinary custom for those noble lords and singles them out with what none other shares with them, so if it were established that perfection of intellect is not customary at that age, it would be permissible for them, as a demonstration of their distinction from others and an indication of their rank with God Almighty and their special status with Him; and they are the people whose distinctions cannot be counted.

The Nawasib (those hostile to the Prophet's family) held that mubahala is permissible to make the truth manifest until the Day of Judgment, except that it is forbidden for children and women to attend. They claimed—may God raise them not in rank nor lower them, nor remove their burden—that what occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ) was merely for the purpose of binding the opponent and silencing him, and that it does not indicate the excellence of those noble persons over our Prophet, and upon them be the best of prayers and the most complete of peace. You know that this claim is a kind of raving and a trace of the touch of Satan.

And nothing is established in minds when daylight needs a proof.

Whoever holds that mubahalah (the mutual invocation of God's curse upon the liar) is permissible today, in the manner that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did, cites what ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Qays ibn Saʿd: that Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be well pleased with them both, had a dispute with another man, so he invited him to mubahalah, recited the verse, raised his hands, and faced the Corner (al-Rukn). It is as if, by this, may God be well pleased with him, he was indicating the manner of ibtihal (earnest supplication) and that the hands are raised in it. And what al-Hakim narrated explicitly confirms this, and that the hands are raised level with the shoulders.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿is indeed the true narrative﴾. This is a nominal clause, the predicate of (inna). It is also permissible that "huwa" be a separating pronoun (damir fasl) with no place in i'rab, and "al-qasas" be the predicate. The separating pronoun conveys restriction of a relative kind (al-qasr al-idafi), as the definiteness of both parts also conveys. "Al-haqq" is an attribute of "al-qasas" and is the intended element of the information: that is, this is the truth, not what the Christians claim concerning the Messiah, peace be upon him, being God and the Son of God. Exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. It has also been said that the pronoun serves restriction and emphasis if there were nothing else in the speech conveying that, and if it is as here, then it is merely for emphasis. The first view is the well-known one, and the majority hold it, and it is probably the most correct. The lam is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), and its original place is to enter upon the subject, but they shift it to the predicate so that two emphatic particles do not follow one another. And if it is permissible for it to enter upon the predicate, its entering upon the separating pronoun is even more permissible, since it is closer to the subject. So understand.

"Al-qasas," according to what is in "al-Bahr," is a verbal noun from the expression: "Fulan narrated the story (qassa al-hadith yaqussuhu qassan and qasasan)." Its original meaning is following a trace. It is said: "Fulan went out tracing the trace of Fulan (yaqussu athar Fulan)," meaning he follows him to learn where he went. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up (qussihi)"﴾, meaning follow his trace. Likewise the narrator (al-qass) in speech, because he follows one report after another, or follows the meanings in order to present them. Here it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle, meaning "the narrated truth." It has been read as "lahwa" with the ha' sukun.

﴿And there is no god except Allah﴾. This is a refutation of the Christians in their trinitarianism, and likewise it is a refutation of all the dualists. "Min" is superfluous for emphasis, as is the case with the particles of connection. The people of the language, as al-Shihab said, understood that it is for emphasizing the comprehensiveness understood from the negated indefinite noun, since it is specific to that in most cases. Muhibb al-Din hesitated over the way in which the superfluous words serve emphasis, since they are not conventionally assigned to it, and he answered that it is a matter of taste known to the people of the language. It was objected that this is a referral to something unknown, so it does not convey anything. Rather, it is better to say that it is conventional, but it belongs to the category of generic convention. So reflect.

﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Mighty﴾, i.e., the one who prevails with complete dominance, or the one who has such complete power, or the one who has no equal, ﴿the Wise﴾ [62], i.e., the one who perfects what He has made, or the one who encompasses all knowable things. The sentence is a concluding appendage to what precedes it, and its purpose is also to restrict divinity to Him, exalted is He, refuting the Christians; that is, restriction of singling out. So the separating pronoun and the definiteness here are like the separating pronoun and definiteness there. As for what has been said, that they are not for restriction, since the usual case regarding other than Him is that there is only one, so the restriction would be void there unless it is made a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb), and the context does not suit that, which has no support, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 3, verse 63:**

﴿Then if they turn away﴾, that is, they turn away from following you and from affirming you after these clear signs. This is on the assumption that the verb is in the past tense. It may also be in the present tense (*yatawallaw*), with one of the two *ta'*s deleted for lightness, its original form being *tatawallaw*. ﴿Then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾ [3:63]. That is, Knowing of them or of you. The clause is, on the surface, the response (*jawab*) to the conditional, but the meaning is what follows from His knowledge of the corrupters, namely His punishing them. So the statement is a threat. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to draw attention to the cause that necessitates the requital and punishment, which is corruption (*ifsad*). It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah is Knowing of these disputants who argue without right, and that they will not dare to engage in mutual imprecation (*mubahala*) with you, because they know your prophethood and the establishment of your mission. On this view too, the clause, on close examination, stands in the place of the response, and not as the requital and punishment. The discourse is directed toward consoling him ﷺ. What this entails is not hidden.

* * *

From the allusive (*ishari*) reading of the verses: ﴿Then when he perceived﴾, that is, witnessed, ﴿Jesus﴾ through the divine light shining upon him ﴿disbelief from them﴾, that is, its darkness, or its essence. For the meanings appear to the perfected ones (*al-kummal*) in different forms according to their differences, and so they see them.

It is related from al-Bazz, may his secret be sanctified, that he said: "The night and the day come to me and inform me of what happens in them." It is also related from one of the gnostics (*'arifin*) that he witnesses the deeds of the servants as they ascend to heaven, and sees the calamity descending from it.
