﴿He said: Who are my helpers﴾ in my call ﴿to Allah﴾, glorified is He, by turning toward occupying oneself with perfecting one's own soul and refining its character, until one becomes fit to educate the deficient, so that He may help me and assist me in perfecting the deficient and guiding the one who has gone astray. ﴿The disciples said﴾, those who whiten the garments of their being with the waters of worship, the hammer of striving, and the sun of watchfulness (*muraqaba*): ﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾, that is, the aides of those who have passed away in Him and remain through Him, and among them is Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿We have believed in Allah﴾, with complete faith. ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, that is, submissive to your command, since it is the command of Allah, glorified is He. ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾, which is what has illuminated the hearts of Your chosen ones with knowledge of Your unseen. ﴿And we have followed the Messenger﴾ in what he has made apparent of Your commands and prohibitions, hoping that this will bring us to Your love. ﴿So enroll us among the witnesses﴾, that is, among those who witness You and who witness with You none other than You; or those present before You, watchful over Your command.

﴿And they schemed﴾, that is, those from whom he perceived disbelief, and they contrived with the people of Allah through a plotting of the self. Their scheming was the scheme of Truth against them, because it is He who adorns this for them, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ [6:108]. So He is the Schemer in reality. This is the meaning of ﴿and Allah schemed﴾ according to some. The better view is to affirm that the two schemes differ, as the context of distinction requires. Someone was asked, "How does Allah scheme?" He cried out and said: "His doing has no cause," and he recited:

*I ransom you; I have been created upon your love,*
*and my soul does not contend with me for other than you.*

*I love You not with a part of me but with all of me,*
*even if Your love leaves me no motion.*

*The deed of another than You is ugly to me,*
*and You do it, and it becomes beautiful from You.*

﴿When Allah said: O Jesus, I am causing you to die﴾ from the mark of temporal origination (*rasm al-huduthiyya*), ﴿and raising you to Me﴾ by the attribute of lordship (*rububiyya*), ﴿and purifying you from those who disbelieve﴾ by occupying your inner secret away from contemplating others (*aghyar*). Or: I am causing you to die from you (taking you away from yourself), and taking you from yourself, and raising you from the qualities of humanity, and purifying you from your own will entirely.

It has also been said: When Jesus, peace and blessings be upon him, perceived disbelief from them and knew that they had sent someone to kill him, he said to the disciples: "I am going to my Father and your heavenly Father," that is, connected to the Holy Spirit and purified from the bond of the world of impurity, so that I may supply you with overflow so that your call to creation may be answered after me. Then there appeared to the people a corporeal form, which was the manifestation of Jesus, the Spirit of Allah, exalted is He, in the likeness of the reality of Jesus. They supposed it to be him, so they crucified it, and they did not know that Allah, exalted is He, raised him to the fourth heaven, which is the sphere of the sun. The wisdom of raising him to that is that his spirituality is an expression of Israfil, peace be upon him, and the Messiah shares with him in the secret of the breathing (*nafkh*). As for one who says that he was raised to the lowest heaven, he explains the wisdom by saying that the outpouring of his spirit occurred through Gabriel, peace be upon him, who is an expression of the spirituality of the sphere of the moon. And the moon is in the lowest heaven, and it is a nocturnal sign that corresponds to the science of the inner (*'ilm al-batin*) which the Messiah, peace be upon him, was given.

The Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, did not take into account the view that he circles around the Throne, because that is the station of ultimate perfection, and for this reason none ascended to it except the owner of the Praised Station (*al-maqam al-mahmud*), ﷺ, who combined the outer and the inner.

﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ in that each of them is a breach of custom, outside its circle, though they differ in that Jesus, peace and blessings be upon him, was without a male, but from the sperm of a female alone, in which there was in some part the power of coagulation and in another part the power of being coagulated, like all composite drops formed from two fluids, one of which has the coagulating power and the other the coagulated. And Adam, peace and blessings be upon him, was without male or female. ﴿He created him from dust﴾, that is, He shaped his form from that. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [3:59], an allusion to the breathing of the spirit into him and its being from the world of command, with regard to his holy spirit, which did not stir in a womb.

﴿So whoever argues with you concerning it﴾, that is, concerning the truth, or concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, with false proofs, ﴿say: Come﴾ etc., that is, call him to mutual imprecation (*mubahala*) in the manner mentioned.

One of the gnostics said: Know that the imprecation of the prophets, peace be upon them, has a great effect, its cause being the connection of their souls with the Holy Spirit and Allah's support of them through it. It is the one that effects, by Allah's permission, in the elemental world. So the elemental world is affected by it as our bodies are affected by our spirits through the accidents that befall them, such as anger, fear, thought about the states of the beloved, and other things. And the human souls are affected by it as our senses and all our faculties are affected by the accidents of our spirits. So when a holy soul connects with it, or with some of the spirits of the celestial bodies and the angelic souls, its effect on the world, at the moment of the connecting orientation, is the effect of what it is connected with. Thus the bodies of the elements and the deficient human souls are affected by it according to what it wills, in accordance with that connection. For this reason, the souls of the Christians were affected by the soul of Jesus, peace and blessings be upon him, with fear, and they recoiled from the mubahala and sought a truce by agreeing to pay the jizya (poll tax). End of quotation.

Some have claimed that every soul has an effect, but it differs according to the differing ranks of souls and the variation in the ranks of orientations toward the universal abstraction (*al-tajarrud al-'amm*). There is a lengthy discussion on this, and perhaps the occasion will lead to its verification. This, and the application of what is in the horizons to what is in the souls, is evident to whoever has comprehensive knowledge of what we have presented in the earlier verses. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 3, verse 64:**

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture"﴾ It was revealed concerning the delegation of the Christians of Najran. This is the view of al-Suddi, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr. It is also reported from Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj that it was revealed concerning the Jews of Madina. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i held that it was revealed concerning both groups of the People of the Scripture, and some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) preferred this view because of the generality of its wording. ﴿Come﴾, i.e., hurry (halumma). ﴿To a word﴾, i.e., a statement (kalam), as al-Zajjaj said. Using it in this sense is a case of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), whose relation ( 'alaqa) is that the part is used for the whole, since it is permissible to apply the word to a compound phrase (al-murakkab al-naqis). However, this usage was not found in the inductive survey of usage (al-istiqra'). It has also been said that it is a metaphor (isti'ara), and this is not far-fetched. It was read as (kilmatan), with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the lam, for ease and transposition (al-naql). ﴿Common﴾, i.e., just (*'adl*). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and Qatada. It has also been said that *sawa'* is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of "equal," i.e., that the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an do not differ regarding it, or that there is no disagreement about it among all the laws (al-shara'i'). In the reading of the majority it is in the genitive, being an attribute (na't) of (*kalima*). It was also read in the accusative as a verbal noun.

﴿Between us and you﴾ is connected to *sawa'*. ﴿That we not worship﴾, i.e., we and you, ﴿except God﴾, by our affirming His oneness in worship and making our worship sincerely for Him. Regarding the position of (*an*) and what follows it, Abu al-Baqa' mentioned two possibilities. The first is the genitive, in apposition (badaliyya) to ﴿word﴾. The second is the nominative, as the predicate (khabariyya) of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is that we do not worship except God." Were it not for the operation of (*an*), it could be explanatory (tafsiriyya). It has also been said that the sentence is complete at ﴿common﴾, and then a new sentence begins: ﴿between us and you, that we not worship﴾, so that the prepositional phrase is the fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) and (*an*) with what follows it is the delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿And that we not associate with Him anything﴾, of things, meaning that we do not make anything other than Him a partner with Him in deserving worship, and we do not consider anything worthy of being worshipped. With this meaning the statement is establishing new content (ta'sis). The apparent view is that it is emphasis (ta'kid) of what precedes it, but establishing new content is more beneficial. It has also been said that the meaning is that we do not associate with Him anything of association (shirk), but this is very far-fetched.

﴿And that some of us not take others as lords besides God﴾, i.e., that some of us not obey others in disobedience to God, the Exalted. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. It is supported by what al-Tirmidhi reported and graded as good (hasan), from the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim: "When this verse was revealed, he said: 'O Messenger of God, we did not worship them.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Did they not make lawful for you and unlawful, and you followed them?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'That is it.'" It has been said that God, may He be glorified, alluded to this with His saying, Mighty is He Who speaks: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God﴾. 'Ikrima reported that this taking meant some of them prostrating to others. It has also been said that it is like the belief of the Jews that 'Uzayr was the son of God, and the belief of the Christians regarding the Messiah, which is similar. The pronoun in *na* (us), under every interpretation, refers to people, not to the possible (al-mumkin), even though it could include idols, because the People of the Scripture did not worship them.

There is a subtle point in the use of the word "some" (al-ba'd): it indicates that they are some of our kind, so how could they be lords? If you say: the addressees did not take some as lords besides God, but took them as gods alongside Him, the answer is that "besides God" means "besides God alone." Or it is said: he used this expression to draw attention to the fact that association does not coexist with the acknowledgment of God's lordship, by reason. This was said by some. As for the Christians, may God blacken their fortune, they have the greatest share of these prohibited matters. Their sects and the detailed account of their disbelief will come, God willing, in the most complete manner.

﴿Then if they turn away, say: "Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ [64] The meaning is: if they turn away from your agreement on what has been mentioned, which the Scriptures and the Messengers all agree upon, after it has been presented to them, then know that the proof has been established against them, and they refused only out of obstinacy. So say to them: "Be fair and acknowledge that we are upon the true religion." This is a challenge to them (ta'jiz) or an allusion (ta'rid) against them, because if they testify to Islam for them, it is as if they had said, "We are not like that." This is the view of some of the verifiers. It has also been said that the meaning is: if they turn away, say: "We do not shrink from Islam, and we do not care about anyone in this matter, so bear witness that we are Muslims, for we do not conceal our Islam as you fear and conceal your disbelief, and do not acknowledge it, because you do not trust in God's help." It is not hidden that this, despite what it contains, is appropriate only if the discourse concerns the hypocrites among the People of the Scripture, because the hypocrites are those who fear and therefore conceal. As for these people, they acknowledge what they are upon, whatever it is, so this statement is not fitting for them. And ﴿turned away﴾ here is in the past tense, and it is not permissible that the implied reading be *tatawallaw* (present tense), because that spoils the meaning: ﴿say﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, while *tatawallaw* would be addressed to the polytheists, and at that point there would be no answer (jawab) left in the sentence.

[p. 194]

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 65:*

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is an address to the Jews and the Christians. ﴿Why do you argue about Abraham﴾, meaning: why do you dispute and debate concerning him, each of you claiming that he (peace be upon him) was upon his religion. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The Christians of Najran and the rabbis of the Jews gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disputed in his presence. The rabbis said, 'Abraham was none but a Jew,' and the Christians said, 'Abraham was none but a Christian.' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse concerning them."

The first adverbial phrase (*al-zarf al-awwal*) is connected to what follows it, and so is the second. *Ma* is interrogative (*istifhamiyya*, an interrogative particle), and the purpose is denial and astonishment, according to al-Samin (a grammarian). Its alif has been deleted when the preposition entered upon it, in order to distinguish it from the relative pronoun (*al-mawsula*). The statement involves an elision of a noun, meaning "the religion of Abraham" or "his law (*shari'a*)", because essences (*al-dhawat*) are not subject to dispute.

﴿And the Torah was not revealed﴾ to Moses (peace be upon him), ﴿nor the Gospel﴾ to Jesus (peace be upon him), ﴿except after him﴾. Between him and Moses (peace be upon them both) there were five hundred and sixty-five years, and it has been said seven hundred, and it has been said a thousand years. Between Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both) there were one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five years, and it has been said two thousand years. There are other opinions as well.

﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ [65] The hamza (*al-hamza*, the interrogative particle) enters upon an implied element, which is the thing conjoined by the stated conjunction, according to one view. The meaning is: "Will you not reflect, so that you do not understand the falsehood of your statement?" or "Do you say that, so that you do not understand its falsehood?" This is a declaration of their ignorance and foolishness in that claim. This is clear if they claimed, as al-Shihab (al-Khafaji, the commentator) said, that Abraham (peace be upon him) was literally one of them. But if their claim was that the religion of Abraham agrees with the religion of Moses or the religion of Jesus, then he would be a Jew or a Christian in this sense. Declaring them ignorant and denying them reason on the basis of the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel after him is problematic, unless it is claimed that the meaning is: if the matter were as they say, Moses would not have been given the Torah, nor Jesus the Gospel, but rather both would have been commanded to convey the scrolls of Abraham. This is what has been said. But you know that this does not satisfy the heart, for one may say: what prevents the unity of the law from coexisting with the revelation of these two Books for a purpose other than explaining a new law? Moreover, the scrolls did not contain rulings but were parables and admonitions, as has come in the hadith. Then, as for what al-Shihab said, although the basis for declaring them ignorant is clear in it, the utterance of that claim by the People of the Scripture is extremely unlikely, because the people were not at this level of ignorance. Among them were the rabbis of the Jews and the delegation of Najran, and it has been mentioned that the latter two were very insistent in debate. Ibn Jarir narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith al-Zubaydi that he said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'I wish there were a veil between me and the people of Najran, so that I would not see them and they would not see me,'" because of the severity with which they disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ).

Unless it is said that Allah the Exalted blinded their insight in this claim, so that they would become a laughingstock for the children of the believers. Or that they said that on the basis of stubbornness and obstinacy, so that each of them would anger his companion. Or to mislead some of the believers, thinking that because they were unlettered and not informed about the histories of the earlier prophets, such a claim would shake them; so Allah the Exalted exposed them. Or that these people in themselves were ignorant and did not know, even though they were People of the Scripture. What Ibn al-Harith mentioned does not indicate their knowledge, as is not hidden.

It has also been said that the intention of the Jews in their saying that Abraham was a Jew is that he believed in Moses before Moses' mission, in the manner that Muslims say about all the messengers (peace be upon them) that they believed in our Prophet (ﷺ) before his mission, as his foretelling of him indicates. And that the intention of the Christians in their saying that Abraham was a Christian is similar to that. Allah the Exalted refuted them with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed except after him﴾, meaning: it is part of the nature of what comes later that it includes reports of what came earlier, especially a matter as important as this, a great honour and a supreme favour. ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ regarding what is in them, so that you would know that they are free of reports of his Judaism and Christianity, which you claimed. Then Allah, glory be to Him, drew attention to their foolishness with His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 66:

﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾ meaning: you are these fools, ﴿you argued about what you have knowledge of﴾ like the matter of Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them both, ﴿so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, which is the matter of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, since there is no mention of his religion in your Book, or no reference to the fact that he believed in Musa and Isa before their missions at all. The intended meaning is not to describe them as truly having knowledge; rather, the meaning is: suppose you argue about what you claim to know, according to what appears to you from the implications and allusions of the expressions of your Book in your opinion. Then how can you argue about what you have no knowledge of and there is no mention, no hint of it in your Book whatsoever?!

"Ha" (ها) is a particle of alerting (harf tanbih). Its entry before a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is a demonstrative noun (ism isharah) is regular, as in ha ana dha ("here I am"). It is repeated here for emphasis. Al-Akhfash held that the original form was a-antum (with a interrogative), and the hamza was changed to ha', and the meaning of interrogation for him is wonder at their ignorance. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it is not good, because the replacement of the interrogative hamza with ha' has not been heard in their speech except in a rare line of poetry; moreover, separating the replaced ha' from the hamza of (antum) is not appropriate, because separation is only made to avoid the heaviness of two hamzas together, and here the heaviness has already been removed by replacing the first with ha'. The demonstrative is for belittling and disparagement, and from it is understood the attribute by which the benefit of the predication becomes apparent. The clause ﴿hajajtum﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the first. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (haliyyah), on the evidence that a circumstantial phrase often occupies its place, as in ha ana dha qa'iman; and this circumstance is obligatory. It was also said that the clause is a predicate of (antum), and ﴿ha'ulaa'﴾ is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been omitted. It was also said: ﴿ha'ulaa'﴾ means "those who," being the predicate of the subject, and the clause ﴿hajajtum﴾ is a relative clause; this is the view of the Kufans. Their reciters read ﴿ha antum﴾ with a long vowel and hamza. The people of Madina and Abu 'Amr read it without hamza or long vowel, except to the extent of the articulation of the quiescent alif. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read it with hamza and short vowel without lengthening. Ibn 'Amir read it with a long vowel without hamza.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ the state of Ibrahim and what he was upon, ﴿while you do not know﴾ [66] that. You may consider the object general, so that what is mentioned enters it as a primary inclusion. The clause is an emphasis for the negation of knowledge from them concerning the matter of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Then he explicitly stated what the established proof had declared, so He, glorified is He, said:

**[Page 196]**

﴿Abraham was not a Jew﴾, as the Jews claimed, ﴿nor a Christian﴾, as the Christians claimed, ﴿but he was a ḥanīf﴾, meaning one who turns away from corrupt creeds (ḥanīf: one who inclines away from falsehood toward the truth), ﴿a Muslim﴾, meaning one who submits to obedience to the Truth, or one who affirms God's oneness (tawḥīd), because Islam is also used in the sense of tawḥīd. It has been said that this is supported by God's words, ﴿nor was he of the polytheists﴾ [67], meaning the idol-worshippers, such as the Arabs who claimed to be upon his religion, or polytheists in general, so that it also includes fire-worshippers like the Magians and star-worshippers like the Sabians. It has also been said that the intended polytheists are the Jews and Christians, because the Jews say, "Uzayr is the son of God," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of God." Exalted is God far above that, greatly exalted.

The original wording would have been "nor was he of you," but the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to imply that they are polytheists. In that case the clause is an emphasis on what precedes it. Interpreting Islam in the sense mentioned above is the view chosen by a group of verifying scholars (muḥaqqiqīn), who claimed that it cannot be correctly interpreted here as the Muḥammadan religion, because it may be objected that he came many centuries later, so how could he be a Muslim? This would be like their claim that he was a Jew or a Christian, which is refuted by God's words, ﴿and the Torah and the Gospel were not sent down except after him﴾. The same objection therefore applies to them, and the argument is shared between the two views. Some scholars interpreted it in that way, and answered the shared objection by saying that the Qur'an has informed us that Abraham was a Muslim, while the Torah and the Gospel do not state that he, peace be upon him, was a Jew or a Christian. Thus the difference is clear.

The scholar al-Nisabūrī said: If it is said, "Your claim that Abraham, peace be upon him, was upon the religion of Islam, if you mean agreement in the fundamental principles (uṣūl), this is not specific to the religion of Islam; and if you mean agreement in the subsidiary rulings (furūʿ), it follows that our Prophet ﷺ was not a bringer of a sacred law (sharīʿah) but rather a confirmer of the law of those before him." It is answered: the first option is chosen, and the specificity holds, because the Jews and Christians in our time oppose the fundamental principles, by their saying in the Trinity, associating ʿUzayr, peace be upon him, with God, and so on. Or the second option is chosen, and what was mentioned does not follow, because God may have abrogated those subsidiary rulings through the law of Moses, peace be upon him, and then our Prophet ﷺ abrogated the law of Moses with his own law, which agrees with the law of Abraham, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him. Thus he, peace be upon him, is a bringer of a sacred law, while his law agrees with the law of Abraham in most of the subsidiary rulings. End of quotation.

It is not hidden what is wrong with the answer to the second option, namely that it is far-fetched, indeed not even valid. This is because the abrogation of Abraham's law by the law of Moses, and then the abrogation of Moses' law by the law of our Prophet, peace be upon them all, which agrees with the law of Abraham, does not make our Prophet the bringer of a new sacred law. Rather, it may also be said that he is a confirmer of the law of one before him, namely Abraham, peace be upon him. Moreover, the agreement of all the subsidiary rulings of our law with all the subsidiary rulings of the law of Abraham is impossible in any way at all, since among the subsidiary rulings of our law is the obligation of reciting the Qur'an in prayer, which was obviously not revealed to any prophet other than our Prophet ﷺ, and there are many similar examples.

Agreement in most of them lies within the realm of what is prohibited, and short of establishing it stands the high mountain. God's words, ﴿that you follow the creed of Abraham﴾, are not evidence for agreement in the subsidiary rulings, since the word "creed" (millah) there means tawḥīd, or tawḥīd together with moral conduct, like the word "guidance" in God's words, ﴿those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾.

Al-Shihāb [al-Alūsī] objected to the answer given to the first option on the grounds of its being far-fetched, just as he objected to the answer given to the second option on the grounds of its being far-fetched by itself. He mentioned that this is the reason some verifying scholars deviated from what the words of this scholar (al-Nisabūrī) imply, namely that the meaning of Abraham being a Muslim is that he was upon the creed of Islam, toward the meaning that he was a submitter, by taking Islam in its linguistic sense. He claimed that this is free of objection. But it was criticized that taking Islam linguistically is not suitable to the discussion of religions, and the discussion of it, so this view is not free from far-fetchedness, and perhaps it is no less far-fetched than the far-fetchedness he claimed for the first answer, as is not hidden from one with sound taste.

This is one matter. There is another interpretation of the verse, perhaps one that can be extracted from amid dung and blood: when the People of the Book disputed, the Jews said, "Abraham is one of us," and the Christians said, "He is one of us." Each group meant that he, peace be upon him, was at that time in the condition he is now in, which is a condition contrary to what their prophet was in reality, but agreeing with him in their claim, in the sense of the agreement of fundamentals with fundamentals, or agreement in what is customarily considered agreement even if it is not in most matters. This claim is not so absurd as to be hidden from anyone. So God the Exalted refuted them by His words, ﴿and the Torah and the Gospel were not sent down except after him﴾, meaning, they do not contain that, and had it been there, it would have been worth mentioning. Then God, exalted is He, pointed to their foolishness in a more complete manner, and then He explicitly stated what He had first alluded to, saying, ﴿Abraham was not a Jew﴾, meaning, from the Jewish sect that opposes what Moses, peace be upon him, brought in reality; ﴿nor a Christian﴾, meaning, from the Christian sect that opposes what Jesus, peace be upon him, brought in the same way; ﴿but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim﴾, meaning, upon the religion of Islam, which is the only religion acceptable to God, and it is the religion of all the prophets, may the blessings and peace of God Most High be upon them all. In this is an indication that those Jews and Christians have nothing to do with religion, because they oppose in reality what the two prophets stood upon, rather, what all the prophets stood upon. Then He pointed to the cause of this by what He hinted at with His words, ﴿nor was he of the polytheists﴾. Accordingly, the Muslim, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ said, and as we have pointed out earlier many times, is the believer even if he is not from this community, contrary to al-Suyūṭī's claim that Islam is specific to this community. This is what I have in this matter. So reflect, for the path of the intellect is broad.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 68:

﴿Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham﴾ *awlā* is an elative form (*af'al al-tafḍīl*) from *waliya*, *yalīhi*, *walyan*. Its *alif* is converted from a *yā'* because its first radical is a *wāw*, so its last radical cannot be a *wāw*, since in the language there is no word whose first and last radicals are both *wāw* except *wāw* itself. The original meaning is "nearer." Among its uses is the hadith: "*li-awlā rajulin dhakarin*" ("to the nearest male"). It can also mean "more deserving," as when you say: "The scholar is more deserving of precedence (*awlā bi-l-taqdīm*)." This is the meaning intended here, that is, the nearest of people and the most special to Abraham ﴿to those who followed him﴾, that is, those who were upon his law in his time, or who followed him in general. The coordination in His words, glorified is He, ﴿and this Prophet﴾ is *'aṭf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm* (coordination of the specific upon the general). It is coordinated upon the relative pronoun before it, which is the predicate of (*inna*). It was also read in the accusative, coordinated upon the object pronoun, and the sense would be: "to those who followed Abraham and followed this Prophet." It was also read in the genitive, coordinated upon "Abraham," meaning: "Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham, and this Prophet, are those who followed him." It was objected that the pronoun in ﴿followed him﴾ should have been dual, and one should say "they followed both of them." It was answered that it is of the type of ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, but in it, according to what has been said, there is the separation between the governor and the governed by a foreign element.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿and those who believe﴾, if it is coordinated upon "those who followed him," then this also applies to it. If it is coordinated upon "this Prophet," then there is no benefit in it, unless it is claimed that it is for honoring them by mentioning them. As for the insistence that it is coordination of attributes, some upon others, in that case, it is as you see. Then, that those who followed Abraham, peace be upon him, in his time are the closest of people to him is evident. That our Prophet (ﷺ) is closer to him than others, because his law agrees with the Abrahamic law more than the laws of the other messengers agree with it, and that the believers of this community are likewise, because they follow their Prophet in what he brought, and among it is what agrees.

﴿Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾ [68] He helps them and rewards them with good, as is the way of a protector. He did not say "their protector," as an indication of the attribute by which Allah, exalted is He, is a protector to His servants, which is belief, based on the principle that attaching a ruling to a derived noun (*mushtaqq*) implies that the basis of derivation is its cause. From this it is known that the ruling applies to the Prophet by the indication of the text.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "The leaders of the Jews said: 'By Allah, O Muhammad, we know that we are more deserving of the religion of Abraham than you and others, and that he was a Jew.' But you only have envy.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

'Abd ibn Humayd related through the chain of Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "Ibn Ghanm told me: 'When the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to the Negus, 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Imarah ibn Abi Mu'ayt caught up with them, and they wanted to trouble them and oppress them. They came to the Negus and informed him that these men who had come to you from the people of Mecca want to overthrow your kingdom, corrupt your land, and insult your Lord.' So the Negus sent for them. When they came to him, he said: 'Do you not hear what your two companions say, to 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Imarah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, claiming that you came to overthrow my kingdom and corrupt my land?' 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and Hamzah said: 'If you wish, leave the matter between one of us and the Negus, so that whichever of us is youngest in age may speak to him. If what he says is right, then Allah will bring it about, and if it is otherwise, you may say: 'He is a young man, and you have an excuse in that.'' So the Negus gathered his priests, his monks, and his interpreters. Then he asked them: 'Tell me about your companion from whom you have come: what does he say to you, what does he command you, and what does he forbid you? Does he have a book that he reads?' They said: 'Yes, this man reads what Allah, exalted is He, has revealed to him, and what he has heard from Him. He commands what is good, commands good neighborliness, commands care for orphans, and commands that Allah, exalted is He, be worshipped alone, and that no other god be worshipped with Him.' Then he recited to him Surat al-Rum, al-'Ankabut, Ashab al-Kahf, and Maryam. When he mentioned 'Isa in the Qur'an, 'Amr wanted to anger him against them and said: 'By Allah, they insult 'Isa and revile him.' The Negus said: 'What does your companion say about 'Isa?' He said: 'He says that 'Isa is the servant of Allah, His Messenger, His Spirit, and His Word, which He cast to Maryam.' The Negus took a bit of straw from his toothstick, about the amount that dust would fall into the eye, and swore that al-Masih did not exceed what your companion says by the weight of that dust in his hand from the straw of his toothstick. So rejoice and do not fear. *Fa-la (dahūnah)*, meaning in the language of Abyssinia, is blame upon the party of Abraham.' 'Amr ibn al-'As said: 'What is the party of Abraham?' He said: 'These men and their companion whom they came from, and whoever follows them.' So this verse was revealed on that day in their dispute with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was in Medina: ﴿Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham﴾ the verse."

﴿Surely a party of the People of the Book wish to lead you astray﴾. It is well known that this was revealed when the Jews invited Hudhayfah, 'Ammar and Mu'adh to Judaism. Accordingly, "the People of the Book" here means the Jews. It has also been said that it refers to both groups. The verse explains that they are callers to misguidance, following its explanation that they themselves are astray. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sufyan that he said: "Everything in Al 'Imran that mentions the People of the Book refers to the Christians." This is probably a general rule (jari majra al-ghalib), not an absolute one. The *min* (مِن) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and "a party" (ta'ifah) means their leaders and rabbis. It has also been said that *min* is explicative (li-bayan al-jins), and that "a party" refers to all the People of the Book, but this is far-fetched. The *law* (لَوْ) is used in the sense of *an* (أنْ), the verbal particle, so that the phrase formed with it (al-muntasabik) is the object of *wadda* (وَدَّ, "wished"). It is also permissible to keep it in its original sense, in which case the object of *wadda* and the response of *law* are both omitted, and the meaning is: "They wish your misguidance; if they could lead you astray, they would rejoice at that." The meaning of ﴿yudillunakum﴾ ("they lead you astray") is: they return you to your disbelief, as Ibn 'Abbas said; or they destroy you, as Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said; or they cause you to fall into error and cast doubts into your religion, as Abu 'Ali said, which is close to the first meaning.

﴿And they lead none astray except themselves﴾. The *waw* (وَ) is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal). The meaning, if "leading astray" is understood as destruction, is that they destroy none except themselves, because they deserve the wrath and anger of God through their preference for destroying the believers. If the meaning of destruction is causing them to fall into error, this requires interpretation, because the people are themselves astray, which would make the one who is astray cause others to be astray. Thus it is said that the intended meaning of leading astray is its consequence, which returns upon them, either by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) or by metaphor (isti'arah), i.e., misguidance does not pass them by but its harm returns only to them, since their punishment is doubled because of it. Or the intended meaning of "themselves" is their likes, those of the same kind as them. In this case, according to what has been said, the statement contains a report of the unseen, and it is a metaphor (isti'arah) or a simile (tashbih) with the implied "likes of themselves," since no Muslim has become a Jew, and to God be praise. It has also been said that the meaning of their leading themselves astray is their persistence in error by what their souls have embellished for them, even though they were able to follow guidance through the clarification of proofs. This is not free from some difficulty.

﴿And they are not aware﴾ [69]. That is: they do not perceive that the leading astray is confined to them, because of the veil that has come over their hearts. This was said by Abu 'Ali. It has also been said: they are not aware that God informs the believers of their error and their leading astray. In the denial of awareness from them there is emphasis in their condemnation.

[Page 199]

ﷻ "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while you bear witness?" [3:70]. That is: why do you disbelieve in what is recited to you of the verses of the Qur'an, while you know what proves its truth and the obligation to affirm it, from the Torah and the Gospel? It has also been said: the meaning is, why do you disbelieve in the verses in your books that indicate his prophethood (ﷺ), while you witness the proofs that indicate that? Or: why do you disbelieve in what is in your books, that the religion with Allah is Islam, while you witness that? Or: why do you disbelieve in the proofs that indicate his prophethood (ﷺ), while you witness that the appearance of a miracle indicates the truthfulness of one who claims to be a messenger? Or: while you witness, when you are alone, the soundness of the religion of Islam. Or: why do you disbelieve in all the signs of Allah, while you know their truth without doubt, with the knowledge of direct observation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 71:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you mix the truth with falsehood﴾ That is, you conceal it with it, or you confuse it with it, and the "ba'" (bi) is redundant (ṣilah). Regarding the intended meaning there are several opinions. The first: it refers to their distortion of the Torah and the Gospel; this was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. The second: it refers to their showing Islam outwardly while concealing hypocrisy within; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The third: it refers to believing in Musa and 'Isa while disbelieving in Muhammad, upon them be blessings and peace. The fourth: it refers to what they know in their hearts of the truth of his prophethood (ﷺ) and what they display of denying him; this is related from Abu 'Ali and Abu Muslim. It is also read as (tulabbisūna) with the doubled letter, and it has the same meaning as the unstressed form. Yahya ibn Wathhab read (talbasūna), which is from labistu al-thawb (I wore the garment), and the "ba'" here means "ma'a" (with). The intended meaning of clothing is being characterized by something and being intertwined with it. This has been reported in what al-Bukhari related in his "Sahih" from 'A'ishah that he (ﷺ) said: "The one who pretends to have what he has not been given is like one who wears two garments of falsehood."

﴿and conceal the truth﴾ That is, the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what you have found in your books of his description and the good news about him, ﴿while you know﴾ [71] that it is true. It has been said: "you know the matters by which the obligation is valid," but this is not correct.

[Page 200]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 72:

﴿And a group﴾ means a company. It is called *ṭāʾifa* because they form a circle around which people go. ﴿From the People of the Book﴾ means the Jews, some of them to others. ﴿Believe﴾ means show belief ﴿in what has been revealed to those who believe﴾, namely the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said that they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions. ﴿At the beginning of the day﴾ means its first part, as in the verse of al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad:

"Whoever is pleased by the killing of Malik,
let him come to our women (at the beginning of the day)."

It is called *wajh* (face) because it is the first thing that confronts you from it. It is also said that it is called so because, like the face, it is its highest and most noble part. Al-Tha'alibi mentioned that this is a well-known *istiʿara* (metaphor).

﴿And reject at its end, perhaps they will return﴾ [72], that is, by means of this act they will turn away from their belief in the truth of what was revealed to them. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "Twelve men of the rabbis of Khaybar and the villages of ʿUrayna agreed among themselves, and some of them said to others: 'Enter the religion of Muhammad at the beginning of the day, with the tongue only and not with belief, and reject at the end of the day, and say: We examined our books and consulted our scholars, and we found that Muhammad is not that one, and his falsehood and the nullity of his religion have become clear to us. When you do this, his followers will doubt their religion, and they will say: They are the People of the Book and they know it best, so they will return from their religion to your religion.'"

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: This was concerning the matter of the *qibla*. When it was changed to the Kaʿba, this grieved the Jews, and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf said to his companions: "Believe in what has been revealed to Muhammad concerning the matter of the Kaʿba, and pray towards it at the beginning of the day, and return to your *qibla* at its end, perhaps they will doubt."

The expression "what has been revealed" is used in accordance with what the believers say; otherwise, they deny and do not accept that God Most High revealed anything to the believers. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that some of them commanded others to say this. As for the carrying out of the command by the one commanded, the verse is silent on whether it occurred or not. It is also reported from some of them that the reports contain what indicates that it did occur.

[Page 201]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 73:

﴿And do not believe except for those who follow your religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you before your Lord.﴾ Regarding the structure and meaning of the verse, al-Shihab summarized several views from the statements of some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin):

The first: the implied sense is: "And do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given," and they are the Muslims, "you were given a heavenly Book such as the Torah and a sent prophet such as Moses," and "that they will argue with you and overcome you by proof on the Day of Resurrection," except for the sake of following you. Its upshot is that they forbade them from disclosing these two matters to the Muslims, lest they become more steadfast, and to the idolaters of the Arabs, lest it move them to Islam. He used *aw* (or) in the manner of ﴿And do not obey any of them who is sinful or ungrateful﴾, and this is more eloquent. Reading it with the sense of *hatta* (until) is correct but less preferred. He placed the saying of the Most High, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, as a parenthetical clause between the verb and its complement.

The benefit of the parenthetical clause is to indicate that their scheming does not harm anyone whom God, the Exalted, has graced by entering Islam, or it increases their steadfastness in it. It also indicates that the guidance is His guidance, so it is He who brings about its manifestation: ﴿They want to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light﴾. The meaning of "belief" here is its public manifestation, as al-Zamakhshari stated, or verbal affirmation, as al-Wahidi stated. By "those who follow" is meant the staunch among them; otherwise what they feared would have occurred.

The second: the intended meaning is: "And do not believe this apparent belief that you have displayed at the start of the day except for one who was following your religion earlier," and they are those among them who had become Muslim, that is, for the sake of their return, because that was more important and more effective to them, and they were more eager and more hopeful regarding it. At this point the speech is complete. Then it is said: ﴿Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, that is, whomever God guides, none can misguide. On this view, the saying of the Most High, ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ etc., is a causal clause explaining an omitted element, that is: "Because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, and because of what is connected to it of prevailing by proof on the Day of Resurrection, you schemed what you schemed." Its upshot is that what calls you to it is nothing but envy. He used *aw* to indicate that each of the two matters independently moves them to anger and to envy, to the point that they schemed what they schemed. Had he used *wa* (and), it would not have had this position, because the second necessarily follows the first: if what they were given is true, then they will certainly prevail over their opponent on the Day of Resurrection, so there would be no added benefit. As for *aw*, it indicates that each one is independently a motive for envy and for concentrated effort in scheming. Reading it with the sense of *hatta* has no place that startles the hearer, although it is an apparent view.

This view is supported by the reading of Ibn Kathir: (a-an yu'ta) with an added interrogative hamza, to indicate its separation from the verb and its independence as a denial. In it is the restriction of belief to what occurs at the start of the day, by the context that the discussion concerns it, and the specification of "who follows" as their Muslims, by the indication of the past tense, since others are also following their religion now. It is also reported from al-Zamakhshari that ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ etc. is part of the quoted speech, as if it were said: "Say to them these two statements." Its meaning is: he emphasized upon them that the guidance is not what God, the Exalted, did by giving the Book to others than you, and he denied to them that they should be vexed that anyone should be given the like of it. It is as if it were said: "Indeed the guidance is the guidance of God, and say: 'Because anyone should be given the like of what you were given'—you said what you said and schemed what you schemed."

The third: that ﴿And do not believe﴾ is established as it was established in the second view, and ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ is made the predicate of *inna* (indeed), and ﴿the guidance of God﴾ is made an appositive of its subject, and *aw* has the sense of *hatta* (until) on the basis that it is a causal limit. In that case, "before your Lord" should not be restricted to the Day of Resurrection, but rather to the true argument, as was indicated in al-Baqarah. If it were taken as coordination, the speech would not hold together.

The fourth: that ﴿And do not believe except for those who﴾ etc. remains on its unrestricted sense, that is: "And reject its end, and persist in what you were in of Judaism, and do not acknowledge anyone except one who is on your religion." This is part of the speech of the group. ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance﴾ etc. is then a command to the Prophet ﷺ to say that in reply to them, in the sense: "Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, so do not deny that anyone should be given, until you argue." The indication of the implied element is that ﴿And do not believe﴾ etc. is an affirmation of Judaism, and that no religion equals it. So when he is commanded to answer them, it is known that what they denied is not deniable, and that it will occur. Taking *aw* in its original sense is also good in this case, because it is a confirmation of the giving and a hint that whoever is given the like of what they were given will be the victors. It is read ("in yu'ta") with the hamza of *in* (if) pronounced with a kasra, on the basis that it is negative, that is: "Say to them: what is given (ma yu'ta)." This is an address to those among them who had become Muslim, hoping they would return. The meaning is: there is no giving and no argument, so *aw* has the sense of *hatta* (until). The word "say" was supplied for clarification and explanation, since it is not a resumptive causal clause. The saying of the Most High, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance﴾ etc., is a parenthetical clause mentioned before their speech is complete, for the sake of attention to making clear the corruption of what they went to. The second of the views is the most preferred, because it is supported by the reading of Ibn Kathir, it is more useful than the first, less strained than the rest of the views, and closer to the context. End of quotation.

I say: What he mentioned in the fourth view, of the sense "do not deny that anyone should be given" etc., is the statement of Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Jubba'i, but they did not take *aw* in the sense of *hatta*, which is one of the two possibilities he mentioned. Likewise, the view of substituting ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ for ﴿the guidance﴾ is the statement of al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj, except that they supplied *la* (not) between *an* and *yu'ta*. Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad objected to both, saying that *la* is not something that is omitted here, and he committed himself to supplying an elided noun that is commonly supplied in such cases, namely "disliking" (karahah). The meaning would be: "Indeed the guidance is the disliking that anyone should be given the like of what you were given," that is, from among those who opposed the religion of Islam, because God does not guide one who is a liar and a disbeliever, so the guidance of God is far from non-believers. It is not hidden that this meaning is strained, and it is not worth anything. Similar to it is what some people said: that ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ etc. is an explanation of "the guidance," that what is given is the Law, that ﴿or they should argue with you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you were given﴾, and that what is argued with is reason. The sense of the speech is: "The guidance of God, the Exalted, is what He legislated or what He entrusted to reason." Among people are those who took the speech from the beginning of the verse to its end as address from God, the Exalted, to the believers. He said: The sense is: "And do not believe, O believers, except for one who follows your religion, which is the religion of Islam, and do not affirm that anyone will be given the like of what you were given of religion. There is no prophet after your Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, and no law after your law until the Day of Resurrection. And do not affirm that anyone will have an argument against you before your Lord, because your religion is the best of religions." Making ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ a parenthetical clause for emphasis and for hastening the joy is also possible, and what it contains is not hidden. The choice of some for it, and their reliance on what al-Dahhak said, that the Jews said: "We will argue before our Lord against whoever opposes us in our religion," so God, the Exalted, showed them that they are the ones refuted and defeated, and that the believers are the victors, is not worth anything, because this explanation does not necessarily bear this interpretation, as is not hidden from one of sound heart. The nominative pronoun in ﴿they argue with you﴾ on every interpretation refers back to (ahad, "anyone"), because it has the sense of the plural, since what is intended by it is other than their followers.

Ibn al-Munir raised an objection to separating ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ from ﴿do not believe﴾ according to some of the previous views, saying that it would require the occurrence of (ahad, "anyone") in an affirmative context, because the interrogative here is a denial, and an interrogative of denial in such a context is an affirmation. Its upshot is that He denied to them and rebuked them for what occurred from them, which was concealing belief, on the ground that prophethood is not restricted to the Children of Israel, for the two reasons mentioned, so it is a firm affirmation. Then he said: It is possible to say: the form of the interrogative was observed even though its real meaning was not intended, so it was proper for (ahad) to enter its context for that reason. But there is consideration in this. Al-Wahidi said: This verse is among the most difficult problems of the Qur'an and the hardest in interpretation.

﴿Say: Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of God﴾ is a rejection and nullification of what they claimed, with the clearest proof. By "the bounty" is meant Islam, as Ibn Jurayj said. Others said: prophethood. It was said: the proofs which the Prophet ﷺ and the believers were given. It was said: the blessings of religion and of this world, and what is appropriate to the context enters into it primarily. ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, that is, of His servants. ﴿And God is All-Encompassing﴾ in mercy. It was said: of wide power, He does what He wills. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ [73] of the interests of the servants. It was said: He knows where to place His message.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 74:

﴿He singles out for His mercy whomever He wills﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is prophethood. Ibn Jurayj said: Islam and the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is also the frequent remembrance of God, exalted is He. The preposition bi (ب, "with") is introduced on the object of restriction (al-maqsur), and it also enters on that which is restricted to (al-maqsur 'alayh). Some scholars have versified this, saying:

"The bi after the restrictive construction (al-ikhtisas) often comes before that which they restricted,
and its reverse is also used and is good; the great scholar and master, the sayyid, has mentioned it."

﴿And God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾. Ibn Jubayr said: [74] means abundant (al-wafir).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 75:

﴿And among the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾. This begins the explanation of another type of their faults. The verb ﴿tamanhu﴾ (you entrust him) comes from amintuhu, meaning i'tamantuhu (I entrusted him). The particle bi (with) is said to mean ʿala (upon), and it is also said to mean fi (in), that is, "in the safekeeping of a qintar." The qintar was discussed earlier in this commentary. It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Salam was entrusted by a Qurashi with a thousand and two hundred uqiyyah of gold, and he returned it to him. ﴿And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you﴾, like Finhas ibn Azura. It is narrated that another Qurashi entrusted him with a dinar and he denied it. It is also said that the trustworthy one with a large amount is the Christians, since trustworthiness is generally found among them, and the treacherous ones with a small amount are the Jews, since treachery is generally found among them. This was narrated from Ikrima.

The word dinar (dinar) is a non-Arabic term, and its yaʾ (ي) is a substitute for a nun (ن). Its original form is dinnar, and the first of the two identical letters was changed to yaʾ because it came after a kasrah. The plural dananir confirms the original form, since the plural returns a word to its root. In the well-known view, the dinar is twenty-four qirat, and the qirat is three grains from the middle of a barley grain, so the total is seventy-two grains. They said that this did not differ in the pre-Islamic period or in Islam. Among the strange reports is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Malik ibn Dinar, that he said: the dinar was named dinar because it is din (religion) and nar (fire). Its meaning is that whoever takes it by right, it is his religion, and whoever takes it without right, for him is the fire. This is perhaps an indication drawn from this word, not that it is so in reality, as is not hidden from anyone who possesses even a little reason, let alone the owner of a dinar. The word ﴿yu'addihi﴾ has been read with a kasrah on the ha' with a yaʾ after it in pronunciation, with a kasrah without a yaʾ, and with a sukun (silence), treating the connection as a pause. It has also been read with a dammah on the ha' and a waw after it in pronunciation, and with a dammah without a waw.

﴿Except while you stand over him﴾. This is an exception from the most general of the states or times. The meaning is: he will not return it to you in any state, or at any time, except while you remain standing over him, or during the time you remain standing over him. Standing (al-qiyam) is a metaphor for extreme insistence in demanding. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, explained it as persistence (al-ilhah). Al-Suddi explained it as remaining with him and being in his company, and al-Hasan explained it as persistent following and demanding repayment. The majority read the dal of ﴿dumta﴾ with a dammah, so it is, in their view, like ﴿qultu﴾. It has also been read with a kasrah on the dal, so it is then on the pattern of ﴿khiftu﴾, and this is a dialect. The present tense in the first dialect is ﴿yadumu﴾, like ﴿yaqumu﴾, and in the second it is ﴿yadamu﴾, like ﴿yakhafu﴾.

﴿That﴾, meaning the refusal to return, which is indicated by His words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿he will not return it﴾. ﴿Because they said﴾: the plural pronoun refers back to ﴿man﴾ (whoever) in ﴿whoever, if you entrust him with a dinar﴾. It is in the plural because the meaning was taken into account. The ba' (because of) is causal, meaning "because of their saying," ﴿There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered (ummiyyin)﴾, that is, there is no blame or reproach upon us for what we have taken from the wealth of the Arabs.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that he said: The Jews dealt with men from the Muslims in the pre-Islamic period. When they embraced Islam, the Jews demanded their dealings from them. They said: "We have no trust obligation or repayment toward you, because you abandoned your religion which you were upon." They claimed that they had found this in their book. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾ [75], that is, they are lying. Al-Kalbi said: The Jews said: "All the wealth was ours, so whatever is in the hands of the Arabs of it belongs to us, and they wronged us and seized it from us, so there is no sin upon us in taking their wealth." Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Said ibn Jubayr, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿And among the People of the Book﴾ up to His words, glorified is He, ﴿That is because they said: there is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered﴾, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The enemies of Allah have lied. There is nothing from the pre-Islamic period except that it is under these two feet of mine, except trust, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked.'"

The prepositional phrase ﴿upon Allah﴾ is connected to ﴿they say﴾, and the meaning is "they fabricate." It is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) of ﴿the lie﴾, placed before it. Abu al-Baqa did not permit its connection to it, because a relative complement (silah) cannot precede the relative noun. Others permitted it, since it functions like an adverb of place or time, in which latitude is allowed that is not allowed in other things.

Page 203

﴿Bala﴾ ("Yes indeed") is a response to their saying ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾, and an affirmation of what they denied. The meaning is: "Yes indeed, there is blame upon them regarding the unlettered." ﴿Whoever fulfills his covenant and is mindful of God—indeed God loves the mindful﴾ [76] is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh clause) that confirms the sentence indicated by ﴿bala﴾, since its implicit contrary meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the meaning understood by contrast) conveys the censure of whoever does not fulfill the rights absolutely. Thus they fall within it at the first level of inclusion. ﴿Man﴾ is either a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a conditional particle (shartiyya). ﴿Awfa﴾ has three dialectal readings: retaining the hamza; omitting it with the fa' lightened; and doubling the fa'. The pronoun in ﴿ahdihi﴾ refers to ﴿man﴾. It has also been said that it refers to God. On the first view it is a verbal noun (masdar) with its agent as the genitive; on the second view it is a verbal noun with its object or its agent as the genitive. In the second clause there must be a pronoun referring back to ﴿man﴾ to link the clauses. If ﴿al-muttaqin﴾ is taken as the same as ﴿awfa﴾, then the noun itself is used in place of the pronoun for the link (rabt, the connecting element between clauses). If ﴿al-muttaqin﴾ is general, then its generality and comprehensiveness serve as the link. The noun was placed in the position of the pronoun on the first view in order to record that those who fulfill the covenant do so through mindfulness, to indicate the cause of the ruling, and out of regard for the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat, the rhyme-endings of the verses). The first view is preferred because of the strength of the link in it. Ibn Hisham said: "Apparently there is no generality, and ﴿al-muttaqin﴾ is equivalent to the one mentioned before." The answer, whether explicit or implied, is omitted, and its estimate is: "God loves him," and ﴿fa-inna Allaha﴾ etc. indicates it. Al-Halabi objected to this, saying that it is an unnecessary artificiality. His statement "apparently there is no generality" is in the domain of denial, for if the pronoun in ﴿bi-ahdihi﴾ refers to God, then the shift from the pronoun to the noun is for the purpose of conveying generality, as is customary in similar cases. This was stated by one of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ Al-Sitta (the six compilers of the canonical hadith collections) and others related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever swears an oath in which he is a liar, in order to seize by it the property of a Muslim man, will meet Allah while He is angry with him." Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said: "By Allah, it was about me that this was said. There was a piece of land between me and a man from the Jews, and he denied it to me. So I brought him before the Prophet ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'Do you have proof?' I said: 'No.' So he said to the Jew: 'Swear.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he will swear and take my property.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who﴾ ..." etc. [Page 204] And al-Bukhari and others related from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa that a man displayed his merchandise in the market and swore by Allah that he had been offered for it what he had not been offered, in order to deceive a Muslim man into it, and so this verse was revealed. Ahmad and Ibn Jarir related, and the wording is his, from Adi ibn Umayra, who said: "There was a dispute between Imru' al-Qays and a man from Hadramawt. They brought it before the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to the Hadrami: 'Your proof, or else his oath.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if he swears, he will take my land.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever swears a false oath in order to seize by it the right of his brother, will meet Allah the Exalted while He is angry with him.' Imru' al-Qays said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is there for one who abandons it while he knows that it is a right?' He said: 'Paradise.' He said: 'Then I call you to witness that I have abandoned it.' So the verse was revealed." Ibn Jarir related from Ikrima, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Rafi', Lubaba ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who distorted the Torah, altered the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the ruling on trusts, and other matters, and took a bribe for that." Other occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) have also been related, and there is no obstacle to the multiplicity of occasions of revelation, as they have verified.

By "they sell" (yashtaruna) is meant "they exchange" (yastabdilun). By "the covenant" is meant the command of Allah and what fulfilling it is obligatory. It has been said: it is what He entrusted to the Jews in the Torah concerning the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been said: it is what is in human reason of restraint from falsehood and submission to the truth. By "oaths" are meant false oaths. By "a small price" are meant paltry compensations or bribes. The description of that price as small is because of its smallness in comparison with the reward that escapes them and the punishment that they incur.

﴿Those have no share in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., they have no portion of its bliss because of that exchange. ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾, i.e., not with what would please them, but with what would grieve them at the time of their reckoning. This is what al-Jubba'i said. Or He will not speak to them at all, and the reckoning will be by the speech of the angels to them by Allah's command, as a humiliation of them. It has been said: the meaning is that they will not benefit from the words of Allah and His signs. Its remoteness is not hidden. It has been inferred that this is a metaphor (kinaya, an allusive expression) for His anger toward them, glory be to Him.

﴿Nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., He will not show favour to them nor have mercy on them, as one says "look at me," meaning "have mercy on me." Al-Zamakhshari made it a figurative usage (majaz) for contempt toward them and displeasure with them. He distinguished between its use for one to whom looking (in the sense of turning the pupil) is permissible and its use for one to whom that is not permissible, on the ground that its origin, for one to whom it is permissible, is as a kinaya, because whoever holds a person in regard turns toward him and lends him the look of his eyes; then it became common until it became an expression for regard and kindness even where there was no looking. Then it came, for one to whom looking is not permissible, purely to mean kindness, as a majaz for what had been a kinaya for one to whom looking is permissible. In al-Kashshaf, it is stated that in this there is a clear statement that a kinaya requires that the literal meaning be capable of being intended even if it is not intended, and that kinayat may become so well known that that aspect is no longer considered, and then they join the majaz; they are not made majaz except after this fame, because the direction of the transition to the figurative meaning at first is not clear, unlike the meaning referred to by the kinaya. By this is removed what many have mentioned as a contradiction between two statements of al-Zamakhshari concerning the extension of the hand in His words: ﴿Rather, His two hands are outstretched﴾, where he made the extension of the hand a majaz for generosity at one time and a kinaya at another. Its substance is that if one sets aside an external impediment, it is a kinaya, then it is joined to the majaz; so it is called a kinaya with regard to its origin before joining and a majaz after it. Thus there is no contradiction between them, as they supposed. So consider this carefully. The adverbial phrase ("on the Day of Resurrection") is connected to both verbs, and in it is an intensification of the threat.

﴿Nor will He purify them﴾, i.e., He will not judge them to be pure, nor will He name them so; rather He will judge that they are unbelievers and wicked. This is what al-Qadi said. Al-Jubba'i said: He will not place them in the station of the pure. It has also been said: He will not cleanse them from the defilement of sins and burdens by forgiveness. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [77], i.e., one that is painful and afflicting. The apparent meaning is that this is in the Hereafter, though it was not restricted to it, being content with the first mention. It has also been said that it is in this world, by humiliation and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax), on the basis that the verse concerns the Jews.

[Page 205]

﴿And indeed among them is a group﴾, meaning: among the People of the Book, the treacherous ones, is a group ﴿who distort their tongues with the Book﴾, meaning they alter it. This is what Mujahid said. It has also been said that the root of al-layy (twisting) is al-fatl (twisting), from your saying: "I twisted his hand (lawaytu yadahu) when I twisted it." From the same root comes: "I delayed the creditor (lawaytu al-gharim) when I postponed his right." The poet said:

*You prolong my delay though you are able to pay, and I am good, O one with the girdle, at demanding.*

In a report it is said: "Delaying payment by one who is able (layy al-wajid) is injustice." So the meaning is that they twist their tongues in the recitation by altering the vowel marks and the like, a change through which the meaning is altered. In the end, this returns to what Mujahid said. Close to it is what has been said: the intended meaning is that they incline the tongues by means of something resembling the Book. Al-alsina (the tongues) is the plural of lisan (tongue). Ibn al-Shihnah mentioned that lisan may be masculine or feminine. It is reported from Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala' that whoever treats it as feminine pluralizes it as alsun, and whoever treats it as masculine pluralizes it as alsinah. It is reported from al-Farra' that he said: "I have not heard lisan itself from the Arabs except as masculine." It is not hidden that the one who affirms takes precedence over the one who denies. The letter ba' (with) is either an extra particle (silah), or indicates the instrument, or indicates the container (zarfiyyah), or indicates accompaniment (mulabasah). The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing al-alsina, meaning: "joined to the Book."

The people of Madinah read ﴿yulawwuna﴾ with shaddah, and so it is like ﴿they turned their heads﴾ (Qur'an 63:5). It is reported from Mujahid and Ibn Kathir that they read ﴿yalunna﴾, by changing the damma'd waw into a hamzah, then easing it by deleting it and transferring its vowel onto the preceding consonant. This is what has been said. It was objected that if the damma of the waw were transferred to the preceding letter and the waw deleted because of two consecutive unvowelled letters, that would suffice for the explanation, so what need is there to change the waw into a hamzah? It was answered that this was done so that it would conform to the morphological rule (al-qa'idah al-tasrifiyyah), unlike transferring the vowel of the waw and then deleting it, as is known in tasrif (morphology). Some verifiers examined this and said that a damma'd waw is only changed into a hamzah when its damma is original, so this too is contrary to analogy. Indeed, ﴿yalu'una﴾ with hamzah has been read among the shadhdh (irregular readings), and it supports this. In either case, there is a combination of two i'lal (morphological alterations), and similar cases are many. As for taking it from al-wali (nearness), meaning they bring their tongues near by inclining them toward the distorted, this is far from the sound and near to the distorted.

﴿So that you may think it is from the Book﴾, meaning: so that you, O Muslims, may suppose that the distorted matter indicated by the twisting, or that which resembles it, is from the Book of God Most High, revealed to one of His prophets, upon them be peace. It has been read ﴿liyahsabuhu﴾ with the ya' (third person), and the pronoun also refers to the Muslims. ﴿But it is not from the Book﴾, rather it is from their own selves. ﴿And they say, "It is from God"﴾, meaning: they claim openly, not content with allusion and indirection, that the distorted or the resembling matter has come down from God. ﴿But it is not from God﴾, meaning: it has not come down from God Most High. The waw is for the circumstantial clause, and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the subject in the predicate. In the clause ﴿and they say﴾ etc. is an emphasis of the negation that precedes it, but the purpose is not emphasis alone, for otherwise the conjunction would not make sense. Rather, it is also a censure: they did not stop at that allusion but committed this explicit statement. By this the difference that requires the conjunction is achieved. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to magnify what they undertook.

Al-Jubba'i and al-Ka'bi used this verse to argue that the act of the servant is not created by God Most High, for otherwise those distorters would have been truthful in saying ﴿it is from God﴾ (Most High). But (it was refuted) that the people did not claim that the distortion was from God and by His creation. They only claimed that the distorted matter was revealed from God, or [it is] one of His rulings. So God Most High's denial was directed at this claim they made.

The summary is that the intended negation, as we have indicated, is its descent from Him, glory be to Him, and this is more specific than its being from His act and creation. Negating the specific does not necessitate negating the general. So it does not indicate the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, who hold that the acts of servants are created by them and not by God Most High.

﴿And they speak falsehood against God﴾, meaning: in attributing that to God Most High, by allusion and by explicit statement. ﴿While they know﴾ [78] that they are lying against Him, glory be to Him. This is a recording against them that what they fabricated was deliberate, not mistaken. It has been said that they know what punishment is upon them for that. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians together, because they distorted the Torah and the Gospel and added to the Book of God what is not from it. Others reported that it concerns a group of Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Abu Yasir, and Shu'bah ibn Amr the poet, who altered what was a proof against them from the Torah.

People differed as to whether the distortion was written into the Torah or not. A group held that nothing in the Torah is other than the word of God Most High, and that the distortion of the Jews was only a change at the time of recitation, or a false interpretation of the texts. As for their writing whatever they desired into the Torah across its many copies, that did not happen. They argued for this by what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "The Torah and the Gospel, as God Most High sent them down, have not had a single letter changed. But they go astray through distortion and interpretation, and through books they used to write from their own selves, and they say: 'This is from God,' and it is not from God. As for the Books of God Most High, they are preserved and not altered." They also argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say to the Jews, as an argument against them: ﴿Then bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾ (Qur'an 3:93), and they refrained from doing so. Had it been altered to agree with their aim, they would not have refrained. Indeed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would not have said that to them, because it would turn against his noble purpose by nullifying it.

Others held that they did change and write that into their own book. They argued for this with many apparent indications. The multiplicity of copies does not prevent this, either because of the possibility of tawatu' (collusion or coordinated agreement) or because the change was made in some copies and not others. Likewise, the Messenger's saying to them does not prevent it, because he (ﷺ) may have known that some part serving his purpose remained unaltered, either because they did not understand its meaning, or because God Most High turned them away from changing it. As for what is reported from Wahb, even if it is established from him, it may be an opinion from his own ijtihad (independent reasoning), or arising from an incomplete survey.

What supports the occurrence of alteration in the Books of God Most High, and that they have not remained as they were on the day they were revealed, is the occurrence of contradiction in the Gospels, their conflict, their mutual falsehood, their incoherence, and their clashing with one another. They are four Gospels:

The first is the Gospel of Matthew (Matta). He was one of the Twelve Apostles (al-Hawariyyin). His Gospel was in the Syriac language, and he wrote it in the land of Palestine eight years after the raising of the Messiah to heaven. The number of its chapters (isahat, sing. isahah) is sixty-eight.

The second is the Gospel of Mark (Murqus). He was one of the Seventy. He wrote his Gospel in the Frankish language in a Roman city twelve years after the raising of the Messiah. The number of its chapters is forty-eight.

The third is the Gospel of Luke (Luqa). He was also one of the Seventy. He wrote his Gospel in the Greek language in the city of Alexandria after that. The number of its chapters is eighty-three.
