The fourth is the Gospel of John (Yuhanna). He was the beloved of the Messiah. He wrote his Gospel in the city of Ephesus (Iqsis) in the land of Rome thirty years after the raising of the Messiah. The number of its chapters in the Coptic copies is thirty-three.

Each Gospel includes narratives and stories that the other omitted, and it contains matters and things of which the other includes the opposite or something contrary to them. Among them are things for which necessity decides that they are not the word of God Most High at all. From that: Matthew mentioned that the Messiah was crucified and that two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and the other on his left, and that both of them used to mock the Messiah along with the Jews and reproach him. Luke mentioned the opposite, saying: one of them used to mock him, and the other said to him: "Do you not fear God? As for us, we have been repaid; but this one has done nothing wrong." Then he said to the Messiah: "My lord, remember me in your kingdom." He said: "Truly, you will be with me today in Paradise." It is not hidden that this leads to contradiction, for in Matthew the two robbers are both disbelievers, while in Luke one of them is a believer and the other a disbeliever. Mark and John omitted this story.

From that: Luke mentioned that Jesus (Yasu') said: "The Son of Man did not come to destroy the souls of people, but to give them life." His companions contradicted him and said: "Rather he said: 'The Son of Man did not come to cast peace upon the earth, but a sword, and to kindle fire in it.'" There is no doubt that this is a contradiction. One says he came as a mercy to the worlds, and the other says he came as a vengeance upon all creation.

From that: Matthew said: Jesus said to the Twelve disciples: "You are those who in the coming age will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." So he bore witness to all of them for success and righteousness in general at the resurrection. Then Matthew and others abrogated that and said: "One of the Twelve disciples departed, namely Judas, the keeper of the alms box, who accepted a bribe against Jesus of thirty dirhams, and brought the police and handed Jesus over to them." Jesus said: "Woe to him; it would have been better for him not to have been born." From that: Matthew also mentioned that when Jesus was brought to Pilate the governor, he said: "What evil has this man done?" The Jews cried out and said: "Crucify him, crucify him!" When he saw their determination and that it did not benefit him among them, he took water and washed his hands, and said: "I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it." John denied that and said: when Jesus was brought to him, he said to the Jews: "What do you want?" They said: "Crucifixion." So he struck Jesus, then handed him over to them. And other things that would be lengthy. If this change and distortion has occurred in the roots and the earlier ones of these people, then what do you think of their branches and later ones?

*And when there is injustice in the reeds, the arrows' feathers are thrown into disorder in the breasts of the arrows.*

Would that I knew whether Ibn Munabbih was aware of this or was not aware, when he said: "The Torah and the Gospel, as God Most High sent them down." Glory be to God! Is this not a wondrous marvel?!

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 79:**

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me, besides Allah."﴾ This is an absolution of the prophets of Allah, upon them be prayers and peace, following the absolution of Allah, exalted is He, from the attribution to Him of what the People of the Book fabricated against Him. It has also been said that it is a refutation and rejection of those who worship ʿIsa, upon him be peace. Ibn Ishaq and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Abu Rafiʿ al-Qurazi said, when the rabbis of the Jews and the Christians of the people of Najran gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he invited them to Islam: 'Do you want, O Muhammad, that we worship you as the Christians worship ʿIsa son of Maryam?' A man from the people of Najran, a Christian called al-Ra'is, said: 'Is that what you want from us, O Muhammad?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'God forbid that we worship other than Allah, or command the worship of other than Him. It is not for this that He sent me, nor for this that He commanded me.' Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse." ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "It reached me that a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we greet you as some of us greet one another? Shall we not prostrate to you?' He said: 'No, but honour your Prophet and recognise the right of those who deserve it, for it is not fitting that prostration be made to anyone besides Allah, exalted is He.'" Then the verse was revealed. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated: "Some people among the Jews were making people worship them besides their Lord by distorting the Book of Allah, exalted is He, from its place. So He said: ﴿It is not for a human being...﴾" etc.

The meaning of *ma kana* is "it is not proper (ma yasihhu)." It has also been said: "it is not becoming (ma yanbaghi)," and it has been said: "it is not permitted for anyone (la yajuzu li-ahadin)." He expressed it with *bashar* ("human being") to indicate the reason for the ruling, for humanness is incompatible with the matter that the disbelievers attributed to those noble ones, upon them be prayers and peace.

The prepositional phrase is the predicate of *kana* placed before its subject, and the subject is what is formed from *an* and the verb following its noun. For the meaning to be correct, it is necessary to observe the conjunction, for if it were left unmentioned the statement would not be sound, because Allah, exalted is He, has given many humans the Book and the two (judgment and prophethood). The verb is conjoined to the subjunctive complement of *an* with *thumma* ("then"), to magnify this statement, for when it is negated after an interval, its negation without the interval is more fitting and more certain. It is as if it were said: "This great giving is not at all compatible with this statement, even if it comes after an interval from this blessing." *Al-hukm* means *al-hikmah* ("wisdom"), whose meaning has already been mentioned. *Al-ʿibad* is the plural of *ʿabd* ("servant"). The qadi said: "Here it is from *ʿibadah* (worship), and he did not say *ʿabid* because it is from *ʿubudiyyah* (servitude), and that cannot be exclusive to other than Allah, exalted is He. For this reason one says: 'These are the servants (ʿabid) of Zayd,' and one does not say: 'His worshippers (ʿibad).'" The adverbial phrase that follows it is attached to an omitted verb and stands as its qualifier, meaning: "worshippers who are belonging to me." ﴿Besides Allah﴾ is attached to the word ﴿worshippers﴾ because of the verbal sense it contains. It may also be a second qualifier, or a circumstantial clause (hal), to specify the indefinite noun with a description, meaning: "transgressing Allah, exalted is He, by associating partners with Him and by singling out (others)," as al-Jubba'i said, for the transgression is definitely realised in both. Then this giving in the verse is literal according to the first two narrations, and metaphorical according to the last narration, as is not hidden.

﴿But rather, be rabbaniyyun﴾ is an affirmation of what was negated previously, namely the statement governed by *an* (the subjunctive). It is as if it were said: "It is not for that human being to say that, but rather he says: 'Be rabbaniyyun.'" So the verb here is also in the subjunctive, conjoined to it. It has been permitted to read it in the nominative according to the meaning, because it carries the sense of "he does not say." It has also been said: it is valid not to supply the word "say," with the meaning: "Do not be those who say that, but be rabbaniyyun." ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained *al-rabbani* as "the learned jurist (faqih)." Qatadah and al-Suddi explained it as "the knowledgeable wise one (al-ʿalim al-hakim)." Ibn Jubayr explained it as "the forbearing, pious one (al-halim al-taqi)." Ibn Zayd explained it as "one who manages the affairs of the people." These statements are close in meaning. The word is Arabic, not Syriac, according to the correct view. Abu ʿUbaydah claimed that the Arabs do not know it, [but it was the jurists and people of knowledge who knew it]. It is derived from *al-Rabb* ("the Lord"), like *Ilahi* from *Ilah*, and the alif and nun are added in the relative form for emphasis, often, as in *Lihyani* ("one with a large beard"), *al-Jummani* ("one with abundant hair"), and *Raqabani* ("thick-necked"). It has also been said that it is derived from *Rabban* as an adjective, like *ʿAtshan* meaning "one who has been nurtured" (murabba).

﴿Because you were teaching the Book and because you were studying﴾ [79]. The *ba'* is causal and is attached to *kunu* ("be"), meaning: "Be thus because of your persistence in teaching the Book and studying it." What is required is that knowledge not be separated from action, since neither of them is considered valid without the other. It has also been said that it is attached to *rabbaniyyin*, because it carries the sense of a verb. It has also been said that it is attached to an omitted word which stands as its qualifier. *Al-dirasah* is repetition; one says: "He studied the Book," meaning he repeated it, and it is also applied to recitation. The repetition of *bima kuntum* serves to indicate the independence of each of the continuity of teaching and the continuity of reading, which is indicated by making the predicate of *kana* a present-tense verb, "by excellence and achieving rabbaniyyah." He placed the teaching of the Book before its study because of its greater nobility over it, or because the first address was to their leaders and the second to those below them. It has also been said: because the object of teaching is the Book in the sense of the Qur'an, and the object of study is jurisprudence (fiqh). But this is a very distant view, even if the speech of some of the early scholars suggests it.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Yaʿqub, Abu ʿAmr and Mujahid read *taʿlamuna* ("you know") in the sense of "knowing (ʿalimin)." It is also read *tudarrisuna* with the doubled letter, from *al-tadris* (teaching), and *tudrisuna* from *al-idrars*, with the same meaning. The coming of *afʿala* in the sense of *faʿʿala* is common. It has been permitted that the well-known reading also has this meaning, on the basis that the intended meaning is "you teach it to the people."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 80:

﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords.﴾ Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb read ﴿wa-lā yaʾmurakum﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, coordinating it with (yaqūla) (the verb governed by the preceding clause). The (wa-lā) here is either an extra particle (zāʾidah), added to emphasise the sense of negation that is common in usage, especially when much time has passed and a separation intervenes; the meaning is: it is not for a human being that God should give him this and send him to call people to devote worship exclusively to Him and abandon rivals, and then tell the people to become His servants, and command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. This is like your saying: "It is not for Zayd that I should honour him and then he insults me and does not show me any lightness." Or the (wa-lā) is not extra, on the basis that the Prophet ﷺ used to forbid worship of the angels, the Messiah and ʿUzayr, peace be upon them; so when it was said to him, "Shall we take you as a lord?", it was said to them: it is not for a human being whom God has chosen as a prophet to then command the people to worship him and forbid them to worship the angels and the prophets. Moreover, whoever wishes to enslave a person says to him: "You should worship the likes of me and my equals." On this view, the intended meaning of the non-command is the prohibition, although the wording is more general than that, since it is more directly aimed at the purpose and better suited to the reality.

The remaining Seven read ﴿wa-lā yaʾmurukum﴾ with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, as a resumptive (istiʾnāf) clause, and it may also be a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. It has been said: the resumptive reading is more apparent (aẓhar), and the reading ﴿wa-lan yaʾmurakum﴾ supports it. The greater apparentness is justified by its freedom from the strain of making the non-command mean a prohibition, and by the fact that coordination would require placing it before (lākin), and likewise the circumstantial reading.
Page 209

It has also been read with a sukūn on the rāʾ, to avoid a succession of vowels. On all the other readings, the subject pronoun refers back to (basharin) (a human being). In some of them its return to God, exalted is He, is also permitted. Both possibilities are likewise permitted in His words: ﴿Would He command you to disbelieve?﴾ where the interrogative is for denial. That the referent of the pronoun in one of the two possibilities is indefinite makes it general. ﴿After you have become Muslims﴾ [80]. Al-Khaṭīb (al-Razi) took this as evidence that the verse was revealed concerning the Muslims who said, "Shall we not prostrate to you?", on the basis of the apparent sense. The justification for the address being to the disbelievers, and the verse having been revealed about them, is that it is permissible to say to the People of the Book: ﴿Would He command you to disbelieve after you have become Muslims?﴾, i.e. submitting, prepared for the true religion, by way of loosening the reins and gradual enticement. As for the claim that every one who affirms his prophet is a Muslim, and the assertion that his prophet commanded him to do what necessitates his disbelief, is an assertion that he commanded him to disbelieve after his Islam; so the indication of this for the address being to the Muslims is very weak and altogether untenable, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 81 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him."﴾ The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is understood and addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "Remember the time of that." Al-Samin preferred that it be the object of ﴿aqrartum﴾ ("you acknowledged") which comes later, but ʿAbd al-Baqi rejected this on the grounds that the address in ﴿aqrartum﴾ comes after the covenant has been established, and there is some hesitation about this. Its being coordinated with what precedes it, namely the Almighty's words ﴿And when the angels said﴾, as transmitted by al-Tabarsi, is far-fetched.

The meaning of the verse has been disputed. It has been said that it is to be taken literally, and this is supported by what Ibn Jarir reported from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, who said: "Allah did not send any prophet, from Adam onwards, except that He took from him a covenant concerning Muhammad ﷺ: that if he is sent while he is alive, he will certainly believe in him and certainly support him, and He commands him to take the covenant from his people." Then he recited the verse. The absence of mention of the nations in it at that point is either because they are known by a stronger implication, or because the mention of the prophets made their mention unnecessary; so there is an elliptical omission in the verse, and there is not in it the combining of two contradictory things.

It has been said that the idafa (construct) of "covenant" to "the prophets" is an idafa to the agent, and the meaning is: "And when Allah took the covenant which the prophets confirmed upon their nations." Ibn ʿAbbas went to this view. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: "I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: 'The companions of ʿAbd Allah recite (And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book, concerning what I have given you, etc.),' whereas we recite ﴿covenant of the prophets﴾." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Allah the Exalted only took the covenant of the prophets upon their peoples." By this, may Allah be pleased with him, he indicated that there is no contradiction between the two readings, as is imagined, to the extent that it was thought that this was the source of Mujahid's statement, which Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from him, that ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ was an error in the copying of the Book, and that the verse was as ʿAbd Allah recited it. But that is not so, since this alone cannot be the source of it; otherwise it would necessitate preference without a preferring factor. Rather, the source of it, if it is authentic, is something else. I do not think that what is known after reflection on what we have previously stated in the introductions, and what we expounded upon in ﴿al-Ajwiba al-ʿIraqiyya ʿan al-Asʾila al-Iraniyya﴾ (The Iraqi Answers to the Iranian Questions), is anything other than this.

It has been said: the intended meaning is "the nations of the prophets," with an omitted modifier (mudaf). This was the view of al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been said: the omitted modifier is "children," and what is meant by them, according to the correct view, is the Children of Israel, because of the abundance of prophets' descendants among them, and because the context concerns them. This is reinforced by the reading of ʿAbd Allah mentioned above, which is also the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

It has been said: the intended meaning is "And when Allah took a covenant like the covenant of the prophets," that is, a binding covenant upon the nations. Then He made their covenant the very covenant of the prophets, by omitting the particle of comparison, for emphasis.

It has been said: what is meant by "the prophets" is the Children of Israel, and He named them so in mockery, because they used to say: "We have more right to prophethood than Muhammad, because we are the People of the Book, and the prophets were from among us." This is like when you say to someone whom you have entrusted with something, and who betrayed it, and then claims to be trustworthy: "O trustworthy one, what have you done with my trust?!" Al-Halabi criticised this, saying that it is very far-fetched, since there is no indication that makes this clear.

It has been answered that the one who holds this view perhaps took their aforementioned statement as a circumstantial indication.

It has been said: the idafa is for causation, for the slightest connection, as if it were said: "And when Allah took the covenant from the people for the sake of the prophets," and then He explained it with the words of the Glorified: ﴿whatever I have given you﴾, etc. It is not hidden that this too is very far off. Al-Shihab said: "We have not seen anyone who mentioned that idafa conveys causation except the one who made this statement."

Many scholars chose the first view, namely that the taking of the covenant from the prophets was for him ﷺ, as indicated by the words of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honour his face. The fact that Allah, the Glorified, knew that they would not reach his time does not prevent this, because in it, together with what Allah taught of exalting him ﷺ, magnifying him, elevating his status and honouring his mention, there is something that befits none but that exalted presence. The benefit becomes greater if that taking was from them in their books and not in the world of the atoms (ʿalam al-dharr), for that is far away, as far as that time is, as some hold. The view that the covenant was taken from the prophets, which obligates belief in him ﷺ by whoever of them reached his time, is supported by what Abu Yaʿla reported from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not ask the People of the Book about anything, for they will not guide you, and they have gone astray. Either you will confirm falsehood, or you will deny truth. By Allah, if Musa were alive among you, it would not be lawful for him except to follow me." There are many reports with a similar meaning, and by their apparent meaning they support what we have said. From here the knowers (al-ʿarifun) went to the view that he ﷺ is the absolute prophet, the true messenger, and the independent legislator, and that whoever else among the prophets, peace be upon them, is in the position of being subordinate to him ﷺ.

This verse has been counted among the difficult verses of the Qur'an in terms of its grammatical construction (iʿrab). The grammarians have dived deep into clarifying it and have split hairs over it. Let us mention some of the discussion on it. We say: many said that the lam in ﴿lamā ātaytukum﴾, according to the reading with fatha and tashdid (lamā, with the lam pronounced as a fatha), which is the reading of the majority, is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwaṭṭi'a) for the oath implied by the taking of the covenant, because it carries the sense of swearing an oath; and it was so named because it facilitates the listener's understanding of the response. The grammarians defined it, as al-Shihab said, as the lam that enters upon the conditional (al-sharṭ), whether it is inna or another, but it has become predominant with inna after the oath has been mentioned explicitly or implicitly, to indicate that the response belongs to the oath and not to the condition, like your saying: "If you honour me, I will surely honour you." But if you said: "I honour you," or "so I honour you," or what resembles that of what is used as the response to the condition, it would not be permitted, as Ibn al-Hajib explicitly stated; al-Farra' disagreed with him and permitted that the condition be answered while the oath precedes it. But the first is the sound view. That this lam must enter upon the conditional is the well-known view, and some grammarians disagreed. They said: it is permitted for it to enter upon something other than the conditional, either absolutely or on condition that it resemble the conditional, as the relative (al-mawsulah) does not, but the redundant (al-zaʾidah) does. Al-Zamakhshari said, in the Surah of Hud, that it is not necessary for it to enter upon the words of conditionality (kalim al-mujazah); al-Azhari transmitted this from al-Akhfash and mentioned that Thaʿlab criticised him for it. So the matter is disputed.

And ﴿mā﴾ is a conditional in a position of accusative governed by ﴿ātaytu﴾ ("I gave"), and the second object is the pronoun of the addressees (kum), and ﴿min﴾ ("of") is an explanatory (bayan) for ﴿mā﴾. It was objected that taking ﴿min﴾ as explanatory is common after the relative, but after the conditional it requires transmission. Similarly, the view that it is redundant (ziyada) is in need of what was mentioned, since its being redundant after the relative too is like its being redundant after the conditional, requiring the same. It was answered that al-Samin transmitted what indicates that this occurs according to the imams. In ﴿Janiy al-Dani﴾ it is said: some of the grammarians said that ﴿min﴾ may be added with conditions outside the chapter of specification (tamyiz), but within it, it is added even if the conditions are not fulfilled, as in ﴿li-llahi darruka min rajul﴾ ("by Allah, what a man you are"). Hence our master ʿAbd al-Baqi said: it is permitted that ﴿min﴾ be partitive, mentioned to explain the conditional ﴿mā﴾, or redundant, entering upon the specification. And ﴿latu'minunna﴾ is the response of the oath alone, according to the correct view. Because of its indication of the response of the condition and the unity of their meaning, some were lax and made it stand in place of both responses. It was not objected that it is the response of the oath and the response of the condition together, because the two are contradictory in that the first has no place (in the sentence), while the second has a place. The claim that one sentence may be judged by both qualities under two considerations is an obligation of something not required.

They also permitted that ﴿mā﴾ be a relative, and the lam that enters upon it in that case is the lam of the inceptive (lam al-ibtida'). The statement of some implies that the lam afterward is preparatory, and it seems to be built upon the view of those grammarians who permitted the preparatory lam to enter upon something other than the conditional, as has passed. In this case ﴿mā﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is [p. 211] either understood, or the sentence ﴿latu'minunna﴾ together with the implied oath. The discussion of this type is well known.

It is objected that if the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to the subject (mubtada'), as is apparent, then the covenant would be their belief in what He gave them, whereas the purpose of the verse is the taking of the covenant to believe in the Messenger ﷺ and to support him. And if it refers to the Messenger, like the second pronoun in the accusative which refers to him absolutely, to avoid the necessity of disjunction, then the sentence that is a predicate of the referent is left without a link. It was answered: since the coordinated sentence contains what has the meaning of the relative subject, and for this reason the link is dispensed with in it, even though it is required in the two coordinated relative clauses according to the well-known view; and since the pronoun ﴿bihi﴾ refers to the Messenger, taking into account ﴿musaddiqun li-ma maʿakum﴾ which takes the place of the pronoun referring to ﴿mā﴾, it suffices with this alone, without a pronoun in its predicate, because the sentences are connected one with another. The words of the Imam al-Suhayli in ﴿al-Rawd al-Anf﴾ point to this. But it is not hidden that, together with the artificiality in it, this is based on the unity of what they were given and what is with them. In this there is a problem: if both ﴿ātaynākum﴾ and ﴿jāʾakum﴾ are future, then the apparent meaning is that what is meant by ﴿mā ātaynākum﴾ is the Qur'an, because it is what they will be given in the future, in view of its being given to the Messenger whom they were charged to follow; and what is with them is the Books which they were given. Taking it to mean the Qur'an is rejected by good taste, since, although it is not with them according to the apparent sense, there is no beauty in the Qur'an confirming the Qur'an, which is necessary on that supposition. If both verbs are past, the corruption appears in that this messenger whom Allah obligated them to believe in and support had not yet come at that time. If the first verb is past and the second future, there is a lack of agreement between the two coordinated verbs, which are both past in form; and there is some remoteness in this. Perhaps the one who answers chooses this alternative and bears this remoteness, because ﴿thumma﴾ ("then"), even though it is not regarded for something of this weakness, eases the matter. Abu al-Baqaʾ, on that supposition, permitted that the predicate be ﴿min kitab﴾ ("of a Book"), meaning: "what I gave you of the Book," and he made the indefinite here like the definite. He also permitted that the returning pronoun to the relative in the coordinated sentence be omitted, meaning "came to you with it," even though the conditions for omitting such a pronoun are not met according to the majority, but rather with a flaw in the meaning, because what is given is the Book of each prophet in his time and his law, whereas what is brought by the Messenger is the Qur'an according to the apparent sense, not the Book of each prophet. The return of the implied pronoun requires that. And on the supposition that what is given is also the Qur'an, as the reading of both verbs in the future requires, it is objected that there is no sense in the Messenger's coming to them with the Qur'an after their being given the Qur'an with a delay, and the coordination with ﴿thumma﴾ is explicit in this meaning. And on the supposition that what is brought by the Messenger is the Book of each prophet, with some kind of artificiality, the description of the Messenger as confirming what is with them becomes almost superfluous. So reflect.

Hamza read ﴿li-mā ātaytukum﴾ with a kasra on the lam, on the basis that ﴿mā﴾ is verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah), and the lam is a causative preposition (jarr ajaliyyah), related to ﴿latu'minunna﴾, meaning: "For the sake of my giving you part of the Book, then the coming of a messenger confirming it, Allah took the covenant that you must believe in him and you must support him." It was objected that this involves operating ﴿mā﴾ after the lam of the oath on what precedes it, and that is not permitted. It was answered that this is not agreed upon, for the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words indicates its permissibility; and perhaps whoever prevents it restricts that to cases where the preceding complement is not an adverb, because that one is given wider latitude than others. Yes, to settle the dispute, the better course is that it be related to the implied ﴿uqsimu﴾ ("I swear"). It is also permitted that ﴿mā﴾ in this reading be a relative too, and the preposition-phrase is related to ﴿akhadha﴾ ("took").

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he recited (لَمّا آتَيْتُكُمْ) with tashdid (the doubled *lam*), and there are two possibilities in it. The first: that it is temporal (ẓarfiyyah, meaning "when"), as the majority hold, in disagreement with Sibawayh. Its response is implied and is of the same kind as the response of an oath, as al-Zamakhshari maintained. That is: when I gave you some of the Book and wisdom, and then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you, it became obligatory upon you to believe in him and support him. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah implied that it is of the same kind as what precedes it, that is: when you were in this state, leaders of the people and their best, the covenant was taken from you. So it occurs in *Tafsir al-Zajjaj*, and its ultimate meaning is causal (taʿlīl, "giving a reason"). The second: that its origin is (مَا), so the nun was changed into a mim because of its resemblance to it, and three mims came together. The second was then deleted, because of its weakness by being a substitute and because repetition occurs through it. Abu Hayyan preferred this in *al-Bahr*.

Ibn Jinni claimed that the first is the more correct, and al-Halabi examined this claim. The (مِن) is either extra (mazīdah) in affirmative speech according to the view of al-Akhfash, or causal (taʿlīliyyah) according to what Ibn Jinni chose. It was said: this is the most correct, because the meaning becomes clear upon it and it agrees with the reading of takhfīf (lightening, i.e., without tashdid). The lam is either extra or preparatory (muwaṭṭi'ah), based on the view that its entry upon a conditional particle is not required.

Nafi' read (آتَيْنَاكُمْ) in the plural form for glorification (taʿẓīm), and the rest read (آتَيْتُكُمْ) in the singular. Each of the two readings has its merit from one aspect, so understand this. It is unlikely that you will find the like of it in your hands.

(He said), i.e., Allah, the Exalted, to the prophets. This is an explanation of the taking of the covenant, or it is a statement (maqūl) following it for emphasis: ﴿Do you affirm﴾ this mentioned matter, ﴿and accept﴾, i.e., you agree, in the manner of ﴿If you are given this, then take it﴾. It was also said that the meaning is: did you accept ﴿My burden upon that﴾ on the nations? The (iṣr), with a kasra on the hamza, means covenant, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. Its origin is from (iṣār), which is what is tied and fastened with. The covenant was perhaps named thus because it is fastened with it. It was also read with a damma (ʿiṣr), which is either a dialectal form of the same word, like (ʿubr) and (ʿubbar) in their saying "a she-camel that is ʿubr asfār" (strong for journeys), or it is a plural of (iṣār) used metaphorically for covenant. It was pluralized either because of the multiplicity of those who make the covenant, which is the apparent reading, or for emphasis.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), built upon an implied question, as if it were said: "What did they say at that?" So it was said: they said, ﴿We affirm﴾. The expected answer would have been "We affirm this, your burden," but the second part was not mentioned, being sufficient with the first. (He said), i.e., Allah, the Exalted, to them: ﴿Then bear witness﴾, i.e., let some of you bear witness against others to that affirmation. Thus he made the one affirming a party and the witness another party, so that the one witnessed against and the witness would not be the same. It was also said that the address in it is to the prophets, peace be upon them, alone: they were commanded to bear witness against their nations. This is attributed to ʿAli, may Allah honor his face. It was also said that it is addressed to the angels, and that would be a metaphorical reference (kināyah) to something unmentioned. This is attributed to Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab. ﴿And I am with you among the witnesses﴾ [81], i.e., over your affirmation and your mutual testimony, according to what the meaning requires, since testimony necessarily involves something witnessed against. What we have mentioned here is suited to the context. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended meaning is: "Know, and I am with you, knowing."

In every interpretation there is emphasis and a great warning. The prepositional phrase (al-jār wa al-majrūr) is the predicate (khabar) of (anā), and (maʿakum) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The sentence is resumptive and has no place in terms of grammatical case (lā maḥalla lahā min al-iʿrāb). It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (fa-ishhadū).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 82:**

﴿But whoever turns away﴾, meaning turns away from faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) and from supporting him. This is what ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his countenance, said. ﴿After that﴾, meaning after the covenant, the affirmation and the confirmation by the testimony (*shahada*). ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to (*man*, مَن), whose meaning is taken into account here just as its wording was taken into account earlier. ﴿They are the defiant ones﴾ [82], meaning those who go beyond bounds in disbelief to its most heinous degrees.

It is the well-known view that the prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, are not included in the ruling of this conditional sentence (*shartiyya*), or in what is similar to its ruling, because they are too exalted in rank for it to be conceivable that the antecedent (*muqaddam*) would hold true of them so that they would be described by it. Allah forbid that they should be described by what the consequent (*tali*) contains. Rather, this ruling applies to their followers. It is also permitted that the meaning be general. The verse is of the same kind as: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾.

[Page 213]

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn) brought their disputes concerning the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Each group claimed that it was the most entitled to his religion. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Both groups are free of the religion of Ibrahim.' They became angry and said: 'By Allah, we will not accept your judgment, nor will we follow your religion.' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse."

The clause in the composition is coordinated (ma'tuf) on the whole conditional structure (al-shart wal-jaza'), though it was also said that it is coordinated on the apodosis (al-jaza') alone. Coordinating an imperative (insha') on an informative statement (ikhbar) is permissible here according to those who allow it. The interrogative particle (al-hamza) is, on both interpretations, placed between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, to express denial (inkar). It was also said that it is coordinated on an elided element, whose supposed form is: "Will they turn away, and so seek other than the religion of Allah?" Ibn Hisham said: "The first view is the position of Sibawayh and the majority, and al-Zamakhshari affirmed it in several places, while he permitted the second in some places. The second is weakened by the artificiality it involves and by the fact that it is not consistent. As for the first, it relies on the claim that the clause is elided. If this is countered by the fronting of part of the conjoined element, it may be said that this is easier than it, because the figurative usage in it, according to their saying, is less in wording. Moreover, this figurative usage carries an indication of the priority of one thing over another, namely the priority of the interrogative particle in initial position. As for the second view, it is impossible in cases like ﴿Is then one who stands over every soul in what it has earned [the same as those who associate partners with Him]?﴾ [13:33]." End of quotation.

Shams al-Din ibn al-Sa'igh objected to this, saying: "What prevents us from supposing the elided phrase to be: 'Is there not a manager of existing things, so that one who stands over every soul...' as an affirmative interrogative (istifham taqriri) intended to establish the existence of the Creator? The meaning is: 'Does the Manager (al-mudabbir) cease to exist, so that no one stands over every soul?' That is impossible; rather, the Manager exists, and He is the one who stands over every soul. This is preferable to the supposition of Badr al-Din ibn al-Damamini: 'They are astray, so one who stands over every soul in what it has earned [is not to be made their equal], for they did not affirm His oneness.' His taking the interrogative particle as a reproachful denial (inkar tawbikhi) and, in general, the detailed treatment of this question, is close to being better: if that supposed element comes to mind, it is to be said by the supposition; otherwise, it is to be said in accordance with what the majority said."

The fronting of the object (taqdim al-maf'ul) is because it is what is intended by the denial, not for restriction (hasr), as is wrongly supposed, because what is denied is taking other than Allah as a lord, even alongside Him. The claim that it indicates that the religion of other than Allah does not combine with His religion in seeking, so that the fronting is for specification (takhsis), with the denial directed at it, meaning: "Do they single out other than the religion of Allah for seeking?" is an artificiality. As for the statement of Abu Hayyan, that the justification of the fronting by what has preceded has no verification, because the denial that the particle expresses is not directed at essences (dhawat) but at actions connected with essences, so that what is denied is the seeking whose object is ﴿other than the religion of Allah﴾, and the fronting of the object came by way of expansion (al-ittisa'), and because ﴿yabghun﴾ resembles a closing rhyme (fasila), it has no verification according to those of verification, because we did not claim that the denial is directed at essences, as is not hidden.

Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in one transmission, and Hafs and Ya'qub, read ﴿yabghun﴾ with the third-person masculine plural (ya'). The rest read it with the second-person (ta'), on the meaning: "Do you then turn away, [or do you] commit transgression and disbelieve, so that you seek other than the religion of Allah?" Some scholars held that this is a shift of person (iltifat), so for them there is no elision. On the view of the elision, the aim of denial is realized in what has been indicated, and it does not conflict with it, because it is included within it.

﴿And to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) that reinforces the denial, meaning: "How do they seek and demand other than His religion, when this is the state [of creation]?" ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾: the two are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: obeying and disobeying. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that they be verbal nouns not of the same root as the verb (ghayr al-masdar), because aslama here means "submitted and obeyed." It was said: "There is a problem with this, because it is apparent for ﴿tawan﴾ (willingly), by agreement of its meaning with what precedes it, but not for ''karhan'' (unwillingly)." And the saying that what is permitted in the subsequent elements is not permitted in the initial ones is not useful. This may be answered by saying that submission (al-kurh) in it is also a kind of compliance (inqiyad). The word ''tawan'' is the verbal noun of ''taa'a yatu'u,'' just as ''al-ita'a'' is the verbal noun of ''aat'a yut'i'u,'' and they did not distinguish between the two. It was also said that ''ta'ahu yatu'uhu'' means "complied with him," ''at'ahu yut'ihu'' means "carried out his command," and ''taw'ahu'' means "agreed with him."

There are several opinions regarding the meaning of the verse:

The first: The intended meaning of submission by willingness is the submission arising from knowledge in general, whether it is attained through reasoning, as is the case with most of us, or without reasoning and reflection, as is the case with the angels. The submission by unwillingness is that which is attained by the sword and by witnessing what compels one to submit.

The second: The intended meaning is that they complied with Him, the Exalted, choosing to obey His command, like the angels and the believers, and [others] were subjected to His will, like the disbelievers, for they are subjected to the will of their disbelief, since what He does not will does not occur. This does not conflict, as some said, with the partial voluntary element (al-juz' al-ikhtiyari), so that they have no choice at all, which would make it a doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists). Nor does it require that their punishment for disbelief is not due, nor that there be no difference between believer and disbeliever on the basis that all do only what Allah wills for them, as was wrongly supposed.

The third: what some of our Sufi masters, may Allah benefit us through them, indicated: that submission by willingness is compliance and obedience to what Allah has commanded without the opposition of a carnal darkness and the barrier of the veils of self-regard, while submission by unwillingness is compliance together with the intervention of oppositions and whisperings, the barrier of veils, and attachment to intermediaries. The first is like the submission of the angels and of some of the chosen righteous on earth, and the second is like the submission of many whom doubts turn from side to side until he says:

I have indeed gone round all those places of worship,
and I have let my gaze wander among all those landmarks.
So I saw none but one placing the palm of a bewildered man
upon his chin, or striking the tooth of a regretful one.

The disbelievers belong to the second category according to the people of Allah, the Exalted, because they also affirmed a Creator, but the darkness of their selves came between them and them and attaining the truth. ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him﴾ [12:106].

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ This is what the statement of Mujahid points to. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah that he said: "Every human being has acknowledged against himself that Allah, the Exalted, is my Lord and I am His servant. Whoever associates others in His worship, this is the one who submitted unwillingly; and whoever sincerely devotes worship to Allah, the Exalted, is the one who submitted willingly." Al-A'mash read ﴿karhan﴾ with a ḍamma (kurhan).

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [83]: that is, you will be returned to His recompense, according to the well-known view. So hasten to His religion and do not oppose submission. They permitted that the clause be a new statement (mustaʾnafa) informing of what it contains of a threat, and that it be coordinated on ﴿And to Him has submitted﴾, in which case it is also circumstantial (haliyya). ʿĀṣim read it with the third-person (ya' of absence), and the pronoun refers either to ﴿those who [seek]﴾ or to whatever the pronoun of ﴿yabghun﴾ refers to. If it is read with the second person, it is a shift (iltifat). The rest read it with the second person, and the pronoun refers back to whatever the pronoun of ﴿yabghun﴾ refers to; so the third-person reading in it is also a shift.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 84:**

﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾. This is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to inform, about himself and the believers, that they believe in what was mentioned. So the pronoun in (āmannā, "we believed") refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the community (ummah). Mawla 'Abd al-Baqi said: When God the Exalted took the covenant (mīthāq) from the Prophets themselves, that they should believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, and support him, He also commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to believe in the Prophets who believed in him and in their Books. Thus ﴿āmannā﴾ stands in the place of āmanta ("you believed"), to honour our Prophet, the best of prayers and the most complete of peace be upon him. Or, since He had made a covenant with the Prophets and their nations that they should believe, He commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community to believe in them and in their Books.

The summary is that the covenant was taken from both sides, on the basis of belief, in one manner. Here he does not mention the wisdom (ḥikmah) of the earlier Prophets, either because belief in the revealed Book is belief in what it contains of wisdom, or to indicate that their law (sharī'ah) is abrogated (mansūkhah, "naskh" meaning abrogation) in the time of this Prophet (ﷺ). Both are on the assumption that "wisdom" means the law. He also does not mention his support (peace be upon him) for them, since there is no room in any way for supporting the predecessors. The claim that the covenant was taken from both sides is supported by what 'Abd al-Razzaq and others transmitted from Tawus, that he said: God the Exalted took the covenant of the Prophets that some of them would confirm others.

﴿And what was sent down to us﴾, which is the Qur'an sent down to him (ﷺ) first, and to them through its being conveyed to them. For this reason he used the plural pronoun. It may be considered that the sending down was to him alone, but what belongs to one is attributed to the plural, metaphorically, as it has been said. It is also possible that the "nūn" is the nūn of majesty (nūn al-'aẓamah), not the pronoun of the plural.

Page 215

The verb "sent down" is governed here by ʿalā ("upon"), while in al-Baqarah it is governed by ilā ("to"), because it has a direction of height in terms of its origin, and of arrival in terms of its end. Here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the sense of elevation fits. There the address is general, so the sense of arrival fits. This is what has been said, but it is refuted by His saying: ﴿Believe in what was sent down upon those who believed﴾. The truth is that there is no difference between the verb with ilā and the verb with ʿalā except by way of consideration. If you consider its origin, you govern it with ʿalā, because it is from above; if you consider its arrival at the one to whom it belongs, you govern it with ilā. One of the two considerations is sometimes observed and the other at other times, for variety of expression. Al-Raghib distinguished that what came from the higher realm (al-malaʾ al-aʿlā) without intermediary is more fittingly expressed with ʿalā, which is specific to height, and what did not come in that way is more fittingly expressed with ilā, which is specific to conveyance. It has also been said that "he sent down upon him" is taken to mean the command to the one upon whom it was sent down to convey it to others, and "he sent down to him" is taken to mean what he alone was given, because ilā marks the end of the sending down. Both views are open to scrutiny.

﴿And what was sent down upon Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾. It has been said: these noble ones were singled out for mention because the People of the Book acknowledge their prophethood and their Books. The intended meaning of the relative pronoun is the scrolls (ṣuḥuf), as is apparent. He placed what was sent down upon him (peace be upon him) before what was sent down upon them, either to honour him and give him priority, or because it is what makes him known, and knowledge of the one who makes known precedes knowledge of the one made known. The "Tribes" (al-asbāṭ) are the grandsons, not the sons of daughters. Their intended meaning, according to the opinion of the sons of Jacob, is the twelve and their descendants. Not all of them were sons, contrary to what he claimed.

﴿And what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾, of the Torah and the Gospel and all the miracles, as the choice of the verb "given" over the verb "sent down", which is specific to a Book, indicates. It has been said that it is specific to the two Books. The change of style is for the sake of attention to the matter of the two Books, and the singling out of these two Prophets for mention is because the discourse is with the Jews and Christians. ﴿And the Prophets﴾ is coordinated with ﴿Moses and Jesus﴾, meaning: and what the Prophets were given, across their multiple individuals and differing names, ﴿from their Lord﴾. The phrase ﴿from their Lord﴾ is connected to (ūtiya, "was given"). In the expression "the Lord" with a pronoun of them attached, there is a gentleness that is not hidden.

﴿We do not differentiate between any one of them﴾, that is, by confirming some and denying others, as the Jews and Christians did. Differentiating in other ways, such as preference, is permissible. ﴿And to Him we are submitting Muslims﴾ [84], that is, we are surrendering in obedience and submission in all that He commanded and forbade, or we are sincere to Him in worship. In both interpretations this sentence is not a supplement after the sentence of belief, as is apparent. It has been said that the people of the religions opposed to Islam all acknowledged belief, but they did not acknowledge the word "Islam". For this reason he followed that sentence with this one.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 85:**

﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him.﴾ It was revealed concerning a group who apostatized. They were twelve men who left Madinah and came to Makkah as disbelievers, among them al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari. As for al-Islam (submission), it has been said that it means tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and inqiyad (submission). It has also been said that it means the sharia (sacred law) of our Prophet (ﷺ). God made clear that whoever seeks, after his mission (ﷺ), a law other than his, it will not be accepted from him. The acceptance of a thing is being pleased with it and rewarding its doer for it. The word dinan (as a religion) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification) of ghayr (other), and ghayr is the object of yabtaghi (seeks). It is also permitted that dinan is the object of yabtaghi and ghayr is an adjective that was placed first and so became a hal (circumstantial accusative). It has also been said that it is a badal (substitute) for ghayra al-Islam. The majority read the two ghayns (gh) clearly, but Abu Amr is reported to have read them with idgham (assimilation of the first into the second). Abu al-Baqa criticized this reading, arguing that the kasra on the first ghayn indicates the omitted ya'.

﴿And he will be among the losers in the Hereafter.﴾ [85] It may be coordinated with the answer of the conditional, in which case it is in the place of jazm (jussive). Or it may be in the place of hal from the pronoun in the genitive, in which case it is in the place of nasb (accusative). Or it may be a new independent sentence, in which case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The phrase fi al-akhirah (in the Hereafter) is related either to a deleted word indicated by what follows it, meaning "and he is a loser in the Hereafter," or it is related to al-khasirin (the losers), on the basis that the alif and lam are not relative (mawsulah) but are the definite article. Losing in the Hereafter is the deprivation of reward and the incurring of punishment. It has been said that the original meaning of khusran (loss) is the loss of the capital. What is meant here is the squandering of the sound fitrah (innate disposition) with which one is created, which is referred to in the hadith: "Every child is born upon the fitrah." It also means not benefiting from that, and its manifestation becomes clear when its opposite is realized: ﴿The Day when wealth and children will not benefit﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart.﴾ The expression "the losers" is more emphatic than "a loser," as we have noted before, and it is treated as an intransitive verb, which is why its object has been omitted. The meaning is that he is among those who have fallen into loss.

The verse has been used as evidence that faith (iman) is the same as Islam, since if it were other than Islam it would not be accepted, and the consequent is false by necessity, so the antecedent is like it. It has been answered that "it will never be accepted from him" negates the acceptance of every religion that is distinct from the religion of Islam and faith. Although it is "other than Islam," it is not different from the religion of Islam but is identical to it in essence, though different in concept. The Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that there is no distinction. But the words of God, ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted.'"﴾ indicate a distinction. The way to reconcile the two is to understand the first verse according to the sharia usage and the second according to the linguistic lexical meaning.

[Page 217]

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 3, verse 86:

﴿How will God guide﴾ to the true religion ﴿a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾? Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from al-Hasan that they were the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who saw the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their scripture, acknowledged it, and testified that he was true. But when he was sent from among others (than them), they envied the Arabs for it, denied him, and disbelieved after their acknowledgment, out of envy toward the Arabs when he was sent from among others. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas something similar. Ikrimah said: they were Abu Amir al-Rahib and al-Harith ibn Suwayd, along with twelve men, who turned back from Islam and joined the Quraysh. Then they wrote to their people: "Is there any repentance for us?" So the verse was revealed concerning them. Most of the narrations are on this view. The meaning of the verse is to consider it unlikely that He would guide them, i.e., that He would give them guidance (dalalah) that leads to the goal (mūṣṣilah), not merely any indication of the way. This was said by some. It is also said that the meaning is: how would He direct them along the path of the rightly guided, with reward for them and praise of them, when they have done what they have done? It is also said that the verse is in the manner of distancing, as one says: "How can I guide you to the road when you have abandoned it?" That is, there is no road by which He could guide them to faith except the way by which He guided them, and they have abandoned it, and there is no other road. It is also said that the intended meaning is: how would He guide them to Paradise and reward them, while the state is what you see?!

﴿And they testified that the Messenger﴾, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿is true﴾ (ḥaqq), with no doubt about his prophethood, ﴿and clear proofs had come to them﴾, i.e., the evidences and arguments that clearly establish the truth of what he claims. It is also said that these are the Qur'an, and it is said that they are the tidings of him (peace be upon him) in their scriptures. ﴿And they testified﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with what is in ﹛their belief﹜ of the sense of a verb, because it carries the meaning of "they believed". Apparently it is a conjunction on the sense (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-maʿnā), as in God's words: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to God a goodly loan﴾, not on the basis of a mistaken assumption (tawahhum) as has been supposed. Some chose to interpret the conjunct so that its conjunction with the explicit noun before it would be valid, by supposing with it the verbal particle "an" (that), i.e., "and that they testified", meaning "and their testimony", in the manner of the poet's words:

"And wearing a cloak, and my eye being comforted, are dearer to me than wearing fine silks."

This view was taken by al-Raghib and Abu al-Baqa. It was also permitted to make it a conjunction with ﴿disbelieved﴾, and the corruption of the meaning is averted by the fact that conjunction does not require sequence; so the denied element may be the testimony concurrent with the disbelief or prior to it. It was objected that the apparent sense requires the conjunct to be restricted by what restricts the element conjoined to, whereas their testimony was not after their belief but with it or before it. It was answered by denying this, because it does not follow that the conjunct must be restricted by what restricts the element it is conjoined to; had that been intended, it would have been placed later. It was also said that what prevents this conjunction is that they were not combining testimony and disbelief; this was answered by denying it: rather they are combining them, even if not simultaneously. Some made it a conjunction with ﴿disbelieved﴾ and did not burden themselves with any of what was mentioned. It was claimed that this refers to the hypocrites, but that is contrary to what is transmitted and to reason. Most of the careful scholars chose that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state) from the pronoun in ﴿disbelieved﴾, with "qad" (indeed) implied with it. The governing element cannot be "yahdi" (He guides), because He guides whoever testifies that the Messenger is true. On the basis of this, and on the basis of the conjunction with belief, it was argued that the verbal acknowledgment by the tongue is outside the reality of faith. The reasoning is that conjunction by its apparent sense requires "difference" (al-mughāyarah) between the conjunct and what it is conjoined to, and that the circumstantial clause requires restriction. If acknowledgment were part of the reality of faith, its mention would be without benefit; and if it were identical with it, this would require restricting a thing by itself, and what is in that is not hidden. Some claimed that by belief is meant belief in God, and by the testimony mentioned is belief in His Messenger (ﷺ), and the matter is then clear. So reflect.

﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [86]: i.e., the disbelievers who wronged themselves by neglecting reflection and placing disbelief in the place of belief. So how about one to whom the truth came, who knew it, and then turned away from it? It is also permissible to take "wrongdoing" in its general sense, so that disbelief enters it by primary inclusion. The sentence is either parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah, an interjected clause) or circumstantial (ḥāliyyah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 87:

﴿Those﴾, i.e., those mentioned, who are characterized by the most abominable qualities. It is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). His, glorified is He, saying ﴿their recompense﴾, i.e., the recompense of their deed, is the second subject (mubtada' thani). His, mighty is His majesty, saying ﴿that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together﴾ [87] is the predicate (khabar) of the second subject. This, together with its predicate, is the predicate of the first subject. It has been said: this indicates by its explicit meaning the permissibility of cursing them, and by its implied meaning it negates the permissibility of cursing others. Perhaps the distinction between them and others, such that the curse was specifically attached to them, is that they are sealed upon their hearts and barred (from guidance) because of the wickedness of their essences and the ugliness of their readiness for guidance, and they are despairing of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, unlike others. The disagreement concerns cursing specific individuals from among those for whom the curse has been reported in terms of their categories, such as a particular wine-drinker, for example, which is well known. Al-Nawawi held its permissibility, citing what was reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a donkey that had been branded on its face, and he said: 'May Allah curse whoever did this.'" and what is authentically established that the angels curse whoever leaves her house without her husband's permission. It has been answered that the curse there is directed at the category, into which the individual also falls. It has been objected that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, like interpreting "inna" and "its rider" as referring to that. Caution is not hidden. The intended meaning of "mankind" is either the believers, because they are the ones who curse the disbelievers, or it is general, because every individual curses whoever does not follow the truth, even if he himself is not a follower according to his own claim.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 88:

﴿Abiding therein⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ﴿upon them⁠﴾, and the governing element (ʿāmil) of it is the sense of being established (al-istiqrār). The genitive pronoun refers either to the curse (al-laʿna), or to the punishment (al-ʿuqūba), or to the Fire (al-nār), even though none of these has been mentioned explicitly, being sufficed by the indication of the curse toward it. ﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved⁠﴾ [88]. That is, they will not be given respite, and the punishment will not be deferred from them from one time to another time; or, it means they will not be looked upon or given any consideration. The sentence is either a new, independent sentence (mustaʾnafa), or it occupies the place of an accusative in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Except those who repent after that﴾, i.e., after the disbelief they committed after believing, ﴿and reform﴾, i.e., they entered upon righteousness. This is based on the verb being intransitive, of the type of *aṣbaḥū* (they entered the morning), i.e., they entered upon the morning. It is also permissible for it to be transitive, with the object omitted, meaning they reformed what they had corrupted. Thus there is an indication, as has been said, that mere regret for what passed of apostasy and resolve to abandon it in the future is not sufficient, because of the rights they had neglected. It has been objected that mere repentance necessitates the lightening of the punishment and the regard of the Truth toward them, so the apparent meaning is that this is not a restriction but an explanation of what it means to set right what has been corrupted.

It is answered that this objection is not valid, because mere regret and resolve to abandon disbelief in the future do not by themselves remove one from it. Thus it is an explanation of the repentance that is considered valid, and the outcome is one in verification. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [89], i.e., He will forgive their disbelief and reward them. It has also been said: ﴿Forgiving﴾ toward them in this world by concealing their ugly deeds, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them in the Hereafter by pardoning them. Its remoteness is not hidden. The sentence is a justification for what the exception implies.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 90:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief﴾. Ata' and Qatada said: it was revealed concerning the Jews who disbelieved in ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and the Injil after their belief in their prophets and their scriptures, and then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. It was also said: it refers to the People of the Book who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before his mission, then disbelieved in him after his mission, and then increased in disbelief through persistence, obstinacy, and barring others from the path. This is attributed to al-Hasan. It was also said: it refers to the companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd, for when he returned [to apostasy], they said: "We will remain in Makkah in disbelief for as long as we wish, and whenever we want to return, we will return," so what was revealed concerning al-Harith was revealed concerning them. It was also said: it refers to a group of his companions who used to disbelieve and then return to Islam; this was narrated from Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani'. The word ﴿كُفْرًا﴾ is a *tamyiz* (specification of the accusative, *tamyiz*: an accusative noun clarifying the sense of a preceding term) that has been transferred from the subject. The first *dal* in ﴿ازدادوا﴾ is a replacement for the *ta'* of the *ifti'al* form (the reflexive/augmented verbal pattern), because it occurs after a *zay*.

﴿Their repentance will never be accepted﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Jubba'i said: this is because they only repent at the presence of death and the moment of witnessing it, and at that point the repentance of a disbeliever is not accepted. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is because it was not from the heart; it was merely hypocrisy. It was also said: this is of the type of the line of poetry:

*"And you do not see the lizard entering it"*

meaning: there is no repentance for them until it is accepted, because they were not granted success in it. Thus it is of the type of *kinaya* (metonymy: using an expression for what it implies, the implied meaning being the intended sense), not *majaz* (figurative usage in which the word itself is used in a non-literal sense), as the *Allama* said, where the speech is taken in its literal meaning so that one moves from it to what it necessarily implies. In any case, this does not contradict what is indicated by the *istithna'* (exception, referring to the exception in the verse), and what is established in the *shari'a* (sacred law), as is well known. It was also said: this repentance was not from disbelief, but rather from sins they used to commit together with it, and they repented of them while persisting in disbelief, so it was rejected from them for that reason. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "These Jews and Christians disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief through sins they committed, then they went to repent of those sins while still in their disbelief, so their repentance was not accepted. Had they been upon guidance, it would have been accepted, but they are upon error." This leads to the question of whether a disbeliever is obligated to the *furu'* (the subsidiary rulings of the law), a matter whose discussion has been extensively expounded in the *usul* (the foundations of jurisprudence).

﴿And those are the astray﴾ [90]. This is a conjunction either with the predicate of ﴿إنّ﴾ (*inna*), so its position is in the nominative case, or with ﴿إنّ﴾ together with its subject, in which case it has no grammatical position. ﴿الضالون﴾ means those who err from the path of truth and salvation. It was also said: the ruined, those who will be punished. The restriction (*hasr*) is understood in the sense that they are complete in misguidance, so it does not negate the existence of misguidance in others as well.

[p. 219]

**"Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers"** (*inna alladhina kafaru wa matu wa hum kuffar*): that is, while they remain upon their disbelief. **"Then none of them will be accepted, even if it were the earth filled with gold"** (*fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim mil'u al-ard*) from its east to its west, **"gold"** (*dhahaban*). It is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (the accusative of specification). al-A'mash read *dhahabun* in the nominative, which is construed as a *badal* (substitute) for *mil'u*, or as an *'atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition), or as the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been objected to this that a qualifier must be supposed for the *badal* to be apt, and there is no indication of one; moreover, an *'atf al-bayan* of a definite by an indefinite is not attested. Making it a predicate is only apt if the clause is taken as a qualifier or a circumstantial clause, and even that is not free of weakness. The *mil'* of a thing, with a kasra on the *mim*, is the quantity that fills it. As for *mal'* with a fatha, it is the verbal noun of *mala'ahu mal'an*. As for *mula'ah*, with a damma and the long vowel, it is a wrapper (a large cloak).

Here there is a well-known question: why is the *fa'* (then) introduced into the predicate of *inna* here, and not in the preceding verse, although the two verses are equal in the soundness of introducing the *fa'* to express causality, as is apparent? Several scholars answered that the relative clause in the first verse is disbelief and its increase, and this does not entail the non-acceptance of repentance; rather, it entails [the non-acceptance] only upon dying in it. For if [the repentance] were performed in the manner it should be, it would be accepted. This is unlike dying as disbelievers in this verse, for that entails the said outcome. For this reason, if one says, "Whoever comes to me, for him is a dirham," it is an acknowledgment (of debt), unlike if he joins it with the *fa'*, as is well known among the jurists. It is not objected that the attaching of a ruling to a descriptive attribute is evidence of causality, because we do not concede that it necessarily entails this, since the expression by a relative pronoun may serve purposes such as signalling the certainty of the report, as in his saying:

*Indeed she who pitched a tent, as an emigrant*
*in the town of the army's camp, the ghoul took her away from them.*

This has been explained at length in the *Ma'ani* [works]. It is also read: **"Then none of them will be accepted, the earth's fill"** (*fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim mil'a al-ard*), with the verb in the active voice, whose subject is God Most High, and *mil'a* in the accusative; and *mil'a al-ard* with the two hamzas lightened.

**"Even if he were to ransom himself with it"** (*wa law iftada bihi*). Ibn al-Munir said in *al-Intisaf*: this *wa* of accompaniment joined to the conditional requires another condition, on which the conditional joined to it is coordinated, as a necessity. The custom in such cases is that the stated element draws attention to the unstated one by way of a fortiori reasoning. An example is your saying: "I honour Zayd, even if he does wrong." This *wa* coordinates what is mentioned with an omitted element, whose supposition is: "I honour Zayd if he does well, and even if he does wrong." You have, by enjoining his honouring even if he does wrong, drawn attention to the fact that honouring him if he does well is a fortiori. Among this is His saying: ﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice, witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves﴾. Its meaning, and God knows best, is: "even if the right were against others, and even if it were against you," but He mentioned what is harder for them, and enjoined it, drawing attention to the fact that what is easier is more fitting for obligation. Since this verse departs from this pattern of usage, because His saying, glorified is He, ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ requires another omitted condition of which this stated one would be a reminder by a fortiori reasoning, and the state mentioned, namely the state of their ransoming themselves with the earth's fill of gold, is the most worthy of the states for the acceptance of ransom, and there is no state beyond it that would be more fitting for acceptance than it. The exegetes laboured over its interpretation. az-Zamakhshari mentioned three aspects. The essence of the first is that the non-acceptance of the earth's fill is a metonymy for the non-acceptance of any ransom, since the context indicates that acceptance is sought for deliverance; and [the expression] was diverted to depict abundance, since it is the furthest limit beyond which no aspiration lies in common usage. Within the implicit meaning, the earth's fill is intended literally, so the meaning becomes: no ransom will be accepted from him, even if he ransomed himself with the earth's fill of gold. In the first there is a consideration of generality and of its taking the place of any ransom; in the second there is a consideration of literal meaning, or [it is] for the sake of maximal hyperbole without regard to its standing in the place of [any ransom]. The essence of the second: the intended meaning is "even if he ransomed himself with its like along with it," as He stated explicitly in another verse; and because it is known that the first is also a ransom, it is as if it were said: "the earth's fill as ransom will not be accepted, even if doubled." This returns to making the *ba'* (with) mean *ma'a* (together with), and supposing *mithl* (like) after it, that is, "together with its like." The essence of the third: a descriptive attribute is supposed that the context specifies, such as "he had given it in charity." In that case the condition mentioned earlier is not meant to emphasise the preceding ruling; rather, it is a conditional whose apodosis is omitted, and the meaning is: "The earth's fill of gold will not be accepted from him, if he gave it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would likewise not be accepted from him." The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the wealth, without regard to the attribute of giving in charity. The utterance is thus of the kind of: ﴿No one is granted a long life, nor is anything taken from his lifespan﴾ and "I have a dirham and its half." End of quotation.

There is no concealing what is in this of obscurity and artificiality. Close to this is what was said: that the *wa* is superfluous, and this is supported by its being read without it in the anomalous readings. Likewise is the view that *law* (if) is not conjunctive but conditional, and the apodosis is what follows it, or it stands in the place of the apodosis. Ibn al-Munir mentioned, as an answer, asserting that applying the verse to it is easier and closer. Indeed he claimed that it is among the easy yet impossible matters that the acceptance of a ransom which is the earth's fill of gold occurs in several states: at times it is taken by compulsion, as the taking of blood-money; at other times the one ransoming says, "I ransom myself with such-and-such," and does not do it; and at other times he says so while the ransom is ready and he hands it over to the one from whom he hopes its acceptance. So what is mentioned in the verse is the most emphatic of the states and the most worthy of acceptance, namely that he ransoms himself with the earth's fill of gold as a ransom that is realised, in that he is able to perform this great matter and hands it over by choice; and yet it is not accepted from him. Then it follows, a fortiori, that the mere statement from him, "I will expend the wealth and I am able to do so," or what resembles this, would not be accepted, by a fortiori reasoning. Thus the *wa* in this state remains in its proper function, drawing attention to the fact that there are other states in which acceptance does not occur, by a fortiori reasoning in relation to the stated state. His, the Exalted's, saying explicitly indicates this. The intended meaning is that there is no deliverance for them from the threat; for otherwise it is known that on that day they are more destitute than Ibn al-Mudhallaq, unable to do anything. A parallel to this is your saying: "I will not sell you this garment for a thousand dinars, even if you hand it to me in my hand." End of quotation. Close to this is what Abu Hayyan mentioned, saying: what this construction requires, and what it should be taken to mean, is that God Most High has informed that whoever dies a disbeliever, there will not be accepted from him what fills the earth of gold, in every state he might intend, even in the state of ransoming himself from punishment; because the state of ransoming is not one in which the ransomer confers a favour upon the one ransomed from, since it is a state of compulsion from the one ransomed from. We have established, in constructions like this one, that *law* comes to signal that what precedes it has come in the manner of exhaustive enumeration, while what follows it has come as an explicit specification of a state which might be thought not to fall under what precedes it. Like his, upon him be prayer and peace: "Give to the beggar, even if he comes on a horse," and "Turn away the beggar, even if with a burnt hoof." As if these were things that ought not to be done: for the beggar's being on a horse indicates his wealth, so it is not fitting that he be given; and likewise the burnt hoof has no sustenance in it, so it would be fitting that the beggar not be turned away with it. Likewise, the state of ransoming would be fitting for the acceptance from him of the earth's fill of gold; yet it is not accepted. Its parallel is: ﴿You would not believe us, even if we were truthful﴾, for they denied that he would believe them in every state, even in the state of their truthfulness, which is the state in which they ought to be believed; and *law* here is for generalising the negation and emphasising it.

This is what has been transmitted. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, and Ibn Jarir (the wording being his), reported from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The disbeliever will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the earth's fill of gold, would you have ransomed yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said: 'You were asked for what is easier than that, and you did not do it.' This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, then none of them will be accepted, the earth's fill of gold, even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾."

**"For them is a painful punishment"** (*ulaika lahum 'adhabun alim*). The demonstrative *ulaika* is the subject, and the adverbial phrase is the predicate. Because it relies on the subject, it raises the agent.
