It is also permissible that *lahum* be a fronted predicate, and *'adhab* a delayed subject, and the clause a predicate of the demonstrative; the first is better. In following what was mentioned with this clause there is an intensification in warning and in despair; for whoever is not accepted with ransom may perhaps be pardoned out of generosity. **"And they will have no helpers"** (*wa ma lahum min nasirin*) [91], in averting the punishment or lightening it. The *min* is superfluous after the negation for totality, and it is inserted after the negation whether it precedes a singular or a plural noun, contrary to those who claimed that this applies only to the singular. The plural form is for the sake of agreement with the pronoun, and in it there is harmony of line-endings. What is meant is that none of them has a single helper.

* * *

Among the allusive interpretations: **"Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is common between us and you"** (*qul ya ahl al-kitab ta'alaw ila kalimatin sawa'in baynana wa baynakum*). This word is the word of tawhid (monotheism), and the abandonment of following desire and the inclination toward other than God; for this has never been subject to disagreement by any prophet or any scripture.

**"Abraham was not a Jew"** (*ma kana Ibrahim*), the Friend [of God], *yahudiyyan* (a Jew), connected to the comparison; **"nor a Christian"** (*wa la nasraniyyan*), one who holds to the Trinity; **"but he was a ḥanif"** (*wa lakin kana hanifan*), inclining away from being toward seeing the Originator through the originated; **"a Muslim"** (*musliman*), submitting when His decree and destiny take their course; or, going to what the Muslims who are chosen go to, those who say: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾.

**"Indeed, the nearest of people to Abraham are those who followed him"** (*inna awla al-nas bi-Ibrahima lalladhina ittaba'uhu*), on the condition of detachment from the two states of being and of preventing the souls from turning toward the worlds. For when the Friend reached the presence of holiness, his sight turned away from the brides of kingship and dominion; so he said: ﴿I am free of what you associate﴾, ﴿I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾.

[p. 221]

**"And this Prophet"** (*wa hadha al-nabiyy*), the great one, meaning Muhammad, upon him from God be the most excellent blessing and the most perfect salutation, is also more entitled to follow his father the Friend and to take his noble path, because he is the pure essence of the churning of his love and the distilled truth of his nature. **"And those who believed"** (*wa alladhina amanu*) in him (ﷺ), upon whom his lights shone and in whose hearts' gardens his secrets came to fruition. **"And God is the Protector of the believers"** (*wa Allahu wali al-mu'minin*), all of them; He guards them from the calamities of subjugation, admits them into the domes of protection, and grants them the abodes of honour. **"And do not believe except in one who follows your religion"** (*wa la tu'minu illa li-man tabi'a dinakum*). The people of God, glorified is He, have taken this as address to the believers, as some of the literalists said; that is: do not disclose the secrets of the Truth except to its people, and do not confess the meanings of the reality to those of the people who are veiled, lest they turn against you and seek to shed your blood. **"Say: Indeed the guidance"** (*qul inna al-huda*), meaning **"the guidance of God, that anyone be given what you have been given"** (*huda Allahi an yu'ta ahadun mithla ma utitum*), of the knowledge of the inner [truth], **"or that they argue with you"** (*aw an yuhajjukum*) with it in their claim, **"before your Lord"** (*'inda rabbikum*), and this is the knowledge of the outer [law].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 91 (part 2 of 2):

The summary of the meaning is that (true) guidance (*al-huda*) lies in combining the outward (*zahir*) and the inward (*batin*). Confining oneself to knowledge of the outward and denying the inward is not guidance. ﴿Say: Surely the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾, so He disposes of it according to His will, which follows His knowledge, which in turn follows the known objects from pre-eternity (*azal al-azal*). ﴿And Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing﴾. How, then, could He be confined by restrictions? Rather, He manifests Himself as wisdom requires, in the manifestations, for the people of witnessing (*ahl al-shuhud*). ﴿He singles out for His mercy﴾, the special mercy, ﴿whom He wills﴾ of His servants, and this is the knowledge of Him, which is higher than unveiling the unseen of the realm of the malakut (the dominion) and witnessing the secret of the jabarut (the realm of sovereignty). ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of Great Bounty﴾, which cannot be comprehended.

﴿Yes, whoever fulfils his covenant﴾, and this is the covenant of the spirit, in the manner of unveiling; the covenant of the heart, in receiving the address; and the covenant of the intellect, in complying with the commands and prohibitions. ﴿And is mindful of Allah﴾ against the passing thoughts of the souls and the sudden assaults of desires. ﴿Then surely Allah loves the mindful﴾, meaning that he has attained the station of the reality of love.

﴿Surely those who sell Allah's covenant and their oaths for a little price﴾, the verse is an allusion to one who inclined toward the greenery of this world and preferred it over witnessing the presence of the Lord (*al-Mawla*). He adorned his outward appearance with the worship of the near ones (*al-muqarrabin*) and mixed it with love of leadership (*hubb al-riyasa*). That person has fallen from the vision of encounter and from being addressed by the Real (*al-Haqq*) in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and prophethood, and then he should say to the people: "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾. This is because prophetic mission (*al-istinba'*) occurs only after annihilation in unity (*al-fana' fi al-tawhid*). Whoever Allah, exalted is He, has erased of his humanity by annihilating him from himself, and has given him a luminous, real existence fit to receive the Book and intellectual wisdom, cannot call people to himself, since one who calls to himself is only veiled by himself, and between the two matters there is contradiction. Rather, he says: ﴿Be Lordly (rabbaniyyin)﴾, that is, ascribed to the Lord. What is meant is worshippers who are disciplined by knowledge, action, and persistence in acts of obedience, so that the lights of the Lord may overwhelm the secrets within you.

There are many expressions among them regarding the rabbani. Al-Shibli said: The rabbani is one who takes knowledge only from the Lord and does not return to anything except Him. Sahl said: The rabbani is one who does not choose any state over his Lord. Al-Qasim said: He is one who is characterized by the morals of the Lord in knowledge and judgment. It was said: He is one who is annihilated in his existence and annihilated from his witnessing. It was said: He is one whom the vicissitudes of destinies, in their variety, do not affect. It was said, and it was said; and all the sayings come from a single watering place.

﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾, for they are some of His manifestations, while He, glory be to Him, is the Absolute, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. ﴿Would He command you to disbelieve after you have submitted?﴾, that is: would He command you to be veiled by seeing forms and looking at likenesses, after the lights of unity (*anwar al-tawhid*) have shone in your secrets and the suns of singularity (*shumus al-tafrid*) have risen in your hearts? ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾, the verse. In it there is an allusion that He, glory be to Him, took the pledge from the deputies of the Muhammadan Reality (*al-Haqiqa al-Muhammadiyya*) in pre-eternity, to submit, obey, and believe in it. He singled them out for mention because they are the people of the first row and the men of the Presence (*al-hadra*). It was also said: Allah, exalted is He, took from them the covenant of mutual acquaintance, establishing the religion, not dividing, confirming one another, calling the creation to monotheism, dedicating worship to Allah, exalted is He, obeying the Prophet, and making some of them known to their nations to others. This is other than the general covenant indicated by His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, etc.

Page 222

﴿Then whoever turns away after that﴾, that is, after he has known Allah's covenant with the prophets, and the prophets' conveying to Him what was entrusted to them, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient (*al-fasiqun*)﴾, that is, those who have departed from the religion of Allah, exalted is He, and there is no other religion that is valid in reality, except in imagination. ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, when to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, whoever is in the world of spirits and the world of souls, or whoever is in the world of the malakut and the world of the mulk (the visible realm), ﴿willingly﴾ by his own choice and awareness, ﴿and unwillingly﴾ from a standpoint he does not know, and does not know that he does not know, because of his being veiled by seeing other things. For this reason he has fallen from the rank of acceptance. ﴿And to Him they will be returned﴾ in the end, when the shin (leg) is uncovered. ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam﴾, which is monotheism, ﴿as a religion﴾ for himself, ﴿it will never be accepted from him﴾, because he does not reach the Real, due to the place of the veil. ﴿And in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾ on the Great Day of Resurrection, those who have lost themselves.

﴿How will Allah guide a people...﴾, the verse. It is a way of finding it improbable that He would guide one whom Allah created without the readiness for knowledge, and who was judged to be a disbeliever in the pre-eternal past. For whoever has no readiness does not fall into the lights of manifestation (*al-tajalli*), and whoever plunges into the sea of subjugation (*al-qahr*) and clings to the bottom of the depth of distance (*ba'd al-bu'd*) has no path to the shore of nearness of nearness (*qurb al-qurb*). And Allah prevails in His affair. How excellent is the one who said:

When a man is not created fortunate, the thoughts of his raiser are bewildered, and what he hopes for is lost.
So Musa, whom Jibril raised, is a disbeliever, and Musa, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger.

This is it. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Guide to the right path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 92:

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) explaining what benefits the believers and is accepted from them, following the explanation of what does not benefit the disbelievers and is not accepted from them. "Tanalu" is from "nala, yanalu, naylan," meaning to reach and find. It is said, "nala al-'ilm" (he attained knowledge) when he reached it and became characterized by it. Al-birr (righteousness) is goodness and perfection of good. Some scholars distinguish between it and khayr (good) by saying that birr is the benefit that reaches another person together with the intention to do so, while khayr is benefit in general, even if it occurs inadvertently. The opposite of birr is ʿuquq (disobedience to parents), and the opposite of khayr is sharr (evil). The definite article in "al-birr" is either for the genus and reality, meaning "you will not be righteous (abrar) until you spend," which is what is narrated from al-Hasan, or it is for a previously known referent (ta'rif al-'ahd), meaning "you will not reach the righteousness of God, O people of His obedience, until you spend." This is the view of Muqatil and ʿAta'.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that birr is interpreted as Paradise, and similar was narrated from Masruq, al-Suddi and ʿAmr ibn Maymun. Some scholars held that the sentence contains an elision (hadhf mudaf), meaning "you will not attain the reward of righteousness." Here "hatta" means "ila" (until), and "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya). This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "ba'da ma tuhibbun" (some of what you love). It was also said that "min" is explicative (bayaniyya), and according to this view there is no difference in meaning between the two readings. "Ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a descriptive noun (mawsufa). Making it a verbal noun (masdariyya), with the verbal noun carrying the meaning of the object, is permissible according to the opinion of Abu ʿAli.

Regarding the meaning of His words, glorified is He, ﴿what you love﴾, there are several opinions. It is said it refers to wealth, and it was expressed this way because all people love it. It is also said it refers to the most precious and noble wealth. And it is said it includes that and other things that a person loves and desires. On this last view, "infaq" (spending) is used metaphorically, while on the first two views it is used literally. The early generation (al-salaf), may Allah be pleased with them, used to dedicate to Allah whatever they loved. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Abu Talha had the most palm trees of the Ansar in Medina, and the property he loved most was Bayruha', which faced the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ used to enter it and drink from its pleasant water. When the verse ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ was revealed, Abu Talha said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, and the most beloved of my property to me is Bayruha', and it is a charity for Allah, the Exalted. I hope for its righteousness and its reserve with Allah, the Exalted. So place it, O Messenger of Allah, where Allah shows you.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Bakh, bakh! That is profitable wealth. I have heard what you said, and I think you should give it to your relatives.' Abu Talha said: 'I will do so, O Messenger of Allah.' So Abu Talha distributed it among his relatives and his paternal cousins [Page 223]." In a narration in Muslim and Abu Dawud: "So he placed it between Hassan ibn Thabit and Ubayy ibn Ka'b."

Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: "When this verse was revealed, Zayd ibn Haritha came with a horse called Sabal, which was the most beloved property to him. He said: 'It is a charity.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ accepted it, and he gave it to his son Usama to ride. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ noticed that in Zayd's face, and said: 'Indeed Allah, exalted is He, has accepted it from you.'" ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "This verse ﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾ and so on came to my mind. I considered what Allah had given me, and I found nothing more beloved to me than Marjana, a Roman slave-girl of mine. I said: 'She is free for the sake of Allah's face. If I were to return to something I had dedicated to Allah, I would marry her.' So I married her to Nafi'." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Nafi', who said: "Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, used to buy sugar and give it in charity. We would say to him: 'If you bought food for them with its price, it would be more beneficial for them than this.' He would say: 'I know what you are saying, but I heard Allah, exalted is He, say: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, and Ibn ʿUmar loves sugar.'"

The apparent meaning of these reports indicates that the spending in the verse includes recommended charity (al-mustahabb). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that what is meant is the payment of obligatory zakat and what Allah has enjoined on wealth. It is as if it were said: "You will never attain righteousness until you pay the zakat of your wealth." This is based on the view that what is meant by ﴿what you love﴾ is wealth itself, not its most noble parts. As for al-Nisaburi's statement that it is objected that the payer of zakat is not obligated to give the best and most noble of his wealth, this arises from a lack of reflection. Had he reflected, he would not have raised an objection against the interpreter of the Qur'an (tarjuman al-Qur'an) and the scholar of the Ummah (habr al-umma). Al-Wahidi reported from Mujahid and al-Kalbi that the verse is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of zakat. Naskh (abrogation, where a later ruling replaces an earlier one) is a technical term in legal theory. This view is considered weak, because the obligation of zakat does not contradict encouragement to give up what one loves in the cause of Allah, the Exalted.

This verse has been raised as a difficulty: its apparent meaning requires that a poor person who never spent from what he loves during his whole life, because he was unable to, would not be righteous, or would not attain the righteousness of Allah, the Exalted, among the people of His obedience. Yet this is not the case. It was answered that the statement is given in the mode of urging spending, and it is restricted by ability; it was stated in absolute terms only as a form of emphasis in encouragement. It was also said that the better view is that what is meant is: "You will never attain complete righteousness, which occurs in its most excellent forms, until you spend from what you love." The poor person who did not spend throughout his life cannot be said to be a perfectly righteous person, nor does he attain the perfect righteousness of Allah among the people of His obedience. It was also said that the better of these views is to say that what is meant is: "You will never attain righteousness through spending until you spend from what you love."

The summary of this is that spending from what one loves results in attaining righteousness, while spending from other than that does not result in attaining righteousness. Nothing in the verse indicates a restriction of the result of righteousness to spending from what one loves, nor a denial that righteousness results from another action among the commanded actions. In that case, it is not far-fetched that the poor non-spender may be righteous, or may attain the righteousness of Allah among the people of His obedience through another avenue. Perhaps his actions free from spending wealth may demand a greater and fuller righteousness than what mere spending demands. The discussion extends to the question of preferring the patient poor person over the thankful rich person, a long-running question about which treatises have been written.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾, that is: whatever thing you spend from among things, or whatever good thing you spend that you love, or a bad thing that you dislike. "Min" in the first case relates to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of the conditional particle (ism al-shart). In the second case it is in the accusative position as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) for the answer of the condition, occupying its place: that is, He will reward you accordingly, for He is Knowing of everything you spend. It was also said that this is the answer of the condition, and the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, knows it existing exactly as you do it, in terms of the goodness or badness of your intention. The fronting of the adverbial phrase is for the sake of the verse endings (fawasil). In the verse there is both encouragement and warning. It was said that it also contains an indication toward urging concealment of charity.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 3, verse 93:**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All food was lawful for the Children of Israel﴾

Al-Wahidi narrated from al-Kalbi that when the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I am upon the religion of Ibrahim," the Jews said, "How can that be, when you eat the flesh of camels and drink their milk?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "That was lawful for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and so we make it lawful." The Jews then said, "Everything we forbid today was forbidden to Nuh and Ibrahim until it reached us." So Allah revealed this verse as a refutation of them.

The word *ṭaʿām* (food) is used in the sense of *maṭʿūm* (that which is eaten). What is meant here is either foodstuffs in general or edible things. Because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) used as a descriptive, it has a meaning in which the singular masculine and other forms are equal, and this is the common rule. Therefore, the statement of al-Radi does not contradict this, that one says *rajulun ʿadlun* (a just man) and *rajulāni ʿadlāni* (two just men), since that is observing the sense of the word. Some scholars mentioned that this interpretation makes *kull* (all) serve as emphasis, because totality is the function of a definite plural noun with *al-* (the definite article). The word *ḥill* (lawfulness) is also a verbal noun, used here in the sense of *ḥalāl* (lawful). The intended meaning is to inform that eating food is lawful, not that the food itself is lawful, because lawfulness, like prohibition, does not attach to essences and is not estimated as with expenditure. Although it is valid for it to be the object of *ḥill*, it may be mistakenly thought so because of the preceding context, but this is contrary to the purpose for which the statement was made.

*Isrāʾīl* is Yaʿqub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them all. According to Abu Mijlaz, a king named him with this name after he wrestled him down and struck his thigh.

﴿Except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾. Mujahid said: he made the flesh of livestock unlawful. Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas that he made unlawful the extra lobe of the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat, except that which was on the back. From Ata: he made unlawful the flesh and milk of camels. The reason for this prohibition is what is in the hadith that al-Hakim and others related with a sound chain from Ibn Abbas: he (peace be upon him) had sciatica, and he vowed that if he were healed he would not eat the food he loved most, and that was camel meat, which he loved. In another narration from Said ibn Jubayr from him: he had that ailment, and he ate camel meat, and then he spent a night groaning, so he swore never to eat it again. It was also said: he made it unlawful for himself as an act of worship, and he asked Allah the Exalted to permit it for him, so Allah, glorified is He, made it unlawful for his offspring. This was attributed to al-Hasan. And it was said: he made it unlawful and restrained himself from it, as an ascetic who is determined in his religion forbids pleasures to himself.

Many scholars held that the prohibition was by a text (*naṣṣ*) that came down concerning it. Some said it was by personal reasoning (*ijtihād*), and the apparent structure of the verse supports this. By it, the permissibility of such a thing for the prophets, peace be upon them, has been argued. The exception is *muttaṣil* (connected, i.e., included in the general statement), because the meaning in every case is that he made it unlawful for himself and for his descendants. It was also said that it is *munqaṭiʿ* (disconnected, i.e., not included in the general statement), and the meaning would be: "but Israel made it unlawful for himself alone, and did not make it unlawful for them." The first view is the one given preference.

﴿Before the Torah was revealed﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is connected to the statement ﴿was lawful﴾. The separation by the exception does no harm, since it is a permissible separation. This is according to the view of al-Kisai and Abu al-Hasan, who permit that what comes before *illā* (except) may govern what comes after it when it is an adverbial (*ẓarf*), a prepositional phrase (*jār*), a genitive (*majrūr*), or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It was also said that it is connected to *ḥurrima* (was made unlawful). Abu Hayyan objected that this is far-fetched, since it would be informing of what is obvious and known necessarily, and there would be no benefit in it. He excused it by saying that the benefit is to show that the prohibition came before it, and that the Torah includes other prohibitions that came upon them as a hardship and restriction. Some scholars preferred that it is connected to an omitted element, and the implied meaning is "was lawful" (*kāna ḥillan*).

﴿Before the Torah was revealed﴾: this is an answer to a question arising from the preceding exception, as if it were said: "When was it lawful?" and so it is answered with this phrase. What prompted this is that the purpose of restricting the prohibition is not apparent, and that restricting the description before its completion would be necessary if it were taken as a qualifier of the lawfulness.

There is no concealing what is in this. The apparent meaning is that all food other than what was excepted was lawful to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed, which included the prohibition of what was made unlawful for them due to their wrongdoing. In this there is a refutation of the Jews in their claim of innocence regarding what was condemned against them, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them﴾ (4:160), and His words, glorified is He: ﴿And upon those who were Jews, We forbade...﴾ (6:146), the two verses. It is also a rebuke to them concerning their denial of abrogation (*naskh*, the annulment of an earlier ruling by a later one), since making unlawful what was lawful can only happen through it. It also repels the criticism against the claim of the Messenger (ﷺ) that he agreed with his father Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in accordance with what the occasion of revelation indicates.

As-Suddi held that nothing was made unlawful for them upon the revelation of the Torah except what they had been prohibiting before its revelation, following their father Yaʿqub, peace be upon him. Al-Kalbi said: Allah, glorified is He, did not make unlawful for them what was made unlawful in the Torah; rather, He made it unlawful after it, because of their wrongdoing and disbelief. For when the Children of Israel committed a great sin, Allah the Exalted made a good food unlawful for them and poured down a punishment (*rijz*) upon them. From al-Dahhak: Allah the Exalted did not make any of that unlawful for them in the Torah or after it; rather, it was something they made unlawful for themselves, following their father. The attribution of its prohibition to Allah, the Exalted, is metaphorical. This is far-fetched.

﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it﴾. This is a command to him (ﷺ) to argue against them with their own Book, which clearly confirms the correctness of what he says concerning lawful and unlawful matters. The name *al-Tawrāh* (the Torah) is stated explicitly because the sentence is an address to the Jews, cut off from what precedes it. The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿if you are truthful﴾, that is, in your claim, is a conditional clause whose answer has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it: that is, "if you are truthful, then bring the Torah and recite it." It is narrated that they did not dare to bring it, and so they were confounded and were struck dumb (*ulqimū ḥajaran*).

In this there is clear proof of the truth of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ), since he knew that what is in the Torah proves their lying, while he had not read it or any other of the scrolls of the earlier peoples. Such a thing can only come through revelation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 94:

﴿Then whoever fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ That is, he invents this by his own claim that the prohibition existed for the prophets and their communities before the revelation of the Torah (al-Tawrat). (Fa-man) refers to those Jews, and it is possible that it is general, in which case they enter it as a primary inclusion. The original meaning of al-iftira' (fabrication) is cutting the leather (adim); it is said: "faraa al-adim yafrihi fary-an" when he cut it. It came to be used for innovating and inventing. The sentence may be resumptive (mustaanifa), or it may be in the accusative position (mansuba al-mahall) coordinated upon the sentence "fa-'tu" (so bring), in which case it falls under the saying. As for "man," it may be conditional (shartiyya) or relative (mawsula), and its wording and meaning have both been observed. ﴿after that﴾ That is, after their being commanded with what was mentioned and what follows from it of the establishment of proof (qiyam al-hujja) and the manifestation of clear evidence.

﴿Those﴾ That is, the fabricators, who are removed from the honor of nearness, ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾ wronging themselves by doing what made punishment obligatory for them. It was also said: they are the wrongdoers to themselves through that, and to their followers by misguiding them, because of their persistence in falsehood and their not affirming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The qualification with "remoteness" was specified even though he deserves the threat for lying against Allah the Exalted at every time and in every state, to indicate the complete ugliness of the act. It was also said: it is to explain that he is only held accountable for it after the proof has been established against him, and whoever lies about what he is not held to account for is like the child who does not deserve the threat for his lie; and there is reflection in this. Then the connection of this verse with what precedes it: eating is a spending of what one loves, but upon oneself, and Ali ibn Isa pointed to this. It was also said: when their argument about the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had preceded, and among what they denied against our Prophet (ﷺ) was the eating of camel meat, claiming that it opposed the religion of Ibrahim, it was fitting to mention the refutation of their claim immediately after that argument.

[Page 4]

﴿Say: Allah has spoken the truth﴾: that is, His truthfulness became manifest and was established regarding that ﴿all food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself﴾. It has also been said that it refers to Muhammad (peace be upon him) being upon the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), and that his religion is Islam. It has also been said that it refers to everything He reported. What was mentioned enters into this initially, and in it, as has been said, there is an allusion (ta'rid) to their outright lying.

﴿Then follow the creed of Abraham﴾, which is the religion of Islam, for you do not follow his creed as you claim. It has also been said: follow the likeness of his creed, so that you may be freed from Judaism, which compelled you to lie against Allah and to make things hard upon yourselves. It has also been said: follow his creed in permitting the eating of camel meat and drinking its milk, which was lawful for him. ﴿Upright (hanifan)﴾: that is, inclining away from all the false religions toward the religion of truth; or steadfast upon what Allah the Exalted prescribed of the true religion in its pilgrimage, its rites, its food, and other matters.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: that is, in any matter of their religion at all. In it there is an allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheism of those addressed. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil), that is, an appended closing remark, to what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "It reached us that the Jews said: 'Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) is greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets, and because it is in the Holy Land.' The Muslims said: 'Rather, the Ka'bah is greater.' This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so there was revealed [the verse] up to ﴿the station of Ibrahim﴾."

The like of this is also related from Mujahid. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that Allah the Exalted commanded the disbelievers to follow the creed (millah) of Ibrahim, and from his creed is the exaltation of the Sacred House of Allah the Exalted. So the mention of the House, its excellence and its sanctity is appropriate for this. It has also been said: the connection is that this is a second doubt they advanced, and Allah the Exalted refuted them in it just as He refuted them in the previous one. The meaning is: indeed the first House established for the worship of mankind of their Lord, i.e., it was prepared and made a place of worship. The one who established it is Allah the Exalted, as is indicated by the reading of the one who read (wadaʿa) with the active voice (bi-l-bina' li-l-fa'il), because the apparent reading then is that the pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted, even though His name is not explicitly mentioned before it in the verse, on the basis that it is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah). The possibility that it refers to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), because of his fame for building the House, is contrary to the apparent meaning. The clause (wudiʿa) is in the position of a genitive, being an attribute of (bayt), and (lil-nas) is connected to it, the lam in it denoting cause (li-l-ʿillah). His saying the Exalted: ﴿that which is at Bakkah﴾ is the predicate of inna, and the lam is displaced (muzahlaqah); and He informed with a definite noun about an indefinite noun in order to specify it, and this is within the chapter of inna. "Bakkah" is, according to most, a dialectal variant of Makkah, and the letters ba' and mim often alternate with one another, as in namit and nabit, lazim and lazib, ratib and ratim. It has also been said that they are different: Bakkah is the place of the mosque, and Makkah is the whole town. Its origin is from al-bakk, meaning crowding; it is said bakkahu yabukkuhu bakkan if he crowded him, and tabakka al-nas if the people thronged. It is as if it was named thus because of the crowding of pilgrims in it. It has also been said: it means pounding (al-dakk), and it was named thus because it pounds the necks of tyrants when they intend it with evil, and humbles them within it; therefore you see them in circumambulation like ordinary people, and if Allah the Exalted enabled them to clear the place of circumambulation, they would do so. It has also been said that it is derived from bakaat al-naqah or al-shah, when her milk decreased, and it is as if it was named thus because of the scarcity of its water and its barrenness. It has been said: from here the town was also named Makkah, taking it from the young camel's sucking the udder when it sucks it and leaves no milk in it. It has also been said: it is from makkahu Allah, when Allah exhausts him by destruction. Then the intended meaning of "first" is first in terms of time; it has been said: first in terms of rank. The first view is supported by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the first House established for mankind, and he said: 'The Masjid al-Haram, then Bayt al-Maqdis.' It was asked: 'How much time is between them?' He said: 'Forty years.'"

This has been challenged, since the builder of the Masjid al-Haram is Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and the builder of al-Aqsa is Dawud, then his son Sulayman (peace be upon them both), and he raised its dome eighteen miles, and between the building of Ibrahim and their building there is a period exceeding forty times over. It was answered that "establishing" (wad') is other than "building" (bina'), and the question concerns the period between their two establishments, not the period between their two buildings. So it is possible that the establisher of al-Aqsa was some prophet before Dawud and his son (peace be upon them both), and then they built it afterwards, and this interpretation is necessary (qalahu al-Tahawi). Some answered, on the assumption that by establishing is meant building, that the builder of the Masjid al-Haram and the Masjid al-Aqsa is Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and that he built al-Aqsa forty years after his building of the Masjid al-Haram; and he claimed that this is understood from the hadith, so reflect.

It is reported in some narrations that the first to build the House were the angels, and they built it two thousand years before Adam (peace be upon him). Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi have what supports this. It is related that the angels' building of it was of red ruby; then Adam built it, then Shith, then Ibrahim, then the Amalekites, then Jurhum, then Qusayy, then Quraysh, then Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, then al-Hajjaj. The building of al-Hajjaj has continued until now, except for the spout, the door and the threshold; and repair has taken place in the wall and the roof more than once, and marble was renewed in it. It has been said that it descended with Adam from Paradise, then was raised to the heavens after his death. It has been said that it was built before him and was raised to the seventh heaven in the Flood, and it has been said the fourth. Most people of reports hold that the earth was spread out (duhiyat) from beneath it. We have already set forth for you what benefits you here, so remember.

﴿Blessed﴾: i.e., abundant in good, because the reward of worship is multiplied in it; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also been said: because sins are forgiven in it for one who performs Hajj to it, circumambulates it and performs i'tikaf beside it.

Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that its blessing is what is mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿to which the fruits of every thing are brought﴾. It has been said: its blessing is the continuance of worship in it and adherence to it. The word "barakah" has come with two meanings: growth, which is the common one, and stability, and from it comes "barakah" for the stability of water in it, and "baraka" for the chest, for the stability of memory in it. And "tabaraka Allah" means He is stable and never ceases. Al-Karmani explained its being blessed by saying that the Ka'bah is like the point, and the rows of those facing it in prayers are like circles surrounding the center. There is no doubt that among them are persons whose spirits are heavenly, whose hearts are holy, whose secrets are luminous, and whose inner selves are divine; and whoever is in the Masjid al-Haram, the lights of those pure, sacred spirits connect with the light of his soul, so the divine lights increase in his heart, and this is the utmost blessing. Moreover, the earth is spherical, and every moment that is assumed is morning for one people, noon for a second, afternoon for a third, and so on; so the Ka'bah is never free of a people turning toward it for the performance of the obligatory prayers, and it is thus always. The accusative word is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase which functions as a relative clause.

Abu al-Baqa' allowed making it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (wudiʿa), and ﴿and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [96]: i.e., a guide for them to Paradise, which He the Exalted intends, or a guide to Him, glory be to Him, by what is in it of wondrous signs, as the Exalted said:

[Page 6]

**"Therein are clear signs"** (﴿فِيهِ آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾): such as the destruction of the tyrants who intended harm to it, like the companions of the elephant (Ashab al-Fil) and others; the wild beasts not attacking the game within it; the birds not fleeing from people there; and that whichever corner of the House the rain falls opposite, fertility falls upon the lands adjacent to it. So if it falls opposite the Yemeni Corner (al-Rukn al-Yamani), fertility is in Yemen; if opposite the Syrian Corner (al-Rukn al-Shami), fertility is in Syria; and if it covers the whole House, it is in all the lands. Also: the scarcity of pebbles (al-jamarat) despite the multitude of those throwing them, and so on. They also counted among the signs the birds' deviation from flying over it throughout the ages. On this there is a discussion by the later scholars (al-muhdathin), because some birds do fly over it. It was said: no bird flies over it except one that has a medicinal property for healing. This was objected to, on the basis that the punishment is its cause, for taking the snake. It was said: the bird whose blood is forfeit (al-muhdar damuha) flies over it, while the pigeon, despite its abundance, does not fly over it. Some have reconciled the two statements with this, but there remains some doubt in the heart about it. Some people have reported that they witnessed that birds in general fly over it at certain times.

[Page 6, continued]

The pronoun in the genitive (al-damir al-majrur) refers to the House, and the adverbial sense of the preposition (al-zarfiyya) is figurative; otherwise, these would not be counted as signs. The clause is either a new independent sentence (mustaʾnafa), brought in as an explanation and elaboration of the guidance (al-huda), or it is another circumstantial clause (hal). There is no harm in omitting the conjunction "wa" in a nominal circumstantial clause (al-jumla al-ismiyya al-haliyya), as ʿAbd al-Qahir and others have indicated. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in "al-ʿalamin" (the worlds), with its governing element being "huda" (guidance); or of the pronoun in "mubarakan" (blessed), which is its governing element; or that it be an attributive adjective (sifa) of "huda," just as "al-ʿalamin" is in that way. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿مَقامُ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ (the Station of Ibrahim), is either a subject whose predicate is omitted (mubtada' mahdhuf al-khabar), meaning: among them, or one of them, is the Station of Ibrahim; or a predicate whose subject is omitted (khabar mahdhuf al-mubtada'). Al-Halabi chose the latter. It was also said: it is a partial substitute (badal al-baʿd min al-kull, substitution of a part for the whole) and this is the view of Abu Muslim. Some have permitted that it be an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). The explanation of the plural by a singular is valid, on the basis that the Station includes multiple signs: the imprint of the two feet in the solid rock is one sign; their sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign; the softening of some of this kind of rock but not others is a sign; its preservation along the passage of time is a sign; and its protection from enemies is a sign. Or, on the basis that this single sign, because of the prominence of its matter and the strength of its indication of the power of Allah, exalted is He, and the prophethood of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is treated as if it were many signs. This is supported by what Ibn al-Anbari transmitted from Mujahid, that he used to recite "fihi ayatun bayyinatun" (there is a clear sign in it) in the singular. In this there is the following: although this is grammatically acceptable in meaning, it is objected to that "ayat" is indefinite (nakira) while "maqam Ibrahim" is definite (maʿrifa). Abu Hayyan has stated explicitly that it is not permissible to differ in explanatory apposition, by the consensus of the Basrans and the Kufans. Furthermore, the cause of this report in this context is what was transmitted from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: that when the building of the Kaaba was raised, he stood upon this stone so as to be able to lift the stones, and his feet sank into it. Other accounts about this have also been mentioned earlier.

﴿ومَن دَخَلَهُ كانَ آمِنًا﴾ (And whoever enters it is secure): the object pronoun refers to the Station of Ibrahim in the sense of the entire Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), according to what Ibn ʿAbbas said, not merely the place of the two feet. It is possible that there is an istikhdam here (a figure in which one word or pronoun is used with two meanings, one for each sense). Al-Jassas said: He mentioned the signs just stated in the Sacred Precinct, then said: "And whoever enters it," etc. Therefore the intended meaning must be the whole Sacred Precinct. The sentence is either an independent statement, not a conditional one; or a conditional sentence coordinated (ʿatf), as many have said, in meaning with "maqam" (the Station), because in meaning it is "the security of whoever enters it." That is, among them, or the second of them, is the security of whoever enters it; or: "In it are signs: the Station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it." On this view, there is no need for the elaborate justification for the plural form, because the two verses are a type of enumeration, like three and four; and it is permissible to mention these two signs and omit mention of the others, indicating the abundance of the signs. Such omission (al-tayy) occurs in prophetic traditions and Arabic poetry. The first is like the report: "Three things of your world have been made dear to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer" (ﷺ), according to what is widely known, although they have authenticated the omission of mention of "three." As for the second, an example is the verse of Jarir:

"Hanifa was (in) thirds: a third of them are slaves, and a third are their clients."

"Man" (من) is either for rational beings, or for them and for others by way of predominance (taghlib, the rule that the masculine rational form is used to include mixed groups), because wild animals, birds, and even plants are secure in it. Thus, "security" here means what can be attributed to all of them by some kind of interpretation (taʾwil). According to the first possibility, it may be that "security" means security in this world from killing, mutilation, and all other punishments. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "In the Jahiliyya, a man would kill another man, then enter the Sacred Precinct, and the son of the one killed, or his father, would meet him and not touch him."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "If I found in it the killer of al-Khattab, I would not touch him until he leaves it."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from his son that he said: "If I found the killer of Umar in the Sacred Precinct, I would not disturb him."

From Ibn ʿAbbas: "If I found the killer of my father in the Sacred Precinct, I would not molest him."

His position on this is that whoever kills or steals outside the Sacred Precinct, then enters it, is not to be sat with, nor spoken to, nor harmed; but he is to be urged (yunashad) until he leaves, then he is taken and the penalty for what he committed is carried out upon him. If he kills or steals within the Sacred Precinct, the penalty is carried out upon him within it. The reports from him on this are numerous, and the detailed positions on the question have been mentioned earlier. As for it meaning, as Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, held, security in the Hereafter from punishment: ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others transmitted from Yahya ibn Jaʿda that whoever enters it is secure from the Fire. Al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever enters the House enters into good deeds, and leaves forgiven of sins." It is also narrated through more than one chain from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever dies in one of the two Sanctuaries will be raised on the Day of Resurrection among the secure." In a narration from Ibn Umar: "Whoever is buried in Mecca as a Muslim will be raised secure on the Day of Resurrection." It is permissible to intend the general meaning by interpreting it as security in this world and the Hereafter, and this is probably the apparent meaning from the unrestricted wording.

﴿ولِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ﴾ (And Hajj to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people): this is an independent sentence whose subject is "hajj" and whose predicate is "lillah" (for Allah). "ʿAla al-nas" (upon the people) is related to what the predicate is related to, or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause of the implicit pronoun in the prepositional phrase, and its governing element is the sense of "settledness" (istiqrar).

It is also permitted that "ʿala al-nas" be the predicate, and "lillah" be related to what it is related to. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause of the implicit pronoun in "al-nas," because the governing element for the circumstantial clause in that case would be a meaning, and a circumstantial clause does not precede its implicit governing element according to the majority; but Ibn Malik permitted it when the circumstantial clause is an adverb or a prepositional phrase and its governing element is likewise, unlike an adverb and a prepositional phrase that do not precede their implicit governing element.

It is also permitted that "hajj" be raised by the first or second prepositional phrase. Linguistically, hajj means simply intending something, or frequenting something to honour it. Here it means a specific intention that became predominant in its usage until it became a technical legal term (haqiqa shar'iyya). "Al" in "al-bayt" is for a known reference (ʿahd).

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and ʿAsim in the transmission of Hafs read "hijj" with a kasra, like "ʿilm," and this is the dialect of Najd.

﴿مَنِ اسْتَطاعَ إلَيْهِ سَبِيلا﴾ (for whoever is able to find a way to it): this is a partial substitute for "al-nas" (badal al-baʿd min al-kull), and the pronoun in the substitute is understood, meaning: from among them. It was also said: it is a total substitute for the whole (badal al-kull min al-kull), and the intended "people" is specific, so no pronoun is needed. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are whoever is able; or the obligated party is whoever is able.

It is also permitted that it be in the accusative (manṣub) by an implied verb, meaning "I mean" (aʿni), and that it be the subject of the verbal noun (fail al-masdar), which is in construct with its object, meaning: "and it is owed to Allah from the people that they make pilgrimage to the House, those among them who are able." There is a well-known objection to this. "Man" in these possibilities is a relative pronoun (mawsula).

It is also permitted that it be conditional, with the answer (jaza') omitted and indicated by what preceded, or the answer is itself, according to the established disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans. A pronoun must refer from the conditional clause back to "ʿala al-nas," and the estimated form is: "whoever among them is able to find a way to it, then it is owed to Allah from him that he make the pilgrimage." This is strengthened by its being contrasted with the conditional that follows it. The pronoun in the genitive refers to the House or to the Hajj, since that is what is being spoken of. It relates to "al-sabil" (the way) because of the sense of reaching or leading to it within it. It is placed before it for emphasis on its importance.

"Istitaʿa" (ability) originally means seeking the compliance and facility of an action. "Intended" here means desire, and desire requires power, so it was applied to power in general, or to power with ease. The latter is more specific, and this is what is intended here. Its verification will come shortly, Allah willing. Power is either physical, financial, or both. Imam Malik held the first view: Hajj is obligatory according to him for one who is able to walk and to earn along the way. Imam al-Shafiʿi held the second view, and therefore he required that a disabled person appoint a proxy (istinaba) if he finds the wage for someone to perform it on his behalf. Our great Imam (may Allah be pleased with him) held the third view. This is supported by what al-Bayhaqi and others transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) who said: "The way is that the servant's body be healthy, and that he have the price of provisions and a mount, without that being a burden to him."

Imam al-Shafiʿi (may Allah be pleased with him) used as evidence what al-Daraqutni transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿ولِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ مَنِ اسْتَطاعَ إلَيْهِ سَبِيلا﴾ (And Hajj to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people, for whoever is able to find a way to it), a man stood and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the way?' He said: 'Provisions and a mount.'" This was narrated through various chains, and it clearly supports the view of al-Shafiʿi, since it restricts ability to financial means and not physical ability. This is a clear contradiction of Imam Malik's view. As for our Imam, he interprets what occurs in it as an explanation of some of the conditions of ability, as evidenced by the fact that if the safety of the road, for example, is lacking, Hajj is not obligatory on him. It is apparent that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not mention physical health because it is obvious. How could it not be, when what is explained is in reality the way that leads the one who is able to the House itself, and that cannot be conceived without health? Among the things that support that what is in the hadith is an explanation of some of the conditions is that in some narrations only one of its elements is mentioned. Al-Daraqutni also transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, "that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the way, and he said: 'That you find a riding camel.'" He did not mention provisions.

This is what is said. The verse has been cited as evidence that ability precedes the action, and that the view that it occurs together with the action is invalid. The reasoning is clear. It was answered that the ability we claim occurs together with the action is the actual power by which the action occurs. "Istitaʿa" is also used with another meaning, namely soundness of the causes, instruments, and limbs, that is, the responsible person being in a state where his causes, instruments, and limbs are sound. We have no dispute that this ability precedes the action, and it is the criterion for the validity of the obligation. What is in the verse, in this sense, is as they said.

[Page 9]

The thorough treatment of this matter, as they have stated it, is as follows. The well-known view attributed to al-Ash'ari (Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari) is that capacity (qudrah) exists together with the act, meaning that it comes into being at the moment the act comes into being and is related to it at that moment. It does not exist before the act, let alone relate to it. Many of the Mu'tazilah agreed with him on this, such as al-Najjar, Muhammad ibn 'Isa, Ibn al-Rawandi, Abu 'Isa al-Warraq, and others. Most of the Mu'tazilah said: capacity exists before the act and is related to it at that time, and it is impossible for it to be related to the act before the act comes into being. Then they differed about whether capacity persists. Some of them said it persists while the act exists, even though the persisting capacity is not a capacity over it. Others denied this. Their proof for this consists of several arguments.

The first: the relation of capacity to the act means bringing it into existence (ijad), and bringing an existing thing into existence is impossible, because it is the producing of what is already produced (tahsil al-hasil). Rather, bringing into existence must come before existence, and for this reason it is correct to say: "He brought it into existence, so it came to be" (awjadahu fa-wujida). It has been answered that this is based on the premise that created capacity is effective, which is disputed. Even if this premise is granted, it can be said: bringing an existing thing into existence by means of that existence, which is the effect of that bringing into existence, is permissible, in the sense that this existence, by which the thing exists at the time of bringing into existence, is dependent on the one who brings it into existence and derived from his bringing it into existence. What is impossible is bringing an existing thing into existence by means of another existence. The reality of this is that the influence, together with the production of the effect, is in terms of time, although it is prior to the effect in terms of essence. This priority is what makes the use of the particle "fa" (then) between them correct.

The second: if it is permissible for capacity to relate to the act at the moment of its coming into being, it would follow that there is capacity over what persists at the moment of its persistence, and the consequent is false. The demonstration of the implication is that the only thing preventing capacity from relating to a thing is that it is actually existing, and what is coming into being at the moment of its coming into being is also actually existing. It has been answered: we accept this, because its existence continues through the continuation of capacity's relation to it, or we make a distinction by which the implication is refuted, namely that what exists after its non-existence needs a cause, but what persists does not. For if capacity did not relate to the first, it would remain in its non-existence, and it was supposed to exist, which is a contradiction. And if it did not relate to the second, it would remain in existence, which is what corresponds to reality. Or we refute the argument first by the influence of knowledge or of being knowing (al-'alamiyyah), by agreement, for that is conditioned at the moment the act comes into being and not at its persistence; second, by the influence of the act on the agent's being an agent, for the act has an effect on this at the moment of its coming into being, and if the act is supposed to persist, it does not have an effect at the time of persistence; and third, by the concomitance of will (irada), since they require it at the moment of coming into being and not at persistence, so the same holds for capacity.

[Page 9 continues]

The third: that capacity's coexistence with the act would necessitate either the creation of God's capacity (may He be exalted) or the eternity of what He has capacity over, and both are false. Rather, His capacity is eternal, and its relation to what He has capacity over is eternal. Thus the relation of capacity to its objects before their coming into being has been established. If it were impossible in created capacity, it would be impossible in eternal capacity, and it is not so. It has been answered: the eternal, persisting capacity differs in quiddity (mahiyyah) from created capacity, which, according to us, cannot persist. Therefore it does not follow from the permissibility of created capacity's precedence over the act that the permissibility of created capacity's precedence over it is valid. Furthermore, the eternal capacity relates to the act in eternity by a nominal relation (ta'alluq ma'nawi) that does not entail the existence of the act, and it has another relation to it at the moment of its coming into being, which necessitates its existence. Therefore it does not follow from its eternity together with its nominal relation that its effects are eternal.

The fourth: it would follow from that assumption that the unbeliever, during the time of his disbelief, is not obligated (mukallaf) to believe, because it is not within his capacity in that prior state. Rather, we say: it would follow that disobedience cannot be conceived of from anyone, for with the act there is no disobedience, and without it there is no capacity, so there is no obligation, and therefore no disobedience. Also, the strongest excuse of the obligated person, which must be accepted to remove blame from him, is that what he was obligated to do is not within his capacity. So if he is not capable of the act before it, it is obligatory to remove blame from him for not doing the obligated act, and this is false by the consensus of the community. Also, if it were permissible to obligate the unbeliever to believe while it is not within his capacity, then it would be permissible to obligate him to create substances (jawahir) and accidents (a'rad). It has been answered: obligating the impossible is permissible according to us, so we accept the permissibility of obligation to that creation. We can also distinguish: abandoning belief is only by his capacity, unlike the non-existence of substances and accidents, which is not within his capacity at all. Therefore it does not follow from the permissibility of obligation to believe the permissibility of obligation to create them. In sum, the condition of obligation according to us is that the thing, or its opposite, be related to capacity. This is found in belief, because abandoning it, by being engaged in its opposite, is within his capacity during his disbelief. This is unlike the bringing into existence of substances and accidents, which is not within his capacity at all, neither as an act nor as an abandonment, so obligation to it is not permissible. As for what has been mentioned about the matter of excuses and the obligation to accept them, it is based on the rule of rational goodness and badness (al-tahsin wa-al-taqbih al-'aqliyyan), and proofs of their invalidity have been established in its proper place. Thus it is in al-Mawaqif and its commentary.

The basis of what became widespread from al-Ash'ari, it has been said, is that capacity is an accident which God (may He be exalted) creates in the living being, by which he performs voluntary acts. Therefore it must be concomitant with the act in time, not preceding it, for otherwise it would follow that the act occurs without capacity, given what has been demonstrated about the impossibility of the persistence of accidents. This has been objected to by what is in the arguments for the impossibility of the persistence of accidents of strong consideration, and that it may be said: even granting the aforementioned impossibility, there is no dispute about the possibility of the renewal of similar accidents after their cessation. So from where does it follow that the act occurs without capacity? It has been answered: we only claim that this follows if the capacity by which the act occurs is the prior capacity. But if you make it the renewed, concomitant similar, then you have acknowledged that the capacity by which the act occurs cannot be except concomitant. Then, if you claim that there must be similars that occur so that the act is not possible with the first moment of capacity's coming into being, then the burden of proof is on you.

It is said in response: this is a claim that the denial of the existence of a prior similar is not included in al-Ash'ari's claim, and this contradicts what is known from what was previously stated in describing his doctrine. In al-Mawaqif, he mentioned another argument of al-Ash'ari's for what he claimed and examined it too. This is their statement. The truth in my opinion on this issue is that the condition of obligation is the power which becomes effective by the permission of God (may He be exalted) when the will is joined to it, a will that follows God's will, based on His saying (glorified is He): ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [2:286]. Its clarification is that just as He (exalted is He) is self-sufficient (ghani bi-al-dhat) above the worlds, so He is wise and bountiful. Just as His essential self-sufficiency means that He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, so the requirement of His bounty and mercy, while observing what His wisdom requires (glorified is He), is as al-Adud indicated in 'Uyun al-Jawahir, and Abu 'Abd Allah al-Dimashqi extensively discussed this in Shifa' al-'Alil.

[Page 10]

It is known that wisdom does not require that one be commanded to do an act who is not capable of carrying it out, nor that one be forbidden from it who is not capable of refraining from it. Therefore, by the requirement of the wisdom which He (glorified is He) observed in what He created and commanded, out of grace and mercy, it is necessary that obligation be according to capacity. If this is so, then the condition of obligation is the power which becomes effective when the will is joined to it. This power exists before the act, while the capacity which is together with the act is the capacity possessing all the conditions of influence, among which is the joining of the will to it. With this, Imam al-Razi, as in al-Mawaqif, reconciled the doctrine of al-Ash'ari, who holds that capacity is with the act, and the Mu'tazilah, who hold that it is before it. He said: perhaps al-Ash'ari meant by capacity the power possessing all the conditions of influence, and that is why he ruled that it is with the act and that it does not relate to opposites. And the Mu'tazilah meant by capacity merely the muscular power, and that is why they said it exists before the act and relates to opposing matters. This is a sound reconciliation. But the statement of al-Sayyid (may Allah sanctify his secret), in explaining the discussion which the author of al-Mawaqif mentioned, that created capacity is not effective according to the Shaykh (al-Ash'ari), so how can it be said that he meant by capacity the power possessing all the conditions of influence, is refuted by what has been made clear in al-Ibanah, which is the last of his works.

According to the reliable view of his books, as Ibn 'Asakir, al-Mujidd Ibn Taymiyyah, and others have stated, the Shaykh holds that capacity possessing the conditions has influence, but not independently as the Mu'tazilah say. Rather, it is by the permission of God (may He be exalted), and this is what kasb (acquisition) means according to him. As for his statement in the commentary on al-Mawaqif that the voluntary acts of servants occur by God's capacity alone, and their capacity has no influence on them, but God (may He be exalted) has made it His custom to create in the servant capacity and choice, and when there is no impediment He creates in him the act he has capacity over, concomitant with both, so the act of the servant is created by God (may He be exalted) as origination and innovation, and acquired by the servant, and what is meant by his acquisition of it is its concomitance with his capacity and will without there being any influence or contribution from him in its existence beyond being its locus, and this is the doctrine of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, there is in it a discussion from several aspects.

(First) this is not the doctrine of the aforementioned Shaykh in the last of his writings, on which reliance has been established, and his mention of it in other places, even if granted, is not to be relied upon, since it is a weaker view and one he retracted.

(Second) the obligation in the explicit texts of the Book and the Sunnah relates, as command or prohibition, only to the voluntary acts themselves, not to the concomitance of capacity and will with them. The servant's acquired matter is the voluntary act itself, and what is meant by his acquiring it is his obtaining it by the influence of his capacity by God's permission, not independently. Thus the claim that what is meant by the servant's acquisition of the act is the concomitance of the act with his capacity and will without influence does not agree with what the explicit texts of the Book and the Sunnah require, nor with the texts of al-Ibanah. What makes this clearer is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that when the verse ﴿Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [2:284] was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then knelt and said: "O Messenger of God, we were obligated with deeds we can bear: prayer, fasting, jihad, and charity, and this verse has been revealed to you which we cannot bear." The hadith [continues]. For it is explicit that what they were obligated with is what they can bear of the actions themselves, which is the prayer itself and its like, not its concomitance with their capacity and will. And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) affirmed them in that.

(Third) because if the concomitance of the act with the servant's capacity and will were the acquisition, then that concomitance would be what he is obligated with, and if so, obligation with what cannot be borne would occur, because concomitance is a matter that follows upon the act of God (exalted is He), namely God's bringing the voluntary act into existence concomitant with both. What follows upon the act of God is not within the servant's capacity at all, because the meaning of a thing being within his capacity is that it can be brought about by his capacity when his will is directed toward it, in accordance with God's will, as is clear from the hadith: "Whoever restrains his anger while being able to act on it." What follows upon the act of God cannot be within the servant's capacity in this sense, for if it were within his capacity from the start—

[Page 11]

[p. 11 continued]

It follows that if the conjunction were not dependent on an act of God, either directly or through an intermediary, then the act of God on which it depends would have to be within the servant's capacity. The consequence is false in both its parts, once it is granted that the servant has no influence at all. Therefore the antecedent is false too.

(Fourth) The conjunction, being something that depends on an act of God, does not vary for the servant in difficulty or ease. So if the conjunction were what the servant is obligated to perform, then obligation with the hardest deeds and obligation with the easiest would be equal for the servant. Yet the text of the Book says: "God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity" (2:286), and the text of the Sunnah says that a subordinate is not obligated except with what he can bear. These two texts witness to the difference, just as self-evidence also witnesses to it. This argument has been objected to in several ways.

First: The claim that it is known that wisdom does not require commanding a deed of one who cannot comply with it implies that the acts and rulings of God Most High must contain wisdom and benefit. This is granted. But we do not grant that this benefit must be manifest to us, since the Wise One is not obliged to make His wisdom known to those beneath Him, as al-Qaffal said in *Mahasin al-Shari'ah*. In that case, what prevents one from saying that there is a benefit we have not come to know? The answer: we have not claimed anything beyond that God Most High has observed wisdom in what He commands and creates, out of grace and mercy, not by obligation. This is established by His saying: "the handiwork of God, who perfected everything" (27:88), His saying: "who made excellent everything He created" (32:7), and by the consensus, which is protected from error by the grace of God. The requirement of wisdom is that the attainment of a thing be sought only from one who is able to attain it and capable of it, as the texts bear witness. We have not claimed that the manifestation of the wisdom in all His acts and rulings is obligatory, nor anything that entails that. Showing the wisdom behind a single ruling does not entail a claim of universality. What this comes to is that God Most High has let us know the wisdom in this matter, without it being obligatory for us to know it.

Second: The claim that obligation in the explicit texts of the Book and the Sunnah attaches only to... [the text continues with the objection, which is addressed here]. As for the objection that the matter is one of attachment, not of mere conjunction: the intended meaning is not conjunction in general but conjunction in the mode of attachment. Acquisition (*kasb*) is an expression for the attachment of created capacity to the thing capable, without influence, as in the words of more than one scholar. Commands and prohibitions are attached to acts that are voluntary in appearance, by way of this attachment in which there is no influence. To claim that these texts are explicit in attachment together with influence is disputed; rather they are open to more than one reading. Even if they are granted to be apparent in influence, the apparent may be set aside for a proof to the contrary. As for the claim that "we do not understand from the attachment of capacity anything but its influence, otherwise it is not capacity, so how can capacity have an attachment without influence?", this is a well-known question. Its answer is what is in *Sharh al-Mawaqif* and elsewhere: that influence is a consequence of capacity, though it may be separated from it. It is answered that interpreting acquisition as an attachment with no influence, meaning only apparent acquisition, contradicts the texts stating that the servant is able to bring about his voluntary acts by the permission of God Most High. There is no proof to the contrary that requires departing from this. That God is "the Creator of everything" (13:16) does not negate influence by permission. Moreover, the attachment of capacity follows will, and its attachment on the view that influence is entirely negated is not valid, as the words of al-Jalal al-Dawani in explaining the principles of voluntary acts indicate. It is clarified by the words of the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali in the *Book of Tawhid and Trust* in the *Ihya'*. As for what is in *Sharh al-Mawaqif* and elsewhere, that influence may be separated from capacity, we say the same: what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. What is denied is the total negation of influence from created capacity. As for the argument with what the Proof of Islam mentions in *al-Iqtisad*, that eternal capacity is attached in eternity to the originated, and there is no originated thing, so attachment is valid with no influence, and created capacity may be like that: this is answered by saying that capacity does not exercise influence except in accordance with will, and will was attached from eternity to bringing things into being through capacity at their fitting times in wisdom. So the non-influence of capacity before its time is because it influences in accordance with will, not absolutely. Therefore it is not obligatory for it to influence before the time, and it is obligatory for it to influence at the time. As for created capacity on the view that its influence is wholly negated, it cannot truly be said that it influences in accordance with will, so its analogy with the eternal is not valid.

[p. 12]

The summary: every attachment of the eternal capacity in accordance with will is not separated from influence at its time. By contrast, created capacity, on the view that influence is wholly negated from it, has no influence at all, and so it has no attachment to influence in accordance with will.

Third: As for the objection made in the third point, namely that if it were so, obligation with what cannot be borne would occur, etc. It may be said in response: we accept its occurrence according to al-Ash'ari, and there is no harm in it. It is answered that it has been established in its proper place that Imam al-Ash'ari did not state this explicitly, and it is not valid to derive it from his words. So to hold that it occurs according to him is to hold what he did not say, neither explicitly nor by implication. The statement that there is no harm in it holds only when looking at self-sufficiency (*ghina dhati*). But when looking at the fact that He is generous and wise, holding it contradicts the text. And what harm is more grievous than this?

Fourth: The claim there as well is that if the conjunction were acquisition, then the conjunction would be what is obligated, is not necessary. Acquisition is used for the verbal noun meaning, and it is used for the object, i.e., the acquired, which is the matter itself and not the acquisition in the sense of conjunction or the attachment of created capacity to the act. So the meaning of "acquisition" is that his capacity is attached to the act. If you wish, you may say: his capacity conjoins the act, so the act is acquired, and it is what is obligated. It is answered: real acquisition, as it occurs in the Book and the Sunnah, means the servant's attaining what his will has attached to, which follows the will of God Most High, by his capacity that exercises influence by His permission. The acquired is what he has attained by the said capacity. So the meaning of the acquired act being obligated is that the obligated servant is required to attain it by acquisition in the verbal noun sense, since the acquired is what is attained by the verbal noun. When the acquired is obligated, acquisition in the verbal noun sense is certainly obligated, since the acquired cannot be attained without the verbal noun subsisting in the obligated person, because what is attained by the verbal noun is absent when the verbal noun does not subsist in the obligated person. Thus the implication in the conditional is evident.

(Fifth) The claim in the objection that the conjunction, being something that is a consequence of an act of God Most High, does not vary, etc., contains two matters.

The first: We do not grant that there is necessary connection between the conjunction being what is obligated and its not varying. What prevents it from varying in terms of the person's states in regard to it? Sometimes God Most High creates in him patience and resolve, and sometimes impatience and slackness, and so on, of what returns to soundness of constitution and its opposite, or other accidents and states that God creates and disposes His servant in as He wills, which entail pain or pleasure.

The second: What you have mentioned applies equally to your position. It is said: if the servant's capacity influences by God's permission, then how does difference arise, such that this is easy and that is difficult, though both are within capacity and both are equal in possibility? It is answered: as for the first, the connection between its being a consequence of an act of God Most High and its not varying is established, since if it is acquisition in the verbal noun sense, it is attaining the acquired, and attainment, as it subsists in the obligated person, certainly varies in degrees of difficulty and ease. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then lying on your side."

The conjunction, being a matter that is a consequence of an act of God Most High, does not subsist in the servant, so it does not vary in relation to him at all. The objection that it may vary by some of it being, by God's creation in the servant, patience, etc., is outside the subject, since the expression is explicit that the intended point is that it does not vary for the servant in difficulty or ease, not that it does not vary at all.

As for the second: the texts have shown variation in degrees of strength and force, as in His saying: "they were more numerous than them and greater in strength" (30:9), His saying: "they were stronger than them in power and in traces" (40:21), and His saying: "We destroyed those stronger in might than them" (50:36).
