And since the degrees of this differ among the strong in accordance with their innate, uncreated dispositions, difference arose in deeds in difficulty and ease. This is what we have found of the verification of the truth from the books of our masters, may God sanctify their secrets and make the highest Paradise their abode.

[p. 13]

I have digressed into this discussion here, although partial allusions to some of it appeared earlier, because it is a matter of great importance that should not be neglected. So keep it in mind, for it is a product of deep inquiry, not of the markets' shops. God Most High is the Granter of success; there is no lord but Him.

"And whoever disbelieves, then God is Independent of the worlds" (3:97). It is possible that "whoever disbelieves" means whoever does not perform the Hajj, and the term "disbelief" is used for abandoning the Hajj as a severe rebuke to the one who abandons it. Something similar occurs in what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad and others narrated from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies without having performed the Hajj of Islam, with no visible obstacle, such as sickness that prevents him, or a tyrannical ruler, or a manifest need, let him die in whatever state he wishes, a Jew or a Christian." Similar to this is what was narrated by a sound chain from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I had resolved to send men to these cities to look at everyone who had means but did not perform the Hajj, and to impose the jizya on them, for they are not Muslims."

It is also possible to keep "disbelief" on its apparent sense, based on what Ibn Jarir, Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Ikrima: when the verse "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion" (3:85) was revealed, the Jews said: "We are Muslims." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "God Most High has prescribed for the Muslims the Pilgrimage to the House." They said: "It has not been prescribed for us," and they refused to perform it. Then "And whoever disbelieves" was revealed.

And through the route of al-Dahhak: when the verse of the Hajj was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gathered the people of the religions: the polytheists of the Arabs, the Christians, the Jews, the Magians and the Sabians, and said: "God Most High has prescribed for you the Hajj, so perform the Hajj to the House." None accepted it but the Muslims, and five religions disbelieved in it, saying: "We do not believe in it, nor do we pray towards it, nor do we face it." So God the Glorified revealed: "And whoever disbelieves," etc.

To the apparent sense of the verse went Ibn Abbas. Al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said concerning the verse, reading "and whoever disbelieves [kufr]" with the Hajj, that he did not consider his Hajj a piety nor his abandoning it a sin. Ibn Jarir also narrated that when the verse was revealed, a man from Hudhayl stood up and said: "O Messenger of God, is whoever abandons it a disbeliever?" He said: "Whoever abandons it does not fear its punishment, and whoever performs it does not hope for its reward; that is the matter."

Taking both possibilities into account, the verse cannot serve as evidence for those who claim that the one who commits a major sin (kabirah) is a disbeliever. The word "man" (من) may be conditional (shartiyyah), which is the more apparent reading, or relative (mawsulah). On both readings, the clause after the fa' (فاء) dispenses with a returning pronoun (rabit) by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, since the original would be "fa-inna Allah ghaniyyun 'anhum" (so Allah is free of need of them).

It is also permissible for the plural to remain in its general sense, and the returning pronoun is dispensed with by the inclusion of those mentioned within it in the primary sense. The phrase "istighna'" (independence, being free of need) in this context is, as some have said, a metonymy (kinayah) for displeasure (sukht). For this reason it is valid to make it the apodosis (jaza'), and if you refuse, then it is its proof. In the verse, as they have said, there are various aspects that indicate the complete care given to the matter of the Hajj and the utmost emphasis upon the one who abandons it. They counted among these: the choice of the form of a declarative statement and its presentation in the shape of a nominal sentence, which denotes permanence and continuity, in a way that indicates that it is a binding right of Allah the Exalted upon the people; the generalization of the ruling at first and its specification afterward; calling the abandonment of the Hajj "disbelief" (kufr) insofar as it is the act of disbelievers; and the mention of "istighna'" and "al-'alamin" (the worlds).

Al-Tibi mentioned that in the specification of the comprehensive proper name (Allah) and the fronting of the predicate (khabar) there is an indication that this is an act of worship which should be restricted only to a worshipped one who combines all perfections entirely. And that in placing the explicit noun, which is the House (al-bayt), in the position of the pronoun after it had been mentioned indefinitely, there is an exaggeration in describing it to the utmost extent, as if He had linked the ruling to the appropriate attribute. Likewise, in mentioning "the people" (al-nas) after having mentioned it in definite form, there is an indication of the causal basis (‘illiyyah) of the obligation, which is that they are people. And in the appendix (tadhyil), "And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need of the worlds" — since in meaning it is an emphatic confirmation of the announcement that this (abandoning the Hajj) is disbelief in its reality, and that the one who does it deserves that Allah the Exalted, in His majesty and greatness, is pleased with him with complete pleasure, just as He is displeased with the one who abandons it with a great displeasure. In the specification of this act of worship and its being the clarification of the religion (millah) of Ibrahim (عليه السلام), after the refutation of the People of the Book in the preceding verses and returning to mention them after a grand matter and a momentous affair concerning that great act of worship, some have drawn support for its being a great act of worship from its being among the ancient laws, based on what is reported that Adam (عليه السلام) performed the Hajj forty years on foot from India, and that Gabriel said to him: "Indeed the angels used to circumambulate this House seven thousand years before you." Ibn Ishaq claimed that Allah the Exalted did not send any prophet after Ibrahim except that he performed the Hajj. Others explicitly stated that there was no prophet except that he performed the Hajj, in contrast to those who excepted Hud and Salih (عليهما الصلاة والسلام). Regarding its obligation upon those before us there are two views. It was said: the correct view is that it was not obligatory except upon us, and this is considered strange. A group claimed that it is the best of acts of worship because it comprises both wealth and body. Regarding the time of its obligation there is disagreement: it was said before the Hijrah; it was said in the first year of the Hijrah and so on up to the tenth year; and it was affirmed that it was in the sixth year. Indeed the Prophet (ﷺ) performed the Hajj before prophethood, after it, and before the Hijrah, a number of times whose count is unknown. The designation (of those earlier pilgrimages as Hajj) is metaphorical, in terms of outward form. Rather, it has been said that this also applied to the Hajj of al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) in the ninth year, but the more correct view is otherwise, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was not commanded except with a lawful (shar'i) Hajj. The same is said of the eighth year, in which 'Attab ibn Asid, the governor of Makkah, was appointed. And after that, there was only the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 98:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?"﴾ He addressed them by the title of being People of the Scripture, which necessitates belief in Him and in what confirms Him, as an intensification of the condemnation of their state in denying that. The interrogative is for reproach and an indication of their being unable to offer an excuse for their disbelief, as if it were said: "Produce your excuse, if you are able."

The meaning of "the signs" (al-ayat) is absolutely all the proofs that indicate the prophethood of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the truth of his claim, of which the Hajj (pilgrimage) and the command to perform it are part. By this the connection of the verse to what precedes it becomes apparent. Its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is what Ibn Ishaq and a group related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Shammas ibn Qays passed by, and he was an old man who had become decrepit in the Jahiliyyah, of great disbelief, of intense rancour toward the Muslims, and of intense envy of them, upon a group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the Aws and the Khazraj, in a gathering that had brought them together, in which they were conversing. What angered him was what he saw of their harmony, their unity, and the good state of their relations upon Islam, after the enmity that had existed between them in the Jahiliyyah. So he said: 'The chiefs of the Banu Qaylah have gathered in this land. By Allah, we have no place among them when their chiefs gather here.' He then commanded a young man with him from among the Jews, saying: 'Go to them, sit with them, then remind them of the Day of Bu'ath and what came before it, and recite to them some of what they used to exchange of poetry about it.' The Day of Bu'ath was a day on which the Aws and the Khazraj fought, and victory on it went to the Aws over the Khazraj. So he did that. The people then spoke, disputed, and boasted, until two men from the two clans leapt up onto their knees: Aws ibn Qayzi, one of the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and Habbar ibn Sakhr, one of the Banu Salimah of the Khazraj. They quarrelled, then one of them said to his companion: 'If you wish, by Allah, we can take it back right now.' Both groups grew angry and said: 'Weapons! Weapons! Our meeting place is al-Zahirah,' and al-Zahirah is al-Harrah. They went out to it, and the Aws joined together, some with others, and the Khazraj joined together, some with others, upon their claim which they had held in the Jahiliyyah. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the emigrants (muhajirun) among his Companions who were with him, until he came to them and said: 'O assembly of Muslims! Allah, Allah! Do you call to the claims of the Jahiliyyah while I am among you, after Allah has guided you to Islam, honoured you with it, cut off from you the affair of the Jahiliyyah, rescued you by it from disbelief, and united your hearts by it? Would you return to what you were upon as disbelievers?' The people then recognised that it was a prod from Satan and a scheme against them from their enemy. So they threw the weapons from their hands, wept, and the men embraced one another. Then they departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), listening and obeying, while Allah had extinguished from them the scheme of the enemy of Allah, Shammas. Allah revealed concerning Shammas and what he did: ﴿Say, 'O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve?'﴾ until His saying, glorified is He: [Page 15] ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ And He revealed concerning Aws ibn Qayzi, Habbar, and those who were with them from their people, who did what they did: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those given the Scripture...﴾ the verse." On this basis, the meaning of "People of the Scripture" is apparently the Jews.

It was also said: what is meant by it includes both the Jews and the Christians.

﴿And Allah is Witness over what you do.﴾ (98) This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah, a clause in the accusative of state), whose governing element (al-'amil) is "you disbelieve." It serves to intensify the reproach. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is for what has passed more than once. The shahid (witness) is the knowing, the one who is fully aware. The intensive form (sigha al-mubalaghah) is for emphasis in the warning. Taking shahid to mean shahid (in the sense of "witnessing") is a forced interpretation for which there is no need. The word "ma" (ما) is either a reference to their disbelief, or it is in its general sense, and it includes that [disbelief] as a primary inclusion. The meaning is: "For what reason do you disbelieve, while the situation is that nothing whatsoever of all your deeds is hidden from Him, and He will recompense you for them in the most perfect manner?" There is no doubt that this is among the things that close off for you the paths of disbelief and sins, and cut off their causes entirely.

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert﴾ meaning, you turn away, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ meaning, His path that leads to Him, which is the religion of Islam ﴿those who believe﴾ meaning, in Allah and in what came from Him; or, those who affirm that path and believe in that religion in actuality, or with a near potential by intending it and resolving upon it. The prepositional phrase is the object of ﴿تَصُدُّونَ﴾ (you avert), and it was placed before it for emphasis on it.

(﴿تَبْغُونَها﴾) meaning, the way. (﴿عِوَجًا﴾) meaning, crookedness and deviation from straightness. The word is used with a kasra on the ʿayn (عِوَجًا) for religion, speech, and land, as in ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness﴾. The word with a fatha on the ʿayn (عَوَجًا) is used for the inclination of any upright thing, such as a spear or a wall, for example. The word here is one of the two objects of ﴿تَبْغُونَ﴾ (you seek), since bagha (بغى) takes two objects, one directly and the other with the preposition *li* (لِ), as the lexicographers have stated. Its transitivity to the pronoun *ha* (الهاء, "it") is by way of elision and conveyance (من باب الحذف والإيصال), meaning, "you seek for it [the way]," as in the verse:

*So their servant turned and called out, "Shall I hunt for you a gazelle or a donkey?"*

He intended, "Shall I hunt for you?" Ibn al-Munir said: "It is better to make the pronoun the object without needing to presume the preposition." And (﴿عِوَجًا﴾) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) that stands in the place of a noun, for emphasis, as if they were requesting that the upright path itself become the crooked thing. Al-Tibi claimed that there is a problem with this, since the meaning is only correct if (﴿عِوَجًا﴾) is the direct object, because it is what they seek; so the preposition must be presumed. There is consideration in this. It was also said: (﴿عِوَجًا﴾) is a circumstantial accusative from the subject of ﴿تَبْغُونَ﴾, and the discussion about it is like the discussion about the previous one. In any case, the clause ﴿تَبْغُونَ﴾ is either a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of ﴿تَصُدُّونَ﴾ or from "the way," or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought as an explanation of that averting.

Most scholars hold that this averting was by stirring up discord and incitement among the believers, so that their word would differ and the affairs of their religion would be disrupted, as is indicated by what we cited in explaining the occasion of revelation. On this basis, the intended meaning of "People of the Scripture" is the Jews as well, and the address by this title is because of what preceded. Repeating the address and the question is for the sake of intensifying the rebuke and reproach against them for their ugly deeds and their details. Had it been said, "Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah and avert from the way of Allah?", it might have been supposed that the reproach was for the combination of the two matters.

It was also said: the address is to the People of the Scripture in general, and their averting from the way was by their denial and their altering of the description of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. This was the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. According to al-Suddi, whenever someone asked them, "Do you find Muhammad in your books?" they would say, "No," thereby averting him from belief in him. This is a censure of them for misguiding others, following their censure for going astray.

It was recited as (﴿تَصُدُّونَ﴾) from *aṣudda* (أصُدُّ). ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of ﴿تَصُدُّونَ﴾ or from the subject of ﴿تَبْغُونَ﴾. Taking it as a new sentence (isti'naf) goes against the apparent sense. The meaning is: how can you do this while you are scholars who know, who are aware of the earlier announcement of him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and who know the truth of his prophethood? Or it means: while you are upright (ʿudūl) in the eyes of the people of your religion, who trust your words and ask you to testify in matters; and your present state requires the opposite of what you are doing. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ (99) is a warning to them for what they have done. It was said: since their disbelief was manifest, it was fitting to mention witnessing alongside it in the previous verse, because witnessing is for what is apparent and known. Or, since their averting from the way of Allah, along with what accompanies it, was by deceit and hidden trickery that passes over the heedless, it was fitting to mention heedlessness alongside it in this verse. For this reason, each of the two verses was concluded with what it was concluded with.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 100:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ (100)

This is an address to the Aws and the Khazraj, in accordance with what the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) requires. Other believers also enter into the general meaning of the wording. God Most High addressed them Himself, after commanding His Messenger (ﷺ) to address the People of the Book, in order to show the greatness of their rank and to indicate that they are the most deserving of being addressed and spoken to directly by God. Therefore there is no need to say that the one addressed is the Messenger, with an implied "say to them" (qul lahum).

By "a faction" is meant some unspecified group, or it is Shammas ibn Qays the Jew. Restricting it to him serves as an intensification of the warning; for this reason, it is said, the object of the verb has been omitted. Some have said: the meaning is, if you obey them by accepting their words that revive the enmities which existed between you in the Jahiliyyah.

As for ﴿kafirin﴾ (disbelievers), it may be a second object of ﴿yaruddukum﴾ (they will return you), with the verb "return" being construed to carry the sense of "make" (tadmin al-radd ma'na al-tasyir), as in the verse of the poet:

"Fate struck the women of the family of Sa'd with a decree, so they became mourners for it, mourning.
So it turned their black hair white, and it turned their white faces black."

Or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its object. They said: the first is more effective in exonerating the believers from being attributed to disbelief, since it explicitly states that the disbelief is imposed by way of compulsion (qasr).

"After" (ba'da) may be an adverbial of time (zarf) for ﴿yaruddukum﴾, or an adverbial of time for ﴿kafirin﴾. Its mention, though there is no need for it since the address itself suffices for it, and the impossibility of returning to disbelief without prior belief, and its placement between the two accusatives, serve to show the full abhorrence of disbelief; and the extreme remoteness of its occurrence is either to increase its ugliness, or because belief prevents it, as if it were said: "after your firm belief." In this there is a strengthening of the believers that is not hidden. He placed the rebuke of the disbelievers before this address because the disbelievers were like the motivating cause for it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 101:**

﴿And how can you disbelieve?﴾ That is, in what state could disbelief come from you, ﴿while the verses of Allah are recited to you﴾, which indicate His oneness and the prophethood of His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿and among you is His Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), who teaches you the Book and the wisdom and purifies you by establishing the truth and removing doubts. This clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the pronoun of the addressees in (takfurun, "you disbelieve"), and the purpose is to make it seem unlikely that disbelief could come from them when they have what rejects it. 

It has also been said that the purpose is to express astonishment, meaning: it is not fitting for you to disbelieve in any circumstance, especially in this situation, in which disbelief is more grievous than in other situations. The purpose is not to deny that it has occurred, as in ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ and the verse that follows. It has also been said that their disbelief refers to their committing the deeds of unbelievers, such as the calls of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period). In that case there is no obstacle to the interrogative being a denial that it has occurred, but the first view is better. In the verse there is also a discouragement to the Jews from what they had sought. Most scholars restrict this address to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to the Aws and Khazraj among them. Some have made it general to all believers and the whole community, and in that case the meaning of his (ﷺ) being among them is that his traces and the evidences of his prophethood are among them, since these remain until the command of Allah comes. Allah, glorified is He, did not attribute the recitation to His Messenger, peace be upon him, to indicate that each of the two matters is independently sufficient in the matter, and to notify that recitation is sufficient for the purpose from whichever reciter it comes.

Page 17

﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah﴾: either a noun is to be understood, meaning, "whoever holds fast to the religion of Allah," and "holding fast" (i'tisam) in the sense of adherence is a subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara tabi'iyya); or no noun is understood, and "holding fast to Allah" is made a metaphor for seeking refuge in Him, glorified is He. Al-Tibi said: according to the first, the clause is conjoined to ﴿and you are being recited to﴾, meaning: how can you disbelieve, while the Qur'an is recited to you and you know the state of the One to whom one holds fast, glorified is His majesty? According to the second, it is a concluding clause (tadhyil) to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, if you obey﴾, etc., since its content is that you only obey them out of fear of their evils and schemes, so do not fear them, but seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, for the averting of their evils, and do not obey them. Do you not know that whoever seeks refuge in Allah, exalted is He, is sufficed against the evil he fears? Thus according to the first, this clause is brought to deny disbelief along with this strong deterrent understood from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you are being recited to﴾, etc. According to the second, it is for urging seeking refuge. It is possible on the first to take it as a concluding clause, and on the second, as a circumstantial clause too, so understand. ﴿Whoever﴾ (man) is conditional, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿has been guided to a straight path﴾ (101) is the response of the condition. Because it is in the past tense with "qad," the statement conveys the certainty of guidance, as though it has already been achieved. It has been said that the tanwin (nunation) is for magnification, and the description of the path as "straight" is to explicitly reject those who seek to make it crooked. Although the straight path is in reality the true religion, and being guided to it is holding fast to it itself, yet since the two considerations differ, and the latter heading is one for which competitors compete, it is presented in the form of a response, to urge and encourage, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has succeeded﴾. End.

You know that this, despite what it contains, is only needed if the meaning of holding fast to Allah is faith in Him, glorified is He, and adherence to His religion, as Ibn Jurayj said. But if its meaning is trust in Allah, exalted is He, reliance upon Him and seeking refuge in Him, as was reported from Abu al-Aliya, then the need for it is far-fetched. In that case the meaning of being guided to the straight path is salvation and success in finding a way out. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted from al-Zuhri, who said: Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "No servant holds fast to Me, apart from My creation, while the heavens and the earth plot against him, but I will make for him a way out from that. And no servant holds fast to a created being apart from Me, but I will cut the means of the heaven before his eyes, and make the earth sink from beneath his feet."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 102:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ He repeated the address with this title to honour them, and the gentleness in its repetition after the address to the People of the Book is not hidden. ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾, that is, with the fear that is due to Him. Many have related from Ibn Mas'ud, both as a statement of his own (mawquf) and as a report traced to the Prophet (marfu'): "It is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, and thanked and not disbelieved." Many have claimed that this verse was abrogated (naskh), and this has been related from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: When it was revealed, the act of worship became burdensome for the people, so they stood (in prayer) until their ankles swelled and their foreheads were ulcerated. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed, as a relief for the Muslims, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾, and this abrogated the first verse. A similar report comes from Anas and Qatadah. One of the two reports from Ibn Abbas is also of this kind, while Ibn Jarir related through some chains from him that he said: It was not abrogated, but "the fear due to Him" means that they strive for Allah with the striving due to Him, and that no blame of any blamer deters them regarding Allah, the Exalted, and that they stand for Allah, glorified is He, with justice, even against themselves, their fathers and their mothers. Whoever holds to abrogation inclines to the view that what is meant by "the fear due to Him" is what is befitting for Him and suitable to His majesty and greatness, and that is not possible, for ﴿they have not esteemed Allah with the esteem due to Him﴾. Whoever holds that there is no abrogation inclines to the view that the word "haqq" (due/right) derives from "haqqa al-shay'" meaning "it became obligatory and established," and the idafa (construction) is of the type of attributing a quality to what it describes, and that the original sense is "fear Allah with a fear that is true," i.e.

صفحة 18

established and obligatory, on the pattern of "I struck Zayd a severe striking," meaning a severe blow. Then His words, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾, would be an explanation of His words ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i claimed that the view of abrogation is invalid because of what it entails regarding the permissibility of some sins. Al-Rummani responded to him that when the words ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ are understood as meaning that they should uphold the truth in fear and in security, what he mentioned does not apply, for it is not impossible that He obligated them to fear Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in every state, and then permitted abandoning the obligation when there is fear for one's self, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith﴾. You know that what al-Jubba'i mentioned only occurs to the mind so as to require an answer if ﴿the fear due to Him﴾ is interpreted, on the assumption of abrogation, as he interpreted it, namely abandoning all sins and the like. But if it is not interpreted that way, and is instead interpreted as the abrogationist inclined to, then what he mentioned hardly occurs to the mind so as to need an answer. Indeed, the denial of abrogation in that case would be based on what the Mu'tazilah held regarding the impossibility of imposing obligations one cannot bear from the outset, as is not hidden. The root of (tuqat) is (wuqayah), whose waw, when it takes a damma, is changed to a ta', as in (tuhmah) and (tukhamah), and whose ya', when it takes a fatha, becomes an alif. Al-Zajjaj permitted three forms for it: tuqah, wiqah, and iqah.

﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ (201), that is, devoted yourselves wholly to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not associating with Him anything at all. Some of the verifiers have mentioned that Islam in such a context does not mean the deeds, but rather the inner faith, because deeds are hardly feasible at the moment of death. That is why it is reported in the supplication at the funeral prayer: "O Allah, whomever of us You keep alive, keep alive upon Islam, and whomever of us You cause to die, cause to die upon faith." So Islam was mentioned first and faith second, since every situation has its own speech. The exception is from the most general of states, meaning: do not die in any state except the state in which your Islam is established and your steadfastness upon it, as the nominal sentence indicates. Had it been said "except as Muslims," it would not have occupied this position. The governing element of the state is what precedes "except" after its removal, and the intended meaning is the prohibition against being in any state other than the state of Islam at death. It returns to the obligation of remaining steadfast upon Islam until death, except that the prohibition was directed at death for the sake of emphasis in forbidding the condition mentioned, and the intent is not a prohibition of death itself, since it is not within their power so that they could be forbidden from it. In al-Suyuti's Tahbir: Among the strange things that have become well known in the interpretation of (muslimun) is the statement of the common people: "that is, married," and this is a view with no known basis. It is not permitted to venture into interpreting the speech of Allah the Exalted merely on the basis of what occurs to the soul or is heard from one who bears no responsibility, end quote.

Abu Abd Allah (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) read (muslimun) with a shadda, and its meaning is "submitting to what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, and yielding to him." In this verse there is an emphasis on the prohibition against obeying the People of the Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 103:

﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾: that is, the Qur'an. This was related with a sound chain of transmission from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him).

More than one narrator reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Book of Allah is the rope of Allah, stretched from the heaven to the earth."

Ahmad reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am leaving among you two successors: the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, stretched between the heaven and the earth, and my family, the People of my House. They will not part from each other until they come to me at the Basin." Many reports with similar meaning have come down. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the rope of Allah" is obedience and community (al-jama'ah), and this too was related from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Sha'bi, from Thabit ibn Qutnah al-Muzani, who said: I heard Ibn Mas'ud giving a sermon, saying: "O people, upon you is obedience and community, for they are the rope of Allah, the Exalted, which He commanded." In another report from him: "The rope of Allah, the Exalted, is the community." This was also related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and Abu al-'Aliyah, that it is sincerity to Allah alone. From al-Hasan, that it is obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From Ibn Zayd, that it is Islam. From Qatadah, that it is the covenant of Allah and His command. All of these are close in meaning.

In the statement there is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah, a metaphor drawn from a whole scene), in which the state of the believers, in seeking support from one of the things mentioned and trusting in its protection, is likened to the state of one who clings to a sturdy rope, secure against breaking, while hanging from a high place. This involves no figurative usage (majaz) in the individual words, and the terms used for the comparison (al-mushabbah bihi) were borrowed for the thing compared (al-mushabbah). It is possible that there are two synonymous metaphors in the statement: the rope is borrowed for the covenant, for example, as a clear, original metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah asliyyah), with the indicator (qarinah) being the genitive construction; and holding fast (i'tisam) is borrowed for trusting in the covenant and clinging to it, as a clear, derivative metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah tab'iyyah), with the indicator being its being joined with the second metaphor. It is also possible that in (i'tasamu) there is a derivative figurative usage (majaz mursal tab'i) based on the relation of generality and specificity. It may even be a figurative usage at two levels, due to the sending of the figurative usage (irsal al-majaz). It is also possible that the metaphor is only in the rope, while holding fast (al-i'tisam) remains in its literal meaning, as a supporting elaboration (tarshih) of it in the most complete manner. The indicator may vary with the manner of treatment: from one perspective it may prevent the literal reading, and from another it may not. Therefore, it is not objectionable that the possibility of a figurative reading depends on a preventing indicator against intending the literal meaning; for with its presence, how could the literal meaning be intended so that both readings are valid in (i'tasamu)? The metaphors may also be non-independent: the metaphor in the rope may be implicit (makniyyah), while in holding fast it is imaginative (takhyiliyyah), because the implicit metaphor entails the imaginative one. This was stated by al-Tibi, though it is far-fetched, as is well known.

We have mentioned in our glosses on the treatise of Ibn Isam what refutes some of these aspects, together with the answer to that. Return to it if you wish. ( ﴿all together﴾ ) is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of (i'tasimu), as is the apparent and obvious reading, meaning: gathered upon it. Then the words of the Exalted, ﴿and do not separate﴾, are an emphasis (ta'kid), based on the meaning: "and do not separate from the truth which you were commanded to hold fast to." It has also been said that the meaning is: there should not occur among you discord and wars, as is intended by those who remind you of the days of ignorance, deceiving you. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not separate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was related from al-Hasan.

﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you﴾: that is, its kind. Among it is guidance and success in Islam, which leads to harmony and the removal of enmity. It may also be that what is intended is what He, glorified be He, explained with His words: ﴿when you were enemies﴾, that is, in the days of ignorance, ﴿and He brought your hearts together﴾ through Islam. ( blessing (ni'mah) ) is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its subject, and ( upon you (alaykum) ) is either attached to it or is a circumstantial state of it. ( when (idh) ) is either an adverbial complement of the blessing or of the settledness in ( upon you (alaykum) ) if you make it a circumstantial state. It has been said: by what He mentioned, the Exalted intended what occurred between the Aws and the Khazraj of wars that lasted one hundred and twenty years, until He, glorified be He, brought them together through Islam and the grudges were removed. This is what Ibn Ishaq said. The Day of Bu'ath was the last of the wars that took place between them, and this is detailed in al-Kamil. It has also been said: He intended what occurred among the polytheist Arabs of long disputes and wide-ranging fighting, including the War of al-Basus. This was related from al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿So by His blessing you became brothers﴾: that is, you became, by means of His blessing, which is that harmony, loving one another. ( aṣbaḥa ) is here a defective verb (naqisah) of the kind that takes a predicate, and ( brothers (ikhwanan) ) is its predicate. It has been said: ( aṣbaḥtum ) means you entered the morning, and in that case the preposition ( bi, by ) is attached to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial state of the subject, and likewise ( ikhwanan ). That is: so you became, being clothed in His blessing, while being brothers. The word ( al-ikhwan ) is the plural of ( akh, brother ), and the plural most commonly used for a brother of friendship is that, according to the correct view. In al-Itqan it is stated: the brother by lineage has the plural ( ikhwah ), and the brother by friendship has the plural ( ikhwan ). This was said by Ibn Faris, though others disagreed. He cited for friendship: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾, and for lineage: (or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or the houses of your brothers).

﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾ [Page 20]: that is, you were on the edge of a pit of Hell, for there was nothing between you and it but death. The interpretation of ( al-shafa, the brink ) as ( al-tarf, the edge ) is related from al-Suddi regarding this verse, and it is attested among the Arabs. It is dualized as ( shafawan ), pluralized as ( ashfa' ), and annexed to the higher part, as in ( shafa jurf hair, the brink of a crumbling cliff ), and to the lower part, as is said to be the case here. That the intended meaning of the Fire is what we have mentioned is the apparent meaning, and taking it to mean the fire of war is far-fetched.

﴿And He saved you from it﴾: that is, through Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Abbas. The pronoun in the genitive case (in "from it") refers either to the Fire, or to ( pit ), or to ( brink ), since it carries the sense of ( the edge ), or because it acquires feminine gender from its annexed noun, as in the verse:

*And she chokes on the word you have spread, as the chest of the spear chokes with blood.*

For an annexed noun acquires feminine gender from the noun annexed to it if it is a part of it, or an action of it, or a qualifier of it, as they have explicitly stated, and what we are dealing with is of the first type. Whoever makes it general is committed to permitting "stood (f.) the boy of Hind." Al-Zamakhshari chose the last possibility. Ibn al-Munir said: The return of the pronoun to the pit is more complete, because it is the one from which the favour of rescue is literally bestowed. As for the favour of rescue from the brink, it rarely entails that being on the brink usually leads to falling into the pit, so the rescue from the brink is a rescue from the pit into which one is expected to fall. Thus attributing the favour to rescue from the pit is more eloquent and more effective. Moreover, acquiring feminine gender from the annexed noun was counted by Abu 'Ali in al-Ta'aliq among the necessities of poetry, contrary to his view in al-Idah. What led al-Zamakhshari to return the pronoun to the brink was only that this is the state they were in, and they were not yet in the pit so that He would favour them with rescue from the pit. He knew that they were heading toward it had it not been for divine rescue, so the favour was emphasized. Do you not see the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "One who grazes around the sanctuary is about to fall into it," and the words of the Exalted: ﴿Is one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, so that it collapsed with him into the Fire of Hell?﴾ Observe how the Exalted made the building's being on the brink a cause leading to its collapse into the Fire of Hell, with the emphasis of that through His words, glorified be He, "crumbling" (hair). End of quote. From this it is known what is in the statement of Abu Hayyan, that the return of the pronoun is only fitting to the brink, because their being on it is one of the two parts of the predication, so the pronoun returns only to it, not to the pit, since the pit is not what is spoken of, nor to the Fire, since it was only mentioned to specify the pit.

Furthermore, rescue from the brink is more eloquent than rescue from the pit and from the Fire, and rescue from those two does not entail rescue from the brink. So its return to the brink is the apparent reading both in terms of wording and meaning. Yes, what he mentioned, that its return to the brink is the apparent reading in terms of wording, is evident on the basis that the default is for the pronoun to return to the annexed noun rather than the annexing noun when it can refer to either, even by interpretation. However, it may be omitted, so it returns to the annexed noun, either absolutely, as is the view of Ibn al-Munir, or on condition that it is a part of it or like a part of it, as in the verse of Jarir:

*I see the passing of years has taken from me.*

For the passing of years is of its kind. This is the view of al-Wahidi, and the condition exists in our case.

﴿Thus﴾: that is, like that clear explanation, ﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾: that is, His proofs regarding what He commanded you and forbade you from, ﴿that you may be guided﴾ (103): that is, so that you may persist in guidance, and that your increase in it, as the fact that the address is to the believers indicates, or the form of the present tense from the reflexive form (iftaʿala), may be implied.

[p. 21]

Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to work for the good of others right after commanding them to perfect themselves, so that they would be guiding and guided, opposed to their enemies. What Allah the Exalted related of their condition in the past indicates that they were astray and leading others astray. Most readers pronounce the lam of the command with a sukun, but it has also been read with a kasra, which is the original form. The verb *takun* (let there be) may be from *kana* (to be) used as a complete verb, in which case *ummah* (a community) is its subject, the clause *yad'una* (who call) is its description, and *minkum* (from among you) is connected to *takun* or to an omitted element, as a description of *ummah* that was moved before it and so became a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Or it may be from *kana* used as a incomplete verb (nāqisa), in which case *ummah* is its subject and *yad'una* is its predicate, and *minkum* is either a circumstantial clause from *ummah* or connected to the incomplete *kana*.

The *ummah* is the group that aims (*taʾummu*), that is, intends a particular matter. It is also applied to the followers of the prophets because they gather around one goal; to a model to be followed, as in *Indeed Abraham was an ummah* (16:120); to religion and creed, as in *Indeed we found our fathers upon an ummah* (43:23); and to a period of time, as in *And he remembered after an ummah* (12:45). It has other meanings beyond these. The intended sense of "calling to good" is calling to what contains religious or worldly welfare. So the joining of "enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong" to it, in His words *and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong*, is an instance of joining the specific to the general, signifying the great excellence of these two over all other goods. This is what has been said. Ibn al-Munayyir said: "This is not of that type, because after the general term he mentioned everything it includes. The good to which one calls is either a commanded act or a forbidden abstention, and it does not exceed either of these two, so that singling them out would distinguish them from the rest of what it includes. Rather, the better view is that the purpose of this specification is to mention calling to good first in general and then in detail. The repetition of the mention in two ways carries the care that is not hidden, unless a custom is established that restricts enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong to some kinds of good, in which case what was mentioned is complete. But I do not see this custom as established." He ended. He has a sound point, because if calling to good were explained as including worldly affairs, even those not connected to any command or prohibition, it would be broader than communal obligation (*fard al-kifaya*), and this is not free of difficulty. Moreover, Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: *And let there be among you a community that calls to good* (3:104), then said: 'The good is following the Qur'an and my Sunnah.'" This indicates that calling to good does not include calling to worldly matters.

Some people explained "good" as a specific kind of right action, namely faith in Allah the Exalted, and took "what is right" (*maʿrūf*) in the verse to be what is other than that among the acts of obedience. In that case, what Ibn al-Munayyir said does not arise either. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil, that "the good" is Islam, "the right" is obedience to Allah, and "the wrong" (*munkar*) is disobedience to Him. The omission of the direct object from the three verbs is either to inform that it is evident, i.e., they call people, even if they are not accountable, and they command them and forbid them; or to aim at the act itself, as in the expression "so-and-so gives," i.e., they perform the calling, the commanding, and the forbidding and bring them about. The address is said to be directed to those to whom the first address was directed in one opinion, namely the Aws and the Khazraj. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak that it is directed specifically to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who were the transmitters. Most scholars hold that it is general, and whoever has been mentioned enters it in the first instance. As for *min* (from) here, it has been said to be partitive (*lil-tabʿīḍ*), and it has been said to be explanatory (*lil-tabyīn*). It is also said to be abstractive (*tajrīdiyya*), as one says: "So-and-so has from his children a soldier," and "the commander has from his servants an army," meaning all the children and servants.

The root of the disagreement on this is that the scholars agreed that enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a communal obligation (*fard al-kifaya*), and only a few have disagreed with this. Among them is Shaykh Abu Jaʿfar of the Imamiyya (Twelver Shiʿa), who said that it is an individual obligation (*fard al-ʿayn*). They differed over whether an obligation of the communal type is binding on all the responsible persons, and falls away from them when some of them perform it, or whether it is binding on only some. Imam al-Razi and his followers held the second view, since it is sufficient that it be fulfilled by some; if it were obligatory on all, the performance by some would not suffice, for it is unlikely that an obligation would fall from a responsible person through the act of another. The majority held the first view, which is the apparent meaning of the text of Imam al-Shafiʿi in *al-Umm*. They argued for it from the fact that all are sinful when it is abandoned; had it not been obligatory on all of them, they would not have sinned by abandoning it.

The first group answered this by saying that their sin in abandoning it is for their failure to bring about what was intended to be achieved from them in general, not because it is obligatory on each of them. The majority objected to this by saying that it is precisely this which is unlikely, namely that a group is sinful for the abandonment by another group of an act they were charged with. The answer to this is that the falling away of the obligation from others through their performance is no more fitting than the sinfulness of others through their abandonment; it may be said that the latter is in fact more fitting, because a parallel of it is established by revelation: the falling away of what is upon Zayd through the payment by ʿAmr; but the sinfulness of a person for another's abandonment has not been established. Thus what the majority said is complete.

The objection that this is what is unlikely is answered: it would only follow if the charge in the apparent sense were tied specifically to that other group alone. But this is not so; rather both groups are equal in the possibility that the command applies to them and is connected to them, with no preference of one over the other. So in the mentioned sinfulness there is no sinfulness of one group for the abandonment by another of an act with which it was charged, since it is not known that the other group was charged with it; rather both groups are equal in the possibility that each is charged with it. Thus the said unlikelihood is misplaced. Moreover, if we follow what a group among the adherents of the second view chose, that the indefinite part is ambiguous, the situation becomes that the responsible one is a group not specified individually. Then the responsible is the common notion shared among the groups, which applies to each group. All groups are then equal in the address being connected to them through its connection to the shared notion, which is equal among them. So there is no difficulty in the name "all," and the dispute between the two groups does not become verbal, since on both views the address then includes everyone. Likewise the sinfulness upon abandonment, because one of the two views claims the connection to each one individually, while the other claims its connection to each through spreading from the connection to the shared notion. The result of this is that whoever doubts whether another has performed that obligation is not bound by it under the view of spreading, but is bound under the view of initiation; and he is not relieved of it unless he thinks the other has performed it. From here one can dispense with answering what was raised against the majority, and what was said about it does not harm us. Moreover, it may be said, according to what has been said, that debt is not entirely a parallel to what we are discussing, because the debt of Zayd is binding upon him alone in the apparent sense, and has no connection to anyone else. Therefore it is valid for it to fall from him through another's payment, but it is not valid that another should be sinful for its non-payment. By contrast, in what we are discussing, the attribution of the obligation in the apparent sense to both groups is equal, so it is possible that each group be sinful for the abandonment of the other, because the obligation is attached to them in the apparent sense, and they are equal with the others in this attachment.

As for their saying: "it has not been established that a person is sinful through another's performance," this does not correspond to the discussion, since the claim is not that someone is sinful through another's performance, but that he is sinful through an abandonment. So the corresponding statement is: "it has not been established that a person is sinful through another's abandonment of performance." It may be resolved from this by saying that the connection in the apparent sense is shared among all the groups, so what Imam al-Razi and his followers held is complete, and this is the view chosen by Ibn al-Subki, contrary to his father. Once this is established, know that those who hold that the responsible are some said that *min* is partitive, and those who hold that the responsible are all said that it is explanatory. They supported this by saying that Allah the Exalted established the command to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong for the whole community in His words: *You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong* (3:110). This does not require that calling to good be an individual obligation (*fard al-ʿayn*), since jihad is a communal obligation by consensus although it is established by general addresses. So reflect.

*And those* (*wa-ulāʾika*): that is, those described by these perfect attributes.

*They are the successful* (*hum al-mufliḥūn*) (3:104): that is, the complete in success. By this, the restriction derived from the separating pronoun and the definiteness of both extremes is valid. Imam Ahmad and Abu Yaʿla transmitted from Durra bint Abi Lahab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Who is the best of people?' He said: 'The one who most enjoins what is right, most forbids what is wrong, is most mindful of Allah the Exalted, and most keeps the ties of kinship.'"

And al-Hasan transmitted: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the vicegerent (*khalīfa*) of Allah the Exalted, the vicegerent of His Messenger (ﷺ), and the vicegerent of His Book." And it has been related: "You will certainly enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or Allah will surely set over you a tyrannical ruler who does not honour your elder and does not show mercy to your young; your best will call, but they will not be answered; and you will seek help, but you will not be helped."

Enjoining what is right is obligatory or recommended according to what it is enjoined to; likewise forbidding what is wrong, if we say that what is disliked (*makruh*) is wrong in the sacred law. But if it is explained as what deserves punishment, just as what is right is what deserves reward, then it is only obligatory. Some have said so, except that it is objected that the two are not opposite poles. The more evident view is that the sinner must be forbidden from what he commits, because it is obligatory to forbid every doer; leaving the forbidding of some, namely himself, does not remove the obligation to forbid the rest. The same is said regarding the command. This is not disturbed by His words: *Why do you say what you do not do?* (61:2), because it is interpreted to mean that the forbidding is of not doing, not of speaking. Nor by His words: *Do you enjoin righteousness upon people and forget yourselves?* (2:44), because the rebuke is only for forgetting themselves, not for their commanding righteousness. And one of the early pious said: "Command the good, even if you do not do it." Indeed, there are well-known conditions for enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, whose place is elsewhere. The basic forms of them are: "Do this" and "Do not do that." Fighting, so that the commanded or forbidden person obeys, is a matter beyond that and is not part of their essence, even if it becomes obligatory for some, such as rulers, at certain times, because that is a separate ruling, as His words (ﷺ) indicate: "Command your children to pray when they are seven years old, strike them for it when they are ten years old, and separate them in their beds."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 105:

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾, namely the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'.

Ibn Majah narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects: one is in Paradise and seventy are in the Fire. The Christians split into seventy-two sects: seventy-one are in the Fire and one is in Paradise. By the One in whose hand is my soul, my community will split into seventy-three sects: one is in Paradise and seventy-two are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they?" He said: "The main body (al-Jama'ah)."

In a narration of Ahmad from Mu'awiyah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The People of the Book split in their religion into seventy-two creeds, and this community will split into seventy-three, all of them in the Fire except one."

In another narration of Ahmad from Anas, also traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Children of Israel split into seventy-one sects, seventy sects perished and one sect was saved. My community will split into seventy-two sects; seventy-one sects will perish and one sect will be saved."

There is no contradiction between these narrations, because the division occurred in some periods in accordance with what is mentioned in them, and that suffices for the truth of the statement, even if the number increased or decreased at another time.

﴿And they differed﴾ concerning monotheism, divine transcendence, and the states of the Hereafter. It has been said: this is the meaning of "became divided," and it was repeated for emphasis. It has also been said: "becoming divided" refers to enmity, and "differing" refers to religious belief.

﴿After the clear proofs had come to them﴾: that is, the signs and arguments that make the truth clear and that necessitate unity of the word. al-Hasan said: "the Torah." Qatadah and Abu Umamah said: "the Qur'an."

﴿And those﴾ refers to those mentioned, considered in terms of their being characterized by what is in the relative clause. ﴿For them is a great punishment﴾ (501), which cannot be fully described, because of their division and the difference mentioned. In this there is a warning for them and a threat to those who imitate them, because resembling those upon whom anger has fallen requires anger.

Furthermore, this blameworthy difference is, as has been said, to be understood as difference in the fundamental principles (usul) and not in the subsidiary rulings (furu'). This restriction is derived from the comparison. It has also been said that it includes both the fundamentals and the subsidiary rulings, because we see the disagreement of the People of the Sunnah on them, such as al-Maturidi and al-Ash'ari. In that case, the prohibition of disagreement refers to disagreement about matters for which there is a text from the Lawgiver or on which there is consensus. This is not a far-fetched view.

The non-prohibition of disagreement in subsidiary rulings is argued from his (peace be upon him) saying: "The disagreement of my community is a mercy," and from his (ﷺ) saying: "Whatever you are given of the Book of Allah, acting upon it is binding, and no one has an excuse for abandoning it. If it is not in the Book of Allah, then there is a practice from me that is established. If there is no practice from me, then what my companions say is like the stars in the sky. Whichever of them you follow, you will be guided. And the disagreement of my companions is a mercy for you."

By "them" he (ﷺ) meant their elite who had attained the rank of ijtihad (independent reasoning). The address is directed to those below them, so there is no difficulty in this, contrary to what whoever erred has supposed. There are many reports from the early generations (salaf) on this meaning.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Madkhal narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who said: "The disagreement of the companions of Muhammad is a mercy for the servants of Allah." Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat narrated it with the wording: "The disagreement of the companions of Muhammad was a mercy to people." In al-Madkhal, from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who said: "It would not please me if the companions of Muhammad had not differed, because if they had not differed, there would have been no concession (rukhsah)."

The Imam al-Subki objected that "The disagreement of my community is a mercy" is not known among the scholars of hadith, that he had not found for it a sound, weak, or fabricated chain, and that he did not think it had any basis, unless it was a saying of people, such that someone said: "The disagreement of the community is a mercy," and someone else took it, thought it was a hadith, and made it a saying of prophethood. He said: "I have always believed that this hadith has no basis." He argued for its falsehood with verses and sound hadiths that state that mercy requires the absence of disagreement. The verses are too numerous to count. Among the hadiths is his (ﷺ) saying: "The Children of Israel were destroyed only through their excessive questioning and their disagreement with their prophets," and his (peace be upon him) saying: "Do not differ, lest your hearts differ." Although this was stated regarding the straightening of rows, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording and not from the specific occasion.

Then he said: "What we are certain of is that agreement is better than disagreement, and that disagreement is of three types. The first is in fundamental principles, and there is no doubt that it is misguidance and the cause of every corruption, and it is what is referred to in the Qur'an. The second is in opinions and wars, and it is indicated by his (ﷺ) saying to Mu'adh and Abu Musa when he sent them to Yemen: 'Cooperate and do not differ.' There is also no doubt that this is forbidden, because of what it involves of wasting religious and worldly interests. The third is in subsidiary rulings, such as disagreement about what is lawful and unlawful and similar matters. What we are certain of is that agreement is also better than this, but is it misguidance like the first two types or not? On this there is disagreement. The statement of Ibn Hazm and those who follow his path, who prohibit imitation (taqlid), indicates the first (that it is misguidance). As for us, we permit taqlid for the layman and taking, when needed, the concession from the opinions of some scholars without seeking out concessions indiscriminately, and this indicates the second (that it is not misguidance). From this perspective, it may be correct to say: 'Disagreement is a mercy,' because concessions are among its fruits beyond doubt. This does not, by any means, negate the certainty that agreement is better than disagreement. There is no contradiction between the two statements, because the aspect of goodness differs and the aspect of mercy differs. The goodness lies in knowledge of the true religion that Allah has obligated His servants to follow, which is the correct position in His sight. The mercy lies in the concession granted to him and the permission to proceed through taqlid on that basis. A 'mercy' in an indefinite form in an affirmative context does not imply generality, so it suffices for its validity that there be some mercy in disagreement, at some time, in some state, in some respect. If that is a hadith, it is to be interpreted in this way, and likewise if it is not. In every case, we do not say that disagreement is commanded. The statement that agreement is commanded depends on whether the correct view is one or many. If we say that the correct view is one, and this is the sound position, then the truth in reality is one, all people are commanded to seek it, and agreeing upon it is desired, and disagreement in that case is forbidden, even though the one who errs is excused and rewarded for his ijtihad and for exerting his effort to seek the truth."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah narrated from the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-'As: "When a judge exercises ijtihad and is correct, he has two rewards; when he exercises ijtihad and errs, he has one reward." The same applies if we hold the view of 'tashabbuh' (that all are correct in some sense), as is the position of some of the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory). However, if we say that every mujtahid is correct, then everyone is commanded to exercise ijtihad and to follow what is predominant in his opinion. It does not follow that they are all commanded to agree, nor that their disagreement is not forbidden. The application of the term "mercy" to disagreement on this assumption is stronger than its application on our view that the correct position is one. All of this is when we understand the disagreement in the report as disagreement in subsidiary rulings. As for when we say the intended meaning is disagreement in crafts and trades, there is no doubt that this is among the blessings of Allah, for which the servant is required to give thanks, as al-Halimi said in Shu'ab al-Iman. However, on this interpretation it would be more appropriate to say "the disagreement of people is a mercy," since this quality is not specific to this community, for all nations differ in crafts and trades, not only this community. Thus there must be some aspect that specifies this community. Imam al-Haramayn explained it by saying that the ranks and positions given to his community (ﷺ) were not given to any other nation, so they are part of Allah's mercy and grace toward them. But the word "disagreement" does not immediately bring to mind this meaning, nor crafts and trades. Keeping the apparent and immediate meaning is the craft, and interpreting the report as stated above is the other option.

This is the summary of his statement, and it is not hidden that it is acceptable. Yes, the claim that the hadith is not known at all among the scholars of hadith is not without qualification. al-Zarkashi attributed it, in his book on well-known hadiths, to Kitab al-Hujjah of Nasr al-Maqdisi, without mentioning its chain or its soundness. However, there is in general what strengthens it from the sayings of the early generations. And the hadith we cited earlier, although al-Tabari and al-Bayhaqi in al-Madkhal narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) with a weak chain, nonetheless, in this matter, what suffices is the hadith that al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated. So the truth from which there is no escape is that what is meant is the disagreement of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and those who shared with them in ijtihad, such as the recognized scholars of religion who are mujtahids and are not innovators, and that this is a mercy for the weak of the community and for those who are not at their level, which is not a matter over which two rams should butt heads or two people should dispute. So let this be understood.

[Page 24]

[Page 25]

﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾. This is governed either by the meaning of settledness contained in ﴿لَهم﴾ ("for them"), or it is object of an implied ﴿اذْكُرْ﴾ ("remember"). It was also said that its governing element is ﴿عَذابٌ﴾ ("a punishment"), but this was judged weak because a qualified verbal noun (al-masdar al-mawsuf) does not govern. It was also said that it is ﴿عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("great"). An objection to this is that it would restrict its greatness to this time, and that has no meaning. It was answered that when it is great on that day, and every great thing is in it, then it is more so in other than it. However, the restriction is not intended, and the whiteness is meant in its literal sense, or its necessary consequence of joy and gladness. The same is said of blackness. Most scholars hold the first view. They said: the people of truth are marked with whiteness of the face and brightness of the complexion, as an honour for them and a manifestation of the effects of their deeds in that gathering, while the people of falsehood are marked with the opposite. The apparent meaning is that the whitening and blackening apply to the whole body, but they are attributed to the faces because the face is the first thing of a person that meets you and that you see, and it is the most noble of his limbs.

It has been disputed when this happens. It was said: the time of resurrection from the graves. It was said: the time of the reading of the scrolls. It was said: the time when good deeds and bad deeds are weighed in the scale. It was said: at His saying, exalted be His majesty, ﴿وَامْتازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ ("And separate yourselves today, you criminals"). It was said: the time when each group is commanded to follow what it worshipped. It is not far-fetched to say that in each of these stations something of this occurs, until it reaches a limit that Allah, exalted is He, knows. For whiteness and blackness belong to what is graded (al-mushakkik, a term whose meaning varies in degree) and not to what is univocal (al-mutawati', a term applied uniformly), as is not hidden. And he read ﴿تَبْيَضُّ وَتَسْوَدُّ﴾ with the vowel of the present-tense prefix kasra, and this is a dialect form, and also ﴿تَبْيَاضُّ وَتَسْوَادُّ﴾.

﴿As for those whose faces turned black﴾. This is a detailed explanation of the states of the two groups. He began with the state of those whose faces turned black because it comes near ﴿وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ ("and some faces turn black"), and so that the beginning and the ending are with what pleases the soul and expands the breast.

﴿Did you disbelieve after your faith?﴾ This is on the supposition of a saying linked with ﴿الْفَاءُ﴾ (the particle fa'), meaning: it will be said to them thus. Omitting the saying and the consequent fa' following it in the omission is more than can be counted. What is prohibited is omitting the fa' alone in the response to ﴿أَمَّا﴾ (amma, "as for"). The interrogation is for rebuke and for expressing wonder at their state. The statement is a narration of what is said to them, so there is no change of address in it, contrary to al-Samin. The apparent meaning from the context and the preceding verses is that these are the People of the Book, and their disbelief after their faith is their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after believing in him before his mission. This is the view of Ikrimah, and al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i preferred it.

It was also said: they are all the disbelievers, because of their turning away from what was obligatory upon them of affirming the Oneness of Allah, when He made them testify against themselves: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾. This is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. It is possible that by faith is meant faith in potential and innate nature, and the disbelief of all the disbelievers came after this faith, since they had the capacity, through sound reasoning, clear proofs and manifest signs, to believe in Allah, exalted is He, and in His Messenger (ﷺ). It is reported from al-Hasan that they are the hypocrites, who were given the word of faith with their tongues but denied it in their hearts and deeds, so faith on this view is metaphorical. It was also said: they are the people of innovations and desires from this community. This is reported from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Abu Umamah, Ibn Abbas, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿So taste the punishment﴾, that is, the known punishment described as great. The command is for humiliation, so that what is commanded is fixed and realized. It was also said: it may be a command of compulsion, that every hair of their limbs tastes the punishment. We seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from His wrath. The fa' indicates that the command to taste the punishment follows from their mentioned disbelief, as His saying, glorified is He, explicitly shows: ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾. So the ba' (bi, "because of") is causal. It was also said it is for exchange, without regard to causation, and it is not in the sense of the lam (al-lam, "for"). Perhaps He, glorified is He, intended ("after your faith"). The combining of the past and the present forms is to indicate the continuation of their disbelief, or its occurrence in the worldly life.

[Page 26]

As for those whose faces turn white, they are in the mercy of Allah, that is, Paradise. This is an instance of al-ta'bir bil-hal 'an al-mahall (expressing the place by what is in it, a figure of speech), and the sense of "in" (al-zarfiyyah, the sense of a container) is literal. It may also be intended that the mercy means reward, in which case the sense of "in" is figurative, as one says: "in everlasting bliss and a pleasant life." This implies the abundance of the mercy and its encompassing of those mentioned, in the way a container encompasses what is in it. It is not permissible to take "mercy" to mean an attribute of Allah, the Exalted, since the sense of "in" does not apply to it. What indicates the above is that the mercy is contrasted with the punishment, and that it is linked with eternal abiding in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ (107). He expressed this by mercy only to indicate that the believer, even if he spends his entire life in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, does not attain what he attains except by the mercy of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason it is related in a report: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."

The clause ﴿they abide therein forever﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah, a new sentence that answers an implied question), which answers what arises from the context, as if it were said: "How will they be therein?" And it was answered with what you see. In it there is an emphasis in meaning on what preceded. It was said that it is a predicate after a predicate, but this is not correct. The fronting of the adverbial phrase ("therein") is for preserving the rhyme-endings (ra's al-ayy, the final sounds of verses). The pronoun in the genitive refers to the mercy. It is among the most remote of interpretations to take it as referring to the call to good, and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, contrary to one who held this view and made the statement an explanation of the reason they are in the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, and their opposites are in punishment, as if it were said: "What is their state that they are in the mercy of Allah, the Exalted?" And it was answered: "They were abiding forever in good deeds."

It is also read: ابياضّت and اسوادّت (with doubled letters).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 108:

( ﴿تِلْكَ﴾ ) That is, the ones previously mentioned and whose status is great. ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you﴾, meaning We recite them to you bit by bit. Attributing this recitation to Him, exalted is He, is a metaphor (majaz), since the one who recites is Jibril, peace be upon him, by the command of Him, glorified and exalted is He. In his departure from the literal sense, together with the shift (iltifat) to the first person plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), there is an evident care for the recitation and for what is recited. The verbal clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the verses," and its governing element is the meaning of the demonstrative.

It is also permitted that it be in the position of the predicate (khabar) of "tilka," with "ayat" as an apposition (badal) to it. It has also been read as "yatluha" in the third person form.

( ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ ) That is, while being characterized by truth or justice, in everything that those verses indicate and express. Thus the prepositional phrase is in the position of an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkada) relating to the subject or object. ﴿And Allah does not intend any injustice to the worlds﴾ (801), by placing upon them punishment they do not deserve, which would be injustice, or by diminishing from them the reward they have earned, which would be a favor they are owed. This clause confirms the content of what precedes it in the most complete manner, since it uses the indefinite noun "zulm," directs the negation to His intention, and uses the present tense, which, with the help of the context, indicates the continuation of the negation. It attaches the ruling to individual members of the definite plural, and it shifts to the august name. Injustice (zulm) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, or abandoning what is obligatory. It is impossible for Him, exalted is He, due to the proofs established for that. Negating a thing does not imply its possibility, for the impossible may be negated, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾.

It has been said: the apparent meaning is that what is intended is that Allah does not intend what is an injustice from the servants among themselves, not that everything He does is not an injustice from Him. This is because the context is one of clarifying that He does not waste the reward of the good-doers, nor neglect the disbeliever, but recompenses him for his disbelief. If what was intended were that everything He does is not an injustice, this would not be derived from it. There is in this what is not hidden.

Page 27

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 109:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ That is, to Him alone, exclusively, belongs whatever is in them of created beings, by way of ownership, creation and disposal. The use of "mā" (what), rather than "man" (who), is either for the sake of predominance, or to indicate that non-rational beings, in relation to His greatness, are no different from rational ones. ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (901). That is, their affairs are returned to Him, so He recompenses each according to what wisdom requires of reward and punishment. The placing of the prepositional phrase first (ilā Allāh, "to Allah") implies restriction: it is to the judgment and decree of Allah Most High, and not to anything else, whether as a partner or independently. This clause confirms the content of what was mentioned concerning the recompense of the two groups. It has also been said that it is coordinated with what precedes it, confirming its content. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is to cultivate awe. Yahya ibn Wathhab read (tarji'u), with a fatḥa on the tā' and a kasra on the jīm, throughout the Qur'an.

﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ is a resumptive statement, introduced to strengthen the believers in what they already possess of agreement upon the truth and of calling to good. This is what has been said. It has also been said that it is part of the first address, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah as He should be feared﴾. After this, addresses to the believers followed, containing commands and prohibitions, and in between them there was a digression about those whose faces turn white and those whose faces turn black, and some of their conditions in the Hereafter. Then he returned to the first address, urging obedience and submission.

Kāna (to be) is a defective verb (al-fi'l al-nāqiṣ). Originally it signifies only existence in the past, without indicating whether that continues or ceases. It may be used for eternity, as in the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, such as ﴿And Allah is ever All-Knowing of everything﴾. It may also be used to express the necessity of a thing and its inseparability, as in ﴿And man is ever most contentious﴾.
