Some grammarians held that it signifies cessation by its convention, like other defective verbs. The sound view is the first, and according to it the verse does not imply that the addressees are not now the best nation. It has been said that the meaning is "you were" in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), or among the nations, that is, in their knowledge that you were thus. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is "you are the best nation." This was objected to on the basis that it requires an extra kāna, and it is not permissible for kāna to be extra at the beginning of a sentence.

﴿Was brought forth﴾ means was made manifest, and the agent is omitted because it is known. ﴿For mankind﴾ is attached to what is at its place (i.e., to the verb "brought forth"). It has been said that it is attached to "best nation." The clause "was brought forth" is a qualifier of "nation." It has been said that it qualifies "best." The first is more preferable. The address has been said to be specifically to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and this is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It has been said that it is to the emigrants (al-muhājirūn) among them, and this is one of two reports from Ibn 'Abbās. In another report, it is general to the Ummah of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. This is supported by what Imam Aḥmad recorded with a good chain from Abū al-Ḥasan, may Allah honour his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "I have been given what none of the prophets were given: I was supported with awe; I was given the keys of the earth; I was named Aḥmad; the earth was made for me as a purifier; and my Ummah was made the best of nations."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Abū Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that the verse concerns the People of the House of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Ibn Jarīr recorded from 'Ikrimah that it was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ūd, 'Ammār ibn Yāsir,
[Page 28]
Sālim the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Mu'ādh ibn Jabal. The apparent meaning is that although the address is specific to those among the believers who witnessed the revelation, or to some of them, its ruling is suitable to be general to all. This is indicated by the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, as related by Qatādah: "O people, whoever is pleased to be among that Ummah, let him fulfil the condition of Allah concerning it." He indicated by this His words, exalted is He: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾. For although it is a resumptive statement explaining that they are the best nation, or a second qualifier of "nation" according to what has been said, it still implies a condition. What is understood by "right" (al-ma'rūf) is acts of obedience, and by "wrong" (al-munkar) the sins that the Law has disapproved.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others recorded from Ibn 'Abbās regarding the verse that the meaning is: you enjoin them to bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and to acknowledge what Allah has sent down, and you fight them over that. "There is no god but Allah" is the greatest of what is right. And you forbid them from what is wrong, and what is wrong is denial (al-takdhīb), which is the gravest of wrongs. It seems that he, may Allah be pleased with him, took the unrestricted term to refer to its complete instance. Otherwise, there is no indication for this specification.

﴿And you believe in Allah﴾: by belief in Him, exalted is He, is meant belief in everything that it is obligatory to believe in. This is because belief is only counted and deserves to be called belief when one truly believes in Allah, exalted is He, and the reality of belief in Allah, exalted is He, is that it encompasses all that it is obligatory to believe in. So if one falls short in any part of it, he has no share of belief in Allah, exalted is He, at all. The context requires this, because it is an allusion to the People of the Book, that they do not believe in all that it is obligatory to believe in, as is indicated by the following statement that denies belief from them, despite the knowledge that they are believers in general. Also, the context is one of praise for the believers by describing them as ﴿the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. This clause is conjoined to what precedes it, which gives the reason for the report (that they are the best nation). So if belief in everything that it is obligatory to believe in were not meant, it would not be praise, and it would not be suitable as a reason, and the conjunction would not fit. The belief was placed after enjoining right and forbidding wrong, though it precedes them in existence and rank, as is apparent, because belief is shared by all nations, whereas enjoining right and forbidding wrong are more evident in indicating excellence. It is also permissible to say that he put those two before it for emphasis, and because the discourse is oriented toward them. As for mentioning belief, it is like a completion (al-tatmīm). It is also permissible that this is to draw attention to the fact that the benefit of enjoining right and forbidding wrong in religion is more evident than what belief in Allah, exalted is He, includes, because it is the duty of the prophets, peace be upon them. Had it been said "they were put first" and the belief placed later for emphasis, and so that it connects with His words, exalted is He, ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them﴾, it would not be far-fetched. That is, if they had believed as belief should be, that belief would have been ﴿better for them﴾ than what they have of leadership in this world, for it averts killing and humiliation from them, and in the Hereafter, for it averts the lasting punishment. It has been said: if the People of the Book had believed in Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, it would have been better for them than believing in Moses and Jesus alone, peace be upon them both. It has been said: what is preferred over is their disbelief, so the excellence is only with reference to their claim, and in this there is a kind of mockery of them. This clause is conjoined to ﴿you were the best nation﴾ and linked to it, in the sense: and if the People of the Book had believed as you believed, and enjoined right as you enjoined it, and forbade wrong as you forbade it, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾.

﴿Among them are the believers﴾, such as 'Abdullāh ibn Salām, his brother, and Tha'labah ibn Su'bah.

﴿And most of them are the defiantly disobedient﴾ (110): that is, those who go outside the obedience of Allah, exalted is He. Disbelief was expressed by "defiant disobedience" (al-fisq) to signal that they have departed from what their Book made obligatory. It has been said: this is to indicate that, among the disbelievers, they are in the position of disbelievers among the sinners, because they have reached a shameful state which is, of them, more heinous and more atrocious.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 111:

﴿They will not harm you, except for a little annoyance.﴾ This is an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil), because al-adha (annoyance) carries the meaning of slight harm, as the contexts of its usage attest. So it is as if it were said: "They will not harm you with any harm, except a slight harm." It has also been said that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because annoyance is not harm. But this is open to question. The verse, as Muqatil said, was revealed when the leaders of the Jews, such as Ka'b, Abu Rafi', Abu Yasir, Kinanah and Ibn Suriya, targeted their believers, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, and harmed them for their embracing Islam. This harm was verbal, as the words of Qatadah and others imply, and that slander was against Allah Most High, as al-Hasan said.

﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾: that is, they will be routed without managing to gain anything from you. Turning the back is a well-known metaphor (kinayah) for defeat.

﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ (111): this is a conjunction (atf) upon the clause of the condition and its consequence, and "thumma" (then) indicates sequence and a delay in the report (al-tarakhi al-ikhbari), meaning: they will have no victory from anyone; then their end will be helplessness and abandonment, whether they fight you or do not fight you. In it is a confirmation of the believers in the most complete manner.

It is also read: "thumma la yunsaru" (they will not be helped), and the clause is then conjoined to the consequent of the condition, and "thumma" indicates a delay in rank between the two reports, not in time, since they are simultaneous. Some scholars permitted that it indicates a delay in time in both readings, based on considering it between the conjoined element and the last part of the conjoined element. The reading with the nominative (al-raf') is more eloquent, because it is free of the restriction. In this verse there is a clear proof of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ), and because it is among the reports of the unseen that reality confirmed: the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and the Jews of Khaybar fought the Muslims and did not stand firm, and did not obtain anything from them, and no banner of theirs was raised after that, and no matter of theirs was set right, and they did not rise up with any wing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 112 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Humiliation has been imposed upon them﴾: that is, the humiliation of having their lives, property, and families made worthless. It has also been said: the humiliation of clinging to falsehood and paying the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects). Al-Hasan said: "Allah has humiliated them, so they have no protection, and He has placed them beneath the feet of the Muslims." This is from the imagery of pitching tents and domes, as Abu Muslim said. It has been said: this contains a metaphor of the implicit, imaginative type (isti'ara makniyya takhyiliyya), and the encompassing and enveloping of humiliation around them may be likened to that imagery by way of a serial metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya). It has also been said: this is from their saying, "So-and-so imposed a tax (darība) on his slave," meaning he obligated him to pay it. The meaning, then, is: they have been bound to humiliation, and it has become fixed upon them, so there is no escape for them from it. ﴿Wherever they are found﴾: that is, wherever they are encountered. It has been said: wherever they are seized and overcome. "Ayna-ma" (wherever) is a conditional particle, "ma" is superfluous (za'ida), and "thuqifu" (they are found) is in the jussive position. The response to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, or it is itself the response according to one opinion.

﴿Except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people﴾: this is an exceptive clause of the "emptied" type (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances. The meaning, in negative form, is: they are not safe from humiliation in any circumstance, except in the circumstance of being under the protection of Allah, the Exalted, or His Book which came to them, and the protection of the Muslims. By that, they are safe from being killed, taken captive, having their children enslaved, and having their wealth uprooted.

It has been said: that is, except in the circumstance of being adherents of Islam and following the way of the believers. In that case, the humiliation of clinging to falsehood and of paying (tribute) is lifted from them.

﴿And they have returned with anger from Allah﴾: that is, they have returned bearing it. This is a metonymy (kinaya) for their deserving it and their being liable to it, from the expression "bā'a fulān bi-fulān" (so-and-so returned with so-and-so), meaning that he became deserving of being killed in retaliation for him. The meaning is that they have become worthy of His anger, glory be to Him. The indefiniteness of "ghadabin" (anger) is for magnification (tafkhim), and the attributive phrase confirms this.

﴿And humiliation (maskana) has been imposed upon them﴾: so they are, for the most part, wretched and needy, and rarely is a Jew found who displays wealth. (﴿That﴾) refers to what has been mentioned of these matters: ﴿because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, which indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾ at all. The attribution of killing to them, although it was the deed of their predecessors, is in the manner that has been explained more than once.

﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ (211). This refers to their disbelief and their killing of the prophets, peace be upon them, according to what the proximity requires, so there is no repetition. It has been said: the meaning is that the imposition of humiliation and what follows it, just as it is caused by their disbelief and killing, is caused by their disobedience and transgression. The expression in the past and present tenses is for what has passed. Then, the clause ﴿Among them are believers﴾, and likewise the clause ﴿They will not harm you﴾, and what is conjoined to them, come as digressions (istitrad). For this reason they were not conjoined to the conditional clause before them. The second digression was not conjoined to the first because they are distant from each other and each is a different type of speech. Some of the scholars of verification said: these two clauses, along with what follows them, are connected to His saying, ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed﴾, explaining it. So His saying, ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, explains that, on the basis that the assumed case is the belief of all of them; otherwise, some of them are believers, in order to lift ill opinion from some of them. His saying, Exalted is His majesty, ﴿They will not harm you﴾, is an explanation of what is better for them, namely that because of their lack of faith they are afflicted with the hardship of plotting to harm you, with grief over failure, and with scheming to overcome you by opposition, and to overcome you, and with seeking leadership by opposing you. For this opposition, Allah imposed humiliation upon them. And in seeking wealth by taking bribes through altering their Book, Allah imposed on them the poverty. Had they believed, they would have been saved from all of that. End of quote. It is not hidden that this, even if accepted and its remoteness borne, does not preclude the view that it is a digression, because a digression is when something suitable is mentioned in the course of speech without being the subject of the context. What precludes it is an interjection (i'tiraḍ), and we do not hold that view, so reflect.

* * *

This (and by way of allusion) ﴿You will never attain righteousness (birr)﴾, which is nearness to Allah, ﴿until you spend from that which you love﴾, that is, some of it. The allusion in it is to the self (nafs), for when the self spends in the way of Allah, the greatest veil is removed, and the spending of everything after it becomes easy. ﴿And whatever you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, so one should seek out what pleases Him. It is related from some of them that he said: Those who spend are of several kinds. Among them is one who spends while observing reward and compensation; among them is one who spends while watching for the lifting of trials and calamities; and among them is one who spends, content with His knowledge. And by Allah, how excellent is the one who said:

He is stirred toward goodness in pursuit of lofty rank, so that one day his qualities may be mentioned near Salma.

﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel had made unlawful for himself﴾. It has been said: the benefit of informing of this is to teach the people of love to abandon what has been made dear to them of delicious foods and worldly pleasures, out of desire for what is with Allah, the Exalted.

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾: it is the Ka'ba, which is among the greatest manifestations of Him, the Exalted, to the extent that they said: it is for the Muhammadans like the tree was for Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿Blessed﴾: with what He clothed it in from the lights of His essence. ﴿And guidance﴾: with what He clothed it in from the lights of His attributes. ﴿For the worlds﴾: according to their readiness. ﴿In it are clear signs, the standing place of Abraham﴾, which includes contentment, submission, expansion, certainty, unveiling, witnessing, intimate friendship, and chivalry; or knowledge and monotheism, annihilation and subsistence, intoxication and sobriety; or all of that.

﴿And whoever enters it shall be safe﴾: from the perils of his own self, because it is the station of establishment (tamkin). (The application of this to what is within the souls is that) the House is an allusion to the true heart. What is reported, that the House was the first thing to appear on the surface of the water when the heavens and the earth were created, and that it was created two thousand years before the earth and was a white foam (zubda) on the surface of the water, so the earth was spread out beneath it on that basis, may be interpreted as follows: its appearance on the water at that time is its attachment to the drop (nutfa) at the creation of the heaven of the spirit, the animal soul, and the earth of the body. Its being created before the earth is an allusion to its eternity and the createdness of the body. Specifying that by two thousand years is an allusion to its precedence over the body by two stages, the stage of the soul and the stage of the heart, precedence in rank, since the thousand is a complete rank. Its being a white foam is an allusion to the purity of its essence. The spreading of the earth beneath it is an allusion to the formation of the body from its influence, and to the forms of its members and their shapes following its states. It is not hidden that the place where the spirit attaches to the body and the true heart first connects to it is the pineal heart (al-qalb al-sanawbari), which is the first of the organs to form, the first organ to move, and the last organ to become still. So ﴿the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾ — the chest is the form; or it is the first place of worship established for them, for the true heart, which is at Bakkah, the spiritual chest, which is the most noble station in the soul and the place toward which the faculties crowd. Its being ﴿blessed﴾ means that it possesses divine blessing because of the overflow of good upon it. Its being ﴿guidance﴾ means that one is guided by it to Allah, the Exalted. The signs that are in it are the sciences, knowledge, wisdoms, and realities. And ﴿the standing place of Abraham﴾ is an allusion to the intellect, which is the station of the footstep of Abraham, that is, the spirit, meaning the place of the connection of its light with the heart. There is no doubt that whoever enters that (﴿shall be safe﴾) from the enemies of the imaginative faculty, the phantoms of the whisperings of the self, the abductions of the devils of illusion, the jinn of imaginings, the assassinations of the beasts of the bodily faculties, and their attributes.

﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way thereto﴾: they are the people of His knowledge, Exalted is His majesty. As for those ignorant of Him, they neither stand nor sit (i.e., they do nothing of substance). It is related from some of them that he said: I said to al-Shibli: "I have performed the pilgrimage." He said: "How did you do it?" I said: "I bathed, put on the ihram, prayed two rak'as, and recited the talbiya." He said to me: "Did you by it tie the pilgrimage (to yourself)?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you, by your tying, dissolve every tie you had tied since you were created that is opposed to this tie?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you have not tied it." Then he said: "Did you take off your garments?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you strip yourself of every deed you had done?" I said: "No." He said: "You did not take them off." He said: "Did you purify yourself?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did you remove from yourself every defect?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not purify yourself." He said: "Did you recite the talbiya?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you find the response to the talbiya, like for like?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not recite the talbiya." He said: "Did you enter the Sacred Precinct (haram)?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you, by entering, resolve to abandon every prohibited thing?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not enter." He said: "Did you overlook Mecca?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did a state from Allah, the Exalted, overlook you?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not overlook." He said: "Did you enter the Sacred Mosque?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you enter the Presence (hadra)?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not enter the Sacred Mosque." He said: "Did you see the Ka'ba?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you see what you intended by it?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not see the Ka'ba." He said: "Did you perform the ramal and the sa'y?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you flee from the world and find safety from what you fled from?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did nothing." He said: "Did you shake hands with the Black Stone?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Whoever shakes hands with the Stone has shaken hands with the Real (al-Haqq), and whoever shakes hands with the Real, the trace of safety appears upon him. Did that appear upon you?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not shake hands." He said: "Did you pray two rak'as afterward?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you find yourself standing before Allah, the Exalted?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not pray." He said: "Did you go out to al-Safa?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you say takbir?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Was your secret purified and the created worlds diminished in your eyes?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not go out, nor did you say takbir." He said: "Did you hasten in your sa'y?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you flee from Him to Him?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not hasten." He said: "Did you stand upon al-Marwa?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you see the descent of tranquility (sakina) upon you while you were upon it?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not stand upon al-Marwa." He said: "Did you go out to Mina?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Were you given what you wished for?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not go out." He said: "Did you enter the Mosque of al-Khayf?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did a fear renew itself for you?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not enter." He said: "Did you proceed to Arafat?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you know the state for which you were created and the state to which you will return? Did you know your Lord, whom you had been denying? Do you recognize the Real through anything?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not proceed." He said: "Did you hasten to al-Mash'ar al-Haram?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you remember Allah, the Exalted, in it with a remembrance that made you forget the remembrance of anything else?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not hasten." He said: "Did you slaughter?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you annihilate your desires and your wills in the pleasure of the Real?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not slaughter." He said: "Did you throw the pebbles?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you throw your ignorance away from you by an increase of knowledge that appeared upon you?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not throw." He said: "Did you visit (the Ka'ba)?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Were you unveiled to the realities?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not visit." He said: "Did you exit the state of ihram (ahlalta)?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you resolve to eat only lawful food, in the amount that preserves your self?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not exit the state of ihram." He said: "Did you bid farewell?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Did you depart from your self and your spirit entirely?" I said: "No." He said: "Then you did not bid farewell, nor did you perform the pilgrimage, and you must return if you wish. And when you perform the pilgrimage, strive to be as I have described to you." End of quote.

This which al-Shibli mentioned is the pilgrimage that deserves to be called a pilgrimage. Allah, the Exalted, has servants whom He has qualified for that and empowered to travel those paths. Their pilgrimage is, in reality, from Him to Him and for Him in Him. Their circumambulation is the enclosures of the village (of the beloved) upon the carpet of reverence, and their standing place is the Arafat of recognition upon the leg of service. They have no aim in the walls and the stones. Far, far is it: the aim of the madman from the abodes is nothing but the abodes. As for one who disbelieves and turns away from the Master by the desire of the self, Allah is Independent of the worlds; He, glory be to Him, is independent of him and does not turn toward him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 3, verse 112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God?"﴾ which indicate His unity (*tawhid*, the oneness of God), ﴿while God is Witness over what you do﴾, since He is nearer to you than your jugular vein. ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of God"﴾ by denying it to the believers, ﴿those who believe, seeking to make it crooked﴾ by raising false doubts, ﴿while you are witnesses﴾, knowing that it is true and that there is no crookedness in it. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾, so He will recompense you for it.

﴿O you who believe﴾ with true faith, ﴿if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture﴾ out of fear of their denial of what you are upon of the reality and of the path that leads to Him, glory be to Him, ﴿they will turn you back, after your faith, to disbelievers﴾ whose faith is firmly established in you, ﴿for the denial of the reality is disbelief, like the denial of the Shari'ah (sacred law)﴾. ﴿And whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path﴾, that is, whoever holds fast to Him from anything other than Him has been guided to Him by Him. Al-Wasiti said: whoever claims that he holds fast to Him through other than Him has ignorance of the greatness of lordship. According to some, the reality of *i'tisam* (holding fast) is the drawing of the heart away from the causes, which are the inner idols, and disavowing oneself before God, exalted is He, of power and strength. It is also said: for lovers, *i'tisam* is taking refuge by casting off what is upright, and for the people of realities it is the lifting of *i'tisam*, because they witness that they are in His grip.

﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared﴾ by guarding the covenants, observing the limits, and remaining still under the flow of divine decree with the attribute of contentment. It is also said: the true fear of God is not seeing one's own piety. ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾, that is, do not die except in a state of Islam of existence, meaning that your death should be annihilation in unity (*tawhid*).

﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of God﴾, which is His covenant that He took from the servants on the day of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾, ﴿and do not separate﴾ through the differing of desires. ﴿And remember God's blessing upon you﴾ through guidance to the landmarks of unity, which produces love in the hearts, ﴿when you were enemies﴾ because you were veiled by the veils of the soul and the coverings of nature, ﴿and He brought your hearts together﴾ through loving one another for the sake of God, exalted is He, so that they would be illumined by His light. ﴿So you became, by His blessing upon you, brothers﴾ in religion. ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾, which is the abode of the corrupt nature and the Hell of deprivation, ﴿and He saved you from it﴾ through true connection among you, up to the lote-tree of the station of the spirit and the spirit of the Garden of the Essence.

﴿Let there be among you a community﴾ like the knowing gnostic scholars, the masters of steadfastness in religion, ﴿who call to good﴾, that is, guide people to the absolute perfection of knowing the Truth, exalted is He, and attaining to Him. ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾, that which brings one near to God, exalted is He, ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾, that which distances one from Him, exalted is He. ﴿And those are the successful ones﴾ for whom no veil remains, and they are the vicegerents of God, exalted is He, on His earth.

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ and followed desires and innovations, ﴿and differed after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, the rational and legal proofs that necessitate unity and agreement of word. ﴿And for those is a great punishment﴾, which is the punishment of being deprived of the Presence.

﴿On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾. They said: the whitening of the face is an expression for the illumination of the face of the heart by the light of the Truth turned toward it, and turning away from the lower, carnal direction, which is dark. This happens only through unity. Its blackening is the darkness of the face of the heart through turning toward the soul, which seeks its portions, and turning away from the higher, luminous direction.

﴿As for those whose faces turned black﴾, it will be said to them: ﴿Did you disbelieve﴾, that is, did you veil yourselves from the Truth with the attributes of the soul, ﴿after your faith﴾, that is, after your illumination by the light of readiness, the purity of nature, and the guidance of reason? ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, which is the punishment of veiling from the Truth, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾ in it. ﴿And as for those whose faces turned white, they will be in God's mercy﴾, the special mercy which is the witnessing of beauty, ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾, remaining after annihilation.

﴿You are the best community brought forth﴾ from the place of pre-eternity, ﴿for mankind﴾, that is, for their benefit, ﴿enjoining what is right﴾, that which leads to the station of unity, ﴿and forbidding what is wrong﴾, which is the claim that multiplicity is real in truth.

﴿If the People of the Scripture had believed﴾ as you believed, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ than what they are upon. ﴿Some of them are believers﴾ like you, ﴿but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, those who have gone outside the sanctuary of the Truth.

﴿They will not harm you except with some hurt﴾, which is their denial against you through speech. ﴿And if they fight you﴾ and do not content themselves with that harm, ﴿they will turn their backs to you﴾ and will not gain anything from you, because of the strength of your inner selves and their weakness. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾: no one will help them at all, but they will remain forsaken because the lights of the Truth do not appear upon them. And God, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "When 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tha'laba ibn Shu'ba, Usayd ibn Shu'ba and Usayd ibn 'Ubayd, and those from the Jews who had embraced Islam along with them, became Muslims, believed, affirmed the truth and desired Islam, the rabbis of the Jews and the disbelievers among them said: 'None believed in Muhammad and followed him except our wicked ones. Had they been among our best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers and gone over to another.' So Allah the Exalted revealed concerning this: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ up to His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And they are among the righteous﴾." The sentence, as Our master Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said, serves as a preface to enumerate the virtues of the believers among the People of the Book. The plural pronoun refers to the People of the Book as a whole, not only to the wicked among them. The word ﴿laysa﴾ (is not) is the verb, with its subject being the pronoun, and ﴿sawa'an﴾ (alike) is its predicate. It is in the singular because it originally was a verbal noun (maṣdar). According to the correct view, the pause here is complete. The meaning of the negation of equality is the negation of sharing in the basic attribute of the vices, not the negation of equality in the degrees of that attribute while the sharing in its basic attribute is established. Similar usage is common in speech.

﴿Among the People of the Book is a standing community﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), explaining how they are not alike and removing the ambiguity in it. Abu 'Ubayda said that it forms one sentence with the preceding one, taking ﴿ummatun﴾ (community) as the subject of ﴿laysa﴾ and ﴿sawa'an﴾ as its predicate, so it is like the expression "the fleas bit me" (akalūnī al-barāghīthu, where the verb's subject is placed after it as a grammatical form). It was also said that ﴿ummatun﴾ is in the nominative case as the agent of ﴿sawa'an﴾ (taken as a verb-like noun). The weakness of both views is evident. Placing ﴿ahl al-kitāb﴾ (the People of the Book) in the position of the pronoun is an addition to honor them and to show concern for them. The word ﴿qā'imah﴾ (standing) comes from ﴿qāma﴾ used intransitively in the sense of ﴿istaqāma﴾ (to be upright), meaning a community that is upright in obedience to Allah the Exalted, firm in His command, not turning away from it or abandoning it as the others abandoned and neglected it. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-Zajjaj claimed that the sentence contains an omitted noun (muḍāf, a governed noun), and the estimated meaning is "one possessing a standing community," that is, one possessing an upright path. But in this there is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence.

By this community is meant those mentioned earlier in the occasion of revelation. Some scholars took ﴿ahl al-kitāb﴾ as general for the Jews and the Christians, and counted among the community mentioned such people as the Negus (al-Najāshī) and his companions from the Christians who embraced Islam. ﴿They recite the signs of Allah﴾ is a description of ﴿ummah﴾ following its description as ﴿qā'imah﴾. It is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿qā'imah﴾, or from ﴿ummah﴾ since it has already been described, or from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase that falls as a predicate about it. The meaning is that they recite the Qur'an ﴿during the hours of the night﴾, that is, its times. Its singular is ﴿anan﴾ on the pattern of ﴿'aṣā﴾ (staff). It was also said that the singular is ﴿anan﴾ like ﴿ma'an﴾, and it was said ﴿anan﴾ with a fatḥah then a sukūn, or a kasrah then a sukūn. Al-Akhfash related that the singular is ﴿anw﴾ like ﴿jarw﴾. So the hamza (glottal stop) is converted from a yā' or a wāw. The phrase is connected either to ﴿yatlūna﴾ (they recite) or to ﴿qā'imah﴾. Abu al-Baqa' prevented its connection to the second, on the basis that the word has been described, so it does not govern what comes after the description. ﴿And they prostrate﴾ (wa-hum yasjudūna) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿yatlūna﴾ according to the apparent view. The meaning is "and they pray," since it is known that there is no recitation in prostration, and likewise in bowing; rather, recitation during them has been forbidden, as in the report. By their prayer here is meant the tahajjud (voluntary night prayer), according to what some scholars held, and it was justified on the basis that the prayer was included in the praise, and that in it recitation is facilitated for them, since in the obligatory prayer leading the recitation is the duty of the imam. Considering their state at prayer as an individual prayer is rejected by the context of praise, and this is more appropriate given the shift away from expressing it with the generic noun, which in its usual sense means the obligatory prayers, and given the expression of its time with the vague word "hours." The reason he did not express it as tahajjud is to avoid the possibility of the linguistic meaning, in which there is no praise. What some of the early scholars held is that it is the 'Atamah prayer (the night prayer).

Evidence for this is what Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani related with a sound (ḥasan) chain, the wording being that of the last two, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delayed the 'Isha' prayer one night, then went out to the mosque, and found the people waiting for the prayer. He said: 'Indeed, no one among the People of the Book prays this prayer.' He said: And this verse was revealed: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ until ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous﴾." On this basis the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿yatlūna﴾. It was also said that it is resumptive. The praise for them is by this, due to their distinction and their being specially singled out by that noble prayer, which the People of the Book were not honored to perform, as the hadith states, and not even the rest of the nations. Al-Tabarani related with a sound chain also from al-Munkadir that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out one night, and he delayed the 'Isha' prayer until an hour or so of the night had passed, while the people were waiting in the mosque. He said: 'Indeed, you will not cease to be in prayer as long as you wait for it.' Then he said: 'Indeed, it is a prayer that none of the nations before you have prayed.'" Perhaps this is the secret of placing this ruling before the ruling on faith. It cannot be objected that recitation is not facilitated for them except by praying individually, and that individual prayer is not praised, although this contradicts the actual situation of the people as the two reports indicate, because recitation was not restricted to prayer in it. Restriction would only be necessary if the sentence were a circumstantial clause from the pronoun, as was mentioned earlier, and it is not so.

Expressing the prayer by prostration is because it indicates the perfection of humility more clearly. This is the secret of using it to refer to prayer in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to one who asked him to pray that he might be his companion in Paradise, out of his excessive love for him and fear of separation being prevented on the Day of Resurrection: "I mean, by much prostration." The same applies in many other places. It was also said that by it is meant the prayer between Maghrib and the late 'Isha', which is called the prayer of heedlessness. It was also said that by prostration is meant the prostration of recitation. It was also said that it means humility, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. The nominal sentence was chosen to indicate continuity, and the predication was repeated to strengthen the ruling and emphasize it. The choice of the present-tense form indicates renewal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 114:

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is another attribute of the community (ummah). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) in the same pattern as what precedes it, or, if you wish, that it be a fresh sentence (isti'naf), as Abu al-Baqa' said. What is meant by this belief is belief in everything that must be believed in, in the accepted manner. Allah the Exalted singled out the Last Day for mention to make clear their opposition to the rest of the Jews regarding what someone might suppose they share with them in it. For the Jews too claim to believe in Allah the Exalted and in the Last Day. However, since this belief is accompanied by their saying: ﴿Uzair is the son of Allah﴾, and their disbelief in some of the Books and Messengers, and their description of the Last Day in a way that contradicts what the Chosen Law (al-Shari'ah al-Mustafawiyyah) has declared, their belief is treated as equal to non-belief.

﴿They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is an indication of their abundant share of the virtue of perfecting others, following the indication of their abundance of the virtue of perfecting the self. In it there is also an allusion against the compromisers (al-mudahinin) who turn people away from the way of Allah the Exalted.

﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾: that is, they hasten to do good works and acts of obedience, fearing that they may be lost through death, for example, or they perform righteous deeds eagerly, not reluctantly, knowing the greatness of their station and the goodness of their outcome. This is a comprehensive attribute encompassing all kinds of virtues and bounties. In mentioning it there is an allusion to the sluggishness and reluctance of the Jews in this regard. The root of musara'ah (hastening) is mubadarah (hastening forward), and it is also used to mean eagerness. The choice of the form of mufa'alah is for emphasis. It has been said: he did not express it with 'ajalah (haste) in order to distinguish it from sur'ah (speed), for sur'ah is advancing in what may be advanced in, and it is praiseworthy, its opposite being delay, which is blameworthy; while 'ajalah is advancing in what should not be advanced in, and it is blameworthy, its opposite being anah (deliberation), which is praiseworthy. The choice of ﴿fi﴾ (in) over ﴿ila﴾ (to) and the frequent use of musara'ah with it (transitively) signifies, as Shaykh al-Islam said, that they are firmly established in the essence of good and move freely within its varieties, not that they are outside it and arrive at it. The plural form of paucity (jam' al-qillah) used here suffices in place of the plural of abundance (jam' al-kathrah), as is not hidden.

﴿And those﴾: that is, those described by these outstanding attributes, by virtue of their being characterized by them, as the turning away from the pronoun indicates, ﴿are among the righteous﴾: that is, among the number of those whose condition is made good in the sight of Allah the Exalted. This is a rebuttal of the Jews' saying: "None but our wicked ones believed in it."

Most scholars have held that the verse contains an elision (istighna') by mentioning one of the two groups in place of the other, following the Arab custom of mentioning one of two opposites instead of the other, and the meaning is: "and among them are those who are not like that."

﴿And whatever good they do﴾, i.e., any obedience that is transitive (extending to others) or continuing in its effect, ﴿they will not be denied it﴾, i.e., they will by no means be deprived of its reward. The root meaning of *kufr* is covering or concealing, and because it is interpreted here in the sense just mentioned, it takes two objects. It has been said that the address is to this Ummah, and it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation﴾. Everything between the two is a digression (*istitrad*). It has also been said that the address is to those who are described by the qualities mentioned, and in this there is a shift of grammatical person (*iltifat*). Its particular purpose here is to indicate that, because they possess these virtues, they are fit to be addressed directly.

The people of Kufa, except Abu Bakr, read both verbs with the *ya'* (third person), while the rest read them with the *ta'* (second person), except Abu 'Amr, for it is narrated from him that he read them as the address form. On the reading in the third person (*ghaybah*), it is permissible that the pronoun refers to what was intended by its counterparts earlier, and the discourse in that case stays on a single course. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the Ummah, and the shift to the third person (*ghaybah*) is in consideration of the Ummah, just as the Ummah was considered at the beginning in the expression *ukhrijat* rather than *ukhrijtum*. This is a well-known method of the Arabs in such cases.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious﴾ (511), i.e., of their states, so He will recompense them. This is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) that confirms the content of what precedes it.

The term "the God-conscious" (*al-muttaqin*) may be either general, in which case those addressed enter it at the first level, or specific to those previously mentioned. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun indicates the reason, and that none attains success in His sight except the people of piety. On this basis, His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah.﴾ (Muʾakkidan li-dhalika wa-li-hadha fasl.) [The passage is introduced here as a confirmation of what precedes, and there is a separate discussion.]

What is meant by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is either all the disbelievers, for they boasted of wealth and children when they said: ﴿We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished﴾, so Allah the Exalted answered them with what you see; or it refers to the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir, since their livelihood was in wealth and children.

This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and it was said: the polytheists of Quraysh. (Wa-qila: wa-qila.) Perhaps those who held to generality, which is the apparent meaning, said: it includes those mentioned by initial inclusion. What is meant by "al-ighna" (avail) is "al-daf'" (repelling). It is said: aghna ʿanhu when he repelled from him a harm that would have befallen him otherwise; that is, on the Day of Resurrection their wealth on which they relied in grave matters will not repel from them, nor will those who are more hopeful than that and greater in their estimation, namely their children, any portion of the punishment of Allah the Exalted. Some of them said: what is meant by "al-ighna" is "al-ijzaʾ" (sufficing), and it is said: ma yughni ʿanka hadha, meaning "what does not suffice for you and does not benefit you." "Min" is for substitution or for the starting point, and "shay'an" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: that will not suffice them against the punishment of Allah the Exalted in any measure of sufficing. On the first explanation of "al-ighna" and making this its literal meaning rather than the other, it is said by way of implication (tadmin), and the matter of its being an object is evident from its transitivity then.

﴿And those﴾ — that is, those characterized by disbelief because of their disbelief — ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾, that is, its constant occupants, and this is the customary meaning of "companions" (al-as'hab).

﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾ (611). This is an emphasis of what is intended by the first sentence. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates permanence and continuity, 
page 36
and the fronting of the adverbial phrase is to preserve the rhyme-endings of the verses.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 117:

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ is like an illustration of the failure of wealth to benefit. It is evident that the failure of children to benefit is not explicitly stated, because if they are disbelievers, which is the apparent case, their ruling is the same as theirs. And if they are Muslims, they will be against them, not for them, in this world. Their hatred of them in the Hereafter is ﴿on the Day when the secrets are tested﴾ (86:9), and ﴿when the shin is uncovered﴾ (68:42). Their disavowal of them, when a person flees from his mother and father, is too obvious to be hidden. The particle "mā" (what) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "they spend it." The demonstrative (this) is for belittling. The intended meaning is an illustration of all the charities and expenditures of the disbelievers, however they were made. This is what is narrated from Mujahid. It was also said that it is an illustration of whatever the disbelievers spend generally in hostility toward the Messenger (ﷺ). It was said that it refers to what Quraysh spent on the day of Badr and Uhud when they united against him, peace be upon him. It was also said that it refers to what the lowly among the Jews spent on their distorting scholars, that is, the state of that matter and its amazing story.

﴿like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾, meaning intense cold. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and a group. Al-Zajjāj said: "al-ṣirr" is the sound of the blaze of fire, and that was in that wind. It was also said: the root of "ṣirr" is like "ṣarṣar," meaning a cold wind. According to this, the meaning of the structure is "a wind in which there is a cold wind." As you see, this needs explanation. It has been mentioned that it is used in the sense of "tajrīd" (abstraction), as in his saying:

"Were it not for that, I would have sent my horse grazing, and in the Merciful there is sufficiency for the weak."

That is, He is sufficient. Some scholars rejected that it originally means a cold wind, and that it is merely a verbal noun meaning cold, as al-Ḥabr said. Its use for what was mentioned is figurative (majāz), and it is not the intended meaning. It was also said that it is an adjective meaning cold, but its noun is omitted, meaning "a cold chill," so it is a figurative attribution, like "a shade that is shady." This is far-fetched, because what is familiar in such cases is mentioning the noun, while omitting and estimating it is not known. It was also said that it originally is the sound of a cold wind, from the "ṣarr" of a pen or door, "ṣarīr," when it makes a sound, or from "al-ṣarra," meaning clamor and shouting. It is used here in its original sense. The objection is that this meaning is not familiar in usage. "Rīḥ" is the singular of "riyāḥ," and in the Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon) it is "al-ṣiḥāḥ wa-al-aryāḥ" (the plural). It may also be pluralized as "arwāḥ," because its root is a "wāw," but it came with a "yā'" because of the kasra before it. When they return to the fatḥa, it goes back to the "wāw," as in your saying: "arwaḥa al-māʾ" (the water became cool in the evening), and "tarawwaḥat bi-al-mirwaḥa" (she fanned herself with a fan). It is also said: "rīḥ" and "rīḥa," as they said: "dār" and "dāra." Scholars will have discussion on this point, if Allah the Exalted wills, when it comes. The word "rīḥ" is used in the singular because the wind at sea is specifically associated with punishment, while the plural is specifically associated with mercy. For this reason it is narrated: "O Allah, make them winds (riyāḥ) and do not make them a wind (rīḥ)."

﴿It struck the tilth﴾, that is, the crop of

﴿a people who wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief and sins, so they incurred anger from Allah the Exalted. They were described this way because it was said that destruction from wrath is more severe and more dreadful, or because the intended point is to indicate the absence of benefit in this world and the Hereafter. This occurs only in the destruction of a disbeliever's wealth. As for others, they may be rewarded for what was destroyed for them because of their patience. It was also said that the intended meaning is that they wronged themselves by sowing in a place other than the place of sowing and at a time other than its time, and ( ﴿so it destroyed it﴾ ) entirely, leaving it with no trace or remnant, as a punishment for them for their sins. It was also said that it was a discipline from Allah the Exalted for them in placing a thing in other than its proper place, which is its right. This is from the compound simile (tashbīh murakkab), in which the essence and the totality are found together. It is not necessary that what follows the particle be the thing compared, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is like water We sent down﴾ (10:24). Otherwise it would have to be said: "like the likeness of a tilth," because the spent thing is the object being compared. It is also permitted that the intended meaning is "like the destruction of what they spend, like the destruction of a wind," or "like what they spend, like a wind's place of destruction." The "mahlak" is a passive noun, meaning the tilth. The aspect, when it is a compound simile, is the scarcity of benefit and the loss. It is also permitted that it is a separated simile (tashbīh mufarraq), so the destruction by Allah the Exalted is compared to the destruction by the wind, and the spent thing is compared to the tilth. Allah the Exalted made their deeds scattered dust by what is in the cold wind of making them debris. It is also read: "tunfiqūna" with a "tāʾ."

﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾. The pronoun may refer to the spenders, meaning He did not wrong them by the loss of their expenditures, which they spent in a manner not suitable or of value. Or it may refer to the mentioned people, meaning Allah the Exalted did not wrong the owners of the tilth by destroying it, because they deserved that. In that case this negation, together with His saying ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ (711), is an emphasis on what was understood earlier, both by implication and explicitly. It is read "wa-lākin" with a shadda (lākinna), with "anfusahum" as its subject and the clause "yazlimūna" as its predicate, and the returning pronoun is omitted. The estimate is "yazlimūnahā" (they wrong it), and it is not a fronted object as in the reading with light pronunciation. Its subject is the pronoun of the matter, because it is not omitted except in poetry, as in his saying:

"I was never one whose heart love enters, but whoever looks at your eyelids falls in love."

Its omission is fixed here because of the conditional "man" which is not preceded by abrogating particles. The fronting of "anfusahum" before the verb is for the rhyme (fāṣila), not for restriction. Otherwise the speech would not match, because its implication would be "Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves," not "they wronged themselves and not others," and restriction is necessary in that. The form of the present tense indicates renewal and continuity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 118:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates (biṭānah) those other than your own.﴾ Ibn Ishaq and others related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Some men among the Muslims used to associate closely with some Jews, because of the neighbourly ties and the alliance that existed between them in the pre-Islamic period. So God Most High revealed concerning them, forbidding them from taking such intimacy with them, warning them of the trial (fitnah) that this would bring upon them: this verse." 'Abd ibn Humayd related that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites (munafiqun) of the people of Madinah. The believers were forbidden to befriend them, and the apparent sense of what follows supports this. The biṭānah (intimate, confidant) of a man is his inner circle, those who know his affairs, named from the biṭānah (lining) of a garment, the side facing the body because of its closeness. It is the opposite of the ẓihārah (outer side). The word is used for the singular and plural, and for the masculine and feminine.

The phrase min (مِن) is connected either to lā tattakhidhū (do not take) or to an omitted element functioning as an adjective of biṭānah. It has been said that it is superfluous (zā'idah). Dūn (دُونَ) is either in the sense of ghayr (other than), or in the sense of "lower and baser." The pronoun of the plural attached to it refers to the believers. The meaning is: do not take as allies and confidants the disbelievers, such as the Jews and the hypocrites, or anyone other than the believers, or anyone whose rank does not reach your rank in nobility and religious commitment. The ruling is general, and although the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was specific, taking an opponent as a friend is a cause of trial and corruption. For this reason, this biṭānah has been interpreted as referring to the Khawarij.

Al-Bayhaqi and others related from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Do not engrave Arabic on your rings, and do not seek light from the fire of the polytheists." This was mentioned to al-Hasan, who said: "Yes. Do not engrave on your rings 'Muhammad is the Messenger of God,' and do not let the polytheists keep secrets with you in any of your affairs." Then al-Hasan said: "And the confirmation of this from the Book of God Most High is: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than your own.﴾ ﴿They do not spare you corruption.﴾" The root of alw (أَلْو) is shortcoming (taqṣīr). It is said: alā, like ghazā, yaluu alwan, when one falls short, slackens, or weakens. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"A man, as long as the remnant of his soul lasts, will not reach the extremes of calamities, nor one who falls short (ālā)."

He meant: nor one who is remiss in seeking. It is intransitive, and it becomes transitive to its object by means of a preposition. It may also be used transitively to two objects, in their saying: lā ālūka nuṣḥan wa lā ālūka juhdan (I will not withhold from you sincere advice or effort), by way of implying the sense of withholding: that is, I will not prevent you from that. It may also be taken in the sense of refraining from something, and then it is transitive to one object. In the Qamus: mā alawtu al-shay' means "I did not leave the thing" (i.e., I did not refrain from it). Khabal (خَبَال), in its original sense, is the corruption that afflicts a person and causes him disturbance, like illness or madness, and it is used in the general sense of evil and corruption. According to the first sense, the meaning of the verse is: they do not fall short in causing you corruption and evil; rather they exert themselves to harm you. On this reading, the pronoun in the accusative and the apparent noun are both in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Ibn 'Atiyyah took this view. It has also been permitted that the second noun be in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "driven mad," or as a tamyīz (specification).

This has been objected to, on the grounds that there is no ambiguity in attributing shortcoming to the agent, and it is not valid to make it the agent except on the basis of metaphorical attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī), and the accusative by removal of the preposition. The use of the verbal noun as a ḥāl is not analogical except where the verbal noun is a kind of the verb itself, as in ataanī surʿatan wa buṭʾan (he came to me quickly and slowly), as al-Radi stated in the discussion of the object and the circumstantial accusative. al-Sialkuti relied upon this. Abu Hayyan related that the tamyīz here is transferred from the object, as in ﴿and We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾. This is extraordinarily strange, because the assumption is that the verb is intransitive, so from where would it have an object from which the tamyīz is transferred? To consider its transitivity to it by the implied preposition is a view of the accusative by removal of the preposition, and you have heard what is wrong with that.

It has been answered by committing to one of the two options: either the ḥāl, or its being in the accusative by removal (of the preposition), with the view that hearing (sama') is required here. The meaning on the second view is: "they do not withhold corruption from you," that is, they do to you whatever corruption they are able to, and they keep none of it back from harming you. This is a sound view. Taḍmīn (implicit combination of meanings) is analogical according to the correct opinion, and the dispute about it is weak and not to be considered. The meaning and the grammar on the third view are clear once one has grasped what has preceded.

﴿They wish for what distresses you.﴾ That is: they love your distress, that is, your severe hardship and harm.

Al-Suddi said: "They wish for your going astray from your religion." The same was related from Ibn Jarir.

﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths.﴾ That is: signs of enmity toward you have become manifest from the slips of their tongues and the implications of their words. Because of the intensity of their hatred for you, they cannot control themselves and cannot guard their tongues. Qatadah said: "Its manifestation is among themselves, in that each of them showed to his brother what indicates his hatred for the Muslims." This is far-fetched, because what follows does not fit it. Afwāh (أفواه) is the plural of fam (mouth), whose original form is fuwh, so its final radical is a hā'. Plurals return things to their roots, and this is also indicated by its diminutive, fuwayh, and its relative form, fuwhī. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: qad bada al-baghḍā'. ﴿And what their chests conceal is greater.﴾ That is, greater than what has appeared, because the latter was a slip, and such a thing can only be little.

﴿We have already made the signs clear to you.﴾ That is: We have made clear to you the signs indicating the prohibition of allying with the enemies of God and His Messenger (ﷺ). Or: We have already made clear to you the evident proofs by which the friend is distinguished from the enemy. ﴿If you are people who understand.﴾ (811) That is: if you are of the people of intellect, or if you know the difference between the friend and the enemy, or if you know the admonitions of God Most High and their benefits. The answer to "if" (in) is omitted, because the context indicates it.

Furthermore, these sentences, other than ﴿and what their chests conceal is greater﴾, since it is only a circumstantial clause, have come as independent resumptive statements answering a question about the prohibition. The omission of conjunction between them indicates that each one is independent in that matter. It has been said that they are in the position of a qualifier (naʿt) for biṭānah, except "we have already made clear," because it is evident that it cannot be such. The first view is better, because of the benefits of the independent statement, and because qualifiers carry an implication contrary to the intended meaning, or at least the possibility of such an implication, namely the restriction of the prohibition, and that is not the meaning intended. It has also been said that "they wish for what distresses you" is an explanation and emphasis of "they do not spare you corruption," so its ruling is the same as that clause. Everything other than that is a resumptive statement giving the reason, in a sequence in which the later clause is the cause of the earlier one, until the first is the cause of the prohibition. The causation is complete with the whole group, meaning: do not take them as biṭānah, because they do not spare you corruption, because they wish for severe harm to you, as is shown by the fact that hatred has already appeared from their mouths, even though they conceal much. On this view, it is necessary to make an exception of "we have already made clear," since it cannot be a cause for the appearance of hatred, but it can be a cause for the prohibition. So understand.

Here you are, loving them while they do not love you. This is a reproach showing that the addressees are mistaken in taking them as intimates (*bitanah*, inner confidants). There are differing grammarians' views on the parsing (*i'rab*) of this construction. Al-Azhari, Ibn Kaysan and a group of others said: *ha* (an interjection of alerting, *tanbih*) is for drawing attention, *antum* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause *tuhibbunahum* is the predicate (*khabar*). *Ula'* is either a vocative (*munada*) or in the accusative by specification (*ikhtisas*). This was judged weak, because it goes against the apparent meaning, and specification does not occur with a demonstrative noun. It was also said that *antum* is the subject and *ula'* is its predicate, and the clause that follows is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*). This is supported by what al-Radi said: that the purpose of *ha ana dha af'alu* and *ha anta dha taf'alu* is not to identify oneself or the addressee, since there is no benefit in that, but rather to express astonishment at the occurrence of the action mentioned afterwards from the speaker or the addressee. Accordingly, the clause after the demonstrative is necessary to explain the astonishing state, and it has no grammatical position (*mahall*) because it is a resumed sentence. The Basrans said: it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "here you are, saying," and the circumstantial clause here is necessary because the meaning depends on it and is completed by it. Its governing element is either the interjection or the demonstrative.

Al-Radi objected to this, saying that there is no sense in a circumstantial clause, since the meaning is not "you who are pointed to, in the state of your doing." It is not hidden that what the Basrans said is the apparent sense of Arabic usage, because they said *ha anta dha qa'iman* and so explicitly stated the circumstantial function, even though the meaning is one of informing about the state, since that is what is intended by the expression of disapproval. The pronoun and the demonstrative share the same referent, and taking account of the meaning of pointing is merely to correct the governing relation, not because the meaning rests on it. With this, al-Radi's objection is answered, although it has also been answered in other ways. Al-Zajjaj said: *ula'* may be in the sense of *alladhina* (those who), a predicate of the subject, and *tuhibbunahum* is in the position of a relative clause (*sila*), but this is not sound. It was also said: *antum* is the first subject, *ula'* is the second subject, *tuhibbunahum* is the predicate of the second subject, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject, on the pattern of "you are Zayd, you love him." It was also said: *ula'* is the predicate, and the clause following it is a second predicate. It was said: *ula'* is in the accusative position governed by a verb that the following words explain, and the clause is the predicate of the subject. The pointing is for belittling, so it is used here for reproach, as if he regarded them with contempt because of the evident error of this taking.

The love of the believers for them is meant as ordinary love arising from things like kindness and friendship. Such love, though strange, is blameworthy when it comes from believers towards enemies of the religion who wait for them to suffer misfortune. However, it does not reach the level of unbelief. It did not reach that level for another reason, which hardly occurs from those addressed. It was also said that the meaning is: "you love them" because you desire Islam for them and invite them to Paradise, while they do not love you because they desire for you unbelief and error, which leads to destruction. What this implies is not hidden.

﴿And you believe in the Book, all of it﴾: that is, the whole genus (*jins*) of Books. This is taken as in the expression "you are the man," meaning the one complete in manhood. In that case, "the Book" would be an allusion to the Qur'an, which is a strained reading. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the object in "they do not love you." Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr objected to this, saying that when an affirmative present-tense verb comes as a circumstantial clause, the circumstantial particle *waw* does not enter upon it. For this reason they interpreted "I stood and I was striking his eyes" as having an elided subject, meaning "I stood while I was striking his eyes." A similar interpretation, though it occurs here, would mean: "and they do not love you while you believe in the whole Book." However, coordination with *tuhibbunahum* is better because it avoids ellipsis. In addition, the discourse is in the context of rebuke, and belief in the whole Book is not like that, since it is purely correct. The reading "you believe in the whole Book while they do not believe in any part of it, because their belief is no belief, and so it does not combine with love" is sound, as the second scholar said in establishing the circumstantial function instead of coordination. With this, what al-Bahr has as an excuse is answered. The meaning is: they love you while you believe in their Book, so why do you love them while they do not believe in your Book?

﴿And when they meet you, they say: "We believe"﴾ out of hypocrisy. ﴿And when they are alone﴾: that is, when some of them are alone with others, ﴿they bite at you﴾: that is, on your account, ﴿the fingertips﴾: that is, the tips of the fingers, ﴿out of rage﴾: that is, on account of anger and fury at what they see of the believers' unity, the agreement of their word, and God Most High's support for them, to the extent that their enemies cannot find a way to vent their anger and are compelled to flatter them. Biting the fingertips is the habit of one who is regretful, sorrowful and powerless. For this reason it is used to indicate the state of these people, and the meaning is not that there is actually biting.

Say (O Muhammad) with your tongue. It was also said: the meaning is "speak to yourself about their humiliation and the glorification of Islam," without there being any actual speech. It was also said: it is an address to every believer and an incitement for them against their enmity and an urging for them to address them with the address of adversaries, since nothing cuts love more than a wound inflicted by the tongue. Accordingly, the intended meaning of His words Most High, ﴿Die in your rage﴾, is merely the address with what displeases them. The correct view upon which their word agreed is that it is an invocation against them. That this involves something obscure is because the one against whom an invocation is made is not addressed; rather God Most High is addressed and asked to afflict him. There is no obscurity in its obscurity, and it is heedlessness of the expressions people use such as "may God fight you," "remain in glory," and "sleep in comfort," and other things beyond counting. The meaning, as it has been said, is the invocation for the rage to endure and increase, with the strength of Islam and its people multiplying until they perish from it. According to the second scholar this is a metonymy of metonymy (*kinayat al-kinayah*), where by the invocation of their dying in rage he expressed what it entails, namely the invocation for their rage to increase until their destruction, and by that he expressed what it entails, namely the strength of Islam and the might of its name. This is because death by rage, or its increase, is not something fit to be requested or invoked.

It has been objected that the figurative usage (*majaz*) is mentioned, and as for metonymy upon metonymy, it is rare, though al-Subki explicitly mentioned it in his usul works and reported a disagreement about it. Along with this, the distinction between metonymy by intermediaries and metonymy upon metonymy needs honest reflection, and perhaps it is a conventional distinction. Also, what he mentioned, that death by rage alone, etc., is refuted by the fact that the factor making it fitting may be the allusion it contains to their blame, since they deserved this terrible death and this shameful state.

﴿Indeed God is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ (911): that is, of what is hidden in them. This may be part of what is said, meaning: say to them, "Indeed God Most High knows what is more hidden than what you conceal of biting your fingertips when you are alone, and He will recompense you for it." It may also be separate from it, meaning: say to them what has preceded, and do not be surprised at my informing you of their secrets, for I know what is more hidden than their inner thoughts. The prohibition of surprise then is either used in its ordinary figurative sense on the basis that the addressee already knows the content of this sentence, or it remains in its literal sense if the addressee is other than that and is one who comprehends this address. There is no difficulty on either reading, unlike those who were mistaken about this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 120:

﴿If good touches you﴾, O believers, ﴿it grieves them﴾, that is, it saddens them and enrages them. ﴿Good﴾ here means a blessing from your Lord, such as unity, the unification of the word (kalima), and victory over the enemies. ﴿And if an evil befalls you﴾, that is, a trial (mihna), such as a enemy striking some of you and disagreement of the word among you, ﴿they rejoice at it﴾, that is, they are delighted (yabtahiju) ( by it ). In this is an indication that their enmity has reached the limit of envy and gloating. As for the verb "massa" (touch), it has been said that it is used metaphorically for "asaba" (befall), so the two are here of one meaning, and He has made them equal in other places, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them, and if an affliction befalls you﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾. The expression here uses "massa" with good and "asaba" with evil merely for variety of expression. Some of the verifiers have said: the best and most fitting to the context is what has been said, namely that it indicates their excess in joy and sorrow, because "massa" is less than "asaba", as is apparent. So if the least good that reaches them grieves them, then other than it is more so; and if they rejoice at the greatest of calamities, at which the one who gloats would pity and the envious would be softened, then other than it is more so. Thus their friendship is not hoped for at all, so how can you take them as intimate companions (bitana)?! As for the view that it is not far-fetched to say: this is an indication that what good reaches them relative to God's gentle care for them is a small good, and what evil reaches them, relative to the great reward that is given in return for it, is a great and distant matter, as is not hidden. ﴿And if you are patient﴾ over their harm, or over obedience to God, and the bitterness of jihad in His way, ﴿and you are mindful of God﴾ regarding what has been forbidden to you, ﴿their scheming will not harm you﴾
Page 41
that is, their plotting. The root of "kayd" is hardship. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (la yadirrakum) with a kasra on the dad and a jazm on the ra', as the response of the conditional, from "daarahu yadiiruhu", meaning "darrahu yadurruhu". The ra' is dammed in the well-known reading to follow the dammah of the dad, as in the doubled imperative with a damma on the middle letter, like "mudda"; the jazm is implied. They permitted in its like a fatha for lightness and a kasra for moving the sakin. It has been said that it is marfu' by the implied fa', but this is an artificial construction that is dispensed with. ﴿Anything﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, that is, ﴿their scheming will not harm you at all﴾ of harm, neither much nor little, by the blessing of patience and piety, because they are among the finest acts of obedience and noble characteristics. Whoever adorns himself with these is under God's protection and guardianship, so that the scheme of an enemy does not harm him. It has been said: ﴿their scheming will not harm you﴾ because He has encompassed them, so for you is the great reward; if it fails, then it is the worldly blessing, so you are not deprived of the good in either case. But this is remote. ﴿Indeed God is encompassing of what they do﴾ of scheming.

Al-Hasan and Abu Hatim read (ta'malun) with a ta' on top, and it is an address to the believers, that is, what you do of patience and piety. ﴿Encompassing﴾ in knowledge, or in the meaning fitting to His majesty, so that He punishes them for it or rewards you for it.

And [remember] when you set out early in the morning from [the house of] your family. That is, remember when you went out at dawn from [the house of] your family. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ alone. The statement is a new sentence, brought to cite what it contains: that the absence of patience and piety brings harm, and that their presence brings what was promised, namely deliverance from the harm of the enemies' plotting. The departure was from the chamber of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, ﴿placing the believers﴾, that is, settling them. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr. It was also said: ﴿placing﴾ means lodging them, and it was said: arranging and preparing for them. The reading "lil-mu'minin" (for the believers) supports this, since the place of strengthening and increase is not an eloquent place for it. ﴿positions for battle﴾, that is, places, stations and standing points for it. The original meaning of "maq'ad" (seat) and "maqam" (station) is the place of sitting and standing, then the usage was extended, and it was applied metaphorically (majaz, figurative usage) to any place in general, even if there is no standing or sitting in it. It may also be applied to the person who occupies it, as in their saying "the exalted assembly" and "the noble station." The clause ﴿placing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿you set out﴾. Because the intended purpose is to recall the extended period of time, which includes the start of the departure, the placing, and what follows from them, since this is what reminds of the story, there is no need to say that it is a prospective circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), meaning intending and aiming at the placing. ﴿Positions﴾ is the second object of ﴿placing﴾. The prepositional phrase is related either to the verb before it or to an omitted element that functions as an adjectival qualifier of ﴿positions﴾. It is not permissible, as Abu al-Baqa' said, for it to be related to the word ﴿positions﴾ itself, because what is meant by it is a place, and a place does not govern.

Ibn Ishaq and a group related from Ibn Shihab, Muhammad ibn Yahya, al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and others, each of whom narrated part of the hadith, that: "When the disbelievers of Quraysh, the companions of the well (al-qalib), were struck on the day of Badr, and their broken remnant returned to Makkah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb returned on his camel. 'Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayya walked with men of Quraysh whose fathers, sons and brothers had been struck on the day of Badr. They spoke to Abu Sufyan, and [spoke to] those among Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, saying: 'O assembly of Quraysh, Muhammad has laid you low and killed your best men. So help us with this wealth against his war, so that perhaps we may obtain our vengeance for those who struck us.' They did so.
