Quraysh gathered for war against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and set out with their full strength, their newcomers and their allies, the Ahabish, and those who followed them from the Banu Kinanah and the people of Tihamah. They went out with them with the women, to stir their zeal and so that they would not flee. Abu Sufyan went out, while he was the leader of the people, with Hind bint 'Utba. Others also went out with women. They came until they halted at 'Ayn'ayn, on a mountain in the lowest part of the salt-flat (sabkha), from the channel (qanat), on the edge of the valley, facing Madinah. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims heard of them, and they had halted where they halted, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I saw cows being slaughtered, I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I saw that I put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted it as Madinah. So if you see fit to remain in Madinah and let them come to where they have halted, then if they stay they will stay in a bad place, and if they enter upon us, we will fight them within it.' The opinion of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul agreed with the opinion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in that he too saw that they should not go out to them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also disliked going out. Some men among the Muslims, those whom Allah honoured with martyrdom on the day of Uhud, and others who had missed the day of Badr, said: 'Take us out, O Messenger of Allah, against our enemies, so that they do not see that we have turned away from them out of cowardice and weakness.' 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said: 'O Messenger of Allah, remain in Madinah and do not go out to them. By Allah, we have never gone out from it to an enemy of ours without them striking us, nor has any enemy entered upon us without our striking them. So leave them, O Messenger of Allah. If they remain, they remain in a bad prison, and if they enter, the men will fight them from above them, and if they return, they will return disappointed as they came.' The people kept at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, those among them whose desire was to meet the enemy, until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered, put on his battle armour, and that was on Friday after he had finished the prayer. Then he went out to them, and the people regretted and said: 'We compelled the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that was not for us. If you wish, sit [here], O Messenger of Allah.' He ﷺ said: 'It is not fitting for a Prophet, when he has put on his armour, to take it off until he has fought.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out with a thousand of his companions, while he had promised them victory if they were patient. He appointed Ibn Umm Maktum to lead the people in prayer. When he reached al-Shawt, between Madinah and Uhud, 'Abdullah [ibn Ubayy] withdrew from him with a third of the people and said: 'He obeyed them and disobeyed me. We do not know why we should kill ourselves here, O people.' He returned with those who followed him from his people, from the people of hypocrisy and doubt. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram, brother of the Banu Salimah, followed them, saying: 'O my people, I remind you of Allah that you not forsake your people and your Prophet at the time when the enemy has gathered.' He said: 'If we knew that you were going to fight, we would not have abandoned you, but we do not think there will be any fighting.' When they disobeyed him and refused except to turn away, he said: 'May Allah banish you, enemies of Allah. Allah will surely suffice His Prophet without you.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went on until he passed through the lava-field of the Banu Harithah. A horse swished its tail and struck the sheath of a sword, which he drew out. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who loved good omens and did not regard omens with birds as bad for the owner of the sword, said: 'Smell your sword, for I see that swords will be drawn today.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went on until he descended into the ravine of Uhud, on the side of the valley, toward the mountain. He placed his back and his camp toward Uhud and said: 'None of you shall fight until we order him to fight.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arranged himself for battle and walked on foot, setting his companions in rows, as if he were straightening them with an arrow-shaft. If he saw someone's chest protruding, he said: 'Step back.' He had seven hundred men. He appointed 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr over the archers, and he was distinguished that day by white garments; they were fifty men. He said: 'Keep the horses away from us with arrows, so that they do not come at us from behind, whether we are winning or losing. Stay in your place; you must not be attacked from your side.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ wore two coats of mail, and he gave the banner to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr. Quraysh arranged themselves, and they were three thousand, among them two hundred horses, which they had placed on the flanks. The fighting broke out, and that was on Saturday, on the middle of Shawwal in the third year after the Hijrah, and what happened happened. Allah the Exalted pointed to this day with this verse." The saying that it refers to the day of Badr, as Muqatil said that it refers to the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), is contrary to what the majority of scholars (al-jumhur) hold.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of all things heard, and what was said in this battle enters into this in the first instance, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ (121) of all things known, among them what was in the hearts of the people that day,
[p. 43]
and the sentence is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) to make known that He had decreed for them words and deeds that should not have come from them. Among that is the statement of the companions of 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr when they saw the Muslims overcoming the disbelievers of Quraysh: "Our companions have taken booty, and we will remain with no booty," and they began slipping away one by one until they vacated their positions, and there remained with 'Abdullah only twelve men, despite the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's injunction to them to remain steadfast in their place.

﴿When⁠ two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾: it is said that this is a substitute (badal) for "when you set out early in the morning" (idh ghadawta), clarifying what is intended by the reminder.

It is also permitted that it be an adverbial clause (zarf) governing either "He prepared" (li-tubawwi'u), or "you set out" (li-ghadawta), or "All-Hearing, All-Knowing" (li-sami'un alim), by way of tanazu' (competition between governors), or both together according to one opinion; and the intention is not to restrict his being All-Hearing, All-Knowing to that time.

﴿Two groups from among you﴾, that is, two factions of the Muslims, and they are two clans of the Ansar: Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Abdullah, al-Hasan and a great many others. Al-Jubba'i said: a group of the Muhajirun and a group of the Ansar were about to lose heart.

﴿That they would lose heart﴾, that is, become weak and cowardly, when they saw the desertion of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul together with those who were with him from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The phrase formed by "an" and the verb is attached to "were about to," with the preposition (ba') omitted, meaning "were about to [commit] cowardice." Here the intended meaning is its necessary consequence, since the act of choice to which intention is attached is what is meant. It is apparent that this intention was not a resolve or firm determination to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) and separate from him, because such a thing does not proceed from a believer; rather it was merely a passing thought and whispering of the self, as in the saying:

I say to her, when she is startled and agitated: "Stay where you are, you will be praised or you will rest."

This is confirmed by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾, that is, their Helper; and this clause is parenthetical (i'tiraḍ).

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "were about to" or from its pronoun in "lose heart," indicating the improbability of their cowardice or their intention, given that they were under the protection of Allah, Exalted. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read: "And Allah is their Protector" with the plural pronoun, after the manner of ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾.

﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely⁠﴾ (3:122): that is, upon Him, glorified is He, and not upon other than Him, as indicated by the fronting of the object and the explicit mention of the Glorious Name, for blessing and for causation. The "al" in "the believers" is for the category, and the two groups enter into it at the first level. In this designation there is an indication that faith in Allah, Exalted, necessitates reliance upon Him, and the object of reliance is omitted to convey generality: that they should rely upon Him, mighty is His affair, in all their matters, great and small, easy and difficult.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 123:

﴿Indeed, Allah had already given you victory at Badr﴾. This explains what follows from patience and God-consciousness (taqwa), after the preceding explanation of what follows from their absence. Alternatively, it is a prelude to making reliance upon Allah the Exalted obligatory, by reminding them of what necessitates it. Badr, as al-Sha'bi said, was a well belonging to a man from Juhayna called Badr, and it was named after him. al-Waqidi said: it is the name of the place. It was also said: it is the name of the valley. It was, as 'Ikrima said, a trading site in the pre-Islamic era.

Qatada said: Badr is a water source between Makkah and Madinah, where the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists met. It was the first battle the Prophet (ﷺ) fought. It took place on the seventeenth of the month of Ramadan, on a Friday, in the second year after the Hijra. The letter ba' (bi) here means "in" (fi), i.e., Allah gave you victory at Badr. ﴿And you were humiliated﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the object of "nasarakum" (gave you victory). The word "adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qilla) of "dhalil" (humble, weak). It was chosen over "dhala'il" to indicate their small number together with their weakness. What is meant by it is the lack of equipment, not the well-known humiliation. Therefore there is no difficulty in the Prophet (ﷺ) being included in this address, if we take it that way. It was also said: there is no objection to taking the well-known meaning, and the intended sense would be "﴿and you were humiliated﴾ in the eyes of others, even though you were honoured in your own eyes." The discussion of their number and the number of the polytheists at that time has already been presented.

﴿So be mindful of Allah﴾ by avoiding His disobedience and by being patient in obeying Him. The command to be patient is not stated explicitly, being sufficed by what preceded and what followed, along with an indication, as some have said, of the nobility and originality of God-consciousness and that patience is one of its foundational requirements. Placing the command to be mindful of Allah after the report of victory informs us that their victory mentioned was due to their God-consciousness. Thus the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾ (321) is: so that you may render thanks for the blessing He bestowed upon you, the near victory, because of your God-consciousness of Him. It may also be a metonymy (kinaya) or a figurative usage (majaz) for attaining another blessing that necessitates gratitude, as if it were said: "So be mindful of Allah, that you may attain a blessing from Allah, the Exalted, and thank Him for it." Thus gratitude is placed in the position of bestowal, because it is its cause and prepares for it.

﴿Idh taqulu lil-mu'minin﴾ ("When you were saying to the believers") is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) modifying *li-nasrikum* ("His help for you"). The time meant is an extended period. He placed the command to *taqwa* (God-consciousness) before it to show the great concern for it. It is also said that it is a second substitute (badal) for *idh ghadawta* ("when you set out"). According to the first view, this statement was made at Badr, and this is the view of al-Hasan and others.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from al-Sha'bi that the Muslims were informed on the day of Badr that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi intended to reinforce the polytheists. This troubled them, so God revealed ﴿Is it not enough for you﴾ and so on. Then news of the defeat reached Kurz, so he did not reinforce the polytheists. According to the second view, the statement was made at Uhud. The condition was patience and God-consciousness, which keeps one from disobedience. Since these two were not found among them, they were not given help. This is attributed to Ikrimah and to Qatadah in one of the two reports from him.

﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ *Al-kifayah* is the meeting of need, and above it is *al-ghina* (sufficiency), on the basis that it is an addition beyond the negation of need. *Al-imdad* is originally giving a thing progressively, one state after another. It is said *madda fi al-sayr* when one continues on the journey, and *amtadda bihimu al-sayr* when the journey lengthens and continues. Some have said that what is by way of strengthening and aid is said *amadda yumiddu imdadan*, and what is by way of increase is said *maddahu madda*. It is also said that one says *maddahu fi al-sharr* and *amaddahu fi al-khayr*. The interrogative *hamzah* is for denying that this would not be sufficient for them. He used *lan* to emphasise the negation, according to the view of some scholars. This implies that at that time they were like those who had despaired of victory, because of the smallness of their number and their equipment. In expressing it with the title of Lordship (*rububiyyah*) together with the attachment to the pronoun of the addressees, there is a subtlety and strengthening of the denial that is not hidden.

*An yumiddakum* ("that He should reinforce you") is, in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), the subject of *yakfi-kum*. *Min al-malaikah* ("of the angels") is either an explanation or a qualifier of *alf* ("thousand") or of what it is attached to. *Munzilin* ("sent down") is a qualifier of *thalathat alaf* ("three thousand"). It is also said that it is a circumstantial (hal) qualifier of *al-malaikah*. Describing them with this indicates that they are among the most noble of the angels. They were sent down, as the Shaykh al-Akbar (may God sanctify his secret) mentioned, from the third heaven, and he mentioned the secret of that in *al-Futuhat*.

It was also read *munazzalin* with the doubled letter, for intensification or for gradualness. It was read in the active form of both patterns, with the meaning "sending down" terror into the hearts of your enemies or victory for you. The majority read the *ta'* of *thalathah* with a kasrah. In the irregular readings (shadhdh) it was read with a sukun, and it was pausally stopped on by replacing it with a *ha'*, on the basis that the connected reading was treated as the pause in both cases. This is weakened by the fact that the construct and what is attached to it are like one thing.

[p. 45]

( ﴿بَلى﴾ ) "Yes" (بَلى) is an affirmation of what follows "lan" (لَنْ, "never"), meaning: yes, that (i.e., the three thousand) suffices you (يَكْفِيكم). Then He promised them an increase conditionally, so the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿If you are patient﴾ under the hardship of jihad and what you have been commanded (﴿وتَتَّقُوا﴾), ﴿and maintain taqwa﴾ toward your Lord by avoiding His disobedience and not opposing Him, ( ﴿ويَأْتُوكُمْ﴾ ) ﴿and they come to you﴾, i.e., the polytheists, or the companions of Kurz, as al-Sha'bi said.

[p. 46]

﴿from their immediate rage this [moment]﴾. The original meaning of al-fawr (الفَوْر) is a verbal noun from "fārat al-qidr" (فارَتِ القِدْرُ), when the pot's boiling became intense. From this comes the saying that the intensity of heat is from the fawr of Hell. It is also applied to anger, because it resembles the boiling of a pot, and to the beginning of anything. Then it was borrowed for speed, and then applied to the state in which there is no delay or lag. The meaning is: they will come to you immediately. It was described thus to emphasize speed by adding specificity and proximity. The arrangement of their coming swiftly within the framework of the two conditions of the reinforcement and its two pivots, together with the certainty of the reinforcement in any case, whether they hastened or delayed, serves as a notice of the certainty of the speed of the reinforcement, not of the certainty of its basic occurrence. Or it is to show that its occurrence is certain in any state in which it is supposed, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, since it was linked to the most remote estimations, so that its certainty in all the others is known a fortiori. For the sudden assault of enemies is among the situations in which reinforcement customarily does not arrive. So when the reinforcement is linked to it, its certainty is established despite its incompatibility with it, which indicates that it is certain beyond doubt along with what is not incompatible with it. So it has been said. It may be understood from this that the reinforcement mentioned in the condition in His saying, ﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾, did occur for them. In this there is hesitation and uncertainty, because if this statement refers to the Battle of Uhud, there is no doubt that this did not occur, nor by the possession of one [person], because the condition did not occur; and therefore the defeat occurred. If it refers to the Battle of Badr, as is the preferred view, then there has been disagreement over whether they were reinforced with these five thousand or not. al-Sha'bi held that they were reinforced with something other than them and were not reinforced with them, based on linking the reinforcement with them to the combination of the three matters: patience, taqwa, and the coming of the companions of Kurz. The third matter was missing, as we mentioned at the beginning, so the combination did not exist because some of its parts did not exist. Thus the mentioned reinforcement did not occur, as al-Sha'bi explicitly stated. Yet a group held the opposite, and perhaps this is the basis of the position of the author of the saying (ṣāḥib al-qīl). However, it remains that interpreting al-fawr in the way it has been interpreted is not definitive, and indeed it has not been found explicitly in the statements of the early scholars (al-salaf). What Ikrimah, Mujahid, and Abu Salih, mawla of Umm Hani, held is that it means anger. In that case, min (مِن) is causal, meaning: they will come to you because of their anger at you. The reference (الإشارة) is either to magnify that anger, insofar as it is intense and firmly rooted in hearts, or to belittle it, insofar as it is not in the proper manner or the praiseworthy way. For it was due to the Muslims' opposition to them in religion, their deriding of their opinions, and their condemnation of their gods, or due to what they inflicted upon them and what they smashed of the heads of their leaders on the Day of Badr. Ikrimah held the second view, and it is based on the premise that this statement occurred at Uhud.

Ibn 'Abbas, in what Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, interpreted it as travel, i.e., ﴿and they come to you from this journey of theirs﴾. It was said: this too is based on what its predecessor was based on, "because the disbelievers, after the Battle of Uhud, regretted after their departure, since they had not passed by Madinah, and they intended to return. So God Most High revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should order his companions to prepare against them. Then He said: If you are patient in jihad and maintain taqwa, and they return to you from this journey of theirs, God will reinforce you with five thousand angels. So they took up jihad and went out following the disbelievers despite their wounds. Whoever passed by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed the polytheists that he had gone out pursuing them, the polytheists feared that if they returned, victory would go to the Muslims, and that those who had lagged behind would join them, and others would join them. So they sent Nu'aym al-Ashja'i to dissuade them by magnifying the matter of Quraysh, and they hastened to Makkah, and God Most High spared the Muslims their affair." The story is well known. Yet the interpretation of al-fawr as travel is something we have not found in the lexicographical books available to us. Perhaps al-fawr in the sense of the state in which there is no delay is what is meant, and this interpretation is an explanation of the resulting meaning. Al-Hasan, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Qatadah, and others held that min (مِن) in ﴿from their fawr﴾ means their direction (وجه). This is not explicit in what the later exegetes (ṣāḥib al-qīl) held, because it may mean the direction that the traveler intends, and it may mean the beginning of the time.

[p. 46 continued]

It may mean the beginning of the time. Unless it is said: although it is not explicit, it is an apparent meaning close to the explicit. For although "direction" is used with the stated meaning in the language, the use of fawr in that sense is disputed. The possibility that it means the beginning of time returns to what they said, so reflect.

Know that this reinforcement occurred gradually. At first it was one thousand, then they became two thousand, then three thousand, then five thousand and no more. So the meaning of ﴿He will reinforce you with five thousand﴾ is that He will reinforce you with a complete five thousand. This is the view of al-Hasan. Others said: the angels were eight thousand, so the meaning is: He will reinforce you with five thousand more ﴿marked﴾ (مُسَوِّمِينَ) (521). From taswīm, which is displaying the sign of a thing. The intended meaning is that they were marking themselves or their horses. The reports differ on this. From 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: al-Zubayr wore a yellow turban, wrapping it around himself, so the angels descended wearing yellow turbans. Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the distinguishing mark of the angels on the Day of Badr was white turbans, letting their ends hang on their backs, and on the Day of Hunayn, red turbans. In another report from him, but with a weak chain: on the Day of Badr they wore black turbans, and on the Day of Uhud red turbans.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others transmitted from 'Ali, may God honor his face, that he said: the distinguishing mark of the angels on the Day of Badr was white wool on the foreheads and tails of the horses. They were, as al-Rabi' said, on piebald horses.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that they were marked with red wool (al-'ihn al-aḥmar).

Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Mujahid that he said: they were marked, with the tails and foreheads of their horses cut and containing wool and red wool.

You know that there is no obstacle to their marking themselves and their horses as well. This is according to the recitation (qirā'ah, القراءة, the variant reading of the Qur'an) of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim, ﴿musawwimīn﴾ (مُسَوِّمِينَ) with a kasra on the waw. As for the recitation of the rest, (مُسَوَّمِينَ) with a fatha on the waw, as a passive participle (ism maf'ūl), it was said: the meaning is marked by God Most High. It was also said: sent forth without restraint. From this comes the saying: a sā'imah camel, meaning sent to graze. This is the view of al-Suddi. According to this recitation, what is evident is that the marking is for them. As for whether it was for their horses, that is not apparent.

﴿وما جَعَلَهُ اللَّهُ﴾ [And Allah did not make it]: that is, the reinforcement (al-imdad) understood from the implied verb mentioned previously, which is indicated by the force of the speech, as if it were said: "So Allah reinforced you with what was mentioned." And Allah, exalted is He, did not make that reinforcement anything but good tidings for you. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the promise of reinforcement. It has been said: it refers to the marking (al-taswim) or to the sending down (al-tanzil) or to the victory understood from your earlier victory, and the object of the good tidings is other than that. It has been said: it refers to the reinforcement indicated by one of the two verbs. All of these are nothing, as is not hidden. The word "al-bushra" (good tidings) is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with "ja'ala" transitive to one object, or it is its object if "ja'ala" is taken as transitive to two objects. On the first reading, the exception is an exceptive construction (al-istithna' al-mufarragh) drawn from the most general of causes (a'amm al-'ilal), meaning: "And He did not make your reinforcement by the sending down of the angels for anything among things except good tidings to you that you would be given victory." On the second reading, it is an exceptive construction drawn from the most general of objects, meaning: "And Allah, exalted is He, did not make it anything among things except good tidings to you."

This sentence is the beginning of a new statement, not included within the scope of speech, but rather sent forth from Him, exalted is He, to clarify that apparent causes have no effect apart from His permission, exalted is He, for the true reality of victory belongs exclusively to Him, mighty is His name, so that the believers may place their trust in Him and not despair of Him when its causes and signs are absent. It is conjoined to a verb that is implied, as we have indicated. The address is directed to the believers in honour of them and as a notification that they are the ones in need of what was mentioned. As for His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, he is independent of it through what He has bestowed upon him of spiritual support and divine knowledge.

﴿ولِتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُكم بِهِ﴾ [and so that your hearts might be at rest through it]: that is, and so that your hearts may be calm through the reinforcement, so that you do not fear the multitude of the enemy and the fewness of your numbers. This [phrase] is either conjoined to "bushra" (good tidings) with regard to its position, and it is, like the thing it is conjoined to, a final cause (illah gha'iyyah) for the making. Except that the first was put in the accusative because its conditions were met, while the second was not put in the accusative because those conditions were absent. It has been said: it is also to indicate its original causality and its importance in itself, as in His saying: ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوها وزِينَةً﴾ [that you may ride them and as adornment]. Or it is connected to an implied verb conjoined to the preceding statement, meaning: "and so that your hearts may be at rest through it, He did that." This is better than estimating "He gave you good news," as Abu al-Baqa did. The second is determined on the second possibility of the first.

﴿وما النَّصْرُ﴾ [And victory is not]: that is, in absolute terms, so that the familiar victory is included in it by primary entry. ﴿إلا مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ [except from Allah's presence], who deposited in the causes, according to the requirement of wisdom, a power that is not affected except by Him. Or: "And the familiar victory is not except from Him, exalted is He, and not from the angels, because the utmost of their matter is what was mentioned of good tidings and strengthening of hearts, and they did not fight; or because the utmost of their matter is that they fought by Allah's exalted empowerment of them, and they had no independent action of their own; and had Allah, exalted is He, willed, they would not have acted. Moreover, the mere fact of their fighting does not necessitate victory, rather the weakness of those opposed to the fighters must be combined with it; and had Allah, exalted is He, willed, He would have given them power over them. So when He weakened and strengthened, empowered and did not empower, and victory was achieved through that, it was from Him, exalted is He. The verse, on this view, is not evidence for one who claims that effects occur alongside causes and not through them; this has already been established, so remember it. Likewise, there is no evidence in it for the occurrence or non-occurrence of their fighting, because it permits both matters. Some have said each of these."

The preferred view is what is narrated from Mujahid: that the angels did not fight in the expeditions of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, except at Badr. They were present in some of them according to what Allah, exalted is He, knew of the benefit, such as their presence at the circles of the people of remembrance. Perhaps they helped without fighting, as they did at the battle of Uhud according to one opinion. From Ibn Ishaq: Sa'd ibn Malik was shooting in the battle of Uhud, and a young man was passing him arrows; whenever his arrows ran out, he brought them to him and said: "Shoot, Abu Ishaq!" When the battle ended, he asked about that man, but he was not identified. Abu Bakr al-Asamm denied the reinforcement with angels and said: "One angel suffices to destroy all the people of the earth, as Jibril, peace be upon him, did to the cities of the people of Lut. So if he attends, commanded to fight, what need is there for fighting by people alongside the disbelievers? Also, what benefit is there in sending the rest of the angels with him, when he is the Strong, the Trustworthy? Also, the one who killed each of the leading disbelievers present in the battle is known from the Companions, and it is not known that any of the angels killed any of them. Also, if they fought, either they would be seen by people or not. If the first, then the observers from the army of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, at the battle of Badr would have been numerous thousands, and no one has said that; and this is also contrary to His saying: ﴿ويُقَلِّلُكم في أعْيُنِهِمْ﴾ [and makes you appear few in their eyes]. If they were in other than the form of the children of Adam, there would have been intense terror in the hearts of creation, and this was not transmitted; and had it been, it would surely have been transmitted. If the second, then it would entail the cutting of heads, the tearing of bellies, and the like among the disbelievers without anyone being seen performing these acts. Such a thing would be among the greatest miracles, and it happened between two groups, sound and broken, so it should have been widely transmitted and become well known to both supporter and opponent. Since it did not become well known, it indicates that it did not happen. Also, if they were dense bodies, all would have seen them; and if they were subtle airy bodies, their staying upon the horses would be impossible." End of his statement.

It is not hidden that these doubts are not fitting to raise against the laws of the Sacred Law, nor against one who acknowledges that He is capable of whatever He wills, the Doer of what He intends. The only fitting thing for al-Asamm would have been to be mute about this, since the explicit text of the Qur'an speaks of reinforcement, and its occurrence in reports is close to mass-transmitted (mutawatir). So al-Asamm is deaf to hearing it, or blind to seeing its marvels. And 'Abd ibn Umayr narrated: "When Quraysh returned from Uhud, they began to speak in their assemblies about what they had achieved, saying: 'We did not see the piebald horses nor the white men whom we saw on the day of Badr.'"

The verification in this matter, as some of the researchers have said, is that obligation (al-taklif) contradicts compulsion (al-ilja'), and that He, exalted is His majesty, although He is capable of destroying all the disbelievers in a single moment with one angel, indeed with less than that, indeed without any cause, and likewise He is capable of [page 48] compelling them to Islam and forcing them. But He, exalted is He, willed to make this religion manifest gradually and in stages, through the call and by way of trial and obligation. Therefore, He arranged affairs as He arranged them. So to Him belongs praise for what He bestowed, and to Him belongs judgment in the Hereafter and in this world. Through this, much of those doubts is dispelled. The destruction of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, took place after their obligation had ended, at the time of the descent of the punishment; so Allah, exalted is He, manifested power and made its highest part its lowest. At the battle of Uhud, the time was a time of obligation, so He manifested wisdom so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, and the steadfast from the wavering. Had the matter there been arranged as at Badr, it would have been likely to lead to compulsion, and would have negated obligation and the attachment of reward and punishment. Furthermore, it is not hidden that the angels are either subtle luminous bodies, or noble holy spirits.

In either case, they are able to appear in the forms of the children of Adam, for example, without changing their essence or transforming their reality, as the knowing gnostics among the researchers have said regarding the appearance of Jibril, peace be upon him, in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi. Something similar applies in one respect. "And to Allah belongs the highest likeness" [16:60]. What is authentically reported of Allah's manifestation to the people of the Place of Standing in a form, when He says to them: "I am your Lord," and they deny Him: the judgment in that case is true, although Allah, exalted and sanctified is He, is beyond that, and He, exalted is He, in that manifestation remains upon His absoluteness, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. Whoever accepts this, and none accepts it except one with a sound heart, the reinforcement with angels and their appearance upon spectral horses, firmly seated upon them as the divine wisdom and the lordly interest require, will not be difficult for him. It does not necessarily follow that every person with sight sees them, because an obstacle preventing that may be created, either in the observer or in the observed. There is no obstacle to their being seen at times and hidden at times, and some being seen while others are hidden, and the reins of that are in the hand of the Wise, the All-Knowing. So whatever He wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. Whenever a thing is possible and the explicit text has come concerning it from the Truthful one, its acceptance is obligatory, and mere improbability does not benefit. If interpretation were permitted for this, it would necessitate interpreting most of this Sacred Law, indeed all the laws together, and perhaps that would lead to a grave matter. So it is obligatory to accept every possible matter the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, brought, and to entrust the details of that and its manner to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿العَزِيزِ﴾ [the Mighty]: that is, the Overpowering who is not overpowered in what He decrees. It has been said: the One able to avenge Himself on the disbelievers through the hands of the believers. The application of this attribute here to Him, exalted is He, is a notification of the reason for the restriction of victory to Him, glorified is He. ﴿الحَكِيمِ﴾ [the Wise] (126): that is, the One who places things in their proper places and acts according to what wisdom requires in all His actions. Among that is His granting victory to the believers through the sending down of the angels. The use of this attribute is a rebuttal of people like al-Asamm in their denial of what the apparent texts have spoken. So glorified is He, the All-Knowing, the Wise, the Mighty, the Forbearing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 127:

﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr﴾. What lies between them is a confirmation of its truth and an explanation of how it occurred. A group of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) held this view, and it is clearly correct on the assumption that ﴿when you said﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "He gave you victory," and not a substitute (badal) for "when you set out in the morning," so that no foreign element intervenes, and because that was the Day of Uhud.

The apparent meaning is that this refers to the matter of Badr. What is restricted to the causes mentioned, namely the good news and the reassurance, is the reinforcement by the angels in the manner described. So there is no objection to the explanation of the basic victory by the cutting off and what is coordinated with it. It has also been permitted that it be connected to what the predicate connects to in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾, on the assumption that it refers to the known victory. What is caused by the good news and the reassurance is only the outward reinforcement, not the inward inner victory which is the essence of the matter and its pillar. It has been said that it is connected to the patience itself. This was objected to on the grounds that, along with the separation between the verbal noun and its object by a foreign element, which is the predicate, it disturbs the soundness of the meaning. How could it not, when its meaning would restrict the specific victory, caused by a specific cause, to coming from Him, exalted is He? The intended meaning is not
Page 49
except to restrict the true reality of victory, as in the first view, or the known victory, as in the second, according to that. The saying that it is connected to a deleted element, the sense being "He did that arrangement," or "He reinforced you with the angels, so that He might cut off," is disconnected from acceptance. The cutting off means destruction. By "a part" is meant a group of them. It was said that the group is not expressed by "the middle" but by "the extremity," because the extremities of a thing are the means by which it is weakened and removed. It was also said that this is because the extremity is closer to the believers, so it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾. It was also said that it is to indicate that they were nobles. In al-Asas (Asas al-Balaghah) it says: "He is from the extremities of the Arabs," meaning their nobles. Perhaps the use of "extremities" for "nobles" is because they go ahead in the march. From this they said: "The extremities are the dwellings of the nobles." So it is not objected that "the middle" also implies nobility. The meaning is: to destroy the chiefs of those who disbelieved and their leaders who were foremost among them, by killing and capture. This happened at Badr, as al-Hasan, al-Rabi' and Qatadah said. Seventy of them were killed and seventy were taken captive. Considering it as referring to Uhud, where eighteen of their chiefs were killed, is an opinion held by some, and they found it unlikely, as we have pointed out. ﴿Or He might subdue them﴾, meaning He might humiliate them. This was said by Qatadah and al-Rabi'. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

I have not forgotten, from a longing, I have not forgotten our standing in bewilderment between one delighted and one humbled.

Al-Jubba'i and al-Kalbi said: that is, He turns them back defeated. Al-Suddi said: that is, He curses them. The basic meaning of "kabt" is intense anger and affliction. It was said: throwing a thing down on its face. It was also said that "kabata" has the meaning of "kabida," that is, it struck his liver, as "ra'aha" means it struck his lung. From this is the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

To enrage an envier, while I see an enemy, as if both of them are your farewell and departure.

The verse is taken to bear this meaning. This opinion is supported by the reading "or He might strike their livers" (yakbida). The "or" is for variety, not for doubt, since both matters occur. ﴿So they return frustrated﴾ (127), that is, so they are defeated with their hopes cut off. Frustration (khaybah) is the severing of hope. Scholars distinguished between it and despair (yas), saying that frustration only occurs after hope, while despair may occur both after it and before it. The opposite of frustration is success (zafar), and the opposite of despair is hope (raja').

[p. 50]

﴿There is nothing for you in the affair﴾ (Q. 3:128). One or more narrators reported: "The right lower canine (rubā'iyya) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was struck at the Battle of Uhud. 'Utba ibn Abi Waqqas struck it, and wounded his face. Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, or 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) was washing off the blood, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: 'How will a people prosper who have done this to their Prophet?' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse."

Al-Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others reported from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of Uhud: 'O Allah, curse Abu Sufyan. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhayl ibn 'Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayya.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿There is nothing for you in the affair﴾, and so they all were forgiven."

From al-Jubba'i: "On the day of Uhud, he (ﷺ) asked permission to invoke curses upon the unbelievers because of how they had harmed him, to the extent that he prayed the Zuhr prayer that day seated because of his wounds, and the Muslims prayed behind him seated. Permission was not granted to him, and this verse was revealed."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and al-Sha'bi said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims saw what the unbelievers had done to his companions and to his uncle Hamza, namely slitting of noses and ears and cutting off of private parts, they said: 'If Allah grants us victory over them, we will do to them the same as they did to us, and we will mutilate them in a way no one among the Arabs has ever mutilated.' Then this verse was revealed."

From Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to invoke curses upon those of his companions who fled from him on the day of Uhud, but Allah the Exalted forbade him from that, accepted their repentance, and this verse was revealed."

[p. 50 continued]
All these narrations agree that the verse was revealed concerning Uhud, and the most reliable among them is that it was occasioned by the polytheists.

From Muqatil: it was revealed concerning the people of Bi'r Ma'una. This was because "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent forty, and it was said seventy, men from among the reciters (qurra') of his companions, and appointed al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr over them, to Bi'r Ma'una, four months after Uhud, to teach the people the Qur'an and knowledge. Then the enemy of Allah, 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, called upon the tribes of Sulaym from 'Usayya, Ri'l and Dhakwan for help against them, and they surrounded them in their camp. They fought until they were killed to the last of them, except Ka'b ibn Zayd of the Banu al-Najjar, for they left him with a little life in him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) learned of this, he grieved deeply and cursed them for a month, invoking curses upon them. Then this verse was revealed, and so he abandoned that."

The meaning is: there is nothing for you in the affair of these people, even a little.

﴿Or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them﴾. This is a coordination (ʿatf) either upon "the affair" or upon "anything," with the particle "an" (that) being understood. That is: there is nothing for you of their affair, or of Allah's turning to them in forgiveness, or of their punishment. Or: there is nothing for you of their affair, or of turning to them, or of punishing them.

The two readings are distinguished as follows: on the first, it negates whatever follows from repentance and punishment for him (ﷺ) entirely, namely acceptance and rejection, deliverance from punishment, and the prevention of salvation. On the second, it negates the very act of turning to them in forgiveness and of punishing them from him (ﷺ), meaning he cannot compel them to repentance, nor prevent them from it, nor is he able to punish them, nor to pardon them, since all affairs are in the hand of Allah the Exalted. On both readings, this is the coordination of the particular upon the general (ʿatf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm), as the second scholar (al-ʿAllama al-Thani) said. However, there is doubt about the use of this kind of coordination with the particle "aw" (or). Some have objected to this, saying that this applies if "al-amr" means "the matter/affair," but you may take it to mean "obligation/command," that is: what you command them is not from you, and the command is not in your hand, nor is the turning in forgiveness nor the punishment. Then there is no coordination of the particular upon the general. But it is objected that taking it to mean obligation is strained, and taking it to mean "affair" is higher in rank.

It is transmitted from al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari that "aw" here means "illa an" (except that), and the meaning is: there is nothing for you of their affair except that Allah turns to them in forgiveness through Islam, so that you rejoice, or punishes them, so that you find relief in them.

Whichever is the case, the sentence is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought to explain some matters related to the Battle of Uhud, or what resembles it, following the explanation of what relates to the Battle of Badr, because of the connection between them: each of the two is based upon the exclusivity of the whole affair to Allah the Exalted, and upon denying it from anyone else.

It was said: all that is in these verses concerns the Battle of Uhud, as we have indicated. It was also said: the words of His the Exalted, ﴿or He will turn﴾ and so on, are coordinated upon "yanqalibu" (they will return), meaning: the outcome of their humiliation is that they return defeated, or that He turns to them, or punishes them. Or they are coordinated upon "yakbitahum" (He will humiliate them), and ﴿There is nothing for you in the affair﴾ is a parenthetical statement placed between the thing coordinated upon, which relates to the immediate result, and the coordinated item, which relates to [the future]. This is to affirm that the victorious have no influence, following the explanation that the helpers have no influence. The negation is restricted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by way of a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), to indicate that it is negated from others by greater necessity. The parenthetical statement is placed in this position because what precedes it, namely cutting down and humiliation, is a matter in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and all those engaged in fighting may have a share in the sentence. The meaning is: the owner of their affair absolutely, who is Allah the Exalted, has granted you victory over them, in order to destroy them, or humiliate them, or turn to them in forgiveness if they accept Islam, or punish them if they persist. There is nothing for you of their affair; you are only a servant commanded to warn them and to strive against them.

By their punishment is meant the severe punishment of the Hereafter, which is specific to the most unbelieving of the disbelievers. Otherwise, the absolute punishment of the Hereafter is realized in both of the first two groups. To interpret it as worldly punishment, through capture and the believers' domination over them, is contrary to what is understood from "punishment" when used without qualification. Likewise it does not fit the apparent sense of His, the Glorified, words: ﴿for they are wrongdoers﴾, since this is in the context of giving the reason for this punishment.

[p. 51]
The reason most commonly given for punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. Yes, interpreting it as worldly punishment is more suitable to the meaning mentioned by al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari, because satisfaction of the heart (tashaffi) generally takes place in this world. The joining of repentance and the Hereafter's punishment within the chain of final causes (ʿilla ghaʾiyya) of the victory, which follows it in existence, is because the acceptance of their repentance is a consequence of its realization, which arises from their knowledge of the truth of Islam, by means of the dominance of its adherents, which follows from the victory, which is among the manifest and radiant signs. And their aforementioned punishment is a thing caused by their persistence in unbelief after the truth has become clear in the manner mentioned. This is as indicated by the words of His the Exalted: ﴿that whoever perishes might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives might live upon clear proof﴾ (Q. 8:42). If it is interpreted as capture, for example, the matter of causation is evident without doubt.

This verse has been raised as a difficulty, on the basis that it indicates what some narrations report, namely that he (ﷺ) had done an action and was prevented from it. The objection is: if that action was from Allah the Exalted, how then did He prevent him from it? And if it was not, then it is damaging to his infallibility (ʿiṣma) and contrary to His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ (Q. 53:3). It was answered that what occurred was of the category of "khilaf al-awla" (acting against what is better), in consideration of his high station (ﷺ). The prohibition understood from the speech is of the category of guidance towards choosing what is more excellent, and this is not at all from desire, on the basis of the view that it is valid for a Prophet to exercise independent reasoning (ijtihad) and to act upon what his reasoning, which is permitted to him, has led him to.

It is also allowed that this action itself was by revelation and permission from Allah the Exalted to him (ﷺ), and that the prohibition concerning it was an abrogation (naskh) of that permission. Whichever is the case, it does not contradict the infallibility established for the Prophets, peace be upon them. So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 129 (part 1 of 2):

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This is a resumed statement, brought to explain that ownership of all existent things belongs exclusively to Him, the Exalted, after the explanation of the exclusive ownership of a part of that. It confirms what preceded it and completes it. The placing of the predicate first (lillah, "to Allah") serves to restrict (qasr). "Ma" (what) is general, covering rational and non-rational beings by way of precedence (taghlib). The meaning is: to Him, glorified is He, belongs whatever is in these two kinds, or whatever is in these two directions, in ownership, possession, creation and power, with no share for anyone alongside Him in that. So the affair is wholly His; He does what He wills and judges what He desires.

﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾: that He forgives him from among the believers, so He does not punish him for his sin, as an act of grace from Him. ﴿And punishes whom He wills﴾: that He punishes him, as an act of justice from Him. The choice of the word "man" (whom) in both places is to restrict forgiveness and punishment to rational beings. The placing of forgiveness before punishment indicates that His mercy precedes His wrath.

The apparent sense of the verse indicates that Allah's forgiveness and His punishment are not restricted by anything. Indeed, it has been claimed that restriction is incompatible with the context, since the context serves to establish that He, glorified is He, is the Owner in the absolute sense, so He may do whatever He wills, with nothing to prevent His will, even if His forgiveness were restricted by repentance. And if His punishment were by way of wrongdoing, He would not be doing what He wills, but rather what repentance or wrongdoing necessitates. Therefore the verse clearly negates any obligation upon Allah the Exalted, and that it is permissible for Him, glorified is He, to forgive the sinner and to punish the righteous. This is the doctrine of the Jama'ah (the Sunni majority). The Mu'tazilah held that forgiveness is conditional upon repentance, so whoever does not repent may not be forgiven at all. They relied on two arguments.

The first: the verses and hadiths that explicitly threaten the disobedient with punishment.

The second: if the sinner knows that he will not be punished for his sin, that would amount to approving of him and encouraging others to do the same, and this contradicts the wisdom of sending the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah the Exalted be upon them.

They interpreted this verse as restricted, and specified similar absolute verses as applying to minor sins, or to major sins accompanied by repentance. They said: the meaning is "He forgives whom He wills" when he repents. They took as evidence for this that the Exalted, after His words "or He punishes them" (Qur'an 3:128), followed with His words "for they are wrongdoers," which is a proof that wrongdoing is the cause that necessitates punishment, so there is no punishment without it, and no forgiveness in its presence. Thus it explains "whom He wills." They supported this interpretation with what was narrated from al-Hasan regarding the verse: "He forgives whom He wills" means with repentance, and He does not will to forgive except the penitent; "and punishes whom He wills" and He does not will to punish except those who deserve it. They also cited what was narrated from 'Ata': "He forgives whom" repents to Him, "and punishes whom" meets Him as a wrongdoer.

The Jama'ah held to the unrestricted nature of the verses, and answered the argument of the opponents. As for the first, the verses and hadiths, even if general, indicate only occurrence and not obligation. The dispute concerns this: the abundance of texts on pardon specifies the sinner who is pardoned from the general forms of threat.

As for the second, the mere permissibility of pardon does not necessitate a presumption that punishment will not occur, let alone certainty of it. How could the permissibility of pardon necessitate knowledge that there will be no punishment? The general threats mentioned in the warnings, which are linked with an ultimate purpose of intimidation, favour the likelihood of occurrence for each individual, and that is enough as a deterrent. So how can knowledge of the permissibility of pardon amount to approval and encouragement of sin in the presence of this deterrent?

Moreover, many of the Mu'tazilah specified verses such as His saying: "Indeed, Allah forgives all sins" (Qur'an 39:53) as referring to minor sins. So if the permissibility of pardon necessitated, as they claimed, knowledge of no punishment, the same objection would apply: that the one who commits minor sins, if he knows he will not be punished for his sin, that would amount to approval of him and encouragement of others to do the same. And there is in this as much corruption as there is. What they took as a restriction indicator is opposed by what indicates absoluteness, namely His saying: "To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth." For it is connected in meaning to His saying, glorified is His name: "You have no part in the affair" (Qur'an 3:128). This indicates that He, glorified is He, has absolute disposal, and this is contrary to what they say, since they made His disposal and His will restricted to conformity with wisdom, and wisdom requires that those who do not repent not be forgiven. But it is clearly open to objection, since will and wisdom are both among His attributes, neither following the other. And even if one follows the other, we do not concede that wisdom requires that those who do not repent not be forgiven. Furthermore, the sequence of "or He punishes them" with His words "for they are wrongdoers" does not indicate more than that wrongdoing leads to punishment. As for whoever denies that it leads to punishment, the denial applies only to the claim that it is an explanation of "whom He wills." And where is the proof that every wrongdoing is like this, since the wording has no generality, nor is it of the category of implicit meaning from a qualifier (mafhum al-sifah), so as to serve as an argument in general terms? As for what is transmitted from al-Hasan and 'Ata', no chain of transmission for it is known at all, and whoever claims it should produce it, if he is truthful. Among what indicates its falsity is that it places a restriction on the vast mercy and narrows its paths without definitive evidence. And such a repugnant view is not to be attributed to someone like al-Hasan. Even if we grant its authenticity and the absence of the consequences mentioned, the statement of al-Hasan and the like does not justify abandoning the apparent sense of the Book, and the truth is more deserving of being followed.

If the opponent says: "We rely in this matter on the argument of contradiction," we say: that would be a return to reasoning by rational argument, and we have already made you taste the red death in it, not by the verses. So the indication of this verse in its generality remains, and that is what we seek here. Moreover, this verse, according to most narrations, refers to the disbelievers, and the belief of the Jama'ah is that forgiveness for them is conditional upon repentance from disbelief and return to faith, as His saying, the Exalted, clearly states: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners should be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" (Qur'an 4:48). They are not an object of disagreement between the two groups. So whoever among the Mu'tazilah uses this verse to support his corrupt aim has indeed strayed from the right path.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (129). This is a concluding statement confirming the content of His saying, "He forgives whom He wills," with an addition. The singling out of this concluding statement indicates the preference for the aspect of goodness and bounty, and in it is what supports the doctrine of the Jama'ah.

* * *

This (and by way of allusion): ﴿They are not all alike﴾ in terms of readiness and the manifestation of truth in them ﴿among the People of the Book﴾, who have had the imprints of the eternal divine Book manifested in them. ﴿They are a standing community﴾ standing with Allah, the Exalted, for Him. ﴿They recite the signs of Allah﴾, that is, they manifest to those who are prepared what has overflowed upon them of secrets. ﴿In the watches of the night﴾, the times of the night of ignorance and the darkness of bewilderment. ﴿And they prostrate﴾, that is, they humble themselves before Allah, the Exalted, and self-conceit does not arise in them, that they are knowers and that others are ignorant. ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾,

[p. 53]

that is, in the Origin and the Return. ﴿And they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ as the Law requires. And because what preceded was in view of the particular, since the entrusting of secrets is to the free, while this is with respect to the general, since the Law has a wider scope than the Reality, the order was reversed. ﴿And they hasten to good works﴾ for the perfecting of themselves and others. ﴿And those are among the righteous﴾, who uphold the rights of the Truth and of creation. ﴿And whatever good they do﴾, which brings you near to Allah, the Exalted, ﴿they will not be denied it﴾. Indeed it has come in a hadith: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running." ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾, that is, those who guard against what veils them from Him, so He manifests Himself to them to the degree that the veil is removed.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, who veil themselves from the Truth by seeing other than Him, and associate with Allah, the Exalted, what has no existence, neither in a caravan nor in a battle-party ﴿will not avail them﴾, will not ward off ﴿from them their wealth nor their children from Allah﴾, that is, His punishment ﴿at all﴾, by way of warding off, because these are among their idols which they worshipped. ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾, which is the veil and distance from the Presence. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾, because the attribute of majesty requires it, given their readiness for that.

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾, the perishable and base life and its swiftly passing pleasures, seeking desires and the praise of people, not seeking thereby the Face of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿is like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾, that is, an intense cold, ﴿which strikes the crop of a people who have wronged themselves﴾ by polytheism and disbelief, ﴿and destroys it﴾ as a punishment to them from Allah, the Exalted, for their wrongdoing. ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾ by destroying their crop, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ because of the bad, unacceptable state of their readiness.

﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates﴾, that is, as an inner circle to whom you reveal your secrets, ﴿other than yourselves﴾, like the deniers and the veiled, since true love exists only among those who affirm divine unity, for it is the shadow of Oneness. It does not exist among the veiled, because they are in the world of opposition and darkness, and purity and harmony, which are the fruit of love, cannot be achieved in that world. Therefore you see that the love of those other than the people of Allah revolves around aims, and from here it changes, because carnal pleasures do not last. If this is the state of the veiled with one another, how can love be realized between them and those who oppose them in origin and attribute? How can light and darkness be alike? How can East and West agree?

O you who wed Thurayya to Suhayl, may God preserve your life, how can the two come together?
She is Syrian when she rises, and Suhayl is Yemeni when he rises.

So in reality there is true enmity between them and a complete distance, to the point that their fires cannot be seen by one another. The traces of this are manifest, as Allah the Exalted has explained by His saying: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, because the essential attribute cannot be concealed, ﴿and what their breasts conceal is greater﴾, because it is the source of that. So the one is fire and the other is sparks; the one is a mountain and the outward appearance is dust. ﴿We have already made the signs clear to you﴾, which are the indications showing love and enmity and their causes, ﴿if you use reason﴾ and understand from the import of the speech.

﴿There you are, you love them﴾ by virtue of what you have of monotheism, because the monotheist loves all people truly for the sake of the Truth, and sees all of them as a manifestation of His Beloved, glorified is His majesty. So he shows mercy to all, and knows that some of them have occupied themselves with falsehood, looking at certain aspects, and have been tested by destiny. This does not contradict what we mentioned earlier, on careful reflection. ﴿But they do not love you﴾ by virtue of the veil and the darkness that have been cast upon them, ﴿while you believe in the Book﴾, that is, in its genus, ﴿all of it﴾, because of what you have of monotheism, which requires that. ﴿And they do not believe﴾ in that, because of the veiling by what they are upon.

﴿And when they meet you, they say: "We believe"﴾, because of the hypocrisy in them, which attracts worldly aims. ﴿But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage﴾, the rage hidden in their breasts. ﴿If good touches you﴾, like traces of the manifestation of beauty, ﴿it distresses them﴾, and they grieve over it. ﴿And if an evil befalls you﴾, that is, what they suppose to be evil, like traces of the manifestation of majesty, ﴿they rejoice at it. But if you are patient﴾ with what you have been tested with, and remain firm in monotheism, ﴿and are God-fearing﴾, seeking help from what is upright, ﴿their scheme will not harm you at all﴾, because the one who is patient under trial, who relies on Allah, the Exalted, who seeks help from Him and turns away

[p. 54]

from anything else, is victorious in his aim, dominant over his adversary, enveloped and protected by the care of Allah, the Exalted. The one who is forsaken is the one who seeks help from another and turns toward someone other than Him, as it is said:

Whoever seeks help from other than Allah in a pursuit,
his helper is weakness and abandonment.

﴿Indeed Allah is encompassing of what they do﴾ of schemes, ﴿so He will nullify them and extinguish their fire.﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 129 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr, when you were humble.﴾ To Allah, the Exalted, under the shade of Majesty and Greatness. ﴿So that you may be grateful.﴾ That is, and by gratitude blessings are increased. ﴿When you said to the believers﴾ because of what you saw of their condition: ﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ Read "munzalin" in the form of the active participle: the tranquillity upon you; or "munzalin" in the form of the passive participle: from the side of the Malakut (the realm of dominion) toward you. ﴿Yes, if you endure﴾ the shocks of His manifestation, glory be to Him, ﴿and fear Allah﴾ regarding whatever is other than Him, ﴿and they come upon you in this very moment﴾ that is, without delay, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out﴾ read in the form of the active participle, meaning marking your spirits with the signs of tranquillity; or ﴿marked out﴾ read in the form of the passive participle, with white turbans. This is an allusion to the divine lights manifest upon them. The specification of five thousand by mention perhaps alludes to the reinforcement of each of the five subtleties (latifah, pl. latā'if; the subtle centres of the spiritual faculties in Sufi psychology) with a thousand, and the thousand is an allusion to complete reinforcement, since it is the final degree of the numbers. The condition for this is patience and God-consciousness, because victory over enemies, and the greatest of your enemies is your own self which is between your two sides, does not occur except when the heart is God-fearing, and likewise all the hosts of the spirit; indeed the spirit itself too, through the support of the Truth and illumination with the light of certainty. Thus a correspondence arises between the heart, for example, and the realm of heaven, and by that correspondence it draws down its powers and attributes into its actions, and perhaps it draws strength from the powers of subjugation against the one with whom it is angry. That is an expression for the descent of the angels, and this does not happen except through patience in bearing what is hateful, seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and through God-consciousness, by refraining from opposing the command of the Truth and from inclining toward worldly benefit and fleeting pleasures.

As for when one becomes distressed and panic-stricken and inclines toward the world, this is not attained by him; for the self then overpowers him and veils him with the darkness of its attributes from the light, so that correspondence no longer remains, the supply is cut off, and the angels do not descend. ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good news for you﴾ that is, only so that you would rejoice in it, and your energy in turning toward the Truth would increase. ﴿And that your hearts might be reassured by it﴾ so that the outpouring is realised according to the degree of purification. ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾ not from the angels; so do not veil yourselves by multiplicity from Unity, nor by creation from the Truth, for all is from Him, the Exalted, and unto Him. ﴿The Mighty﴾ so the manifestation by whatever He wills and however He wills is not beyond His power. ﴿The Wise﴾ who concealed His victory in the forms of angels for a wisdom. ﴿That He may cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ that is, destroy them, ﴿or subdue them﴾ humiliate them and abase them, ﴿so that they turn back defeated﴾ returning without having gained what they hoped for.

﴿You have no part﴾ in respect of yourself ﴿in the matter﴾ and all of it belongs to you from another aspect. ﴿Or He turns to them in mercy﴾ if they submit, so that you rejoice, for you are the manifestation of the vast mercy. ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾

﴿Or He punishes them﴾ on your account, so that you are gratified by them, inasmuch as they opposed the command with which you were sent to all mankind, for they are wrongdoers by that opposition.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ of the world of spirits, ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾ of the world of natural things; He disposes of both as He wills and chooses. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ because He has absolute disposal over the dominion and the realm of dominion. ﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

We ask Allah, the Exalted, to forgive us and have mercy upon us.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 130:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury (riba)﴾. This begins a statement that includes a command, a prohibition, encouragement, and warning, as a completion of what preceded it of guidance toward what is most beneficial in matters of religion and in the matter of jihad. Perhaps the specific prohibition of riba is mentioned here because encouragement to spend in ease and in hardship, whose principal form is spending in the way of jihad, implies encouragement to acquire wealth. So people might hasten to the means of earning, and among them, indeed the easiest of them, is riba, so they were forbidden from it.

Page 55

He placed it before the command, out of concern for it, and so that this command would come after closing off what would damage it. Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that this statement is connected to what precedes it, in that most of the wealth of the polytheists had been gathered from riba, and they spent that wealth on the armies. It was possible that this would lead the Muslims to engage in it, so that they would gather wealth and also spend it on the armies, and be able to avenge themselves on their enemy. So the prohibition against that came as mercy upon them and kindness toward them. It was also said: when He, exalted is His glory, mentioned that He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, He connected that to the prohibition of what, if they had done it, would have made them deserving of punishment, which is riba. He singled it out for the prohibition because it was widespread at that time, and out of concern for it, He did not suffice with what indicated its prohibition in surah al-Baqarah, but explicitly stated the prohibition. He brought the statement to it first and foremost, as a notice of the severity of the ban.

The meaning of "consuming" is taking. He expressed it by this because it is the main thing sought by it, and because it is common in foodstuffs, along with what it contains of added severity of reproach. The discussion of riba has already passed. ﴿multiplied manifold﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of riba. "Adʿaf" is the plural of "ḍiʿf," and the ḍiʿf of a thing is its equal; its two ḍiʿfs are its two equals, and its adʿaf are its equals. Some verifiers (muḥaqqiqin) said: ḍaʿf is the name of what doubles a thing, like thanī is the name of what doubles it, from ḍaʿaftu al-shayʾ (I lessened the thing) with lightening, so it is maḍʿūf, as Al-Raghib transmitted, meaning ḍaʿʿaftuhu (I doubled it). It is a term that applies to a number provided there is another number along with it, or more, and its reference is upward, unlike the zawj (pair), whose reference is downward. So when it is said "ḍiʿf of ten," it necessarily means you make it twenty without disagreement, because that is the first level of its doubling. If someone says: "I owe him the ḍiʿf of a dirham," he is obligated to two dirhams, by the necessity of the stated condition, just as when it is said: "He is the brother of Zayd," it implies that Zayd is his brother. And when the pairing is necessary, it enters into the acknowledgment. Based on this, "two ḍiʿfs of a dirham" is reduced to three dirhams. This is not based on what is supposed, that the ḍiʿf of a thing is originally its two equals, and its two ḍiʿfs are its three equals. Rather, that is because its original meaning is the equal, under the stated condition.

This is the view of the jurists regarding acknowledgments and bequests. It is clear that they obligated, for the two ḍiʿfs of a thing, three times its equivalent. If the original meaning of ḍiʿf were the two equals, the two ḍiʿfs would be four equivalents. Its basis is not common popular usage but the linguistic meaning, as al-Azhari said.

From here it appears that if someone says: "I owe him the two ḍiʿfs: a dirham and a dirham," or "the two ḍiʿfs of dirhams," he is obligated to only two dirhams, just as if he said "the two brothers." Then he said: The summary is that doubling a thing is adding another number to it, and it may be increased, and it may be looked at in terms of its first level, because that is the certain one. Then, the doubled thing may be taken along with it, so its two ḍiʿfs are three, and it may not be, so they are two. All of this is what is linguistically established, not by custom. This state is not for restricting what is prohibited, so that the essence of riba would not be prohibited. Rather, it is for observing the reality. Many narrators reported that a man would lend at interest until a term, and when it came due, he would say to the debtor: "Increase the money for me, and I will extend the term for you." He would do so, and so on at every term, until the thing doubled would consume all his wealth entirely. So they were forbidden from that, and the verse was revealed. It was also read as "muḍaʿʿafa" (with doubling of the ʿayn), without an alif.

﴿And fear God﴾, that is, regarding what you have been forbidden, and among it is the consuming of riba. ﴿So that you may succeed﴾ (130), that is, so that you may prosper, or hoping for success. Then the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause. It was said: It is not hidden that the joining of hope with fear indicates that the servant should be between hope and fear; they are his two wings with which he flies to the courts of holiness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 131:

﴿And guard yourselves against the Fire﴾ — that is, beware of following the usurers and engaging in what they engage in of consuming interest (ribā), which leads to entry into the Fire ﴿which has been prepared﴾ — that is, made ready ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ (131). It is the tier whose heat is intense and whose punishment is multiplied, and it is other than the Fire into which the sinners of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) enter, for theirs is less than that. In this is an indication that the consumers of interest are on the brink of the pit of the disbelievers. It may also be said that the Fire in general is created for the disbelievers, prepared for them primarily and essentially, while others enter it by way of following. So the qualifier is not for restriction. To this view the majority of scholars went. It is narrated from the Greatest Imam (Abu Hanifa), may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: this verse is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, since Allah threatened the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not guard against Him by avoiding His prohibitions. And it is not an explicit text on restriction.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 132:**

﴿And obey Allah﴾ in all that He has commanded you and forbidden you, so this does not repeat the earlier command to taqwa (God-consciousness). ﴿And the Messenger﴾, i.e., the one who legislated the religion for you and conveyed the message to you, for his obedience is the obedience of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿That you may receive mercy﴾ (132). That is, so that you may attain the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, or hoping for His mercy. He followed the threat with a promise, as a warning against opposition and an encouragement to obedience. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: this verse is a rebuke to those who disobeyed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he commanded them with what he commanded them at Uhud, and they were likely the archers who abandoned their position.

ۚ﴿And hasten﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿obey﴾ or ﴿fear God﴾.

Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir read it without the conjunctive waw, as a fresh sentence (istiʾnaf); this is the reading of the people of Madina and Syria. The well-known reading, that of the people of Makka and Iraq, is ﴿وسارِعُوا﴾ with waw, meaning "hasten and race to it." It was also read in the latter way: ﴿to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾, i.e., to the causes of them, namely righteous deeds.

From ʿAli, may God ennoble his face: "Hasten to the performance of the obligatory duties." From Ibn ʿAbbas: "to Islam." From Abu al-ʿAliya: "to emigration (hijra)." From Anas ibn Malik: "to the first takbir." From Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "to the performance of acts of obedience." From Yaman: "to the five daily prayers." From al-Dahhak: "to jihad." From ʿIkrima: "to repentance." The apparent meaning is generality, and all kinds of good works are included.

The mention of forgiveness before the Garden is because clearing (takhliya) precedes adorning (tahliya). It has also been said that forgiveness is like the cause of entering the Garden. The phrase ﴿مِن﴾ ("from") is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective modifying ﴿forgiveness﴾. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the pronominal suffix addressing the audience serves to show added kindness towards them. Describing forgiveness as coming from the Lord, rather than describing the Garden that way, exalts its matter and highlights its importance.

The occasion of revelation of the verse, according to what ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others narrated from ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah: "The Muslims said: O Messenger of God, the Children of Israel were more honoured by God Most High than us. When one of them committed a sin, the expiation of his sin would be written on the threshold of his house: 'Slit your nose, slit your ear, do such and such.' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, and these verses were revealed up to His words, Most High: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves﴾ (the verse). The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: 'Shall I not inform you of something better than that?' and then recited it to them."
