The tanwin on ﴿مَغْفِرَةٍ﴾ (forgiveness) is for magnification, and the description supports this; likewise in ﴿جَنَّةٍ﴾ (Garden), and it is also supported by the description of it in His words, Glorified be He: ﴿whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾. The intended meaning is "like the breadth of the heavens and the earth," and this is in the manner of his saying:

I thought the bellowing of my she-camel was a she-goat's, and it was not, by your life, a she-goat's cry.

He meant "like the cry of a she-goat." Breadth is the shorter of the two dimensions, and mentioning it without mentioning length is an intensification. Further intensification comes from omitting the particle of comparison and supplying an omitted genitive. So the purpose is not to delimit its breadth such that its being in the heaven would be impossible; rather the statement is a metaphor for the utmost vastness, in a form the hearers can picture. The Arabs often describe a thing as having breadth when they wish to describe it as vast, and from this is their saying: "He expanded (aʿrada) in noble deeds" when he extended himself in them. By "the heavens and the earth" is meant the seven heavens and the seven earths. From Ibn ʿAbbas, through al-Suddi, he said: "The seven heavens and the seven earths are joined together as garments are joined one to another; that is the breadth of the Garden." The majority hold that it is above the seven heavens, beneath the Throne, and this is related from Anas ibn Malik. It has also been said that it is in the fourth heaven, and a group went to this view. It has also been said that it is outside this world, wherever God wills. Its being "in the heaven" means that it is in the direction of height. We see no obstacle to God creating in the height the likes of the heavens and the earth many times over. This does not contradict the report that it is in the fourth heaven, if sound, nor what is related from the majority, because this is like your saying "the garden is in the house" when it has a door through which one enters it, for it does not contradict the garden's being outside it. On this interpretation, the report is also not contradicted by the Garden's breadth being like the breadth of the heavens and earth, without any need to say that by "the heavens" the seven heavens are not meant, as has been said.

Some people hold that it is in the heaven beneath the Throne or in the fourth, except that this breadth will exist only on the Day of Resurrection, when God increases in it what He increases.

This is related from Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn ʿAli. It was said: this resolves the objection that if the breadth of the Garden is ﴿like the breadth of the heavens and the earth﴾, where then is the Fire? The answer is that this is on the Day of Resurrection; now it is far less than that. On the day it attains that, the heavens and the earth as they now are, to which its breadth is compared, will not be the same. It is not hidden that the claim of increase in breadth on the Day of Resurrection, even if sound, while its being now far less than these heavens and earth is open to denial and hardly acceptable. The objection mentioned was answered by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in another way.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Tanukhi, envoy of Heraclius: "I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with Heraclius's letter, in which was: 'You wrote calling me to a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, so where is the Fire?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Glory be to God, then where is the night when the day comes?'" Perhaps the purpose of the answer is to dismiss the question and show that One able to take the night wherever He wills is able to create the Fire wherever He wills. To this points the report of Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani held that breadth here is not the opposite of length, but from your saying "I offered the goods for sale" (ʿaradtu al-matāʿ), and the meaning is that its price, if it were sold, would be like the price of the heavens and the earth; the intended sense is the greatness of its magnitude and the sublimity of its rank, and that nothing equals it however great. Thus "breadth" means the price offered against the merchandise. Perhaps on this view one can dispense with the omitted genitive, but it is not hidden that, despite its remoteness, this is contrary to what is transmitted from the pious predecessors, that the intended meaning is describing it as vast.

﴿Prepared for the God-fearing﴾: i.e., made ready for those who obey God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ). It is attributed to them to indicate that they are the intended ones in essence, and that the entry of others, such as sinning believers, children and the insane, is by way of following. If taqwa is taken in this place as fear of shirk and not what encompasses it and all other prohibitions, we still cannot dispense with this statement, because the insane, for example, do not truly possess taqwa even if it were fear of shirk, as is not hidden.

It is permissible that there are multiple gardens, and that this Garden is for the God-fearing described with these attributes, and that others do not share in it either in essence or by following. Perhaps it is the Firdaws, which is explicitly mentioned in his (ﷺ) saying: "When you ask God for the Garden, ask Him for the Firdaws." There is room for reflection here. The verse clearly indicates that the Garden is created now, as the past tense verb shows. Taking it as of the type of ﴿and the Horn is blown﴾ is contrary to the apparent meaning, and there is no call for it, as explained in its proper place. Similar to this is ﴿prepared﴾, which precedes concerning the Fire.

As for the indication of the verse that the Garden is outside this world, on the basis that it implies the Garden is greater than it, so it cannot encompass it, there is room for consideration, as consideration of what has preceded will guide you.

The clause is in the genitive position as an adjective of ﴿Garden﴾. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it, since it has been described. It is also permitted that it be a fresh sentence. Abu al-Baqa said: It is not permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the genitive-attached noun, for three reasons. First, the genitive-attached noun does not govern; what comes of that is interpreted despite its weakness. Second, "breadth" here is not meant as the true verbal noun but the distance. Third, this would entail separation between the circumstantial clause and its referent.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 134:**

﴿Those who spend﴾ is in the genitive position as a qualifier (*na't*) of *al-muttaqin* (the God-conscious), praising them. It has also been said that it is a specifier (*mukhassas*), or a substitute (*badal*), or an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or that it is in the accusative position by an implied verb, or in the nominative position by an implied *hum* (they). The object of *yunfiquna* (they spend) is omitted, so that it encompasses everything suitable for praiseworthy spending, or it is left entirely unstated, as in the saying of people: "So-and-so gives."

﴿in ease and in hardship﴾ means in prosperity and in adversity. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: in states of joy and of grief; in life and after death, by making a bequest; in what pleases, such as spending on children and relatives, and in what harms, such as spending on enemies; in hosting a wealthy person and giving gifts to him; and in what one spends on people in distress and gives in charity to them. The root of *al-sarra'* (ease) is the state that gladdens, and *al-darra'* (hardship) is the state that harms. What comes first to mind is what the scholar (Ibn 'Abbas) said. The intended meaning of the two is either their apparent sense or generality, as is customary in similar expressions, meaning that they never, in any state, fail to spend whatever they are able to, whether much or little. It has been narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she gave away a single grape, and of one of the early Muslims (*salaf*) that he gave away an onion. In a report: "Protect yourselves from the Fire even with half a date," and "Turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof."

﴿and those who restrain their anger﴾. The root of *al-kazm* is tying the mouth of a waterskin when it is full, and it is said: *fula kazim*, meaning a man filled with grief. *Al-ghayz* (anger, rage) is the stirring of the temperament upon seeing what is disliked. The difference between it and *al-ghadab* (wrath), as has been said, is that wrath is necessarily followed by the desire for retaliation, whereas rage is not. It has also been said that wrath is what appears on the limbs and skin without choice, while rage is not like that. It has further been said that the two are mutually entailing, except that wrath may be attributed to Allah the Exalted, whereas rage may not be attributed to Him.

The intended meaning is those who swallow their rage, who hold it back when their souls are full of it. So they do not take revenge on one who harms them, and do not show him what they dislike, but rather endure this while being able to carry out and take retaliation. This is the praiseworthy quality. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever restrains rage while he is able to act upon it, Allah fills his heart with security and faith."

Ahmad reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever restrains rage while he is able to carry it out, Allah will call him before the heads of all creation until He lets him choose from whichever of the Houris he wishes." In the first report the reward is of the same kind as the deed, and in the second it is among its consequences. This attribute is coordinated with what precedes it. The shift to the active participle form here indicates continuity, whereas for spending, since it is a renewed action, it was expressed with a form that indicates renewal and occurrence.

﴿and those who pardon people﴾, meaning those who overlook the punishment of those who deserve to be held to account, when that does not involve harm to the religion. It has been said: (pardoning) slaves when they do wrong, but generality is preferable.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah the Exalted says: Let those stand up who have a reward with Allah the Exalted. None will stand except a person who pardoned."

Al-Tabarani reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would be pleased that buildings be raised high for him and his ranks be elevated, let him pardon the one who wronged him, give to the one who denied him, and maintain ties with the one who severed them."

[page 59]

Al-Daylami in *Musnad al-Firdaws* reported from Anas ibn Malik concerning the verse: "Indeed, these in my nation are few, except those whom Allah protects, though they were many in the nations that passed." The exception is disjunctive (*munqati'*) if the fewness is taken in its literal sense, and connected (*muttasil*) if it means non-existence. That some of these qualities were abundant in past nations does not require that they be preferred over this nation in every respect. Whoever supposes that has strained in interpreting the hadith, saying that the meaning is that those who restrain anger in my nation are few, except by Allah's protection, because anger overpowers them, while they were numerous in earlier nations because of their weak zeal, and for this reason enjoining good and forbidding evil among them was rare. And because this nation has been trained in anger for the sake of Allah the Exalted, and committed to avoiding flattery, executing anger has become their habit, so they do not restrain it when tested, except by Allah's protection. Thus, the few in the hadith are those who restrain (anger) despite their weak zeal, and they were the many in the earlier nations, so there is no distinction for them that would lead one to suppose they are preferred over this nation, even in some respects. It is not hidden that this interpretation is one that the indication and the wording reject. Better than it, indeed, there is no relation, is that the abundance is considered relative to all nations together, not relative to each nation individually. And the scarcity of those described by that quality among us does not harm, when considered relative to all creation from Adam, peace be upon him, until our Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, because this whole nation is few relative to all nations, let alone its elite. So reflect on this.

In mentioning these two attributes, as some verifiers have said, there is an indication of the perfect appropriateness of his pardon (ﷺ) toward the archers, and his not holding them to account for what they did of disobeying his command (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) was also urged to abandon what he had resolved upon, namely retaliating against the polytheists for what they had done to Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, to the point that when he saw him mutilated he said: "I will mutilate seventy in your place." Perhaps the expression here is again in the form of the active participle rather than the verb, because pardoning is more akin to restraining than to spending.

﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ (134) is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) summarizing what precedes it. The definite article (*al-*) is either generic, in which case those mentioned are included in it primarily, or it is the article of previous reference (*'ahd*). They were described as *al-muhsinin* (good-doers) according to what has been said, signifying that the qualities enumerated fall under *ihsan* (excellence), which is performing actions in the proper manner, which is their descriptive goodness that entails their intrinsic goodness. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."

It may be said: *ihsan* here means conferring benefit upon others in a manner free of any ugliness. He described them by this to indicate that in all those qualities they are good-doers toward others, not only in spending.

What supports that *ihsan* here means conferring benefit is what al-Bayhaqi reported: a slave-girl of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was pouring water on him so he could prepare for prayer, when the ewer slipped from her hand and struck him, wounding his head. He raised his head toward her, and she said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted says: *and those who restrain their anger*." He said to her: "I have restrained my anger." She said: "*and those who pardon people*." He said: "May Allah the Exalted pardon you." She said: "*And Allah loves the good-doers*." He said: "Go, for you are free for the sake of Allah the Exalted."

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 3, verse 135 (part 1 of 2):

Some scholars preferred reading the definite article as *al-'ahd* (the specific, known reference) rather than *al-jins* (the generic sense), because it is more fitting for praise and better suited to its mention before His saying, ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves﴾, as part of what was revealed when the Muslims said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "The Children of Israel were more honoured by Allah than us," and so on, as we indicated earlier.

It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the condition of the Children of Israel was mentioned in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed, without mention of the beginning of the verse."

In the narration of al-Kalbi: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ established a bond of brotherhood between two men, one from the Ansar and one from Thaqif, and they were never apart. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out on one of his expeditions, and the Thaqafi went out with him, and he left the Ansari in charge of his family and his needs. The Ansari would look after the family of the Thaqafi. One day he came and saw the wife of his companion, who had bathed, and she had let her hair down. It stirred something in his soul, so he entered without asking permission until he reached her. He went to kiss her, but she placed her palm over her face, so he kissed the back of her palm. Then he regretted it and felt shame, and turned back. She said: 'Glory be to Allah! You have betrayed your trust and disobeyed your Lord, and you have not reached your goal.'" He said: "He regretted what he had done, and went out wandering in the mountains, repenting to Allah the Exalted for his sin. Then the Thaqafi returned, and his family informed him of what had happened. He went out searching for him until he was guided to him, and found him prostrating and saying: 'My Lord, my sin, my sin! I have betrayed my brother.' He said to him: 'Rise, so-and-so, and go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ask him about your sin; perhaps Allah will grant you relief and repentance.' So he went with him until they returned to Madinah. One day, at the time of the 'Asr prayer, Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with his repentance, and recited: ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency﴾ until His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And excellent is the reward of the doers﴾. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this for this man specifically, or for people in general?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, peace be upon him, said: 'Rather, it is for people in general.'"

In the narration of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas: "A beautiful woman came to Tayhan the date-seller, buying dates from him. He drew her to himself and kissed her. Then he regretted that, so he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned it to him, and this verse was revealed."

You know that there is no obstacle to multiple causes of revelation. Whatever the case, by the general wording the verse encompasses what the archers did, in an initial sense. Al-Tirmidhi related from 'Attaf ibn Khalid that he said: "It has reached me that when it was revealed, Iblis cried out to his troops, threw dust upon his head, and called for destruction and perdition, until his troops came to him from every land and sea. They said: 'What is wrong with you, our master?' He said: 'A verse has been revealed in the Book of Allah, after which no sin will harm any of the children of Adam.' They said: 'What is it?' He told them. They said: 'We will open for them the door of desires, so they will not repent, nor seek forgiveness, and they will see nothing but that they are upon the truth.' So he was content with that from them."

As for the relative pronoun (*alladhina*), it is either separated from what precedes it, being a subject (*mubtada'*), or it is said to be conjoined to what precedes it as one of the attributes of the God-fearing. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾, is a parenthetical clause between them, indicating the difference between them, for the rank of the first group in piety is higher and their portion is fuller. Or it refers to the God-fearing, in which case the difference is clearer and greater.

"Indecency" (*fahisha*) refers to the major sins, and "wronging oneself" refers to the minor sins, as stated by Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar al-Hamdani. It is also said: "Indecency" is an overt act of disobedience, and "wronging oneself" is disobedience in speech. It is also said: "Indecency" is that which extends to others, including the spreading of sin, because it is the cause of people's audacity toward it and their falling into it, whereas "wronging oneself" is not of this kind. It is also said: "Indecency" is everything whose ugliness is extreme among sins and transgressions, and it is used for every ugly quality of speech and action, and it often occurs with the meaning of fornication. The root of *fuhsh* is exceeding the limit in evil, and from this is the saying of Tarafa:

*"The treasured wealth of the excessive, the rigid one..."*

He means the one who exceeded the limit in stinginess. So perhaps what is meant here is an act of disobedience extremely ugly, and "wronging" is sin in general. Mentioning it after the former is mentioning the general after the specific. The "or" in the interpretations is for diversification. It is not objected that according to some interpretations there is an alternation between the specific and the general, though its acceptance has been questioned, because they said: this is an alternation between two groups: one who seeks forgiveness for indecency, and one who seeks forgiveness for any sin that proceeds from them, and how far apart these are.

The answer to *idha* (when) is His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿they remember Allah﴾, meaning: they remember His great right and His threat; or they remember being presented before Him; or His questioning about the sin on the Day of Resurrection, or His prohibition, or His forgiveness. It is also said: "they remember" His beauty, so they feel shame; and His majesty, so they fear. It is also said: "they remember" His sacred essence, exalted above all ugliness, and they love to draw near to Him by what is fitting to Him, by purifying themselves from blameworthy traits. In every case, the intended meaning is not merely the mention of His name, glorified is His name.

﴿So they seek forgiveness﴾, meaning they ask Him, exalted is He, for forgiveness, ﴿for their sins﴾, whatever they may be. The object of "they seek forgiveness" is omitted because the meaning is understood, i.e., they sought forgiveness from Him. The intended meaning is not merely the request for forgiveness, but with repentance; otherwise, seeking forgiveness while persisting in sin is like mocking the Lord, may His majesty be exalted. For this reason Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya said: "Our seeking forgiveness itself needs seeking forgiveness."

﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?﴾ This is a parenthetical clause between the two conjoined elements, or between the circumstantial clause and its subject. The construction, according to what some verifiers have stated, indicates matters from Allah's side and matters from the servant's side.

As for the first, there are several aspects. One: the denotation of the proper name (Allah), in accordance with what the context requires of the meaning of broad forgiveness. The construction is in the form of a question rather than an assertion, not saying "and none forgives sins except Allah," which confirms and emphasizes that meaning, as if it were said: "Do you know anyone who can forgive all sins, small and great, past and future, other than He whose mercy encompasses everything?" Two: placing it out of its normal position and removing it from its place, because it is a parenthetical clause between the subject, which is "those who," and the predicate that follows, and then between the conjoined and the element it is conjoined to, or between the circumstantial clause and its subject, to indicate the great concern for it and to alert that whenever seeking forgiveness exists, forgiveness does not fail to follow. Three: the use of the plural with the definite article, to inform that the penitent, when he approaches with seeking forgiveness, is met with forgiveness of all his sins, so he becomes as one who has no sin. Four: the denotation of negation by restriction and affirmation, indicating that there is no refuge for sinners except His generosity and bounty, for whoever His mercy encompasses everything, no one shares with Him in its dispersal through generosity and bounty. Five: the attribution of forgiveness of sins to His own self, glorified is He, and its affirmation for His sacred essence after the existence of seeking forgiveness and the servants' disavowal, indicates that this is realized with certainty, either according to the promise, as we say, or according to justice, as the Mu'tazila claim.

As for the second, there are also several aspects:

The first: displaying the vastness of mercy and hastening forgiveness is a great glad tiding and a consolation to souls. The second: when the servant considers this intense care and great concern regarding repentance, his energy is stirred and his inclination is moved, so he does not hold back from it. The third: within the sense of comprehensiveness is the removal of despair and despondency, and for this reason He, glorified is He, gave the reason for the prohibition in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ by His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾.

The fourth: sins are mentioned without restriction and generalized after the mention of indecency and wronging oneself and the abandonment of what the apparent meaning requires, to indicate that there is no concern about forgiveness, for although sins may be great, the pardon of Allah the Exalted is greater.

The fifth: the all-encompassing name in the construction, as it indicates the breadth of forgiveness according to the context, also indicates, together with the intended restriction, that He alone, exalted is He, possesses the requirements of forgiveness: being Mighty, with none above Him to overturn His judgment, and being Wise, forgiving whom His wisdom requires to be forgiven.

Some have insisted that the "al-" in "al-dhunub" (the sins) is for the genus, so that the verse indicates the impossibility of the forgiveness of any single sin from anyone other than Allah. This, in his view, is not indicated by the verse if all sins (*al-dhunub*) are intended, and then the matter of emphasis increases. As for making the clause circumstantial with the assumption that those speaking say this, it is a forced interpretation that removes many of these subtle aspects, as is not hidden.

"Man" (*man*) is the subject, and "yaghfiru" (forgives) is its predicate. The glorious Name is either a substitute for the pronoun in "yaghfiru" or its agent.

﴿And they do not persist in what they have done﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they sought forgiveness﴾, or is a circumstantial clause of its subject, meaning: they do not remain, or they are not remaining, upon what they committed of sins, whether an indecency or a wrong, or upon their deed. The root of *al-israr* (persistence) is binding tightly, from *al-sarr* (tying). It is also said: steadfastness upon something. From this is the saying of al-Hutay'a describing horses:

*"Grim, with their tousled, bold riders, when they seek their harvest with what is reaped..."*

In the Shari'a it is used to mean remaining upon wrongdoing without seeking forgiveness and returning through repentance. It appears that it is not correct to intend this meaning here, lest what is in the implicit meaning be repeated along with what is in the explicit meaning. Perhaps it is used here with the meaning of remaining. If seeking forgiveness is understood merely as the request for forgiveness, then this indicates repentance, which is the essence of the matter, except that seeking forgiveness is mentioned first because it indicates repentance outwardly. If it is understood as the state in which repentance accompanies it, then this is an explicit statement of part of what is meant, and an indication of attention to it, as they said regarding mentioning the specific after the general.

Al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, as a statement of a companion: "Every sin that the servant persists in is a major sin, and no sin is major from which the servant repents."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* related from Ibn 'Umar, as a raised report: "Show mercy, and you will be shown mercy; forgive, and you will be forgiven. Woe to the bombastic talkers; woe to those who persist."

﴿And they know﴾ (135). It is said that the clause is a circumstantial clause of the subject of "they sought forgiveness," and this has a verbal remoteness. The well-known view is that it is a circumstantial clause of the subject of "they persisted." The object of "they know" is omitted, meaning: they know the ugliness of their deed. It has been mentioned that a circumstantial clause after a negated verb, and likewise all qualifiers, may refer back to the negation as a qualifier of it, not of what is negated, as in: "I did not come to you occupied with your affairs," meaning: "I abandoned coming while occupied with that." It may also refer back to what the negation entered, as in: "I did not come to you riding." This has two meanings: one, which is the more common, is that the negation refers only to the qualifier, and the act itself is affirmed, so the meaning is "I came not riding." The second is that the negation is intended to apply to both the act and the qualifier together, meaning the absence of both: in the example, "I did not come and did not ride." It may also be that the negation is directed only to the act, without considering the negation or affirmation of the qualifier.

It has been said: in this verse it is not correct for "and they know" to be a qualifier of the negation, because there is no benefit, since abandoning persistence entails reward and recompense whether it is with knowledge of the ugliness or with ignorance; rather, with ignorance it is more fitting. Nor is it correct that the negation be directed to the qualifier only while affirming the act itself, since the meaning is not the affirmation of persistence and the negation of knowledge. Likewise, it is not correct that it be directed to both the act and the qualifier together, since the meaning is not the negation of knowledge. The apparent view is that the appropriate reading here is that the negation is directed to the act only, without considering the negation or affirmation of the qualifier, and the intended meaning is: "they did not persist while knowing," in the sense that the absence of persistence is certainly realized.

[Page 60] [Page 61] [Page 62]

You could say: why should it not be possible that the circumstantial clause here restricts the negation, so that the meaning is "they did not persist in the sin because they knew that the sin is ugly"? For a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) may come in the sense of giving a reason (taʿlīl).

As for the hadith that abandoning persistence (iṣrār) entails reward and recompense, whether it is accompanied by knowledge of the ugliness [of the sin] or by ignorance, so the content of the circumstantial clause has no bearing on the requirement of reward: this is answered by saying that the purpose of mentioning the circumstantial clause is not to restrict the persistence by it so that it brings about the reward, such that the above objection would apply. Rather, the intention is to praise them, that their abandoning persistence in sin is because there is in them something that restrains them from it, namely their knowledge of the ugliness of the sin. Thus it is a praise of them that among their attributes is guarding against vices. Some later scholars claimed that it is necessary for the circumstantial clause to be a restriction of the negated element, and that the negation relates to the restriction, meaning: "persistence was not for them while knowing the ugliness [of the sin], for the one who persists while not knowing the ugliness is not deprived of reward, and one who does not persist out of laziness or because the inclination of his nature is absent does not attain it, since the reward is for restraint, not for mere absence; otherwise everyone would have endless rewards for the endless vices they never thought of committing." What is wrong with his saying "and one who does not persist etc." and his saying "since the reward etc." is not hidden from one who looks carefully. It seems that whoever made it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "istaghfarū" wanted to flee from this difficulty. I say: the circumstantial clause is restricted to the negation and to the object of knowledge, and what is known is not the ugliness [of the sin] but rather that He forgives whoever seeks forgiveness and accepts the repentance of whoever repents. This is also what is related from Mujāhid, as a group of scholars transmitted from him, and it is also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The meaning is that they abandoned persistence in sin, knowing that God Most High accepts repentance from His servants and forgives them. This is an indication that they do not despair of the mercy of God, glorified is He. This interpretation is not subject to the objection of lack of benefit as was raised at first, for it is well known, beyond any doubt, that abandoning persistence only brings reward when it is not accompanied by despair, for none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people. Perhaps praising them for knowing this is more fitting than praising them for knowing the ugliness of the act. It may be said that the sentence is inserted parenthetically for this purpose, just as the sentence "And who forgives sins except God?" is inserted for what it was inserted for. As for taking it as coordinated with the sentence "they did not persist," many things are valid as a subordinate but not valid independently, so this is not what the soul inclines to.

(﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾) is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned last, in view of their possession of the praiseworthy attributes mentioned earlier. The use of the distal form serves to indicate how exalted their rank in virtue is. Most scholars held this view. It has also been said that it refers to those mentioned, who constitute a single group, and that it is the subject (mubtada'). The words ﴿جَزاؤُهُمْ﴾ are then either a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for it or a second subject. The words ﴿مَغْفِرَة﴾ are the predicate of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾, or the predicate of the second subject, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first. On the first reading, this clause is the predicate of ﴿والَّذِينَ إذا فَعَلُوا﴾ and so on. Our master Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) claimed that this is the most evident and best suited to the arrangement of the word "forgiveness" in the series of rewards, since it indicates a previous sin. On the last two readings, ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ and what follows is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustanifah) explaining what precedes it and disclosing the state of both groups, the good-doers and the penitents. He did not mention, among the attributes of the first group, anything that involves a trace of sin, so that the forgiveness common to both would be mentioned at the outset of the reward. Restricting the demonstrative to the last two, even though both share the ruling of the preparation of Paradise for them, is an evident forced interpretation. End of quotation.

What appears from the apparent meaning of what Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan is that he recited ﴿الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ في السَّرّاءِ والضَّرّاءِ﴾ up to the end of the verse, then recited ﴿والَّذِينَ إذا فَعَلُوا فاحِشَةً﴾ up to the end of the verse, and said: "These two descriptions belong to one man." On this view, the demonstrative is one of the last two readings mentioned, or rather the first of them, and this demonstrative is as the author of the Qil (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, as it is said) stated. This forgiveness is the forgiveness to which all believers, whether they have sinned or not, are commanded to hasten by means that lead to it. Therefore its occurrence at the outset of the reward does no harm.

﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ is connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of "forgiveness," reinforcing what the indefiniteness (tanwin) conveys of intrinsic magnificence with the magnificence conveyed by the annexation. The meaning is: a great forgiveness proceeding from Him, may He be exalted. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the annexation to their pronoun serves to indicate the cause of the ruling and to confer honour.

﴿وجَنّاتٌ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ﴾ is coordinated with "forgiveness." What is meant by it is gardens included within that Garden whose breadth, God the Glorious informed us, is as wide as the heavens and the earth. There are no gardens beyond it, according to what the words of the author of the Qil imply. However, [God] did not suffice with the preparation of what was described first. He specified its description by its containing what increases its delight: rivers flowing, after describing it as vast. The statement that these are their reward and their recompense, which by the dictates of bounty must reach them, is above the statement of preparation, or it reinforces it. Thus the tanwin is for magnification, in the same mould as what was mentioned of the thing coordinated with.

Shaykh al-Islam claimed that the indefiniteness indicates that these gardens are lower in rank than the Garden mentioned previously, and that this supports the preponderance of the first reading that he indicated. There is some hesitation about this.

﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾ is a predicative state (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun in the genitive in ﴿جَزاؤُهم﴾, because it is in meaning an object: it is in effect equivalent to "God will recompense them with gardens, abiding therein." It cannot be a state of "gardens" in wording, while the abiding belongs to its people in meaning, for had it been so, the pronoun would have been made explicit, according to the majority view.

﴿ونِعْمَ أجْرُ العامِلِينَ﴾ (136). The object of praise is omitted, meaning: "and excellent is the reward of those who work, [namely] the Garden." Muqatil confined himself to this. Others held that it refers to what was mentioned of forgiveness and the gardens.

Page 64

Certain rhetorical embellishments (muhassinat) are found in the sentence, as some scholars of verification have stated:

First: it functions as a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the preceding discourse, and so it adds emphasis to the pleasure of hearing the promise.

Second: placing the word "reward" (ajr) in the position of the pronoun of recompense. The original would be "and excellent is it," i.e., their recompense is the obligation to fulfil this promise. It also depicts the image of work as hired labour, to stimulate the worker.

Third: generalizing "those who work" and putting it in the place of a pronoun indicates, in a demonstrative manner, that what is sought has been attained by those mentioned.

As for the preceding discourse which this has been made a concluding statement to, it is either the discourse concerning the penitents, or the whole preceding discourse according to the disagreement we mentioned just now. Whoever holds the first view said: "It suffices you to distinguish between the two groups, namely: the God-fearing (muttaqun), who performed all the obligations and avoided all sins; and those who seek forgiveness for their sins after committing them and perpetrating indecencies and wrongdoing. God, may He be exalted, distinguished the verse about the first group with His words, glorified be He and exalted: ﴿واللَّهُ يُحِبُّ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾, which indicates that they are good-doers beloved by God, the Exalted. He distinguished the verse about the others with His words, Mighty and Sublime be He: ﴿ونِعْمَ أجْرُ العامِلِينَ﴾, which indicates that these are hired workers, and that what they were given of reward is a recompense for their making up for some of what they had lost for themselves. How far is this from that! The distance between the fish and the fishmonger is great."

It is not hidden that, on the supposition that the two attributes belong to one man, as was related from al-Hasan, it is possible to say that the mention of this sentence after that one is due to what some scholars of verification stated. What prevents the statement that they are beloved by God, the Exalted, and that God fulfils what He promised them without fail? Their being good-doers is not contradicted by their seeking forgiveness and repenting when they sin. As for if by "good-doing" is meant bestowing benefit upon others, it is evident. As for if by it is meant performing actions in the proper manner, or "that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you," as stated in the Sahih, then if that were contradicted it would follow that the term "good-doer" applies only to one like the infallible, and it would not apply to one who worshipped God and obeyed Him for a long period in the most fitting and best manner, then disobeyed Him for a moment, then regretted with the utmost regret, and sought forgiveness, "the master of forms of seeking forgiveness." I do not think anyone holds that. So reflect.

Furthermore, in these verses, according to what the majority hold, there is an indication that believers are three categories: the God-fearing, the penitent, and the persistent. There is also an indication that those who are not persistent will have their sins forgiven and will enter the Garden. As for whether they indicate that the persistent will not have their sins forgiven nor enter the Garden, as some claimed, that is not so, because silence about a ruling is not an explanation of their ruling according to some, while it indicates the contrary according to others. It suffices for its establishment that they hesitate between fear and hope, and that they are not free from reproach, the least of which is reproaching them for what they committed, in detail, and what a disgrace that is. This is necessary according to what the texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate. In that case, complete forgiveness is not achieved for them as it is for the penitent. Moreover, what the verses imply is that the Garden is not the reward of the persistent, and likewise forgiveness. As for negating bounty (tafaddul) with respect to these two, that is not so. This is clear according to the principle of the Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist school that held obligation on God to reward and punish), because of the difference between reward and bounty in terms of obligation and non-obligation. As for the principle of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni orthodox school), it is likewise, because bounty is of two kinds: one kind is consequent upon the work, like satiety following eating, and it is called a reward and a wage. The other kind is not consequent upon the work. Of it is that which completes the reward in quantity or quality, as He promised multiplication and other things. Of it is that which is purely bounty in reality and in name, like pardon for those who committed major sins, and the vision of God in the abode of permanence, and other things known only to God, the Exalted. This was stated by some scholars of verification.

Al-Allamah al-Tibi mentioned that God's words, ﴿واتَّقُوا النّارَ الَّتِي أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ (Fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers), were addressed to believing consumers of usury, as a deterrent from persisting in what would lead them to the ranks of the perdition of the disbelievers, and as an encouragement to repentance and to hastening to attain the degrees of the successful among the God-fearing and the penitent. Therefore, including the persistent in this context is far from the target, because it is an incitement and encouragement to sin, not a restraint or a warning. Thus the verses clarify the meaning of the God-fearing for the purposes of encouragement and warning, and further depict the stations and ranks of the friends of God, so that they may be an impetus for them to join their ranks. It is necessary to mention the penitent, their seeking forgiveness and their not persisting, so that this may be a kindness to these people. All the benefits mentioned in God's words, glorified be He and exalted: ﴿ومَن يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إلا اللَّهُ﴾ (And who forgives sins except God?) are included in the meaning. It is therefore known from this that the implication of ﴿ولَمْ يُصِرُّوا عَلى ما فَعَلُوا﴾ (and have not persisted in what they did) is abandoned, because the context of exhortation and urging excluded the persistent. The conclusion is that the condition for the validity of implication (mafhum) here is absent, so it is not at all valid for the Mu'tazilah to argue with this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 137:

﴿Indeed, there have passed﴾, i.e., have gone by, ﴿before you ways (sunan)﴾, i.e., occurrences among the rejecting nations which Allah, exalted is He, brought about according to His custom. Al-Mufaddal said: what is meant by them is the nations (umam). The word sunnah has indeed come in their speech with the meaning of ummah (community), and among this is his saying:

"The people have not witnessed such excellence as yours, nor have they seen anyone like you in the ways of bygone times."

ʿAtaʾ said: what is meant by them is the sharʿ (revealed laws) and religions (adyan), so the meaning is: there have passed before you ways and religions which were abrogated. It is not hidden that the first (view) is more suitable to the context, because this is either directed at encouraging the obligated (mukallafun) or the consumers of usury (akilu al-riba) to act in obedience or to repent from disobedience, or to both, in a manner other than what preceded, as has been said; or it is a return to detailing the rest of the story after laying the foundations of guidance and righteousness and arranging the preliminaries of success and salvation, according to one opinion. The mention of the passing of religions has little connection with that. Although some claim that in it there is a reinforcement of the believers upon the religion of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, lest they weaken by the saying of the Jews that the religion of Moses, peace be upon him, cannot be abrogated, and that abrogation is impermissible for Allah, exalted is He, because it is a change of mind (bada'); and an incitement of the Jews and an urging them to accept the religion of Islam; and a warning to them that there may befall them the like of what befell the deniers; and a strengthening of the hearts of the believers that He will give them victory over the deniers. Yes, the application of sunnah to the sharʿ is closer than its application to an occurrence, because originally it means the way and the custom, and from this is their saying: "the sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him." The prepositional phrase is either related to "passed" or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "ways," i.e., ways existing from before you.

﴿So travel through the earth﴾, i.e., with your feet or with your understanding, ﴿and observe﴾, i.e., reflect.

﴿How was the end of those who denied﴾ (137), i.e., the final outcome of their affair which their denial of their prophets led to. The fa' (so) indicates the causal link between passing away and travelling and observing, or the command to them. It was said: the meaning is conditional, i.e., if you doubt, then travel, etc. The address in every case is directed to the believers. Al-Naqqash said: it is addressed to the disbelievers, and there is remoteness in this. The word "kayfa" (how) is a predicate preceding "kana" (was), and it is suspended for the verb of observing (nazar), and the clause is in a position of accusative after the removal of the preposition, because the original usage is with the preposition; and the verb is stripped of the feminine marker tāʾ because the subject is metaphorically feminine.

This is a clarification for mankind, and guidance and admonition for those who are mindful of God (138).

The demonstrative "this" may refer to the Qur'an, which is the view reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah. It has been criticized as far from the context. Or it may refer to what was summarized earlier concerning the disbelievers, the God-fearing, and those who repent. The words of God, Glorified is He, "Precedents have passed before you" (137), are a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad, a clause interposed between parts of a sentence) urging faith, God-consciousness, and repentance, as has been said. The purpose of the parenthetical insertion is to answer an objection: a parenthetical clause confirms the matter it interrupts, but here this is not the case. Those verses are addressed as encouragement and warning to those who consume usury, whereas this verse conveys a warning. Its meaning returns to encouragement by way of contrast. Likewise, some verses addressed to the Most Merciful (surah 55) concerning threats are counted among the bounties (al-ala')[^1] by way of restraining from sins. Thus the emphasis is achieved without deficiency. It has been objected that this is a forced interpretation.

Or the demonstrative may refer to what preceded in the words of God, Glorified is He, "Precedents have passed before you," and so on. This is the view reported from Abu Ishaq, and it was chosen by al-Tabari, al-Balkhi, and many later scholars. The definite article (al-) in "mankind" (al-nas) is for a specific reference (al-'ahd)[^2], and the intended people are the deniers. The adverbial phrase may be connected either to "clarification" or to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of them. That is, this is an explanation of the evil outcome of what they are upon of denial. Although the preceding command is specific to the believers according to the preferred view, acting upon its requirement is not restricted to them. Therefore it includes the deniers as well, in that they should look into the outcome of their predecessors so that they may take heed.

Admonition (al-mawi'za) is that which softens the heart and calls to adherence to what contains obedience. Guidance (al-huda) is the explanation of the path of right direction so that it may be followed rather than the path of error. The difference between it and clarification (al-bayan) is that the latter is the manifestation of meaning, whatever it may be. Because what is meant here by clarification is that which is devoid of guidance and admonition, it was specifically assigned to mankind, although its apparent scope includes the God-fearing.

The intended "those who are mindful" are the opposite of the deniers. It seems that the second-person pronoun was replaced by this noun, on the basis that the meaning is "and an increase in insight and admonition for you," to indicate the cause of the ruling. For the matter of its being guidance and admonition for them depends on their God-consciousness and their not denying it. The clarification of its being a clarification for the deniers was mentioned first, although it is not directed to it, over its being guidance for the God-fearing, although that is the intended aim of the context. This is because the first thing that follows from witnessing the traces of the destruction of their predecessors is the manifestation of the state of their descendants. As for guidance, it is something that follows from that. The restriction to the two matters with regard to the God-fearing, despite their following from the clarification, is because they are the primary objective. It has also been said that the definite article in "mankind" is for the generic sense (al-jins)[^3].

The intended meaning is a clarification for all people, but the one who benefits from it is the God-fearing, because they are guided by it and seek admonition from it. This is not far-fetched. Some have permitted that the God-fearing be understood as those who are becoming God-fearing, so that guidance and admonition remain without addition. Or they may be understood as those who include both them and others who are already God-fearing in fact. Then guidance and what is conjoined to it would require taking into account what includes both the beginning and the increase in it. There is no concealing the greater remoteness of the second interpretation, since it involves departing from the apparent meaning in two places. As for the first, there is remoteness in that it departs from the apparent meaning in one place. Although it shares with what we have said this aspect, what we have undertaken is indicated in general by the nunation (tanwin)[^4] found in the word, whereas what they have undertaken is not so indicated. Rather, considering perfection, which the absoluteness of the expression suggests, may reject it. Perhaps it is because of both matters combined that the matter of removing the khuff (leather sock)[^5] has become trivial.

[^1]: al-ala': the bounties or blessings of God.
[^2]: al-'ahd: the definite article indicating a previously known or specific referent.
[^3]: al-jins: the definite article indicating the class or genus in general.
[^4]: tanwin: the nunation, the "n" sound marking indefinite nouns in Arabic.
[^5]: khuff: a leather sock or boot worn over which one may wipe in ablution.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 139:

﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve﴾. Al-Wahidi related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were routed on the day of Uhud. While they were in that state, Khalid ibn al-Walid came up with the cavalry of the polytheists, intending to overpower them on the mountain. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O God, we have no strength except through You. O God, none worships You in this city except these few men.' Then God sent down this verse. A group of Muslims rallied, climbed the mountain, shot at the cavalry of the polytheists, and defeated them."

It is also related on the authority of al-Zuhri and Qatadah that it was revealed as a consolation to the Muslims for what befell them on the day of Uhud of killing and wounds.

It is related on the authority of al-Kalbi that it was revealed after the day of Uhud, when "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered his companions, may God be pleased with them, to pursue the enemy, although they had sustained the wounds that they had sustained. He (ﷺ) said: 'None shall go out except those who were present with us yesterday.' This was hard on the Muslims, so God sent down this verse."

In any case, it is coordinated (ma'tufah) with God's words ﴿Travel through the earth﴾ in terms of wording, and connected to it in terms of meaning if we say that it returns to the detailed account (al-tafsil); and with what preceded of the story of Uhud, if we do not say that. This is the view of a group, who regard the interposing of the discussion of usury as a digression (istitrad) or an allusion to another kind of enmity toward the religion and warfare against the Muslims. By this the connection becomes apparent. Its orientation has also been explained in other ways, as has already been mentioned.

Some people have made the verbal connection of this verse depend on an elided element, meaning: "Be diligent, and do not weaken." This is in line with the disagreement (over the connection), but it is an unnecessary strain (takalluf) that can be dispensed with.

The weakening (wahn) is weakness, meaning: do not become weak in fighting your enemies and in striving in the cause of God because of the wounds you have received. ﴿Nor grieve﴾ over what you have suffered of the killing of the noble ones. In that battle, five of the Emigrants were killed: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib; Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, bearer of the banner of the Messenger of God (ﷺ); 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh, the son of the paternal aunt of the Prophet (ﷺ); 'Uthman ibn Shammas; and Sa'd, freed slave of 'Utbah, may God be pleased with them; and seventy of the Helpers. It has also been said that ﴿nor grieve﴾ means over what you missed of the spoils of war. Its remoteness is not hidden. The apparent meaning is that the literal sense of the prohibition is not intended here; rather what is intended is consolation and encouragement. If the literal sense is intended, then perhaps it refers to the voluntary consequences that follow from weakness and grief, meaning: do not do what follows from that.

﴿While you are the superior ones﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) relating to the subject of the two verbs, meaning: and the situation is that you are "the superior ones," the victors over your enemies, since their outcome is the outcome of their predecessors who denied. This is an explicit statement after the implication of victory and triumph.

Al-Qurtubi related that after that they did not go out on any campaign without being victorious, in every expedition that took place during his (ﷺ) lifetime, and likewise in every expedition that took place afterward, even if only one of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, was in it. Or the meaning, with the situation being that you are higher than them in rank, is that you are upon the truth and your fighting is to raise the word of God, and your slain are in Paradise, whereas they are upon falsehood and their fighting is to support the word of Satan, and their slain are in the Fire. Their sharing with you in this superiority is based on the outward appearance and their claim. If superiority is taken in the sense of victory, this is not needed, because war is a matter of alternation (sijal), and the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿while you are the superior ones﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to them, in that you inflicted on them at the Battle of Badr greater than what they inflicted on you today.

Some people permitted the clause to have no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and made it a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) between the aforementioned prohibition and His, glorified is He, words ﴿if you are believers﴾ (139), because it is related to it in meaning. Even if the answer (of the condition) is elided, meaning: if you are believers, then do not weaken and do not grieve, for faith necessitates strength of heart, greater trust in God, the Exalted, and indifference to His enemies. It is not hidden that the claim of a connection is not objectionable, but the ruling that the clause is parenthetical is considered far-fetched. It is also possible that this conditional is connected to "the superior ones," with the answer likewise elided, meaning: if you are believers, then you are the superior ones, for faith in God, the Exalted, necessarily requires superiority. It is also possible that by faith is meant the affirmation of God's promise of help and victory over the enemies of God, the Exalted. This possibility is not restricted to the last of the two possibilities of connection, as the way some of them have phrased it may suggest. In every case, the purpose of the condition here is to confirm what is linked to it, as in the words of the hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my wage," or like your saying to your son: "If you are my son, then do not disobey me." Some have taken the condition to indicate causation (ta'lil), meaning: do not weaken and do not grieve because you are believers, or "while you are the superior ones" for that reason. The view that the meaning is "if you remain upon faith" does not have full suitability to the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 140:

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched that people.﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Asim, read *qarh* with a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*, while the rest read it with a *fatḥah*. Both are dialectal forms, like *ad-duff* and *ad-daff*, and *aḍ-ḍu'f* and *aḍ-ḍa'f*. Al-Farra' said: *al-qarh* with a *fatḥah* means the wound itself, and with a *ḍammah* means the pain of it. It is also read with a *ḍammah* on both the *qāf* and the *rā'*, by *ittiba'* (vowel harmonization, the following vowel being copied onto the preceding one), as in *al-yusr* and *al-yusul*, and *aṭ-ṭunb* and *aṭ-ṭunub*. Abu as-Simal read both with a *fatḥah*, and it is the verbal noun of *qaraḥa*, *yaqraḥu*, when a person develops a sore. The meaning is: if they inflicted a wound on you on the day of Uhud, then you had already inflicted one on them before that, on the day of Badr. Yet that did not weaken their hearts or deter them from renewing the fight against you. You are more entitled not to weaken, for you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. The imperfect verb (*al-muḍāri'*) here, according to what al-Taftazani held, is for the narration of a present state (*ḥikāyat al-ḥāl*), because the touching has already taken place. As for the use of *in* (if) with *kāna* (was) implied, meaning "if a wound had touched you," *in* does not conjugate with *kāna*, because its indication of the past is strong. Or it is said that *in* may come merely to express a condition, without transferring the verb from the past to the future. What occurs in the position of the answer of the condition is not a true answer, since it is realized before this condition, but rather an indicator of the answer. The meaning is: if a wound had touched you, that does not excuse you or justify your withdrawal from jihad afterwards, because it has touched your enemies, and they remain as they are. Or it is said: if a wound touches you, then be consoled, for a similar wound has touched that people. The similarity is in terms of the large number of the slain in general. So it is not objected that the Muslims killed seventy of the polytheists at Badr and took seventy captive, while the polytheists killed seventy-five of the Muslims at Uhud and wounded seventy. Some scholars insisted on interpreting *qarḥ* as mere defeat, without counting the dead, to avoid this objection. Some went too far in interpreting the verse and carried it to a meaning that the words of Allah Most High should not be carried to. He said: the more likely view is that the intended meaning is ﴿if a wound touches you﴾, so do not weaken, because ﴿it has touched the people﴾, that is the men, ﴿a similar wound﴾. Wounds belong to men, not to women. Whoever belongs to the company of men should not turn away from what is his due, but should strive for it. By this, the expression in the imperfect tense remains valid and is on its apparent meaning. This also dispels what has been said: that the wound of the people was not like their wound. This does not require the previous answer.

It is also said: both touchings took place at Uhud, for the Muslims inflicted wounds upon them before they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They killed more than twenty of them, including their standard-bearer, wounded a large number, and hamstrung nearly all their horses with arrows. It is also said that the wound which touched them was that they returned disappointed despite their numbers and their dominance, by the protection of Allah Most High for the believers.

﴿And those days﴾: the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*) refers to what follows it, as in ambiguous pronouns (*ḍamā'ir mubhamah*) which are explained by what follows, such as *rabbahu rajulan* (its lord, a man). Such usage conveys magnification and exaltation. The word *al-ayyām* (the days) means the times, not the conventional days. Its definiteness is for the known (*al-'ahd*), indicating the times of triumph and dominance that run among the past and future nations. The two days of Badr and Uhud are included in this primarily.

﴿We alternate them among people﴾: we turn them among them, so we grant victory to these at one time and to those at another time, as happened on the day of Badr and the day of Uhud. *Al-mudāwalah* is the transfer of a thing from one to another. It is said: "the hands passed it around" (*tadāwalathu al-aydī*) when it moved from one to another. *An-nās* (people) is general, but Ibn Sirin interpreted it as the rulers. The demonstrative noun is the subject, and *al-ayyām* is its predicate. *Nudāwiluhā* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the element governing it is the sense of the indication, or it is a second predicate. It is permissible for *al-ayyām* to be an adjective, a substitute, or an explicative apposition (*'aṭf bayān*), and *nudāwiluhā* is then the predicate. *Bayna an-nās* is an adverbial complement of *nudāwiluhā*, and it is permitted for it to be a circumstantial clause of the *hā'* (the pronoun). The form of the imperfect, which indicates recurrence and continuity, is to inform that this alternation is a practice followed among all nations until the command of Allah Most High comes. Among their sayings: "The days are turns and war is a bucket-exchange" (*sijāl*). In this there is a kind of consolation for the believers. It has also been read as *yudāwiluhā*.

﴿And so that Allah may know those who believe﴾: this is a causal clause (*ta'līl*) for one specific instance of the absolute alternation mentioned before, namely the known alternation occurring between the two groups of believers and disbelievers. The *lām* is connected either to what is indicated by the unrestricted verb, restricted by occurring between the two mentioned groups, or to the unrestricted verb itself in terms of its occurrence between them. The sentence is conjoined to another cause considered for it, either specifically and definitely, because of the indication mentioned, as if it were said: "We alternate them between you and your enemy so that your condition may become manifest and be known," or generally and vaguely, to alert that causes are not limited to those enumerated, and that the servant is distressed by what happens to him without perceiving what Allah has hidden within it of subtle kindnesses. As if it were said: "We make them turns among you so that they may be wisdoms and many benefits," and ﴿so that Allah may know﴾ etc. In this there is what is clearly an emphasis on consolation. The restriction of the explanation to the cause of this instance from the absolute alternation, rather than its other instances occurring among the rest of the nations, is either definite or vague, because the scientific purpose does not concern its explanation. You may also take the omitted, undetermined element as an expression of the causes of all its other instances, in order to indicate in summary that each instance of it has a cause that calls for it apparently. As if it were said: ﴿We alternate them among people﴾ all of them, so that such-and-such wisdoms may be the motivations for those instances, ﴿and so that Allah may know﴾ etc. The first *lām* is then connected to the unrestricted verb in terms of its restriction to those instances, and the second to the restriction to the known instance. This is what Mawlana Shaykh al-Islam said. They also allowed that the verb is conjoined to what precedes it in meaning, as if it were said: "The days alternated among you, because this is our custom, [and so that Allah may know] etc." It has been said that the verb being causally explained is elided and is to be estimated as postponed, the estimate being: ﴿And so that Allah may know those who believe﴾ did that. Some thought the *wāw* is additional, but this is from narrowness of scope. The speech is of the figurative kind (*tamthīl*), meaning: He treats you in the manner of one who wishes to know the sincere ones who remain steadfast in faith from others. Knowledge here is a metaphor for distinguishing, by the device of naming the cause after its effect, meaning: to distinguish those steadfast in faith from others. To take knowledge as distinguishing in the figurative sense is an unnecessary elaboration. Many have preferred taking knowledge as the cognitive attachment (*ta'alluq tanjīzī*) upon which the reward is consequent. Some of this was discussed earlier concerning al-Baqarah.

In sum, it is not objected that the knowledge, which is an attribute subsisting in His Essence, Exalted is He, would entail its occurrence, nor that the word "believe" is used although the intended meaning is firmness and sincerity in it, for it is a sign that the name of faith does not apply to anything else.

Some claimed the estimate is: so that Allah may know the believer from the hypocrite, but he dispensed with mentioning one of them over the other, and there is no need for this. Similar is the view that an annexed noun is elided, meaning: the patience of those who... The turning to the third person by attributing it to the Majestic Name serves to nurture awe, and to indicate that the issuing of each of the things mentioned, which are in the process of being causes, from His acts, Exalted is He, is in respect of a specific source among His attributes, which this Greatest Name comprises, distinct from the source of the other.

﴿And that He may take martyrs from among you﴾: *shuhadā'* is the plural of *shahīd*, which is the slain in battle. The intended martyrs are the martyrs of Uhud, as said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Ishaq. The *min* (from) is either initial (*ibtidā'iyyah*) or partitive (*tab'īḍiyyah*), attached to *yattakhidh*, or to an elided element that stands as a circumstantial clause of *shuhadā'*. It has been said that it is the plural of *shāhid* (witness), meaning: and that He may take from among you witnesses, who are vouched for by what appeared of their steadfastness upon the truth, their patience in hardships, and other tokens of sincerity, so that they may bear witness over the nations on the Day of Resurrection. In this view, the *min* is explicative (*bayāniyyah*), because that testimony is the duty of all, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation so that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾. The first view is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ikrimah, who said: When the news was delayed for the women, they went out to inquire. Then they saw two men slain on a riding animal or on a camel. A woman of the Ansar said: "Who are these two?" They said: "So-and-so and so-and-so, her brother and her husband," or "her husband and her son." She said: "What has the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) done?" They said: "He is alive." She said: "I do not mind, for Allah Most High takes martyrs from among His servants." The Qur'an was revealed in accordance with what she said: ﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾. Taking is here a metonymy for honouring, because whoever takes something for himself has chosen it and approved of it. So the meaning is: that He may honour some of you with martyrdom.

﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ (140): that is, He hates them. By "the wrongdoers" is meant either the hypocrites, like Ibn Ubayy and his followers, who withdrew from the army of Islam as we related earlier, and they stand in contrast to the believers mentioned before, described as steadfast in faith and firm in it, whose outward appearances agree with their inward ones. Or it means the disbelievers who openly profess disbelief. Whichever it is, the sentence is parenthetical (*mu'tariḍah*), to affirm the content of what precedes it. It contains an alert that Allah Most High does not truly help the disbeliever, but only overpowers him at times as a respite and a trial for the believer. Also, if victory were always for the believers, people would enter faith out of hope for blessing and as an omen, and the aim is other than that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 141:

﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾, i.e., that He may cleanse them of sins and purify them of misdeeds.
Page 70
The root of tamhis (purification through testing) is, as al-Khalil said, the refining of a thing from every defect; one says: "I refined the gold (mahhastu al-dhahab) when I removed its impurity."

The clause is conjoined to (yattakhidha) [﴿and that He may take [some of you] as martyrs﴾]. The repetition of the lam (li-) serves to give importance to this cause, and for this reason the Glorious Name was placed in the position of a pronoun [i.e., Allah was mentioned explicitly rather than as a pronoun]; or it serves to emphasize the causal sense, because of the interposition between them of a parenthetical clause. These three matters, as our master Shaykh al-Islam said, are causes for the alternation (of victory and defeat, al-mudawala al-mahhuda) in terms of its being directed at the believers; they were placed first in the mention because they are the ones in need of explanation. Perhaps the last cause was delayed beyond the parenthetical clause so that it would not be assumed that the sinners are included among the wrongdoers (al-zalimin); or so that it would be connected with His words, Exalted and Glorious be He: ﴿and that He may destroy the disbelievers﴾ (141), because of the correspondence between them, since both tamhis and mahq involve removal. However, in the first is the removal of traces and the lifting of burdens, while in the second is the removal of the very substance and the ruin of the self. The root of mahq is the gradual diminishing of a thing bit by bit, and from it comes "mihaq" (the waning of the moon). The meaning is: and that He may destroy the disbelievers and leave none of them remaining, blowing out the fire. This is a cause for the alternation in terms of its being directed against them. Here "the disbelievers" refers to a specific group, namely those who fought the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Uhud and persisted in disbelief, for Allah Most High destroyed them all. It has also been said: it is permissible that this be a cause for the alternation in terms of its being directed against the believers as well, for when the disbelievers prevail at times they become deluded, and Satan leads them into vain hopes and whispers to them, so they remain persistent in disbelief, and Allah Most High destroys them for their sins and makes them abide forever in the Fire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 142:

﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise﴾ is an address to those who fled on the day of Uhud. It is a new sentence (kalam mustani'af) explaining the ultimate purpose of the alternation of fortunes (al-mudawala), and it is the conclusion drawn from the three earlier causes mentioned. The (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'a), with an implied (bal) (rather) and the interrogative hamza of denial (al-istifham al-inkari). That it is connective (muttasila), with an implied counterpart (adil), is far-fetched (takallluf). The turn away from consolation, by explaining the causes of the hardship they suffered, leads to the affirmation that these are among the beginnings of attaining the sublime goal and the highest station. The meaning is: rather, it is not fitting for you to think that you will enter Paradise and attain its bliss and what Allah the Exalted has prepared for His servants within it. ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (tadkhulu) (you enter), emphasizing the denial. The hope for reward without action from one whom it is known is bound to that action is, in the minds of people, improbable. For this reason it was said:

*You hope for salvation but have not taken its paths;*
*Indeed, a ship does not sail on dry land.*

It is related from Shahr ibn Hawshab: seeking Paradise without action is one of the sins; awaiting intercession without a cause is a kind of delusion; and hoping for mercy from one who is not obeyed is foolishness and ignorance. The negation of knowledge, in terms of its being an immediate connection (ta'alluq al-tanjizi), is as was mentioned concerning the affirmation, according to one opinion.

It is also permissible that the statement be a metonymy (kinaya) for the negation of the realization of that, because the negation of knowledge is a necessary consequence of the negation of realization, since realization necessitates the knowledge of Allah the Exalted; and the negation of the necessary consequence entails the negation of what necessitates it. It is often said: "Allah the Exalted has not known any good in so-and-so," meaning that there is no good in him until He knows it. Whether this applies to the negation of our knowledge or not is a matter of doubt, and what the author of al-Intisaf decided upon is the second view. The preference for metonymy over explicit statement is for emphasis in establishing the intended meaning, namely that the striving (jihad), which is the cause of the greatest success for them, has not been realized, since speech based on it is like claiming a thing with proof. In this there is also an allusion to abandoning ostentation (riya'), and that the intended object is the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, not people. The negation was directed at the qualified persons (al-mawsufin), although what is negated is the attribute (al-wasf) which is striving, in order to emphasize the negation of that and its non-realization at all; and how can an attribute be realized without a qualified subject?

The choice of (lamma) over (lam) indicates that striving is expected from them in the future, based on what is understood from the words of Sibawayh: that (lamma) indicates the expectation of the action negated by it. Al-Zajjaj also mentioned that if it is said: "So-and-so has done," its answer is: "lamma yafʿal" (he has not yet done); and if it is said: "Did he do?" its answer is: "lam yafʿal" (he did not do); and if it is said: "Indeed he has done" (laqad fa'ala), its answer is: "ma fa'ala" (he did not do), as if he had said: "By Allah, indeed he has done," and the responder said: "By Allah, he did not do." And if it is said: "He does" meaning the future, its answer is: "la yafʿal" (he does not do); and if it is said: "He will do" (sa-yafʿal), its answer is: "lan yafʿal" (he will not do). Abu Hayyan's statement, that the view that (lamma) indicates the expectation of the action negated by it in the future is one that I do not know any of the grammarians to have mentioned except one who is not relied upon, is correct. Yes, this expectation is not considered here in emphasizing the denial.

(wa-ya'lama) is read with a fatha on the mim, on the basis that its original form is (ya'lamanna) with a light nun, which was dropped in connected speech. They have permitted its omission, either on condition that a following consonant (sakin) meets it, or absolutely. Among examples of this is the verse:

*When I say "qadni" (enough for me), he swears by Allah an oath*
*That will suffice me, you and all your kin together.*

This is according to the reading with a fatha on the lam. It was also said that the fatha on the mim is to follow the lam, so that the glorification of the name of Allah, may His name be exalted, remains. The (min-kum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (alladhina), and the (min) in it is partitive (lil-tab'id), which indicates that striving is a communal obligation (fard kifaya). ﴿and that He may know the patient﴾ (142) is in the accusative by the implied (an) (that). It was also said that it is governed by the waw of change (waw al-sarf), and the speech follows the pattern of "Do not eat fish and drink milk," meaning: "Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet realized among you the striving and the patience," that is, the combination of the two. The choice of "al-sabirin" (the patient) over "alladhina sabaru" (those who were patient) is to indicate that what is considered is continuous perseverance in patience, and for the preservation of the rhyme-endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy). It was also said that the verb is jussive (majzum) by coordination with the jussive before it, and it was moved by fatha to avoid the meeting of two sakins, for lightness and by assimilation. This is supported by the reading of al-Hasan: (wa-ya'lami al-sabirin) with a kasra on the mim.
