It was also read (wa-ya'lamu) with a damma, on the basis that the waw is for resumption of speech (li'l-istinaf) or for circumstance (li'l-hal), with the implied (wa-huwa ya'lamu, "while He knows"), and the subject of the circumstance is the relative pronoun, as if it were said: "While you have not yet striven, and you are patient."

[Page 71]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 143:**

﴿And you had certainly wished for death﴾ is addressed to a group of the believers who had not witnessed the Battle of Badr, because they did not expect war when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for it. When what happened, happened, they regretted it and began to say: "Would that we had been killed as the companions of Badr were killed, and had been martyred as they were martyred." Then, when Allah made them witness Uhud, none remained except those whom Allah willed.

The meaning of "death" here is death in the way of Allah, which is martyrdom (shahada). There is no harm in wishing for it. It is not an objection that wishing for this would mean wishing for the victory of the disbelievers, because the aim of the one who wishes is only to attain the honour of the martyrs and nothing else, and this idea does not occur to his mind. This is like someone who drinks a Christian's medicine, for example, intending healing and not its benefit to him or the promotion of his trade. This wish was expressed by Abdullah ibn Rawahah, one of the senior Companions, and it was not rebuked. It is also permissible that "death" means war (harb), since war is one of its causes, and the words of al-Rabi' and Qatadah point to this. In that case, what is wished for is war, not death itself.

﴿before you met it﴾ is connected to (tamannawna, "you wished"), explaining the reason for their wishing, meaning: before you had seen and known its terror. It was also read with a damma on the lam (lāmi), by omitting the genitive (muḍāf ilayhi, the word it is attached to) and intending its meaning. In that reading, "an talqawhu" (that you meet it) is a substitute (badal) for "al-mawt" (death) in the grammatical category of badal ishtimal (a substitute that is related to what it replaces, by inclusion), meaning: you had wished for death, that you would meet it before this. It was also read as talaqawhu, from the form of mufa'alah, which occurs between two parties, and "what met you" and "you met it" are the same. It is also permissible that it is of the type of "safarta" (you travelled), and the pronoun refers to death. It has been said that it refers to the enemy, understood from the context, but this is not correct.

﴿then you have surely seen it﴾ means: what you wished for of death, by seeing its causes or its causes themselves. The fa' (fa' faṣīḥa, the "eloquent fa'," which signals an unstated condition) implies: as if it were said, "If you are truthful in your wish, then you have indeed seen it." The choice of "seeing" over "meeting" is either to indicate their flight, or to emphasise their witnessing of it, like the qualifying of this by His words, glorified is He: ﴿while you were looking on﴾. This is because it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees, meaning: you saw it while you were beholding it. This is in the manner of your saying: "I saw him, and there is no defect in my eye," meaning: I saw him with a real seeing, with no concealment in it and no doubt. It has been said that (tanẓurūna, "you look on") means "you contemplate and reflect," meaning: while you contemplate the situation, how it is. It has also been said that its meaning is "while you look on" at Muhammad (ﷺ). In every case, the purpose of this statement is to rebuke the fleeing ones

[Page 72]

for their wishing for martyrdom while they had not stood firm until they were martyred, or for their wishing for war and their causing it, then their cowardice and flight, not for the wish for martyrdom itself, because that is not something for which one is rebuked, as has been wrongly imagined.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 144 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Muhammad is nothing but a Messenger; messengers have passed away before him.﴾ It is narrated that when the two armies met on the day of Uhud and the fighting grew fierce, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Who will take this sword with its right and strike the enemy with it until it bends?" Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha al-Ansari took it. He then tied a red turban around his head and began to strut, saying:

I am the one whom my close friend pledged to me, while we were at the slope of al-Nahil:
that I would not stand in fetters for all time. ∗∗∗ I will strike with the sword of Allah and His Messenger.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, this is a gait that Allah and His Messenger detest, except in this situation." He then did not meet anyone without killing him. Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, also fought a severe battle until his sword was bent. Allah sent His help to the Muslims, and the polytheists turned their backs. When the archers saw the enemy in retreat and the Muslims plundering the spoils, they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), except for a few of them, and went down to the camp. When Khalid ibn al-Walid saw the scarcity of archers, the people busy with the spoils, and their backs left unguarded, he shouted to his cavalry among the polytheists and attacked the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from behind them with two hundred and fifty horsemen. They scattered them and killed about thirty men. Abdullah ibn Qami'a al-Harithi threw a stone at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which broke his front tooth and wounded his noble face. He then advanced intending to kill him, but Mus'ab ibn Umayr, the standard-bearer, may Allah be pleased with him, defended him until Ibn Qami'a killed him.

It is also said that the one who threw the stone was Utba ibn Abi Waqqas. He returned believing that he had killed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: "I have killed Muhammad." A crier cried out, whom no one knew, until it was said that he was Iblis: "Indeed, Muhammad has been killed!" So the people fell back, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began calling out: "To me, servants of Allah!" Thirty men gathered around him, protected him, and drove the polytheists away from him. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shot until the string of his bow snapped, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) handed him his quiver, saying: "Shoot, may my father and mother be your ransom." The hand of Talha ibn Ubaydullah was struck and became paralyzed. The eye of Qatada was dislodged until it fell onto his cheek; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put it back, and it returned as well as it had been before.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) withdrew, Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi caught up with him, saying: "You will not escape if you escape!" The people said: "O Messenger of Allah, should one of us not turn against him?" He said: "Leave him." When he drew near, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took a spear from al-Harith ibn al-Simma, then faced him and stabbed him in the neck, inflicting a scratch. He fell from his horse, bellowing like a bull, saying: "Muhammad has killed me." Before this, Ubayy used to meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and say: "I have a mare that I feed every day with a faraq of grain, and I will kill you on her back." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would reply: "Rather, I will kill you, if Allah wills." His companions carried him away and said: "There is no harm for you." He said: "Yes, indeed. If this blow had struck Rabi'a and Mudar, it would have killed them. Did he not say to me, 'I will kill you'? Had he spat on me after that statement, he would have killed me." He did not survive more than a day before he died at a place called Sarif.

When the news that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been killed spread among the people, some of the Muslims said: "If only we had a messenger to Abdullah ibn Ubayy, to obtain safe conduct for us from Abu Sufyan." Some of them sat down and laid down their arms. Some of the people of hypocrisy said: "If Muhammad has been killed, then return to your former religion." Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, said: "If Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad has not been killed. What is the point of living after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Fight for what he fought for, and die for what he died for." Then he said: "O Allah, I apologize to You for what these people have said, meaning the Muslims, and I disavow to You what these people have said, meaning the hypocrites." Then he drew his sword, fought until he was killed, may Allah be pleased with him.

[Page 73]

It is also narrated that the first person to recognize the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "I recognized his eyes beneath the helmet, shining, so I called out at the top of my voice: 'O assembly of Muslims, rejoice! This is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)!' He signaled to me: 'Be quiet.' A group of his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, gathered around him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) rebuked them for fleeing. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we ransom you with our fathers and sons. News reached us that you had been killed, so our hearts were terrified and we turned our backs.' Then Allah revealed this verse."

"Muhammad" is a proper name for our Prophet (ﷺ), derived linguistically from the passive participle of the doubled verb ḥammada. His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib named him this on the seventh day after his birth, because his father had died before that. When he was asked about this, he said, referring to a vision he had seen: "You hoped that he would be praised in the heavens and on earth." Its meaning before being transferred as a name is "one who is praised greatly," and its opposite is "Mudhammam" (the one who is censured). In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Have you not seen how Allah has turned away from me the curses and insults of the Quraysh? They revile Mudhammam, but I am Muhammad."

This noble name contains countless secrets, to the extent that it is said that it alludes to the number of the Prophets, just as it alludes to the Messengers among them, peace be upon them all. The Prophet (ﷺ) referred to himself by this name here because it is his first and most famous name, and it was by it that the crier cried out. It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows "illa" (except). There is agreement that "ma" (not) does not operate here, because its negation is annulled by "illa." Scholars differed over whether this restriction (qasr) is a qasr qalb (restriction by reversal, correcting a mistaken belief) or a qasr ifrad (restriction by singling out, excluding partners). Al-Allama al-Tibi and a group of scholars held that it is a qasr qalb, because the addressees, through their turning back on their heels when news of the Prophet's (ﷺ) death spread, behaved as though they believed that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not have the same status as the earlier Messengers, whose communities were obligated to follow their religion even after their deaths. Rather, they thought his case was different from theirs. Allah therefore rebuked them for this and clarified that the Prophet's (ﷺ) status is the same as that of the earlier Prophets, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them all: they died, and their followers remained holding fast to their religion and steadfast upon it. Thus the clause "messengers have passed away" (qad khalat) and what follows is a descriptive phrase modifying "Messenger," indicating that he (ﷺ) shares in the honor of having passed away. For the fact that his fellow Messengers passed away is a clear sign that he too will pass away, as if it were said: "Similar messengers have passed away before him, so he too will pass away just as they did." The restriction applies to this description, so it cannot be objected that a qasr qalb would imply that the addressees denied the Messengership, because that arises from forgetting the description.

It has also been said that the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to the pronoun in "Messenger," and the sense of restriction is the same.

Sahib al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki, author of Miftah al-'Ulum) held that it is a qasr ifrad, a restriction that excludes partners, departing from the apparent sense of the sentence by treating their great dismay at his not remaining as equal to their disbelief in and avoidance of it, as if they believed two attributes about him: Messengership and distance from death. So it is restricted to Messengership, denying distance from death. It has been objected that on this view, the clause "messengers have passed away" must be read as a separate statement explaining that he (ﷺ) is not distant from non-permanence like the other Messengers. For if the description is taken as the basis, the restriction can only be a qasr qalb, since the restriction falls on it. The objection notes that taking the clause as separate is remote, because it departs from the usual rule for clauses following indefinite nouns. It was answered that this is not necessary, since it is permissible for it to be a descriptive clause that also emphasizes the meaning of the restriction, placed after it in conception. Ibn Abbas read "rusul" (messengers) with indefiniteness (tanwin).

[Page 74]

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ The interrogative particle "hamza" is for denial, and the "fa" is either resumptive or merely indicates sequence. "Inqilab 'ala al-a'qab" (turning back on one's heels) originally means retreating backward, and here it is intended to mean apostasy and returning to the disbelief they were previously in, according to the well-known view. The purpose is to deny that they would apostatize from the religion upon his (ﷺ) passing by death or killing, given that they knew that the Messengers before him had passed away while their religion remained held fast. This was questioned: the Companions did not apostatize, so how can the expression "turning back on the heels," which normally implies that, be used? It was answered that the intended meaning is not literal apostasy but a severe rebuke for their flight and their withdrawal from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and for abandoning him to destruction. It was also said that the denial here means that this did not happen and should not happen, not a denial of what actually occurred. It was also said that it is a report about what happened to the people of apostasy after his death (ﷺ), and an allusion to the defeat that occurred, because of its resemblance to that.

Some scholars took "turning back" here to mean a decrease in faith, not disbelief after it, relying on what Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Zuhri, who said: "When this verse was revealed, 'that they may increase in faith along with their faith,' they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we know that faith increases; does it decrease?' He said: 'Yes, by Him who sent me with the truth, it does decrease.' They said: 'Is there any evidence for this in the Book of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾" And "turning back" is a decrease, not disbelief. It is not hidden that this report is not strong enough to be used as evidence, and I do not find in it the force of the sound hadiths.

Some of the view that the *fa'* (the particle "then") links the conditional sentence to the one before it, in the sense of causation, and the *hamza* (the interrogative particle) is for denying that. That is, it is not fitting for you to make the absence of the Messengers before him a cause for you to turn back on your heels after his death or his killing. Rather, make him a cause for holding fast to his religion, as is the rule for all the other Prophets, peace be upon them. Thus, turning back on your heels reverses the requirement of the established fact, which is that he is a Messenger who will pass away just as the Messengers before him passed away. The mention of death with the word *in* ("if"), though his death is certain, is to place the addressees in the position of those who are in doubt about it, because of their extreme dismay at it. The Master (al-Mawla) said: The situation is the same in all other instances, for the word *in* in the speech of God Most High does not operate on its apparent meaning at all, since God Most High knows with certainty whether something will occur or not. Rather, it is interpreted in light of the listener's condition, or in light of another matter that suits the context. By death is meant death on one's bed, and by killing is meant death through the destruction of the body. Death was mentioned first, although the mention of killing is what nearly brought about the great death, because death is more likely to occur, so deterring people from turning back at his death and keeping them steadfast then is more important. Also, the common attribute that truly joins him (ﷺ) and the Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, is death rather than killing. This differs from those who claimed it, arguing from what was reported about the poisoned meal at Khaybar, although killing and death did occur among them. He (God) mentioned killing, even though He knows that he would not be killed, because of the addressees' supposition about it. As for the verse ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾, if it was revealed before Uhud, it is possible that it did not reach those fleeing defeat, and even if it reached them, it is possible that it would not be present in their minds in such a terrifying situation. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, forgot this verse on the day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died.

Abu Hurayrah narrated that he (may God be pleased with him) stood up that day and said: "Some hypocrites claim that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has died. By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not die, but he has gone to his Lord just as Musa ibn 'Imran went, for he was absent from his people for forty nights, then he returned to them after it was said: 'He has died.' By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) will return just as Musa returned. Let him cut off the hands and feet of men who claim that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has died." Then Abu Bakr came out and said: "Gently, O 'Umar, be silent." He praised God and extolled Him, then said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, Muhammad has died. And whoever used to worship God Most High, God Most High is living and does not die." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And Muhammad is not but a Messenger...﴾ to its end. By God, it was as if people did not know that this verse had been revealed until Abu Bakr recited it that day, and the people took it from Abu Bakr. 'Umar said: "By God, it was only when I heard Abu Bakr recite it that I was stunned, until I fell to the ground, my legs not carrying me, and I knew that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had died."

As for the excuse that the understanding of the verse of protection is restricted to the scholars among the Companions and those of insight among them, despite the apparent meaning of the wording, as al-Zamakhshari offered as an excuse, there is much wrong with it. And the claim that its intended meaning is protection from people's temptation and misguidance is clearly far-fetched, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is not suspected of that; such wording is only used in the context of stirring up and admonition. ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels, he will not harm God﴾ by what he has done of turning back, because God Most High cannot be harmed at all, even slightly. He only harms himself by exposing himself to wrath and punishment, or by depriving himself of greater reward. The negation being directed at the object indicates this, for it implies that he harms someone other than God Most High, but there is no one other than himself. ﴿And God will reward the grateful﴾ (144), that is, He will reward those who remain steadfast in the religion of Islam. The expression "the grateful" is used in place of "the steadfast," because steadfastness in that arises from certainty of its truth, and that is gratitude for it. In this there is an allusion to the ingratitude of those who turned back. 'Ali, may God honor his face, also interpreted "the grateful" as "the steadfast," and Ibn Jarir narrated it from him. He used to say: "The steadfast are Abu Bakr and his companions." Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, is the leader of the grateful. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the intended ones are the obedient among the Emigrants and the Helpers. The explicit mention of the majestic Name in place of a pronoun is to declare the greater care for the matter of their reward. The connection of this with what precedes it is the connection of promise with threat.

Page 75

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 145 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to urge (hadd) toward jihad and to censure abandoning it out of fear of being killed, while completely cutting off the excuse of those who fled out of such fear. It is also possible that it is a consolation for what befell the people by the death of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and an indication that he, peace be upon him, like others, does not die except by the permission of Allah the Exalted, so there is no excuse for anyone to abandon his religion after his death.

By "soul" (nafs) is meant the species, and restricting it to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as narrated from Ibn Ishaq, is "nothing" (laysa bi-shay'). "Death" (al-mawt) here is more general than death by natural causes (hatf al-anf) and death by killing, as we will verify. The verb "kana" (was) is defective (naqisah), its subject is "an tamuta" (that it die), and "li-nafsin" (for a soul) is attached to an omitted element that falls as its predicate. The exception is an exceptive construction (mufarragh) from the most general of causes.

Abu al-Baqa' held that "bi-idhni Allah" (by the permission of Allah) is the predicate of kana, and "li-nafsin" is attached to it, with the lam being for specification (lil-tabyin). It is transmitted from some of them that the prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element whose estimate is "the death for a soul," and "an tamuta" is an explanation of the omitted element. It is related from al-Zajjaj and some from al-Akhfash that the estimate is: "And it was not a soul to die," then the lam was moved forward. All these opinions are weaker than weakness itself, especially the last. The meaning is: death did not occur to any soul among souls, absolutely, through any of the causes, except by the will of Allah the Exalted and His facilitation. "Permission" (idhn) is a metaphor for that, because it is one of its necessary consequences. The apparent structure of the sentence indicates that death is among the acts that one undertakes by choice, as it is commonly said, "It was not for Zayd to do such-and-such," when that act is voluntary. But the apparent meaning here is set aside, by taking this as an illustration: that the forms of death in relation to souls are like a voluntary act which is not undertaken except with permission.

The intended meaning is the inability to do it, or by treating the undertaking of souls toward its beginnings, such as fighting for example, as equivalent to undertaking it itself, for the sake of emphasis in establishing the aim. For since its death is impossible to occur when it undertakes it or its beginnings and strives to bring it about, then it is all the more impossible and clearer when that is absent. It is also possible on this view that "permission" remains in its literal sense, with its object omitted because it is known. The intended meaning, "by His permission, the Exalted," is His permission to the Angel of Death, for he is the one who seizes the spirit of every living being, human or not, martyr or not, on land or at sea. So much so that it is said: he seizes the spirit of his own self. Some excepted the spirits of martyrs of the sea, for Allah the Exalted Himself seizes them without intermediary, and he relied on the hadith of Juwaybir, which is very weak, and in its chain from the route of al-Dahhak there is a break in transmission. The Mu'tazilah held that the Angel of Death seizes only the spirits of the two groups (jinn and humans) and not others. Some innovators said: he seizes all, except the spirits of animals, for his assistants are those who seize them. There is no contradiction between "Allah seizes the souls at the time of their death" (39:42), "The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you" (32:11), and "Our messengers take him" (6:61), because the attribution of that to Him, the Exalted, is by way of true creation and origination, to the angel because he is the one who directly performs it, and to the messengers because they are his assistants who labor at extraction from the sinews, bones, flesh and veins.

"Kitaban" (a decree) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing its verb, derived from the preceding clause. The meaning: that death which was permitted was decreed as a decree, "mu'ajjalan" (specified), i.e. determined by a known time that neither advances nor delays. It was said: a binding, firm ruling, and it is an adjective of "kitaban." Describing it does not harm the fact that the masdar is emphatic, on the basis that it is known from what preceded; and not every adjective goes out of the category of emphasis. You may, however, because of the obscurity in that, make the masdar, with its adjective, specifying the type, and this is better than making it emphatic. "Mu'ajjalan" was taken as a circumstantial state (hal) of "al-mawt" (death), not an adjective of it, due to the extreme remoteness of that. So reflect.

"Mu'ajjalan" was also read with waw in place of hamza, according to the rule of easing. The apparent meaning of the verse supports the position of the People of the Sunnah, who say that the one who is killed has died at his term (ajal), meaning at his appointed time, and that had he not been killed he could have died at that time, or not died, without certainty of extension of life, nor of death instead of killing; for on the assumption of no killing there is no certainty of the existence or non-existence of the term, so there is no certainty of death nor of life. The Mu'tazilah disagreed on this. Al-Ka'bi among them held that the one who is killed is not dead, because killing is the act of the servant and death is the act of Allah, Glorified be He, meaning His product and the effect of His attribute; and that the one killed has two terms: one is killing and the other is death; and that had he not been killed he would have lived until his term, which is death. Abu al-Hudhayl held that had the one killed not been killed, he would have died absolutely at that time.

The majority held that the killer has cut short the term of the one killed, and that had he not been killed he would have lived until a limit which is his term, the one at which Allah knew his death would be were it not for the killing. The dispute between the Companions (Ash'arites) and the majority is not verbal, as the Ustadh (Ustadh Abu Ishaq) and many of the verifiers saw, where they said: if the term is the time of the cessation of life in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, then the one killed is dead at his term without any dispute from the Mu'tazilah in that, for they do not deny that the one killed is dead by the term which Allah knew, namely the term by means of killing. And if the cessation of life is restricted to not being consequent upon an act of the servant, then it is not so, with no dispute from the Companions in that, for they hold that the one killed is not dead at a term other than that consequent upon the servant's act. We say: the essence of the dispute is that what is meant by the term of the one killed, as an attribute, is the time of the cessation of his life such that there is no escape from it, nor any advance or delay, as His saying the Exalted indicates: "When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it" (16:61 / 7:34). The disagreement returns to whether this has been realized in the case of the one killed, or whether what is known in his case is that if he is killed he dies, and if he is not killed he lives. Thus in Sharh al-Maqasid. Perhaps this is an answer by choosing the first alternative, which is that what is meant is the time of the cessation of life in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, but not absolutely; rather according to what He knew and decreed by way of certainty. Then it is suitable as a locus of dispute, for it does not follow from the non-realization of that in the one killed, as the Mu'tazilah say, a divergence of knowledge from the known, since it is possible that his death by killing is known to precede while the term which cannot diverge from it is later. It may be said that it is possible this is an answer by choosing a third alternative, namely what is determined by way of certainty, since in stating the answer there is no reference to knowledge; and what is determined is more specific than the known term in general, and the difference between it and being an answer by choosing the first is that the condition of knowledge is considered in the term which is the locus of dispute on the assumption of choosing the first, and not considered in it on the assumption of choosing the third, though it is known in reality as well. So understand.

Then Abu al-Husayn and those who follow him claim necessity (darurah) in this question, and so too the majority in the view of some; and according to others it is, for them, an inferential (istidlaliyyah) matter.

They argued for their position by the hadiths reported that some acts of obedience increase one's lifespan, and by the argument that had the one killed died at his term, the killer would not deserve blame or punishment, nor would retaliation be incumbent upon him, nor the payment of blood-money, nor value in slaughtering another's sheep; for he has not cut short a term, nor brought about death by his act. And that perhaps thousands are killed in a battle or war, while custom makes it impossible that all of them die at that time by their terms. Abu al-Hudhayl relied on the argument that had the one killed not died, the killer would be cutting short a term that Allah decreed and changing a matter that He knew, which is impossible. Al-Ka'bi relied on the saying of Allah: "Then if he dies or is killed" (3:144), where He made killing a counterpart to death, on the basis that by killing is meant the state of being killed, and that this is the very cessation of life, and that death is specific to what is not in the manner of killing; and whenever death is other than killing, the one killed has two terms: one is killing and the other is death.

As for the argument of the first group, the first point is answered: those hadiths are solitary reports (akhbar ahad), so they do not oppose definitive verses such as His saying the Exalted: "When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it." Or it is answered that what is meant by obedience increasing lifespan is that it increases in what is the chief aim of it, namely the acquisition of perfections and goods and blessings by which human souls are perfected and attain everlasting happiness. Or that lifespan (umr) is other than term (ajal), for linguistically it means time, and the term of a thing is said of its whole duration and of its last part, as one says "the term of the debt is two months" or "the end of such-and-such month." Then its use became prevalent for the end of the duration of life, and from here it is explained as the time at which Allah the Exalted knew the cessation of the animal's life, as we have established.

Lifespan (umr) linguistically is the duration of life, as in "the lifespan of Zayd is such-and-such," and the duration of remaining, as in "the lifespan of the world." It is very often used figuratively for the duration of the persistence of people's remembrance of a person for good after his death. From this is the saying: "The remembrance of a young man is his second lifespan." From here it is said of one who has died and left a good reputation and a beautiful trace: "He has not died." Perhaps he, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, meant that those acts of obedience increase this lifespan, because they are a cause of good remembrance; and this is most often reported regarding charity and maintaining ties of kinship, and that these two are among what brings about the praise of people, which is beyond doubt. It is said: for this reason he, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, did not say in that case that it increases the term (ajal). Or it is answered that Allah the Exalted knew that this obedient person, had he not performed this act of obedience, would have had a lifespan of, say, forty years, but He knew he would perform it and his lifespan would be seventy years. So the attribution of this increase to that obedience is based on Allah's knowledge that without it this increase would not exist. The summary of this is that He, Glorified be He, decreed his lifespan as seventy in such a way that advance or delay from it is not conceivable, given His knowledge that his obedience would become a cause of thirty years, so that with forty years from non-obedience it becomes seventy. The summary of this is not that He decreed it seventy on one condition and forty on another, so as to entail a multiplicity of terms; and the Companions do not hold that.

The second answer: that the obligation of blame and punishment, or the incurring of retaliation or the payment of blood-money for example upon the killer, is not something established in the locus from death; rather it is by what he has acquired and committed of undertaking a forbidden act, which Allah the Exalted makes a means of death, as in all other causes and effects, especially when signs of survival are apparent and what would make the arrival of the term seem likely is absent. Even if the death of a sheep were known by the report of a truthful, infallible informant, or the signs producing certainty appeared, then according to some jurists he would not be liable.

The third answer: that custom is also broken by the occurrence of the death of thousands at one time without fighting or warfare, as in times of plague for example; moreover that

The Ka'bi (Abu al-Ka'bi) ... ? No, I will proceed with the translation.

Relying on this kind of proof for this kind of question is utterly untenable. As for the argument of Abu al-Hudhayl (Abu al-Hudhayl al-'Allaf), it is answered by saying that the non-occurrence of killing is only conceivable on the supposition of God's knowledge that he will not be killed. In that case, we do not concede that an impossibility follows. It is also answered that there is no impossibility in the cutting short of a predetermined term (ajal) that would have been fixed had there been no killing, since this is a confirmation of what is known, not a change of it. As for the argument of al-Ka'bi, who opposed the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilah) and the Ash'ariyyah (Ash'ariyyah) in affirming two terms, it is answered that killing subsists in the killer and is an attribute of him, not of the one killed. What befalls the one killed is death and the departure of the soul, which is by God's bringing into being, permission, and will, together with the state of being-killed (maqtuliyyah) that arises from the killer's act of killing, and this is the state of the one killed, since it is the cessation of life. Specification by what is not in the manner of killing is also implied by this.

﴿Then if he dies or is killed﴾. This contradicts his school, which denies qada' (divine decree) and qadar (divine measure) in the acts of servants, since the cessation of life resulting from the killer's killing is a term (ajal) that God has decreed, determined, and fixed. The meaning of the verse, as we have indicated, is: "Then if he dies of his own accord without any cause, or dies by the cause of killing." It indicates that the mere cessation of life is death. From this it has been said that in the one killed there are two meanings: killing, which is from the act of the agent, and dying, which is from God alone.

The philosophers (falasifah) went the same way as al-Ka'bi regarding the multiplicity of terms. They said: for the living being there is a natural term (ajal tabi'i) through the dissolution of its moisture and the extinction of its innate heat, and there are also premature terms (ajal ikhtiramiyyah) which multiply with the multiplicity of countless causes, such as diseases and calamities. Its explanation: the bodies in which the moist parts predominate are composed with the innate heat, and it becomes for them like oil for the burning wick. Whenever those moistures are diminished, the innate heat follows them in that, until, when the diminution reaches its end and dryness increases, the heat is extinguished, like the extinguishing of a lamp when its oil runs out. Thus natural death occurs. It varies according to the differences of temperaments, and in humans it is, for the most part, a full one hundred and twenty years.

Calamities may befall, such as freezing cold that congeals, heat that melts, various kinds of poisons, various kinds of separation of connection, and bad temperament, which corrupt the body and take it out of its soundness for accepting life, since its condition is the balance of temperament. So it perishes because of this, and this is the premature term. This is refuted because it is built upon their principles of the influence of nature and temperament, and this is false according to us, since there is no influence except His, glorified be He. Those matters, according to us, are customary causes (asbab 'adiyyah), not rational causes as they claimed.

Some researchers have claimed that the dispute between us and the philosophers is like the dispute between us and the Mu'tazilah, according to the view of the master (al-Ustadh), that it is verbal (lafzi). For they do not deny qada' and qadar. The time at which God knows the cessation of life, by whatever cause, is one time for them too. And what they mention of the natural term, we also do not deny. But they make the balance of temperament, the soundness of heat and moisture, and the like, into real rational conditions for the continuation of life, whereas we make them customary causes. That is another discussion, and the completion of the discussion on this question will come, for affairs are held in pledge to their appointed times, and for every term there is a Book.

﴿And whoever desires﴾, that is, by his deed, such as jihad, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, such as spoils of war, ﴿We will give him﴾ with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), ﴿of it﴾, that is, some of its reward, if We will. It is in accordance with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾. This is an allusion to those whom the spoils distracted on the day of Uhud from the interest of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and its detail has already been mentioned.

﴿And whoever desires﴾, that is, by his deed, also such as jihad and defending the Messenger of God (ﷺ),
﴿the reward of the Hereafter﴾, of what God, exalted be He, has prepared for His servants therein of bliss, ﴿We will give him of it﴾, that is, of its reward what We will, according to what the gracious promise has decreed. This is an indication of praise for those who stood firm with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on that day. And the verse, although it was revealed specifically concerning jihad, is general in all deeds.

﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾ (145). It may be that by them are meant those who desire the Hereafter, and it may be that by them is meant the category of the grateful, who enter it in the first instance.

The sentence is a concluding addition (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it and a promise of increase upon it. In beginning it with the sin (the future particle) and leaving the reward indefinite, there is emphasis and an indication of the grandeur of the reward's status, and that it is such that the scope of explanation falls short of it, which is not hidden. By this the joining of the two worships in regard to the two groups is made complete, and the difference becomes clear to one who has two eyes. The three verbs have also been read with the ya' (third person).

* * *

This (and by way of allusion): ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba, doubled and redoubled﴾. This is either an allusion to the command to put trust in God, exalted be He, in seeking sustenance and to turn wholly to Him, or a symbol of the command to do good to the needy servants of God without seeking benefit from them. For it has been reported in some narrations that "a loan is better than charity." Or it is a hint at not seeking a reward for deeds, by doing them purely to manifest servitude.

﴿And fear God﴾ from consuming riba, ﴿that you may succeed﴾, that is, that you may win the truth.

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, that is, fear Me regarding the Fire, for its burning and its punishment are from Me. This is the secret of the unity of the unity (sirr 'ayn al-jam'). They said: in reality it returns to the manifestation of the manifestation of Majesty (taajjli al-qahr), and it is, in its outward sense, a warning for the common folk, while the first warning is for the elite, and they are few.

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾, which is the covering of your acts, which are your greatest veil from seeing the Truth, ﴿and a garden whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, which is the garden of the unity of acts, which is the unity of the world of dominion (malakut). Therefore He, glorified be He, mentioned the heavens and the earth, and mentioned the width without the length, because acts, considered in the horizontal chain, which makes each act depend upon another act, are confined to the world of dominion that human understandings reach and estimate. But considered in length, they are not confined to it, and its measure cannot be estimated, for the act is the locus of manifestation of the attribute, the attribute is the locus of manifestation of the essence, and the essence has no end and no limit.

﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure﴾. So those veiled from the Essence and the Attributes see only this garden, while those who have emerged for the One, the Subduer, the width of their garden is the very same as its length, and there is no limit to its length, so its measure cannot be estimated in length or in width. ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾: He veiled their acts and left the attribution of acts to other than the Truth, majestic is His majesty. It is also possible that He, glorified be He, called His creation, according to the differences of their ranks, to doing what leads to forgiveness according to the differences of its ranks, for sin varies. The sin of the infallible is lack of knowledge of his Lord, in view of the greatness of His beauty and majesty in the reality of the matter.

It is reported from the master of the knowers (ﷺ): "Glory be to You, we did not know You with the true knowledge of You." So the knowers did not know Him from the standpoint of what He is, but they knew Him from the standpoint of what they are, and there is a difference between the two knowledges. For this reason it has been said: "None knows God except God."

He also called them to what draws them to the Garden. If the address is to the knowers, it is a call to the very unity of union, so that He may manifest Himself to them through intermediaries, for their remaining in knowledge. In reality, His knowledge is His nearness, and His Garden is the contemplation of Him, and in the reality of realities it is the Essence, the Gathering, which strangers cannot reach. For this reason it has been said: "There is nothing in the Garden but God." If the address is considered with respect to individual believers, then by it is meant the kinds of beautiful manifestations, or their outward aspect which the language of the Shari'ah has made clear. Their call to it is by way of education and drawing human souls, which have not yet been weaned from suckling the breast of pleasures, to what makes them desire the acquisition of human perfections and ascent to the summit of divine ascensions. Those are the ones who spend the precious things of their souls for their Master in ease and hardship, in the states of beauty and majesty. It is also possible that what is meant is those whom contrary states do not prevent from spending in what pleases God, exalted be He, because of the soundness of their trust in Him, glorified be He, through seeing all acts as from Him.

﴿And those who restrain anger﴾, which arises in a person according to human nature, and their restraint of it may be by binding it with the cord of submission and contentment. This is with regard to one who is in the station of the Garden of Attributes. As for those below them, their restraint is less than this restraint,
[Page 80]
and the cause of restraint is that they see the offense against them as the act of God, exalted be He, and creatures have no part in it.

﴿And those who pardon people﴾, either because they are in the station of the unity of acts, or because they are in the station of the unity of attributes.

﴿And God loves the doers of good﴾, according to their ranks in goodness. ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾, that is, a grave sin among the major sins, which is seeing their own acts that are forbidden to them, like the prohibition on looking at non-mahram women with desire, ﴿or wrong themselves﴾ by diminishing their rights and holding back from perfecting them, ﴿remember God﴾, that is, they recall His greatness and know that there is no real doer besides Him, ﴿and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾, that is, they seek the covering of their acts from them by disavowing power and strength except through God. ﴿And who forgives sins﴾, which is seeing acts, or looking at all other things, ﴿except God﴾, who is the Great King whom nothing can magnify beyond Himself. ﴿And they do not persist in what they did﴾ in their heedlessness and their diminishing the right of their souls, ﴿while they know﴾ the reality of the matter and that there is no doer but Him. ﴿Those, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord﴾, which is His covering them, as they exist through His existence and ascend from the station of the unity of acts to what is above it. ﴿And gardens﴾, that is, hidden things, which are the gardens of the unseen and orchards of contemplation and nearness, which are the springs of the attributes of the Essence. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is, from them flow rivers of eternal attributes. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ without staying or cutting off, and without the passage of time, and without the veil of place, and without change. ﴿And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾. Among them are those who stand, with the condition of fidelity in love, upon the ancient presence, without breaking covenants and without forgetfulness in witnessing.

﴿Indeed there have passed before you examples﴾, that is, punishments and events, concerning those who denied the prophets in calling them to monotheism. ﴿So travel﴾ with your thoughts ﴿in the earth and observe﴾ and reflect upon their traces, so that you may know ﴿how was the end of those who denied﴾, that is, their final outcome and their ultimate fate, which denial had invited. It may also be that this is a command to the souls to look at the traces of the soul's powers that are in the earth of nature, so that it may know what befell them and how their state ended, so that perhaps by this it may rise from the lowest point of attachment to them. ﴿This﴾, that is, the speech of God, exalted be He, ﴿is a clarification for mankind﴾, clarifying for them the realities of the affairs of both worlds, ﴿and guidance and an admonition﴾ by which one reaches the Divine Presence, ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, who are the people of God and His elect.

The state varies according to the variance of the readiness of the listeners to the speech. For among them are a people who hear it with the ears of the intellects, and among them a people who hear it with the ears of the secrets. The share of the first is compliance and taking admonition, while the share of the latter is, in addition to that, unveiling and contemplation of the lights. The Truth has manifested Himself in it to the elect of His servants and the near ones of the people of His election, so they witnessed lights manifesting, an eternal attribute beyond the world of letters that are recited.

﴿And do not weaken﴾, that is, do not be feeble in jihad, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over what escaped you of victory and what afflicted you of the killing of brethren, ﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾ in rank, ﴿if you are believers﴾, that is, monotheists, since the monotheist sees all as from his Master, so the least of his degrees is patience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 145 (part 3 of 3):

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched that people.﴾ Yet they did not falter, even though they were inferior to you. ﴿And these are the days; We alternate them among the people﴾, that is, the battles: one day for one group and another day for another. ﴿That Allah may know those who believe﴾, that is, that His detailed knowledge, which follows the occurrence of the known thing, may become manifest. ﴿And that He may take martyrs from among you﴾, and they are those who witness the truth and are thereby oblivious of themselves. ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who wronged themselves, wasted their rights, and did not perfect their upbringing.

﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾, that is, to cleanse them from sins and the veils which keep them away from Allah the Exalted, through punishment and affliction. ﴿And destroy﴾, that is, annihilate ﴿the disbelievers﴾ with the fire of their egoism.

﴿Or did you think﴾ that you would enter Paradise, that is, enter the world of holiness? ﴿While Allah has not yet known those of you who strive and known the steadfast﴾, that is, there has not yet appeared from you striving which bequeaths witnessing, and patience in purifying the souls and clarifying the hearts in accordance with the Shariah and the law of the Path, so that the lights of the Reality may be manifested to the spirits.

﴿And you certainly wished for death﴾, that is, the death of the souls from their attributes ﴿before you met it﴾ through striving and spiritual exercises ﴿and now you have seen it﴾ by seeing its causes, which is war with the enemies of Allah the Exalted ﴿while you were looking on﴾, that is, you knew that this striving is one of its causes: the death of the soul from its attributes. It may also be said: when the one who has certainty does not possess his certainty as a state, he wishes for things and claims conditions, until, when he is tested, there appears from him what contradicts his claim and opposes his wish. Hence it was said:

"And when the coward is alone in a land, he seeks the spear-thrust and the duel for himself alone."

But when that certainty becomes firm and established, becoming a faculty and a station rather than a passing state, the matter does not differ for him at the time of testing. The verse alludes to rebuking the fleeing, that their certainty was a state and not a station.

﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾, that is, he is a human being like his brothers among the messengers; just as they passed away before him, he too will pass away after them. ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ and return to the rear. The allusion in this is that Allah the Exalted rebuked those who were shaken by the departure of the great intermediary from among them, and this is incompatible with witnessing the truth and beholding it. Hence the Greatest Truthful one (al-Siddiq al-Akbar), may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has died; and whoever used to worship Allah the Exalted, then Allah the Exalted is living and does not die." ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾ because of His essential self-subsistence ﴿and Allah will reward the thankful﴾ with true faith, ﴿those who are thankful﴾ with conventional faith, by fulfilling its rights: obeying the commands of the Shariah and refraining from its prohibitions. ﴿And it was not for a soul to die﴾ this known death, or the death from its base attributes and vile morals ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾ and His will, or His drawing it by the radiance of His light. ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ according to the capacity of his preparedness ﴿We will give him thereof﴾ as wisdom requires ﴿and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter﴾ as recompense for his deed ﴿We will give him thereof, and We will reward the thankful.﴾ Perhaps these are the ones who desired neither reward, and had no aim except servitude; He left their recompense unspecified to indicate that it is a matter beyond expression, and perhaps it is the manifestation of the Truth to them. This is the ultimate wish of the lovers and the final goal of the seekers. We ask Allah the Exalted for His pleasure and His success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 146 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And how many⦆ is an independent statement, brought as a rebuke to the defeated as well, since they did not follow the ways of the godly (rabbaniyyun) who fought alongside the messengers, peace be upon them, although they were more deserving of this, since they were "the best community brought forth for mankind."

The word has been disputed. It has been said that it is a simple (basit) word, formed this way from the start, with the nun being original (asliyyah). Ibn Hayyan and others adopted this view, and on it the matter is clear and agrees with the orthography. It has also been said, and this is the well-known view, that it is compound (murakkabah), made up of ʾayyin (with tanwin) and the kaf of comparison. Regarding this ʾayyin there is disagreement. It has been said that it is the ʾayy found in the expression ʾayyu al-rijal ("which of the men"). Ibn Jinni said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of awa, yaʾwi, meaning to gather and come together, and its original form was awyin. The waw and the ya' came together, one of them was preceded by a sukun, so it was changed and assimilated, like tayyin and shayyin. After the compounding, a meaning of multiplicity arose in it, which is understood from kam, just as another meaning arose in kadha after compounding. Thus kam and ka'ayyin have one meaning.

They said: it shares five features with kam: indefiniteness (ibham), need for a specifier (tamyiz), indeclinability (bina'), obligatory initial position (luzum al-taslir), and the expression of multiplicity, which is the usual use. It also shares interrogation, which is rare, and only Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Usfur and Ibn Malik affirmed this. It is cited as evidence the statement of Ubayy ibn Ka'b to Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with both of them: "Ka'ayyin you recite a verse of Surat al-Ahzab?" He said: "Seventy-three." 

It differs from kam in five respects as well. First, it is compound according to the well-known view, whereas kam is simple according to it, contrary to those who claimed it is compound from the kaf and the interrogative ma, and then its alif was deleted because of the entry of a preposition, and it was made sakin for lightness because the word is heavy through compounding. Second, its specifier is generally in the genitive with min. Ibn Usfur even claimed that this is obligatory, but Sibawayh's explicit statement that it is not obligatory refutes this. Among the examples is his saying:

"Drive away despair with hope, for many a one pained, whose ease came after hardship."

Third, it is not used interrogatively according to the majority. Fourth, it is not used in the genitive, contrary to Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Usfur, who permitted "bi-ka'ayyin tabi'u al-thawb" (with ka'ayyin you sell the garment).

Fifth, its predicate does not occur as a singular noun. They said that between it and kadha there is agreement and disagreement too. Kadha agrees with it in four respects: composition, indeclinability, indefiniteness, and need for a specifier. It differs from it in three respects. The first is that kadha does not have the initial position; you say "qabadtu kadha wa kadha dirhaman" (I received such and such dirhams). The second is that its specifier must be in the accusative, so it is not permitted to put it in the genitive with min by agreement, nor with an idafah (construct), contrary to the Kufans, who permitted, without repetition or conjunction, that one says "kadha thawbin wa kadha athwab" (such and such a garment, and such and such garments), by analogy with the explicit number. For this reason their jurists said: if someone says to another "I owe you kadha dirham mi'a" (such and such dirham hundred), or "kadha dirham thalatha" (such and such dirham three), or "kadha kadha dirhaman ahada 'ashar" (such and such, such and such dirhams eleven), or "kadha dirham 'ishrun" (such and such dirham twenty), or "kadha wa kadha dirham ahad wa 'ishrun" (such and such, such and such dirham twenty-one), he is held liable for the determined amount, by analogy with the explicit numbers. Apart from the two issues of the idafah, al-Mubarrad, al-Akhfash, al-Sirafi and Ibn Usfur agreed with them on this detail. Ibn al-Sayyid erred in claiming a consensus on permitting what al-Mubarrad and those mentioned with him permitted. The third is that kadha is generally not used except coordinated with another, as in his saying:

"Count the soul favours after your misery, remembering such and such, with kindness, through which the hardship was forgotten."

Ibn Kharuf claimed that they did not say "kadha dirham," but Ibn Malik mentioned that it is attested though rare, as Ibn Hisham said.

Furthermore, the retention of the tanwin of ka'ayyin, according to the well-known view, both in pausal pronunciation and in writing, is contrary to analogy, since it reverses its original form. The word has several dialectal forms, and all of them have been read in the Qur'an. The first is ka'ayyin with shadda (doubling) on the original basis, and this is the well-known form, and the majority of reciters read with it. The second is ka'in, with an alif after it, followed by a kasra-marked hamza without a ya', on the pattern of kahin, like the active participle. Ibn Kathir read with it, and among its examples is his saying:

"And many a one has shown us favour and bounty over you in the past, and you do not know who the benefactor is."

Its interpretation has been disputed. According to al-Mubarrad it is an active participle of kana yakunu, but this is hardly correct, since there is then no reason for it to be indeclinable, nor for it to express multiplicity. It has also been said that its original form is the doubled form, and the doubled ya' was placed before the hamza, and it became ka-ya'in, with a fatha-marked kaf and ya', a kasra-marked hamza, and a nun. Its pattern is like 'alaf. A parallel to this kind of alteration in the single word is what they do with the compound, as occurs in a rare dialect, ra'milî for la'amri (by my life), with the ra' placed before the lam. Then the first ya' was deleted for lightness, and the second was changed into an alif because it was vowelled and the preceding letter was open. Or the second ya' was deleted because it was heavy through the vowel and the doubling, and the sakin ya' was changed into an alif, as in ayah (sign). A parallel to this, in deleting one of the two ya's and changing the other into an alif, is the Ta'i form in the relative adjective of Tayy, the name of a tribe, for its original form is tayyi'i with two doubled ya's with a hamza between them. One of the two ya's was deleted and the other changed.

The third form is ka-'ay, with a ya' after the hamza, and it was read by Ibn Muhaysin. Its basis is that the second ya' was deleted and the hamza made sakin, because the two words became mixed and treated as one word, just as they made the ha' sakin in lahw and fahw. The ya' was given a vowel because the letter before it was sakin.

The fourth is ka-yi'in, with a sakin ya' followed by a kasra-marked hamza. The fifth is ka'in with a fatha-marked kaf, a kasra-marked hamza, and a nun. Its pattern is ka'i'. This occurs in his saying:

"Among a friend whom I thought sincere in brotherhood, whose testing revealed that he is a flatterer."

Its basis is that one of the two ya's was deleted, and then the other was deleted for the tanwin, or both were deleted at once. This is possible when the two letters have merged and the kaf has no governing element, because it has left its meaning. Whoever said this, such as al-Hufi, went too far.

Its place is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). And the saying of God, ﴿from a prophet⦆, is a specifier (tamyiz) of it, like the specifier of kam. This has been discussed a moment ago. Perhaps the intended meaning of the prophet here is the messenger, and al-Tabarsi stated this explicitly.

﴿There fought alongside him many rabbiyyun⦆ means large crowds. This is the well-known interpretation from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them. He cited as evidence, as narrated by Ibn al-Anbari, when Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him, the verse of Hassan:

"And when a group turns away from the goal, we have set upon them rabbiyy."

On this basis it is related to rabbah with a kasra on the ra'. That the damma is a dialectal form is not established, and it means a group, and for emphasis. Al-Dahhak restricted it to the alif. Sa'id ibn Mansur reported from al-Hasan that they are the scholars and jurists. Ibn Jubayr also reported it from Ibn Abbas, and on this basis it is related to al-Rabb, like rabbani, contrary to analogy, like the damma reading. The reading that corresponds to it is the fatha, and it has been read with it.

Ibn Zayd said: the rabbiyyun are the followers and the rabbaniyyun are the rulers. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read qutila with the passive form. In the predicate of the subject there are several possibilities. The first is that it is the verb with the implicit pronoun in it, referring to ka'ayyin or to nabi, and in that case "ma'ahu rabbiyyun" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah) relating to the pronoun, or to nabi, because it is specified in meaning, or "ma'ahu" is a circumstantial element (hal), and rabbiyyun is its subject.

The second is that it is the clause "ma'ahu rabbiyyun," and in this case the verbal clause with its nominative element is an adjective of nabi.

The third is that it is elided, and its estimated form is "mada" (passed) or something similar. In that case the verb may be an adjective of nabi and "ma'ahu rabbiyyun" a circumstantial element as stated before, and the verb may also be ascribed to rabbiyyun, so there is no pronoun in it, and the clause is an adjective of nabi.

The fourth is that rabbiyyun is in the nominative by the verb, so there is no pronoun, and the clause is the predicate.

It is also read qutthila with shadda. Ibn Jinni said: in that case there is no pronoun in the verb, because doubling carries the meaning of multiplicity, which is incompatible with ascribing it to one person. It was answered that there is no impediment to its having the pronoun of the first, because it has the meaning of a group. It was objected that this is contrary to the apparent sense. From here it has been said that this reading supports ascribing qutila to the rabbiyyun, and what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jubayr also supports it, that he used to say: "We have never heard that a prophet was killed in battle." And the saying of al-Hasan and a group: "No prophet was ever killed in war." Then, whoever claims that the killing is ascribed to the prophet, and that it was also in war, as the context suggests, takes the help promised in the saying of God, ﴿Indeed We shall help Our messengers⦆, to mean help through raising up the word and the like, not help against enemies absolutely, so that the two verses do not contradict. This is one of the answers in this context, the indication of which was given earlier, so recall it. The tanwin in nabi is for exaltation. Al-Jahhuri claimed that it is for multiplicity.

﴿So they did not falter⦆ is coordinated with "qatalu" (fought), on the basis that what is meant is the absence of the faltering expected from fighting, and persistence in a matter after what calls for the opposite has occurred. Although it is continuation in appearance, in reality it is, as our master Shaykh al-Islam said, a new act. From here the particle fa' is correct, indicating that what follows is a consequence of what precedes. Among this is their saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed," and "I rebuked him, but he did not desist." The root meaning of wahn is weakness. Qatada and Ibn Abi Malik explained it here as incapacity, and al-Zajjaj as cowardice, that is, "they were not incapacitated" or "they were not cowardly."

﴿For what befell them in the way of God⦆ means in the course of the fighting. This is a cause for the negated, not for the negation. Yes, the negated is understood from restricting the affirmed by this adverbial phrase. "Ma" is a relative (mawsulah) or a qualifier (mawsufah). If the two pronouns are taken to refer to all the rabbiyyun, it is an expression for what is other than killing, of the hardships of war that affect all. If they are taken to refer to the remaining ones after the others were killed, which is the more fitting, as it has been said, in the context of rebuking those who gave up after the martyrs were martyred, then it is also an expression of that, together with what befell them after the killing of their brothers, such as fear and sorrow. This is according to the well-known reading. As for the two other readings, namely qutila and qutthila, in the passive form, both lightened and doubled, they have said: if the verb is ascribed to the apparent noun, then the two pronouns refer definitely to the remaining ones, and the statement in that case is like "the Banu Fulan were killed," when the killing fell among them but did not wipe them out. If it is ascribed to the pronoun, as is the more apparent and fitting view for some, with the rebuke for giving up because of the rumour of his killing, may God bless him and grant him peace, then this is also the view of Qatada, al-Rabi', Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Suddi, as has been said. In that case the two pronouns refer to the remaining ones too if the rabbiyyun are considered to have been with the prophet in the killing, and to all of them if they are considered to have been with him in the fighting.

﴿Nor did they weaken⦆ means they did not slacken in jihad, as al-Zajjaj said. It has also been said: they were not affected by weakness in religion, such that their belief changed because of the absence of victory. ﴿Nor did they submit⦆ means they did not apostatise from their insight, nor from their religion, as Qatada said. It has also been said: they did not submit to their enemy, and the words of Ibn Abbas point to this. The verb istakana is often used in this sense, and also in the sense of entreating. It has been disputed whether it is from sukun (stillness), so its pattern is iftaʿala, because the submissive one becomes still before the one to whom he submits, and its alif is for lengthening, which is common and not an error, contrary to Abu al-Baqa', and not restricted to poetry, contrary to Abu Hayyan. Or it is from kawn (being), so its pattern is istaf'ala and its alif is changed from a waw, and the sin is added for emphasis, as if he sought from himself to be for the one who overcame him. It has also been said: because it is like non-existence, so it seeks from itself existence.

It could also be that it comes from the Arabs' saying: "Fulan spent the night (bāta fulānun) in a bad state (bi-kaynatin sū'in)," meaning in a bad condition. Or it may derive from "kānahu yakīnuhu," when he humiliated him. This is attributed to al-Azhari and Abu 'Ali. In that case, the alif in it (the ā in wahanū's root) is converted from a yā'. The majority read the ha' in ﴿وهَنُوا﴾ with a fatha. It was also read with a kasra, which is a dialect form, but the fatha is more well-known. It was also read with sukūn, as a lightening of the kasra. In the statement there is an allusion that is not hidden.

﴿وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ (146) in enduring the hardships and bearing the adversities in His cause, so He grants them victory and elevates their station.

The intended meaning of "the patient ones" (al-ṣābirīn) is either the rabbiyyūn (the godly scholars), and the explicit mention in place of a pronoun is to openly praise them for patience, which is the foundation of the matter, while also indicating the reason for the ruling; or it refers to a general category that includes them and others, with them entering into it by primary inclusion.

The sentence, under both interpretations, is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 147:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their saying was not﴾ is like an emphasis and an intensification of their steadfastness in the religion and of the complete absence of weakness and feebleness reaching them. It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with what precedes it. It has also been said: it is a statement explaining their verbal excellences immediately after the explanation of their practical excellences. The word (qawlahum), in the accusative, is the predicate of kana (was), and its subject is the verbal noun (masdar) formed from (an) and what follows it in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except that they said﴾. The exception is a restricted (mufarragh) exception from the most general of things. That is: their saying, in that situation and amid the clashing of the points of hardships and pains, was not ﴿except that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾, that is, our minor sins, ﴿and our excesses in our affair﴾, that is, our transgression beyond the limit, and what is meant is our major sins. This is narrated from al-Dahhak. It has also been said: excess (israf) is transgression in doing what is obligatory, and sin (dhanb) is general in this and in negligence. It has also been said: it stands in opposition to excess, and both are blameworthy. In this surah, God willing, the application of the term "sins" to major sins will come, so understand.

The adverbial phrase (zarf) is connected to what is "with them" or is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. They attributed these to themselves, although the apparent meaning is that they were free of negligence in the matter of God Exalted, out of belittling themselves, considering their aspiration small, and ascribing what afflicted them to their own deeds. Moreover, it is not far-fetched that by those sins and that excess may be meant what was really a sin and an excess, but relative to them: the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to God). It has also been said: by seeking forgiveness they meant seeking the acceptance of their deeds, since nothing is obligatory upon God Exalted; but there is in this what is not hidden. They placed the supplication for forgiveness before what is more important according to the situation, from the supplication in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And make firm our feet﴾, that is, at the time of striving against Your enemies, by strengthening our hearts and aiding us with spiritual support from You, ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾. (147)
Page 85
Bringing it closer to the sphere of acceptance, for a supplication accompanied by humility and issuing from purity and cleanness is closer to being answered.

Some people have said: what is meant by (make firm our feet) is: make us firm upon Your true religion. Thus the placing of the request for forgiveness before this firmness is by way of placing clearing (takhliyah) before adornment (tahliyah). Placing both before the request for victory is for what has preceded. It has also been said: they requested forgiveness first so that they would be entitled to request victory over the disbelievers, by their being preferred through their purity from sins over them, while they were encompassed by sins. In their request for victory despite their exceedingly great numbers, which what preceded indicates, is a notification that they did not look to their numbers nor rely upon them, but ascribed the firmness of their feet to God Exalted and believed that victory is from Him, glorified and exalted is He. In the report about them that their saying was nothing but this, rather than anything containing a trace of distress, feebleness or wavering, there is an allusion against the defeated, which is not hidden.

Ibn Kathir and Asim, in one narration from them, read (qawluhum) with the nominative, making it the subject, while the predicate is (an) and what is in its sphere, meaning: their saying was not any thing among things except this saying which indicates the most excellent of excellences. Our master Shaykh al-Islam said: this, as you see, is more firmly grounded in terms of meaning and more suited to the requirement of the context, because the report that their saying in general is the particular saying of theirs narrated in detail, as their two readings convey, is more informative to the hearer than the report that the particularity of their stated saying is their saying, since the locus of the benefit and the place of clarification in declarative sentences is the predicate. The more appropriate predicate is what is more informative and more evident in indicating the event, and richer in containing specific relations far from occurrence in the external world and in the hearer's mind. It is not hidden that this here, in that (an) with what is in its sphere is more complete and perfect. As for what the annexation conveys of general, absolute, collective relation, since it is easily present both externally and mentally, its proper treatment is to be considered in a collective manner and made a heading for the subject, not intended in itself in the discourse of clarification. The majority chose what they chose, and the rule of grammar is that when two definites meet, the more definite of them is more entitled to be the subject. There is no doubt in the greater definiteness of (an qalu) because it indicates the aspect of the relation and the time of the event, and because it resembles the pronoun in that it is neither described nor does it describe. And (qawlahum) is annexed to a pronoun, and it is in the position of a proper noun, so reflect. End.

Abu al-Baqa said: what follows illa is made the subject of kana, and the explicit verbal noun as its predicate is stronger than the reverse, for two reasons: first, (an qalu) resembles the pronoun in that it is not described, and it is more definite; second, what follows (illa) is affirmative, and the meaning is: their saying was "Our Lord, forgive us our sins," etc., being their custom in supplication. Allamah al-Tibi said: it seems the meaning is that nothing proper or fitting from the men of the Lord in that situation was except this saying, and that other than this saying would be contrary to their state. This particularity is conveyed by the placement of (an) with the verb as the subject of kana. Its verification is what the author of al-Intisaf mentioned: that the benefit of introducing (kana) is the intensification of negating the act it governs, by enumerating the aspect of its act generally in terms of occurrence and specifically in terms of the particularity of the utterance; so it is a negation twice. Then he said: on this basis, if you make the main part of the sentence (an qalu) and rely upon it, and make (qawlahum) like a complement, what you intended is achieved; but if you reverse it, you ride into strain. Do you not see how Abu al-Baqa made the predicate a forgotten thing in the second aspect and relied upon what follows (illa)? End.

From this one knows what is in the words of our master Shaykh al-Islam, for whenever it is possible to consider the eloquence of the meaning while observing the grammatical rule, one should not turn away from that to something else, especially since they have stated that making the less definite noun the subject is weak. Al-Mughni says: know that they ruled that (an) and (inna), when they are presumed with a definite verbal noun, have the rule of a pronoun, because it is not described, just as the pronoun is likewise; for this reason the Seven read ﴿What was their argument except that they said﴾ and ﴿So what was the answer of his people except that they said﴾. The nominative is weak, like the weakness of reporting about something by a pronoun regarding what is less definite. End. Some have explained the definiteness of the derived verbal noun by saying that it is not denied.
Page 86
Objections have been raised against each of the two explanations of Ibn Hisham and of the some.

As for the objection to the first, it is that its not being described does not necessitate placing it in the position of the pronoun; how many a noun is not described, indeed does not describe, yet is not in that position? It was answered that it is possible that in that noun there is an impediment preventing its being placed in the position of the pronoun, since the absence of an impediment is not part of the cause nor a condition for its existence. As for the objection to the second, it is that it is not accepted, for it may be indefinite, as in ﴿And it was not that this Qur'an be fabricated﴾, that is, a fabrication, as al-Shihab said.

It was answered that the intent of whoever said that the derived verbal noun is not indefinite is that in such a position it is not indefinite, not that the verbal particle cannot be interpreted with an indefinite verbal noun at all. This is supported by restricting the verbal noun to the definite in the wording of al-Mughni, from which it is understood that (an) and (inna) sometimes are presumed with a definite verbal noun and sometimes with an indefinite one, and that when they are presumed with a definite verbal noun, it has the rule of a pronoun. From here Sahib al-Matla said regarding that explanation: the saying of the believers, if it is stripped of annexation, remains indefinite, unlike (an qalu). Remaining in al-Mughni's text are matters. The first: is the restriction to (an) and (inna) incidental or exclusionary? Some verifiers held the former, arguing that in the sixth aspect of the fifth chapter it is stated without qualification that the verbal particle and its complement in such cases are definite, so they do not function as adjectives for an indefinite, and it was not limited to (an) and (inna). And for one who holds the latter it may say: there is a difference between absolute definiteness and being in the rule of the pronoun, as is not hidden.
