Ibn Hisham took the absolute in the absolute and restricted the restricted, so there is no harm in leaving both expressions as they appear.

The second: it is understood from its apparent meaning that if the two particles were presumed with an indefinite verbal noun, it would not be in the rule of the pronoun, and the apparent sense of this is that description is then permitted, and there is hesitation in this, for it may be said: the non-establishment of the rank of the pronoun for it does not necessitate the permissibility of description, since the prohibition of description is more general than the rank of the pronoun, and negating the more specific does not entail negating the more general.

The third: it is understood from his words that the presumed verbal noun defined by annexation, whether annexed to a pronoun or to something else, has the status of a pronoun; but none of the imams has explicitly stated this. However, since Ibn Hisham is trustworthy and an imam in the discipline, and nothing has been transmitted from his imams contrary to it, what he says is accepted.

The fourth: his ruling that the nominative is weak, like the weakness of reporting by a pronoun about what is less definite, is far removed from the view of Ibn Malik that it is permissible to report a definite noun about a purely indefinite noun in the chapter on the abrogating particles. A great difference lies between them. Ibn Malik's statement is supported by the verse ﴿For indeed, God is sufficient for you﴾. And perhaps for the sake of verifying this position, and of what we indicated at the outset regarding the meaning of the verse, the Master, may his secret be sanctified, said: reflect, reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 148:

﴿So Allah gave them﴾ i.e., as a consequence of their saying that, as the particle fa' indicates, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, i.e., victory and booty; this is what Ibn Jurayj said. Qatadah said: conquest, dominance, establishment, and victory over their enemy. It has been said: calling that a "reward" is because it follows from their obedience, and in it there is honour and exaltation for them. It has also been said: calling that a "reward" is a metaphor, because it resembles a reward.

The interpretation of Ibn Jurayj has been questioned on the grounds that spoils of war were not made lawful for anyone before Islam; rather, when the prophets took booty, a fire would come down from heaven and consume it. So how can booty be a worldly reward, when none of it reached those who fought? It has been answered that the property which the fire would consume is other than living beings; as for living beings, they would remain for those who fought, not for the prophets, peace be upon them. Thus that was the worldly reward.

﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, i.e., and the good reward of the Hereafter. According to Ibn Jurayj, this is Allah's pleasure and mercy; according to Qatadah, it is Paradise. The specification of the "good" for this reward is to signal its excellence, its distinction, and that it is the one that is truly counted with Him, Exalted. Perhaps the mention of the worldly reward before it is out of regard for the actual order of occurrence, or because it is more fitting to what precedes it, namely the supplication for victory over the disbelievers.

﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ (148). This is a concluding statement confirming what precedes it, for Allah's love for His servant is the source of every good and happiness. The lam [in "the good-doers"] is either for a specific reference (ʿahd), and the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that what was related about them is of the category of excellence (iḥsān); or it is for the category (jins), and they are included in it as a primary inclusion. In both interpretations, there is encouragement for the believers to attain the noble qualities that were related.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 149:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve﴾ This begins the admonition of the believers against following the disbelievers, by explaining the harms of doing so, right after encouraging them to emulate the helpers of the prophets, peace be upon them, by explaining their virtues. The address is introduced with the vocative and the attention-drawing particle to show concern for what falls within its scope. Describing them with faith serves to remind them of a state that is incompatible with that obedience, so the admonition comes in the most complete form. As for the phrase ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, it may refer to the hypocrites, because the verse was revealed, as narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, when they said to the believers at the time of the defeat: "Return to your brethren and enter into their religion." Expressing them by this description is intended to increase the aversion to them and the warning against obeying them. It may refer to Abu Sufyan and his companions; in that case, obeying them means submitting to them and seeking safety from them, and this is the view taken by al-Suddi. It may refer to the Jews and the Christians; in that case the meaning is: do not take the Jews and Christians as advisers concerning your religion, and do not believe them in anything of that matter. This is the view taken by Ibn Jurayj, who related that they used to cast doubts about the religion upon them, saying: "If Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were truly a prophet, he would not have been defeated, nor would what befell him and his companions have befallen him; he is merely a man whose situation is like that of other people, a day for him and a day against him." So they were forbidden to pay attention to these. It may refer to the rest of the disbelievers.

Some later scholars held that such obedience is permissible, and the particle ﴿إن﴾ was used to signal that obedience is far from occurring among the believers.

﴿they will turn you back on your heels﴾ That is, they will return you to your original state, which is associating partners with Allah, the Exalted, and the verb is the answer to the conditional.

This is valid on the basis of what is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, although the sense of the statement with respect to him is, in effect: ﴿if you obey those who disbelieve﴾ in their saying: "Return to your brethren and enter into their religion," they will bring you into their religion; and this reverts to your saying: if you enter into their religion, you will enter into their religion. In this there is the unity of the condition and the consequence, on the basis that turning back on one's heels is a sign of the reversal of affairs and a proverbial expression for returning after advancing. It has been said that the intended meaning of obedience is intending it and resolving upon it, that is: if you resolve to obey them in this, you will be turned back and return to what you were upon of disbelief. This is more emphatic in admonition, but it is far from the wording. It was also permitted that its conditional character be taken in consideration of it serving as a preparation for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so you will turn back as losers﴾ (149), that is: you will return as losers, deprived of the good of this world and the happiness of the Hereafter, and that is the greatest loss.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 150:

﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector (mawla)﴾ This is an idrab (a turning away from the previous statement, leaving it without negating it). The meaning is: the disbelievers are not allies (awliya') whose commands you should obey in anything, nor can they give you victory; rather, Allah is your Helper, and none other. It is a mubtada' and khabar (subject and predicate). It was also read with the noun of majesty (al-ism al-jalil) in the accusative, as a direct object of a verb omitted, and the meaning then is: "So do not obey them; rather, obey Allah, your Protector," ﴿and He is the best of helpers﴾ (150), because He is the Mighty who is not overcome, and the true Helper, so He alone should be singled out for obedience and for seeking aid. The clause is conjoined to what precedes it.

It was also permitted, on the basis of the irregular (shadhdh) reading, to take it as a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) clause and as a circumstantial clause (hal).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 151:

﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ This serves as an explanation of what precedes it. He expressed it with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), in keeping with the customs of grandeur, to inspire awe. The sin (in sa-) is for emphasis on the casting. And (al-ru'b), with a sukun on the ain, means fear and dread; that is, "We shall hurl that into their hearts." The intended referent of the relative clause is Abu Sufyan and his companions. Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi, who said: "When Abu Sufyan and the polytheists departed on the day of Uhud, heading toward Makkah, Abu Sufyan set out until he reached part of the way, then they regretted and said: 'Evil is what you have done; you killed them, until only the fugitives remain. Leave them! Return and annihilate them.' Then Allah the Exalted cast terror into their hearts, so they fled, and they met a Bedouin and made him a reward, saying to him: 'If you meet Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, inform them of what we have gathered against them.' Allah the Exalted informed His Messenger (ﷺ), so he pursued them until he reached Hamra' al-Asad. Allah the Exalted then revealed this verse in that regard, mentioning the matter of Abu Sufyan and his companions." It was also said that the verse was revealed on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been helped with terror against the enemy."

Ahmad and others related from the hadith of Abu Umamah: "I have been helped with terror for a distance of a month; it is cast into the hearts of my enemies."

It was read as (sa-yulqi) with a ya'. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read (al-ru'ub) with a damma on the ain, and this is a dialect of the word. It was also said that the damma is the original and the sukun is for lightness; and it was said that the original is the sukun and the damma is for assimilation.

﴿because they associated with Allah﴾ that is, because of their association (ishrak) with the Essence that necessarily exists, possessing all attributes of perfection. Since this Name indicates greatness, which is incompatible with partnership, He used it. The first prepositional phrase is connected to (sa-nulqi), not to (al-ru'b). The connection of (fi) to it does not prevent this, because the meanings differ. The second is connected to what is near it. Association was a cause of the casting of terror, because it is among the things that necessitate their abandonment and the victory of the believers over them, and both of these are among the motives for terror.

﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾ that is, for their association with Him. It was also said: for worshipping Him. (Ma) is an indefinite noun, described or relative, and not a verbal-source particle. ﴿authority﴾ that is, proof. Its mention indicates that what is followed in the matter of monotheism is the heavenly proof, not opinions and baseless desires. It is called (sultan) because by it one is strengthened against an opponent and gains power over him. The nun is extra; it was also said to be original. Mentioning the non-sending down of proof, together with the impossibility of its realization, falls under the negation of the qualified because its qualifying condition is negated; that is, there is no proof until He sends it down. This is in the manner of his saying, describing a desert:

It is not frightened by its terrors, the hare, nor do you see the lizard there hiding in its hole.

Since the meaning is that there is no lizard there to hide, the intention is to negate both together. This is like their saying: "a negative proposition does not require the existence of its subject." What we have mentioned about the impossibility of realizing proof for association almost amounts to being known as necessary by religion. As for association in lordship, it is evident, for how could Allah, glory be to Him, command belief that the Creator of the world is two who share necessary existence and the attribution of every perfection? As for association in divinity, which most of the polytheists in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held to, it leads to commanding belief in things contrary to reality of what the polytheists believed about their idols, and He has refuted them for it. So the statement of Isam al-Millah: "We say: the proof for association is within His power; if He willed, He would send it down, for if He commanded the association of idols with Him in worship, worship would become obligatory" — I see this only as a solution by Isam al-Din; "There is no god but Allah" is addressed to the dualists and the idolaters, and they reject the possibility of that, as is not hidden from one who has understood the meaning of this good word. May Allah grant us death upon it, and not make us among those who associate with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for.

﴿And their refuge﴾ that is, where they take refuge in the Hereafter ﴿is the Fire﴾ there is no refuge for them other than it.

﴿And wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾ (151). That is, their abode. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for severity, for explanation, and to indicate that they are wrongdoers in their association, placing a thing in other than its place. Al-mathwa is the place of dwelling, on the pattern of maf'al from thawaytu, and its final radical is a ya'. The object of the dispraise is omitted, that is: "wretched is their abode, the Fire." He did not express it with al-ma'wa to signify eternity, since residence is included in al-mathwa but not in it.

[p. 89]

﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾. Al-Wahidi narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah, after they had been afflicted with what they were afflicted with on the Day of Uhud, some of his Companions said: 'From where has this befallen us, when Allah the Exalted had promised us victory?' So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse."

"Wa'dahu" (His promise) is the second object of "sadaqa" (to fulfil, to be true to). Clearly, it takes two objects in such constructions, and it can also take the second object with a preposition, as in "sadaqtu Zaydan fi al-hadith" (I was truthful to Zayd in the statement). From this, some have permitted that "wa'dahu" is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naṣb bi-naz' al-khāfid).

The promise meant here is what Allah, glorified is He, promised them of victory by His saying, ﴿If you are patient and fear Allah﴾, and so on, and through His Prophet ﷺ when he said to the archers: "Do not leave your place. We will never cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your place."

In another narration: "Do not leave this place, for we will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in this place."

The first view is supported by what al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dala'il from 'Urwa, who said: "Allah had promised them, on condition of patience and piety, that He would reinforce them with five thousand angels bearing marks, and He had indeed done so. But when they disobeyed the command of the Messenger and abandoned their ranks, and the archers abandoned the Messenger's covenant with them, that they should not leave their positions, and they desired the world, Allah lifted the reinforcement of the angels."

Our master Shaykh al-Islam (al-Bayḍawi) chose the second view, and what would benefit you here has already been mentioned earlier.

The view that the promise meant is what He, majestic is His glory, said: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ is not valid, as is not hidden.

Imam Ahmad and a group narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah did not help His Prophet in any battle as He helped him on the Day of Uhud." They denied this, so Ibn 'Abbas said: "Between me and whoever denies this is the Book of Allah. Allah the Exalted says about the Day of Uhud: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them﴾ (taḥussūnahum), i.e., you were killing them." This is the transmitted explanation (al-tafsir al-ma'thur, explanation based on transmitted reports), and the scholar (Ibn 'Abbas) cited in support the words of 'Utba al-Laythi:

"We strike them with the swords until it is as if we are splitting from them, with the skulls, a colocynth."

And his words:

"And among us is one who met with the sword of Muhammad, who (haassa) the enemies, the breadth of the armies."

The original meaning of "hassahu" is that he struck his sense (ḥāssa) with a blight which nullified it, like his liver. Hence it is used to express killing. From this comes "jarād maḥsūs" (a locust destroyed), which is one killed by cold. It is also said that it is one touched by fire. The verb "hass" is often used for killing in the sense of complete extermination.

The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to ﴿sadaqakumu﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it could be an adverbial phrase of the promise, ﴿bi-idhnihi﴾, i.e., by His facilitation and granting of success. The restriction with it is to establish that their killing of them was through what Allah had promised them of victory. ﴿Until when you lost heart﴾, i.e., you became fearful and cowardly regarding your enemy, ﴿and disputed concerning the matter﴾, i.e., the matter of war, or the matter of his ﷺ command to you regarding guarding that position, as its explanation has already been mentioned, ﴿and disobeyed﴾, by not standing firm there and turning towards the spoils, ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾, namely the defeat of the polytheists and your victory over them.

Mujahid said: "Allah gave the believers victory over the polytheists to the extent that the women of the polytheists mounted every hard and sliding thing." Then the polytheists gained the upper hand over them because of their disobedience to the Prophet ﷺ. It is also narrated that Khalid ibn al-Walid came with the cavalry of the polytheists, and with him was 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, saying: "Charge against him." He charged against him and defeated him and those with him. When the archers saw that, they went back, except a few, and entered the camp, opposing the command and vacating the position they had been in. So the cavalry of the polytheists entered from that place upon the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and some of them struck others, and they became confused. Many Muslims were killed because of that.

﴿Among you are those who desire the world﴾, and they are the archers who coveted the plunder and left the position for it. ﴿And among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾, like 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, the commander of the archers, and those who remained steadfast with him, obeying the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until

[p. 90]

he was martyred. ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, i.e., He restrained you from them until the situation changed from victory to its opposite. ﴿That He might test you﴾, i.e., that He might deal with you as one who is tested, so that your condition and your steadfastness in faith would become manifest. Thus in the speech there is a figurative metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya, an extended metaphor by representation), since testing is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Regarding "ḥattā" (until) here there are two views. One is that it is a preposition (ḥarf jarr) meaning "ila" (to), and its complement is ﴿taḥussūnahum﴾ or ﴿ṣadaqakum﴾, or something omitted whose estimate is "dāma lakum dhālika" (that continued for you). The second is that it is a conjunction of beginning (ḥarf ibtidā') which introduces the conditional sentence of "idhā" (when) and what follows it. As for the answer of "idhā", it is said to be ﴿tanāza'tum﴾, with the "wāw" being superfluous; this was preferred by al-Farra'. It is also said to be ﴿ṣarafakum﴾, with "thumma" being superfluous, and this is very weak. The correct view is that it is omitted, and this is the view of the Basrans. Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "bi-an amarakum" (that He commanded you). Abu Hayyan estimated it as "inqasamtum ila qismayn" (you divided into two groups), based on what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "mana'akum nasrahu" (He withheld His victory from you). Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "inhazamtum" (you were routed). Each has its direction. Some later scholars estimated it as "imtahanakum" (He tested you). This was refuted on the basis that the beginning would then be the endpoint of the turning away which results from withholding victory. In every estimate, ﴿ṣarafakum﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūf, conjoined) upon that omitted element. It is also said that "idhā" is a noun, as in the saying: "idhā yaqūmu Zayd, idhā yaqūmu 'Amr" (when Zayd stands, when 'Amr stands), and "ḥattā" is a preposition meaning "ila" (to), connected to ﴿ṣadaqakum﴾ by way of its including the meaning of victory, as if it were said: "Allah the Exalted had given you victory until the time of your weakness and your disputing," and so on. And ﴿thumma ṣarafakum﴾ in this case is coordinated upon that. These two clauses, being adverbial, form a parenthetical interjection between the two conjoined elements.

﴿And certainly He pardoned you﴾, either by pure bounty, or because He knew of your great remorse over the disobedience. It is said that what is meant by that is pardon for the sin, and it is general for all who turned away.

This is supported by what al-Bukhari narrated from 'Uthman ibn Mawhab, who said: "A man came to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: 'I will ask you about something, so tell me. I adjure you by the sanctity of this House: Do you know that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan fled on the Day of Uhud?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you know that he was absent from Badr and did not witness it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you know that he failed to take part in the Pledge of al-Ridwan and did not witness it?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he exclaimed 'Allahu akbar!' Ibn 'Umar said: 'Come, let me inform you and explain to you what you asked me about. As for his fleeing on the Day of Uhud, I testify that Allah the Exalted pardoned him. As for his absence from Badr, he had under him the daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and she was ill. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "You will have the reward of a man who witnessed Badr, and his share."'

As for his absence from the Pledge of al-Ridwan: had anyone been more honoured in the valley of Makkah than 'Uthman, he would have sent him instead. So he sent 'Uthman, and the Pledge of al-Ridwan took place after 'Uthman had gone to Makkah. Then the Prophet ﷺ struck with his right hand upon his other hand and said: "This is the hand of 'Uthman. Take it now with you."'"

Al-Balkhi said: "It is a pardon from total extermination." This was also narrated from Ibn Jurayj. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i claimed that it is specific to those who did not disobey Allah by their turning away. All of these are contrary to the apparent meaning. It may be said that the motive for al-Balkhi's view is that the pardon for sin will be indicated by something that comes later in the clearest manner, and that founding a new meaning (ta'sis) is better than emphasising an existing one (ta'kid). The statement of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, contains nothing more than that Allah the Exalted pardoned the sin of those who fled, and this is the clear meaning of the following verse. As for whether it is understood from it, even by implication, that what is meant by the pardon here is pardon for the sin, I do not think any fair-minded person would claim this.

﴿And Allah is full of bounty towards the believers﴾ (152). This is a concluding clause (tadhyīl, a closing statement that confirms what precedes) which affirms the content of what came before. In it is an indication that this pardon, even if it came after repentance, was by way of bounty and not obligation. That is, it is His way to show bounty to them by pardon, or in all circumstances, "they were given the trial," or "it was turned against them," since the trial is also mercy. The tanwin (nunation) of "faḍl" is for magnification. "Al-mu'minin" (the believers) refers either to those addressed, and the explicit mention in place of the pronoun is for honour and to indicate the reason for the ruling, or it refers to the category in general, and they enter into it in the primary sense. Perhaps generalising here and in what precedes is better than restricting. Restricting the bounty to pardon is better than restricting it to the absence of total extermination, as some have claimed.

(Page 91)

*Idh tus'idūna* (when you were ascending) is connected either to *sarafakum* (He turned you away) or to *yabtalīkum* (He tested you). Its connection to *'afā* (He pardoned), as al-Ṭabarsī said, "is nothing," and similarly its connection to *'aṣaytum* (you disobeyed), *tanāzaʿtum* (you disputed) or *fashiltum* (you lost heart), as Abū al-Baqā' said. It was also said that it is connected to an implied *udhkur* (remember). This raises a difficulty: the meaning would become "Remember, O Muḥammad, when you were ascending," and this contains two addresses without a conjunction, so the correct form would be *udhkurū* (remember, plural).

It is answered that what is meant by *udhkur* is the category of this action, so *udhkurū* is implied and not *udhkur*. It may also be of the type of "O Prophet, when you divorce women" (65:1). It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Al-Shihāb answered that *udhkur* includes the sense of saying, and the meaning is: "Say to them, O Muḥammad, when they were ascending..." Similarly, there is no objection to this, just as you say to Zayd, "Do you say such-and-such?", because the quoted address is intended in its wording, so it does not contradict the aforementioned rule. They overlooked this, so consider it. It is not hidden that this is also contrary to the apparent meaning.

*Al-iṣʿād* means going off and moving away across the land. Some distinguished between *al-iṣʿād* and *al-ṣuʿūd*, saying that *al-iṣʿād* is on level ground while *al-ṣuʿūd* is upward movement. It was also said there is no difference between *aṣʿada* and *ṣaʿida* except that the hamza in the first indicates entering, like *aṣbaḥa* (he entered the morning). Most scholars follow the first view.

al-Ḥasan read, as transmitted by Ibn Jarīr from him, *taṣʿadūna* with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ* and the *ʿayn*, and some interpreted it as ascending a mountain. Abū Ḥaywah read *tasaʿʿadūna* with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ* and a shaddah on the *ʿayn*. This is either from *tasaʿʿada* in the ladder, meaning he climbed, or from *ṣaʿʿada* in the valley, *taṣʿīdan*, meaning he descended into it. al-Akhfash said: "*Aṣʿada* in the land means he went and travelled, and *aṣʿada* in the valley and *ṣaʿʿada* in it mean he descended." He recited:

*"Though you see me today driving my camel-litter, I go up at times into the lands and go down."*

al-Shammākh said:

*"If you dislike my satire, then avoid my anger; let not my descent and my ascent overtake you."*

It has been narrated by more than one that when the people were tested, they fled into the valley of Uḥud. Abū Zayd said: "It is said *ṣaʿʿada fī al-sullam ṣuʿūdan* (he climbed the ladder), and *ṣaʿʿada fī al-jabal* or *ʿalā al-jabal taṣʿīdan* (he climbed the mountain). They did not know *ṣaʿida* in this sense." Ubayy read *idh tuṣʿidūna* in the valley, and this supports the view of those who said that *al-iṣʿād* is going on level ground, not upward movement. It was also read *yuṣʿidūna* with the letter *yāʾ*, and the connection of *idh* to *udhkur* is clear on this reading.

*Wa lā talwūna ʿalā aḥad* (and you did not turn back for anyone): that is, you did not stay for anyone, and you did not turn aside. It is from *lawā*, meaning "to turn" or "to bend," and it is often used with the meaning "to stop and wait," because the one who waits typically turns his neck. It was also explained as "you do not return," which is close to that meaning. al-Ṭabarsī mentioned that this verb is only used in negation, so one does not say *lawaytu ʿalā kadhā*. al-Ḥasan read *talūna* with a single *wāw*, changing the dammed *wāw* into a hamza and dropping it for lightness.

It was also read *talūna* with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ*, as being from *alwā*, a dialectal form of *lawā*, and *yulūna* with a *yāʾ*, like *yuṣʿidūna*. Abū al-Baqā' said: "It is read *ʿalā Uḥudin* with two ḍammahs, and it is the mountain. The rebuke upon it is not clear." Some explained it as meaning the companions of Uḥud, or the place of the battle. This indicates their distance in sensing fear and their haste in the defeat, to the point that they did not turn their attention even to the place itself.

*Wa al-rasūlu yadʿūkum fī ukhrākum* (while the Messenger was calling you from behind): that is, he was calling out to you from your rear, or to your other company, or calling to you from behind you. It is said, "So-and-so came at the end of the people, their last, and their hindmost, when he came after them." Mentioning him, upon him be blessings and peace, with the title of Messenger is to indicate that his call was by way of the message from Allah, Exalted, in order to emphasise the rebuke of those who fled. It was narrated that he (ﷺ) used to call: "To me, servants of Allah! To me, servants of Allah! I am the Messenger of Allah; whoever turns back will have Paradise." This was when the people had been defeated and had hastened to flee, before they reached a distance where the voice cannot be heard. This does not contradict what was previously related from Kaʿb ibn Mālik, that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recognised them and called with his loudest voice, "O company of Muslims, rejoice! This is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," he gestured to him to be silent. That was at the end of the affair, when the defeated had gone far away. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

*Fa-athābakum* (so He rewarded you) is a conjunction upon *sarafakum* (He turned you away). The hidden pronoun refers to Allah, Exalted. The expression "rewarded" is figurative, in the manner of His saying, "Their greeting therein is a painful blow" (a sarcastic usage). Or it is a metaphor for requital, meaning: Allah, Exalted, requited you for what you disobeyed, *ghaman bi-ghammin* (grief upon grief). That is, distress upon distress. Most scholars hold that there is no difference between *al-ghamm* and *al-ḥuzn* (sorrow). The *bāʾ* is either for accompaniment, and the adverbial phrase is stable, meaning: He requited you with *ghaman* (grief) joined with *bi-ghammin* (grief). The first grief was what befell them from killing, wounding, and the overpowering of the polytheists over them. The second grief was what befell them from the rumour of the killing of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the loss of the spoils. This was the view of Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ.

It was also said: the second grief was the polytheists, Abū Sufyān and his companions, looking down upon them while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with them on the rock. This was related from al-Suddī. It was also said that what is meant is mere multiplication, meaning: He requited you with many griefs, some connected to others. Or the *bāʾ* is for causation, and the adverbial phrase is connected to *athābakum*. The first grief was for the companions, may Allah be pleased with them, through the killing of their fellows, and the second grief was for the Messenger (ﷺ) through their disobedience of his command. The meaning is: He rewarded you with grief because of a grief you caused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through your disobedience and opposition to his command.

al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Maghribī said: the first grief was for the polytheists, because of what they saw of the strength of the Muslims in pursuing them and their going out to Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad, and the second grief was for the believers because of what was inflicted upon them. That is: He requited you with the grief of your enemies, the polytheists, because of a grief they caused you. It was said that the *bāʾ* here is for substitution (*badal*). Both these views are distant, and the connection to them is not clear. More distant still is what was narrated from al-Ḥasan, that the first grief was for the believers because of what befell them on the day of Uḥud, and the second grief was for the polytheists because of what befell them on the day of Badr. The meaning is: He requited you with grief on the day of Uḥud, through killing and wounding, because of a grief you caused the polytheists on the day of Badr in the same way. This was objected to, on the ground that what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr at the hands of the Muslims only requires a requital of honour, not grief.

It was also said that the hidden pronoun in *athābakum* refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), and *athābakum* means *ā-sākum* (he consoled you), that is, he made you equal to him, sharing in the sorrow. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was grieved by what descended upon you, just as you were grieved by what descended upon him. He did not blame you for your disobedience, as consolation to you and relief for you. This was objected to, on the ground that it is contrary to the apparent meaning, because it would lead to a disconnection if the conjunction were upon *sarafakum*, and the sequence would not be apparent except with strained interpretation if the conjunction were upon *yadʿūkum*. Yes, the causation based on His saying, "So that you may not grieve over what escaped you, nor over what afflicted you" (3:153), is clear on this view, since the meaning is: He consoled you with this, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you of victory, nor over what afflicted you of hardships. The same applies to the view of al-Maghribī. As for the other views, the meaning is: so that you may train yourselves in patience during hardships, so that you do not grieve over a benefit that has passed or a harm that is coming. This interpretation was needed because requital with grief is only a cause of sorrow, not of its absence.

It was also said: the particle *lā* (not) is superfluous, and the meaning is: "so that you may feel regret for what escaped you of victory and spoils, and for what afflicted you of wounds and defeat, as a punishment for you." Then the causation is clear. It is not hidden that the emphasis of *lā* and its repetition weakens the view that it is superfluous. It was also said: the causation is on its apparent meaning, and *lā* is not superfluous, and the statement is connected to His saying, "And indeed He pardoned you" (3:152), meaning: Allah, Exalted, pardoned you so that you would not grieve, and so on, for the pardon of Allah, Exalted, removes every sorrow. What is in this is not hidden. Perhaps it may be said that the matter of causation is also clear according to what was related from al-Suddī, without need for interpretation or for saying that *lā* is superfluous. This is clarified by what Ibn Jarīr narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "The people were afflicted with grief and sorrow over what had befallen them among their companions who were killed. When they gathered in the ravine, Abū Sufyān and his companions stopped at the mouth of the ravine. The believers thought they would turn upon them and kill them as well, so sorrow befell them which made them forget their sorrow over their companions. This is His saying, 'So He rewarded you with grief upon grief,' and so on." The *ḥadīth* that "the requital with grief is only a cause of sorrow, not of its absence" is not accepted in an unrestricted way. What prevents a particular grief from being a cause of the removal of another particular grief, by the second being greater so that it makes the first forgotten? So reflect.

*Wa Allāhu khabīrun bi-mā taʿmalūn* (and Allah is Aware of what you do) (153): He knows your deeds and what you intended by them. In *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*, it says: "*Al-khabīr* means *al-ʿalīm* (the All-Knowing), but when knowledge is attributed to hidden inner matters it is called *khibrah* (inner knowledge), and its possessor is called *khabīr*." In this there is encouragement to obedience and warning against disobedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 154 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then He sent down upon you﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿then He rewarded you﴾, and the address is to the believers in truth. The meaning is: then He bestowed upon you, O believers, ﴿after the distress﴾ that had overtaken you. The explicit statement of the delay of the sending down after it, despite the implication of "then" (thumma) for it and for its being delayed after it, is for the sake of added clarification and to remind of the magnitude of the favour.

﴿security (amanah)﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) like "manaʿah," and it is the object (maf'ul) of "sent down," i.e. He sent down upon you security. ﴿Slumber (nuʿas)﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it. It was also said to be an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). It was permitted that ﴿nuʿas﴾ be in the accusative as an object, and ﴿amanah﴾ be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, the meaning being "possessed of security." It does no harm that it is indefinite, since it precedes it, or that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the addressees with an elided genitive, i.e. "possessors of security," or that it is the plural of "āmin" like "barr" and "bararah."

It was said that ﴿amanah﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for ﴿nuʿas﴾. This was objected to on the grounds that its apparent sense requires placing the object of the verbal noun before it, and even if one posits an elided verb, i.e. "you slept security," it is answered that the verb has no good placement. It was also said that it is an object of purpose for "sent down."

This was objected to on the grounds that it is invalid because its condition is violated, which is the unity of the agent, since the agent of "sent down" is God Most High, and the agent of the security is those upon whom it was sent down. It is answered that just as "amanah" can be a verbal noun for the one to whom security happens, it can be a verbal noun for the one who causes it, and the intended meaning here is the second, as if it were said: "He sent down slumber upon you so that He would make you secure by it," and then there is no doubt about the unity of the agent. It was read with the letter mim sukun (amnah), as if because it occurs in a brief time, it is one instance of security, so this does not contradict that the intended meaning is absolute security. The fronting of the two adverbial phrases before the direct object is for the sake of attention to the matter fronted and arousing anticipation for the postponed element, and the singling out of fear from among the varieties of distress for removal, because it is the most important to them in that situation.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi that the polytheists withdrew on the day of Uhud after what had passed between them and the Muslims, and they promised the Prophet ﹙ﷺ﹚ a meeting at Badr the following year. He said to them, "Yes." The Muslims became fearful that they would descend upon Medina, so the Messenger of God ﹙ﷺ﹚ sent a man and said: "Look: if you see them sitting upon their baggage and having their horses on the side, then the people are leaving; but if you see them sitting upon their horses and having their baggage on the side, then the people will descend upon Medina. Fear God and be patient," and he prepared them for fighting. When the Messenger saw them sitting on their baggage quickly and hastily, he called out at the top of his voice that they were departing. When the believers saw that, they confirmed the Prophet of God ﹙ﷺ﹚ and slept. Some of the hypocrites remained, thinking that the people were coming to them. That is His saying, ﴿Then He sent down upon you﴾ etc.

From Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse he said: God gave them security that day by a slumber that covered them, for only one who feels secure sleeps, and the one who is afraid does not sleep.

Many transmitters reported from Anas that Abu Talhah said: "Slumber overcame us on the day of Uhud while we were in our ranks, and you were among those whom slumber overtook that day, so my sword kept falling from my hand, and I would take it, and it would fall, and I would take it." In another narration from him he said: "I raised my head on the day of Uhud and began to look, and there was not one of them but he was swaying beneath his shield, i.e. his buckler, from slumber." Similarly from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam.

It was said: this is the custom of God Most High with the believers, that He makes slumber in battle a sign of victory. This happened in this way to ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, at Siffin, and it is among the divine outpourings and the divine tranquility. ﴿He covers a group of you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the Emigrants and the majority of the Helpers. This implies that it did not cover everyone, and that does not detract from the generality of the sending down for all. The clause is in the accusative position as an attribute of ﴿slumber﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisai read ﴿tughshā﴾ with the feminine ta, so that the pronoun refers to ﴿security﴾, and the apparent sense is that the clause is then a new (mustaʾnafah) sentence, answering an implied question: "What is the ruling of this security?" It is answered: "It covers a group." It was said: it is in the position of an attribute of ﴿security﴾. This was objected to on the grounds that an attribute should precede the substitute and the explicative apposition, and should not be separated from the noun it qualifies by the object of purpose, and that it is customary to speak about the substitute rather than the thing substituted. ﴿And a group﴾, namely the hypocrites.

﴿Their own selves had caused them concern (ahammathum anfusuhum)﴾, i.e. made them people of concern and brought them into it; or: nothing concerned them except their own selves, not the Prophet ﹙ﷺ﹚ nor anyone else. From "ahamm," meaning he made it a matter of concern and an aim for himself. The restriction (hasr) is derived from the context. Some scholars mentioned that the Arabs use this expression for one who is afraid and whose concern for himself has occupied him away from others. ﴿A group﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿their own selves had caused them concern﴾ is its predicate (khabar). This is permitted even though it is indefinite, because it occurs after the waw of circumstance, as in the verse:

"We journeyed while a star had shone, but when your face appeared, it eclipsed the light of every dawn-rising one."

Or because it stands in the place of detailing, as in his saying:

"When I die, people will be of two kinds: one who gloats, and another who praises me for what I am doing."

It was permitted that the clause be an attribute of it, and the predicate then elided, i.e. "and with you" or "there is there a group," and the estimate "and among you a group" requires that the hypocrites be included in the address regarding the sending down of security. In any case, the clause is either a circumstantial clause explaining the severity of the terror and emphasizing the magnitude of the blessing in being delivered from it, or a new sentence brought to explain the state of the hypocrites, so the waw is either circumstantial or resumptive. That it means "when" (idh) is not correct, as Abu al-Baqa' explicitly stated.

﴿They think about God other than the truth﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ﴿had caused them concern﴾, not of ﴿a group﴾, even though it is specified, because of what the coming of a circumstantial qualifier from a subject entails in speech. It was permitted that it be an attribute after an attribute of ﴿a group﴾, or a predicate after a predicate, or that it be the predicate itself, and ﴿had caused them concern﴾ is an attribute or a new sentence explaining what precedes it. "Other than" (ghayr) is in the accusative as an absolute verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid), since it is annexed to an elided verbal noun, and it takes the form of what it is annexed to, i.e. "other than the true thought," which is the thought that befits being attributed to Him. Some said it is a generic absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq nawʿi). The saying of God Most High, ﴿the thought of the Jahiliyyah﴾, is a substitute for what precedes it.

Ibn al-Hajib said: "other than the truth" and "thought" are two verbal nouns, one for comparison and the other as an emphasis for the other, meaning: they say other than the truth. The two objects of "they think" are elided, i.e. they think that the non-fulfilment of His promise, glory be to Him, has occurred. Abu al-Baqa' makes "other than the truth" the first object, i.e. a matter other than the truth, and "by God" is in the position of the second object. The annexation of "thought" to "the Jahiliyyah" is said to be either an annexation of the qualified noun to the verbal noun of its attribute, whose meaning is restriction to the Jahiliyyah, like "a man of truth" and "Hatim of generosity," so it has the sense of the preposition "lam" (belonging to), i.e. the one restricted to truth and generosity; here the ya is a relative ya and the ta is the feminine marker inherent in it. Or it is an annexation of the verbal noun to its agent with an elided noun, meaning the thought of the people of the Jahiliyyah, i.e. of polytheism and ignorance of God Most High, and this too is a genuine restrictive annexation.

﴿They say: is there for us any part of the matter?﴾ That is, some of them say to others by way of denial: is there for us any share of victory, conquest, and triumph? I.e., there is nothing of that for us, because God, glory be to Him and exalted, does not help Muhammad ﹙ﷺ﹚. Or those present among them say to the Messenger of God ﹙ﷺ﹚ in the form of seeking guidance: is there for us any share of the command of God and His promise of victory? Some researchers chose this.

It was said that the clause is either a circumstantial qualifier, or a predicate after a predicate, or an attribute after an attribute, or a new sentence explaining what precedes it, or a substitute for "they think." It is a substitute of the whole according to the truth, and a substitute of inclusion according to the meaning. A difficulty was raised: the saying "they say: is there for us" etc. is an explanation of "they think" and a rendering of it, and an interrogative cannot be a rendering of a declarative, just as one cannot say: "Zayd informed me, he said: do not go," or "he ordered me, he said: do not strike," or "he forbade me, he said: strike," because correspondence between the report and what is reported is obligatory.

The essence of the difficulty is that the object of thinking is a propositional relation, so how can an interrogative of rendering occur as its object? It was answered that the interrogative is a request for knowledge concerning what is doubted and thought, so it may be the object of thinking. Its verification is that thought or knowledge attaches to what is said in answer to that interrogative, as mentioned in the chapter on the suspension of verbs of the heart by an interrogative. It is not hidden that this holds only on the assumption that the interrogative is genuine; but if it is a denial, there is no difficulty, and "it was not said, nor did he say," because it is a declarative and so corresponds with what precedes it in declarativity. Some who took it as a denial held that the meaning is: we have been prevented from managing our own selves and directing them by our choice, so nothing of the matter remains for us. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy said this when the hypocrites informed him of the killing of the Banu al-Khazraj, then he said: "By God, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." It was said: their evil thought on this view is their approval of the opinion of ʿAbd Allah and those who followed him. It was also said: the interrogative is on its apparent sense, and the meaning is: will this subjugation be removed from us, so that we would have some share of the matter? It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent sense. The second "min" is a sword-stroke of an orator (i.e. an emphatic or superfluous particle). The word "shay'" is in the nominative position as a subject, and as Abu al-Baqa' said, there are two possibilities for its predicate: the first is "for us," and "of the matter" is then a circumstantial qualifier; the second is "of the matter," and "for us" is then an explanation, and the complete benefit is achieved by it.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad: ﴿Indeed the matter, all of it, belongs to God﴾, i.e. the true authority and dominance belong to the party of God and His friends, so He helps His Messenger ﹙ﷺ﹚ and his Companions, and disgraces his enemies and subdues them. He expressed the dominance belonging to God Most High as a metaphor for its belonging to His friends, because they are in a position of nearness to Him, glory be to Him. Or the decree or the management belongs to Him Most High alone, in which none shares with Him, so He does what He wills and conducts affairs as the pen has run in the eternal decree. On this view there is no metaphor in the speech. It came as an emphasis for what the speech that preceded it stands in opposition to, which is likewise.

Al-Bahr estimated from this that the interrogative in what preceded it remains on its literal sense, for if its meaning were a denial that they had any part of the matter, they would not have been answered by affirming that the matter, all of it, belongs to God, unless one posits with the negative clause an affirmative clause, so that the meaning is: nothing of the matter belongs to us, but to others who compelled us to go out and forced us to it; then that could be an answer to this posited clause. It is objected that there is no need for this posit on that view either. As for when their intention is the denial of God's help to His Prophet ﹙ﷺ﹚ and those with him, it is clear, because in that statement there is an affirmation of that help in the fullest way. As for when their intention is that no part of the matter remains for them since they were prevented from managing themselves, then in that denial there is an indication that they had some management, and that if they were left to themselves and their management, their side would not have been bent; and this affirmation undertakes to reject that and nullify it in a veiled way, as is not hidden. So I see the positing, as it stands, to be only from narrowness of mind.

Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read ﴿kulluhu﴾ with the nominative, as the subject, the preposition-phrase being related to an elided predicate which occupies the position of the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "indeed" (inna). As for the reading with the accusative, ﴿kull﴾ is an emphasis of the noun of "indeed," and ﴿li-llah﴾ is its predicate. Abu al-Baqa' claimed that ﴿kulluhu﴾ may be a substitute for ﴿al-amr﴾, but this is far-fetched.

﴿They conceal within themselves﴾, i.e. they hide

[Page 97 begins partway through this passage.]

...in them, or they conceal among themselves ﴿what they do not reveal to you﴾, meaning what they are unable to show you. The clause is either a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (they say). The words ﴿Say: Indeed, the matter entirely belongs to Allah﴾ are a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) between the circumstantial clause and the word it modifies. The meaning is: they say what they say while showing that they are seekers of guidance and seekers of victory, while concealing denial and rejection. This is evident on the second possibility in the first verse. For one who takes the interrogative in it as denial, the resumed-sentence reading is required by his view, or the declarative and similar readings are permitted, as already mentioned. The answering clause is a parenthetical insertion in every case, except the possibility that it is a resumed sentence, according to the correct view. As for making this clause a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (Say), with ﴿for you﴾ as the connecting element, its status is not hidden.

(They say) means: within themselves, or secretly to one another. For if the speech were openly spoken, they would not be hypocrites. The clause is either a substitute (badal, a word that replaces and clarifies the earlier one) for (they conceal), or a resumed sentence that comes as an answer to a question arising from what precedes, as if it were asked: "What is it that they concealed?" and it was answered with that. Some scholars of verification (muḥaqqiqūn) preferred this, on the grounds that it is more beneficial, and that if the speech is taken in its literal sense, the two statements do not differ. Their saying ﴿Is there any say for us?﴾ to the believers is not in the same circumstance as their saying ﴿If there had been any say for us﴾ to their companions, and a substitute for a circumstantial clause is itself a circumstantial clause. You know that this last argument is based on the premise that the first statement was made to the believers, and you know that this is not certain. It has also been said that it is because two statements cannot come from one speaker at the same time. Against this it is objected that the time of a concurrent circumstance is not restricted in this way, as is not hidden. For this reason some learned scholars (fuḍalā') justified the denial of concurrence by the sequence of this statement after what precedes it, but they abandoned this justification, for...

﴿If there had been any say for us in the matter, we would not have been killed here.﴾ The meaning is: if we had any share of that, as Muhammad promised and claimed that the matter belongs to Allah and to His allies, ﴿we would not have been killed.﴾ So this, in their view, is a rejection of what they were answered with first. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: if we had choice and planning, we would not have left, as was the opinion of Ibn Ubayy and his followers. The meaning of ﴿we would not have been killed﴾ is ﴿we would not have been overcome﴾, because the speakers are not among those who were killed, since that is impossible for them. It is also possible that the attribution is figurative (majāz, a use of language beyond its literal sense), by attributing to all what belongs to some, so the meaning is: if we had any share of that, those of us who were killed in this battle would not have been killed. Further, it is clear that the view of sequence requires that the answering verse had already been revealed and that they had heard it, so that the claim of rejecting it with this corrupt doubt can be made. The apparent evidence from the reports is that it had not been revealed at that time. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he was asked about this verse, and he said: "Because of those who were killed from among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), they came to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and said to him: 'What do you think?' He said: 'By Allah, we are not consulted'" (﴿If there had been any say for us in the matter, we would not have been killed here.﴾).

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir, and a great many others related from al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I saw myself with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the fear grew intense upon us. Allah sent sleep upon us, so that none of us was without his chin on his chest. By Allah, I was hearing the speech of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr as if it were a dream: ﴿If there had been any say for us in the matter, we would not have been killed here.﴾ So I memorized it from him, and concerning that Allah revealed..." up to "here" (hahuna).

It may be said that this statement from them is like an argument for the first statement, and that both statements came from them initially, and Allah related them to us, refuting them. This is evident if the interrogative is denial. As for if it is a genuine question, there is obscurity in it, so consider this.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, in answer to that: ﴿If you had been in your houses﴾, O hypocrites, and in your dwellings in Madinah, and had not gone out to fight with your aggression, ﴿those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone forth﴾, meaning they would have come out for a cause among the causes calling for going forth, ﴿to their resting places﴾ that were written in the Preserved Tablet, or decreed in the prior knowledge of Allah the Exalted, ﴿upon them, in that battle﴾. That is, to their places of falling, where Allah the Exalted knew and decreed their killing, and where they were killed without doubt, for the decree of Allah cannot be turned back, [Page 97 continues]

[Page 98]

and His judgment cannot be overturned. And in it there is an emphasis in refuting their false statement that is not hidden. Some claimed that the more eloquent reading is that by those decreed killing are meant the killers, meaning that those who kill from among their people would have gone forth to the resting places of those killed, and not one of them would have been spared, despite their fortification in Madinah and their safety in their houses. The remoteness of this is not hidden, because it involves disconnection, and because what is apparent from (upon them) is that they are the ones killed, not the ones killing. It was also said: the meaning is, if you remained in your dwellings, O hypocrites and doubters, and stayed back from fighting, the believers who were obligated to fight would have gone forth to combat, patient and seeking reward, and they would have killed and been killed. This returns to our statement: if you had stayed back from fighting, the believers would not have stayed back.

The word al-muḍāji' is the plural of maḍja', so if it means a sleeping place, then its use for the place of falling is a metaphor (isti'āra, a borrowed use of a word), and if it means the place where the body extends in general, for the living and the dead, then it is literal (ḥaqīqa). It was recited (kataba) with the active verb and the object (al-qatl) in the accusative, and (kutiba 'alayhimu al-qitāl), and (lubarraza) with the doubled letter, in the passive form.

﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts﴾, that is, that Allah the Exalted might examine what is in your breasts through your deeds, for He knows it unseen, and wants to know it witnessed, so that the reward is established upon it. This is said by al-Zajjaj. Or that He might deal with you as one who is tested and examined, as said by several scholars. This is an address to the believers. The lam is for causation, and what follows it is the cause of an implied verb placed before a conjunction with other omitted causes, to indicate their multiplicity, as if it were said: He did what He did for many benefits, ﴿and that He might test...﴾ etc. Or it is for an implied verb after "that is," and for the mentioned testing: He did what He did, and not because of lack of concern for the affairs of His allies and the helpers of His Prophet (ﷺ), for example.

The conjunction here, according to some scholars of verification, is upon His saying: ﴿He sent down upon you﴾, and the separation between them is permissible, because the separating element is part of the complements of the conjoined term, verbally or in meaning. It was also said: there is no omission in the speech, and it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿So that you would not grieve﴾, meaning He rewarded you with grief for two matters: not grieving and being tested. This is deemed weak, because placing those matters in between requires a point at that stage, and that point is not apparent. Even weaker is that the conjunction upon His saying ﴿that He might test you﴾ is hardly acceptable, meaning He turned you away from them in order to test you and to test what is in your breasts. Some made it conjoined to a deleted cause, and both causes are: ﴿it would have caused to go forth﴾, as if it were said: ﴿It would have caused those for whom killing had been decreed to go forth to their resting places﴾, for the execution of the decree, or for many benefits, and for testing.

It is objected that sound taste rejects this, for the context requires explaining the wisdom of what occurred on that day of severity and terror, not explaining the wisdom of the prescribed going forth. The address was directed to the believers because they are the ones counted, and because displaying their condition reveals it to others.

It was also said: it is for both them and the hypocrites, meaning to test what is in your hidden thoughts of sincerity and hypocrisy. It was said: it is for the hypocrites alone, because the context of the verse is directed to them. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and that He might purify what is in your hearts﴾, that is, to clear what is in them of belief from whisperings, favors the first view, because the hypocrites have no belief to be purified and cleansed of whisperings. Perhaps those who hold that the address is only to the hypocrites, or to them with the believers, explain purification as uncovering and distinguishing: that He might reveal what is in your hearts of hidden matters or hypocrisy and distinguish them. However, interpreting purification in this sense makes this clause a kind of emphasis on what precedes it. The word "hearts" is used here, as it has been said, because purification relates to belief, as indicated, and the use of "heart" with this is common, so one says: "he believed with his heart," and you hardly hear them say "he believed with his breast" or "he believed with his chest." In the Qur'an: ﴿Those, He wrote faith in their hearts﴾, and there is not "He wrote faith in their breasts." However, the breast is mentioned with Islam, as in His saying: ﴿So is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam...﴾. Hence some masters said: the heart is the seat of faith, the breast is the place of Islam, the fu'ād (inner heart) is the dawn of witnessing, and the lubb (core of the heart) is the station of true unity. Perhaps the verse on this view returns to our statement: that He might test your Islam and purify your faith. It may be said [Page 98 continues]

that He used that expression while using "breasts" earlier, for variety, on the basis that the meaning of both plurals is one.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ (154), that is, of what is in the hearts which are in the breasts of hidden thoughts. It is described thus because, since the hearts are settled in the breasts, they are treated as if they possess them. So "dhāt" here means "possessor of," not "essence or self of a thing." In the verse there is promise and warning, or one of them alone, depending on the disagreement about the address. It also contains an indication that Allah the Exalted is free of need for testing, and He only displays the form of testing for wisdoms He knows, such as training the believers or displaying the condition of the hypocrites. He chose "breasts" here because the testing free of need for Him, glory be to Him, was connected to what is in them. Purification under the first meaning is cleansing and purifying, and this is not what this clause indicates, namely that He is free of it; rather He did it for a wisdom. Yet if it is meant as uncovering and distinguishing, it is correct to say that this clause indicates that He is also free of need.

From here some scholars of verification permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the object of the two verbs, meaning: He did what He did for testing and uncovering, while He is free of both and encompasses hidden matters. However, it does not then appear why the hidden and secret things are expressed by "possessors of the breasts" rather than "possessors of the hearts," even though the second expression is better suited, because the hearts are their seat directly, while the breasts are their seat only apparently through the hearts. Unless it is said that "possessors of the breasts" means the things that hardly leave the breasts, because they are inherent in them, and are accompanying and inseparable from them, and this is more comprehensive than "possessors of the hearts," because the first applies both to the secrets within the hearts and to the hearts themselves. For each of these two is inseparable from the breasts in that it is inherent in them, unlike the second, which applies only to the secrets, since it is inherent in them rather than in the breasts. In that case, "possessors of the breasts" can be meant in this comprehensive sense, and the expression is used for that reason.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 3, verse 155:

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away﴾ from the enemy (*al-dubur*) at Uhud, O Muslims, or: indeed, those of you who fled to Madinah ﴿on the day the two hosts met﴾, and the two hosts were the host of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the host of Abu Sufyan.

﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip﴾, that is, he sought from them a slip and invited them to it, ﴿because of some of what they had earned﴾ of their sins. The meaning is: the cause of their turning away was that they had obeyed Satan and committed sins, and so they were deprived of divine support and of strengthening of their hearts, until they turned away. On this reading, the slip is not the turning away itself, but the sins that led to it. It is also permissible that the slip into which Satan led them and to which he invited them was the turning away itself. In that case, "some of what they had earned" may mean either: the earlier sins, with the sense of causation being that these sins drew them towards it, since one sin drags another, just as obedience drags obedience; or the acceptance of what Satan adorned for them of defeat, which is what is related from al-Hasan; or the disobedience of the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to remain steadfast in the position, which led them to defeat; or earlier sins not by way of causation but because they disliked jihad while those sins remained upon them. Al-Zajjaj said: Satan reminded them of their faults, which they disliked to bring before God, so they postponed jihad and turned away until they could set their affairs right and fight in a state that is pleasing (to God). The construction, on both interpretations, is for the affirmation of the report (*tahqiq al-khabar*), like the poet's saying:

*Indeed she who struck a tent, emigrating, in Kufa of the army camp, the ghoul has consumed her love.*

It is not of the type where the attribute is the cause of the predicate, as in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are gardens of bliss﴾, because ﴿because of some of what they had earned﴾ rejects that and affirms the affirmation. It is also of the type of *al-tardid lil-ta'liq* (the hedging that suspends a judgment), as in the poet's saying:

*Yellow (of complexion), sorrows never descend upon her courtyard; if a stone touched her, joy would touch it.*

Because ﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip﴾ and so on is the predicate of *inna*. *Inna* was added for emphasis and to lengthen the speech, and *ma* was added to restrain it from governing (the verb).
Page 99
The original structure is: Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met turned away only because Satan caused them to slip, because of some of what they had earned, and so on. This is like your saying: "Indeed, the one who honored you honored you only because you deserve it." Mentioning "some" indicates that among their earnings there were acts of obedience, which do not necessitate the slip. Or it is because this punishment was not for all that they had earned, since the whole would call for more than this; but He, exalted is He, bestowed pardon for much of it. ﴿Had God taken people to account for what they have earned, He would not have left upon its back a single creature﴾.

﴿And God has certainly pardoned them﴾. Glorified is He, He repeated the mention of pardon to reinforce the hope of the sinners in it, to prevent them from despair, and to make their expectations as good as possible. It may be said: this is an establishment (*ta'sis*, introducing new information), not an emphasis (*ta'kid*), so reflect on this.

﴿Indeed God is All-Forgiving﴾ of sins, minor and major, ﴿All-Forbearing﴾ (155), who does not hasten to punish the sinner. This sentence has come as a reason for the pardon of these who turned away, and they were the majority of the people. Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi mentioned that there remained with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud only thirteen people: five of the Emigrants (*al-Muhajirun*): Abu Bakr, Ali, Talha, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; and the rest were from the Helpers (*al-Ansar*), may God be pleased with them all. Among the well-known fugitives were: Uthman, Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla, Kharija ibn Zayd, Abu Hudhayfa ibn Utba, al-Walid ibn Uqba, Sa'd and Uqba, the two sons of Uthman, from the Helpers, from the clan of Banu Zurayq.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning the first three, and from others something different. No explicit report has been found naming more than these. Perhaps the restriction to them is because they went to the greatest extremes in fleeing and did not return to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until a period of time had passed, to the point that some of them did not return until after three days. It is claimed that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You have indeed gone off with it (the defeat) wide and far." As for the rest of the fugitives, they gathered on the mountain on that day. Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, was among this category, as in the report of Ibn Jarir, contrary to the Shi'a. And even if we grant it, there is no reproach after God's pardon for all of them. We do not claim infallibility for the Companions, may God be pleased with them, nor do we make it a condition for the caliphate.

[Page 100 begins where indicated.]

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾. "Those who disbelieved" here means the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), such as Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. This is the view of al-Suddi and Mujahid. Their disbelief is mentioned at the start of the sentence to make clear that their condition differs from that of the believers, and to warn against resembling them, since they are who they are. This indicates that faith (iman) is not merely the verbal profession of the tongue, as the Karramiyya (a sect that holds this view) maintain. Otherwise the hypocrite would not be called a disbeliever. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is all disbelievers in general, that is, "do not be like the disbelievers in reality." ﴿And they said to their brothers﴾ regarding their way (madhhab) or their lineage (nasab). The lam here is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), meaning "they said on account of them." Ibn al-Hajib took it to mean "about" (ʿan). It is not permissible for the intended meaning to be addressing the brothers directly, as appears most obvious, because what follows indicates that they were absent at the time of this statement. As for the view of some that it is valid for the saying to be attributed to their brothers by considering the present ones among them, and that the following phrase refers to another group, this is an artificial interpretation with no need for it, apart from the excess of superfluous elaboration.

﴿When they travel through the land﴾, that is, journey in it for trade or to seek a livelihood, and then die. This is the view of al-Suddi. The root meaning of ḍarb is to strike one thing against another, and it was used for travel because of the striking of the earth by the foot, and then it became a literal term for it. It has also been said that the original meaning of ḍarb fi al-ardh is to go far in travel, and this is disputed. The earth is specifically mentioned because most of their journeys were by land. It has also been said that mentioning "the earth" alone, meaning the land, suffices in place of mentioning the sea. It has also been said that "the earth" includes both land and sea, and this is not far-fetched. The word idhā (when) is used, whereas the proper form of the sentence would have been idh (since/when in the past), as they said, "They said..." (lamma qalū). The word idhā indicates time by its form, which contradicts the time indicated by the verb it governs, and it is used [Page 101 is not here yet; continue] to observe the narration of a past situation (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl), meaning the representation of a past state as if it were present. The meaning of this is that you imagine yourself existing in that past time, or you imagine that past time as if it existed now. This is like your saying: "They said that when they strike (on the earth)," where the meaning is "when they struck," except that you have used the present form to evoke the image of their striking in the land. Two objections have been raised. The first is that the narration of a present state occurs only where the form of the present is used, whereas this is a form of the future, since the meaning of ﴿idhā ḍarabū﴾ is "when they strike" in what is yet to come. The second is that their statement, "If they had been with us," came only after their death, so how can it be restricted to striking in the land?

The first objection is answered by saying that ﴿idhā ḍarabū﴾ carries the sense of continuity, as in ﴿when they meet those who believe﴾, and so it spoils the representation for the sake of the present situation. The second is answered by saying that ﴿they said to their brothers﴾ stands in the position of the conditional's response in meaning, so the meaning is: "Do not be like those who disbelieved, and when their brothers are struck and die, or are [out] raiding and are killed, they say: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died nor been killed﴾." The striking and the killing are both in the sense of the future. The restriction of the saying to striking is in reference to the last part, which is death, while killing, although not mentioned explicitly, is indicated by what is in the saying, and so it is intended in meaning. What is considered is the concurrence (muqaranah) according to common usage, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you depart from ʿArafat, remember Allah at the Sacred Landmark﴾, and as when you say: "When the crescent of Muharram appears, I will come to you in its middle."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Here idhā substitutes for what has passed of time and what is yet to come," meaning that it is for mere time, or for the intention of continuity. What the correct analysis requires is that ﴿idhā ḍarabū﴾ not be made a circumstantial adverb of qālū, but rather a time-adverb for what occurs to the brothers when this is said on their account and concerning them, as if it were said: "They said on account of the circumstances afflicting their brothers, ﴿when they strike﴾, meaning when they were striking." This is what the Allama al-Thani said. You know that stripping idhā of the meaning of the future and making it mean time in general is sufficient to explain the verse and removes its difficulty. The intention of continuity from it does not dispel the objection to that explanation, because if it is for continuity, it includes the past, and so it is not for the narration of a present state. Likewise, if qālū is the response, it becomes future, and so the mentioned narration cannot apply to it either. What the correct analysis requires is refuted by the fact that establishing the validity of such a usage in Arabic is like pulling thorns from a thornbush, and more firmly grounded, though still distant, is what Abu Hayyan said: that idhā may remain for the future, by supposing that its governing element is a future-oriented noun in construction, with the pronoun in ﴿if they had been﴾ referring to their brothers in wording but not in meaning, in the manner of "I have a dirham and its half." The estimate is: "They said, out of fear for the destruction of their brothers, ﴿when they strike﴾ or ﴿are [out] raiding﴾, ﴿if they had been﴾, that is, our other brothers whose death and killing had already occurred, ﴿with us, they would not have died nor been killed.﴾" In that case this saying is a discouragement to their remaining brothers from journeying and raiding, lest they suffer what befell the earlier ones. The reason they did not take idhā here to mean the narration of a present state, as some have said by taking it that way after an oath, as in ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, is that for them to claim the narration of a present state free of turbidity would not be accepted by the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) there, for they have deemed that its remaining for the future is without any objection.

It is also permissible in the verse for qālū to mean yaqūlūna (they say), and the use of the past form in the sense of the future has occurred in their speech, such as his saying:

*And indeed I come to you, to thank what has passed of the matter, and to claim what was to be tomorrow.*

Likewise it is permissible that it remain on its meaning, and idhā be taken to mean the past, since it comes for that, just as it came for the future according to some, as in His saying exalted: ﴿And when they saw a trade or a diversion, they dispersed toward it﴾, and His saying:

*And a companion who increases the cup's sweetness, I gave him drink when the stars had set.*

In that case there is no conflict between the time of the condition and the time of the conditioned. So reflect on all of this. The clause that specifies the aspect of resemblance and similarity which they were forbidden from is the clause coordinated with the relative clause, and the meaning is: "Do not imitate the disbelievers in their saying to their brothers, when they travel, ﴿or are [out] raiding﴾."

[Page 101]

Ghuzzan (ﻏُزًّى) is the plural of ghāzin (raider), like ʿāfin and ʿuffan (ʿāfin being "forgiving"), and it is one of the rare plurals of defective roots. Some cited as evidence for it the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*A land of dust-covered horizons, its landmarks humble, its ponds worn out, its spring-water murky.*

It is also pluralized as ghuzāh, like qāḍin and quḍāh (judges), and as ghaziyy, like ḥājj and ḥajīj (pilgrims) and qāṭin and qaṭīn (residents), and as ghuzzāʾ, like fāsiq and fussāq (wicked people). They recited for it the verse of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:

*One day among raiders, one day at Surayah, and one day at Khashkhash of the leg, with its ridges.*

It is also pluralized as ghāzūn, like ḍāribin and ḍāribūn (strikers), and it is in the accusative case with a fatḥah estimated on the alif that replaced the elided waw, due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters.
