Its original form was ghazawā: the waw was vocalized, the letter before it was opened, so it was changed to an alif, and then it was elided. It has been read with the lightening of the zāy. Abu al-Baqa said: "In this there are two possibilities. The first: its original form was ghuzzāʾatan, and the hāʾ was elided for lightness, because the tāʾ marks the plural, and that has been achieved by the form itself." The second: "It was intended as the reading of the majority, and one of the two zāys was elided to avoid doubling." This second part was mentioned together with what precedes it, though it is included in it, because it is what is intended in this context, and what precedes it is a preparation for it. It has been said that the striking on the earth may be found without travel, on the basis that by it is meant long travel, so the striking was specified on this reading. That they were raiders is general in one respect and specific in another. The reason He did not say ghazwan (an infinitive) is to indicate the continuation of their characterization by the title of being raiders, or that this has ended, meaning they were raiders in what had passed.

﴿If they had been﴾ residing ﴿with us﴾, by not traveling or raiding, ﴿they would not have died nor been killed﴾. Rather, they would have remained longer than what they remained. The conditional clause (al-jumlah al-imtināʿiyyah) is in the position of an accusative object of qālū, and it indicates that there is an omitted element in the preceding speech, namely: "when they strike in the land and die, ﴿or are [out] raiding﴾ and are killed." Estimating "and die" or "or are killed" in each of the two parts is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿So that Allah may make that a cause of anguish in their hearts﴾. This is connected to qālū and falls within its scope, and it is part of the thing being compared. The reference to the statement is with regard to what it contains of belief. The lam is the lam of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), and the meaning is: "Do not be like them in the false statement and corrupt belief, which lead to anguish, regret, and destruction in the end." To this the words of al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli point. It has also been said that it is connected to "do not be" (lā takūnū), as the reason for the prohibition. In that case it falls outside the scope of the thing being compared, but the statement and belief are both included in it. The meaning is: "Do not be like them in uttering that statement and holding that belief, so that Allah may make your not being with them in that statement and belief a cause of anguish in their hearts alone." Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is a statement without verification, because making anguish is not a cause of the prohibition. It is only a cause of the fulfilment of the prohibition, which is the absence of similarity, so the attainment of that absence and of opposition in what they say and believe results in what angers and grieves them, since you did not agree with them in what they said and believed, and so the striking in the land and raiding is abandoned. It seems that the speaker was confused about requiring the absence of similarity by the attainment of absence, and understanding this is obscure and subtle.

Al-Safaqusi criticized him by saying that this objection would necessarily entail that "do not disobey, so that you may enter Paradise" is impermissible, because the prohibition is not a cause of entering Paradise. Likewise, "obey Allah, exalted is He, so that you may enter Paradise" would be impermissible, because the command is not a cause of entering it. Then he said: "The truth is that the lam is connected to the verb prohibited and commanded, in the sense that refraining from the act or performing the commanded act is a cause of entering Paradise or the like, and this presents no difficulty." It has also been said that it is connected to "do not be," and that what is indicated by the prohibition is what is referred to. In that case all of this falls outside the scope of the thing being compared, and the meaning is: "Do not be like them, so that Allah may make your not being like them an anguish in their hearts." On this view, "and they said" is the beginning of a new statement, coordinated with various implied things, as the sayings, states, and actions of the hypocrites require. The connection of this with what precedes it is that, since warning had been given against being like them, it encompassed all the vices connected with them, and the mentioned saying was singled out because it is more shameful and clearer as evidence of their hypocrisy. That is, they are enemies of the religion, who did not fall short in harm and opposition, but rather did such-and-such and said such-and-such. From this one may know what those implied things are. According to each of the three aspects, the pronoun in ﴿in their hearts﴾ refers to the disbelievers. Although anguish occurs only in the heart, the heart is mentioned to indicate firm establishment and to signal that it does not cease.

Ibn Tamjid permitted the pronoun to refer back to the believers. In that case the lam is connected only to qālū, and he explained the verse in a way that calls for wonder.

﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾. This is a refutation of their false saying immediately after explaining its harm. That is, Allah alone is the true agent in life and death, not residing or traveling. He, exalted is He, may give life to the traveler and the raider even as they plunge into the places of death, and He may cause death to the resident and the one sitting at home even though they are under the shade of blessings. It is not meant that He, exalted is He, brings life and death into existence, although this is the apparent meaning, because the discourse is not about that, and the refutation is not achieved by it. The discourse concerns the bringing about of what produces them. It has also been said that the meaning is that He, exalted is He, gives life and causes death whether one is traveling or at home, at the presence of the appointed term, and no one can delay what He has advanced, nor advance what He has delayed, nor reverse what He has decreed, nor escape what He has determined. In this there is a prohibition on the believers from staying behind in jihad out of fear of being killed. The waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl), so there is no objection that it is impermissible to coordinate a report with a non-report (inshāʾ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 156 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ (156) This is an encouragement to obedience and a warning against disobedience, or a threat to the believers lest they resemble the disbelievers. For the seeing of Allah, like His knowledge, is used in the Qur'an to mean recompense for what is seen, just as for what is known. The believers, although they did not resemble them in what was mentioned, nevertheless their regret over leaving Madinah calls for this warning. Ibn Kathir and the people of Kufa, except ʿAsim, read *yaʿmalūna* with the *yāʾ* (they do), and the plural pronoun then refers to the disbelievers. The "deed" is general, encompassing the aforementioned statement, its source, which is the corrupt belief, and what follows from that of actions. For this reason the verse uses the attribute of sight rather than the attribute of hearing. The mention of the Exalted Name, and the fronting of the adverbial phrase, are for reasons already mentioned more than once.

* * *

Here, by way of allusion (*ishara*), ﴿And how many a prophet﴾, that is, how many, a prophet of elevated rank and exalted station, who in the realm of the souls is the holy spirit, ﴿fought alongside him﴾, the enemy of Allah, the Most High, namely the commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammara*), ﴿large companies (*ribbiyyun*)﴾, those who take on the character of the Lord, and they are the spiritual powers. ﴿They did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah﴾, that is, the path to reaching Him, from the fatigue of spiritual striving. ﴿Nor did they falter﴾ in seeking the truth, ﴿nor did they submit﴾ or yield to other than Him. ﴿And Allah loves the patient﴾, those who endure the hardships of the struggle against the self. ﴿And their words were only: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, that is, cover over for us our existences by pouring upon us the lights of true existence, ﴿and our excesses in our affair﴾, that is, our transgression of the bounds of the outward Shariah at the shocks of the theophanies (*tajalliyyat*), ﴿and make firm our feet﴾ in the places of the battles of our souls, ﴿and help us﴾ with Your support and aid, ﴿against the disbelieving people﴾ who conceal Your lordship.

﴿So Allah gave them﴾ because of their supplication, expressed through the tongues of their readiness and their turning to Him, the Most High, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, which is the station of the unity of acts and the unity of attributes, ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, which is the station of the unity of the Essence. ﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾ in seeking, who do not turn toward the others.

﴿O you who believe﴾, true belief, ﴿if you obey those who disbelieve﴾, and they are the disbelieving souls and their attributes, ﴿they will turn you back on your heels﴾ down to the lowest of the low, which is the prison of animality, ﴿and you will turn back losing﴾ yourselves.

﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector﴾, your Helper, ﴿and He is the best of helpers﴾ for whoever relies upon Him and cuts off his gaze from anything other than Him.

﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, fear, ﴿for that they associated with Allah that for which He had sent down no authority﴾, that is, for which there is no existence, ﴿authority﴾, that is, proof, since there is no proof for its existence that He could send down, given that its non-existence is established by its very nature. He, glorified is He, made the casting of terror into their hearts a consequence of their polytheism, [Page 103] because courage and all the other virtues are balances (*iʿtidalat*) in the powers of the soul when it is kindled by the light of the heart illuminated by the light of tawhid. Therefore they are not complete or real except for the monotheist who is certain. As for the polytheist, he is veiled from the source of strength by what he has associated with Allah, which has no existence and no essence in reality, so he is weak, clinging to a straw (*qarmala*). ﴿Their refuge is the Fire﴾, which is the fire of deprivation, ﴿and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾, who placed things in other than their proper places, and worshipped names they had named, which Allah has not sent down any authority for.

﴿Allah had already fulfilled His promise to you﴾, which was conditional upon patience and piety, ﴿when you were killing them﴾, that is, you were slaughtering the armies of the human attributes with a devastating slaughter, ﴿by His permission﴾ and command, not according to the dictates of nature. ﴿Until, when you lost courage﴾, that is, became cowardly at the manifestation of majesty, ﴿and disputed about the matter﴾, that is, you differed concerning the affair of seeking, ﴿and disobeyed﴾ the guiding, nurturing teacher, ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾, namely the attainment of the lights of the Presence. ﴿Among you were those who desired this world﴾ because of the deficiency of their resolve and the weakness of their judgment, ﴿and among you were those who desired the Hereafter﴾ because of the length of their reach and the strength of their intellect. ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, that is, from the enemies of your souls and their armies, ﴿to test you﴾, that is, to try you with concealment after the manifestation through the lights of the contemplations, and with sobriety after intoxication by the cups of the ecstatic states, and with weaning after being nourished by the milk of tenderness, as the majesty requires. ﴿And He certainly pardoned you﴾ after that, so you turned to Him, as the requirement of beauty demands. ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾ in both the stages of nearness and distance. How graceful is the saying of the one who said:

*So he was harsh that they might be deterred, and whoever is wise, let him sometimes be harsh toward the one he loves.*

﴿When you were climbing﴾ the mountain of turning toward the Truth, ﴿and not turning﴾, that is, not looking, ﴿to anyone﴾ of the two affairs, this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And the Messenger﴾, that is, the Messenger of the inspirations, ﴿was calling you﴾: "To Me, servants of Allah! To Me, servants of Allah!" ﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾, that is, in place of the grief of this world and the Hereafter He repaid you with the grief of seeking the Truth, ﴿so that you would not grieve over what escaped you﴾ of the adornments of this world, ﴿nor over what befell you﴾ of the shocks of the manifestation of subjugation. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, because He, glorified is He, is closer to you than you are to yourselves.

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after the grief, security, a drowsiness﴾, that is, a meaning from His gentle graces that appeared in the form of drowsiness, and it is the divine tranquility (*sakina rahmaniyya*), ﴿enveloping a group of you﴾, and they are the truthful in seeking, ﴿while a group was concerned only with themselves﴾, and they are the people of the souls, for they have no concern except the share of their souls and the enjoyment of their pleasures. ﴿They thought about Allah other than the truth﴾ according to the requirement of the evil of their readiness. ﴿They say: "Do we have any say in the matter?"﴾, that is, the creation has come between us and the management of affairs, and if they had not, we would have done what is good for us. ﴿Say: "Indeed, the matter is entirely Allah's﴾, so He alone is the One who disposes of affairs as readiness requires, so there is no management alongside His management, and no existence for anyone besides Him. ﴿They conceal within themselves﴾, in their wicked souls, ﴿what they do not disclose﴾ to you, in their claim, O guide, the perfect one. ﴿They say: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here"﴾ by the sword of desires. (﴿here﴾), that is, in this created state. ﴿Say: "Even if you had been in your houses"﴾, which are the abodes of original non-existence before the manifestation of these determinations, ﴿those whom death had decreed would have gone forth﴾ according to knowledge, ﴿to their resting places﴾ that were decreed for them in the tablet of eternity, namely the wasteland of desires. For He, glorified is He, said: ﴿No calamity befalls on the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being﴾, that is, before We make it manifest in this determination. Allah, glorified is He, did what He did for many wisdoms. ﴿And that Allah may test what is in your breasts﴾, that is, that He may try what is in your readiness of truthfulness, sincerity, reliance upon Him, and the like of these traits, and bring them forth from potentiality into actuality. ﴿And that He may purify what is in your hearts﴾, that is, He may refine what has come forth from the hidden place of the breast into the storehouse of the heart, from the impurity of whisperings and the thoughts of the self. For affliction is a whip with which Allah, the Most High, drives His servants toward Him. Hence the report: "The people most severely tested are the prophets, then the saints, then the next best, and the next best." And how well the one said:

*By Allah's grace on the calamities, for they are the rust of the base and the polisher of the free.*

*I was but a lump, and they forged me into a sword, and the edge of their vicissitudes brought out my blade.*

[Page 104] This is because at that time they turn to the Truth, and there appears in each of them only what lies in the hidden place of his readiness, as it is said: "In the time of testing, a man is either honored or disgraced." The address in both places is to the believers. It has also been said: the first address is to the hypocrites and the second to the believers. And He, glorified is He, specified the breasts for the first group because the breast is the mine of rancor and whispering, and so it is more fitting to the state of the hypocrites. He specified the hearts for the second group because the heart is the seat of faith and tranquility, and it is more fitting to the state of the believers. The relation of Islam by the tongue to faith in the heart is like the relation of the breast to the heart. It has been said: For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And Allah knows the secrets of the breasts﴾, on the basis that what is meant by it is warning and admonition against being associated with the qualities He does not approve of, of which the breast is the hiding place.

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met﴾, the gathering of the spirit and its powers, and the gathering of the soul and its powers, ﴿it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ of sins, for these produce darkness, and Satan has no way over the son of Adam through adornment and whispering except when he finds darkness in the heart. You may also leave the two gatherings on their outward meaning, and the rest of the allusion remains as it is. ﴿And Allah has already pardoned them﴾ when their hearts were illuminated by the light of regret and repentance. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾. In accordance with this, the acts of disobedience appeared and were followed by repentance, so that this would be a mirror for the manifestation of the attributes of Allah, the Most High.

From this comes the report: "Were you not to sin, Allah would bring about a people who sin and then seek forgiveness, and they would be forgiven."

It is related that Ibrahim ibn Adham, may Allah be pleased with him, one night repeated in the circumambulation more than anything else his saying: "O Allah, preserve me from sins." He then heard a voice from his heart saying: "O Ibrahim, you ask Him for preservation, and all His servants ask Him for preservation. So if He preserves you, upon whom does He bestow favor, and upon whom does He show generosity?"

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ by seeing others and believing in the influence of other than Him, and who said, concerning their brothers when they journeyed in the land, that is, when they left them by abandoning what they were upon, and traveled in the land of their souls and took the path of right guidance, ﴿or were raiders﴾, that is, fighting alongside their greatest enemies, which are their souls that lie between their sides, and their powers and armies of caprice and Satan. ﴿Had they been﴾ staying ﴿with us﴾, agreeing with us, ﴿they would not have died﴾ from the hardship of spiritual discipline, ﴿nor been killed﴾ by the sword of striving, and they would have been relieved of this fatigue. ﴿That Allah may make that﴾, that is, not being like them, ﴿a regret﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿in their hearts﴾ when they see what Allah, the Most High, has prepared for you. ﴿And Allah gives life to whom He wills﴾ with eternal life, ﴿and causes to die whom He wills﴾ with the death of ignorance and distance from the Presence. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, a warning against inclining toward the words of the deniers and believing in them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 157:

﴿And if you are killed﴾, O believers, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, that is, in jihad, ﴿or die﴾ a natural death, ﴿while you are engaged in it, in deed or intention﴾.

﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾ (157). That is, what the disbelievers amass of the worldly benefits and pleasures throughout their lifetimes. This is an encouragement for the believers to engage in jihad, and that it is something the competitors should compete for. It also brings consolation and solace to them for what has befallen them in the way of Allah, the Exalted, after the nullification of whatever might deter them from raising the word of Allah, the Exalted. The first lam is a preparatory lam for the oath (lam al-tawtiah), the second falls in the answer to the oath, and the answer to the conditional clause is omitted, because the answer to the oath indicates it and fulfils its meaning. ﴿Forgiveness﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and (min) ﴿from﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as its attribute. It was described thus to show concern for it and as a sign of the certainty of its occurrence. Some scholars took the view that another attribute is to be assumed, meaning: ﴿surely there is forgiveness for you from Allah﴾, and the attribute of ﴿mercy﴾ is omitted because of what is mentioned indicating it. The tanwin in both words is for diminution (ta'qil), and this does not contradict what the description points to. The affirmation of the basic notion of goodness (khayriyyah) in what the disbelievers amass, as the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) requires, is either on the basis that what they amass in this world may be of what is lawful, which is in reality good, or that it comes according to their own statement and belief that those possessions are good. For ma (ما) it is permitted that it be a relative pronoun (mawsulah), or an indefinite described noun with the returning pronoun omitted, or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), in which case the object is then omitted, meaning: from their gathering of wealth.

Nafi' and the people of Kufa, other than Asim, read (مِتُّمْ) with a kasra. Hafs agreed with them in all other instances except here. The rest read it with a damma on the mim. On the first reading it is from (مات يموت) in the pattern of (خفتم من خاف يخاف), and on the second from (مات يموت) in the pattern of (كنتم من كان يكون). Hafs, on the authority of Asim, read (يَجْمَعُونَ) with the ya, in the third-person form, and the rest read (تَجْمَعُونَ) with the ta, in the second-person form, the pronoun referring to the believers. He placed killing before dying because it carries greater reward and is greater in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, so the consequence of forgiveness and mercy upon it is stronger.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 3, verse 158:

He reversed the order in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you die or are killed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾ (158), because death is more common than killing, and both are equal in being gathered. The meaning is that whatever cause of your perishing occurs, you will be gathered to Allah, the Exalted, and to no other, so that He will recompense each of you as he deserves: He will reward the good-doer for his good deeds and the evil-doer for his evil deeds. There is no one other than Him from whom reward is hoped for or from whom the averting of punishment is expected. So prefer what brings you near to Him and draws His pleasure to you, namely acting by His obedience and striving in His way, and do not incline toward the world.

It is attributed to al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with him):

Since bodies were created for death,
the killing of a man by the sword, by Allah, is better.

The discussion of the two lams is like the discussion of their two counterparts with two lams. The introduction of the lam of oath before the fronted complement indicates emphasis on restriction and exclusivity, that His divinity (ulūhiyyah, divinity) is what requires this. Some have claimed that the fronting of this complement is merely for the sake of emphasis, and that what follows it, being a fāṣilah (verse-ending), adds to its beauty. What we pointed out first is better. They said: Were it not for this fronting, the verb would have to be emphasized with the nun (nūn al-tawkīd, emphatic nun), because an affirmative imperfect verb referring to the future must be emphasized when accompanied by the lam. This is contrary to the Kufans, who permit the interchange of the two. The apparent sense of the practice of some verifiers (muhaqqiqūn) indicates that there is an implied element in this sentence, by the context of what precedes it, i.e., "And if you die or are killed in the way of Allah." The reading of it as general is likely better.

Some claimed that the verse contains a division of the stations of servanthood into three categories. Whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, out of fear of His Fire, He grants him security from what he fears, and to this points His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah﴾. Whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, out of longing for His Paradise, He grants him what he hopes for, and to this points His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and mercy﴾, because mercy is among the names of Paradise. Whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, out of longing for His noble Face, desiring nothing else, he is the sincere servant upon whom the Truth, majestic is His majesty, manifests itself in the abode of His honor, and to this points His saying, may His name be exalted: ﴿to Allah you will be gathered﴾. It is not hidden that this is a matter of interpretation (ta'wil), not of exegesis (tafsir).

[Page 106]

**"So by mercy from Allah you were gentle with them"** is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). The *fa'* (فاء) indicates the sequence of the statement's meaning with respect to what the context implies: that those who fled deserved blame and reproach from him (ﷺ), by the requirement of human nature, since they had fled from him while the pools of terror were full and they had hurried to flee while the war was still standing on its shin. Or (it indicates) the vastness of the scope of His forgiveness and mercy. The *ba'* (باء) is connected to *linta* (لنت), and the fronting of the word (*bihi*, بما, i.e. the *ba'* with *ma*) is for restriction. *Ma* (ما) is superfluous, for emphasis, and the leading exegetes hold this view. It is what is transmitted from Qatada. Al-Zajjaj reported the consensus (ijma', إجماع: agreement of the scholars) on it, but there is room for examination of this, for al-Akhfash and others said: it is permissible that it be an indefinite noun in the sense of "a thing," and "mercy" (*rahmatin*, رحمة) is an apposition to it. It is also permitted that it be a qualifier of it. It was also said: it is interrogative for expressing wonder, and the estimate is "by what mercy were you gentle with them?" The tanwin in *rahmatin* in every interpretation is for magnification. *Min* (من) is connected to an omitted element which takes the position of a qualifier of it, meaning: "by a great mercy from Allah, the Exalted, you were gentle with them, and did not rebuke them." Perhaps what is meant by this mercy is that He, glory be to Him and exalted, strengthened his heart (ﷺ) and singled him out with noble character. The gentleness and softness of demeanour is taken as a consequence of the strengthening of the heart, because whoever controls himself at the time of anger is perfect in courage.

It was said: the statement in this context conveys two benefits. One of them indicates his courage (ﷺ), and the second indicates his gentleness. It is therefore of the category of completion, and these two attributes were combined in him (ﷺ) on the Day of Uhud, when he stood firm until his companions returned to him, although what befell him had befallen him. Then he neither reprimanded them nor rebuked them for fleeing, but rather shared with them in their grief.

**"And had you been harsh"**, i.e. rough of demeanour, coarse of character, and boorish in dealing, in speech and in action, **"hard-hearted"**, i.e. severe. Al-Kalbi said: **"harsh"** in words, **"hard-hearted"** in deeds.

Some said that the *fazz* (فظ) is one of bad character in outward matters, in speech and deeds, while **"hard-hearted"** is one of bad character in inward matters. The second is the cause of the first, and the cause was put first because of its evidence, since it is what can be perceived. It is possible to say that what is meant is: "had you been contrary to those two attributes expressed by mercy," which is rashness, alluded to by harshness and bad character, indicated by hardness of heart. For the hardness of the heart and its failure to be affected is followed by every blameworthy attribute. For this reason it has been transmitted: "The hearts furthest from Allah, the Exalted, are the hard hearts."

It seems that because of its remoteness it was introduced with "it is possible" (*yumkin*, يمكن). In every interpretation there is an ellipsis in the statement, meaning: "had you been harsh and hard-hearted, and did not soften toward them, and were severe toward them, **they would have scattered from around you**", i.e. they would have dispersed from you, fled from you, and not inclined to you, and thrown themselves into the pits of destruction, and the matter of what you were sent with, of guiding them and directing them to the path, would not have been organized.

**"So pardon them"** is consequent upon what precedes it, meaning: since the matter is as such, pardon them in what concerns your rights. **"And ask forgiveness for them"** from Allah, in what concerns His rights, glory be to Him and exalted, completing compassion and perfecting training. **"And consult them in the matter"**, i.e. in war. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it by way of Ibn Sirin from Ubayda, and it is suitable to the context. Or it means: in this and similar matters in which consultation is customarily practised. This view was taken by a group.

It has been disputed concerning his (ﷺ) consulting his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, in matters of religion when there is no revelation. Whoever rejects his (ﷺ) use of independent reasoning (*ijtihad*, اجتهاد: independent legal reasoning) holds that it is not permissible. Whoever does not reject it, and this is the more sound view, holds that it is permissible. Its benefit is seeking support from their opinion. This is supported by what Imam Ahmad transmitted from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr and Umar: "If you two were to agree on a counsel, I would not oppose you both." Or it is for consoling their hearts. Qatada took this view, for Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to consult his companions in matters, while revelation from heaven was coming to him, because it is more pleasing to the hearts of the people, or so that it would be a sunnah after him for his community." Al-Hasan took this view, for al-Bayhaqi transmitted from him that he said concerning the verse: "Allah knew that there was no need for them, but He wished that those after him should follow his example." This is supported by what Ibn Adi and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted with a good chain from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the verse 'and consult them in the matter' was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Allah and His Messenger are free of need of it, but Allah made it a mercy for my community. Whoever among them consults will not lack right guidance, and whoever abandons it will not lack error.'"

It was said: the benefit of this is that He tests them, so that the sincere advisor is distinguished from the deceiver. This is not correct. Al-Jassas claimed that it is impermissible for the command to consult to be for the sake of consoling the souls, for if it were known to them that when they exhaust their effort in deriving the correct answer to what they were asked about, and then it was not acted upon, there would be no consoling of their souls in that; rather there would be in it a causing of their unease, by informing them that their opinions were not accepted and not relied upon. He affirmed that there must be a benefit in his (ﷺ) consulting them, which is seeking support from what they have, and that there must be for the Prophet (ﷺ) with them a kind of independent reasoning, so that what agreed with his opinion was acted upon, and what opposed it was left without reproach. In this is guidance toward independent reasoning and its permissibility in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and an indication of the rank of the Companions, and that they were all people of independent reasoning, and that their inner states are pleasing to Allah, the Exalted. End of quotation.

There is room for examination in this, since it is no secret to whoever consults his own conscience that in the words of an elder to a younger, "What do you see in such-and-such a matter?" and "What do you have concerning it?" there is consoling of his soul and encouragement for it to acquire opinions and exercise thought, especially when his opinion sometimes coincides with the opinion of the elder, even if the opinion that agrees is not the one acted upon, but rather the opinion that agrees is acted upon. As for what he claimed, that if the opinion is not acted upon there is unease in it, this is not accepted, especially in what we are concerned with, because the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, knew the exalted rank of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that their minds in comparison to his noble mind are like the faint star in comparison to the sun at midday. Moreover, whoever said that the benefit of consultation is the consoling of the soul indicated that revelation came to him, so he was free of it, and in that case the intention of consoling is more complete and more evident, because in consultation at that time there is an exposure of them to what might agree with revelation. And the unease caused by non-action here is more remote, because its basis is following revelation, and it is known to them that it is more deserving of being followed, because it comes from Allah, the Subtle, the All-Aware, as is not hidden. Then what was mentioned, that in this there is an indication that all the Companions are people of independent reasoning, is within the scope of prohibition. For a ruler's command, for example, to his agent to consult the people of his town in his affairs does not require that he consult each and every one of them in that; rather it is hardly intended at all. Rather the intention is that he consult the people of opinion among them and those trained in them. And that all the Companions were so is the first point of the claim, and without proving it there is the battle of the Camel and the battle of Siffin.

What supports that the Companions whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to consult are the people of opinion and planning, and not all of them without distinction, is what al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, from Ibn Abbas, that he said concerning "and consult them in the matter": Abu Bakr and Umar. And by the route of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from the scholar (Ibn Abbas, al-Habr) that the verse was revealed concerning the two of them. Yes, if the consultation were merely for consoling the souls without seeking support, there would be a basis for consulting any one of them, even if he were not among the people of opinion. But al-Jassas did not build his statement on that.

It remains that between what Imam Ahmad transmitted of "his (ﷺ) saying to the two Umars, may Allah be pleased with them both: 'If you two were to agree upon a counsel, I would not oppose you both,'" and what Ibn Adi and al-Bayhaqi transmitted of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), at the revelation of the verse: "Indeed Allah and His Messenger are free of need of it, but Allah made it a mercy for my community," there is a contradiction, unless the report of their not being opposed if they agreed is understood as pointing to the elevation of their rank and the exaltedness of their station, and that their agreement on a matter would be nothing but in accord with what is with Allah, the Exalted, which is what is relied upon and acted upon. And it seems that in his saying (ﷺ): "I would not oppose you both," rather than "I would act upon your words," for example, there is a kind of indication of what we have said. So reflect.

Ibn Abbas read, as al-Bukhari transmitted in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* from him: "and consult them in some of the matter" (*fi ba'di al-amr*, في بعض الأمر). **"And when you have resolved"**, i.e. when you have firmly determined your heart upon the action and its execution after consultation, as the *fa'* (فاء) indicates.

**"Then put your trust in Allah"**, i.e. rely upon Him, have confidence in Him, and entrust your affair to Him, for He is the most knowing of what is most fitting. The origin of *tawakkul* (trust in God; توكل) is the manifestation of helplessness, reliance upon another, and being content with him in doing what one needs. This, for us, is upon Allah, glory be to Him, and it does not negate observing the causes; rather it is with observing them together with delegating the matter to Him, exalted is His glory. The saying "tie it and trust" (*i'qilha wa tawakkal*) guides to this. But according to our masters the Sufis, it is the complete neglect of planning. It is transmitted from Khalid ibn Zayd that he read "when I have resolved" (*fa-idha 'azamtu*, فإذا عزمت) in the first person, and the meaning is: "when I have settled something for you and specified it for you, then put your trust in Me, and do not consult anyone about it." The shift of person is for cultivating awe, for explaining the trust, and for the command to it, for the title of divinity, comprising all the attributes of speech, requires trust in Him, glory be to Him, and the command to it.

**"Indeed Allah loves those who put their trust"** in Him, who have confidence in Him and are devoted to Him, so He helps them and guides them to what is better for them, as love requires. The sentence is a reason for trusting in Him, glory be to Him. The fine order of the verse has been observed, for he (ﷺ) was first commanded to pardon them in matters concerning his own person; when they reached this station, he was commanded to ask forgiveness for them regarding what is between them and Allah, so that the two obligations would be lifted from them. When they arrived here, he was commanded to consult them in the matter, since they had become free of the two obligations and purified of them. Then after that he (ﷺ) was commanded to trust in Allah, the Exalted, and to devote himself to Him, because He, glory be to Him, is the most upright support and the greatest refuge, by which causes alone have effect, and whose needs are fulfilled only at His door.

This is a sentence begun anew, presented through a shift of address (talwin al-khitab (a shift in the mode of address)), to honour the believers, to make reliance upon Him obligatory, to encourage obedience to Him, through which one deserves victory, and to warn against disobeying Him, through which one deserves abandonment. That is: if He wills your victory, as He willed it on the day of Badr, then no one will overcome you, by way of the negation of the genus (nafy al-jins (the generic negation)), which encompasses all the individuals of the overcomer, in essence and attribute. Thus it is more eloquent than "no one will overcome you," since it indicates the negation of the attribute only.

Then, the implication (mafhum) from the apparent wording of the noble text is, as Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud)) said, although the negation of their being overcome is stated without an explicit reference to the negation of equality, which is what the context requires. Nevertheless, what is understood from it with certainty is the negation of equality and the affirmation of the superiority of those addressed. So when you say, "There is no one more generous than so-and-so, and none more excellent than him," what is understood is necessarily that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. This is a matter that holds across all languages. The explicit negation is not the only case; it also holds for what comes in the form of a denying interrogative (istifham inkari (interrogative of denial)), as in His saying, ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God?﴾, in many places of the Revelation. We have indicated this topic earlier.

﴿And if He forsakes you﴾, that is, and if He wills your abandonment (khidhlan) and withholds His aid from you, as He did on the day of Uhud.

It has also been read as ﴿yakhdhulukum﴾, from akhdhalahu, when one makes him forsaken (makhdhul).

﴿Then who is it that will help you﴾ is a denying interrogative, indicating the absence of a helper in the manner of the absence of an overcomer. It has been said: the answer to the condition in the first case came as an explicit negation, but in the second it did not come in that way, out of gentleness towards the believers, since He stated plainly to them the absence of victory, without stating explicitly that they have no helper, although the speech implies this.

﴿after Him﴾, that is, after His abandonment, or after God (Allah) Himself, meaning: if you go beyond Him. On the first reading, "ba'd" (after) is a temporal adverb, which is its original use. On the second, it is used metaphorically for place. ﴿And upon God﴾, not upon anyone else, as the placing of the object first indicates.

﴿So let the believers put their trust﴾ (160). By "the believers" is meant either the genus of believers, with those addressed included in it in the primary sense, or those addressed specifically, by way of the shift of person (iltifat (shift of grammatical person)). On either reading, the honour of those addressed is evident, together with an allusion to the reason why reliance upon Him, exalted is He, is necessary. The fa' (then) is, as they have said, either for the sequence of what follows it, or for commanding it upon what has passed concerning the believers' victory and defeat, given God's aid to them or His abandonment of them. For knowledge of this necessarily calls for restricting reliance to Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 161 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate﴾ (yaghulla). That is, it is not valid or fitting for any of the prophets to betray the trust in the spoils of war (maghnam), because betrayal is incompatible with prophethood. The root meaning of ghull (misappropriation, embezzlement of booty) is taking something secretly, and for this reason the term is used for theft. Then, in the lexicon, it was specialized to mean stealing from the spoils before their division, and it is also called ghulul. It has been said that it was named this because hands are "shackled" (maghlula) in it, meaning restrained. It is "a ghull," which is the iron ring that joins a captive's hand to his neck, and it is also called jami'a. Al-Rummani and others said: the root of ghulul is from ghalal, which is the entry of water into the gaps of trees. Betrayal was called ghulul because it occurs in possession covertly, through a means other than that which is permitted. From the same root come ghill (rancour), ghalil (the burning of thirst), and ghilala (a shirt of mail, or a fine undergarment). The purpose is to clear the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the most emphatic way from what the archers suspected of him on the day of Uhud. Al-Wahidi related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that when the archers abandoned their position that day in pursuit of booty, they said: "We fear that the Prophet (ﷺ) will say, 'Whoever takes something, it is his,' and that he will not distribute the spoils, as he did not distribute them on the day of Badr." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You thought that we would misappropriate and not distribute to you?" And for this reason the verse was revealed. Or the purpose is to clear him (ﷺ) of what some hypocrites accused him of on the day of Badr. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Jarir, and they graded it as hasan, related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "This verse was revealed concerning a red cloak (qatifa) that was lost on the day of Badr. Some people said: 'Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it.'" The first narration is more suitable to the context, and its connection with what precedes it is more complete, because the incident is from Uhud. However, in it there is an indication that the spoils of Badr were not distributed, and this contradicts what will come in Surat al-Anfal. Its verification, if Allah the Exalted wills, will come. The second narration is more acceptable to the scholars of this discipline. It is possible that the intended meaning is an emphasis on the prohibition of ghulu (excess, or exaggeration in this context). Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Musannaf and Ibn Jarir, as a mursal narration, related from al-Dahhak who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out vanguards (tala'i'). The Prophet (ﷺ) gained a booty, and he distributed it among the people and did not give anything to the vanguards. When the vanguards arrived, they said: 'The Prophet (ﷺ) distributed and did not distribute to us.' So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse." So the meaning is: it is not for a prophet to give some of the army and withhold from others; rather, he must distribute equally among all. The Glorified One expressed the deprivation of some of the warriors as ghulul, to completely wean them from this act, or to magnify its gravity. Some scholars took the speech under this possibility in the manner of ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾, which was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while another was intended, namely whoever does the like of this after the prohibition against it. Its remoteness is not hidden. The form of the sentence under the first possibility is an informative statement both in wording and meaning, but it does not exclude an allusion to a prohibition against holding that belief in that sacred presence. Under the last possibility, it is a report that is treated as a demand. This form has come as a prohibition in several places in the revelation, such as His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives﴾, and ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists﴾, and ﴿And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾. Likewise, it is used for rational impossibility, such as His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾, and ﴿It is not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub read ﴿yughalla﴾ in the passive voice. There are three aspects to its interpretation. The first: its past tense is aghlaltuhu, meaning I attributed to him ghulul, just as you say akfartuhu, meaning I attributed kufr to him. Al-Kumayt said:

"A group has declared me a disbeliever (akfarat-ni) for loving you, and a group said: 'A wrongdoer and a sinner.'"

The meaning is: it is not valid for a prophet that anyone attribute ghulul to him. The second: it is from aghlaltuhu, when you find him to be a ghall (one who misappropriates), just as they say ahmadtuhu (I found him praiseworthy), abkhaltuhu (I found him stingy), and ajbantuhu (I found him cowardly), meaning I found him so. The meaning is: it is not valid for a prophet to be found misappropriating. The third: it is from ghall (the verb yaghulla), and the meaning is: it is not for a prophet that another should misappropriate him, that is, betray him and steal from his booty. The reason for the specification of the prophet with this, even though it is not permissible for anyone else, such as an imam or commander, to misappropriate, is either because of the great gravity of his betrayal, or because he is the one in charge of the matter of the spoils. So if betrayal is forbidden for him, and he is the one in charge of the matter, then its prohibition for others is more fitting. This is what has been said. You know that there is no need to explain the specification by what has been mentioned, after taking into account the occasion of revelation and considering what comes after it.

Some people claimed that the verse was revealed concerning the conveying of revelation. They said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was reciting the Qur'an, and in it was the fault of their religion and the reviling of their gods. So they asked him to omit that, and Allah the Exalted revealed the verse." It is not hidden that this is very far-fetched. I do not know how the chain (sanad) of this report is, and I do not think the report is anything but fabricated (mawdu'). What makes it even more remote, indeed, what almost does not permit it, is His saying: ﴿And whoever misappropriates will come with what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This is a conditional sentence that is newly begun (mustanfa), having no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). Ma is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, meaning "with that which he misappropriated." It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), and the estimate would be "in a state in which the misappropriator knows the punishment for misappropriation." The apparent reports indicate that "coming" is in its literal sense. Al-Shaykhan and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us one day and mentioned misappropriation, magnified it and magnified its matter. Then he said: 'Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck, making a noise, and he says: "O Messenger of Allah, help me!" And I will say: "I have no power for you against Allah at all; I have already conveyed to you." Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a horse on his neck, neighing, and he says: "O Messenger of Allah, help me!" And I will say: "I have no power for you against Allah at all; I have already conveyed to you." Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with rags on his neck, flapping, and he says: "O Messenger of Allah, help me!" And I will say: "I have no power for you against Allah at all; I have already conveyed to you." Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with gold or silver on his neck, and he says: "O Messenger of Allah, help me!" And I will say: "I have no power for you against Allah at all; I have already conveyed to you.'"

Reports with this meaning are numerous. Perhaps the secret in that is that he is exposed before the heads of the witnesses, as an increase in his punishment. Al-Jubba'i went to this, and there is no rational obstacle to it. The objection to it is not valid, and something that suggests objection has occurred from ancient times. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayra that a man said to him: "Have you seen the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And whoever misappropriates will come with what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection﴾? This one misappropriates a thousand dirhams and two thousand dirhams, and he comes with them. Have you seen the one who misappropriates a hundred camels or two hundred camels? How does he deal with them?!" He said: "Have you seen one whose molar is like Uhud, whose thigh is like Warqan, whose shin is like Bayda', and whose seat is from al-Rabadha to Madina; will he not carry the like of this?"

It has come in some reports that the coming with misappropriated goods is from the Fire. Then in the verse there is an omission, meaning "he will come with what he misappropriated from the Fire." Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A stone will weigh seven khalifat (pregnant she-camels), and it will be thrown into Hell, and it will fall in it for seventy autumns. And the misappropriated goods will be brought and thrown with it. Then its owner will be ordered to bring it, and this is the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And whoever misappropriates will come with what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "If I were to consider lawful the small amount of ghulul, I would consider lawful the large amount of it. No one misappropriates except that he is ordered to bring it from the lowest level of Hell." It has been said: bringing it is a metaphor for bringing its sin. It is an expression of what he did for what he was obligated to of sin; that is, he will come with what he bore of its burden and sin. Al-Balkhi chose this and said: "It is possible that what the reports contain came in the form of a parable, as if Allah the Exalted, when He exposed the misappropriator and punished him with severe punishment, acted as if he were coming with it, carrying it, and it had a voice." It is not hidden that Abu Hurayra's answer to the man refuses this interpretation.

It has been said: meanings will appear in corporeal forms on the Day of Resurrection, as the report of the coming of death in the form of a ram indicates, and the Qur'an meeting its companion in the form of a pale man when the grave splits open for him, and other such things. Many have mentioned that it is not far-fetched for deeds, both acts of obedience and sins, to appear in forms that suit them. Then it is possible to say: the sin of every misappropriator will appear on the Day of Resurrection in the form of his misappropriation, and he will come with it there. On this basis, the reports are upon their apparent meaning, without any need to resort to figurative representation. Abu Hurayra's answer does not refute it. Casting it into the Fire is also not problematic. As for the People of the Apparent (Ahl al-Zahir), perhaps they say that he is thrown in without punishment. Even if we assume this, there is no prohibition on it, because Allah the Exalted is not obligated to anything. It has been reported in some reports that He creates a creation at the time when Hell says: ﴿Is there any more?﴾, and He places them in it. Nevertheless, even with this, and even granting the soundness of the report, it is necessary to say that some of the misappropriation is excepted from being thrown, since the misappropriated goods may be a mushaf (copy of the Qur'an). I do not think anyone would dare to say that it is thrown.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾. That is, every accountable soul will be given the full and complete recompense for what it did, whether good or evil. So in the speech there is an omitted mudaf (qualifier), or the earned thing has been placed in the position of its recompense. In making the full payment dependent on "every earned thing," even though the intended point is to explain the state of the misappropriator when he comes with what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection, there is an indication of the magnitude of the matter of that Day and an emphasis on the atrocity of the state of the misappropriator, which is not hidden. For when every earner is recompensed for his deed, and nothing is diminished from it, even if his offense is very small and insignificant, then the misappropriator, with the great gravity of his offense, is more deserving of this. This is the reason for turning away from what the apparent wording would require, such as "then he will be paid for what he earned," because this is more suitable to what precedes it. It has been said: it is possible that the intended meaning is: then from it (the booty) every soul that has a share in that spoil will be paid what it earned of the deficiency of its share from his misappropriation. In that case, the wording is in accordance with the apparent meaning. The word "then" (thumma) indicates the gap between his carrying what he misappropriated and his recompense, or it indicates temporal delay, meaning after his carrying what he misappropriated by a long period, and he is made to wait among the people, disgraced, carrying what he misappropriated; from it every soul will be paid. It is not hidden that this kind of possibility is something that the speech of the Sovereign, the Exalted, should be protected from. So the truth that should not be turned away from is the first saying, which includes the point of the turning away. The meaning of "then" according to it is clear, whether it is taken to indicate temporal delay or delay in rank.

As for the first, that is because bringing what he misappropriated when he rises from the grave is the apparent meaning, and the recompense is after that by a long time. As for the second, that is because the recompense and punishment of the misappropriator are more atrocious than carrying what he misappropriated and the disgrace of it. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that this carrying is like an addition to the burden, and it almost is a bliss in comparison with what he will face afterward. The sentence in every case is coordinated (ma'tufa) with the conditional sentence.

"And they" — i.e., all people, indicated by "every soul" — "will not be wronged": that is, in accordance with wisdom and justice, the reward of their obedient ones will not be diminished, nor will the punishment of their disobedient ones be increased.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 162:

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ meaning: strives to attain it and aims toward it, ﴿like one who returns with wrath﴾, i.e. returns (bā᾽a, "returned"), ﴿with wrath﴾, i.e. great, very intense anger. It is (bi-fatḥatayn) a regular verbal noun (maṣdar qiyāsī), and it is said (bi-ḍammin fa-sukūn), which is not a regular form. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb before it, and it is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in which case it is connected to an implied element, i.e. he returned accompanied by wrath.

﴿from Allah﴾, i.e. proceeding from Him, exalted is He.

There are several opinions regarding the meaning of the verse. The first is that the meaning is: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾, exalted is He, in acting in obedience, ﴿like one who returns with wrath﴾ from Him, glorified is He, in acting in disobedience. This is related from Ibn Ishaq. The second is that its meaning is: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ in abstaining from misappropriation (ghulūl), like the Prophet and those who walk in his way, ﴿like one who returns with wrath from Allah﴾, exalted is He, by committing misappropriation. This is related from al-Hasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Ṭabarī chose it because it is more suited to the context. The third is that the intended meaning is: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾, exalted is He, through striving in His way, ﴿like one who returns with wrath﴾ from Him, majestic is His majesty, through fleeing from it. This is transmitted from al-Jubba᾽ī and al-Zajjāj. It is also said that this agrees with what is reported as the occasion of revelation: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to go out to Uhud, a group of the hypocrites stayed behind, while the believers followed him, so Allah revealed this verse. However, there is distance in this view. The use of the noble Name in the place of the pronoun has been explained more than once.

﴿And his abode is Hell﴾, i.e. his destination is that. In this clause there are two possibilities. The first: that it is a new independent sentence, brought to explain the state of the one who returns with wrath, and from its counterpart it is understood that the one who follows the pleasure (of Allah) has Paradise as his abode. It was not mentioned so that the warning would be more forceful. It is also said: Paradise was not mentioned with the pleasure because the pleasure of Allah is greater and entails every bliss, and wrath entails every punishment; so it requires that Hell be mentioned with it within the sphere of prohibition, since beauty precedes majesty; so understand. The second: that it falls within the scope of the relative clause, so it is coordinated with ﴿returns with wrath﴾, as a nominal relative clause coordinated with a verbal relative clause. In both possibilities it has no place in terms of i'rab.

﴿And evil is the destination﴾: this is either a concluding remark (tadhyīl), or a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), or coordinated with the relative clause by an implied element. It is said that this applies to them. In any case, the element specified by the dispraise is omitted, i.e. Hell. ﴿Al-maṣīr﴾ (destination) is a noun of place, and it may also be a verbal noun. Scholars distinguished between it and al-marji᾽ (return) by saying that al-maṣīr implies that what one arrives at in Hell is different from what one was in this world, because ṣayrūra (becoming) entails a transition from one state to another, as in ṣāra al-ṭīnu khazafan ("the clay became pottery"), whereas al-marji᾽ is the reversion of a thing to a state it was previously in, as in your saying: "the return of the son of Adam is to the dust." As for their saying "the return of the servants is to Allah, exalted is He," it is in view of the fact that they revert to a state in which they own nothing for themselves, just as they did not own anything before they were given ownership.

﴿Hum﴾ refers back to the relative pronouns (al-mawsulun) according to their meaning, and it is the subject (mubtada'). The phrase ﴿darajat﴾ ("degrees") is its predicate (khabar). The intended meaning is that they vary in rank. This is a case of naming the thing that necessitates (al-malzum) to mean what it necessitates (al-lazim). Alternatively, they are likened to steps (al-darj) in their variation, rising and falling, by way of metaphor (isti'ara). Or they are treated as the degrees themselves, for emphasis on the variation, and this would be an eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh) with the particle of comparison omitted. It has also been said that the sentence contains an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), and there is no comparison. The meaning is: "they are people of degrees," that is, ranks or varying states. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid and al-Suddi: "They have degrees." Some scholars hold that in this case the verse includes a grouping of the degrees (al-darajat) over the lower levels (al-darkat), since the first term is for the first group and the second for the second group.

﴿'inda Allah﴾ means "in the sight of God," that is, in His knowledge and His judgment. The adverbial phrase is connected to ﴿darajat﴾ according to meaning, or to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier of it.

﴿wallahu basir bima ya'maluna﴾ means "And God is All-Seeing of what they do," that is, of the deeds and their degrees, and He will recompense them according to them. As Hujjat al-Islam (Proof of Islam) said, al-Basir ("the All-Seeing") is the One who witnesses and sees, such that nothing beneath the earth escapes Him. His seeing is also exalted above being by means of a pupil and eyelids, and He is sanctified above its returning to the impression of forms and colors in His essence as they are impressed in the pupil of a human being. That would be change and being affected, which requires temporality. When He is exalted above that, seeing in His regard is an expression of the attribute by which the perfection of the qualities of the things seen is disclosed. This is clearer and more manifest than what we understand from the perception of sight, which is limited to the surfaces of visible things. End of quote.

From this it is understood that seeing (al-basar) is an attribute additional to knowledge ('ilm). This is the view of the majority of our scholars, and of the Mu'tazila and the Karramiyya. They say: when we know something with clear knowledge and then see it, we find a difference between the two states by immediate intuition, and in the second state there is an additional state, which is sight (al-ibsar).

The philosophers, al-Ka'bi, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, and al-Ghazali according to some, said that God's seeing is an expression of His knowledge of visible things. Al-Ghazali claimed that his statement just quoted indicates this. The same disagreement applies to hearing (al-sam'). The truth is that both are additional to the attribute of knowledge, that neither can be specified in modality (la yukayyafan) nor defined (la yuhaddan), and that affirming them is obligatory, just as He described Himself with them. The righteous predecessors (al-Salaf al-Salih) adopted this view, and it is with this that the heart is at peace.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, Allah has bestowed favour﴾ i.e., He bestowed blessing and graciousness. The root of *mann* (favour) is "cutting off" (qat'), and blessing is called *minnah* because by it one is cut off from affliction. Likewise, reckoning one's good deed against someone (*i'tidad bil-sana'a*) is called *mann* because it cuts the recipient off from the obligation of gratitude for it. The clause is the answer to an implied oath, i.e., "By Allah, Allah has indeed bestowed favour ﴿upon the believers﴾, i.e., from among their own people, or from among the Arabs in general, or from among mankind (*al-Ins*). The middle of the three is the best. This is the view taken by ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her; al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from her that she said: "This is specific to the Arabs." The first is better than the third. In any case, the intended people, as al-Ajhuri said, are: the believers among them in Allah's knowledge, or those whose affair came to faith.

﴿when He sent among them﴾ i.e., among them, ﴿a Messenger﴾ of great rank and lofty standing ﴿from themselves﴾ i.e., from their lineage, or from their kind, an Arab like them, or from the children of Adam, not an angel nor a jinn. The word *idh* (when) is an adverb governed by *manna* (bestowed). Although it has the meaning of time, it occurs in the position of causal explanation, as most verifiers have stated. The prepositional phrase is either attached to *ba'atha* (sent) or to an implied element that functions as a qualifier of *rasulan* (a Messenger). The favour in this regard is either because being of mankind brings familiarity, so that receiving from him is easy and the natural aversion and estrangement between the two different kinds is removed; or so that they may understand his speech with ease and take pride over the other kinds of the human species; or so that they may understand, take pride, and be aware of his circumstances in truthfulness and trustworthiness, which is closer to their believing him and trusting him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The singling out of the believers for the favour, despite the generality of the blessing of the mission, is as indicated by His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾, for their greater benefit from it, though opinions differ concerning them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

It has been read as *limin manna Allahi* with the preposition *min* and *manna* with a doubled nun, as the predicate of an omitted subject, such as "his favour" or "his sending", which was omitted because the indication is clear. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *idh* be in the nominative position, like *idha* in your saying: "The Amir is most eloquent when he is standing", meaning: "Allah's favour upon the believers is at the time of His sending him." It should not be hidden from you that this requires *idh* to be the subject and the prepositional phrase the predicate. This has been objected to on the grounds that it is not known that any of the grammarians said that *idh* occurs in this way, and that what is in the example is *idha*, not *idh*. Here too it is not a subject at all; rather, they permitted two cases: the accusative, on the basis that the predicate is omitted and it stands in its place, and the nominative, on the basis that it is itself the predicate. According to the first, the sentence is of the type "his grandfather is great", because the Amir is most eloquent in the state of standing, not in its being; according to the second, it is of the type "his day is fasting". The first case is the well-known one. ʿAbd al-Qahir permitted the second, relying on the saying of some: "The Amir is most eloquent on Friday" with the nominative. So al-Zamakhshari seems to have analogized *idh* with *idha* and the subject with the predicate.

Some defended al-Zamakhshari by saying that a group of verifying grammarians have stated explicitly that *idh* has come out of the adverbial function, so it is an object and a substitute for the object. This amounts to their explicit statement that it occurs as a subject and a predicate, for example, since this is a claim of its inflectional freedom. Once this is held, all states are equal in permitting its use in any position, without distinguishing one state from another, except where an impediment prevents that state in it and in the other nouns. That is a matter beyond what we are discussing. Yes, al-Shalubin related in his commentary on al-Jazuliyya from some that the basis of the inflectional freedom of adverbs is transmission (*al-sama'*). If this is the rule for the basic freedom only and not its types, the dust is settled regarding what al-Zamakhshari said, on the basis of what we have mentioned, clearly. But if the rule for the types is also thus, then one may not proceed to make it an agent merely because it is established as an object, nor to make it an inchoative merely because it is established as a predicate, for example, except by the occurrence of transmission in that. Thus there is a clear doubt about the soundness of al-Zamakhshari's statement, because the mere statement of theirs at that point that *idh* occurs as an object and a substitute, and that *idha* occurs as a predicate, for example, is of no benefit, since transmission may have come only for that and not for something else, as is not hidden.

In the recitation of the Messenger of Allah and Fatima, may Allah bless him and her and grant them peace, it is *min anfasihim* with a fatha on the fa, i.e., "from their noblest," because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was from the noblest of tribes and their clans. This is a well-known matter that needs no explanation, and it is befitting for every believer to hold it.

Al-Shaykh Wali al-Din al-ʿIraqi was asked: Is knowledge that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was a human and from the Arabs a condition for the validity of faith, or is it a communal obligation (*fard al-kifaya*)? He answered that it is a condition for the validity of faith. Then he said: If a person said: "I believe in the mission of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to all creation, but I do not know whether he is from humans, angels, or jinn, or I do not know whether he is from the Arabs or non-Arabs," then there is no doubt of his disbelief, because he has denied the Qur'an and rejected what the generations of Islam have transmitted from predecessor to successor, and it has become known by necessity to the elite and the common folk; I know of no dispute on this. So if he were ignorant and did not know this, it would be obligatory to teach him; if he then denied it, we would judge him to be a disbeliever. End of quotation. As for whether belief that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was from the noblest tribes and clans is analogous to this, so that it is required for the validity of Islam, or it is not analogous, so that the faith of one who does not know that is valid while he nonetheless holds that sacred station free from every blemish, there is room for reflection. The second is apparent, and it is the more suitable for the common believers.

﴿He recites to them His verses﴾: it is either a qualifier, or a circumstantial clause, or a resumptive clause, and in this there is remoteness; i.e., He recites to them what is revealed to him of the Qur'an, after they had been a people of ignorance, to whom nothing of revelation had reached their ears, or after some of them had been so and some of them were yearning for it, since the Book in the hand of the People of the Book had informed of its descent and gave good news of it.

﴿and purifies them﴾: i.e., He calls them to that by which they become pure and clean from the defilement of ignorance that was in them, or from the evil beliefs such as those held by the idolaters of the Arabs and the People of the Two Books; or He bears witness that they are pure in religion; or He takes from them the zakat by which He purifies them, as al-Farra' said. Its remoteness is not hidden, and similar to it is what is close to it. ﴿and teaches them the Book and wisdom﴾: the discussion of this has already preceded.

This teaching is conjoined to what comes before it, following upon the recitation. He placed purification between them, which is an expression for perfecting the soul according to the practical faculty and refining it, branching from its perfection according to the theoretical faculty, which is attained by teaching following upon recitation, in order to signal that each of the ordered matters is a sublime blessing in itself, deserving of gratitude. If the order of existence were observed, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a Messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them﴾, then the mind would immediately count all of them as one blessing. This is the secret of expressing the Qur'an sometimes by "verses" and sometimes by "the Book and wisdom", as a signal that by each title it is a separate blessing. So said our master Shaykh al-Islam. It may be said: what is meant by reciting the verses is the recitation of what is revealed to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of the verses that indicate tawhid and prophethood; and by purification is the call to the good word, which includes testifying to Allah's oneness and to His Prophet's messengership, upon him be blessings and peace; and by teaching the Book is teaching the wording of the Qur'an and the manner of its recitation so that thereby the pillar of religion may be established for them; and by teaching wisdom is coming to know the secrets hidden in the treasuries of Allah's speech. The ordering of these conjoined items is then clear, for the sum of it is that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prepares the paths of tawhid, calls to it, and teaches what is necessary after one has become engaged in it, adding sweetness upon sweetness. So recitation comes first because it belongs to preparation; then purification, because it follows it, and it is the first matter that produces a quality with which the believers are adorned, and it belongs to the category of clearing away (*takhliya*) which precedes adorning (*tahliya*), because averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits; then teaching, because it is needed only after faith. There remains the question of why teaching is placed before purification in the verse of al-Baqara; perhaps it was a signal of the nobility of adornment, as we indicated there, so reflect.

﴿And indeed they had been before﴾ i.e., before the sending of the Messenger ﴿in manifest error﴾ (164), clear. (*Inna*) here is the lightened form, and the *lam* is the differentiating *lam*; the meaning is: indeed the matter was that they had been before, etc.

This is the view of some verifiers, and Makki mentioned the like, except that he said: the estimate is "and indeed they had been before", so its subject was made a pronoun referring to the believers. Abu Hayyan said: we know of no grammarian who held either of these two views; what is established for us in the books of grammar and from the teachers is that when you say "inna Zaydan qa'imun" and then lighten it, the Basrans have two views concerning it: one, that it is permissible to keep its governance, its state being as it is when it is heavy, except that it does not govern an pronoun; the Kufans prohibited this, and they are refuted by the established transmission from the tongue of the Arabs.

The second view, which is the more prevalent among them, is that it is rendered inert, so it governs neither an explicit nor an implicit noun, neither pronounced nor estimated at all. If a nominal sentence follows it, it takes the nominative by the inchoative and predicate, and the *lam* becomes obligatory in the second of its two items if it is not negated, and in the first if it is postponed; so you say: "inna Zaydun la-qa'imun", whose meaning is the meaning of "inna Zaydan qa'imun". If a verbal sentence follows it, then according to the Basrans it must be one of the abrogators of the inchoative; if the verb comes from another source, it is anomalous and is not analogized upon according to their majority.

Al-Halabi answered those who estimated the subject as "the matter" by saying that it is an explanation of meaning, not a statement of inflection. ʿIsam al-Milla said: whoever said "the matter" did not intend an estimate of a pronoun of the matter; rather he made the sentence a circumstantial clause by way of interpreting it as a narrative, so that the time of the state does not differ from the time of the governing element. The time of being in manifest error is before the time of teaching, but the narrative's being so is continuous. Then he said: this is a common and well-known interpretation regarding a circumstantial state whose time of realization precedes the time of realization of the governing element; so memorize it, do not recite it. End of quotation.

You know that what al-Halabi mentioned is contrary to the apparent meaning, and ʿIsam al-Milla's statement is open to scrutiny, because what suits his point, if it is specified as estimating "the matter", would be estimating it before *anna* rather than after it, as is not hidden. Some permitted that the sentence be a resumptive clause with no place in inflection, while most hold the circumstantial view; on both estimates it explains the completeness and perfection of the blessing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 165:

The saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Why is it that when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), you said, "How is this?"﴾ is a new statement, brought to refute one of the false assumptions that arose after the refutation of another. The hamzah (the interrogative particle) is for rebuke and affirmation. The waw is a conjunction joining what follows it to an omitted element before it. (Lamma) is a temporal noun meaning "when," governing what follows it, and it functions as a conditional, as al-Farisi held, and this is the correct view according to a group of the verifying scholars. Its governing element is (qultum, "you said"), which is the apodosis. The clause ﴿qad asabtum﴾ ("you had inflicted") is in the nominative position as a descriptive clause modifying "a calamity." Taking it as being in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause requires an unnecessary strain.

The "calamity" refers to what befell them on the day of Uhud, the killing of seventy of them. "Twice as much" refers to what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr, the killing of seventy of them and the capture of seventy. This is counted as double either by treating the capture as equivalent to killing, or because they were able to kill and it was Allah's will, so their failure to do so was from their side, and abstaining from killing while able does not negate the infliction.

It has been said: the "two-fold" refers to the two equal defeats, not to the number of the slain.
