This is because the Muslims defeated the unbelievers on the day of Badr, and they (the unbelievers) also defeated the Muslims on the day of Uhud at the beginning of the battle. On this view, the "calamity" is the defeat of the Muslims by the unbelievers after they had left their position. ﴿How is this?﴾ is a nominal clause with the predicate placed first. The meaning is "from where is this?" rather than "how is this?", because the answer given indicates the object of the saying. It has also been said that (anna, "how/from where") is accusative as an adverb of place, governed by the implied "it struck us," and (this) is its subject. The clause is then the direct speech of "you said." The placement of the adverbial phrase and what depends on it between the hamzah and the thing it governs, although the thing actually being denied is what is connected by the waw, serves to intensify the denial and sharpen the rebuke, since committing a foul act at the wrong time is more foul, and rejection of its doer is more emphatic. The meaning is: when the polytheists inflicted on you half of what you had inflicted on them before, did you turn back and say, "From where is this, while we are Muslims fighting out of zeal for Allah, the Exalted, with His Messenger among us, while these are polytheists, enemies of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)?" Or: "Has Allah not promised us victory?" This is the view of al-Jubba'i. This interpretation applies on the basis that the denial and rebuke are directed at the utterance of that saying by them at that time specifically, given that this was not expected to come from them, but rather that the calamity of their enemy being twice their own calamity would ease the affliction and produce consolation. Or: did you do what you did of cowardice and disputing, or of leaving Madinah and insisting on pressing the Prophet (ﷺ)? When the consequences of that struck you, you said, "How is this?" This interpretation applies to the denial of their finding the event improbable while they were directly responsible for its cause. It is also permitted that the element joined by the waw be the saying, as an indication that their words were not a single one, but rather they uttered statements that they should not have uttered.

A group of scholars held that the element joined by the waw is what came before in the saying of Allah, ﴿Allah certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ up to here, and because it concerns one narrative with no foreign element intervening between them, this view is not remote, as Abu Hayyan claimed. In that case the hamzah is placed between the two conjoined elements for affirmation, meaning confirmation, or to lead them to admit, and the rebuke is directed at the content of the conjoined element. The meaning is: was the promise of victory from Allah, the Exalted, on the condition of patience and piety? Then when you lost heart, disputed, and disobeyed, and Allah, the Exalted, afflicted you with what afflicted you, you said, ﴿How is this?﴾

[Page 116]

Most scholars hold that the hamzah is advanced from a later position, while the waw originally belongs at the front. This is the view of Sibawayh and others, and al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) preferred it. The interrogative clause is conjoined to what precedes it. The attribution of "striking" to "calamity" is figurative (majaz, non-literal usage), while its attribution to the addressees is literal (haqiqah). The two attributions were not put in the same form in order to add to the rebuke. The demonstrative in ﴿How is this?﴾ is masculine in agreement with the meaning of "calamity" that it points to, which is the well-known view. Alternatively, it is because their pointing was only to what they had witnessed in the battle as such, without the name of anything occurring to their minds, let alone the name "calamity." Their pointing happened only at the time of narrating. According to what has been said, the verse contains an implicit answer to their astonishment at that infliction: the conditions of this world do not remain in one state. If you inflicted on them the same as what they inflicted on you, and more, what is the basis for astonishment? However, He, glorified is He, explicitly stated a different answer that heals the sick and quenches the thirst, and before which heads bow down. He said, ﴿Say,﴾ O Muhammad, in answer to their corrupt question, ﴿It is from yourselves﴾, meaning this which struck you is from your own selves, that is, they were the cause of it, since the archers disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), left their position, and were greedy for booty, so Allah, the Exalted, punished them for that. This was said by Ikrimah. Or, because you chose, before seventy of you were killed, in exchange for the ransom you had taken from the captives of Badr. This has been attributed to al-Hasan, and what supports it is what Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as hasan), al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'O Muhammad, Allah, the Exalted, has disliked what your people did in taking the captives. He has commanded you to offer them a choice between two matters: either they be brought forward and their necks struck, or they take the ransom on condition that an equal number of them be killed.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people and told them this. They said, 'O Messenger of Allah, they are our clansmen and brothers. We take their ransom to strengthen ourselves for fighting our enemy, and an equal number of us will be martyred. That is not what we dislike.' So seventy men were killed on the day of Uhud, equal to the number of captives of the people of Badr." Or, because you chose to leave Madinah and did not remain until you fought the polytheists within it. This was said by al-Rabi' and others.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions on the day of Uhud, when Abu Sufyan and the polytheists arrived: 'We are in a fortified garden,' meaning Madinah. 'Leave the people to come in to us, and we will fight them.' Some of the Ansar said to him, 'We dislike being killed in the streets of Madinah, and we used to refrain from that in the days of ignorance, so in Islam we have more right to refrain. Lead us out to the people.' He went and put on his battle armour. The people blamed themselves and said, 'The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) proposed one matter, and you proposed another. Go, O Hamzah, and tell him: our matter follows your matter.' Hamzah came to him and said, 'It is not for a prophet, when he has put on his battle armour, to take it off until he engages in battle. And there will certainly be a calamity among you.' They said, 'O Prophet of Allah, specifically, or generally?' He said, 'You will see it.'"

This statement has been objected to on the grounds that it is contradicted by the fact that the promise of victory was given after the choice to go out was made, and that the Prophet's (ﷺ) acting upon it lifted the danger from him and lightened their offence in it. Moreover, the choice to go out and insisting on it came from those whom Allah honoured with martyrdom that day, and how could they utter such a word? It was answered that the refusal mentioned is within the scope of prohibition, and how could it be, when the promised victory was conditional on something Allah knew would not occur? And that the Prophet (ﷺ), although he acted upon it, his noble self was not at ease with it, nor was his blessed heart inclined to it. It is as if the arrows of destiny were shot when they opposed his lofty opinion and turned away from drinking from the sweet sea of his overflowing intellect. This is indicated by his saying, peace be upon him, after he had put on his battle armour, "There will certainly be a calamity among you," and his answer to their question about it, "Specifically or generally?", "You will see it." For this is almost explicit in showing dissatisfaction and clearly implies that that choice required the descent of decree. It is also answered that the address in the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Say, it is from yourselves﴾ is not explicit that those responsible for it are those who uttered that word, so the martyrdom of those who chose to go out does not harm the intended meaning. It is permissible that it be in the manner of your saying to a tribe, "You killed so-and-so," while the killers among them are specific individuals who did not exist at the time of the address. Many similar examples occur in discourse. Moreover, that the calamity of those who uttered the word was the killing of those martyrs is explicit in regret over them, so this fits with an indirect reference to them in attributing shortcoming to them, so that this regret may be lessened, and so that they may know that the ill omen of deviating from the course of the will of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) covers both the great and the small. Indeed, it may even be said that the martyrdom of those persistent ones is evidence that they were the ones who were the cause of that calamity, and for this reason they were martyred, so that they might go to their Lord in the best condition.

This, and it should not be concealed that this answer is not free from strain. It seems that the motive for it is that those who interpret ﴿from yourselves﴾ as referring to going out of Madinah and following Abu Sufyan and his people are a group of eminent scholars, so it is remote to attribute error to them. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Hasan, and Ibn Juraij, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it through Ibn Juraij from Ibn Abbas. So reflect upon this.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ (165). Among what is included in this is victory when obedience is shown, and abandonment when disobedience occurs. Since you disobeyed, He, glorified is He, afflicted you with what afflicted you. The clause is a concluding statement confirming the content of what precedes it, included within the command. It has been said that its purpose is to comfort their hearts and to mix the bitterness of rebuke with the sweetness of promise, meaning that He, glorified is He, is able to grant you victory again, because He is over all things competent. So do not despair of the mercy of Allah. It also expresses care for the matter of consolation and guidance for them to the reality of the situation about which they asked, and an explanation of some of the wisdoms in it.

ورَفْعًا لِما عَسى أنْ يُتَوَهَّمَ مِنَ الجَوابِ مِنِ اسْتِقْلالِهِمْ في وُقُوعِ الحادِثَةِ رَجَعَ إلى خِطابِهِمْ بِرَفْعِ الواسِطَةِ وجَوابِ سُؤالِهِمْ بِأبْسَطِ عِبارَةٍ فَقالَ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿وما أصابَكُمْ﴾ أيُّها المُؤْمِنُونَ مِنَ النَّكْبَةِ بِقَتْلِ مَن قُتِلَ مِنكم ﴿يَوْمَ التَقى الجَمْعانِ﴾ أيُّ جَمْعُكم وجَمْعُ أعْدائِكُمُ المُشْرِكِينَ، والمُرادُ بِذَلِكَ اليَوْمِ يَوْمُ أُحُدٍ، وقَوْلُ بَعْضِهِمْ - لا يَبْعُدُ أنْ يُرادَ بِهِ يَوْمُ أُحُدٍ، ويَوْمُ بَدْرٍ - بَعِيدٌ جِدًّا ﴿فَبِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ أيْ بِإرادَتِهِ، وقِيلَ: بِتَخْلِيَتِهِ، و(ما) اسْمٌ مَوْصُولٌ بِمَعْنى الَّذِي في مَحَلِّ رَفْعٍ بِالِابْتِداءِ، وجُمْلَةُ (أصابَكُمْ) صِلَتُهُ، وبِإذْنِ اللَّهِ: خَبَرُهُ.

(Translation of the above passage follows.)

Here is the translation:

"And to remove what might be suspected from the answer, namely that they (the believers) could be thought to have been independent in the occurrence of the event, He returned to addressing them directly, removing the intermediary, and answering their question in the plainest expression. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And whatever befell you﴾, O believers, of the calamity of the killing of those among you who were killed, ﴿on the day the two hosts met﴾, meaning your host and the host of your enemies, the polytheists. The intended day is the Day of Uhud. The statement of some that it may mean both the Day of Uhud and the Day of Badr is very far-fetched. ﴿then it was by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His will. It was also said: by His allowing it. Here (mā) is a relative pronoun meaning 'that which', in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, the clause (aṣābakum) is its relative clause, and 'by the permission of Allah' is its predicate."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 167:

Page 118

﴿And that He might make evident those who were hypocrites﴾, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon what precedes it, of the same kind. The repetition of the verb (yaʿlam) is either for the sake of giving attention to this cause, or to honour the believers and to purify them from being counted in the same rank as the hypocrites; and it is also to indicate the difference in the state of knowledge according to its relation to the two groups. For it is related to the believers in the manner of its earlier relation, and to the hypocrites in a new manner, which is the secret (al-sirr) — as Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyya) said — in that the first are mentioned with the active participle form (ism al-fa'il), which indicates continuity, and the latter with a relative pronoun whose clause is a verb indicating occurrence (ḥudūth). ﴿And it was said to them﴾ is a conjunction upon "they were hypocrites", indicating that this was a particular hypocrisy which they displayed in that situation.

It has also been said: it is the beginning of a statement conjoined to the whole of what precedes it, a conjunction of one narrative upon another narrative. Its reasoning is that when He, exalted is His mention, mentioned the states of the believers and what befell them and against them in the preceding verses, and made clear that the turn of fortune was only for trial, and so that the believers might be distinguished from the hypocrites, and so that each of the two groups might know that what God Most High has decreed of the afflicting of the believers is bound to occur, He brought in a narrative from their stories suitable to this situation, as a digression. The "and" (wāw) was used because it suits the original speech. In this view, "hypocrisy" is unrestricted and commonly understood. It is also permitted that it be an independent statement, as a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ) to draw attention to the manner of the manifestation of their hypocrisy, or to their not remaining steadfast in faith.

In every case, the speaker is either the Messenger of God (ﷺ) — and al-Asamm held this view — or ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥarām of Banu Salama, and the majority held this view. The content of the saying is His statement: ﴿Come, fight in the way of God, or defend﴾. Al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿or defend﴾ us against the enemy by increasing the numbers, and this is what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also been said that they were given the choice between fighting for the sake of the Hereafter, or for defending the unbelievers away from themselves and their property, or between the first and defending the believers from that; as if it were said: fight for God Most High, or for the sake of defending yourselves and your property against hypocrisy. The conjunctive particle (fa or wa) is omitted between "come" (taʿālaw) and "fight" (qātilū), because the intended meaning of both is one, namely the second; the first is mentioned as a preparation for it and an encouragement towards it, because of what it contains of the indication of mutual support and cooperation. It was also said: the conjunction is omitted to indicate that each of the two sentences is intended in itself. It was also said: the second command is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), but its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿They said﴾ is a explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), as if it were said: what did they do when they were told that? So it was said: they said: ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you﴾, that is: if we were knowing that you would be fighting, we would not have abandoned you, but we do not see that there will be fighting. Ibn Jarir and others narrated this from Ibn Shihab. It was also said: they meant that we do not well know fighting and are not able to do it, because knowledge of a voluntary action is one of the necessary concomitants of the ability to perform it; so by negating the knowledge he expressed the negation of the ability. It is also possible that they made the negation of knowledge of fighting a metonymy for the claim that what they are engaged in is not fighting, on the basis that the negation of knowledge is by negating the known; because fighting requires parity on both sides together with the hope of repelling or overpowering, and when this is not realised, casting oneself into destruction results. Some people allowed that the meaning is: ﴿If we knew fighting﴾ in the way of God, we would follow you; or: if we knew fighting alongside us, we would follow you — but the opponent has no hostility toward us except toward you. It is not hidden that this statement, in all its possible readings, is fit to be an answer to what they were told in all readings other than the first; and on the first reading, this is fit as an answer to it in all readings other than the second, since lack of knowledge of fighting would not be an excuse for not increasing numbers, except in a remote sense. And from their speech:

"If you do not fight, O coward, then at least cheer."

The meaning of "following" (ittibāʿ) is either going out to fight; and they did not express it this way because their tongues, due to the complete discouragement of their hearts from it, do not assist them in declaring it. Or it is going with the believers in general, whether for fighting or for defence and increasing numbers; and to take it as obeying the command, i.e. "if we knew fighting we would have obeyed your command," is not free from remoteness.
Page 119

﴿They were, that day, nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾, that is: they, on the day they said ﴿If we knew﴾ etc., were nearer to disbelief than they had been before that, because the sign of it became apparent upon them by their abandoning the support of the believers, and their making excuses to them in a manner of deceit and mockery.

All the adverbial expressions (ẓurūf), according to the well-known view of the grammarians (muʿarrabūn), relate to ﴿nearer﴾ (aqrab). It is among their rules that two prepositional phrases or two adverbs with the same meaning do not relate to a single governed item, except in three cases: first, that one of them relates to it absolutely and then the other relates to it after being restricted by the first; second, that the second is a follower of the first by apposition (badaliyya) or the like; third, that the governed item is a superlative (af'al al-tafḍīl), because it implies the superior and the inferior, which makes it like having two governed items, as in "the restricted and the unrestricted." What we are concerned with is of this kind: as if it were said, their nearness to disbelief exceeds their nearness to faith. The preposition "lam" in both places is in the sense of "ila" (to), according to what has been said: that the complement of nearness is with "min" and "ila" only; one says "qariba minhu" and "qariba ilayhi," and one does not say "qariba lahu." Or it remains in its own sense, according to what is in al-Durr al-Masun, that nearness, which is the opposite of distance, is transitive with three particles: lam, ila, and min. It was also said: here "aqrab" is from "qarab" with a fatha on the ra', meaning seeking water, and from it comes "al-qarib" for his ship, and "laylat al-qarb," i.e., the arrival; so the meaning is: they are more seeking after disbelief, and in that case it is transitive with "lam" by agreement.

Some claimed that the "lam" here is causal, and the estimate is: they, because of their disbelief that day, are nearer (aqrab) — of the unbelievers — from among them, than from the believers because of their faith. It should not be taken that the speech of God Most High is to be interpreted in this way, due to its great remoteness and the weakness of its composition if the omitted element were stated explicitly.

It was also permitted that a noun be estimated in the speech, namely "ahl" (people of), and the "lam" relates to a omitted specification, namely "nuṣra" (support), and the meaning is: they are nearer, in support, to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith, since their abandonment and their speech were a strengthening of the polytheists and a discouraging of the believers. This is like your saying: "I am harder in striking for Zayd than I am for ʿAmr," and you know that it is possible for "lam" to relate to the specification even when the omission of the noun is not considered. Al-Wahidi claimed that in the verse there is evidence that one who utters the word of monotheism is not declared a disbeliever, because God Most High did not openly state their takfir.

Al-Hasan said: when God Most High says "aqrab," it is for certainty that they are polytheists. It is not hidden that the verse is like a clear statement of their disbelief; but nevertheless they do not deserve to be treated with this treatment as unbelievers, and perhaps this is for another matter.

﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining their state absolutely, not only on that day, and therefore it is separated. It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "nearer." The restriction of the saying to the mouths is either an explanation, because it is a verbal speech and not a mental one, or an emphasis in the manner of His statement ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾. The meaning is that they show the opposite of what they conceal. Shaykh al-Islam said: the mention of the mouths and the hearts is a depiction of their hypocrisy and a clarification of the contradiction between their outward and inward states; and "what" (mā) is an expression for the saying, and what is meant by it is either the very speech manifest on the tongue at one time, and in the heart at another; so the affirmed and the negated are identical in essence and attribute, though they differ in manifestation; or it is the uttered saying alone, in which case the negated thing is its source, which the saying never separates from at all, and it was expressed by it only to show the strength of the connection between them. The meaning is: they utter a saying for which there is no existence, or for whose source there is none in their hearts at all, from among the falsehoods of which is what He related of them just before; for they manifested two matters of which there is nothing in their hearts: first, lack of knowledge of fighting; and second, following on the assumption of knowing it. They lied in both, a manifest lie, since they were knowing of it, and yet persisted in abandonment, resolved upon apostasy. Some chose that "what" is an expression for the spoken saying, and the meaning of its not being in their hearts is that it is not believed by them nor conceived by them, except as one conceives the marital status of three (as an impossibility), for example; and the ruling is general, and it includes the ruling on what they uttered from the whole of the conditional proposition, not only the antecedent alone, nor only the consequent alone, nor both together without the collective form considered in the proposition. Perhaps what the Shaykh mentioned is better.

Page 120

﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾ is an increase in verification of their disbelief and hypocrisy, by clarifying that their hearts are occupied with what contradicts their sayings, of the various kinds of evil and corruption, following the statement of their emptiness of what agrees with them. The meaning is: He knows more than the believers, because God Most High knows it in detail with certain knowledge, whereas the believers know it in summary through signs. It is also permitted that the circumstantial clause is to draw attention to the fact that hypocrisy does not benefit them, and that the meaning is: He knows more than them, because God Most High knows the outcome of their secrets and hopes.

**﴿Those who said﴾** is in the nominative, either as a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for the *waw* of *yakтumun* (they conceal), as if it were said: "And God knows best what those who said [it] conceal." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "They are those who..." It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is **﴿Say﴾**, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "Say to them..." Or it is in the accusative, by way of censure (*dhamm*). Or it is an epithet (*na't*) for **﴿those who were hypocrites﴾**, or a *badal* of it. Or it is in the genitive, as a *badal* of the pronoun in **﴿their mouths﴾** or **﴿their hearts﴾**. The substitution of a noun for a pronoun of absence in their speech has occurred, and from it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*On a state in which, if among the people there were Hatim,*
*With his generosity, he would be stingy with water, Hatim.*

Here *Hatim* is in the genitive as a *badal* of the pronoun in *jūdihi* (his generosity), because the rhyme is in the genitive. The meaning is: they say with the mouths of those who said [it], or they say with their mouths what is not in the hearts of those who said [it]. The expression on both readings is of the type of *tajrid* (abstraction, a rhetorical device in which a speaker addresses a figure of himself), as in his saying:

*O best of those who ride the mounts,*
*And who does not drink a cup from the hand of one who is stingy.*

The speaker, as al-Suddi and others said, was ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and they said this on the day of Uhud. **﴿For their brothers﴾**, that is, on account of their brothers who went out with the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and were killed on that day. What is meant is their blood relations, or those of their kind. **﴿And sat [at home]﴾** is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *qālū* (they said), with *qad* (already) understood, meaning "they said while they had remained back from fighting by abandoning [the Prophet]." It is also permitted that it be coordinated (*ma'tuf*) to the relative clause, so that it becomes a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*) between *qālū* and its complement, which is his saying, exalted is He: **﴿If they had obeyed us﴾**, that is, in abandoning the fighting, **﴿they would not have been killed﴾**, just as we were not killed. In this there is an indication that they had commanded them to abandon [the Prophet] at the time they abandoned him. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, went out with a thousand men, and he had promised them victory if they were patient. When they went out, ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy returned with three hundred. Abu Jabir al-Salami followed them, calling them back. When they overpowered him, they said to him: **﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly have followed you﴾**, and they said to him: 'If you obey us, you will certainly return with us.'" God, exalted is He, thus disclosed the reprehensibility of their saying "If you obey us, you will certainly return with us" by His saying, glorified is He: **﴿Those who said﴾**, and so on.

Some interpreters took the sitting [at home] to mean what Ibn Ubayy recommended during the consultation, namely remaining in Medina from the start, and took obedience to mean accepting his opinion and acting upon it. This view is not free of difficulty. Indeed, our master Shaykh al-Islam said: it is refuted by the fact that the clause is circumstantial, since such a clause serves to specify what constitutes disobedience and opposition, while Ibn Ubayy was not among those who sat [at home] in that sense. Moreover, restricting the non-obedience to their brothers indicates that the command is also restricted to them, so it is impossible to take it to refer to what was addressed to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, during the consultation.

**﴿Say﴾**, O Muhammad, as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of their lying: **﴿Avert from yourselves death﴾**, that is, repel it from yourselves. This is the answer to a condition that has been omitted, because of the indication of His saying: **﴿if you are truthful﴾** (168) regarding it, just as the condition's answer has been omitted because of the indication of **﴿avert﴾** upon it. Whoever permits the answer to precede the condition does not need what has been mentioned. The object of the truthfulness is what their statement contains, namely that the cause of their salvation was sitting out of the fighting. What is meant is that what you claim as the cause of salvation is not sound, and even if its soundness were granted, it would not be beneficial. As for the first point, the causes of salvation are many, and at best sitting out and salvation existed together, but that does not indicate causation. As for the second point, what is fled from in essence is death, of which killing is only one cause. So if what you mention is correct, then repel the rest of its causes, for the causes of death are equal in the possibility of repelling them by stratagems and in the impossibility of doing so. Your own selves are dearer to you, and their affair is more important to you.

It has also been said that the object of the truthfulness is what was expressly stated in their saying **﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾**, and the meaning is that if they had obeyed you and sat [at home], they would have been killed while sitting, just as they were killed while fighting. In that case **﴿Avert﴾** and what follows is a mockery of them, meaning: if you are men who repel the causes of death, then **﴿avert﴾** all its causes, so that you do not die, as you supposedly averted this particular cause.

In the *Kashshaf* it is related that seventy hypocrites died on the day they uttered this statement, corresponding to the number who were killed at Uhud.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 169:

﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead.﴾ Imam Ahmad and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the bodies of green birds, which go to the rivers of Paradise and eat of its fruits, and which take shelter in lamps of gold suspended in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the beauty of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us,'" and in another wording: "They said: 'Who will convey to our brothers that we are alive in Paradise and provided for, so that they will not lose interest in jihad and will not shrink from war?' Allah the Exalted said: 'I will convey it to them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed these verses."

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it hasan, and al-Hakim related it and graded it sahih, and others besides them, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me and said: 'O Jabir, why do I see you downcast?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my father has been martyred and has left behind dependants and debt.' He said: 'Shall I not give you good news of what Allah the Exalted did with your father?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Allah the Exalted has never spoken to anyone except from behind a veil. He brought your father to life and spoke to him face to face, and said: "O My servant, wish of Me and I will give you." He said: "O Lord, return me to life so that I may be killed for You a second time." The Lord the Exalted said: "It has already been decreed from Me that they will not return." He said: "O my Lord, then convey to those behind me." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.'"

There is no contradiction between the two reports, since both matters may have occurred, and Allah revealed the verse concerning both. The reports concur that it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Uhud. In the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from Ishaq ibn Abi Talha, who said: "Anas told me concerning the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) whom the Prophet, peace be upon him, sent to Bir Ma'una," and he related the hadith at length, until he said: "And Anas told me that Allah the Exalted revealed a Qur'an concerning them: 'Convey on our behalf to our people that we have met our Lord, so He is pleased with us and we are pleased with Him.' Then it was abrogated and lifted after we had recited it for a time. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not think...﴾ etc."

From this it was said that the verse was revealed concerning them, and you know that the report is not explicit on that. Some claimed that it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr. The scholar al-Suyuti asserted that this is an error, and that it is the verse of al-Baqara that was revealed concerning them, being a new statement placed directly after the explanation that caution does not fatten nor avail, to clarify that the killing they fear and warn against is not something to be feared, but rather is among the most noble goals for which competitors compete. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to whoever comes upon the address in general.

It was said: [the verse is addressed] to the hypocrites who said: ﴿If they had obeyed us and stayed behind...﴾. Their belief was expressed as "thinking" because it is not counted as such. It was read as ﴿yahsabanna﴾ with a ya' on the basis of attribution to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), or the pronoun of whoever is considered, in the same manner as what was mentioned in the address. It was also said: [the verb is attributed] to ﴿those who were killed﴾, and the first object is omitted, because originally it was a subject (mubtada') which may be omitted when there is an indicator, that is: "and let not those who were killed think themselves dead."

Abu Hayyan objected that this only holds according to the opinion of the majority, who permit this omission, but for them it is very rare. Ibrahim ibn Malakun al-Ishbili prohibited it entirely. What is prohibited according to some and rare according to the majority should not be attributed to the speech of Allah the Exalted. In response: this is partisanship, because omitting one of the two objects in the category of "thinking" does not prevent abridgement, indeed brevity, according to the correct view; and "ma" here is from the first [category], so it is permissible, although some have permitted brevity, and a parallel suffices for the justification.

The scholar al-Tibi mentioned that omitting one of the two objects in this category is the view of al-Akhfash, and the apparent practice of some implies that it is understood to be an implied pronoun, that is: "and let not those who were killed think them [to be dead]," and the meaning is "let them not think themselves." Abu Hayyan objected to this with another matter, namely that it involves placing the pronoun before its explanatory noun, which is restricted to certain places, and this is not one of them. Al-Saffaqusi answered that although this is not one of them, the return of the pronoun to the grammatical subject verbally is permissible, since it is prior in meaning, and the transitivity of verbs of the heart to the pronoun of the subject is permissible. Al-Sirafi and others held the permissibility of "I thought Zayd departing" and "I thought the two Zayds departing," and this is the parallel of what that scholar mentioned, so the objection to it is most strange. Furthermore, the purpose of directing the prohibition to those who were killed is to alert the hearers that they deserve to be consoled by this and to be given the good news of eternal life and lasting bliss. But not at all times; rather at the beginning of the killing, for once their state becomes clear to them, there is no remaining benefit in considering their consolation and good news, nor any point in alerting and reminding the hearers. So said Shaykh al-Islam.

It was said: it is a prohibition with the meaning of a negation, and this occurs, though rarely. Or it is a prohibition against their thinking themselves dead at any time, even though at the time of the address they knew of their being alive. It was read ﴿wa-la tahsibanna﴾ with a kasra on the sin, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿qutthilu﴾ with the doubled letter because of the large number of those killed.

﴿Rather, they are alive﴾, that is, rather they are living and continuing in that state. It was read in the accusative, and al-Zajjaj construed it as the object of an omitted verb, that is: "rather, consider them living." Al-Farisi rejected this on the grounds that the matter is certain, so one is not commanded to think about it, and the omission of a verb other than the verb of thinking, such as "believe them" or "make them," is weak, since there is no indication of it. Moreover, regarding the estimate "make them," Abu Hayyan said that it is not valid at all, whether you take it to mean "create them," "make them," "name them," or "compose them." Yes, al-Saffaqusi said: it is valid if it means "believe them," but the point that there is no indication remains. Al-Jalabi answered that the absence of a verbal indication is granted, but when the meaning points to something, it is estimated without weakness, although the indication of the wording is better. The second scholar said: there is no prohibition on commanding thinking, because it is supposition not certainty, and obligation through supposition occurs, as in His saying: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾, a command to analogy and to attaining supposition. Some said: the intended meaning is certainty, and "I suppose them" is estimated for the sake of agreement of form. It is not hidden that this is forced, for omission for the sake of agreement of form is not known.

﴿With their Lord﴾ is in the place of nominative, as a second predicate of the omitted subject, or as an attribute of ﴿alive﴾, or in the place of accusative, as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in ﴿alive﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an adverbial complement of it or of the verb following it. "Inda" here is not for physical nearness, because that is impossible, nor in the sense of "fi" (in) of knowledge and judgment, as you say: "this is with (inda) Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, so-and-so," since that is not suited to the context; rather it means nearness and honor, that is, they are those of closeness and lofty rank. Some claimed that the meaning "in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted" suits the context, because it indicates certainty, that is, their life is established without doubt. It is not hidden that the context is one of praise, so explaining "inda" as nearness is more fitting to it.

In the statement there is indication of certainty from other aspects, and in mentioning the title of Lordship together with its attachment to their pronoun there is additional honor for them.

﴿They are provided for﴾ is an attribute of ﴿alive﴾, or a circumstantial state of the pronoun in it or in the adverbial complement, and in it there is emphasis on their being alive. The discussion of their life has already been treated in the most complete manner. The claim that their souls attach themselves to the spheres and stars, and so take delight in that and gain increase of perfection, is a statement that descends to the dust. I do not think its proponent has heard the sound reports or the clear traditions, nor has he tasted the flavor of the radiant Shari'a, nor has the white path of the way appeared to him. The report of the lamps does not illuminate his speech, nor does it remove his darkness.

By my life, the state of the martyrs and their life is beyond all that.

**Fariheen** (joyful) may be taken as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) either from the pronoun in *yurzaqūn* (they are provided for), or from the pronoun in *aḥyā'* (alive), or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase (ẓarf). It may also be in the accusative as a term of praise (madḥ), or as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifa) of *aḥyā'* in the accusative reading, and its meaning is "gladdened."

﴿*bi-mā ātāhumu-llāh*﴾ (with what God has given them), after their departure from the world, ﴿*min faḍlihi*﴾ (of His bounty). *Bi-mā ātāhum* is connected to *ātāhum*. The *min* here may be causal (sababiyya), or denoting the starting point (ibtidā' al-ghāya), or it may be connected to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial state of the elided pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun; in that case the *min* is partitive (tab'īḍ), and the sense is: "with what He gave them, it being a part of His bounty."

What is meant by this "given" is the various kinds of blessings which the martyrs attain on the Day of Resurrection, or after martyrdom, or the very attainment of success through martyrdom in the way of God, exalted is He.

﴿*wa-yastabshirūn*﴾ (and they rejoice), that is, they are made glad by good tidings (*bishāra*). The original meaning of *istibshār* is seeking good tidings, which is news that delights; however, the meaning here is joy, the word being used for what necessarily accompanies its meaning. It is either a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) or conjoined to *fariheen*, since it is interpreted as *yafraḥūn*.

It is also permitted that the sense be "while they rejoice," so the clause is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in *fariheen*, or of the object pronoun in *ātāhum*. A subject must be supposed when it is made a circumstantial clause, because the affirmative present verb does not take the conjunction *wāw* when it is a circumstantial state.

﴿*bi-l-ladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim*﴾ (concerning those who have not joined them), that is, concerning their brothers who have not yet been killed in the way of God, so that they might join them. ﴿*min khalfihim*﴾ (from behind them) is connected to *yalḥaqū*, and the meaning is that they remained after them while they had already preceded them.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial state of the subject of *yalḥaqū*, meaning: they did not join them, being left behind them, remaining after them in the world.

﴿*allā khawfun 'alayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn*﴾ (no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve). It is a substitute (badal) for *alladhīna*, a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) that clarifies that their rejoicing concerns the condition of their brothers and not their persons. That is: they rejoice at what has become clear to them of the good state of their brothers whom they left alive, namely that when they are killed in the way of God, they will succeed as they succeeded, and will obtain bliss as they obtained it. This view was held by Ibn Jurayj and Qatada. It has also been said that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning *li-allā* (so that not) or *bi-an lā* (that not), and it is an object of *yastabshirūn* standing in the position of an object of purpose: they rejoice at the arrival of their brothers who remain after them to them, because there is no fear upon them, etc. In that case, the rejoicing is not by the states.

This is supported by what is narrated from al-Suddi: that the martyr is brought a book containing the names of those of his brothers who will come to him, and he is given good tidings of this, so he rejoices as the family of an absent person rejoices at his arrival in the world. On this reading, the pronoun in *'alayhim* and what follows it refers to the first *alladhīna*, and on the first reading it refers to the second.

Among the people there are those who interpreted *alladhīna lam yalḥaqū* as those who are left behind in rank below the martyrs, namely the warriors who strove in the way of God but were not killed, rather remained until they died upon their beds. Although they did not attain the ranks of the martyrs, they also have great merit, such that no fear is upon them and they do not grieve, owing to the great excellence of jihad. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent sense of the verse, though the merit of the warriors, even if they were not killed, is something over which two rams do not butt heads.

And *an* (that), in every reading, is the light (mukhaffafa) form, its noun being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate the negated clause; the meaning is "no fear shall be upon them" regarding those whom they left behind of their offspring, for God, exalted is He, takes charge of them.

﴿*wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn*﴾ (nor shall they grieve) over what they left behind of their wealth, because God, exalted is He, has abundantly granted them recompense. Or: "no fear shall be upon them" regarding what they are about to face, because God, exalted is He, has purified their sins through martyrdom; "nor shall they grieve" at parting from the world, rejoicing in the Hereafter. Or: "no fear shall be upon them" in the world from being killed, for that is the very life which one should desire, let alone fear and beware of; "nor shall they grieve" at separation. It has also been said that both of these negated matters concern the Hereafter, and the meaning is that they do not fear the befalling of anything disagreeable from its terrors, nor do they grieve over the loss of a beloved bliss of it; and this is a sound view.

The purpose is to show the continuous absence of that, not the absence of its continuity, as might be suggested by the predicate in the second clause being a present verb; for negation, even when it enters upon the present verb itself, indicates permanence and continuance according to context, and the reference to this has already been made.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 171:

﴿Yastabshiruna﴾ is repeated for emphasis, and so that the phrase ﴿with a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾ (171) may be connected to it. Thus it becomes an explanation and elucidation of His, glorified is He, words: ﴿No fear shall be on them, nor shall they grieve﴾, because fear is a distress that befalls a person from what he anticipates of evil, and grief is a distress that befalls him from the loss of something beneficial or the occurrence of something harmful. So whoever is enveloped in a blessing from Allah the Exalted and a bounty from Him, glorified is He, will never grieve, and whoever has his deeds made thankworthy and not wasted will not fear the outcome. It is also possible that the explanation of that negation is by the mere words of the Majestic, Exalted One: ﴿with a blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, without adding what follows to it. It has been said: the first "yastabshiruna" is for the rejection of harms, which is why it was placed first, and the second is for the existence of delights; or the first is concerning their brethren and the second concerning themselves. Some of the people have parsed ﴿yastabshiruna﴾ as a substitute for the first, which is why the conjunction waw is not entered upon it. And ﴿min Allah﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurred as a qualifier of ﴿ni'mah﴾, confirming what the indefiniteness conveyed of inherent grandeur with grandeur through annexation. Bounty and blessing are mentioned together although they are often expressed by one meaning, either for emphasis, or to indicate that what He, glorified is He, granted them is not a blessing merely to the measure of sufficiency without multiplying joy and delight, but rather exceeds it, multiplying that in it. Its parallel is His, exalted is He, words: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and an increase﴾. And "anna" is conjoined to ﴿fadl﴾ or to ﴿ni'mah﴾, and on both assessments the content of what follows it is included in what is rejoiced in.

Al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis that it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) on the content of what precedes it from the earlier verses, or a parenthetical insertion between the follower and the followed, on the basis that the relative clause that comes next is a follower of ﴿alladhina lam yalhaqu﴾. The intended meaning of "the believers" is either the martyrs, and referring to them by this designation serves to inform of the loftiness of the rank of faith and that it is the criterion for the happiness they attained; or all the believers, and the fulfilment of their rewards is mentioned and counted among what is rejoiced in, in accordance with what the conjunction requires by virtue of the brotherhood in religion. Many have preferred this view.

This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, that this verse encompassed all the believers except the martyrs. Allah, exalted is He, rarely mentions a bounty with which He honoured the prophets or a reward He gave them without mentioning, glorified is He, what Allah the Exalted gave the believers after them. And in the verse there is an indication that whoever has no faith, his deeds are nullified and his rewards are wasted.

[Page 125]

**﴿Those who answered﴾**, that is, obeyed, **﴿Allah and the Messenger﴾**, by carrying out the commands, **﴿after the wound had befallen them﴾**, that is, after they had been struck by injuries on the Day of Uhud. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is in a position of genitive as an attribute of **"the believers,"** or in a position of accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni), or in a position of nominative by an implied "they are," or it is the first subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the clause of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good among them and feared Allah, there is a great reward﴾ (172). Al-Tabarsi said: "This is the more likely."

**"Among them"** (minhum) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in **"did good,"** and **"min"** is partitive (lil-tab'id), which is the view of some. Others held that it is explicative (lil-bayan). In that case the speech contains an abstraction (tajrid): from those who answered Allah and the Messenger, the one who does good and fears Allah is abstracted. The purpose of combining the two attributes is praise and explanation, not restriction, since all those who answered are good-doers and God-fearing.

Ibn Ishaq and others said: "When it was Sunday, sixteen nights had passed of Shawwal, and the battle of Uhud had been on Saturday, in the middle of it, the caller of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to pursue the enemy, and that none should go out with us except those who had been present at our battle yesterday. Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Hizam spoke to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my father had left me in charge of seven sisters of mine, and said: "O my son, it is not fitting for me or for you that we leave these women without a man among them, and I am not one who would prefer you to myself in jihad with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So stay behind with your sisters." So I stayed behind with them.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave him permission, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to strike terror into the enemy, until he reached Hamra' al-Asad, eight miles from Medina, and he stayed there on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, then returned to Medina. Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i passed by him, and Khuza'a, its Muslims and its polytheists, were a trusted repository of advice for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Tihama; their covenant with him was such that they concealed nothing from him that happened there. Ma'bad was at that time a polytheist, and he said: 'O Muhammad, by Allah, what has befallen you among your companions has grieved us greatly, and we wished that Allah had granted you well-being regarding them.' Then he left, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at Hamra' al-Asad, until he met Abu Sufyan and those with him at al-Rawha'. They had resolved to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, and they said: 'We have struck the best of his companions, his leaders and his nobles; then we will return before we uproot them. We will certainly charge against them and finish them off.' When Abu Sufyan saw Ma'bad he said: 'What is behind you, O Ma'bad?' He said: 'Muhammad has set out with his companions seeking you, with a force the like of which I have never seen, and they are burning against you with a burning, and those who had stayed behind from him on your day have joined him, and they regret what they did to them, out of rage against you, something I have never seen the like of.' He said: 'Woe to you, what are you saying?' He said: 'By Allah, I do not think you should depart until you see the forelocks of the horses.' He said: 'By Allah, we have resolved to make a charge against them, to uproot what remains of them.' He said: 'Then I forbid you from that. By Allah, what I have seen has moved me to compose verses of poetry about them.' He said: 'And what did you say?' He said: 'I said:

The she-camel I ride nearly collapsed from the clamour, when the earth flowed with the dark, massed horses,

They hurl lions, noble ones, not archers, ***
at the meeting, nor ill-favoured, lean men.

So the earth seemed to be tilting beneath them ***
when they advanced upon a leader who was not forsaken.

And I said: "Woe to the son of Harb (Abu Sufyan) because of their meeting, ***
when the valley of Batha' surges with horses."

I am a warner to the people of the arrows, ***
to every one of them, the bold and the bound.

Of the horses of Ahmad, not cowardly archers, ***
and what I have warned of cannot be described by mere talk.'

Then Abu Sufyan and those with him turned back. A caravan from Abd al-Qays passed by him, and he said: 'Where are you heading?' They said: 'We want Medina.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'We want provisions.' He said: 'Will you convey a message from me to Muhammad, which I send you with, and I will bring these for you tomorrow, raisins, at 'Ukaz, when you reach it?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When you reach him, tell him that we have resolved to march against him and his companions, to uproot what remains of them.' The caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was at Hamra' al-Asad, and they informed him of what Abu Sufyan and his companions had said. He said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'"

Ibn Hisham reported that when Abu Sufyan wished to return to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf said to them: "Do not do it, for the people have been tested, and we fear that they will have a fight other than the one that was. So return to your places." So they returned. When it reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was at Hamra' al-Asad, that they had resolved to return, he said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, I have marked stones for them, which, had they attacked us with them, would have made them like yesterday's departed." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions returned to Medina, and Allah, Exalted is He, revealed these verses. Most of the exegetes adopted this view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 173 (part 1 of 2):

Then His saying, ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾, is either a substitution (badal) for ( ﴿those who responded﴾ ) or a qualifier (sifah). The intended meaning of "the people" is: the first, the riders of ʿAbd Qays; and the second, Abu Sufyan and those with him. The definite article (alif lam) in both is for a specific reference ('ahd), and the second "the people" is other than the first.
[p. 126]
It has been related from Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah and others that they said, and the report is interwoven: "These verses were revealed concerning the minor Battle of Badr. That is because Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud, when he wanted to turn back: 'O Muhammad, the appointed meeting between us and you is the season of Badr next year, if you wish.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'That is between us and you, if Allah the Exalted wills.' When the following year came, Abu Sufyan set out with the people of Mecca until he halted at Majannah, on the side of Marr al-Zahran. It was also said that he reached ʿUsfan. Then Allah the Exalted cast terror into him, and turning back appeared to him. He met Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud al-Ashjaʿi, who had come performing ʿumrah, and Abu Sufyan said to him: 'I have made an appointment with Muhammad and his companions that we meet at the season of Badr, and this is a year of drought, and only a year in which we graze the trees and drink milk will suit us. It has become clear to me, and I dislike that Muhammad goes out and I do not go out, for that would embolden them. So go to Madinah and dishearten them, and for you I will give ten camels, which I will place in the hands of Suhayl ibn ʿAmr.' Nuʿaym came to Madinah and found the people preparing for Abu Sufyan's appointment. He said to them: 'What a wretched opinion is your opinion! They came to you in your homes and your dwellings, and none of you escaped except a fugitive, and now you want to go out to them when they have gathered against you at the season? By Allah, not one of you will escape.' The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked going out. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will certainly go out, even if I go alone.' So he went out with seventy riders, saying: '(Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian).' Until he arrived at Badr, and he remained there eight days waiting for Abu Sufyan. Abu Sufyan and those with him had returned from Majannah to Mecca, and the people of Mecca named them 'the army of the sawiq' (parched grain), meaning you had done nothing but drink sawiq. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not meet any of the polytheists, so he turned back to Madinah.'" Concerning that, ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah or Kaʿb ibn Malik says:

We promised Abu Sufyan a promise, but we found no truth in his appointment, and it was not fulfilled.
So I swear, if you had come to us and met us, you would have returned disgraced and lost your allies.
We left there the sinews of ʿUtbah and his son, and ʿAmr, Abu Jahl, we left him lying prostrate.
You disobeyed the Messenger of Allah, fie upon your religion and your affair, which was the thing that was misguided.
And though you have reproached me, I am one who says: my family and my wealth be a ransom for the Messenger of Allah.
We obeyed him, and we did not exchange him among us for anything else, a torch for us in the darkness of the night, guiding.

On this reading, the intended "people" in the first instance is Nuʿaym, and the term is applied to him as the plural and collective noun with the definite article of genus (alif lam al-jinsiyyah) is applied metaphorically to one of its members, as the scholars have explicitly stated. Or it is on the basis that those who spread the report to them are like those who said it to them. But whether the speaker was Nuʿaym is open to discussion.
Ibn Saʿd has mentioned it in his Tabaqat, and some have mentioned that the speakers were people of ʿAbd Qays.
﴿So it increased them in faith﴾. The hidden pronoun refers either to what was said, or to the verbal noun (masdar) of "said," or to its agent if by it is meant Nuʿaym alone, or to Allah the Exalted. Abu Hayyan criticized the first, saying it is weak, because what increases faith is only the uttering of it, not the thing itself. Likewise the third is criticized, because when the plural form is used metaphorically for a single individual, the pronouns refer to that plural, not to the singular. So one says "their hair (mafariquhu) has turned grey" with regard to the plural, and it is not permissible to say "its hair (mafriquhu) has turned grey" with regard to the singular. But there is room for discussion in both objections. As for the first, al-Halabi has objected that what was said is in reality what produced the increase in faith. As for the second, al-Saffaqsi has objected that it is not far-fetched to permit it, based on what is known from the inductive survey of their speech regarding a term that has both a word-form and a meaning, where sometimes the word-form is taken into account and sometimes the meaning.
The intended meaning is that they did not give attention to that; rather, their certainty in Allah the Exalted was established by it, and they became more tranquil, and they showed zeal for Islam.
[p. 127]
Those who say that faith admits of increase and decrease have used this as evidence. This is clear if obedience is made part of faith. But if faith is taken to be the assent and conviction itself, they have said concerning that: certainty increases through repeated practice, the frequent reflection, and the mutual support of proofs, without doubt, and numerous reports strengthen that. Whoever holds that faith is the assent itself and denies that it is capable of increase and decrease interprets what has come in that regard by considering the object of the belief. Among them is one who says that its increase is metaphorical for the increase of its fruit, the manifestation of its effects, and the shining of its light and radiance in the heart, and its decrease is the opposite of that. It seems that the increase here is a metaphor for the manifestation of zeal and for disregarding what discourages them. You know that the first interpretation here is very obscure, because for the people, according to the outward sense, at that statement nothing new had arisen that must be believed in, like the obligation of a prayer or a fast for example, so as to say that the increase of their faith is with regard to that object. Likewise, adopting the second interpretation for the verses and reports which hardly submit to the confines of restriction is extremely far-fetched.
So the preferable view is to accept that faith admits of increase and decrease without interpretation. And if we say that it is the assent itself, that its decrease would make it supposition or doubt, and would take it outside being faith and assent, is something on which there is no supposition or doubt, and its unqualified form is disallowed.
Yes, it may be that assent has a level, and if it descends from it, it goes outside being assent, and that is something on which no one disputes that it does not admit of decrease while remaining assent. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have pointed to this.
﴿And they said, "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾. That is, "our reckoner and our sufficiency," from the verb "ahsaba" when he suffices him. The evidence that ḥasb in the sense of muḥsib is an active participle is its occurrence as a qualifier of an indefinite noun in the phrase "rajul ḥasbuka," together with its being attached to a second person pronoun. Were it not an active participle, and its attachment merely verbal and not conferring definiteness like the attachment of the verbal noun, it would not be valid for it to be a qualifier of "rajul," so they said. From this it is known that the verbal noun used as an active participle has its ruling in attachment. The verbal sentence is conjoined to the sentence before it.
﴿And excellent is the Guardian﴾ (172). That is, the one entrusted to, so faʿil is in the sense of maf'ul, and the one specified for praise is omitted, which is His pronoun, the Exalted. The apparent reading is that this constructive sentence is conjoined to the preceding informative sentence. The waw is either from the narration (ḥikayah) or from what is narrated. If it is the first, and we say that conjoining the constructive (inshaʾi) to the informative is permitted in what has a place in grammatical case (iʿrab), since both are then in the status of single words, the matter of the conjunction is clear without the strain of interpretation, because the sentence conjoined to has the place of an object in the accusative. (They said.) However, the claim that this conjunction is permitted without interpretation is, according to the majority, disallowed, and it requires a witness, and none has been established.
If it is the second, and we say that conjoining the constructive to the informative is permitted absolutely, as Al-Saffar held, or we say that conjoining narrative to narrative is permitted, meaning conjoining the resulting content of one of the two sentences to the resulting content of the other without regard to the wording, as the second Allamah indicated, then the matter is also clear. But if we say that this is not permitted, as the majority held, then interpretation is necessary, either on the side of the conjoined-to or on the side of the conjoined. Those who go to the first said: the first sentence, though informative in form, is intended to produce reliance or sufficiency, not to inform that He, the Exalted, is sufficient in reality. Those who go to the second differed. Some of them estimated "we said" (qulna), i.e., "and we said: excellent is the Guardian."
It is objected that this is an estimate to which the mind does not incline, and there is no indication of it in the context, and moreover there is no well-considered connection between informing that Allah the Exalted is sufficient for them and informing that they said "excellent is the Guardian," such that it would be good to conjoin the two. Others made the content after the waw conjoined to what precedes it by estimating a subject: either deferred, to match the conjoined-to, for "ḥasbuna" is the predicate and "Allah" is the subject, by the indication of its mention in the conjoined-to and the omission of it being common in usage and the mind's moving to it; or fronted, out of regard for the closeness of the reference together with what preceded.
[p. 128]
It is objected that it is not hidden that after estimating the subject, if "excellent is the Guardian" is not interpreted as a statement made about Him, the sentence is also constructive, since a nominal sentence whose predicate is constructive is constructive, just as one whose predicate is a verb is verbal in meaning. How could it not be so, when there is no difference between "excellent is the man, Zayd" and "Zayd is excellent of men," in that the meaning of each is a relation that does not admit of truth or falsehood. And after interpretation, the conjoined is not the sentence "excellent is the Guardian," but the sentence of which its predicate's complement is "excellent is the Guardian." The difficulty lies only in conjoining "excellent is the Guardian," unless it is said that this is chosen, and it is said: an answer to something may be by affirming that thing and presenting something else, and it may be by changing that thing, and what is here is of the second kind. So from the apparent standpoint the conjoined is the sentence "excellent is the Guardian," and the difficulty returns. From the standpoint of reality the conjoined is the sentence of the statement, and there is no difficulty. But it is objected that after interpretation the general praise, for which the verbs of praise were established, is lost, and it becomes informing of a specific praise, namely that it was said about Him, "excellent is the Guardian." Also, the being-said of the said statement is only by way of predication and informing about Him by "excellent is the Guardian," so it is necessary to estimate a statement made about Him a second time, and this leads to infinite estimates. And it seems that for this reason the majority did not interpret the constructive that occurs as a predicate in that way. This is the choice of Saʿd, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him. Some have permitted, on the supposition that the waw is from what is narrated, conjoining "excellent is the Guardian" to "ḥasbuna," considering that it has the sense of a verb, as "ja'ala" is conjoined to "fāliq" in His saying, ﴿He splits the dawn and made the night for rest﴾, according to one opinion. In that case it is conjoining a sentence that has a place in grammatical case to a single word, since it is then a predicate about a single word. Some of the verifiers permit this, and it is not conjoining the constructive to the informative. Although this is, in reality, without objection, nonetheless the matter of conjoining to the predicate, based on what Shaykh al-Radi mentioned, that "niʿma al-rajul" has the sense of a single word and its estimate is "ay rajul jayyid" (i.e., a good man), is clearer, as is not hidden.

Some people claimed that the verse is evidence for the permissibility of conjoining the constructive to the informative in what has a place in grammatical case, based on the premise that the waw is from narration only.

It is not hidden from you that, even granting that the *waw* there is of this kind, it cannot serve as evidence for what has been mentioned, because it is possible that (*qalū*, "they said") is implied in the conjoined clause, the proof being that it is mentioned in the clause it is conjoined to (*al-maʿṭūf ʿalayhi*). In that case it would be a conjunction (*ʿatf*, the grammatical linking of one element to another) of a verbal declarative clause (*jumla fiʿliyya khabariyya*) onto another verbal declarative clause. Furthermore, just as the apparent reading requires that there be a conjunction onto the declarative (*ikhbar*, declarative speech), and there is the disagreement you have learned about, so too it requires the conjunction of a verbal clause onto a nominal clause, and this too has a well-known disagreement, as does its reverse. The answer to this can be derived from what we mentioned concerning the performative (*insha'*) and the declarative (*ikhbar*). The scholars have spoken at length on this matter, and what we have mentioned is little of much, and a trickle from a great pool.

Then, this phrase was the last thing Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said when he was thrown into the fire, as al-Bukhari recorded in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and ʿAbd al-Razzaq and others from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you encounter a matter, say: Hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil (Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs)."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya recorded from ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that "the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever his distress intensified, would pass his hand over his head and beard, then exhale a long sigh and say: Hasbi Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil."

Abu Nuʿaym recorded from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hasbi Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil is the security of every fearful person."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 174:

﴿Then they returned⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ ...﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with an implied element understood from the context, meaning: so they went out to them and returned. ﴿with a blessing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (inqalabū). It is also permitted that it be a direct object (mafʿūl bihi). The bāʾ, according to the first view, is for transitivity (taʿdiyah), and according to the second, for accompaniment (muṣāḥabah). The tanwin (indefinite ending) on it, under both assessments, is for magnification, i.e., (with a blessing) that is great, whose extent cannot be measured. ﴿from Allah﴾ is a qualifier of "blessing," emphasizing its greatness.

Page 129

The intended meaning of it is safety, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas; or steadfastness upon faith and obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, as said by al-Zajjaj; or their humiliation of the enemies of Allah from a distance, as has been said; or the combination of all these matters, according to what we say.

﴿and bounty﴾, which is profit in trade. Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that "a caravan passed by during the days of the season, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bought it, profited wealth, and distributed it among his companions; that is the bounty."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he went out to the Lesser Battle of Badr at Badr, gave his companions dirhams with which to buy goods in the season, and they gained trade."

And from Mujahid: the bounty is what they obtained of trade and reward.

﴿No harm touched them⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠ ...﴾ That is, no killing struck them, which is narrated from al-Suddi; or no one harmed them, which is narrated from al-Habr (Ibn ʿAbbas). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of (inqalabū), or from the implicit pronoun in (bi-niʿmah) if it is a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they returned blessed, cleared of harm. When the circumstantial clause has a present-tense verb negated by (lam) and contains a pronoun referring back to the subject, it is permitted to include the particle "wāw" or omit it.

﴿And they followed⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠ ...﴾ is a conjunction with (inqalabū). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, with "qad" implied, meaning: and they had certainly followed in everything they were given, or in going out to meet the enemy. ﴿the pleasure of Allah﴾, which is the basis of every good. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ (174), in that He bestowed upon them what He bestowed. In what preceded, together with concluding with this verse containing the noble all-encompassing Name, and the attribution of "Possessor of bounty" to Him, and the description of the bounty as great, there is an indication that those who remained behind lost for themselves a great matter whose reality cannot be fully grasped, and they deserve to regret it with a regret beyond which there is none.

[Page 130]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 175 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is only that [demonstrative] Satan (al-shaytan)...﴾ The demonstrative (ishara, "that") refers to the one who discourages, either directly or through an intermediary. The address is to the believers, and it is the subject (mubtada'). His saying "al-Shaytan" means Iblis, because it is his name by dominance (ghalaba). It is the predicate (khabar), in an intensive simile (tashbih baligh). His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿frightens his allies﴾" is a new, explanatory clause (jumla mustan'afa) clarifying his being a devil (shaytana), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal), as in His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiya)﴾."

It is permissible for "al-Shaytan" to be an attribute of the demonstrative, also as a simile. It is also possible that it is a figurative usage (majaz), where he is made to be the one who frightens, and "frightens" is the predicate. It has also been permitted that "dhalika" (that) refers to the statement of the one who discourages. In that case a genitive noun must be supplied, meaning "the statement of Satan." What is meant by him is also Iblis. There is no figurative usage in it according to the sound view. The figurative usage lies only in the attribution to him, because the saying was by his whispering and causing, so it was made as if it were his saying. The pronoun in "yukhawwifu" (frightens) is either for the implied subject or for Satan, with the returning pronoun removed, meaning "he frightens by it."

As for "his allies" (awliya'ahu), they may be Abu Sufyan and his companions. Then the first object of "yukhawwifu" is omitted, meaning "he frightens you with his allies," by making them great in your hearts. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿to warn of severe punishment﴾." Ibn 'Abbas read it with this object mentioned.

Some read "yukhawwifukum bi-awliya'ihi" (he frightens you with his allies). Most of the exegetes follow this meaning, and al-Zajjaj, Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and others went this way. It is supported by His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿So do not fear them﴾," meaning do not fear his allies whom he has caused you to fear, "﴿and fear Me﴾" in opposing My command.

Or the allies are those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then "awliya'ahu" is the first object, and the second object is either left unmentioned or omitted because it is understood, meaning "he causes them to fall into fear," or "he frightens them of Abu Sufyan and his companions." On this view it is not correct for the pronoun in "takhafuhum" (fear them) to return to the allies; rather it returns to the people.

The second [view]: the pronoun is like that in "ikhshawhum" (fear them), and so it is a rejection of it, meaning "do not fear the people, and sit back from fighting and be cowardly," "﴿and fear Me﴾," so fight with My Messenger and hasten to comply with what he commands you. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi went to this view. Al-Tibi claimed that the structure of the verse supports it. The address then is to both groups, those who went out and those who stayed behind, and the aim is an indirect rebuke of the last group. It has been said that the address is to the latter alone, and "awliya'ahu" in that case is placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, to censure them by saying they are the allies of Satan. Some have preferred this statement absolutely, giving as its reason that those who went out did not fear anyone but Allah, may He be exalted.

"﴿And they said, Allah is sufficient for us﴾." You know that the presence of the possibility of indirect rebuke weakens this reason. The "fa" (then) is for the sequence of the prohibition or the cessation based on what precedes it, since the frightener being a devil, or a statement of his, is something that requires the absence of fear and the prohibition against it.

Abu 'Amr read the "ya'" of "wakhafuni" (and fear Me) when connected, and omitted it when pausing. The rest omit it in all cases, and it is the pronoun of the object.

His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿If you are believers﴾" (175). If the address is to those who stayed behind, the matter in it is clear. If it is to those who went out, it is directed to urge them on and stir them, given the certainty of their faith. If it is to all of them, then it contains a grammatical priority of the masculine (taghlib). In any case, the response (jaza') is omitted. It has been said: if the address in what precedes is to the sincere believers, it does not require a response, because it has the meaning of a cause (ta'lil). If it is to the others, then a response is required. As if the meaning is: "If you are believers, then fear Me and fight with My Messenger," because faith requires that you prefer fear of Allah, may He be exalted, over fear of people.

* * *

Here (and from the category of allusion, ishara) in the verses, "﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah﴾" by the sword of love, "﴿or you die﴾" by the experiential death, "﴿surely forgiveness﴾," meaning a covering over of your existence, "﴿from Allah and mercy﴾" from Him, may He be exalted, by your being adorned with His attributes, may He be mighty and majestic, "﴿is better than what they gather﴾," meaning the people of abundance.

"﴿So by a mercy from Allah﴾," meaning by your being characterized by a mercy of the Merciful, that is, a mercy following your bestowed divine existence, not your human existence. "﴿You were gentle with them, and had you been harsh (fazz)﴾," characterized by the attributes of the self, such as coarseness and roughness, "﴿they would have scattered from around you﴾," and not borne the burden of that. Or it may be said: if the attributes of beauty in you did not prevail over the qualities of majesty, they would have dispersed from you and not endured with you.
