Or it may be said: if you had given them pure wine of unity, unmixed with what has any share for them, they would have scattered, wandering on their faces, unable to stand with you even for a moment. Or it may be said: if you had been scrupulous with them about the rulings of realities, their chests would have been constricted and they would not have borne the weights of the reality of courtesies on the path, but you were lenient with them through the Shari'a and its concessions.

"﴿So pardon them﴾" regarding what relates to you of their shortcomings with you, because of the loftiness of your rank and because you see nothing in existence except Allah. "﴿And ask forgiveness for them﴾" regarding what relates to the right of Allah, may He be exalted, because of their apology. Or: ask forgiveness for them for what passes through their hearts of thoughts that do not befit knowledge. "﴿And consult them in the matter﴾" when you are in the station of action, as a test for them and an examination of their station. "﴿And when you have resolved﴾," and that is when you are in the station of witnessing the lordship and emerging from distinction into unity, "﴿then rely upon Allah﴾," for He is sufficient for you in what He wants from you and what you want from Him.

Some Sufis mentioned that it is possible to understand from the verse that the address is with the human spirit, and that the faculties of the self and its appetitive and irascible powers exist so that they may take their share, and that the continuation of the offspring and the good ordering of livelihood are connected to this. Were it not so, those powers would have vanished and perished, wisdom would have been disrupted, and the perfections for which man was created would have been lost.

"﴿If Allah helps you, there is none to overcome you﴾," a realization of the meaning of reliance (tawakkul) and unity (tawhid) in actions.

Some of the masters, may Allah sanctify their secrets, mentioned that Allah's help for His servants varies in degrees. His help for the seekers (murids) is by granting them success in suppressing desires; His help for the lovers (muhibbin) is by the description of nearness; His help for the knowers ('arifin) is by the unveiling of witnessings. It has been said: the help of Allah, may He be exalted, is perceived only by one who disowns his own power and strength and holds fast to his Lord in all his means.

"﴿And it is not for a prophet to deceive (yaghull)﴾," because of his perfect holiness and the utmost of his trustworthiness, so he did not hide the right of Allah, may He be exalted, from His servants. He gave the knowledge of truth to the people of truth, and did not place his secrets except with the trustworthy among his community.

"﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾," that is, the Prophet, in the station of pleasure, which is the garden of the attributes, by his being characterized by the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted, "﴿like one who has earned anger from Allah﴾," and that is the one who deceives, veiled by the attributes of his own self, "﴿and whose refuge is Hell﴾," which is the lowest abyss of the dark self. "﴿They are of degrees with Allah﴾," meaning each of the people of pleasure and of wrath differs in ranks according to their readinesses.

"﴿Certainly Allah conferred favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾," since he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the mirror of the Truth, through which It manifests to the believers. Had it manifested to them directly, they would have been burned by the first assault of its greatness. The meaning of his being "from themselves" (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) is his being in the garb of a human, apparent in the form they have. To understand "the believers" as "the knowers," and "the messenger" as the human spirit illuminated by the light of the Names and Attributes, sent to reform the faculties, is not far-fetched in the station of allusion. "﴿When a disaster struck you﴾" in the course of traveling in Allah, may He be exalted, and it is the disaster of spiritual dryness (fatra) relative to you, "﴿you have struck twice as much﴾" [i.e., the faculties of the self have been struck twice as much]: once when you reached the station of the unity of actions, and once when you reached the station of the unity of attributes. "﴿You said, From where is this?﴾" that is, how has this befallen us while we are in the wilderness of the journey in Allah, may He be exalted and mighty? "﴿Say, It is from yourselves﴾," because a remnant of its own attributes remains in it. This does not contradict His saying, may He be exalted, "﴿Say, all is from Allah﴾," because the efficient cause in all is the Truth, may His majesty be exalted, and the receptive cause is themselves. Nothing overflows from the Agent except what befits and is required by the readiness. So in relation to the Agent it is from Allah, and in relation to the recipient it is from themselves. It may be said that what is from themselves is also from Allah, may He be exalted, when viewed from the standpoint of unity, since there is nothing else there.

"﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the way of Allah﴾," whether they were killed in the lesser struggle (jihad asghar), by giving up their lives seeking the pleasure of Allah, may He be exalted, or in the greater struggle (jihad akbar), by breaking the self and suppressing desire through discipline, "﴿are dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord﴾," with the true life, brought near in the presence of holiness, "﴿being provided for﴾" with the spiritual provisions, which are the knowledges and realities. It has been reported in some traditions: "The spirits of the martyrs are in the bodies of green birds, roaming in the rivers of Paradise, eating from its fruits, and taking refuge in golden lamps suspended in the shade of the Throne." Some Sufis transmitted this with this wording, and took the green birds as a reference to the celestial bodies, the golden lamps as a reference to the stars, the rivers of Paradise as the sources and channels of knowledge, and its fruits as states and knowledges.

The meaning is that the spirits of the martyrs attach themselves to the luminous celestial bodies in their purity, and approach the channels of knowledge, acquiring there knowledges and states. It is not hidden that this is something that should not be believed, as we have pointed out before. If interpretation is nevertheless necessary, then let the bird be taken as a reference to the forms through which spirits appear, on the basis that they are immaterial substances. The name "bird" is applied to them as an indication of their lightness and their swift arrival wherever they are permitted.

A similar thing in general is His saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith: "Children are the dada'mis of Paradise." The dada'mis are plural of du'mus, a small creature found in stagnant water, very active and hardly ever still. It is known that children are not that creature in Paradise, but he (may Allah bless him, his family and grant him peace) intended to inform that they will be wanderers in Paradise. He expressed this by way of intensive simile (tashbih baligh). The description of the birds as green is a reference to their beauty and freshness. From this also is the report: "Indeed the world is sweet and green," and the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed, raiding is sweet and green." Among their proverbs is: "The self is green," and by this they may mean that it inclines toward everything and desires it.

The matter of the locative (zarfiyya) in the report is simple. The rest of what is in it is either on its apparent sense or is interpreted. On the second view, "Paradise" is intended as the Paradise of intention, which is the Paradise of the Essence and the Attributes. Its rivers are what arises from the manifestations (tajalliyat). Its fruits are the effects that follow those manifestations. The lamps suspended in the shade of the Throne are stations that cannot be comprehended, suspended in the shade of the throne of all-encompassing absolute existence. Their being of gold is a reference to their greatness, and that they are not attained except by the exertion of the souls.

[Page 132]

The sum of the meaning on this reading is that the spirits of the martyrs, who gave their lives seeking the pleasure of God Most High, or whom longing for Him, exalted is His glory, slew, take the forms of beautiful, delicate, tender images that whoever sees them finds pleasing. They fly on the wings of acceptance and contentment through the various kinds of divine manifestations, and by this they acquire kinds of spiritual delights whose worth cannot be measured. A sublime station is renewed for them with the measure of every night, which is attained only through the like of their deeds. That is the enduring bliss and the great triumph.

It seems that whoever interpreted this report and similar ones intended to close the door of transmigration (tanasukh, the passage of souls between bodies). Perhaps, in the sense held by the people of misguidance, it is not necessary, as we pointed out in the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿rejoicing in what God has given them of His bounty﴾, of honour, favour and nearness to Him. ﴿And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾, namely the warriors who have not yet been killed, or the wayfarers who strive against their souls and have not yet reached their rank at that time. ﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, because of their triumph in the greatest refuge and the most noble Beloved. ﴿They rejoice in a blessing from God﴾, a great one, which is the Paradise of the Attributes, ﴿and bounty﴾, i.e., an increase upon it, which is the Paradise of the Essence. And despite that, ﴿God does not waste﴾ the reward of the faith of the believers, which is the Paradise of Actions and the reward of deeds. ﴿Those who responded to God and the Messenger﴾ by annihilation in the Essential Unity and by upholding the right of steadfastness, ﴿after the wound had afflicted them﴾, i.e., the breaking of the self, ﴿for those of them who did good﴾, and they are those who remained firm in the station of contemplation and perfected their looking at their own selves, ﴿there is a great reward﴾ beyond the reward of faith.

﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, the deniers before reaching contemplation, ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ and massed to oppose you, ﴿so fear them﴾, and abandon what you are upon. ﴿But that increased them﴾, that saying, ﴿in faith﴾, i.e., in certainty and monotheism through negating the other and disregarding it. By negating what is other than God Most High, they arrived at affirming Him. ﴿And they said, God is sufficient for us﴾, so they witnessed Him, then returned to the details of the Attributes with steadfastness, and said: ﴿an excellent Guardian﴾. ﴿So they returned with blessing from God and bounty﴾, i.e., they returned with the Real Existence in the Paradise of the Attributes and the Essence. ﴿No harm touched them﴾: no one harmed them, for there is none but the One. ﴿And they followed God's pleasure﴾ in their journey, until they attained the Paradise of the Essence alluded to in His saying: ﴿and God is Possessor of great bounty﴾, as we pointed out.

﴿That is only Satan who frightens his allies﴾, the ones veiled by their selves, ﴿so do not fear them﴾, the deniers, ﴿and fear Me﴾, since there is nothing in existence besides Me, ﴿if you are believers﴾, i.e., monotheists in true monotheism. God Most High is the Granter of success to what is right, and He is our sufficiency and an excellent Guardian.

[Page 132]

﴿Let not grieve you those who race to disbelief﴾: this is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is directed to him as an honour, to console him, while also indicating that he is the leader whose affairs are the principal concern. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers either to the hypocrites who held back, which is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq; or to a group of Arabs who apostatised from Islam, because of their closeness to the idol-worshippers, which is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i; or to all the disbelievers, which is the view of al-Hasan; or to the hypocrites and a group of the Jews, as specified in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, let not grieve you those who race to disbelief from among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths while their hearts have not believed, and from among those who are Jews﴾. Some scholars held this view. The meaning of (yusari'una fi al-kufr, "they race into disbelief") is that they fall into it quickly, out of their extreme eagerness for it and their intense desire for it. Because racing (al-musara'a) includes the sense of falling into something, it takes the preposition "fi" (in) rather than "ila" (to), which is the usual construction, as in ﴿And race to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾ and elsewhere. This construction was chosen. It was said that this is to indicate their settled state in disbelief, and their constant engagement with it from the beginning of their racing to its end, just as in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿They race to good deeds﴾, regarding the believers. As for the use of "ila" in the verse of the Garden, the reason is that forgiveness and the Garden are the endpoint and goal of racing. The relative clause is the subject of (yahzunuka, "grieves you"). The relative clause is not the cause of the absence of grief, as is customary in such constructions, because grief over falling into disbelief is the fitting response, since it is ugly in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, and one must grieve when witnessing it. Thus it would not be correct to forbid grief over that. Rather, the cause here is what results from that racing, namely the spite toward the believers and the causing of harm to them. He expressed it this way for the sake of emphasis in the prohibition.

What is meant is: let not grieve you the fear that they will harm you and aid against you. This is supported by the juxtaposition of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾, as a rejection and denial of the supposition of fear. The sentence contains an elided noun, and what is meant is "the friends of Allah," as an example, because of the rational indication of it. Omitting this and attaching the negation of harm to Him, exalted is He, is an honour for the believers and indicates that harming them is like harming Him, glorified and exalted is He. In this there is further emphasis in the consolation. (Shay'an, "at all") is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they will never harm Him with any harm whatsoever. It was said that it is the object by means of a preposition, meaning: they will never harm Him with anything at all. Interpreting "yadurru" as something that takes two objects directly is unnecessary, and the context probably calls for something other than that.

Nafi' recited (yuhzinu) with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the zāy throughout the Qur'an, except His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾, where he read it with a fathah and a dammah on the zāy. The rest of the readers recited as Nafi' did in the excepted place. Abu Ja'far recited the reverse of what Nafi' recited. The past tense on the reading with the fathah is (hazina), and on the reading with the dammah it is from (ahzana). Their meaning is the same, except that (hazina) is a rare dialect form. It was said that (hazantuhu) means I caused him grief, and (ahzantuhu) means I exposed him to grief. Al-Khalil said: (khazantuhu) means I put grief in him, as (dahantuhu) means I put oil in him, and (ahzantuhu) means I made him grieved. It is also read (yusri'una) without an alif, from (asra'a), and (yusari'una) with imalah and with tafkhim.

﴿Allah intends not to give them any share in the Hereafter﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the cause of their racing, as if it were said: why do they race into disbelief when they gain nothing from it? It is answered that He, exalted is He, intends that He will not give them any portion of reward in the Hereafter. Thus He intends that for them; so how would they not race? In this is evidence that disbelief occurs by the will of Allah, the Exalted, even though He punishes its doer and blames him, because that is due to the badness of his predisposition, which requires that this be overflowed upon him. Some scholars of verification (muhaqqiqin) mentioned that mentioning the will indicates the complete sincerity of the motive to deprive them and to punish them, since the will of the Most Merciful of the merciful is attached to both. Some claimed that this is based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, but that is not so, as is not hidden; for He did not say, "He did not will their disbelief," nor did He allude to it. The form of the present tense indicates the continuity and persistence of the will, and it returns to the continuity and persistence of the source of this intended outcome, which is disbelief. Thus there is an indication that they will remain in disbelief until they perish in it. And for them, along with this complete deprivation of reward, there is a great punishment whose extent cannot be measured.

It is reported from some of them that since racing toward a thing indicates the greatness of its importance and the exaltedness of its value in the eyes of the one who races, the punishment was described as great, in keeping with the correspondence, and as a warning about the baseness of what they raced toward and its lowness in itself. It was also said that since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ indicates the greatness of the One whom they intended to harm, the punishment was described as great, as an indication that intending harm to the Great is a great matter, and that a great punishment follows from it. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (lahum, "for them"), meaning: Allah, the Exalted, intends to deprive them of reward, while a great punishment is prepared for them; or it is a new sentence, indicating their share of punishment immediately after the explanation that they have no portion of reward.

Some claimed that these two clauses are in the position of a reason for the earlier prohibition, and that the meaning is: "Let not grieve you that they race to elevate disbelief and to demolish Islam, neither out of fear for Islam nor out of compassion for them." As for the first, because they will never harm Allah at all, so they are not able to demolish His religion, which He intends to exalt; and then there is no need to take the friends of Allah as an elided noun. As for the second, because Allah intends that they will have no share in the Hereafter, and for them there is a great punishment.

He supports this by noting that the Prophet (ﷺ) was often forbidden from putting his noble self into hardship for their guidance, and from being distressed at their disbelief, and he was addressed with: (You are not responsible except for conveying), and: "You are not over them a controller." But this is not free from distance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 177:

﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith﴾, i.e., they took disbelief in place of faith, out of desire for what they took and aversion to what they left behind. For this reason he placed "ishtaraw" (bought, exchanged) in the position of "baddalu" (replaced), since the former is more evident in desire and more indicative of bad choice. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They will never harm Allah at all﴾, has already been discussed, and there is in it here a clear allusion, by restricting the harm to themselves, as if it were said: rather, they harm only themselves. The intended meaning of the relative clause here is the same as what was intended there. The repetition serves to establish the ruling and confirm it by stating its cause, by changing the title of the subject, for what is mentioned in the relative clause is a sign of total loss. Everlasting deprivation clearly indicates that their harm falls on themselves, and that it never reaches anyone else at all, and it indicates the complete feebleness of their minds and the weakness of their opinions. How could they accomplish, from harming the friends of Allah Exalted, whom He has guaranteed victory, what depends on strength of resolve, soundness of judgment and firmness of planning? They are more unassailable than Jalima and more protected than the lion's palate. It is also permissible that the relative clause here be general and that it be specific there, namely excluding what al-Hasan went to about it. The sentence affirms the content of what precedes it: it establishes the universal principles for the particular rulings that fall under them. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the first be general for the disbelievers, and this be specific to the hypocrites, and he singled them out for mention because they are more harmful and more treacherous. It has been objected that the intention of the general meaning there is not fitting to the grandeur of the revelation, because the occurrence of hastening into disbelief in the stated sense, and its being a likely cause of grief for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is understood from the prohibition against it, can only be conceived of in those known to be characterized by it. As for those disbelievers whose condition is unknown, who are in distant lands, attributing the aforementioned hastening to them and considering it among the origins of his grief, peace and blessings be upon him, has no basis. It may be said: the one who holds the generality in the first case did not intend by the disbelievers the opposite of the believers wherever they are and in whatever state they are found, but rather what includes those who lag behind and apostates, for example, from among those whose harm to him, Allah bless him and grant him peace, is expected. In that case this objection is not raised.

It has been said: the intended meaning of the first is the hypocrites, or those who apostatized from what is here, the Jews. The intended meaning of faith is either actual faith, as is the case with apostates, or potential faith close to it, obtained by witnessing its proofs in the Torah, as is the case with the Jews for example, or the faculty-faith, obtained by witnessing the revealed speech and the proofs set up in the horizons and in the souls, as is the habit of all disbelievers other than these, or the common element shared by all, as is the habit of all. So reflect.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., painful. The sentence is independent, clarifying the complete severity of their punishment by mentioning the extreme degree of its pain after mentioning the extreme degree of its magnitude. Or it confirms the harm that the first sentence indicated. It has been said: since it is customary for the buyer to rejoice in what he bought and be delighted at obtaining it when the transaction is profitable, and to be pained when it is a loss, their punishment is described as painful, in consideration of that. This was related by our master Shaykh al-Islam.

[Page 135]

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with His saying, ﴿And let not those who disbelieve grieve you﴾ [3:176]. The verb takes the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl, "those who") as its subject. "That" (anna) and what follows it stand in place of both objects (sādd masadd) according to Sibawayh, because the intended meaning is achieved: the heart-verbs are linked to a predication between the subject and the predicate. According to al-Akhfash, the second object is omitted. "What" (mā) is either verbal (maṣdariyyah) or relative (mawṣūlah). In both cases it should have been written separately, but in al-Imam (the ʿUthmanic codex) it is written joined. Following al-Imam is obligatory, and perhaps the reason is harmony with what follows it and the adoption of the more common usage in it. "Good" (khayr) is the predicate. It has also been read as (khayran) in the accusative, with "for themselves" (li-anfusihim) then being the predicate. "For them" (lahum) is either a clarification or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "good." Al-imlāʾ (granting respite) originally means prolonging a period. Al-malaʾ is a long span of time, and from it comes al-malawān, the night and the day, because of their long succession.
[Page 136 note: this page break is part of the source text.]

As for imlāʾ al-kitāb (dictating writing), it is so called because of the long period spent pausing at every word.

It has been said: al-imlāʾ means leaving free (al-takhliyah). The saying is: "He granted his horse (amlā li-faraṣihi)" when he loosened its tether for it to graze as it wished.

The sense of the construction is: "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite, or that what We grant them, is good for themselves"; or "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is good for them"; or "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that the goodness of what We grant them is established or actual." The outcome of this is a prohibition against rejoicing in the outward prolonging of their lives and in God's leaving them to continue in their state, or against leaving them to their own affairs on the basis of supposing it is good for them. It also rebukes them by showing that it is pure deception and sheer harm. Ḥamzah read (wa-lā taḥsabanna) with the ta, and the address is either to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which is most fitting for the context of consolation, though the intention is a veiled reproach to them, since they supposed what has been mentioned; or it is addressed to everyone who is capable of supposing, aiming to publicise the horror of their condition. The relative pronoun is the object, and "that We grant them respite" etc. is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from it. Since the primary aim is the substitute, and since here it serves in place of two objects, it is permissible to limit it to one object; otherwise, without this, the limitation would not be correct according to the sound view. It is also permissible that "that We grant them respite" be a second object, but because it is in the sense of a verbal noun it cannot be understood as referring to persons, so an ellipsis is necessary. In the first case, the meaning is: "Let not the state and affair of those who disbelieve be supposed (to be good)"; in the second: "Let not those who disbelieve be supposed to be the people for whom 'that We grant them respite' etc. [is good]." The restriction of the good by His saying, ﴿for themselves﴾, is because granting respite is good for believers, owing to its many benefits. As for one who makes khayr in this context an elative of preference (afʿal al-tafḍīl), and makes the thing compared to it fighting in the way of God, he makes the preference based on the assumption of opinion and mere accommodation. The verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca, as narrated from Muqatil, or concerning Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr, as narrated from ʿAṭāʾ. ﴿We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ is a resumptive clause giving the cause of the ruling preceding it. Those who hold that good and evil are by His will, may permit the stating of cause with the like of this, either because it is a purpose, or because it is willed together with the act, which resembles cause according to whoever does not permit explaining His acts by purposes. As for the Mu'tazilah, although they affirm that His acts are caused, the ugly is not willed by Him, nor sought, nor a purpose for them. Therefore they made the increase in sin here a motive, like the saying: "I sat out of the battle through cowardice," not a purpose whose attainment is intended. Since the increase did not precede the granting of respite here, and a motive must precede, they made it a metaphor, on the ground that its being prior in God's eternal knowledge, which cannot be contradicted by the known, likens it to the precedence of the motive in external reality. Its artificiality is not hidden; therefore it has been said: the easier view is that the lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿāqibah).

It has been objected that although this is less forced, the saying is not correct, because this clause is a causal explanation of what precedes it. So if the granting of respite were for a sound purpose which results in this corrupt and ugly matter, that would not be valid, and this would not be suitable as a cause, since it is a prohibition against supposing that granting respite to them is good. So reflect. This was said by one of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqīn).

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read (annamā) here with a fatḥah, and the first with a kasrah, and with the yā of the third person in (yaḥsabanna), so that "those who disbelieve" is the subject of yaḥsabanna, and "that We grant them respite that they may increase in sin" stands in place of the two objects of supposing. The meaning: "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is for the increase of sin; rather it is for repentance, entering into faith, and making up for what has been missed." The clause ﴿that We grant them respite is good for themselves﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the verb and its object, and its meaning is: "Our granting respite is good for them if they awaken and repent." The difference between the two readings is that on this reading the granting of respite is for the desire of repentance, and the granting for the purpose of increase is negated; on the other reading, the first is affirmed and the second is negated implicitly. There is no contradiction between them, because according to Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni scholars) it is permissible for either to be intended, and it does not follow that the intended thing is separated from the will, since it is conditional on conditions, as you have known.

Some have claimed that the clause ﴿that We grant them respite is good for them﴾ etc. is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), meaning: "Let not this be supposed in this state, and this state contradicts it." This is nothing.

﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is an independent clause describing their state in the Hereafter after describing their state in this world. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the waw (of the plural), meaning: "that they may increase in sin, with a humiliating punishment prepared for them." This is the strongest reading in the last reading, as many verifiers have held, so that the content of this falls within the scope of the prohibition against supposing, as if one said: "that they may increase in sin, and that there may be for them a punishment." Some have made it coordinated with the clause "that they may increase," so that "a humiliating punishment" is the subject of the adverbial phrase, with the implied meaning "and there will be for them a humiliating punishment." This is very weak. Indeed it has been said it may also be parenthetical, and there is some merit in this in general.

Further, the reason their punishment is described as humiliating: as Shaykh al-Islam said, since granting respite entails enjoying the good things and adornments of this world, and that calls for arrogance and tyranny, it is described thus so that their recompense is a fitting recompense. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam. It may also be said that this is an indication of refuting what might be the source of their supposing, namely that they are honoured before Him, mighty and majestic, following the indication of its refutation in another way.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 179 (part 1 of 2):

﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in⦆ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to promise the believers and to threaten the hypocrites with a worldly punishment, namely disgrace and humiliation, following the explanation of their punishment in the Hereafter. The explanation of this was given first because it is more effective in giving respite (al-imla') so that sins increase. In this promise and threat there is also, as is not hidden, a consolation for him (ﷺ), as in the preceding discourse. It has been said: the verse is brought to explain the wisdom behind God's granting respite to the disbelievers, following an explanation of their disbelief. But it is not hidden that this is distant, let alone being the closer view. By "the believers" is meant the sincere ones (al-mukhlisun). The address, as taste requires, is to the general body of the sincere and the hypocrites; so there is an iltifat within a tilwin (shift of address). By "the state you are in" is meant the mixing of some of them with others and their equal standing in the application of the rulings of Islam upon them. To this view lean the verifying scholars of exegesis (al-muhaqqiqun min ahl al-tafsir). Most of them said: the address is to the hypocrites alone, so there is only tilwin (shift of address). Most of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) held that it is specifically to the believers, so there is tilwin and iltifat as well.

Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jarir and others, from Qatadah, that it is addressed to the disbelievers. Perhaps what is meant by them is the hypocrites; otherwise it is very distant.

The lam in ﴿li-yadhar⦆ is connected to an omitted element, which is the predicate (khabar) of kana, and the verb is put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" after it, as the Basrans held; that is, God was not willing to leave the believers, etc. The Kufans said: the lam is extra (mazidah) for emphasis, and it itself governs the verb in the subjunctive, and the predicate is the verb. Its being extra does not detract from its governing, since the extra element may govern, as in the extra prepositions (huruf al-jarr al-mazidah). So there is no weakness in their position from this aspect, as has been wrongly thought. The original of "yadhar" is "yawdhar," and the waw was dropped from it, by analogy with "yada'" (yadaʿa). There is no reason for its dropping there, since it did not fall between a ya' and a kasrah, nor what is in the position of a kasrah. This differs from "yadaʿa," where the original is "yawdaʿa," and the waw was dropped because it fell between a ya' and what is in the position of a kasrah. The dal was vowelled with fatha because its final radical is a guttural letter (harf halqi), so the preceding letter takes fatha; similar are "yasaʿa," "yatao" and "yaqaʿa." They did not use from "yadhar" a past tense, a verbal noun, or an active participle, for example, relying on the inflection of its synonym, which is "yatruku."

God's words ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good⦆ are a limit (ghayah) for what the preceding negation implies, as if it were said: He does not leave them in that mixture, but rather He decrees affairs and arranges causes until He separates the hypocrite from the believer. It is not a limit for the preceding statement itself, since the meaning would become: He does not leave the believers in the state you are in until this limit; and it would be understood from it, as al-Samin said, that once the limit is reached He leaves the believers in the state you are in, and that is not the meaning. He expressed the believer and the hypocrite by the good and the wicked, to record upon each of them what befits it, and to indicate the cause of the ruling. He used the singular "the wicked" and "the good" although many individuals are intended by each; this signals that the basis of separating one of the two groups from the other is their being characterized by their attributes, not the particular essence or the plurality of their individuals. The distinction is linked to "the wicked," although what is apparent from what preceded, namely that the believers are not left in mixture, would link it to them and their separation from the hypocrites; because the distinction that occurs between the two groups is by acting upon the hypocrites and changing them from one state to another state, while the believers remain in what they were in of the basic faith, even though their greater sincerity becomes apparent, not by acting upon them, and changing them from state to state while the hypocrites remain in what they are in of concealment. The non-leaving was not attributed to them because it implies concern for the one to whom it is attributed; for what is apparent from it is that they are not left in an unsuitable state, as taste sound attests; this was said by some verifying scholars. It has also been said: he placed the wicked before the good and linked the verb of distinguishing to it, to indicate the greater baseness of that kind, since what is cast away of two things is the lesser.

Hamzah and al-Kisai read "yumayyiz" with shaddah, its past being "mayyaza," and the past of the unshaddah form "maza." Both, as several said, are two dialects with one meaning; the doubling is not for making the verb transitive, as in faraha and farrraha, because maza and mayyaza both take one object. A parallel is ʿada and ʿawwada. From Ibn Kathir it is related that he read "yumiz" with a dammah on its first letter and without shaddah, as from amaza with the meaning of mayyaza. It was disputed by what this distinction is achieved: it was said by calamities and afflictions, as happened on the day of Uhud; it was said by raising the word of religion and breaking the power of opponents; it was said by revelation to the Prophet, and for this reason God follows it with His words: "God would not disclose the unseen to you, but God chooses from His messengers whom He wills" (Qur'an 3:179). From here Our master Shaykh al-Islam made what precedes the istidrak (the corrective "but") a preparation for explaining the distinction promised, by way of addressing the sincere directly as an honour to them; and the istidrak is an indication of how it occurs in summary, and that the meaning is: God would not leave the sincere in mixture with the hypocrites, but rather He arranges the beginnings until He brings the hypocrites out from among them; and He does not do that by disclosing to you what is in their hearts of disbelief and hypocrisy, but He reveals to His messenger, and informs him of that, and of what appeared from them of words and deeds, as He related some of it previously, so He disgraces them before all witnesses and delivers you from what you dislike. He mentioned that he had permitted that the meaning be: He does not leave you mixed until He distinguishes the wicked from the good by imposing upon you hard duties which only the sincere endure, whose hearts God has tested, in place of their lives, in jihad and in spending wealth in the way of God; so He makes that a touchstone for your beliefs and a witness to your inner selves, until some of you know what is in the heart of others by way of inference, not by reaching the essence of the breasts, for that is something God has reserved for Himself. He follows this with: the istidrak, by the choice of messengers, which indicates their greater excellence and the superiority of their knowledge over creation after the explanation of the deficiency of their rank in reaching the hidden secrets of hearts, is explicit that the intended meaning is the disclosure of those secrets, brought about through revelation and not through a duty, in a way that leads to their secrets coming out of the rank of concealment.

You know that the claim that the istidrak is explicit in what he asserts is intended is hardly established by proof. For this reason it was said: the upshot of the meaning is that you do not have the rank of knowing the unseen; you have only the rank of inferential knowledge arising from setting up signs and proofs, and God will grant you that, so do not covet anything beyond it; for the rank of knowing the unseen belongs to whom He wills of His messengers. Where are you from those chosen, good men! Indeed, what this master mentioned is more apparent and more appropriate. Abu Hayyan had preceded him to it. As for the intended meaning of His words ﴿to disclose to you⦆: either it is that one of you be given knowledge of the unseen and so be informed of what is in hearts, or that He disclose it to all of you; that is, God does not disclose that to all of you, but it is specific to whom He wills. The first was supported by the fact that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) fits it better,

for Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi that "the disbelievers said: if Muhammad is truthful, let him tell us who among us believes and who disbelieves; so this was revealed."

Al-Wahidi related from al-Suddi that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My community was shown to me in their forms, as Adam was shown them, and I was informed who among them believes in me and who disbelieves." This reached the hypocrites, who mocked and said: "Muhammad claims he knows who believes in him and who disbelieves, and we are with him and he does not recognize us." So God revealed this verse. Al-Kalbi said: "Quraysh said: 'You claim, O Muhammad, that whoever opposes you is in the Fire, and God is angry with him, and that whoever follows you in your religion is among the people of Paradise, and God is pleased with him; so inform us who among us believes in you and who does not,' and God revealed this verse."

The second was supported by the fact that the apparent context requires it. It has been said: the truth is to follow the context. A slight relevance to the story suffices for its being an occasion of revelation. Moreover, there is some discussion in the chains of these reports, so much so that some of the memorizers of hadith said of one of them: "I have not found it." Something contrary to them has also been related from Abu al-ʿAliyah, namely that the believers asked to be given a sign by which they might distinguish between the believer and the hypocrite, and so this was revealed.

Al-ijtiba' means selection (al-istikhlas), as related from Abu Malik, and it comes back to choosing and preferring; this is the well-known meaning in its exegesis. One says "jabautu al-mal" and "jabaytuhu," with waw and with ya'. The ya' in "yajtabi" here is either on its original basis, or it is changed from a waw because of the kasrah before it. He expressed it with this to indicate that standing over the unseen secrets is not attainable except by one whom God has prepared for a lofty office, the aspirations of nations fall short of, and whom He has chosen over the multitudes for guiding them. The "min" is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The generalization of the choosing to all the messengers, peace be upon them, is to show that his (ﷺ) condition in this domain is a clear matter with an established origin, proceeding according to the practice of God which has been followed among the messengers, may God's blessings and peace be upon them all.

It has also been said that the "min" is partitive, since knowledge of the hidden matters is specific to some of the messengers and at some times, as His will requires. It is not hidden that this occurring at some times is accepted, but that it is specific to some messengers is something about which there is some unease in the heart. The correct view is probably the opposite. This is not objected to by the fact that God may disclose the unseen to some of the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf), those of holy souls, because that is by way of inheritance and not independently; and they say that what is specific to the messengers, peace be upon them, is the second (i.e., independent knowledge). Moreover, if what is meant is what the context supports, after this objection and the display of the majestic name in both places, to instill awe, and like it, as has been said, is what is in His words: ﴿So believe in God and His messengers⦆, and the intended meaning is: believe with the attribute of sincerity; so it does no harm that the address is general to the hypocrites who are apparently believers.

The generalization of the command, although the context of the noble discourse is for belief in the Prophet (ﷺ) so as to make belief in him obligatory by the demonstrative method, and to indicate that this entails belief in all, since he confirms what is before him of the messengers, and they are witnesses to the soundness of his prophethood, and the command is belief in everything the one (ﷺ) brought, it therefore includes, at the first level, believing him in what he reported about the conditions of the hypocrites. It may also be said that the intended belief in God Most High is that they know Him alone as the one who knows the unseen.

And of belief in His messengers is that they know them as servants chosen, except what God has taught them, and that they say nothing except what is revealed to them regarding the laws. That the intended belief in God Most High is belief that He, glory be to Him and exalted, does not leave the sincere in mixture ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good⦆ by setting up signs and attaining knowledge by inference through recognizing the believer and the hypocrite.

And of belief in His messengers is belief that they are the ones fitted to know the unseen and no others, which is remote, as is not hidden.

﴿And if you believe⦆ that is, in God Most High and His messengers

the right of faith (ḥaqq al-īmān). ﴿And you fear (Allah)﴾: that is, you avoid opposing the commands and prohibitions; or, you avoid hypocrisy (nifāq). ﴿Then for you﴾ in return for that, ﴿there is a great reward﴾ from Allah, the Exalted, as a bounty (faḍl) that cannot be fathomed nor limited, in this world and the Hereafter.

[Page 140]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 180:

﴿Let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty think that it is good for them.﴾ This is an explanation of the state of stinginess (bukhl) and its evil outcome, and a refutation of its people's claim that it is good for them, in line with the explanation of the state of being granted respite. For this reason the verse is connected to what precedes it.

It has also been said that the connection is this: when Allah, exalted is He, had emphasized urging the sacrifice of lives in jihad and other things, He began here to urge the sacrifice of wealth, and He explained the severe threat for whoever is stingy. He presented what they were stingy with under the description of Allah's giving it to them from His bounty, in order to emphasize the evil of their conduct, since that is one of the things that necessitate spending it in His cause, glorified is He. The verb "yahsabanna" (think) is attributed to the relative pronoun (alladhina), and the first object is omitted because the relative clause indicates it.

It has been objected that the object in this construction is required from two directions: from the direction of the governing verb, and from the direction of its being one of the two parts of the sentence. Therefore, when its requirement is repeated, its omission is prohibited. This is refuted by the predicate of "kana" (was), since it is also required from two directions, and there is no disagreement about the permissibility of omitting it when a proof indicates it.

Al-Tayyibi transmitted from the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) that omitting one of the two objects of "hasiba" (to think) is only permissible when the subject of "hasiba" and its two objects are one and the same in meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the way of Allah are dead﴾ according to the reading with the yaa' (the third-person form). Then he said: this verse is not like that, so an interpretation is necessary, namely that one says: "inna alladhina yabkhaluna" (those who are stingy), the subject, since it includes stinginess, is in the status of the unity of subject and object, and for this reason it was omitted. It has been said that al-Zamakhshari alluded to the strength of the indication by the unity he mentioned. Both of these views are worthless. The correct view is that the basis for the validity of the omission is the indication. Whenever it exists, omission is permissible, and whenever it does not exist, it is not permissible.

As for the claim that "huwa" (it) is a nominative pronoun used in the place of an accusative, referring to stinginess or to the giving, as the first object, it is extremely forced and does not befit the noble arrangement of the text. Even though Mawla Isam al-Din permitted it following Abu al-Baqa', al-Durr al-Masun said that it is an error. The correct view is that it is a separating pronoun (damir fasl) between the two objects of "hasiba," not an emphasis of the apparent noun, as is imagined. It has also been said that the verb is attributed to the pronoun of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, or to the pronoun of whoever thinks, and the first object is the relative pronoun with an implied genitive noun, meaning "the stinginess of those who...", and the second is "khayran" (good), as in the first view. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. Indeed, it is definite in the reading with the second-person address.

In every case, a genitive noun is understood between the preposition (ba') and its object, meaning: "let not...think," or "let not those who are stingy with spending or the zakat of what Allah has given them of His bounty think it is a good quality" (or "good") for them in respect of spending, ﴿but it is an evil﴾, a great one, ﴿for them﴾. The explicit statement of this, despite its being known from what came before, is for emphasis.

﴿They will have what they were stingy with hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This explains the manner in which it will be their punishment. The "sin" (sa) is added for emphasis. The statement, according to most scholars, is either to be taken according to its apparent meaning, for al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever Allah has given wealth but does not pay its zakat, his wealth will be depicted for him as a bald-headed venomous snake with two black spots, which will be hung around his neck on the Day of Resurrection. It will take hold of him by his two jowls and say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.' Then he recited this verse."

Also, more than one narrator transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "There is no relative who comes to his relative, asking him for some of the bounty Allah has given him, and he is stingy toward him, except that a snake comes out for him from Hell on the Day of Resurrection, smacking its lips, until it hangs around his neck." Then he recited the verse.

Abd al-Razzaq and others transmitted from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "What they were stingy with will be made into a collar of fire around their necks."

Some scholars held that the apparent meaning is not intended. The meaning, as Mujahid said, is: they will be charged, on the Day of Resurrection, to bring the equivalent of what they were stingy with of their wealth, as a punishment for them, but they will not be able to do so. Abu Muslim said: they will be bound by the burden of what they were stingy with, in the manner of a collar being bound, with the genitive noun omitted and the noun in the genitive put in its place, to indicate complete suitability between the two. Among their proverbs is "you have hung it like the collar of the dove" (taqlid-ha tawq al-hamamah). Whatever the case, the verse was revealed concerning those who withhold zakat, as this was transmitted from al-Sadiq, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, and other people, and this is the apparent meaning. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the People of the Book who concealed the description of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his prophethood, which the Torah had spoken of. So "stinginess" means the concealing of knowledge, and "bounty" means the Torah which they were given. The meaning of "they will have it hung" is what Abu Muslim said, or it means that they will be hung with a collar of fire as a recompense for this concealment.

In that case the verse is similar to the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled with a bridle of fire." On this view, this is a return to what the discourse had drifted from, namely the story of Uhud, and that is the explanation of the conditions of the People of the Book. It has been said that this is supported by the fact that many verses of the rest of the surah concern them: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: to Allah alone, not to anyone else, either independently or jointly, belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth of what is inherited, of wealth and other things, such as states that pass from one to another, like the messages which the people of heaven inherit, for example. So what is the matter with these people, that they are stingy toward Him with His dominion and do not spend it in His way and seeking His good pleasure? "Inheritance" (mirath) is a verbal noun like "mi'ad" (promise); its origin is "mirwath," and the waw was changed to yaa' because of the kasra before it. The meaning of it is what is inherited, and the discourse is on its literal meaning, without metaphor. It is also possible that Allah, exalted is He, inherits from these people what is in their hands, of what they were stingy with, and it passes from them to Him when He destroys and annihilates them, and regret and remorse remain upon them. In that case there is a metaphor in the statement. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, Allah, exalted is He, will annihilate their people, so that the two (the heavens and the earth) remain with what is in them, with no one having ownership of them. He therefore addressed them with what they know, because they regard what returns to a person as an inheritance that becomes his property.

﴿And Allah is well aware of what you do﴾ of withholding and stinginess, ﴿Acquainted﴾, so He will recompense you for it. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name is to cultivate awe, and the shift to address (the second person) is for emphasis in the threat, because threatening the Great One face to face is more severe. This is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i. The rest read it with the yaa' in the third person.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 181:

﴿Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said: "Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾ Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) entered the House of Study (bayt al-midras), and found the Jews gathered around a man among them called Finhas, who was one of their scholars and rabbis. Abu Bakr said: 'Woe to you, Finhas! Fear Allah and embrace Islam. By Allah, you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; you find him written with you in the Torah.' Finhas said: 'By Allah, Abu Bakr, we are not in need of Allah; rather, He is in need of us. We do not humble ourselves before Him as He humbles Himself before us. We are rich without Him. Had He been rich without us, He would not have borrowed from us, as your companion claims. He forbids you from usury and yet gives us (it). Had He been rich without us, He would not have given us usury.' Abu Bakr became angry (may Allah be pleased with him) and struck Finhas's face with a severe blow, saying: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike your neck, O enemy of Allah!' Finhas went to the Messenger of Allah and said: 'O Muhammad, look at what your companion has done to me!' The Messenger of Allah said to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): 'What moved you to do what you did?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he said a grave word. He claims that Allah, exalted is His majesty, is poor, while they are rich. When he said that, I became angry for the sake of Allah at what he said, and I struck his face.' Finhas denied it and said: 'I did not say that.' So Allah revealed concerning what Finhas said, confirming Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), this verse, and revealed concerning Abu Bakr, and the anger that reached him over that: ﴿And you will certainly hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah﴾ — the verse." 

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that it was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, when Allah revealed: ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ He said: 'Our Lord is asking us for a loan! It is only the poor who borrow from the rich.'"

Al-Diya' and others transmitted through the chain of Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah when Allah revealed ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan﴾, and they said: 'O Muhammad, is your Lord poor, asking His servants for a loan?' So Allah revealed the verse."

The plural (in the first two narrations) alongside the speaker being one person is because the rest were content with that statement. The specification of this saying as something heard, although Allah is All-Hearing of all that is heard, is a veiled allusive expression (kinayah talwihiyyah, an indirect allusion) to the threat, because hearing is a necessary consequence of knowing what is heard, and knowing it entails the threat in this context. So it is a hearing of manifestation and warning, not a hearing of acceptance and approval, as in ﴿Allah hears whoever praises Him﴾. He expressed this by hearing because it signals that the saying is so shameful and blatant that its speaker would not be content for any listener to hear it. Since their denial of the saying was equivalent to denying that they had heard it, He emphasized it with an oath-based emphasis. In this there is also, beyond doubt, an intensification of the threat and an exaggeration of the warning. The governing element (al-ʿamil) in the position of inna and what it governs (the clause that follows it) is taken as the reported speech (al-mahkiyyah bihi). It is also permitted that the phrase be governed by the verbal noun (qawl) to which it is attached, since it is a verbal noun. Abu al-Baqaʾ said: "This follows the view of the Kufans on the operation of the first of two governing words (iʿmal al-awwal), which is a weak principle. It is weakened further here, because the second is a verb and the first is a verbal noun, and the operation of the verb is preferred because of its greater strength."

﴿We will record what they have said﴾, that is, We will record it in the scrolls of the scribes. Then the attribution is metaphorical (majaz), and the recording is literal (haqiqah). Or, We will preserve it in Our knowledge and not neglect it; then the attribution is literal, and the recording is metaphorical. The sin (sin) is for emphasis, meaning that it will never escape Us to record and document it, because it is of the utmost gravity and horror. How could it not be, since it is disbelief in Allah, whether it stems from conviction or from mockery of the Qur'an? This is the apparent meaning. For this reason the words ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ are joined to it, as a signal that the two are brothers in gravity, and as an indication that this is not the first crime they committed or the first sin they permitted themselves. Whoever dared to kill the prophets without right, in his own belief as well as in reality, would not be deemed unlikely to say such a thing. The attribution of killing to these speakers is on the basis of their approval of the deeds of their ancestors who killed. It has also been said that the meaning is: "We will gather what they have said ﴿and their killing of the prophets﴾ in the place of punishment, and recompense them with a matching recompense, since both share the feature that each of them nullifies what the messengers brought." It is not hidden that interpreting the speech of Allah in this way is something that should not be done.

﴿And We will say: Taste the punishment of the burning﴾, that is: and We will take vengeance upon them through this saying, which is never uttered except when the punishment has already come into being.

Al-Harīq (the burning) is in the sense of al-muhraq (that which burns). The annexation of punishment to it is an explanatory annexation (idafah bayaniyyah), meaning the punishment which is burning, because the one who punishes is Allah, exalted, and not the fire. Or the annexation is one of causation, treating the cause as if it were the agent, as some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said. Al-Dhawq (tasting), as al-Raghib said, is the perception of taste in the mouth. Its original sense concerns what is consumed in small quantity, not what is consumed in large quantity, for the latter is called eating (akl). It was then extended and used for perceiving all sensible things and states. Its mention here, as Nasir al-Din said, is because the punishment is consequent upon their saying, which arises from miserliness and from excessive attachment to wealth, and from people's great need for it to obtain food. Most of a person's miserliness comes from fear of losing it. For this reason the mention of eating alongside wealth is frequent. You may also say: when the Jews said what they said and killed those they killed, they caused the Muslims and the followers of the prophets to taste sorrows, and kindled in their hearts the fire of jealousy and grief, and burned their hearts with the blaze of harm and distress. So they were recompensed with this severe punishment, and it was said to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾, just as you made the friends of Allah taste in this world what they disliked. The one who says this to them, as al-Dahhak said, is the guardians of Hell (khazanat Jahannam). Then the attribution is metaphorical. In this verse there are intensifications of the threat: the punishment, the burning, and the tasting are mentioned, which indicates despair. Al-Zajjaj said: "Dhuq (taste) is a word said to one who has despaired of pardon, meaning: taste what you are in; you will not be freed from it." It also signals that what they are in of punishment and humiliation is followed by something even harsher and more calamitous. The saying is for vindication, which indicates complete rage and anger. The preceding verse also contains exaggerations, which are not hidden.

Hamzah recited (sa-yuktabu) with the ya' and in the passive voice, and (wa-qatluhum) with the nominative case, and (wa-yaqulu) in the third person form.

[Page 142]

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the established punishment, which is placed in the position of something sensed and witnessed. To indicate its great importance and its extreme remoteness in terror and horror, He used the demonstrative noun accompanied by the *lam* and the *kaf*. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is His, exalted is He, words: ﴿for what your hands have sent before﴾, meaning: because of your deeds which you have sent forward, such as the killing of the prophets. This is the statement at which the heavens nearly split apart. By "hands" is meant the selves, and the expression of the whole by a part, on which most of the action depends, is a kind of figurative speech. It is permissible that "hands" not be understood figuratively, but rather that their sending forward, which is their action, be made an expression for all the deeds, most of which, or many of which, are performed by the hand, by way of synecdoche (*taghlib*). ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with "what your hands have sent before," so it falls under the rule of the causal *ba'* (*ba' al-sababiyyah*). Its causality for the punishment is because the negation of injustice necessitates justice, which requires rewarding the good-doer and punishing the evildoer. This is the view taken by the leading exegetes (*al-fuhul min al-mufassirin*). Our master Shaykh al-Islam (*Shaykh al-Islam*) criticized this, saying: "Its corruption is evident, for abstaining from punishing one who deserves it is not injustice, either by revelation or by reason, so that the negation of injustice could be a cause of punishment."

The summary of this objection is by way of the exceptive syllogism (*qiyas al-istithna'i*): if abstaining from punishment were injustice, then the negation of injustice would be a cause of punishment; but abstaining from punishment is not injustice; therefore the negation of injustice is not a cause of it. It has been answered that the source of this objection is the failure to distinguish between a cause (*sabab*) and an effective reason (*'illah mujibah*). The distinction is as clear as the morning. A cause is a purely instrumental means that does not necessitate the occurrence of the effect; just as the pen, the cause of writing, does not necessitate it. The justice that necessarily follows from the negation of injustice is a cause of the punishment of the one who deserves it, even though it does not necessitate it. Thus, inferring the absence of causality from the absence of necessitation is extremely corrupt. As for their statement "the justice that necessitates, etc.," it is an explanation of its requirement when left to its own nature, and an affirmation of its being a means. It does not follow from this that it necessitates reward and punishment. This is what the saying of the Exalted in the hadith qudsi indicates: "My mercy precedes My wrath." The essence of this is that the necessary connection between the antecedent and the consequent in the exceptive syllogism is denied, on the ground that there is no reason why abstaining from punishment should not fail to be injustice while the negation of injustice is a cause, namely a cause that is not necessitating and carries no prohibition in that case.

It cannot be said that this objection may be based on the concept of implication (*mafhum*) recognized by al-Shafi'i, and not on the cause being necessitating, because we say: if by the implication is meant the implication of His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah﴾ and so on, then we say: its import is that justice is a cause of the punishment of those who deserve it, and what is implied from it is that justice is not a cause of the punishment of those who do not deserve it. This is a meaning agreed upon, with no dispute about it. If it is meant that what is implied from our saying "the cause of their punishment is His not being unjust" is that, had He not punished them, He would have been unjust, then we say: this, apart from its remoteness from the context of the objector's speech, is of the type of inferring the non-existence of the effect from the non-existence of the cause. It would then be based on the cause being understood as the necessitating cause, as we have said, and the objection we raised applies to it. It is not at all a matter of implication. If something other than this and that is meant, let it be explained so that we may discuss it.

Some people have repelled the objection by saying: the sum of the meaning of the verse is that the punishment has befallen you and was not withheld on account of Allah's not being unjust to the servants. It indicates by its explicit wording that the negation of injustice is not a cause for withholding punishment from one who deserves it, and it does not indicate that injustice is a cause for withholding punishment; rather, withholding it has another cause, namely His kindness, exalted is He. Therefore the objection is not raised. But you know that this is also a failure to grasp the objector's intended point, for whether the speech indicates that injustice is a cause for withholding punishment, or does not, lies outside the objector's aim, as you know from the statement of his argument. Moreover, if by the cause is meant the necessitating cause, as is the basis of the speech of that master, then its indication of this is clear; for the existence of a necessitating cause, just as it is a cause for the existence of the effect, its non-existence is a cause for the non-existence of the effect, as in the rising of the sun and the existence of daylight. So justice, i.e., the negation of injustice, when it is a cause for punishing the one who deserves it, its non-existence, i.e., injustice, is a cause for the non-existence of punishment.

It has been said: it is coordinated with "what you have sent before," to indicate that the causality of their sins for their punishment is restricted by the negation of His injustice, for were it not for this, He might punish them without their sins, not that He would not punish them for their sins.

Our master Shaykh al-Islam also criticized this by saying: "You know that the possibility of His, exalted is He, punishing His servants without sin, indeed its actual occurrence, does not contradict the fact that the punishment of these unbelievers is because of their sins, so as to require considering its absence along with it. This would be necessary only if the claim were that all of the punishments of Allah, exalted is He, are due to the sins of those punished." End of quote. It is not hidden from you that "that He would not punish them for their sins" in the words of the speaker is coordinated with his words "that He would punish them," and the meaning is that the mention of this restriction removes the possibility that He might punish them without their sins, in view of the possibility that He would not punish them for their sins; for this is a good matter by revelation and by reason. As for his statement "to indicate that the causality of their sins for their punishment is restricted, etc.," he intended that the determination of the causality comes about only through this restriction; for with the possibility of His punishing without sin, it is possible that the cause of punishment is the will to punish without sin, so the sum of the meaning of the verse would be: "this punishment of yours has arisen only from your sins and from nothing else." When you know this, it becomes clear to you that the shaykh's rejection of the speaker's words, "that the possibility of His, exalted is He, punishing, etc.," arises from neglecting his intended meaning. For his words are not about the incompatibility of these two matters in themselves, but about the incompatibility of the possibility of punishment without sin with the determination of the sins as its cause. Likewise his statement after that, "This would be necessary only if the claim were, etc.," arises from neglect too, because the need for that restriction in each of the two cases is only to rebuke and reproach the addressees and to make them confess their shortcomings, namely that there is no cause of punishment except from their side.

Hence the claim of a need in one case and its absence in another is extremely feeble. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between this statement and what was first reported from the leading exegetes, where the coordinated clause was taken there as a cause, and here as a restriction on the cause. For the cause is meant as the purely instrumental means, as we indicated earlier, so it is a means whether it is considered an independent cause or a restriction upon the cause. Yes, between the two there is, as will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, an apparent contradiction from another aspect, but this too is not valid, as we shall verify by His power, exalted is He.

The conclusion is that the coordination here is acceptable, and it is the apparent reading, and this is the view of those who held it. It is also permissible to take (*an*) and what follows it as being in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a concluding parenthetical statement (*i'tiradh tadhyili*) affirming the content of what precedes it. That is: "The matter is that He, exalted is He, does not punish His servants without a sin on their part." Expressing this by the negation of injustice, although punishing them without sin is not injustice according to the principle of the people of the Sunnah, is an intensification, not merely an injustice, to show His, exalted is He, complete freedom from that, by presenting it in the form of what is impossible for Him, exalted is He, namely injustice. This is like the way one expresses the withholding of reward for deeds as their being wasted, although deeds do not necessitate reward, so that it would follow from their non-fulfillment that they were wasted. The intensive form (*sigha al-mubalaghah*) is for emphasizing this meaning, by displaying the mentioned punishment without sin in the form of exaggeration in injustice. From here the answer is known to what has been said: that the negation of injustice as such is more emphatic than the negation of its abundance, and the negation of abundance does not negate its root, but may even suggest its existence. It has been answered to this also: it is a negation of the root of injustice and of its abundance with respect to individual persons who are wronged, so the intensification in *zallam* (very unjust) is with respect to quantity, not quality. And: when abundant injustice is negated, little injustice is negated, because one who wrongs, wrongs for the sake of benefit from the wrong; so when abundant injustice, along with its greater benefit, is abandoned with respect to one on whom benefit and harm are possible, then its little, with its small benefit, is abandoned even more. And: *zallam* is for the relative (*li al-nasab*), like *'attar* (perfumer), i.e., injustice is not attributed to Him at all. And: every attribute of His, exalted is He, is in the highest degree of perfection, so if He, glory be to Him, were unjust, He would be *zallam*; thus the negation of the consequent is for the negation of the antecedent. It has been objected that it does not follow from the fact that His attributes are at the furthest degree of perfection that the supposed attribute is so; rather, the basic rule for attributes of deficiency, if they were supposed to be established, is that they would be deficient. It has been answered that when an attribute is supposed for Him, exalted is He, it is supposed together with the perfection that it necessitates; and the claim that this applies to attributes of perfection but not to attributes of deficiency only necessitates that they are not established, not that they are established as deficient. The completion of the discussion on this point will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 183:

﴿Those who said﴾ is in the accusative or nominative case, by way of censure (dhamm). It is also permitted that it be in the genitive case, as a substitute (badal) for its preceding counterpart.

What is meant by the relative clause is a group of Jews, among them Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, Zayd ibn al-Tabut, Finhas ibn 'Azura', and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said this statement: ﴿Indeed, God has covenanted with us﴾, that is, He commanded us and enjoined upon us in the Torah ﴿that we should not believe﴾, that is, that we should not affirm and acknowledge ﴿a messenger﴾ who claims to be sent to us from God Most High ﴿until he brings us a sacrifice﴾, meaning that which is offered to draw near to God Most High, of livestock or other things, as stated by more than one scholar. It has also been read as (qurubun) with two dammas. ﴿Which the fire consumes﴾ is meant to be a white fire that descends from heaven and has a crackling sound. The meaning of the fire consuming the sacrifice is its reducing it to its nature by burning. The use of this expression in that sense is either by way of metaphor (isti'arah) or by way of the unrestricted figurative (majaz mursal). The matter of fire burning the sacrifice when it was accepted was well known in the time of the earlier prophets. However, the claim of those Jews that this covenant exists is among their fabrications and falsehoods, because the fire consuming the sacrifice only compelled belief by being a miracle, and it, like all other miracles, is a matter of law (shar') in that regard. Since their aim from this false speech was non-belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because he had not brought what they said, and if it had been brought, belief would have been realized according to their claim, God Most High replied to them with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to these speakers, as a rebuke to them and a manifestation of their lie, ﴿Messengers have certainly come to you﴾, numerous in number and great in measure, such as Zechariah, John and others, ﴿before me with clear proofs﴾, that is, evident miracles and arguments indicating their truthfulness and the soundness of their messages, and the rightness of their word, ﴿and with what you say﴾, exactly, which is the sacrifice that the fire consumes, ﴿why then did you kill them﴾, that is: what then prevented you from believing in them, so that you dared to kill them, although they came with what you say along with other miracles? ﴿If you are truthful﴾, that is, in what your speech indicates of your belief in a messenger who comes to you with what you have proposed. The address is to those in the time of our Prophet (ﷺ), even though the action belonged to their predecessors, because of their approval of it, as has passed more than once. God, glorified is He, did not cut off their excuse with the sacrifice they asked for, because He, glorified is He, knew that bringing it would be a corruption for them, and miracles follow what is beneficial. It is reported from al-Suddi that this condition came in the Torah thus: Whoever comes claiming that he is a messenger of God Most High, do not believe him until he brings you a sacrifice that the fire consumes, except for the Messiah and Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace; when they come to you, believe in them, for they come without a sacrifice. The apparent view is that this condition is not established at all.

[p. 145]

﴿Then if they deny you﴾ concerning what you have brought to them, ﴿messengers before you were denied too﴾, who came with the like of what you have brought. The clause is the answer to the conditional, but by way of its necessary implication, which the context indicates: it serves to console him for the denial of his people and the Jews. Mujahid confined himself to the second point, as if it were said: "If they deny you, then do not grieve and be consoled." Some of them held that the answer is omitted and that this clause is the reason for it. Many similar constructions occur in speech.

Isam al-Millah said: "There is no need for this interpretation or for positing an omission, since the meaning is: if they deny you, then your denial is the denial of messengers before you, inasmuch as they foretold your mission.
