This contains the utmost rebuke of them, a clarification of his truthfulness (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), and a consolation for him that nothing surpasses." This was criticised on the ground that consolation, according to the majority (al-jumhur) view, is more complete, because on that view there is a sharing between him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and his brother messengers (upon them be blessings and peace) in being denied to their faces and openly. On the second view, there is sharing only in the denial itself, but for him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) it is to his face and explicit, whereas for the messengers it is not so. No one of taste doubts that the first is more eloquent in consolation. On this view, the word "min" (from) may be connected either to "kuththiba" (were denied) or to an omitted element functioning as an adjective of "rusul" (messengers), meaning "existing before you."

On the second view, the second possibility is determined. The description of the messengers by His words, glorified is He, ﴿they came with the clear proofs﴾, that is, the manifest, dazzling miracles, ﴿and the scriptures﴾, the plural of zabur, like rasul and rusul, which is the writing confined to wisdom, from "zabartuhu" in the sense of "I embellished it," as said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: the zubur are admonitions and deterrents, from "zabartuhu" when "I rebuked him." ﴿And the illuminating Book﴾, that is, the clarifying one, or the clear, radiant one.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi that it is the Qur'an. The meaning of the messengers' coming with it is their coming with what it comprises of the foundations of religion, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, concerning it: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾, in a certain respect. From Qatada, the intended meaning is the scriptures (zubur), and the one thing is multiplied by consideration, though it is one. It was also said: the intended meaning is the Torah and the Gospel. The zabur, in the usage of the Qur'an, is what contains laws and rulings, and for this reason it and wisdom (al-hikmah) come conjoined in most instances. The reason for the singular "the Book" is clear on the first view. Perhaps the reason for its singularity on the second and third views, if the generic sense is intended, which applies to one or many, is to signal that the heavenly books, though many, are in certain respects like one thing.

Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-bi-l-zuburi" with the preposition repeated, to indicate that they are distinct from the clear proofs in essence, so that by them are meant miracles other than the books, because repeating the governing element requires difference. Without it, it would be permissible for it to be an instance of the specific being conjoined to the general.

Among the strange views is the claim that by the "clear proofs" are meant the letters considered by their names, such as alif and lam; by the "zubur" the letters considered by their referents and written form, such as ab; and by the "Book" the letters gathered and uttered as a word and as speech.

The proponents of this view claimed that each of these has meanings and secrets which only the knowledgeable understand. They therefore investigate the word from the standpoint of its pronunciation, from the standpoint of each of its written letters, and from the standpoint of the name of each letter, which is itself three letters. It is not hidden that this is a technical convention which should not be used to interpret the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

From tracing the sound reports, the apparent position is that nothing has been established from the Lawgiver, the greatest one (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) concerning this. Short of establishing that is the Red Death: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, that is, it will certainly befall them, so they are as though they taste it. It is both a promise and a threat, to the one who believes and to the one who denies. It also contains an emphasis on the consolation for him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), because recalling death and keeping it in mind removes worldly cares and sorrows.

And in a report: "Remember much the destroyer of pleasures (hadhim al-ladhdhat), for it is not mentioned in abundance except that it diminishes it, nor in little except that it increases it." Likewise is knowledge that beyond this abode there is another abode in which the good-doer is distinguished from the evildoer, and each sees the recompense of his deed. This universal proposition cannot be applied in its full generality, owing to the apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills﴾. If "soul" is taken to mean the essence, the exceptions become very numerous. Do the angels enter into this generality? There are two opinions, and the majority hold that they do.

From Ibn 'Abbas: when His saying, exalted is He, was revealed, ﴿Everyone upon it is perishing﴾, the angels said: "The people of the earth have died." Then when it was revealed…

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 185:

﴿Every soul shall taste death.﴾ The angels said: "We have died."

The occurrence of death to souls in this animal, corporeal mode of existence is something beyond doubt. However, the philosophers (al-Hukama') built this on the premise that this life is only attained through the innate moisture (al-rutubah) and the innate heat (al-hararah).

Then, heat acts upon the dissolution of moisture: when moisture decreases, heat weakens. This state continues until the original moisture is exhausted, the innate heat is extinguished, and death occurs. From here they said: disembodied souls (al-arwah al-mujarradah) do not die, and their death cannot be conceived, since there is neither heat nor moisture there. The Muslims disputed with them on this, and their basis is the heat (the letter kaf) and the moisture (the letter nun). Perhaps they distinguish between death and death. The verse has been used as evidence that the one who is killed is dead, and that the soul remains after the body, because the one who tastes must necessarily be existing at the time of the tasting. So reflect.

Al-Yazidi read (dha'iqatan al-mawt) with tanwin and the accusative on al-mawt, according to the original form; al-A'mash read (dha'iqata al-mawt) with the tanwin dropped and the accusative, as in his saying:

"So I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little."

On all three readings, (kullu nafs) is the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible even though it is indefinite, because of the generality it contains; (dha'iqatu) is the predicate (khabar). It is feminine in accordance with the meaning of (kull), because (kullu nafs) means souls. Had it been mentioned outside the Qur'an in the form of (kull), it would be permissible.

﴿And you will only be paid your rewards in full﴾ i.e., you will be given the recompense of your deeds complete and whole, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ i.e., the time of your standing up from the graves. Al-qiyamah is a verbal noun, and the singular is used because they will stand up all at once. In the word "tawfiyah" (full payment) there is an indication that some of their recompense, good or evil, reaches them before that day. This is supported by what al-Tirmidhi reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat from Abu Hurayrah, raised (marfu'): "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fires." It was said: the point in this is that recompense may occur for some deeds in this world. Perhaps whoever denies the punishment of the grave finds this point decisive for himself.

﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire﴾ i.e., after that day, away from the Fire of Hell. The origin of zahzahah is repeated zahh, which is pulling with haste, and here the necessary meaning is intended. ﴿And is admitted into Paradise has indeed succeeded﴾ i.e., he has been made happy and saved, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The origin of fawz is attaining the desired goal. Some people supplied a complement here, i.e., he succeeded in salvation and attaining what is sought; and it is possible that it was omitted for generality, i.e., with everything he desires. In a report: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and what is in it." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse.

Ahmad and Muslim reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to be drawn away from the Fire and to enter Paradise, let his death come upon him while he believes in God and the Last Day, and let him treat people as he loves to be treated."

The mention of entering Paradise after distance from the Fire is because distance from it does not necessarily entail entering Paradise, as is evident.

﴿And the life of this world is only the enjoyment of delusion﴾ i.e., in its essence, its desires, and its adornment. (185) Mata' (enjoyment) is what is enjoyed and benefited from, of what is sold and bought. God, glorified is He, has likened it to that merchandise which is deceptively presented to the buyer and altered so that he buys it, indicating its extreme worthlessness in the sight of one who considers it closely:

"When an intelligent man tests the world, it reveals itself to him as an enemy in the garments of a friend."

And from Qatadah: It is a goods that is left behind; it is about to vanish from its people, by God. So take from this goods the obedience of God, the Exalted, if you are able, and there is no power except by God. And from 'Ali, may God honor his face: Its touch is soft, its poison deadly.

It was said: the apparent of the world is a source of joy, and its inner is a mount of evils.

Some have mentioned that this comparison applies to one who prefers it over the Hereafter; as for one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is for him a provision for reaching (the goal).

And in a report: "How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man."

Al-ghurur is either a verbal noun or the plural of ghar (deceiver).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 186:**

﴿You will surely be tested﴾ is the response to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, you will surely be tested." What is meant is that you will be treated as those who are tested, so that what is in you of steadfastness upon the truth and good deeds may become manifest. It is not correct to take *ibtila'* (testing) in its literal sense, because that is impossible for the Knower of the unseen, as has already been explained. The address is to the believers, or to them together with the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah, glorified is He, informed them of what would happen only so that they might prepare themselves to bear it when it occurs, equip themselves to meet it, and confront it with fine patience and steadfastness. The onset of trial increases hardship, and readiness for distress makes the matter easier to bear. To establish the meaning of *ibtila'* for this easing, the verse uses emphasis (*ta'kid*). It may also be said that the emphasis is used to establish the actual occurrence of what is tested, as an intensification of the exhortation to the readiness and preparation that is required of them. In any case, the sentence is brought to console the friends of Allah, Exalted is He, about what they will encounter from His enemies, following their consolation about what has already befallen them. It has also been said that the sentence was brought to show that the world is a place of tribulation and testing, and that it was withheld from the believers so that they might be patient and be rewarded, following the statement that it is "the enjoyment of delusion." The first explanation, however, is likely more preferable, as is not hidden.

The *waw* that is vocalized with a *damma* is the pronoun of the subject (*damir al-raf'*). The final radical of the word is omitted for a morphological reason. This *waw* was given a vowel to remove the heaviness resulting from the meeting of two consonant-vowel sequences (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), and this vowel was *damma* so as to indicate the omitted element in the sentence. The *waw* was not converted into an *alif*, despite its being left unvocalized and the preceding letter being *fatha*-vowelled, because that vowelling is incidental.

﴿in your possessions﴾ through the obligatory duties concerning them and through calamities. Some have restricted the meaning to the second, claiming that the first, exemplified in their saying by the spending commanded in the way of Allah, Exalted is He, and by *zakat*, does not fit being placed within the category of testing, since it belongs to the category of diminishing rather than destroying. There is consideration of this, and its reference was already mentioned in al-Baqarah. It is reported from al-Hasan that he restricted it to the first. The better view is to affirm generality. ﴿and in your selves﴾ through killing, wounds, captivity, illnesses, the loss of relatives, and all other hardships, fears, and afflictions that befall them. The verse mentions possessions before selves either for ascending to what is more noble, or because calamities concerning possessions are more numerous than calamities concerning selves.

﴿And you will surely hear much hurtful speech from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, that is, before your being given the Qur'an, and they are the Jews and the Christians. The description of them in this way is either to indicate the basis of the discord and to announce that what they say is grounded, in their claim, in the Scripture, or to point to the gravity of what is uttered by them and the severity of its impact upon the ears, since it is speech issued by one from whom it is not expected, because of an existing restraint with him, which is his being given the Scripture, as has been said. The explicit mention of priority is either to emphasize the indication and strengthen the basis, or to intensify the matter of the restraint against the issuance of that heard speech from those who utter it.

﴿and from those who associated partners [with Allah]﴾, who are the disbelievers of the Arabs, ﴿much harm﴾, such as slandering the religion, denouncing those who believed, fabricating lies against Allah, Exalted is He, and His Messenger (ﷺ), and composing amorous verses about the women of the believers.

﴿And if you are patient﴾ upon those hardships when they come, ﴿and fear Allah﴾, that is, hold fast to the fear of Allah, Exalted is He, and obedience to Him, devote yourselves wholly to Him, and turn away completely from all else, to the extent that the arrival of what is loved and the meeting of what is hated are equal to you. ﴿then indeed that﴾ refers to what was mentioned implicitly of patience and piety. The sense of distance in the demonstrative may be either because it is not mentioned explicitly, as has been said, or to indicate the elevated rank of these two matters and the remoteness of their station.

The singularity of the second-person particle may be either in consideration of each one of the addressees, as an attention to the matter addressed, or because the address intends merely to alert, without the particularity of the circumstances of the addressees.

﴿of the matters requiring resolve﴾ (186). That is, the matters that everyone should resolve upon, because of their complete excellence, nobility, and honour, or what Allah, Exalted is He, has resolved and made obligatory upon His servants. On both interpretations, *'azm* is a verbal noun in the sense of the thing resolved upon. It is derived from their saying *'azamtu al-amr* ("I resolved the matter"), as al-Raghib transmitted, though the more well-known usage is *'azamtu 'ala al-amr*. The claim that no usage other than this has been heard is not accepted, just as the claim that it is not correct to ascribe resolve to Him, Exalted is He, because it is the settling of the self and the binding of the heart upon what is seen as doable, and that is impossible for Him, is also not accepted. What supports the correctness of the ascription is that it was read as *fa-idha 'azamtu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, and in that case it carries the sense of will and command. From this is the saying of Umm 'Atiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her: "We were forbidden to follow funeral processions, but it was not made a firm obligation (*'azimah*) upon us." And what is in another hadith: "He encouraged us to perform the night prayers of Ramadan without it being a firm obligation."

And their saying, *'azamat Allah* (the resolutions of Allah), as al-Azhari transmitted; and from this category is the statement of the jurists that abandoning prayer during menstruation is an *'azimah* (a firm legal ruling). The sentence is an explanation of a response occupying its place, as if it were said: "And if you are patient and fear Allah, that is better for you," or "then you have done well," or something similar, followed by ﴿then indeed that﴾, etc.

It is also permitted that *dhalika* refers to the patience and piety of the addressees. In that case the sentence itself is the answer of the conditional. In presenting the command of patience and piety in the form of a conditional, there is a manifestation of the perfect kindness toward the servants that is not hidden.

Some claimed that this command indicated by the verse was before the revelation of the verse of fighting, and that by its revelation it was abrogated (*naskh*). It was corrected that there is no abrogation, and that the command to what was mentioned was a matter of conciliation (*mudara'ah*), which does not contradict the command to fight. The occasion of revelation of this verse, according to one account, is what was previously indicated.

Al-Wahidi reported from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that Usamah ibn Zayd informed him that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode a donkey with a Fadakiyyah saddle-cloth, and had Usamah ibn Zayd ride behind him, and he went to visit Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah in the tribe of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj, before the battle of Badr, until he passed by a gathering in which was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. That was before 'Abd Allah had embraced Islam. In the gathering were mixed groups of Muslims, polytheists who worshipped idols, and Jews, and in the gathering was 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah. When the dust raised by the animal covered the gathering, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy covered his nose with his cloak and said: 'Do not raise dust over us.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) greeted them, then stopped, dismounted, invited them to Allah, Exalted is He, and recited the Qur'an to them. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: 'O man, there is nothing better than what you say, if it is true, so do not trouble us with it in our gatherings. Return to your camp, and whoever comes to you, relate it to him.' 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, come to us with it in our gatherings, for we love that.' The Muslims, the polytheists, and the Jews began to revile one another until they nearly came to blows. The Prophet (ﷺ) kept calming them until they settled down. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted his animal and went until he entered upon Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and said to him: 'O Sa'd, did you not hear what Abu Hubab (meaning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy) said?' He said: 'So-and-so and so-and-so.' Sa'd said: 'O Messenger of Allah, pardon him and overlook it, for by Him who revealed the Book to you, Allah, Exalted is He, has brought the truth that was revealed to you, and the people of this region had agreed to crown him and wrap him with a turban. When Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked on it with rage.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pardoned him, and Allah, Exalted is He, revealed the verse."

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, from his father, that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the Jew, was a poet who used to satirize the Prophet (ﷺ) and incite the disbelievers of Quraysh against him in his poetry. The Prophet (ﷺ) had come to Madinah, and its people were mixed: among them were Muslims, among them were polytheists, and among them were Jews. The Prophet (ﷺ) wished to win over all of them, but the polytheists and the Jews harmed him and his companions most severely. So Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient in this, and concerning them Allah, Exalted is He, revealed ﴿And you will surely hear...﴾, the verse.

In another narration from al-Zuhri: "This Ka'b used to satirize the Prophet (ﷺ) and compose amorous verses about the women of the believers. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Who will deal with Ibn al-Ashraf for me?' Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: 'I will, O Messenger of Allah.' So he went out, together with his foster-brother Abu Na'ilah and a group, and they killed him by stealth. They brought his head to the Prophet (ﷺ) at the end of the night while he was standing in prayer."

Then He, glory be to Him, described some of the harms done by the People of the Book, saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾. By them is meant either the rabbis of the Jews specifically, which is the view of Ibn Jubayr and is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas through the chain of 'Ikrimah, or those who include them along with the rabbis of the Christians, which is reported from him through the chain of 'Alqamah. They are mentioned by the description of having been given the Book in order to emphasize the ugliness of their condition. It has also been said that this is a hint that the taking of the covenant took place in the Book that they were given.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that the companions of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) would read: "And when your Lord took from those who were given the Book their covenant."

﴿You shall surely make it clear to the people﴾ is the answer to the covenant, since it contains the meaning of an oath. The pronoun refers to the Book, meaning: by God, you will surely make manifest all that is in it of rulings and reports, among which is the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and this is the intended subject of the narrative. The apparent meaning of the words of al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr is that the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), even though his noble name is not explicitly mentioned.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim, in the transmission of Ibn 'Ayyash, read *la-yubayyinunnahu* with the *ya'* of the third person. The scholars of Arabic grammar have established that when you report about an oath that is sworn by something, there are three ways of doing so. The first: that it be in the form of the absent third person, as if you were reporting about something, such as saying: *istahlaftuhu la-yaqumanna* ("I made him swear that he would surely stand"). The second: that you use the form of the second person, intending the wording that was addressed to him, so you say: *istahlaftuhu la-taqumanna*, as if you had said to him: "You shall surely stand." The third: that you use the form of the first person, so you say: *istahlaftuhu la-aqumanna* ("I made him swear that I would surely stand"). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They swore to one another by God, "We will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾, with the *nun*, the *ya'*, and the *ta'*. And if *taqasamu* were an imperative, the *ya'* of the absent form would not come in it, because it is not an absent third person. This was stated by some of the verifiers.

﴿And do not conceal it﴾ is coordinated with the answer. It was not emphasized with the *nun* because it is negated. Abu al-Baqa' said: this is because the emphasis was sufficient in the first verb.

It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the addressees, either by supposing a subject after the *waw*, meaning "while you do not conceal it," or on the opinion of one who permits the *waw* to precede a negated present verb when it functions as a circumstantial clause, meaning: "you shall surely make it manifest without concealing it." The prohibition of concealment after the command to make clear is either for the sake of emphasizing the obligation of the commanded act, as many have taken, or because the clarification that is commanded means mentioning the verses that declare his prophethood, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the concealment that is forbidden means abandoning the deviant interpretations and the false doubts, as has been said.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan that he used to explain ﴿You shall surely make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ with the words: "you shall surely speak the truth, and you shall surely be truthful in deed." The command following the command is apparently also clear on this reading, and perhaps the discourse on it is more beneficial.

Ibn Kathir and those with him read *wa-la yaktumunahu* with the *ya'*, as in the preceding case.

﴿But they threw it behind their backs﴾, that is, they cast aside the covenant that had been taken from them, and did not heed it or pay any attention to it at all. Throwing behind the back is a figure of speech and a metaphor for abandoning regard and not paying attention. The opposite of this is placing a thing before the eyes and in front of them.

﴿And they sold it﴾, that is, the Book which they were commanded to make clear and forbidden to conceal. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the covenant, but the first is preferable. The meaning is that they took in its place ﴿a small price﴾ from the transient goods of this worldly life and its corrupt aims. ﴿Evil is what they bought﴾ (187), that is: evil is the thing they bought with that price. So *ma* is an indefinite accusative noun explaining the subject of *bi'sa*, and the clause *yashtaruna-hu* is its qualifier. The one specified by the blame is omitted. It has been said that *ma* is a verbal noun serving as the subject of *bi'sa*, and the one specified is omitted, meaning: "evil is their buying this purchase, since they deserve through it the painful punishment."

The verse has been cited as evidence for the obligation of making knowledge manifest and the prohibition of concealing any matter of religion for a corrupt purpose, such as facilitating matters for the oppressors, pleasing their souls, seeking their favor, attracting their benefits, and similar things. In a report: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled with a bridle of fire."

Al-Tha'labi narrated with his chain from al-Hasan ibn 'Umara, who said: I came to al-Zuhri after he had stopped narrating hadith, and I found him at his door. I said: "If you see fit, would you narrate to me?" He said: "Do you not know that I have stopped narrating hadith?" I said: "Either you narrate to me, or I narrate to you." He said: "Narrate to me." So I said: "al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna narrated to me from Najm al-Kharraz, who said: I heard 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face, say: God did not take a covenant from the people of ignorance that they should learn until He took a covenant from the people of knowledge that they should teach." He said: So he narrated to me forty hadiths.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu Hurayra: "Were it not for what God, exalted is He, took from the People of the Book, I would not have narrated to you," and he recited this verse.

Ibn Sa'd reported from al-Hasan: "Were it not for the covenant that God, exalted is He, took from the people of knowledge, I would not have narrated to you much of what you ask about."

What supports the use of the verse for what has been mentioned is what Ibn Jarir reported from Abu 'Ubayda, who said: A man came to a group of people in the mosque, among whom was 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and said: "Ka'b sends you greetings and gives you good news that this verse: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾, etc., is not among you." 'Abd Allah said to him: "And you, convey to him greetings, that it was revealed"; and he was a Jew. Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, meant that Ka'b did not know what it pointed to, even though it was revealed concerning the People of the Book.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 188:**

﴿Do not think﴾ is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. That is, do not suppose.

﴿those who rejoice in what they have done﴾: that is, in what they did. Ubayy read it this way. It is also read as (bimā ātaw) and (bimā ūtaw). The second reading is related from ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face.

﴿and love to be praised﴾: that is, to be praised by people. It was said: by the Muslims. It was also said: by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿for what they did not do﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said, in what Ibn Abi Hatim related from him through al-ʿAwfi: "They are the People of the Book. The Book was sent down to them, but they judged by other than the truth, distorted the words from their places, rejoiced in that, and loved ﴿to be praised for what they did not do﴾, namely the prayer and the fasting."

In a narration of al-Bukhari and others from him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked them about something, and they concealed it from him and informed him of something else. They went out, having shown him that they had told him what he had asked about, and they sought praise from him for that, and they rejoiced in having concealed what he had asked them about."

Ibn Jarir related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that they rejoice in concealing the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which their scribes had stated, ﴿and love to be praised﴾ for being followers of the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. According to this view, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers to those mentioned earlier, ﴿those to whom the covenant was given﴾, and it has been placed in the position of their pronoun. The sentence was brought to explain what follows from their deeds, which were mentioned, of punishment,
*(page 151)*
immediately after explaining their ugliness. There is also no small consolation in this. Along with it, another part of their vile and shameful conduct has been included, namely their persistence in what is ugly, their joy in it, and their love of being described with praiseworthy qualities that they do not possess. Allah, glorified is He, expressed this in the manner of something already known, to announce that this quality is famous among them.

It was also said that the relative pronoun refers to a group of hypocrites, a known party among those already mentioned and others. This is supported by what al-Bukhari, Muslim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman related from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him: "Some hypocrites, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to military campaign, stayed behind from him and rejoiced in their sitting out, contrary to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the campaign, they offered excuses to him and swore oaths, and they loved ﴿to be praised for what they did not do﴾. Then this verse was revealed." Similar narrations are related from Rafiʿ ibn Khadij, Zayd ibn Thabit, and others. It was also said that the intended meaning of these people is all the hypocrites, and most of them were from the Jews.

Some have claimed that this reading is more suitable to what is within the scope of the relative clause, because it was well known that they rejoiced in what they did, namely displaying faith while their hearts were settled in disbelief, and they sought praise from the Muslims for faith while they were a thousand miles from it. They used to show love for the believers while they were in the utmost enmity. But you should not fail to notice that, even if it is granted that this is more suitable, there is no sound report known to us that supports it. From here it is known that, after the saying that it is better to apply the relative pronoun to its general sense, including everyone who does any good deed and then rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration and wishes that people would praise him for virtues he does not possess, it fits the people already mentioned in a primary way. However, it has been objected that the inclusion of the previously mentioned people, even in a primary way, is not accepted unless the phrase ﴿what they did﴾ is generalized so that it includes true good deeds and other things. But if it is restricted to good deeds, as the apparent meaning of this view suggests, then the inclusion is not accepted, because those rejoicing did not actually perform a good deed for which they would rejoice with the joy of self-admiration, as is not hidden. Perhaps the matter here is easy. Yet what increases its distance is what Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman related through Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman: Marwan said to his doorkeeper, "Go, O Rafiʿ, to Ibn ʿAbbas and say: If every one of us rejoices in what he has been given and loves to be praised for what he did not do, we will all be punished." Ibn ʿAbbas said, "What is it to you with this verse? This verse was only revealed about the People of the Book." Then he recited: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the two verses. For if it were better to apply the relative pronoun to its general sense, the scholar of the community and interpreter of the Qur'an would have applied it, and he would have removed the difficulty by restricting the joy to the joy of self-admiration, as the proponent of this view did. It does not follow from the statement of this scholar that the prohibition of joy in the sense of self-admiration, and of loving to be praised for what one has not done at all, is not valid. Rather, the most that follows from it is that this is not the meaning of the verse, as has been said, and that does not require that it is not the meaning of anything at all, so that this would be a claim that there is no prohibition. How could that be, when many texts clearly state the prohibition of this, to the extent that some counted it among the major sins?! So let this be understood. In any case, the relative pronoun is the first object of ﴿do not think﴾. The statement of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿so do not think them﴾, is an emphasis of it. The Arabs, as al-Zajjaj said, when the story is long, repeat (ḥasibta) and similar forms, to inform that what has occurred is connected to the first and is an emphasis of it. You say: "Do not suppose Zayd, when he comes to you and speaks to you with such and such, that he is truthful." So (lā taẓunnanna) gives emphasis and clarification. The fāʾ is extra (zāʾidah), as in the line of poetry:

"Then when I perish, (then) at that, lament."

The second object in the statement of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿with a success from the punishment﴾, means: while being clothed in deliverance from it. Here (mafāzah) is a mīmī verbal noun (a noun formed with the prefix mīm) meaning "success," and the tāʾ is not for a single unit, since the noun is formed on this pattern. (min al-ʿadhāb) is connected to it. It is also permitted that (mafāzah) be a noun of place, meaning a place of success and deliverance. It may also be borrowed from (mafāzah), meaning a desert, and in that case (min al-ʿadhāb) is an adjective describing it, because a noun of place does not govern. It is necessary to supply a specific complement: meaning, "a place that delivers" ﴿from the punishment﴾. To supply it generally, meaning "a success existing from the punishment," is not valid, because success is not from the punishment. It was objected that supplying it specifically, although it goes against the basic rule, is an unnecessary strain. It was also read with a ḍamma on the unpointed bāʾ in both verbs, on the basis that the address includes the believers too. And with the yāʾ of the third person and a fatḥa on the bāʾ in both, on the basis that the verb belongs to him, upon him be prayer and peace, or to everyone who is capable of supposing. Its two objects in both readings are as mentioned earlier.

Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read with yāʾ and a fatḥa on the bāʾ in the first verb, and with yāʾ and a ḍamma on the bāʾ in the second verb, on the basis that the subject of (lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna) is what follows, and its two objects are omitted, indicated by the two objects of its emphasis. The subject of its emphasis is the relative pronoun, and its objects are their pronoun, and (bimafāzah). That is: "Let not those who rejoice in what they have done suppose; so let them not suppose themselves to be in success."

It is also permitted that the first object of (lā yaḥsabanna) is omitted and the second object is mentioned, meaning: "I mean (bimafāzah)," that "those who rejoice do not suppose themselves successful." The statement of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿so let them not suppose them﴾, is an emphasis, and the fāʾ is extra as already mentioned. It is also permitted that both objects of (lā yaḥsabanna) are mentioned: the first is their pronoun connected to the second verb, and the second is ﴿with a success﴾. This is built on taking the emphasis to be only the verb and its subject, which is the most suitable, since nothing else was mentioned before them. It was objected that this involves attaching an object pronoun to something other than its governing verb or its subject connected to its governing verb, and none of the grammarians has said so. Although there is an avoidance of omission in this construction, there is consideration here, since many have explicitly permitted that. I have devoted a separate work to this question. It was also permitted that the first verb has as its subject the pronoun of the Prophet, may prayer and peace be upon him and his family, or of every person who supposes. The first object is the relative pronoun, and the second object is omitted, indicated by the object of the second verb. The second verb has as its subject the pronoun of the relative. The fāʾ is for conjunction, because it is clear that the non-supposing of those people follows from the non-supposing of him, upon him be prayer and peace, or from the non-supposing of every supposer. Its two objects are the attached pronoun and ﴿with a success﴾.

The introduction of the threat with their prohibition from the supposing mentioned, according to what the Shaykh al-Islam said, is to alert to the invalidity of their weak opinions and to cut off their empty hopes, since they used to claim that they would be saved from the punishment of the Hereafter by what they had done, just as they had been saved from worldly accountability. On this their joy was based. As for the prohibition addressed to him, may prayer and peace be upon him and his family, it is an allusion to their supposing mentioned, not because supposing might occur from his side, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

You know that the justification of the introduction by what was mentioned, on the assumption that the relative pronoun is applied to its general sense, as already explained, is not clear, unless it is said that it is by the method of predominance (taghlīb).

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ (188): an explanation of the establishment of a specific kind of punishment, without a limit in duration or severity, following what was indicated about their not being saved from punishment in general. The nominal sentence, the emphatic indefinite noun (al-tanwīn al-tafkhīmī), and the descriptive adjective all hint at this.

It is also permitted that this refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and the negation of salvation from punishment mentioned earlier is taken to mean the negation of immediate punishment, which is that they are blamed and rejected among the people, because the garment of falsehood does not last, and the state of its wearer is exposed and disgraced.

[Page 153]

**"To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth"** (3:189). This confirms what precedes it, since it conveys that Allah alone holds the overpowering authority over the whole world, disposing of it as He wills and chooses, by bringing into existence and by annihilating, by giving life and causing death, by punishing and rewarding. Whoever is like this is the owner of their affair, and none can turn back what He wills for them.

**"And Allah is powerful over all things"** (3:189). This is a confirmation following a confirmation. The explicit naming of Allah in the place of a pronoun serves to cultivate awe, while also indicating the basis of the ruling. The comprehensiveness of power over all things is one of the attributes of divinity. The implication is that each of the two sentences stands independently as an affirmation. It has also been said that both sentences together are directed at refuting the earlier words of the Jews, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." This view is judged weak because of its remoteness. Even if it were said, the refutation would be made light of.

* * *

This is an allusive (isharah) interpretation of the verses:

**"And let them not grieve you"** (3:176), either out of fear of harm or because of intense jealousy, **"those who race to disbelief"** (3:176), because of their original veil and their innate darkness. **"Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all"** (3:176), for the court of greatness is sanctified from the assaults of the shadows of error. Or the meaning is: they will not harm you, O supreme manifestation, except that He, exalted is He, has placed His own Self in the station of the Self of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The verse contains an allusion to both separation and unification. **"Allah wills"** (3:176), to show the attribute of His dominance, **"that He not give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment"** (3:176), because of the greatness of their veil and their looking toward others.

**"Indeed, those who have bought disbelief"** (3:177), and taken it in exchange for faith, because of the ugliness of their receptivity and the evil of their choice that is not divinely ordained, **"will not harm Allah at all"** (3:177). But they harm themselves, by depriving themselves of the manifestation of Beauty, **"and for them is a painful punishment"** (3:177), because they have by this become a locus of Majesty.

**"And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite"** (3:178), and Our increasing them in provision, **"is better for them"** (3:178), for they would benefit from it in nearness to Us. **"Indeed, We give them respite only so that they may increase in sin"** (3:178), as a result of this, since they increase in veil upon veil and distance upon distance, **"and for them is a humiliating punishment"** (3:178), because of their extreme distance from the source of might.

**"Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in"** (3:179), that is, in the outward appearance of Islam and the verbal affirmation, **"until He distinguishes the wicked from the good"** (3:179), namely the attributes of the self, the portions of Satan, and the motives of desire, **"from the good"** (3:179), which are the attributes of the heart such as sincerity, certainty, unveiling, witnessing of the spirit, and intimate converse with the innermost secret. This happens through the occurrence of trials and calamities among you. **"Nor would Allah give you knowledge of the unseen"** (3:179), that is, the unseen of your existence, namely the realities hidden within you, without the intermediary of the Messenger, because of distance, lack of affinity, and the absence of readiness to receive from Him, glorified is He. **"But Allah chooses of His messengers whom He wills"** (3:179), so He informs him of that, and guides you to what has been hidden from you of the treasures of your existence and its secrets, because of the kinship that exists between you and him.

**"So believe in Allah and His messengers"** (3:179), by affirmation and by adherence to the Sacred Law, so that it becomes possible for you to receive from them. **"And if you believe"** (3:179), after that true faith, which is attained through spiritual journeying and following the path, **"and fear Allah"** (3:179), that is, the veils and the barriers, **"then for you is a great reward"** (3:179), from the unveiling of the reality. It may be said that Allah, exalted is He, has unseen realms: the unseen of the outward, the unseen of the inward, the unseen of the unseen, the secret of the unseen, and the unseen of the secret. The unseen of the outward is what He, glorified is He, has informed of concerning the matter of the Hereafter. The unseen of the inward is the unseen of the decreed matters that are concealed from the hearts of others. The unseen of the unseen is the secret of the attributes within the acts. The secret of the unseen is the light of the Essence within the attribute. The unseen of the secret is the unseen of eternal pre-existence, the secret of the reality, and insight through an intermediary. Insight into what precedes the last is attained by the travellers according to their stations. As for insight into the last, it does not occur for anyone at all, for eternity is exalted above perception and is specific to our Prophet (ﷺ). In this sense is his seeing through the mode of unveiling granted to him, and the smile of the dawn of eternity upon his face, not by the mode of encompassing and perception.

**"And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty"** (3:180), of wealth, knowledge, power, or self, and so do not spend it in the way of Allah upon those who deserve it, or upon those who are prepared for it, or upon the prophets and the truthful in defending them, or in annihilation in Allah, exalted is He, **"think that it is better for them"** (3:180). **"Rather, it is worse for them"** (3:180), because they are veiled by it. **"They will be encircled with what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection"** (3:180). They will be made to bear its burden, and that will remain as regret in their hearts at their destruction, as indicated by His saying: **"And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth"** (3:180). Some of the gnostics have mentioned that among the greatest kinds of miserliness is withholding secrets from their people, not manifesting the gifts of Allah, exalted is He, to the seekers, and leaving them in the deserts of the path while having the ability to guide them. It is said that the foundation of the path is generosity, that generosity with wealth is the attribute of the seekers (murids), generosity with the self is the attribute of the lovers (muhibbun), and generosity with the spirit is the attribute of the knowers (arifun).

Ibn 'Ata' said: Generosity is giving up the self, the secret, the spirit, and everything. Whoever is miserly on the path of the Truth with his wealth is veiled and remains with it,

[Page 154]

and whoever looks toward others is deprived of the benefits of the Truth and the radiant lights of nearness.

**"Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, 'Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich'"** (3:181). They are the Jews, who heard the request for a loan and did not understand its secret, so they fell into what they fell into and said what they said. This statement is only drawn out by tyranny, the dominance of blameworthy attributes, and the domination of the authority of desire over the commanding self. Then it seeks to clothe itself in the garment of lordship, and from here it says, sometimes, "I am your Most High Lord," despite its veiling and distance from the Presence.

**"Those who said, 'Indeed, Allah has covenanted with us that we not believe any messenger until he brings us a sacrifice which the fire will consume'"** (3:183). It is said that it was reported: "The prophets of the Children of Israel had as their miracle that they would bring a sacrifice, and call upon Allah, exalted is He, and a fire would come down from heaven and consume it." Its interpretation is that they would bring their own selves, drawing near to Allah, exalted is He, by them, and be summoned through asceticism and worship, and then the fire of love would come from the heaven of the spirit and consume them and annihilate them in unity. After that their prophethood would be established and manifest. When the common people of the Children of Israel heard of this, they believed its possible outward meaning in the world of power, so they demanded that sign from every prophet, until our Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace, came, and they demanded it from him as well. Allah, exalted is He, related that to us and refuted it against them.

More fitting, in the domain of interpretation, is that the Jews, who represent the animal and satanic attributes of the self, said to the messenger of the divine inspiration and the lordly insight: "We will not submit to you **until he brings us a sacrifice**," which is this world and what is in it, that you make into an offering to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, so that the fire of love consumes it. **"Say"** (3:183), O one through whom the Truth descends, **"Indeed, there came to you messengers before me"** (3:183), that is, the descents of the Truth, **"with clear proofs"** (3:183), with dazzling arguments, **"and with what you have said"** (3:183), which is making this world and what is in it a sacrifice, **"so why did you kill them"** (3:183), that is, you overcame them and effaced them until you left no trace of those descents, **"if you are truthful"** (3:183) in that you would believe in whoever brings you that.

**"And if they deny you"** (3:184), this is an address to the greatest Messenger (ﷺ), **"then messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs"** (3:184), for the common people, **"and scriptures"** (3:184), for the intermediate ones, **"and the illuminating Book"** (3:184), for the elite. It is possible that the first refers to the oneness of acts, the second to the oneness of attributes, and the third to the oneness of the Essence, indicated by His saying: **"Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth"** (24:35). For this reason He brought the word "Book" in the singular and described it as "illuminating." It is also permissible that the address is to the divine descent and the messengers, indicating the various and diverse descents.

**"Every soul will taste death"** (3:185). This is a comprehensive ruling for all souls, whether they are abstract or simple, interpreting death to include natural death and annihilation in Allah, glorified is He and exalted is He. Then **"you will be paid your full rewards"** (3:185), differing in their kinds, on the Day of Resurrection. **"Whoever is removed from the Fire"** (3:185), that is, the fire of the veil, or what encompasses it and the well-known Fire, **"and admitted to Paradise"** (3:185), which is varied, according to what we have mentioned more than once, or Paradise in the more general sense, **"has truly succeeded"** (3:185). **"And the life of this world is not but the enjoyment of delusion"** (3:185), and its perishable pleasures, **"because it is the greatest veil for whoever looks at it in itself"** (3:185). **"You will surely be tested"** (3:186), you will be examined in your wealth by being obligated to spend it while you are inclined toward it, and in your selves by being exposed to what almost leads to their destruction while you love them.

Some of the gnostics said: Allah, exalted is He, manifested the self and adorned it with the garment of lordship, filled it with gentleness and majesty, and clothed it with the adornment of kingship through wealth, as a trial and test. Whoever looks at his self with the eye of the adornment of lordship, his self passes away within it, and the tongue of lordship speaks through him, and he becomes like the tree of Moses, peace be upon him, from which the Truth spoke. This is like al-Hallaj, who said, "I am the Truth." Whoever looks at the adornment of wealth, which is the adornment of kingship, his state becomes like the state of Solomon, peace be upon him, who would look through that adornment at the greatness of the majesty of the Lord. Whoever looks at his self in that it is his own self and is deceived by the mirage, and does not realize by taste what is with Him, his state becomes like the state of Pharaoh when he cried out, **"I am your Most High Lord"** (79:24). Whoever looks at the greenery of this world, sips the cup of its desires, and becomes intoxicated by it, becomes like Balaam: **"So his likeness is like that of a dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants"** (7:176). This is the aspect of being tested with wealth and selves. What trial is greater than seeing the King and seeing lordship in the cosmos, which is the place of confusion?

**"And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you"** (3:186), who are the people of the station of unification (maqam al-jam'), **"and from those who associate others with Allah"** (3:186), who are the people of multiplicity, **"much hurt"** (3:186), by their speech that contradicts your way. The address is to the intermediate among the travellers, for they reject both the people of the station of unification and the people of multiplicity, as long as they have not reached the oneness of the Essence and have not drunk from the seas of distinction after unification. **"And if you are patient"** (3:186), in striving against your selves, **"and fear Allah"** (3:186), that is, looking at others, **"indeed, that is among the matters of determination"** (3:186), that is, among the required matters that lead to the goal and success in attaining what is sought.

**"And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: 'You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it'"** (3:187). The apparent meaning here is that it is not correct to intend by "those who were given the Scripture" the meaning that was intended earlier, and whoever construes it that way has strained greatly. Perhaps it remains on its apparent meaning, or it is an allusion to the scholars in general. The pronoun in **"but they threw it behind their backs"** (3:187) and what follows refers to them with respect to some of them. So reflect.

**"Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done"** (3:188), that is, who are pleased with the acts of obedience they have performed and are veiled by seeing them, **"and love to be praised"** (3:188), that is, that people praise them, so they are veiled by the aim of praise and commendation from people, or that they should be praised before Allah, **"for what they did not do"** (3:188), but rather Allah, exalted is He, did it through their hands, since there is truly no act except by Allah, exalted is He. **"Then do not think them safe from punishment, and for them is a painful punishment"** (3:188), which is the punishment of deprivation and veiling.

**"And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth"** (3:189). Nothing in them belongs to anyone, and He is the one who disposes of them and of what they contain. So how can one who has an act appear through his hand be astonished by what appeared? **"And Allah is powerful over all things"** (3:189), no one other than Him is capable of any act at all, so that one would be veiled by seeing it.

[Page 156]

﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an emphasis on what precedes it and the establishment of proof for it, and for this reason it is not conjoined with a conjunction. He used the word *inna* (surely) to draw attention to the certainty of the content of the sentence, meaning: surely in their origination and their production, in the form in which they are, there are wonders and marvels; ﴿and the alternation of night and day﴾, meaning their succession, each of them coming after the other according to the rising and setting of the sun, which follow its gliding in the sea of His power, glorified is He, according to His will. The report of the two pebbles (*al-kharazatayn*) lies outside the thread of acceptance, and if one forces it into this context it requires interpretation, and the openings for interpretation are wide. The view that this [alternation] follows the motion of the heavens and the stillness of the earth, as stated by our master Shaykh al-Islam, contradicts what was held by the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), including the hadith scholars and others, namely that the heavens are still and the stars themselves move by the decree of God, the Exalted, the All-Knowing. What he [al-Shaykh al-Islam] held is the well-known view of the philosophers (*hukama'*) among the people. Our master al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned also what contradicts it, saying: "Surely God, glorified is He, made these heavens still, and created in them stars that swim through them, and He made for them in their swimming fixed movements that neither increase nor decrease, and He made them travel in the body of the sky, which is their extent, so they pierce the air adjacent to them, and by their movement there arise sounds and melodies that are pleasing, because their movement is according to a known measure. Those are the melodies of the spheres, arising from the stars traversing the celestial distances. The astronomers (*ashab 'ilm al-hay'a*) arranged the spheres in a possible order according to the judgment of reason, and they made the stars in the spheres like moles on the surface of a body. All that they have said gives the balance of their movements, and if God, the Exalted, did as they described, the movement would be exactly the same. For this reason they are correct in predicting eclipses and the like. They said: the heavens are like spheres and the earth is within them. All of this is a conventional arrangement, and other arrangements are possible; they are correct in the measurements but mistaken in claiming that the matter is as they arranged it. The matter is nothing other than what we have mentioned, by witnessing (*shuhudan*)." End of quotation.

The claim that another arrangement is possible is supported by what was held by the adherents of the New Zij (*Zij al-Jadid*, astronomical tables), that the sun is entirely still and does not move at all, and that it is the centre of the universe, and that the earth, as well as the other planets and fixed stars, move around it. They set forth proofs and demonstrations for this according to their claim [page 156 continues] and built upon it the eclipses, lunar eclipses and the like, and nothing of that failed. This indicates that there is no certainty in what the astronomers held. It is possible that what is meant by the alternation of night and day is their differing and varying, by each increasing at the expense of the other and decreasing as the other increases, according to the changing position of the sun relative to us, near and far, according to the seasons; or [it refers] to their differing and varying according to places, either in length and shortness, for the lands near the North Pole have longer summer days and shorter summer nights than the lands far from it; or in themselves, for the sphericity of the earth requires that at some times in some places it is night while in the opposite place it is day, and in some places morning, in others noon or afternoon or otherwise. This is something about which many people have no doubt. Shaykh al-Islam also mentioned this, and it is not far-fetched. Indeed, the difference of times in places is observed and sensed; no two people dispute it. However, there is a difference regarding the sphericity of the earth. Our master al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that God, after creating the starred sphere within the outermost sphere (*falak al-atlas*), created the earth in seven layers, making each earth smaller than the other, so that over each earth there is a dome of sky. When its creation was completed and its sustenance was decreed within it, and the air took the form of vapour, which is smoke, that smoke split into seven heavens, layered, and transparent bodies, and He placed them over the earths like domes, over each earth a heaven whose edges rest upon it as a half-sphere. The sphere of the earth is for it like a carpet, so it is spread out (*madhiyya*), which He spread for the sake of the heaven that is to be over it. In each of these heavens He placed one of the moving bodies (*jawari*) according to the well-known order. End of quotation. The heart inclines to sphericity, and God is not shy of the truth. What al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, held is a matter of witnessing, and within it there is agreement and disagreement with what the majority of the hadith scholars and most of the religious scholars held.

What some verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) have decided is that no sound hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) has come that explains the matter of the heavens and the earth in the most complete detail, since this question is not among the important matters in the view of the Lawgiver (ﷺ). The important matter in his view is clear and free of doubt. Glory be to Him whose power nothing can thwart. The word *al-layl* (night) is singular in meaning as a collective noun, and its singular is *layla*, like *tamra* (a date) and *tamr* (dates). It was pluralised as *layali* by adding a *ya'* contrary to analogy, and a parallel is *ahl* and *ahali*. It is said that the original form was *laylah*, which was dropped, because its diminutive is *lubayliyya*, as stated in *al-Sihah*. However, a number of scholars have affirmed that it is singular, and that no plural for it is known, and that the view that it is a plural, with *al-layali* being a plural of a plural, is not accepted. Understand this. The discussion of night and day has been treated fully before, and the reason for mentioning the first before the second has been explained.

﴿Are signs﴾, meaning indications of the oneness of God, the Exalted, and the perfection of His knowledge and power. It is the noun of *inna*, and the *lam* has entered upon it because it is placed after its predicate. The nunation (*tanwin*) in it is for magnification, both in quantity and quality, meaning: many great signs. The plural of paucity (*jam' al-qilla*) here stands in the place of the plural of abundance. It was said: in this there is an allusion that the apparent signs, although numerous in themselves, are few in comparison with what remains hidden from them in the treasuries of knowledge and the hidden depths of the unseen, which has not yet appeared. ﴿For people of understanding﴾, meaning for those with intellects pure of the impurities of sense and imagination. From this is the report: "Surely God, the Exalted, prevented me from the Banu Mudlij, because of their keeping of the ties of kinship and their criticism of the *albab* of camels," meaning the pure and noble ones among their camels. It is said *labba yalubbu* like *'adda ya'uddu* when one becomes intelligent (*labib*), and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; the people of Najd say *labba yalibbu* like *farra yafirru*. It is said *labiba al-rajulu* with a kasra, *yalabbu* with a fatha, when one becomes possessed of intellect (*lubb*), and *labuba* with a damma is reported, which is rare and has no parallel in doubled roots.

The way in which the things mentioned indicate His oneness is that they indicate the existence of the Maker, because of their change, which entails their origination, and their dependence upon an eternal agent. Once they indicate this, oneness follows from it. The way they indicate what comes after is that they are in the utmost perfection and the highest precision [page 157] for whoever reflects upon them and considers their outward and hidden aspects, and this requires perfect knowledge and power, as is clear. The theologians (*mutakallimun*) have two methods for proving the existence of the Maker by means of such things: one is the method of change (*taghayyur*), and the second is the method of possibility (*imkan*). Most of them prefer the second. The discussion is detailed in its proper place.

The reason God, glorified is He, limited Himself here to these three after mentioning more in al-Baqara is that the signs, despite their multitude, are confined to the heavenly, the earthly, and what is composed of both. He indicated the first two by the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the third by the alternation of night and day, because they result from the revolution of the sun around the earth, or because they occur by means of an outpourer (*mufid*) that is apparent, namely the upper body (*al-jirm al-'ulwi*), and a receiver of the outpouring, namely the lower body (*al-jirm al-suflī*) which is receptive to darkness and light. So said some. Nasir al-Din said: perhaps this is because the criterion of inference is change, and these three touch upon the totality of its types: for it occurs either in the essence of a thing, like the change of night and day, or in part of it, like the change of the elements through the transformation of their forms, or in what is external to it, like the change of the spheres through the alteration of their positions. It has been objected that this is based on the view of the philosophers regarding the affirmation of prime matter (*hayuli*), form (*suwar*) and the celestial positions, so it is not appropriate to derive the Book of God from it. Perhaps the better explanation, from both this and that, is what Shaykh al-Islam said regarding not treating what was mentioned in that surah: that the aim here is to demonstrate His exclusive possession of the sovereignty and power that was mentioned, and these three are the principal evidences indicating this, so He was content with them. As for there, He intended, within an exposition of His exclusive divinity, to demonstrate that He is characterised by vast mercy, so the proofs of grace and mercy were woven into the thread of the proofs of unity, for what was detailed there of the signs of His mercy, exalted is He, is among the signs of His divinity and oneness.

Among what supports the view that the things mentioned are the principal evidences of unity is what al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh came to the Jews and said: What signs did Moses bring you? They said: his staff, and his hand, white to the onlookers. They came to the Christians and said: How was 'Isa (Jesus) among you? They said: He healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Pray to your Lord to make Safa into gold for us. He prayed to his Lord, and there was revealed: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding﴾."

Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, Ibn 'Asakir and others transmitted from 'Ata', who said: "I said to 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: Tell me of the most wondrous thing you saw from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). She said: And what matter of his was not wondrous? He came to me one night and entered under my covering, then said: Let me worship my Lord. He stood, performed ablution, then stood and prayed, and wept until his tears flowed down upon his chest. Then he bowed and wept, then prostrated and wept, then raised his head and wept, and he continued thus until Bilal came and called him to prayer. I said: O Messenger of God, what makes you weep when God has forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what followed? He said: Shall I not be a grateful servant? And why should I not do so when God has revealed to me this night: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ up to His words: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. Then he said: Woe to him who recites it and does not reflect upon it." It is reported from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) rose at night he would use the siwak, then look at the sky, then say: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens﴾, the verse.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymuna. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) slept until midnight or a little before or after it. Then he woke, and began to wipe sleep from his face with his hands, then he recited the last ten verses of Surat Al 'Imran until he finished."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 191 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ is in the genitive position as an adjective (na't) of ﴿Ulu⁠ (the people of)⁠﴾. It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative or accusative position as a praise (madh). Making it a subject (mubtada') with its predicate (khabar) omitted, its estimated form being "They say: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed﴾," is far-fetched, because of what it entails of disrupting the arrangement of the discourse (tafkik al-nazm).
Page 158
What makes it even more far-fetched is what al-Asbahani recorded in al-Targhib from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: Where are the people of understanding (Ulu al-Albab)? They will say: Which people of understanding do you mean? He will say: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾, etc. He will raise a banner for them, and the people will follow their banner, and He will say to them: Enter it, abiding therein forever."

The apparent meaning is that remembrance (dhikr) here refers to remembrance by the tongue, but together with the presence of the heart, since one is not praised for remembrance without it. Indeed, they have agreed that there is no reward for a heedless remembrancer. Many have held this view. Ibn Jurayj counted the recitation of the Qur'an as remembrance, so it is not disliked for one who is lying down and able to do so. Yes, some of the Shafi'is explicitly stated that it is disliked for him if he covers his head for sleep.

Some of the researchers (muhaqqiqun) said: What is meant by it is the remembrance of Him, the Exalted, in an absolute sense, whether that is in respect of His essence or in respect of His attributes and actions, and whether it is accompanied by remembrance of the tongue or not. The meaning according to this is: those who do not neglect Him, the Exalted, during the majority of their times, with their hearts at rest in remembering Him and their inner selves absorbed in watching over Him. According to this, what is narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and a group, may Allah be pleased with them, is to be understood: that they went out on the day of the Eid to the musalla and began to remember Allah, the Exalted, and some of them said: Did not Allah, the Exalted, say: ﴿They remember Allah standing and sitting﴾? So they stood up remembering Allah, the Exalted, on their feet. Their purpose in this was seeking blessing (tabarruk) through a kind of conformity with the verse, within one instance of its referents, and it was not their purpose to interpret it or to specify its fulfillment definitively; otherwise they would have lain down and remembered as well, to complete the interpretation and the realization of its fulfillment.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the verse that he said: This is only in prayer: if you cannot stand, then sitting; and if you cannot sit, then on your side. Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Imran ibn Husayn, who had hemorrhoids, as al-Bukhari recorded from him. With this report al-Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that the sick person prays lying on his right side, facing the qiblah with the front of his body, and it is not permissible for him to lie on his back, according to the view of al-Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. He made the verse a proof for this, on the basis that when it restricted the state of the remembrancer to the mentioned postures, it indicated that other than these is not among its forms. The prayer includes remembrance, so it should not be in other than its form. This is a matter for reflection. The restriction of remembrance to prayer by Ibn Mas'ud does not stand as a proof, and it is far from the context (siyaq) and the sequence (sibaq) of this sublime arrangement.

"Al-qiyam" and "al-qu'ud" are the plurals of qa'im and qa'id, like niyam and ruqud are the plurals of na'im and raqid. Their being in the accusative is as circumstantial states (hal) from the pronoun of the subject in "yadhkurun." It is also possible that they are two verbal nouns (masdar) interpreted as qa'imin and qa'idin, so that the circumstantial state can be realized.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and on their sides﴾ is attached to an omitted element coordinated with the circumstantial state, meaning: "and being on their sides," i.e., reclining. It is also permitted that the attached coordinated element be estimated as specific: "and reclining on their sides." The purpose of mentioning these states is to indicate continuity, and continuity is understood from them by convention, which is beyond doubt. It is not the true continuity, since that is impossible, but rather in most of their states. Some take continuity from the present tense, which indicates habitual repetition. Whichever is the case, the meaning is: they remember Allah, the Exalted, abundantly.

﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is coordinated with "yadhkurun." Its coordination with the preceding states is not evident. The placing of remembrance in those states before reflection is because in both there is acknowledgment of servanthood (ubudiyyah). The servant is composed of the inner self and the outer body. In the first there is an indication to the servanthood of the second, and in the second there is an indication to the servanthood of the first, because reflection occurs only with the heart and the spirit. In explaining servanthood after completing the signs of lordship (rububiyyah) there is kindness that is not hidden. It was said: He placed the first because it indicates reflection on the selves, and placed the second because it indicates reflection on the horizons. There is no doubt in the precedence of the first over the second. Our master Shaykh al-Islam stated explicitly that this is an explanation of reflection on Allah's actions, while what preceded is an explanation of reflection on His essence in an absolute sense. What the leading scholars of tafsir hold is that He, glorified is He, only specified reflection to creation because of the prohibition against reflecting on the Creator, since the essence and attributes of Allah, exalted is His majesty and mighty is His authority, cannot be reached. This prohibition has been reported in more than one hadith. Abu al-Shaykh and al-Asbahani narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his companions while they were reflecting, and he said: Do not reflect upon Allah, the Exalted, but reflect upon what He has created."

And from Amr ibn Murrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a people reflecting, and he said: ‘Reflect upon the creation and do not reflect upon the Creator.’" And from Ibn Umar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Reflect upon the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, and do not reflect upon Allah, the Exalted." And from Ibn Abbas: Reflect upon everything, and do not reflect upon the essence of Allah, the Exalted, and so on. In that case, is the first being an explanation of reflection on His essence in an absolute sense open to question? Some of the virtuous scholars mentioned in its explanation that reflection upon Allah, glorified is He, is impossible, because it requires encompassing Him who encompasses all things. So reflect.

It was said: He placed remembrance before reflection to alert that the intellect does not suffice for guidance unless it is illumined by the light of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, and His guidance. So the reflector must return to Allah, the Exalted, and observe what has been legislated for him. And an intellect that opposes the Shari'ah is clothed in misguidance, and its reflection yields nothing but misguidance.

And "al-khalq" (creation) is either in the sense of the created thing (makhluq), with the idafah in the sense of "in," meaning: they reflect upon what He created in the heavens and the earth, which is more general, whether by way of part to whole or by way of indwelling in them. Or it is explanatory, meaning: upon the created thing which is the heavens and the earth. Or it remains as a verbal noun, meaning: they reflect upon their origination and their innovation, with what is in them of wondrous made things, subtle secrets, and fine wisdoms, and they derive from that proof of the Creator, His unique oneness of essence, that He is the King who subdues, the Knowing and Capable, the Wise and Perfecter, and so on through the other attributes of perfection. This leads them to recognize the truthfulness of the messengers and the truth of the books that speak of the detailed legislative rulings, the realization of the return (ma'ad), and the establishment of recompense. Because of the nobility of this fruit that results from reflection, and because it is among the acts specific to the heart and far from the places of showing off (riya'), it is among the best of worships. Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: An hour of reflection is better than a night of standing in prayer.

Ibn Sa'd narrated from Abu al-Darda' the like of it. Al-Daylami narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it. And from Abu Hurairah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An hour of reflection is better than sixty years of worship."

And from him too, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "While a man was lying on his back looking at the stars and the sky, he said: By Allah, I know that You have a Lord and a Creator. O Allah, forgive me. So Allah, the Exalted, looked at him and forgave him."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn who said: I asked Umm al-Darda', "What was the best worship of Abu al-Darda'?" She said: Reflection and taking lessons.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Amir ibn Qays who said: I heard more than one, not two or three, of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) saying: Indeed the light of faith, or the radiance of faith, is reflection. He, glorified is He, limited Himself to mentioning reflection ﴿on the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ and did not, exalted is His majesty, include the alternation of night and day within that thread, though He mentioned it previously. The excellence of reflection on it as well is evident, as the reasoning requires. The apparent meaning of what al-Daylami narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "An hour of reflection on the alternation of night and day is better than eighty years of worship," is either to indicate that its inclusion in what was mentioned is manifest, since the alternation is among the states following the states of the heavens and earth, as has been indicated; or to signal the swiftness of those mentioned in arriving at the conclusion merely by reflecting on some of the signs, without needing another of them in establishing what is sought.

﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾.
