The reference "this" is to the heavens and the earth, since they, in terms of the connection of creation to them, are in the sense of the created thing (page 160), or to the creation, on the assumption that it means the created thing. It was said: the reference is to them in regard to what is reflected upon. In either case, the matter of the singular and masculine is clear, and the shift from the pronoun to the demonstrative is to indicate that they are wondrous created things that must be attended to with full distinction, magnifying them. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾. "Batil" (vain) means futility (abath), which is what has no benefit at all, or what has no benefit that is counted, or what is not intended for any benefit. It was said: it is that which passes away and ceases, having no strength or firmness. It is not hidden that this saying has neither strength nor firmness. It is either an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a vain creation," or a circumstantial state from the object.

The meaning: Our Lord, You did not create this created thing, or this great reflected-upon matter, devoid of wisdom and empty of benefit, as the conditions of those heedless of it, those turning away from reflecting upon it, and those lacking the wing of sight in front and behind, indicate. Rather, You created it containing sublime wisdoms and organized for great benefits, at which thoughts stand bewildered short of encompassing them, and the feet of minds tire short of standing upon all of them. Among them is that it be a source of sustenance for the servants and a beacon guiding them to knowledge of the states of the origin and the return, as Your books have declared and Your messengers have brought.

The whole sentence is in the accusative position by an omitted saying: meaning "they say: Our Lord..." etc. The clause of saying is a circumstantial state from the hidden pronoun in "yatafakkarun," meaning: they reflect upon that, saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. This is the view of the majority of the commentators.

The Objection and Its Response

It has been objected that the noble text does not support this reading, because (ma) lies within the relative clause (ṣila), and that which qualifies the relative clause (qayd) should properly be among the grounds of the ruling that is applied to the relative pronoun and the motives for its establishment. Examples are their remembrance of God Most High at all times and their reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth, for these two lead to observing those signs and inferring the sought-after conclusion from them. Without doubt, their saying that is not among the grounds of the aforementioned inference but rather among its consequences that follow from it. Treating it as a qualifier of what lies within the relative clause is therefore unworthy of the sublime revelation. Rather, the fitting reading is that the clause of speech be a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the result of the reflection, and that the meaning of the signs arise from what preceded. When the soul hears the restriction of the signs placed in the creation of the world to "people of understanding" (ulū al-albāb), and then their description with the remembrance of God Most High and reflection upon the domain of those signs, it remains awaiting what appears from them of their effects and rulings. It is as if it were said: "What happens when they reflect on that, and what result follows from it?" So it is said: "They say such-and-such," which indicates their awareness of the secret of creation, leading to knowledge of the truthfulness of the messengers and the veracity of the books that speak of the details of the legal rulings.

This applies if the relative pronoun is a relative clause qualifying (naʿt) "ulū" (people of understanding). If, however, it is a separate clause, in the accusative or nominative for example by way of praise, then the circumstantial reading (ḥāliyyah) comes from it, since there is no doubt that their saying this is among the beginnings of their praise and the excellences of their virtues. Presenting this saying in the form of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) indicates that it accompanies their reflection without hesitation or stammering. End of quotation. It is a statement bearing the marks of verification and the signs of precision.

The claim that the circumstantial reading is compatible with the said saying being among the results is not free from difficulty. Then, that this saying is among the results of reflection is something no person of thought would hardly deny. The clarification of this, according to one opinion, is that when the people reflected on His creatures, glory be to Him, especially the heavens with what is in them of the sun, the moon and the stars, and the earth with what is upon it of seas, mountains and minerals, they knew that these have a Lord and Maker, and so they said: ﴿Our Lord﴾. Then, when they acknowledged that in each of these there are wisdoms, purposes and benefits whose details thought cannot encompass, they said: ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾. Then, when they contemplated and compared the states of these created things to their Maker, they saw that the Maker must be exalted above resembling any of them; therefore He is not a body, nor an accident, nor in a place, nor in need (and so on), so they said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, that is, exaltation of You above what is not befitting to You. Then, when they became absorbed in the seas of greatness and majesty and reached this supreme station, and realized that whoever has power over the aforementioned origination without a model to imitate or a law to follow, and is described by all-encompassing power and perfect wisdom, is more capable of restoring those whom the heavenly books speak of restoring, and that this is only for a manifest wisdom, namely the recompense of the responsible according to their deserving, which depends on their inward and outward deeds, they sought deliverance from what befalls the negligent and what is due to those who fall short. So they said: ﴿Protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ (191), that is, grant us success in acting upon what we have understood from the indication. From here it is said that the "fa" (so) indicates that the supplication for refuge from the Fire follows from what is indicated by ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾, namely the obligation of obedience and avoidance of disobedience, as if it were said: "So we obey You; ﴿protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, which is the recompense of whoever disobeys You." And "Glory be to You" (subḥānaka) is a verbal noun in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) to strengthen and emphasize the speech. This does not preclude that it also emphasizes the negation of purposelessness from His creation.

Some have said: "With this emphasis," without calling it a parenthetical insertion, and they made what follows "fa" a consequence of the glorification indicated by "Glory be to You." They claimed this is more apparent, since His exaltation includes not rejecting the request of those who submit and seek refuge in Him. It is not hidden that the request is a branch of the exaltation against the disappointment of the hopes of the hopeful.

It has also been said that it is the answer to a presumed condition, and that the presumed meaning is: "If we exalt You or affirm Your oneness, then ﴿protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, which is the recompense of those who did not exalt or did not affirm." Al-Ṭabarsī used the verse as evidence that unbelief, misguidance and vices are not created by God Most High, because all these things are vain by consensus, and God, glory be to Him, has negated that in relating the statement of the people of understanding, whose saying has been approved, that there is nothing vain in what He, glory be to Him, has created. Therefore, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that all vices are not attributed to Him, exalted is His majesty, and are negated from Him in terms of creation and origination. In this there is room for examination, because all things are equal in that they are the creation of God Most High and include benefits and wisdoms, as His saying indicates: ﴿Who gave everything its creation and then guided it﴾. Their differentiation is only with respect to the relation of some of them to others, and that some of them are the object of command and others the object of prohibition, for example, not with respect to some including wisdom and others being devoid of it. So vices, insofar as they are the creation of God Most High, are not vain, because the vain, as you know, is that which has no benefit at all, or that which has no benefit deserving of account, or that which is not intended for any benefit. They are not such, because in themselves they include wisdoms and abundant benefits, and it is not far-fetched that God Most High intends them, while He is independent of them in His essence. It is not required that these benefits belong to the one through whom they occur; otherwise many of God's creatures would be devoid of benefit. Calling them vices is only because they are the object of prohibition for a wisdom as well, and this does not require that they be devoid of wisdom. Rather, at most it entails that He, glory be to Him, does not approve of them legally, and this demands punishment for them, because their outpouring was according to the eternal predisposition. Thus the claim that all these things are vain is itself vain, like the claim of consensus on it. The one who said this seems not to have understood the meaning of vain, so he said what he said.

Some have also used it as evidence that God Most High's actions are caused by purposes. This is apparently based on the vain being purposelessness in the third sense. You know that the meaning of purposelessness is not confined to it. Even granting the restriction, there is no harm in this view, according to what many verifying scholars have held, but only together with the doctrine of essential independence and the absence of perfection through another, as we indicated in al-Baqarah.

The scholars of Islamic philosophy (ḥukamāʾ al-Islām) used it as evidence that God, glory be to Him and exalted, created the spheres and the stars and placed in them particular powers, and arranged that from their motions and the connection of some to others there arise benefits in this world, for otherwise they would be vain. It is not possible to restrict their benefits to serving as evidence of the Maker alone, because every particle of water and air shares in this, so their particular properties would have no benefit, and that contradicts the text. The theologians (mutakallimūn) disputed this, saying that it is possible for the celestial bodies to be customary causes (asbāb ʿādiyyah) for terrestrial things, not real causes, and that the effect is with them, not by them, and that this suffices as a benefit for their creation.

You know that the claim that powers are placed in the celestial bodies, indeed in all causes, together with the claim that they have influence by God Most High's permission, is not objectionable. Indeed, it is the preferred doctrine that the early community (salaf al-ummah) followed, and we verified it before. It does not contradict the attribution of all things to the Causer of causes, nor does it conflict with the course of all affairs by His decree and destiny, exalted is His majesty. Yes, the claim that the celestial bodies and the like have influence by themselves, even if God Most High did not permit it, is misguidance, and believing it is unbelief. On this basis is understood what occurred in the report: "Whoever says: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ),' he is a disbeliever in God Most High and a believer in the star; and whoever says: 'We were given rain by God Most High's grace,' he is a believer in God Most High and a disbeliever in the star." So let this be preserved.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 3, verse 192:

﴿Our Lord, indeed, whoever You admit into the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him.﴾ This is an intensification in seeking protection from the Fire, and an explanation of its cause. The sentence begins with the address "Our Lord" to intensify the supplication to the One who bestows goodness, as the word *Rabb* (Lord) implies. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: "The greatest Name of Allah, the Exalted, is *Rabb, Rabb*." The emphasis by *inna* (indeed) indicates complete certainty in the content of the sentence and announces the intensity of fear. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to inspire awe. The admission into the places of punishment was mentioned to specify its manner and to show the extent of its horror. As al-Wahidi said, *al-ikhza'* (disgrace) has several closely related meanings. According to al-Zajjaj, one says "Allah disgraced the enemy" meaning He distanced him. It was also said that it means He humiliated him; it was said that it means He exposed him; it was said that it means He destroyed him, and this was transmitted from al-Mufaddal. It was also said that it means He placed him in a station and situated him in a position of shame.

Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-khizy* (disgrace) in the language means destruction, either by loss, or by the cutting off of an argument, or by falling into affliction. The meaning is: "You have certainly disgraced him with a disgrace beyond which there is no further end." Among the established principles is that when the consequent is made an obviously necessary result of the condition, whether the necessity is by generality and specificity, as in their saying, "Whoever reaches the pasture of *al-Summan* has certainly reached [it]," or by implication, as in this verse, it is to be understood in its greatest and most specific instance, in order to magnify the benefit. For this reason, the disgrace was restricted by what it was restricted by. The philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*) argued from this verse that spiritual punishment is stronger than bodily punishment. This is because the spiritual punishment, which is disgrace, is mentioned as the consequence, on the basis that it is humiliation and shaming, while the bodily punishment, which is the admission into the Fire, is made the condition. The first is made the consequence and the second the condition. The purpose of the conditional sentence is the consequence, and the condition is a qualifier of it. This indicates that the consequence is stronger and more terrible; otherwise it would be reversed, as al-Imam al-Razi said. Also, what is understood from the Exalted's saying, "And protect us from the punishment of the Fire," is a request for protection from it, and His saying, "Our Lord, etc.," is evidence for it. So it is as if they asked for protection from the mentioned [punishment] because disgrace follows from it, and this indicates that it is an extreme that is feared, as some of the verifiers said.

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) argued from it that the perpetrator of a major sin is not a believer, because when Allah the Exalted admits him, He has certainly disgraced him, and the believer is not disgraced, by His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾. It is answered that it does not necessarily follow, from the fact that those who believed with the Prophet (ﷺ) are not disgraced, that anyone else who is a believer is not disgraced in the same way. Also, the verse is not general, due to His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it; that is ever a decree of your Lord that must be carried out﴾ and ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾. So it is understood as referring to those who are admitted into the Fire for eternity, and they are the disbelievers. This is what is narrated from Anas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, and Ibn Jurayj.

It is also possible to say that everyone who enters it is disgraced at the time of his entry, even though the outcome for the people of major sins is their coming out. His saying, "On the Day when He will not disgrace, etc.," is a negation of disgrace in it absolutely, and an absolute statement is satisfied in its truth by a single instance, which is the negation of eternal disgrace. Also, it is possible to say that *al-ikhza'* is shared between shaming and destruction. The affirmed is the first, and the negated is the second, and in that case there is no contradiction.

The Murji'ah (a theological school) argued from it that the perpetrator of a major sin does not enter the Fire, because he is a believer, by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the murdered﴾, and His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The believer is not disgraced, by His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾, etc. And the one admitted into the Fire is disgraced by this verse. It was answered by rejecting all of the premises: as for the first, there is the possibility that he is no longer called a believer after the killing, even though he was a believer before. As for the other two, they are [rejected] by the specificity of the predicate and the particularity of the subject, as has been established just above.

﴿And there are not for the wrongdoers any helpers﴾ (192). That is, there is not for each of them a helper who would support him and rescue him from what he is in. The sentence is a concluding statement to show the horror of their condition. In it there is an emphasis on the supplication. Placing "the wrongdoers" in the position of the pronoun referring to those admitted [into the Fire] is to condemn them and to indicate that their entry into the Fire is due to their wrongdoing. The Mu'tazilah used the negation of helpers to negate intercession for the rest of those admitted [into the Fire]. It is answered that the wrongdoer in the absolute sense is the disbeliever, by His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾. It was also said: the negation of a helper does not prevent the negation of an intercessor, because *nasr* (help) is repelling by strength, while intercession is rescue by submission and supplication. This has a basis. The view that custom does not support it is not valid.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf* (a Qur'an commentary): The apparent meaning of the verse is that whoever enters the Fire has no helper from entering it. As for whether he has no helper from leaving after entering, that is not implied. That is because it is general in negating the individual helper, unrestricted by times. The apparent meaning is to restrict it to what he seeks help for first, as when someone is being punished and you say, "What is his case? There is no helper for him," it is not understood from this that the punishment does not end by itself, nor that after the punishment he was not interceded for. Rather, it is understood from it that no one prevented what befell him. Then, even if the equivalence is granted, it does not indicate negation. Several scholars answered, on the assumption of the generality of "the wrongdoers" and the lack of distinction between help and intercession, that the evidences indicating intercession, which are more than can be counted, specify the generality. What benefits you here has already been mentioned.

[Page 164]

Also, [the verse can be read as] in the sense of speech (qawl). This is, as Shaykh al-Islam said: a report of another supplication, based on their reflection upon the transmitted evidence (al-dalil al-sam'i), after the report of their earlier supplication, which was based on their reflection upon the decisive proofs (al-adillah al-qat'iyyah). It is not hidden that this reflection necessarily calls for this statement in general. In beginning the supplication with the call (al-nida'), there is an indication of the completeness of their turning toward their Master and of their not being heedless of Him, together with a display of complete humility and supplication to the One who bestows goodness and favour. In the emphasis (of the verb "we heard") there is a notice that this (statement) came from them with great eagerness, increased care, and complete energy.

The one calling (al-munadi) is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jurayj, and al-Jubba'i and others chose it.

It has been said: what is meant by it is the Qur'an. This is what is reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and Qatadah, and al-Tabari chose it, giving as the reason for that that not everyone hears the Prophet (ﷺ) or sees him, whereas the Qur'an is manifest and remains through the passing of days and ages; whoever reached the age of its revelation hears it, and whoever did not reach it (also hears it).

For the proponents of the first view, they may say: whoever has reached him (i.e., has received word of) the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his call, it is permissible for him to say, "We heard a caller," even though there is in it a kind of metaphorical extension (tajawwuz). Also, what is meant by the call is the invitation (du'a'), and its attribution to him (ﷺ) is more well known and more apparent, for the Most High said: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord﴾, ﴿I call to Allah﴾, ﴿and as one who calls to Allah﴾. And the call is (directed) to him (ﷺ) literally, and to the Qur'an by way of the figure in the saying of the poet:

Graves call out to you, though they are silent,
and their inhabitants beneath the dust are silent.

The tanwin in "munadi" is for magnification (tafkhim). Choosing it over "da'i" (one who calls) is to indicate the completeness of his care for the matter of the call and its conveyance to the near and the far, because of what it contains of a notice of raising the voice. His exalted state (ﷺ) in sermons was indeed that raising in reality. In a report: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon, his eyes would grow red, his voice would rise, and his anger would intensify, as if he were a warner of an army saying: 'They will attack you in the morning and in the evening.'"

Since the call is specific to what leads to it and ends at it, it is transitive with the preposition lam (la-) and sometimes with ila (to). So the lam in ﴿li'l-iman﴾ (for faith) is on its literal sense, and there is no need to make it mean ila or ba' (bi), nor to make it mean causation ('illah), as some have held. The clause ﴿yunadi﴾ (calls) is in the position of the second object of "sami'a" (heard), according to what al-Akhfash and many of the grammarians held, namely that this verb "sami'a" is transitive to two objects, and that there is no deletion in the speech. But the majority held that it is transitive only to one object, and this was chosen by Ibn al-Hajib, who said in his Amali:

"It may be imagined that 'sama'' (hearing) is transitive to two objects in terms of meaning and usage. As for meaning, because it depends on a heard thing. As for usage, because of their saying: 'I heard Zayd saying that,' and 'I heard him speaking,' and the Most High's saying: ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾. But this has no basis, because for its connection it suffices to have the heard thing without the one from whom it is heard. The one from whom one hears is like the one from whom one smells: just as smelling is transitive only to one object, so too hearing. So it is a case in which the mudaf (the word governed by the genitive) is deleted and the mudaf ilayh (the genitive noun) is put in its place because of knowledge of it, and after it a circumstantial phrase (hal) is mentioned that explains it. And in ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾, the (implied) meaning is 'hear your voices'." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari made the heard thing a descriptive phrase (sifah) after an indefinite noun and a circumstantial phrase (hal) after a definite noun, and this is the apparent view. Some scholars of verification (muhaqqiqin) claimed that what is more suitable in meaning for what he made a hal or a sifah is to make it a substitute (badal), by interpreting the verb as a verbal noun (masdar), according to what some grammarians hold; but this is rare in usage, so the descriptive or circumstantial function was preferred.

Some claimed that if hearing falls on something other than a sound, then after it there must be mentioned a present-tense verb that indicates the sound, and nothing else is permissible. This is not correct, because the adverbial phrase and the active participle occur (after it), as in "as you heard it." And tying the hearing to the essence (dhat) is an exaggeration in establishing it, and an indication that it occurs without intermediary when the heard thing comes from the speaker. In the unrestricted use of "caller" at first, where He, glorified be He, said ﴿a caller﴾ and did not mention what he was called to, and then His saying, exalted be His majesty, afterwards ﴿calling to faith﴾: there is a magnification of the status of the caller and of the one to whom he calls that is not hidden. Had it been said from the beginning "a caller to faith," it would not have had this rank.

The deletion of the explicit object of "yunadi" (calls) is to indicate generality, i.e., he calls everyone: "that believe in your Lord," meaning "believe in Him." This is on the basis that "an" (that) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), or it is "that believe" on the basis that "an" is verbal (masdariyyah). On the first view, "aminu" (believe) is an explanation of "yunadi," because his calling specified his saying "believe"; the meaning is "he calls to faith," i.e., he says "believe." It is not an explanation of "faith," as was mistakenly thought. On the second view, "an aminu" is connected to "yunadi," because it is the thing called to, and it is not a substitute (badal) for "faith," as some claimed. Some scholars of verification restricted themselves to the possibility of the verbal reading, because many grammarians reject the explanatory reading on account of what it involves of artificiality. Those who chose it said: the verbal reading requires interpretation as a verbal noun, and this loses the intended sense of command (talab) from the speech. It was answered: the sense of command is understood in the interpretation (ta'wil) when it is joined to the imperative, and similarly what suits the past and future is understood when it is joined to them. And the outcome of all of this should not be taken to be merely the meaning of a verbal noun, lest the intended sense of the imperative and its sister forms be lost.

In the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) there is an indication of some of the proofs for Him, glorified and exalted be He, and an allusion to His blessing, exalted be His majesty, upon the addressees, so that they might recall it and hasten to obey the command. In the unrestricted use of "faith" and then its restriction, there is a magnification of its status.

﴿So we believed﴾ is conjoined to "we heard." The conjunction with "fa'" (so) indicates the speedy acceptance and that faith is the consequence of hearing without any delay. The meaning: "So we believed in our Lord when we were called to that." Abu Mansur said: "In this there is evidence for the invalidity of the exception (istithna') in faith (i.e., saying 'I am a believer, God willing')." But its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿Our Lord﴾ is a repetition, as has been said, for supplication (tadarru'), and to show complete submission, and to present an acknowledgment of His lordship, exalted be He, together with belief in Him.

﴿So forgive us﴾ is arranged upon belief in Him and the affirmation of His lordship, as the "fa'" indicates. That is: "cover us (so that we are not punished for) our sins" ﴿our sins﴾, i.e., our major sins; ﴿and remove from us our evil deeds﴾, i.e., our minor sins. It has been said: what is meant by "sins" is what preceded of disobedience, and by "evil deeds" what came after of it. It has also been said: the first is what a person does knowing it to be disobedience, and the second is what he does out of ignorance of that. The first is the interpretation transmitted from Ibn Abbas.

It has been supported by the argument that it is the one appropriate to the language, because "dhanb" (sin) is taken from "dhanab," meaning "tail," so it was used for what has a severe consequence, which is the major sin, because of the great sin that follows from it. For this reason it is called "tabi'ah" (consequence), by regard to what punishment follows it, as al-Raghib explicitly stated. As for "sayyi'ah" (evil deed), it is from "su'" (evil), which means what is considered repugnant; for this reason it is contrasted with "hasanah" (good deed), so it is lighter. Its support by the argument that forgiveness is specific to Allah's act, while covering (takfir) may be used of a servant's act, as one says "he expiated for his oath," requires that the second be lighter than the first in bearing what is in it; but it requires only the mere lightness, while the claim that the first is major sins and the second minor sins in the intended sense is not permissible. The first and second in the meaning of the third view are not intended, because lightness and its absence in that view is something without any covering, as is not hidden.

Then, what is understood from many of the expressions of the lexicographers is that there is no difference between forgiveness (ghufran) and covering (takfir). Indeed, some explicitly stated that their meaning is one.

It has been said: in covering (takfir) there is an additional meaning, namely concealment, for safety from disgrace. It has also been said: it is often considered in it the meaning of removal and elimination, and for this reason it is transitive with "'an" (from), whereas forgiveness is not like that. In the mention of "for us" (lana) and "from us" ('anna) in the verse, although had it been said "forgive our sins and cover our evil deeds" it would have conveyed the intended meaning, there is an indication of the abundance of desire for these two matters. Some claimed that the first supplication includes a request for Allah's grace (tawfiq) to repent, because that is the cause of forgiveness of major sins; and that the second supplication includes a request from Him, glorified be He, for grace to avoid major sins, because that is the cause of covering minor sins. You know that forgiveness is not conditioned upon repentance according to the Ash'ariyyah, and that some of them argued with this verse for that, since they requested forgiveness without mention of repentance, indeed without repentance by the indication of the "fa'" of consequence. Thus it was said; the verification of what is in it will come, so reflect.

﴿And cause us to die with the righteous﴾, i.e., specifically included in their company and counted among their group. There is no room for the togetherness (ma'iyyah) to be temporal, since among them are those who died before, and those who will die after. In their asking for the causing to die and attributing it to Allah, exalted be He, there is an indication that they love to meet Allah, and whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him.

"Al-abrar" (the righteous) is the plural of "barr," like "arbab" is the plural of "rabb." It has been said: it is the plural of "barr" as "as-hab" is the plural of "sahib." This was rejected on the ground that the pattern fa'il is not pluralised as af'al. "As-hab" is the plural of "sahb" with sukun, or "sahib" with kasra, a lightened form of "sahib" by deleting the alif. Some grammarians of Arabic affirmed it and considered it rare.

The point of saying "with the righteous" (ma'a al-abrar) rather than "righteous" (abraran) is humility, and that the meaning is: "We are not righteous, so join us with them and make us among their followers." In al-Kashshaf: in that there is a belittling of the self and a good manner, together with an inclusion of exaggeration, because it is of the type of "he is one of the scholars" in place of "he is a scholar."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 194:**

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. That is, after death. "What You promised us" means "by it" or "it itself," and what is meant is the reward. "Through Your messengers" may be connected either to the promise, or to a deleted element that serves as an adjective to a deleted emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar). On both readings there is a deleted genitive noun in the sentence. On the first reading the sense is: "You promised us [the reward] in return for affirming (taṣdīq) or obeying (imtithāl) Your messengers." This is like the saying "God Most High promised Paradise in return for obedience." On the second reading the sense is: "You promised us a promise uttered through the tongues of Your messengers." It is also permissible to connect the preposition to the promise on the reading that supposes "tongues," which lightens the burden of deletion. Connecting it to "give us" (ātinā), as Abu al-Baqa' permitted, goes against the apparent meaning.

Some scholars of verification (muḥaqqiqūn) permitted connecting it to a restricted state-verb (kawn muqayyad) that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "mā," meaning: "sent down" or "carried" ﴿through Your messengers﴾.

Abu Hayyan objected to this: the rule is that when the complement of an adverbial phrase is a restricted state-verb, it may not be deleted; it is deleted only when it is a general (muṭlaq) state-verb. Moreover, the adverbial phrase here is a circumstantial clause, and when it functions as a circumstantial clause, predicate, or adjective, it is connected to a general state-verb, not a restricted one. The reply to this is that connection is not confined to a general state-verb; it may be connected to either a general or a restricted one, and deletion is permitted when there is evidence for it. The strength of this reply is not hidden. Abu Hayyan's denial is nothing, except that positing a restricted state-verb in this context is a forced interpretation (taʿassuf) that is unnecessary.

Some claimed that ʿalā ("upon") may mean maʿa ("with"), and that it is connected to "give us" (ātinā). Nothing is deleted at all. The meaning would be: "Give us with Your messengers, and make them share with us in our reward, for the one who guides to good is like its doer." The purpose of asking that they share with them is to fulfil their right and to multiply their merit through the blessing of their participation. It is not hidden that this is something on which the noble speech of God Most High should not be construed, nor the speech of any of the eloquent Arabs.

The repetition of the address (nidāʾ) is for what has passed many times. The plural "messengers" is used even though the one who calls is a single individual, Muhammad (ﷺ) alone, because his call, especially on the platform of tawhid, and what all the sacred laws (sharāʾiʿ) agreed upon, contain the call of all of them. Therefore his affirmation, may Allah bless him, his family and grant them peace, is an affirmation of them, peace be upon them. Likewise, the reward promised through his tongue is promised through their tongues.

Using the plural in the first case rather than the singular is to show desire for the overflow of Allah's bounty (tayyār faḍl Allāh), since it is known that the reward for affirming multiple messengers is greater than the reward for affirming one messenger. On the second reading, the plural shows complete confidence in the fulfilment of what was promised, based on the multiplicity of witnesses.

The delay of this supplication is based on what we mentioned in explaining the relative clause (al-mawṣūl), and it is nearly certain and evident, because the matter is about the Hereafter.

As for when it is explained as victory over enemies, as has been said, its placement after what precedes it is either because it belongs to the category of adornment (taḥliyah, adorning with virtues) and the other to the category of emptying (takhliyah, clearing of vices), and adornment comes after emptying; or because the first is something whose realization results in salvation in the afterlife and whose absence results in perdition there, while the second is not like this, as is not hidden, so it is lower in rank, and for this reason it is placed after it.

What supports the meaning being victory and not the reward in the Hereafter is the sequel to it in God Most High's words: ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This is because seeking the reward would make this supplication unnecessary, since once the reward is obtained, disgrace is far removed from them. This is unlike the case in which the first supplication means a request for victory in this world, for then it is clear that the first would not suffice for the second. Indeed, in joining the two supplications in that case there is a subtlety, since the outcome of the first, "Do not disgrace us," is in this world, through the enemy's domination over us. So it is as if they said: "Do not disgrace us in this world, and do not disgrace us in the Hereafter." They varied the expression, using a different phrase for each of the two requests, to show the difference between the two things sought.

It was answered that the benefit of the sequel on that reading is to indicate that they asked for a complete reward that was not preceded by disgrace or falling into affliction. As if they, when they asked for what is the greatest wish and the utmost hope of those who hope on that most momentous day, which is the reward, turned to asking for what makes its matter great and its rank elevated in that station, namely the complete removal of punishment. In joining the two matters on this reading there is subtlety that is not hidden.

Also, it may be said that they first asked for the reward on the basis that by it the physical punishment is averted, then they asked for the averting of spiritual punishment, on the basis that disgrace is humiliation and shaming. Thus there is a progression in the speech from lower to higher, as if they said: "Our Lord, avert from us physical punishment, and avert from us what is worse than it, which is spiritual punishment." And if You refuse this and that, and claim that reward entails the absence of disgrace, then we may say: because of their intense eagerness and great desire for salvation on that day, when terrors are manifest and children turn grey, they did not suffice with one of the two supplications, even if it entails the other, but joined them, so that this would be part of insistence (ilḥāḥ), and God Most High loves those who insist in supplication. Thus it is closer to being answered. They put the first first because it is more suitable in form to what precedes it.

Some people interpret this supplication as a request for protection (ʿiṣmah) from what would bring disgrace. The closing of supplications was placed here so that their conclusion would be musk (fragrant), because what is sought in it is a great matter. The adverbial phrase is connected to what is before it in meaning and wording, and this is necessary with certainty if the speech is interpreted, or if the relative clause refers to victory. It is preferred, indeed almost necessary, also if the relative clause refers to the reward. The possibility that it is among what is disputed between "give us" (ātinā) and "do not disgrace us" on that reading is, as you see, [weak].

﴿Indeed You do not fail in the promise﴾ (194). This is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) to confirm what they arranged in the thread of supplication. It has been said that it is connected to what comes before the last clause, which is necessary for it, and al-Ajhuri's words point to this. The word "al-mīʿād" is a noun of time or place in the mīmī form, meaning "the promise." Most commentators restricted it here to reward and answering, and this is the apparent meaning. As for explaining it as resurrection after death, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, it is correct, since it is the appointed time of people for recompense, and it may also return to the first meaning.

The omission of a conjunction (ʿaṭf) in these supplications, which open with the address using the title of Lordship, is to indicate the independence of the requests and the loftiness of their status. We have already pointed out the secret of repeating the address with that name.

In some reports it is said that Moses, peace be upon him, once said: "O my Lord," and God Most High answered him: "At your service, O Moses." Moses, peace be upon him, marvelled at this and said: "O my Lord, is this for me alone?" He said: "No, but for everyone who calls upon Me with lordship."

From Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: whoever is grieved by a matter and says "Our Lord, our Lord" five times, Allah will deliver him from what he fears and give him what he wants. Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: "There is no servant who says 'O my Lord' three times except that God Most High looks at him." This was mentioned to al-Hasan, who said: "Do you not read the Qur'an: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling﴾, and so on?"

If you say: God's promise is necessarily fulfilled, since it is impossible for Him, glory be to Him, to break His promise, by consensus (ijmāʿ). Then how do they ask for what is certain to occur? I answer: it was replied that God's promise to them is not according to their essences but according to their deeds. Therefore the purpose of the supplication is granting success in the deeds by which they become worthy of attaining what was promised. Or the purpose is merely humility and submission before God Most High, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿Indeed You do not fail in the promise﴾. With this the concluding clause fits most perfectly. This was chosen by al-Jubba'i and ʿAli ibn ʿIsa. Or the supplication is devotional (taʿabbudī), according to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Call upon Me﴾. So it does no harm that it is connected to what is necessary to occur or what cannot be otherwise. Among this is ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾. It has also been said that what was promised is only victory, and the people already knew this, but a time was not specified for them in the promise, so they desired that God Most High hasten it, because of the joy of triumph in it. So what was promised is not what was asked, and what was asked was not promised, and there is no difficulty. This is the view of al-Tabari, who said: the verse is specific to those among the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who emigrated and were slow to see victory over their enemies after being promised it, and they said: "We have no patience with Your delay and forbearance." This is strengthened by the verses that follow. The words of Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi also point to this, and there is discussion in it that is known from what we have presented. It has also been said that there is no real supplication here at all, but the speech is in the form of a request while its intent is a statement of fact. It is not hidden that this is far from verification, and it adds weakness upon weakness.

[Page 168]

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾. *Istijaba* (response) is *ijaba* (answering). It is transmitted from al-Farra' that *ijaba* may be used for a reply even if it is a rejection, whereas *istijaba* is a reply that brings about the desired outcome, because the extra *sin* indicates this, since it is for seeking a response, and what is sought is what agrees with the desire, not what contradicts it. It may take *lam* (li-), which is the common usage, and it may also take the object directly, as in his saying:

*Wa-dā'in da'ā, yā man yujību ilā al-nidā, fa-lam yastajibhu 'inda dhāka mujību*
(And a caller called, "O You who answer the call," but the answerer did not answer him at that moment.)

This, as al-Shihab and others said, concerns the transitivity to the caller. As for the transitivity to the supplication, it is common without *lam*, such as: "God the Exalted answered his supplication." For this reason it has been said that this line is elliptical, with an omitted modifier, meaning: "he did not answer his supplication."

The *fa* is conjunctive, and what follows it is coordinated either with the implied resumption in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. There is no harm in their differing in form, since the form of the imperfect there serves to indicate continuity, which suits the context of supplication, while the form of the perfect here serves to announce the realization and establishment of the response. It may also be coordinated with an implied element that the mind is led to, that is: they called with these supplications, "so He answered them," etc.

If that implied saying is considered a circumstantial clause (*hal*), then it is coordinated with (they reflect), in view of its being contemporaneous with what occurred as a circumstantial clause from its subject, namely His, the Exalted's, saying: (Our Lord), etc., for the response is consequent upon their supplications, not upon their mere reflection. Since it is among their beautiful attributes which follow from their deeds in the Hereafter, it deserves to be placed in the sequence of their virtues enumerated in the course of praising them.

[Page 169 is not here; continuing] As for the case where the relative clause is an attribute of "those of understanding" (*ulu al-albab*), there is no justification for this coordination, for reasons you already know. Our master Shaykh al-Islam has clarified this. The well-known view is coordination with what is led to by the mind, which is what the mind is led to. In mentioning "the Lord" here with a pronoun, there is a subtlety that is not hidden.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, and a great many others transmitted from Umm Salama that she said: "I said, 'O Messenger of God, I do not hear that God the Exalted mentions women in the emigration with anything,' so God the Exalted revealed: ﴿So He answered them﴾ to the end of the verse." The Ansar said: "She is the first woman-traveler who came to us." Perhaps what is meant is that it was revealed as a completion of what precedes it.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from her that she said: "The last verse revealed was this verse: ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾."

﴿That I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾. That is, "that I," and thus Ubayy recited it. Its analysis has been disputed. Al-Allama Shaykh al-Islam analyzed it as the *ba'* being causal, as if it were said: "So He answered them because He does not waste the work of any worker among them," that is, His established practice continues in this way. The first person in (*anni*) and the second person in (*minkum*) are considered an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person). The specific point in it is to show the complete concern for the matter of the response and to honor those who supplicate by the honor of direct address, and the statement of the cause serves to emphasize the response and to indicate that its basis is their deeds which they performed before the supplication, not merely the supplication.

Some verifiers said: it is an attached phrase (*silah*) to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of (*istajaba*) or from the pronoun in the genitive in (*lahum*). The estimate is: "addressing them that I," or "being addressed that I," etc. It was said: it is connected to (*istajaba*) because it contains the meaning of saying, which is the view of the Kufans. What supports both views is that (*inni*) was read with a *kasra* on the hamza, and in that case the meaning of saying is definitely intended, and its position is circumstantial, that is: "saying, 'I...'" or "being said to them, 'I...'" etc. The agreement of the two readings is better than their disagreement. This agreement is evident according to the view of the one who held it and the author of the saying, even if they differ in strength and weakness. As for what al-Allama stated, the manifestness barely appears, and in itself it is not evident, as is not hidden.

It was also read: (*la uday'ia*) with doubling. In mentioning the promise to workers in general, together with an allusion to the threat for those who turn away, there is the utmost kindness toward these supplicants, especially since there the abandonment of reward is expressed by "wasting," although it is not literal wasting, since deeds do not necessitate reward so that their non-recompense would entail their being wasted. But this expression was used to emphasize the matter of recompense, so that it is as if it were obligatory upon Him, the Exalted. So it was said.

The well-known view is that *idaa'a* (wasting) originally means destruction, and similar to it is *tadyi'* (losing). It is said: *daa'a yadii'u da'a'atan wa-diya'an* (with a fatha) when it perishes. Here it is used in the sense of nullification, that is: "I do not nullify the work of any worker existing among you," ﴿whether male or female﴾, is an explanation of "worker," and an emphasis of its generality, either in the sense of "a person who works," or by way of predominance (*taghlib*).

It was permitted that it be a substitute for (*minkum*), a substitute of a thing for a thing, since both refer to the same entity; and that it be a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in it. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Some of you are from others﴾ is a subject and predicate. The *min* is either initial (*ibtida'iyya*), with an implied annexed noun, that is: "from the origin of some," or without it, since the male is from the female and the female from the male; or it is connective (*ittisaliyya*), and the connection is either according to the unity of origin, or what is meant is connection in mixing or cooperation, or unity in religion, so that each is as if of the other because of the brotherhood of Islam. The sentence is a resumptive, parenthetical clause clarifying the reason for including women in the category of those who enter with men in the promise.

It was permitted that it be a circumstantial clause or an attribute. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So those who emigrated﴾ is a kind of detailed explanation of what was summarized in the work, and an enumeration of some of the finest examples of it, together with praise and exaltation.

[Page 169 continues] The root of *muhajira* (emigrant) is from *hijra*, which is abandonment. It is most often used for emigration from land to land, that is, leaving the first for the second in general, or for the sake of religion, as is common in the usage of the Shari'a. The understanding in the verse is this meaning, and according to it His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and were expelled from their homes﴾ is an explanatory coordination, with an indication that that emigration was under compulsion and necessity, because the polytheists harmed them and oppressed them until they were forced to leave. It is possible that what is meant is that they abandoned polytheism and left it, and in that case ﴿and were expelled﴾, etc., is a foundational statement. ﴿And were harmed in My way﴾, that is, because of My obedience, My worship, and My religion, and that is the way of God the Exalted. What is meant by harm is what is more general than being expelled from homes, or other things that befell the believers at the hands of the polytheists. ﴿And fought﴾, that is, the disbelievers in the way of God the Exalted. ﴿And were killed﴾, that is, were martyred in battle.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in reverse, and there is no difficulty in it, since the *waw* does not necessitate sequence. The killing was placed first because of its excellence through martyrdom. This is when the killing and the fighting are from one person. As for when what is meant is that some were killed and some fought, and they did not weaken by the killing of their brothers, then considering sequence in it is also not harmful. What supports this intention is that the meaning is not that every individual of the relative clause's referents is characterized by each of the things mentioned in the relative clause's scope, but rather that all are characterized by all in general, whether that is by each individual of the relative clause being characterized by one of the attributes mentioned, or by two of them, or by more. Then what was mentioned can be realized, either by way of distribution, that is, some of them were those who were killed and some of them were those who fought, or by way of omitting some of the relative pronouns from the middle, as is the view of the Kufans, that is: "and those who were killed and those who fought." What supports that the meaning is characterization of all by all in general is that if the meaning were that each individual is characterized by all, then the work of one who is characterized by only some would have been wasted, whereas the matter is not so. The view that what is meant is "they were killed, and they had [already] fought," with an implied *qad* (indeed), and the clause being circumstantial, is not something by which the sublime discourse should be interpreted.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (*qutthilu*) with doubling, for intensification. ﴿Surely I will expiate from them their misdeeds﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, that is: "By God, I will surely expiate." The oath clause is the predicate of the subject, which is the relative pronoun. Tha'lab claimed that a clause does not occur as a predicate, and he justified this: the predicate has a grammatical position, while the answer to the oath has no position, and that is the second. Either it is said that it has a position from the standpoint of predicativeness and no position from the standpoint of answering; or that the answer, which has no position, and the predicate, is the combination of the oath and its answer. It does not matter that the clause is a performative (*insha'iyya*), since it is interpreted as a declarative or by implying a saying, as is well known in such cases.

Expiation (*takfir*) originally means concealment, as we indicated earlier. Because it requires the continuance of the concealed thing, which is not intended here, some verifiers interpreted it here as erasure. What is meant by erasing misdeeds is erasing their traces from the heart, or from the register of the recording angels, and establishing obedience in their place, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous work; for those, God will replace their misdeeds with good deeds﴾. What is meant by misdeeds in what we are discussing are minor sins, since they are the ones expiated by acts of devotion, as Ibn 'Abd al-Barr transmitted from the scholars. However, this is on condition of avoiding major sins, as Ibn 'Atiyya related from the majority of the People of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the Sunni community). They used as evidence for this what is in the two Sahihs from the statement of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: "The five prayers, and the Friday prayer to the next Friday, and Ramadan to the next Ramadan, are expiations for what is between them, so long as major sins are avoided."

The Mu'tazila (a theological school that held a distinct doctrine of sin and reward) said: minor sins are expiated merely by avoiding major sins, and acts of devotion have no role in their expiation. They used as evidence His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will expiate your misdeeds from you﴾. The majority interpreted it as meaning: "We will expiate your misdeeds from you by your good deeds." It was objected to the Mu'tazila that it has been reported: "Fasting the day of 'Arafa is an expiation for two years," and "Fasting the day of 'Ashura is an expiation for a year," and many reports of this kind. If the mere avoidance of major sins is expiating, then what is the need for fasting this day, for example?

The misdeeds were not interpreted as covering major sins because they require repentance, and acts of devotion do not expiate them at all according to the well-known view, by consensus that repentance is an obligation upon the elite and the common people, based on His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And turn to God in repentance all together, O believers﴾. And it would follow from expiating major sins by other than repentance that the obligation of repentance is void, and that contradicts the explicit text.

Ibn al-Salah said in his fatawa: Some acts of devotion, such as prayer, may expiate some major sins, provided that it is not a minor sin. Al-Nawawi stated explicitly that acts of obedience do not expiate major sins, but they may lessen them. Some others said: an act of devotion erases a sin, whether it is major or minor. It is used as evidence for this His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾, and the Prophet's, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, saying: "Follow the bad deed with a good deed, and it will erase it." There is a discussion in this, since the good deed in the verse and the hadith means repentance, if misdeeds are taken in general. On that assumption it is not possible to take it in its apparent sense, because then misdeeds would include the rights of people, and there is consensus that good deeds do not remove these; rather, repentance with its recognized conditions removes them. Also, if the general ruling were taken, it would lead to corruption, namely that there would be no fear in the afterlife. Moreover, the context of revelation indicates restriction of both the good deed and the bad deed. Al-Shaykhan transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that "a man kissed a woman, then came to the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and told him about it. The Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, remained silent until the verse was revealed. He summoned him and recited it to him. A man said: 'Is this for him specifically, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'Rather, it is for all people in general.'"

ووَجْهُ الإرْشادِ إمّا إلى تَخْصِيصِ الحَسَنَةِ بِالتَّوْبَةِ فَهو أنَّهُ جاءَهُ تائِبًا ولَيْسَ في الحَدِيثِ ما يَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّهُ صَدَرَ مِنهُ حَسَنَةٌ أُخْرى، وإمّا عَلى تَخْصِيصِ السَّيِّئَةِ بِالصَّغِيرَةِ فَلِأنَّ ما وقَعَ مِنهُ كانَ كَذَلِكَ لِأنَّ تَقْبِيلَ الأجْنَبِيَّةِ مِنَ الصَّغائِرِ كَما صَرَّحُوا بِهِ، وقالَ بَعْضُ أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ (Ahl al-Sunnah, the Sunni scholars): إنَّ الحَسَنَةَ تُكَفِّرُ الصَّغِيرَةَ ما لَمْ يُصِرَّ عَلَيْها سَواءٌ فَعَلَ الكَبِيرَةَ أمْ لا مَعَ القَوْلِ الأصَحِّ بِأنَّ التَّوْبَةَ (tawbah, repentance) مِنَ الصَّغِيرَةِ واجِبَةٌ أيْضًا، ولَوْ لَمْ يَأْتِ بِكَبِيرَةٍ لِجَوازِ تَعْذِيبِ اللَّهِ سُبْحانَهُ بِها خِلافًا لِلْمُعْتَزِلَةِ (Mu'tazilah) وقِيلَ: الواجِبُ الإتْيانُ بِالتَّوْبَةِ أوْ بِمُكَفِّرِها مِنَ الحَسَنَةِ، وفي المَسْألَةِ كَلامٌ طَوِيلٌ.
ولَعَلَّ التَّوْبَةَ إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ تَعالى تُفْضِي إلى إتْمامِهِ، هَذا ورُبَّما يُقالُ: إنَّ حَمْلَ السَّيِّئاتِ هُنا عَلى ما يَعُمُّ الكَبائِرَ سائِغٌ بِناءً عَلى أنَّ المُهاجَرَةَ تَرْكُ الشِّرْكِ وهو إنَّما يَكُونُ بِالإسْلامِ، والإسْلامُ يَجُبُّ ما قَبْلَهُ، وحِينَئِذٍ يُعْتَبَرُ في السَّيِّئاتِ شَبَهُ التَّوْزِيعِ (shabah al-tawzi', a kind of distributive application) بِأنْ يُؤْخَذَ مِن أنْواعِ مَدْلُولِها مَعَ كُلِّ وصْفٍ ما يُناسِبُهُ، ويَكُونُ هَذا تَصْرِيحًا بِوَعْدِ ما سَألَهُ الدّاعُونَ مِن غُفْرانِ الذُّنُوبِ وتَكْفِيرِ السَّيِّئاتِ بِالخُصُوصِ بَعْدَ ما وُعِدَ ذَلِكَ بِالعُمُومِ، واعْتُرِضَ بِأنَّ هَذا عَلى ما فِيهِ مَبْنِيٌّ عَلى أنَّ الإسْلامَ يَجُبُ ما قَبْلَهُ مُطْلَقًا، وفِيهِ خِلافٌ، فَقَدْ قالَ الزَّرْكَشِيُّ (al-Zarkashi): إنَّ الإسْلامَ المُقارِنَ لِلنَّدَمِ إنَّما يُكَفِّرُ وِزْرَ الكُفْرِ لا غَيْرَ، وأمّا غَيْرُهُ مِنَ المَعاصِي فَلا يُكَفَّرُ إلّا بِتَوْبَةٍ عَنْهُ بِخُصُوصِهِ كَما ذَكَرَهُ البَيْهَقِيُّ (al-Bayhaqi)، واسْتَدِلُّ عَلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وآلِهِ وسَلَّمَ (ﷺ): «إنْ أحْسَنَ في الإسْلامِ لَمْ يُؤاخَذْ بِالأوَّلِ ولا بِالآخِرِ، وإنْ أساءَ في الإسْلامِ أُخِذَ بِالأوَّلِ والآخِرِ».
ولَوْ كانَ الإسْلامُ يُكَفِّرُ سائِرَ المَعاصِي لَمْ يُؤاخَذْ بِها إذا أسْلَمَ، وأُجِيبَ بِأنَّهُ مَعَ اعْتِبارِ ما ذُكِرَ مِن شَبَهِ التَّوْزِيعِ يُهَوَّنُ أمْرُ الخِلافِ كَما لا يَخْفى عَلى أرْبابِ الإنْصافِ فَتَدَبَّرْ.
﴿ولأُدْخِلَنَّهم جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ﴾ [And I will certainly admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow] إشارَةٌ إلى ما عَبَّرَ عَنْهُ الدّاعُونَ فِيما قَبْلُ بِقَوْلِهِمْ: ﴿وآتِنا ما وعَدْتَنا عَلى رُسُلِكَ﴾ [Grant us what You promised us through Your messengers] عَلى أحَدِ القَوْلَيْنِ، أوْ رَمْزٌ إلى ما سَألُوهُ بِقَوْلِهِمْ: ﴿ولا تُخْزِنا يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ [And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection] عَلى القَوْلِ الآخَرِ ﴿ثَوابًا﴾ [as a reward] مَصْدَرٌ مُؤَكِّدٌ (absolute emphatic infinitive) لِما قَبْلَهُ لِأنَّ مَعْنى الجُمْلَةِ لَأُثِيبَنَّهم بِذَلِكَ، فَوَضَعَ ثَوابًا مَوْضِعَ الإثابَةِ وإنْ كانَ في الأصْلِ اسْمًا لِما يُثابُ بِهِ كالعَطاءِ لِما يُعْطى، وقِيلَ: إنَّهُ تَمْيِيزٌ (tamyiz, specification) أوْ حالٌ (hal, circumstantial accusative) مِن جَنّاتٍ لِوَصْفِها، أوْ مِن ضَمِيرِ المَفْعُولِ أيْ مُثابًا بِها أوْ مُثابِينَ، وقِيلَ: إنَّهُ بَدَلٌ (badal, substitute) مِن جَنّاتٍ، وقالَ الكِسائِيُّ (al-Kisa'i): إنَّهُ مَنصُوبٌ
صفحة 171
عَلى القَطْعِ، وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ [from Allah] صِفَةٌ لِثَوابًا وهو وصْفٌ مُؤَكِّدٌ لِأنَّ الثَّوابَ لا يَكُونُ إلّا مِن عِنْدِهِ تَعالى لَكِنَّهُ صَرَّحَ بِهِ تَعْظِيمًا لِلثَّوابِ وتَفْخِيمًا لِشَأْنِهِ، ولا يَرِدُ أنَّ المَصْدَرَ إذا وُصِفَ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ مُؤَكِّدًا، لِما تَقَرَّرَ في مَوْضِعِهِ أنَّ الوَصْفَ المُؤَكِّدَ لا يُنافِي كَوْنَ المَصْدَرِ مُؤَكِّدًا.
وقِيلَ: إنَّهُ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِثَوابًا بِاعْتِبارِ تَأْوِيلِهِ بِاسْمِ المَفْعُولِ، وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿واللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ حُسْنُ الثَّوابِ﴾ [And with Allah is the best reward] (195) تَذْيِيلٌ مُقَرِّرٌ لِمَضْمُونِ ما قَبْلَهُ، والِاسْمُ الجَلِيلُ مُبْتَدَأٌ خَبَرُهُ ( عِنْدَهُ ) و(حُسْنُ الثَّوابِ) مُرْتَفِعٌ بِالظَّرْفِ عَلى الفاعِلِيَّةِ لِاعْتِمادِهِ عَلى المُبْتَدَأِ، أوْ هو مُبْتَدَأٌ ثانٍ، والظَّرْفُ خَبَرُهُ، والجُمْلَةُ خَبَرُ المُبْتَدَأِ الأوَّلِ، والكَلامُ مُخْرَجٌ مُخْرَجَ قَوْلِ الرَّجُلِ: عِنْدِي ما تُرِيدُ يُرِيدُ اخْتِصاصَهُ بِهِ وتَمَلُّكَهُ لَهُ، وإنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ عِنْدَهُ فَلَيْسَ مَعْنًى عِنْدَهُ ﴿حُسْنُ الثَّوابِ﴾ أنَّ الثَّوابَ بِحَضْرَتِهِ وبِالقُرْبِ مِنهُ عَلى ما هو حَقِيقَةُ لَفْظِ عِنْدَهُ، بَلْ مَثَّلَ هُناكَ كَوْنَهُ بِقُدْرَتِهِ وفَضْلِهِ بِحَيْثُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ غَيْرُهُ بِحالِ الشَّيْءِ يَكُونُ بِحَضْرَةِ أحَدٍ لا يَدَّعِيهِ لِغَيْرِهِ، والِاخْتِصاصُ مُسْتَفادٌ مِن هَذا التَّمْثِيلِ حَتّى لَوْ لَمْ يُجْعَلْ ﴿حُسْنُ الثَّوابِ﴾ مُبْتَدَأً مُؤَخَّرًا كانَ الِاخْتِصاصُ بِحالِهِ، وقَدْ أفادَتِ الآيَةُ مَزِيدَ فَضْلِ المُهاجِرِينَ ورِفْعَةَ شَأْنِهِمْ.
وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ (Ibn Jarir) وأبُو الشَّيْخِ (Abu al-Shaykh) والبَيْهَقِيُّ وغَيْرُهم عَنِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ (Ibn Umar) قالَ: سَمِعَتْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ (ﷺ) يَقُولُ: «إنَّ أوَّلَ ثَلاثَةٍ يَدْخُلُونَ الجَنَّةَ لَفُقَراءُ المُهاجِرِينَ الَّذِينَ تُتَّقى بِهِمُ المَكارِهُ إذا أُمِرُوا سَمِعُوا وأطاعُوا، وإنْ كانَتْ لِرَجُلٍ مِنهم حاجَةٌ إلى السُّلْطانِ لَمْ تُقْضَ حَتّى يَمُوتَ وهي في صَدْرِهِ، وإنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى يَدْعُو يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ الجَنَّةَ فَتَأْتِي بِزَخْرَفَتِها وزِينَتِها فَيَقُولُ: أيْنَ عِبادِي الَّذِينَ قاتَلُوا في سَبِيلِي وأُوذُوا في سَبِيلِي وجاهَدُوا في سَبِيلِي، ادْخُلُوا الجَنَّةَ، فَيَدْخُلُونَها بِغَيْرِ عَذابٍ ولا حِسابٍ، وتَأْتِي المَلائِكَةُ فَيَسْجُدُونَ ويَقُولُونَ: رَبَّنا نَحْنُ نُسَبِّحُ لَكَ اللَّيْلَ والنَّهارَ ونُقَدِّسُ لَكَ ما هَؤُلاءِ الَّذِينَ آثَرْتَهم عَلَيْنا ؟ فَيَقُولُ: هَؤُلاءِ عِبادِي الَّذِينَ قاتَلُوا في سَبِيلِي وأُوذُوا في سَبِيلِي، فَتَدْخُلُ المَلائِكَةُ عَلَيْهِمْ مَن كُلِّ بابٍ: ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكم بِما صَبَرْتُمْ فَنِعْمَ عُقْبى الدّارِ﴾ [Peace be upon you for what you endured; how excellent is the final abode]».

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 196:

﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community (ummah). Often the leader of a people is addressed with something while his followers are meant, so his address stands in place of addressing them. It is also possible that it is general, covering the Prophet (ﷺ) and others, by way of taghlib (predominance of one party within a general address), to console the hearts of those being addressed. It has also been said that it is an address to him (peace be upon him) with the aim of strengthening him (ﷺ) in what he is upon, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾. This has been deemed weak, on the grounds that the Prophet (peace be upon him) would never waver to the point of being commanded to stand firm. There is room for scrutiny in this, which is not hidden. In meaning, the prohibition is directed at the addressee, i.e., do not be deceived by what the disbelievers have of expansion in gains, trade, and farms, and abundance of fortune. The prohibition was made apparent upon the "going to and fro" only by treating the cause as if it were the effect: the deceptive going to and fro is a cause for the addressee, and his being deceived by it is the effect. So the cause is blocked by the prohibition directed at it, so that the effect, which is the addressee's being deceived by that cause, is prevented, by way of a demonstrative argument. This is more eloquent than directing the prohibition at the effect from the outset. They said: this is the reverse of someone's saying, "Let me not see you here," for in that the prohibition is directed at the effect, which is seeing, so that the cause, which is the addressee's presence, is prevented.

It was objected to this that "being a deceiver" (gharriyyah) and "being deceived" (maghrurriyyah) are correlatives (mutadayifan), and they have stated that cutting and being cut, and similar things, are correlatives. It has been established that two correlatives cannot be such that one is the cause of the other; rather they are both at one level. So it is better to say: the prohibition is tied to the going to and fro being deceptive, in order to convey the prohibition of the addressee from being deceived, because the negation of one of two correlatives entails the negation of the other. It is not hidden that this is based on what has not been agreed upon by consensus, and perhaps sound reflection requires otherwise. The relative clause (al-mawsul) has been interpreted as referring to the polytheists of Mecca. Al-Wahidi mentioned that "they were in ease and softness of living, and they used to trade and enjoy comforts, so some of the believers said: the enemies of God, Exalted is He, are, as we see, in good, while we have perished from hunger and hardship, so the verse was revealed." Others interpreted it as referring to the Jews, and he related that they used to travel through the land and acquire wealth while the believers were in hardship, so it was revealed. Al-Farra' went to this view. The first opinion is more apparent. Whichever it is, the sentence is brought to console the believers and to make them patient, by explaining the ugliness of what the disbelievers were given of worldly portions, immediately after explaining the goodness of what they will attain of abundant reward and enduring bliss. Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways and Zayd, read (wa-la yaghurrannaka) with the light nun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 197:

﴿مَتاعٌ قَلِيلٌ﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "it is" (huwa), meaning: "their fluctuating about [in the land] is a little enjoyment (mata'un qalil)." This description of it as "little" is either in view of the brevity of its duration, or in comparison with what they have missed of the reward Allah has prepared for the believers. In what Muslim transmitted with a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) chain: "The likeness of this world compared to the Hereafter is nothing but that of one of you dipping his finger into the sea and looking to see what it brings back." It has also been said: the description of that enjoyment as "little" is in comparison with the hardship of striving and bearing difficulties, let alone what befalls one of reckoning and punishment in the abode of reward. Its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿ثُمَّ مَأْواهُمْ﴾ meaning: their final destination (masir) to which they resort and in which they settle after moving on from the places in which they fluctuate.

﴿جَهَنَّمُ﴾ whose punishment cannot be described, ﴿وبِئْسَ المِهادُ﴾ (197). Meaning: how wretched is what they prepared for themselves and spread out as a bed, namely Jahannam. In this there is an indication that their destination to that abode is among what their own souls have earned and their hands have acquired.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 198:

﴿But for those who have feared their Lord, there are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾. (Lakin) is a particle of istidrak (exception or correction) according to the grammarians, and it serves to remove a misconception arising from what precedes it. According to the scholars of ma'ani (the science of meanings, rhetoric), it is for qasr al-qalb (restriction by reversal), refuting the belief of the addressee. The direction of the verse according to the first view is that when He described the disbelievers by the paucity of benefit in their going back and forth in trade and their movement through the lands for its sake, it was possible for someone to imagine that trade, as such, necessarily entails that. So it is corrected: the God-fearing, even if they engage in trade, are not harmed by it, and what has been promised them is theirs. Or it may be said that when He made the enjoyment of those who move about small, despite the breadth of their circumstances, this might suggest that the Muslims, who continue in hardship and hunger, are in utterly small enjoyment. This is rebutted by saying that their enjoyment is for piety and for abstaining from the world, and there is no enjoyment of the world above it, because it is a means to a great, everlasting blessing, which is abiding forever in the gardens. According to the second view, it is a refutation of the belief of the disbelievers that they enjoy life while the believers are in great loss. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) explained placing taqwa within the relative clause by the implication that the qualities mentioned belong to the category of taqwa, and that what is meant by it is guarding oneself against shirk and sins. The relative pronoun (alladhina) is the subject and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, and (jannat) is raised by it as an agent, since it relies on the subject, or it is raised as the subject, with the prepositional phrase as its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the subject. (Khalidin) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal muqaddara) from the pronoun in the genitive (lahum), or from (jannat), since it is specified by the descriptive clause. The governing element is the meaning of settledness contained in the prepositional phrase. Abu Ja'far read (lakinna) with a doubled nun.

﴿As a welcome gift from God﴾. Nuzul, with two dammas, and likewise nuzl with a damma and then a sukun, is what is prepared for a guest upon his first arrival of food, drink and gifts. Al-Dabbi said:

"And when a tyrant came to us with his army, we made spears and sharp swords his nuzl."

It is also used in the sense of provision in general, and it may be a plural meaning those who alight, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

"Or they alight, for we are a people of nuzl."

Abu 'Ali permitted this in the verse, and likewise it may be a verbal noun (masdar). It is said that the basic meaning of nuzl, in the singular, is abundance and surplus in food, and it is borrowed for what results from something. Its accusative case here is either as a circumstantial qualifier from (jannat), since it is specified by the description, and the governing element is the meaning of settledness in the prepositional phrase if it means what is prepared, etc., and making the garden itself, in that case, (nuzl) is a figure of speech, or by supposing an omitted genitive, i.e., possessor of a nuzl. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in (khalidin), if it is plural. Or it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of an omitted verb, if it is a verbal noun, and in that case it means alighting, i.e., they alighted in them as a nuzl. It is also permitted, on the supposition that it is a verbal noun, that it has the sense of the passive participle, so it is a circumstantial qualifier from the genitive pronoun in (fiha), meaning "placed down." The prepositional phrase is an adjectival qualifier of (nuzulan), if you do not make it plural. If you make it plural, then there are, as Abu al-Baqa' said, two views: first, that it is a circumstantial qualifier from the omitted object, because the estimate is "nuzulan" (as a welcome) them; second, that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., that is from God, i.e., by His bounty. Many scholars held that nuzl has the first meaning, and some of them relied on the verse to argue for the seeing of God Most High, because when the Garden in its entirety is a nuzl, there must be something else that is the origin in relation to it, and there is nothing beyond God Most High. This is, as you see, not sound. Yet in this case there is an indication that the people are the guests of God Most High, and in that is complete kindness to them.

﴿And what is with God﴾, of the aforementioned matters, is lasting, due to its abundance and permanence, ﴿is better for the righteous﴾ (198) than the small, passing enjoyment in which the wicked move about, due to its paucity and disappearance. The expression of them as "the righteous", and the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, as it is said, is to indicate that the qualities counted are works of righteousness, just as they belong to the category of taqwa. The clause is a concluding summary (tadhyil). Some claimed that this may be an indication of the vision (of God), because it contains an announcement of the station of nearness and proximity to Him, which nothing of the blessings of Paradise equals. The relative pronoun is the subject, the prepositional phrase is its relative clause, and (khayrun) is its predicate, and (lil-abrar) is an adjectival qualifier of (khayrun).

It is permitted that (lil-abrar) be the predicate, with the intended order being inverted: "And what is with God is settled for the righteous," and (khayrun) in this case is a second predicate. It is also said that (lil-abrar) is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, and (khayrun) is the predicate of the subject. Abu al-Baqa' criticised this, saying it is remote, because it involves separating the subject and predicate by a circumstantial qualifier that belongs to neither, and separating a circumstantial qualifier from its owner of the circumstance, other than the subject, is not permitted in the preferred usage.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 3, verse 199:

﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God﴾. Ibn Jarir reported from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, when al-Najashi died: "Go out and pray over your brother." So he went out and led us in prayer, and he said four takbirs. The hypocrites said: "Look at this man, praying over a Christian foreigner ('ilj) whom he has never seen!" So God revealed this verse.

This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas and Qatadah. From 'Ata', it was revealed concerning forty men from the people of Najran, from the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b: thirty-two from the land of Abyssinia and eight from the Romans. They were all upon the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also narrated from Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who embraced Islam, among them 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those with him. From Mujahid, it was revealed concerning all the believers among the People of the Book. The most well-known narration, however, is that it was revealed concerning al-Najashi, and his name is pronounced with a fatha on the nun according to the well-known report, as al-Zarkashi said.

Ibn al-Sayyid reported it with a kasra (Najishi), and Ibn Dihya adopted this. The jim is with a fatha and is light (not doubled), and doubling it is an error. It ends with a silent ya', and this is the more common transmission, because it is not a nisba (relative adjective). Ibn al-Athir reported it with doubling, and some regarded that as an error. It is a title given to every king of Abyssinia. His personal name was Ashamah, with a fatha on the hamza, a silent sad, and an unpointed ha'. The Abyssinians pronounce it with an unpointed kha', and its meaning in their language is "gift of the idol." Muqatil, in Nawadir al-Tafsir, mentioned that his name was Makhul ibn Sa'sa'ah, but the first is the well-known one. He died in Rajab of the ninth year (AH).

The sentence is a new (independent) clause, brought to show that the People of the Book are not all like those whose characteristics were described, such as breaking the covenant, distorting the Scripture and other things. Rather, among them are those who possess noble virtues. There is also in it an allusion to the hypocrites, who are the most despicable kinds of disbelievers. With this, the connection between this verse and what precedes it of verses is established. If you consider that these (believers among the People of the Book) share with those (the believing emigrants) in the reward with God, the relevance becomes strong. And if you note that what came before praised the emigrants (muhajirun), and this praises those to whom they emigrated, since the first emigration was to them, the relevance becomes even stronger. If the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in His saying: ﴿Let them not deceive you﴾ is taken to refer to the Jews, the strength increases further. The lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') enters upon the subject of inna, and this is permitted because the predicate has been placed first.

﴿And what has been sent down to you﴾, namely the Great Qur'an, ﴿and what has been sent down to them﴾, namely the Gospel and the Torah, or both. The mention of their belief in that (the Scripture revealed to them) after their belief in the Qur'an is delayed, although in reality the order is reversed, because the Qur'an is the criterion (i'yar) and the guardian (muhaymin) over it. Their belief in that is considered only insofar as it follows their belief in the Qur'an, since there is no value in what is in the two Books of abrogated rulings (mansukh). What has not been abrogated is considered only insofar as it is established by the Qur'an, and because what follows is connected to this. It is said: the belief in what was sent down to the believers was put first in order to hasten bringing joy to them. The intended meaning of belief in the second is belief in it without distortion or concealment, as is the practice of those who distort and conceal, and the following of each of the common people.

﴿Humbling themselves before God﴾, that is, submitting to Him, glorified is He. Ibn Zayd said: fearful and humbled. Al-Hasan said: khushu' is the fear that abides in the heart of God, the Exalted.
